(MT_1,14.10) "O Sage, having abandoned the ego-sense and being thus tranquil in mind, I remain free from agitation, finding an unshakable refuge amidst the flood of enjoyments. MU_1,14.11
"I abide" means "I remain. Of what nature is this ego-sense?
It is within the flood of enjoyments, that is, within the multitude of enjoyments.
It is the unbreakable abode and the imperishable foundation.
O Brahman, as long as the cloud of egoism expands,
so long does the cluster of jasmine blossoms of craving put forth its bloom.
This is clear.
When the dense cloud of egoism has been stilled, the lightning-stalk of craving will quickly vanish somewhere, like the movement of a lamp’s flame that has gone out. (MU 1.14.13)
This is clear.
(MT 1.14.13) Upon the great Vindhya mountain of egoism, the intoxicated elephant of the mind roars with thunderous slaps, like a rain-cloud with its peals of thunder. (MU 1.14.14)
He roars and flashes;
with the slapping of his thick ears— that is, with dense claps of his hands—
he is the lion of dense egoism within this great cave of the body.
That which expands and shines forth intensely—it is by this that this world is pervaded. (MU 1.14.15) [Note:
*dehamahādaryām* as found in Ś4 is read as *deham ahaṃ darpām*; N11 reads *maha°*.]
For if there were no egoism (*anahaṅkāritva*), the world, though existing, would not exist, because it would lack the status of being an object of dependence.
(MT 1.14.15) The succession of many births, strung upon the fine thread of craving, has been fashioned by the fierce hunter of egoism into a necklace around his neck. (MU 1.14.16)
For a weaver indeed places a string of pearls threaded upon a thread around his neck. But this son, wife, and household— a mere thread devoid of mantra—
has been spread out here by this enemy of false pride.
This is clear.
(MT 1.14.17) When this word "I" has been wiped away by one who is himself free from distress, all mental afflictions are indeed wiped away. MU 1.14.18
This is clear.

(MT_1,14.18) When the cloud of "I" has subsided and gradually becomes characterized by perfect tranquility, the mist of the mind's conceptualization and delusion vanishes somewhere beyond reach. MU_1,14.19

That which is the delusion of the mind's thinking, having the very form of thought— that alone is the mist, the frost. (MT 1,14.19) For me, whose mental activity is devoid of ego, who am sinking in grief due to my own folly—
"O Brahmin, you ought to tell me whatever is appropriate here.
The sense is: "First, I myself shall abandon my egoism; afterwards, I will do as you have instructed."
With this verse at the end of the chapter, he concludes his condemnation of the ego-sense:
"I do not take refuge in that abode of all calamities, unstable, situated within, and abandoned by the Supreme Being;
the state of the ego-sense is exceedingly painful on all sides—O Great-Souled One, instruct me with your remaining grace. (MU 1.14.21)
The term *ahaṅkṛtipada* refers to the state known as the ego-maker (*ahaṅkṛti*).

By the word "the rest," the intended meaning is: "Setting aside reliance on the ego, I shall accomplish whatever you command. Furthermore, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) should be understood as the production of the status of being the object of "I-ness" within the body, which is otherwise fit to be the object of "this-ness" (*idantā*). Thus all is auspicious.
The production of the state of being an object of the notion of "I-ness" (Ś4:
°tvāsañ°; N11:
°tv*ā*saṃjanaṃ).
Thus ends the fourteenth canto in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus offered this censure of the ego, he introduces the censure of the mind:
"The fickle mind, having become worn out by its own faults, wavers from the noble deed practiced by the Aryas, like a tuft of cotton blown by the wind. (MU 1.15.1)
[āryasevitāt] Ś4:
°tam vātāttapiñchalavavac; Ś4: °piccha°; N11: °lavavaś

"By the defects" means by the defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth. "He deviates from the true goal" means that he does not remain steadfast in the true goal. (MT_1,15.1) He runs here and there, extremely agitated and indeed in vain.
Like a dog in a village, [he flees] from afar to a place even further away, wretched; "kauleyaka" means a dog. (vyartham) is read as "vyaktārtham" in N11. (MT_1,15.2)
One does not obtain anything anywhere, even with the acquisition of great wealth;
one reaches no internal fullness, like a basket with water.
The sense is that once something has been obtained, one should not desire even the slightest thing more.
The mind, though eternally empty, is always ensnared by the net of vain hopes; it finds not even the slightest peace, like a deer strayed from its herd. (MU 1.15.4)
nirvṛtiṃ] Ś4: nivṛ°;
mṛgo] Ś4: mṛgyo; empty and devoid of essence. (MT_1,15.4)
Bearing a state as flickering as a wave, the mind— having fallen into a condition of being lopped off and shattered— does not attain peace even for a moment.
It refers to a state of being torn and shattered, an inability to endure the touch of the hand—
in other words, mental instability.

The flickering of the intellect: The mind, agitated by its own cogitation, rushes in all ten directions, like the water of the milk-ocean stirred up by the gentle striking [of Mount Mandara]. (MU 1.15.6)
Agitated by reflection, disturbed by the pursuit of enjoyments,
possessing whirlpools of surging waves and garlanded with the crocodiles of *māyā*—
I am not able to stem this great ocean of mental delusion. (MU 1.15.7)
That which is the mental construction (kalanā) in the form of waves is volition (saṅkalpa);
that [ocean] has this very [volition] as its whirlpool.
That [is what is meant].
Illusion is erroneous cognition.
O Brahmin, the deer of the mind, longing for the sprouts of grass that are enjoyments and not considering the fall into the abyss, runs far astray. (MU 1.15.8)
Desiring the sprouts of dūrvā grass in the form of enjoyments—
[this is] clear [in Ś4]. Never has my mind experienced that state of being torn and shattered.
He abandons [his state] through a distracted mode of being, like the ocean casting off its turbulence.
It refers to being torn and shattered, the inability to withstand the touch of a hand, and, in short, the instability of the intellect.
[The inability to endure the touch of a hand] (hastasparśāsahatvam);
[the extreme fickleness of the mind] (maticāñcalyam). With a flickering mental state, the mind is restless amidst a multitude of anxieties.
He binds his resolve to no single place, like a lion in a cage;
[he is] restless with a multitude of thoughts, a dense mass of anxiety.
The mind, mounted upon the chariot of delusion, seizes the bliss of tranquility from the body as it exerts its effort, just as a swan extracts milk from water.
(MU 1.15.11) This is clear. (MT 1,15.11)

"O Lord of Munis, the mental fluctuations, having settled upon the bed of manifold conceptualization, do not awaken; therefore I am tormented and distressed. The sense is that the mind and its objects always exist as being swallowed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

[Seized by conceptual construction] Ś4: [seized by conceptual construction] sadāsanmano N11: [always with a mind] kroḍīkṛtadṛḍhagranthitṛṣṇāsūtrombhitātmanā / [by one whose self is woven together with the threads of craving, which have been made into firm knots and embraced].

"O Brahmin, I am bound by the mind as if a bird were caught in a net. Here, the knots should be understood as being of the nature of passion (*rāga*) and the like. [I am bound] by the constant smoke of impatience and by the soot of the flames of anxiety.
O Sage, I have been consumed by my mind as dry grass is by fire—
by that [mind] which has constant impatience and anger itself as its smoke.
"O Brahmin, my mind has been devoured by a cruel beast—a dog-like intellect that has become dull through ignorance and follows after its wife, craving. (MU 1.15.15).
This is clear.
"O Brahmin, I have been carried away by the mind— which is insentient in nature and whose activity consists of tossing and surging like waves— as a tree on a riverbank is swept away by a flood.
(MU 1.15.16) [The phrase "taraṅgavat taralāsphālā" means "extremely flickering, like the tossing of waves."]

By such a mind— whose activity is of that nature— as if by a void wind for the purpose of intermediate falling and for the purpose of assailing, I have been driven far away, like a blade of grass by a fierce gale. (MU 1.15.17)
*Tuṇam*:
[The word] *tuṇa* is a particle used in the intermediate sense of "steps" (*padaiḥ*) that consist of the forms of enjoyments and are devoid of supreme rest.
"For him" means for the purpose of attacking;
"by the void" is an epithet of the mind.
In these words: "I, who have been constantly intent on crossing this ocean of saṃsāra, have been blocked by that evil-minded one, like a flood of water by a dam. (MU 1.15.18)
This is clear.
(MT_1,15.18) As I was going from Pātāla to the surface, and from the surface back to Pātāla, I have been ensnared by that evil-minded one, like a wooden post in a well by a rope-loop. MU_1,15.19
This is clear.
(MT 1.15.19) I have been seized by my own mind—which is false yet expansive in form and fragile under investigation—just as a child is seized by a Vetāla spirit. MU 1.15.20
[With a vast form] he has seized and brought under his own control [the world].
He is hotter than fire and his course is more difficult to traverse than even a mountain.
O Brahmin, the mind-grasper is firmer even than a diamond;
its sequence of transgression is more difficult to restrain and more intense than heat.
That mind is of most difficult course; it is hard to restrain, meaning it can only be subdued with great difficulty.
Its "graha" means its seizing;
it is the seizing of the mind, which is difficult to restrain.
The mind, difficult to restrain, falls upon objects of action like a bird upon pieces of meat;
yet in an instant it turns away from them, just as a child ceases playing with his toys.
This is clear.

(MT 1.15.22) O dear one, this ocean of the mind—whose nature is inert, which is restless, which possesses the movement of vast whirlpools, and which has desires for its serpents—drags me away from afar. (MU 1.15.23)
He whose nature is inert, whose inherent character is insentient, and whose very essence is cold; he whose mental fluctuations consist of vast whirlpools.
His very desires and longings are like predatory beasts, snakes;
he who [has such].
And that [place] in which there are serpents engaged in movement;
it leads one far away, causing one to wander through various realms.
[The snake] endowed with movement; [the reading] *°rpaś saḥ* in Ś4;
[Ś4] omits *saḥ*; [the verb] *bhramayati* in Ś4 is written as *°ma* *ya* *ti*.
"If you possess such a mind as this, then restrain it. To this, he says:
"In that case, even compared to that [mind], the drinking of the great ocean or even the leaping over Mount Sumeru..."
O virtuous one, the restraint of the mind is even more difficult than eating fire or leaping over Mount Sumeru.
[Objection: "Surely the restraint of the mind must be impossible to accomplish; what will be achieved by it? To this he replies: "The mind is difficult to master... [N11: *cittam* ... *duḥsādha*]
Regarding this, it is said:
Mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist;
when it is exhausted, the world is exhausted; therefore, it must be treated with diligent effort.
This is clear.

(MT_1,15.25) These hundreds of pleasures and pains have surely come from the mind, like forests from a preeminent mountain. O Sage, I believe that when the mind has reached attenuation through the power of solitude, they truly dissolve away. MU_1,15.26
These are being experienced;
from Agavarā, the best of mountains,
skillfully and correctly.
With this verse at the end of the chapter, he concludes his censure of the mind:
"I have risen here to conquer that enemy, the mind, upon whom the great ones have fixed their hope for victory over all virtues;
yet, because I find no delight within it, I do not welcome its splendor, which is dull, impure, and vast, just as the moon does not welcome a mass of clouds."
"Lakṣmī" [Ś4]:
in which mind; "abhyutthitaḥ" means having become endowed with exertion. Thus may there be auspiciousness. (MT_1,15.27)
Thus ends the fifteenth canto in the Section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus censured the mind, he now begins the censure of craving:
"By this craving, which is a night of darkness within the heart and is difficult to overcome, rows of owls that are the mental afflictions roam here in the sky of consciousness. (MU 1.16.1)
In the space of volition, which is the space of the mind,
there are defects such as passion and the like;
and it is fitting that the movement of owls occurs during the night.
My moisture and softness having been completely absorbed by this anxiety, which brings about an internal burning,
I have been brought to desiccation by my thoughts, just as a mire is dried up by the heat of the sun.
*Samūḍha* means held or retained.
Taste and softness consist of that which is produced by flavor and that which is produced by water;
herein, "thought" (cintā) should be understood as craving (tṛṣṇā) itself.
Because craving does not depart from its nature as thought;
thus it should be understood in subsequent cases as well.
[jalakṛtaṃ] Ś4: omits jalakṛtaṃ; jñeyā Ś4: °yaḥ; tṛṣṇāyāḥ Ś4: °yā (MT_1,16.2)

In the great forest of my mind, which is crowded with the darkness of delusion and empty, the demoness of hope—meaning craving—dances wildly and is utterly intoxicated. (MU 1.16.3) *Āśā* means *tṛṣṇā* (craving). (MT 1.16.3)
"Surely my *aśoka* blossom of anxiety is coming into full bloom— dusty with the mist of sorrow yet radiant with the accumulation of gold.
(The word *nūnam* signifies certainty.)
My thought, like an Ashoka blossom, is coming into bloom;
in what manner?
By passion—that is, by greed—arisen of its own accord.
She by whom frost was produced— that is, coldness— [she who was] with dust,
that is,
pollen.
"Racitaḥ" means produced or created; "nīhāraḥ" refers to that by which [the frost] is formed;
and "kāñcanāvacayena" means by a collection or accumulation of gold.
Radiant and blazing, she is as brilliant as a heap of refined gold. Enough of this craving that devours the inner disposition and causes wandering within; it is no longer fit for existence.
It has arrived, possessing a stainless radiance like a wave in the ocean;
within the mind,
it leads to delusion, that is, to false knowledge.
The river of craving, with its surging waves, seems to flow upon the mountain of my body; it crosses over, its form rippling with waves,
as it crosses over craving itself.
Like an old blade of grass driven by a whirlwind,
this mind-cātaka bird has been led away somewhere by a turbid intellect that has arisen to obstruct its momentum.
One's own momentum;
by means of an intellect (*dhī*) possessed by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
"Whichever excellence of qualities (*guṇaśrī*), which I have studied and upon which I rely... (MT 1.16.7).
That craving of mine cuts away each [strand] like a small mouse gnawing at a string—
[a string] that has been studied, trained in, and made firm;
that is to say, one that is solid.
Like a withered leaf in water, like an old blade of grass in the wind,
or like an autumn cloud in the sky, I wander in the wheel of thought. (MU 1.16.9)
[Jaratparṇa] Ś4:
*tyar*°; in the wheel of anxiety, in the wheel of craving:
"We, whose intellects are powerless, are unable to go to our own abode."
We are utterly bewildered by the snare of thought, like birds caught in a net.
[The phrase] "those of inept intellect" refers to one's own abode, the innate station known as the reality of the Supreme Self.
"O Father, I have been so scorched by the flame called craving that I do not hope for the cessation of my burning even through ambrosias. (MU 1.16.11) This is clear.
Having gone far, far away from here, and having met again and again,
the mare of craving, intoxicated, wanders swiftly toward the ends of the quarters.
This is clear.
Thirst, which clings to the insentient, causes constant coming and going between the upper and lower realms;
agitated and full of knots, it is like the fierce rope of a water-wheel. (MU 1.16.13) [Note:
*jaḍasaṃsaṅgiṇī* is read as *°sargiṇī* in Ś4.]
"Granthimatī" means possessed of the knots of passion and so forth.
(MT_1,16.13) Like a bull being driven by a rope knotted within its body, which it struggles to sever, a person is swiftly led away by craving. MU_1,16.14
In the body— that is, in the physical frame—
with agitation and not through logical reasoning,
by that which was being cut off— meaning it had begun to be destroyed.
Wherever one is driven, there one is led.
By a constant craving for sons, wives, and kin— a craving that is ever black—
the Kirātī weaves a net here in the worlds, just as she does among the birds.

[Due to craving for sons, wives, consorts, and so forth] Ś4: [by means of Kirātīs here] Ś4: [for the sake of pleasure] Indeed, it is through sons and the like that people incur bondage in saṃsāra. (MT_1,16.15)
Craving, like the night of the dark fortnight, terrifies even the wise, blinds even the eye of wisdom, and exhausts even the joyful;
this is clear. (MU 1.16.16)
Crooked, soft to the touch, and signaling the imbalance of poison, craving burns like a black female serpent even when only slightly touched. (MU 1.16.17) [spṛṣṭā] Ś4: sṛṣ°
This is clear.
(MT 1.16.17) Like a black ogress, wretched craving—which creates a world of illusion—shatters the hearts of men and bestows misfortune. (MU 1.16.18)
Illusion itself is the disease, the affliction;
she who produces that is such [a one].
She bestows misfortune and causes discoloration.

O Brahmin, the lute of craving— worn out and wrapped in a bundle of strings that are lassitude— does not shine in the presence of bliss. (MU 1.16.19) *Tandrā* refers to exhaustion regarding sense objects.
These are the strings;
their collection is the bundle;
that [bundle] is properly wrapped and firmly tied.

In bliss—that state of resting in bliss—and in drama; (MT_1,16.19) it is eternally exceedingly defiled, characterized by bitter madness, long, slender, thick with affection, and a creeper in the abyss of craving. MU_1,16.20
Craving itself is a creeper in a thicket, a vine in a chasm;
it brings no joy, it is empty, utterly fruitless yet highly exalted, inauspicious and cruel—craving is like a withered cluster of blossoms. (MU 1.16.21)
The flower-cluster is withered; the flower-cluster is sapless.
(MT 1.16.21) Even when the mind is not attracted, it pursues everything;
yet it does not obtain any fruit at all—craving is like an aged woman in love. (MU 1.16.22)

With minds not yet won over because of their lack of delight, they have failed to bring the hearts of people under their control. In the great dance of saṃsāra, crowded with various sentiments, craving is the aged dancer upon the stages of the world’s expanse. (MU 1.16.23)

Various tastes consist of forms such as pleasure and so forth, as well as forms such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth. In the long wilderness of *saṃsāra*, the poisonous creeper of craving has spread; it is in full bloom with old age, it is grown up, and it bears a succession of fruits consisting of falls and rises.
Having taken root, it has grown;
even where it cannot find support, it adopts a dancing gait.
Devoid of joy, craving dances like an aged actress.
This is clear.
(MT 1.16.25) When the mist thickens, it quivers violently; when light arrives, it subsides. Yet the peahen of craving, restless with thirst, sets foot upon the floods of suffering. (MU 1.16.26)
He bestows [it] upon delusion when there is mist,
and upon knowledge when there is light. (MT_1,16.26)

The river of craving, thick with dull waves and for long empty within, momentarily attains a surge of exuberance. (MU 1.16.27) "With dull waves" means with waves in the form of insensibility, as well as with waves of water. (MT 1.16.27)
Leaving behind the man who has perished, craving moves from one person to another like a restless bird flying from tree to tree;
craving leaves the man who has perished and departs from that deceased person.
He approaches a man who stands in another form, possessed of stability.
Like what?
Like a bird.
Just as a bird, having abandoned a ruined tree, [flies] away from that ruined tree.
Another form is:
"The tree stands while it goes.
The meaning is "in that manner."

Therefore, even though she has reached her goal, the female monkey of craving—restless and fickle—makes a foothold even on that which is unassailable; though satisfied, she still seeks further fruit; she does not remain in one place for long. (MU 1.16.29)
This is clear.
Having done this, that follows; everything is entirely inconsistent.
And craving exerts itself incessantly, like a divine impulse.
*Daivikī* means pertaining to the divine (*deva*).
[Connected with fate: For a moment she enters the underworld, for a moment she goes to the vault of heaven;
for a moment she wanders through the groves of the quarters—thirst is the bee in the lotus-heart. (MU 1.16.31)
This is clear.
(MT_1,16.31) Among all the defects of saṃsāra, craving alone bestows long-lasting suffering;
it casts even one dwelling in the inner apartments into extreme peril. (MU_1,16.32)
Regarding "of all the defects of saṃsāra" (*sarvasaṃsāradoṣāṇām*): the genitive case here is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*).
He explains the state of long-term suffering (*dīrghaduḥkhatvam*) itself with the second half of the verse, beginning with "dwelling in the inner apartments" (*antaḥpurastham*).
The garland of clouds of craving, dense with the mist of delusion and obstructing the supreme light, bestows the highest dullness.
(MU 1.16.33) [This is clear. (MT 1,16.33)
For all the multitudes of living beings wandering in saṃsāra,
craving is the binding rope, with the garlands of their minds woven together.
This is clear.

(MT 1.16.34) Thirst, possessing variegated colors, devoid of qualities, long, and having a soiled appearance; its locus is both empty and non-empty, and it shares the nature of Indra’s bow. (MU 1.16.35)
In the case of the rainbow (*śakrakārmuka*), its state of being a locus for impurity (*malināspadatva*) should be understood as its dependence upon the clouds.
In the case of autumn (*śarad*), it is the ripening of the crops of virtues (*guṇasasya*); yet, in times of calamity (*āpad*), it is like a thunderbolt (*aśani*).
Frost is the lotus-pond of the [night of] dissolution; the long night is the darkness.
What is thirst? It is for the sake of calamity, meaning for the purpose of misfortune.
Autumn is the fruition, being endowed with fruit.
The meaning is "a bringer of calamity.
She is the actress in the drama of saṃsāra, the female bird dwelling in the body-abode, the doe in the forest of the mind, and the lute for the song of passion. (MU 1.16.37)
This is clear.
(MT 1.16.37) It is a wave in the ocean of worldly affairs, a chain for the elephant of delusion;
it is as beautiful as a banyan tree at a crossroads, and a moonlight for the night-lotus of suffering. (MU 1.16.38)
The meaning is that it brings about the suffering of transformation, like the shade of a banyan tree on a path.
It is a single jewel-casket for the sufferings of old age and death;
it is a perpetually intoxicated courtesan for the dalliances of mental anguish and physical disease. (MU 1.16.39)
A small casket, a box. (MT_1,16.39) For a moment it is pure light, for a moment a fragment of darkness;
for a moment craving is like the path of the sky, for a moment dense with mist. MU_1,16.40
This is clear.
(MT 1.16.40) May craving go to its rest for the sake of quieting the exertion of activity, just as the darkness of thick, black night [subsides] for the sake of warding off demons. (MU 1.16.41)
That exertion which is performed for the sake of a task—
for its cessation,
that night [is prescribed]. (MT 1,16.41)

This world remains deluded, mute, and its inner disposition agitated, for as long as it continues to pursue the cholera-like sickness of the poison of craving (*tṛṣṇā-viṣa-viṣūcikā*). (MU 1.16.42) "Poison-cholera" refers to a specific type of disease caused by the ingestion of poison. (MT 1.16.42)
This entire world abandons all suffering when it is freed from anxiety;
for the abandonment of anxiety is said to be the mantra against the cholera of anxiety.
Suffering has anxiety as its very nature; [it is] suffering.
Grasping at everything—grass, stones, wood, and so forth—with the suspicion that it is something to be enjoyed, craving throbs within like a female fish in a pond. (MU 1.16.44) [Note:
*āmiṣaśaṅkayā* as found in N11]
It throbs clearly in the lake, according to N11 and Ś4: *°ranty hrade*. (MT 1.16.44)
The affliction of disease and thirst, residing within the limbs, quickly brings even a man of profound depth to a state of superficiality, just as the rays of the sun cause a lotus to open.
"Utānatām" means the state of having palms turned upward.
That is to say, the state of being a beggar.
Oh, how truly marvelous it is that those of great intelligence cut away even their craving—which is so difficult to sever—by means of the stainless joy of discernment! (MU 1.16.46)
[duśchedām] N11: ducche° is clear.
Neither the edge of a sword, nor the fire of a thunderbolt, nor the glowing sparks of heated iron [can compare].
"O Brahmin, just as this craving (tṛṣṇā) residing in the heart is sharp, so too [are these lamps]—sharp-tipped like collyrium-black, with wicks long with oil.
(MU 1.16.47). This is clear.
(MT 1.16.47) [The lamps] have tips black as collyrium and are sharp, possessing wicks that are long with oil.
Luminous, yet lacking the sensations of burning or heat, these [desires] are like the flames of a lamp—
black as soot and possessing sharp points.
* Sneha means affection, passion, and oil; *daśā* means state and the wick of a lamp. Even one who is wise as Mount Meru, even one who is brave, and even one who is steadfast—
Craving alone makes even the best of men as light as a blade of grass in the blink of an eye; "makes as light as a blade of grass" means it renders him insignificant.
It is vast, dense, terrifying, thick with webs of clouds and dust.
Craving is a vast and dense great forest of the Vindhya mountains, filled with blinding darkness and fierce mist;
in the case of the Vindhya forest, it is one in which the expanses are thick with impenetrable thickets.
It is dense because it binds, and it is of the nature of a net;
such is it, consisting of passion (rajas) and composed of the quality of rajas.
In the sense of the wilderness, it is "pervaded by a net of clouds and dust";
it is "enveloped in darkness," meaning possessed by the blindness of ignorance; and it is "filled with fierce mist," meaning possessed by harsh delusion.
[Regarding "vyāptā": Ś4 reads *rajasā vyāptyety*.
With this verse at the end of the section on creation, he concludes the censure of craving (*tṛṣṇā*):
"Though it is but one, having found its mark within all worlds, it has become difficult to perceive, as if standing right before us."
In this world, which has waves of flickering movement, craving resides like the power of sweetness within the mass of waters of the milk-ocean;
the sense is that it has become difficult to perceive because of its extreme subtlety.

The sweet power is the quality known as sweetness. Thus all is auspicious. (MT 1.16.51) Thus ends the sixteenth canto in the chapter on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus censured craving, he begins the censure of the body:
"Oṃ!
It is dense with the strings of moist intestines, subject to transformation, and full of torment."
The body flickers within saṃsāra, and even that leads only to suffering. The moist ones are those sinew-strings drenched in blood.
By these [qualities], it is dense, difficult to traverse, subject to transformation, and afflicted by disease.
[antratantryaḥ] N11: °try(ā)aḥ (MT_1,17.1).
He qualifies the body itself in detail;
[viśinaṣṭi] N11, Ś4: viśana°.

Though ignorant, he resembles one who knows; though possessed of the self-refulgence of the *valita-ātman*, he is, by reason of logic, neither fit for liberation (*bhavya*) nor unfit (*abhavya*); he is neither inert (*jaḍa*) nor conscious (*cetana*).
Though ignorant, he is like a stone, and thus insentient.
Because it appears as a cognizer similar to one who knows that [reality].
"Valita" means that the wonder of the Supreme Self (paramātmacamatkāra) is obstructed by the very notion of "I-ness" (ahambhāvanā) regarding the body.
"By means of reasoning" refers to reasoning in the form of yoga and so forth.
He is both capable and supreme because he is a means to liberation;
yet he is "incapable" (*abhavya*) from my perspective, meaning incapable according to my view.
Between those who perceive the insentient and those who perceive the sentient, his evil inclinations are swinging like a pendulum.
Neither one who possesses discernment nor one whose self is deluded would attribute delusion [to it].
The sense is that if it were insentient, like a stone, it could not be the locus of activity; if it were sentient, it could not become an object of perception.
Like a stone,
he attains joy with a little and with a little he attains distress.
There is no one so pitiable as this lowly person, who is equal to a body and excluded from virtue.

For a base person attains joy with only a little, and likewise falls into distress. (MT 1.17.4) He is adorned at every moment by a blossoming flower of a smile, which is ever-changing in its appearance and beautiful with teeth for filaments. (MU 1.17.5)
This is clear.

(MT 1.17.5) With the multitude of his arms as its branches, well-supported by the pillars of his teeth, overspread by the forest of the bees of his eyes, and possessing the large fruit of his head-throne; MU 1.17.6.
[He is] approached by the multitude of the branches of his arms;
he stands firmly upon the pillars of his teeth.
With streams of flowing tears for its sap-flow, with hands and feet as its beautiful sprouts, possessing ankles,
it is the dwelling place for the birds that are the multitudes of karmic effects.
The vast and extensive abode for the birds that are the aggregates of effects;
this tree of the body, possessing good shade, is the resting place for the multitude of travelers that are living beings.
Whose is it as "one's own," and whose is it as "another's"? For what concern can there be here regarding possession or non-possession? (MU 1.17.8)
The meaning is that, regarding what is real and what is unreal, equanimity alone is appropriate here.
Furthermore, when the boat of the body has been taken up for the purpose of crossing over the burden [of saṃsāra], who could possibly conceive of it as a self? (MU 1.17.9)
In the context of the body, it is for the purpose of crossing over the burden, that is, for the sake of bringing an end to the burden of saṃsāra;
for without the body, saṃsāra perishes.
In the empty forest named "body," which is crowded with many pits—
Who can place their trust in this tree with countless hairs?
Here, the sense-objects are the pits.
In this firm drum of the body, bound together by skin, sinews, and bones, [who would find confidence?]
Like a cat, I do not remain within the interior of this incessant noise;
[for] the skin, sinews,
and bones are like the subtle channels within the drum.
For the cat does not remain there.
The monkey of the mind, which has grown wild in the forest of saṃsāra,
takes the form of a *cintāmaṇi* flower-cluster, yet it is scarred by the woodworms of long-standing suffering.

The glorious tree has its trunk as the serpent of craving, its dwelling as the crow of anger, flowers as smiles, and bears great fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds; it is the monkey of the flickering mind.
With shoulders as its trunk, a network of vine-like arms, and beautiful clusters of hands,
with all the sprouts of its bodily limbs stirred by the wind,
it was the support for the birds of all the senses— possessing well-formed knees, excellent skin, and a lofty stature.
Endowed with the luster of fresh sap, frequented by travelers in the form of desire,
it possesses a long row of hair-grass grown upon its summit,
and its hollow interior serves as a nest for the aged vultures of egoism.
Because its root—the web of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*)—has been severed, this tree of the body is weak in appearance; it has ceased all exertion and brings me no pleasure.
Only the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is a vulture [preying upon it].
That which is its hollow cavity, serving as a nest,
is within its belly;
it is such [a being].
The body is of a weak form and a flaccid form; indeed,
it is only when seized by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) that it becomes firm through physical exercise or impact.
That which has cessation as its destruction;
such is it. [This is] a *kulaka*.
The body is the great house for the householder that is the ego;
whether it rolls about or attains stability, O Sage, what does it matter to me? (MU 1.17.18)
"Let it come [to me].
The meaning is that neither pleasure nor pain is appropriate in the plundering or the stability of another's house.
Thus [it is said]. [N11: ...iti; Ś4:
iti] "This body-house, bound like a beast by its senses, with the courtyard of its house filled with leaping thirst, and all its limbs stained by passion—this is not desired by me. (MU 1.17.19)

By this, the body's resemblance to a rustic house has been stated. (MT_1,17.19) This house of the body, with its hollows crowded by the friction of wood-like bones and its rafters bound together by strings of intestines, is not desired by me. MU_1,17.20
"Wood" refers to the form of wood, namely a skeleton of bones; its "clashing" is its state of being joined together without gaps, and by that it is "constricted," meaning crowded on all sides.
That which has a hollow interior;
such [is it].
With "antradāmabhiḥ," meaning with cords of entrails.
A hollow cavity, with strings of entrails spread out like lute-strings, and a mire made of blood-water; [N11: *koṭaraṃ*]. [Ś4: *°dhāma°* for *°dāma°*]. MT_1,17.20.
My house of a body, white with the *makkola* dye of old age and turned into mud by the blood-red water, is not desired.
I do not desire this house of the body, whose structural stability is maintained by endless activities like those depicted in a painting, and which has false delusion as its great pillar.
°sthitiḥ; Ś4: °sthitiḥ [mithyāmohamahāsthūṇaṃ] N11:
°sthū(n) *l*aṃ; Ś4: °sthūnaṃ.
In various artistic works and manifold tasks,
they are supported and maintained;
those [energies] which possess infinite activities.
That whose stability is supported and filled by them.
In the case of a householder, various artistic works are to be painted;
that [house] is such that its great pillar is nothing other than false delusion, which is to say, false knowledge.
Such is it.
For it is by false knowledge alone that the body is sustained.

This house of the body, with its various functions, where the cries of suffering children are heard, which is charming only in its comfortable bed, and where the maidservants are consumed by wicked desires— this is not desired by me.
The beds are indeed pleasures;
with them it is enchanting.
He whose miserable desires—those wretched longings—are like burnt-out servants, that is, destroyed servants.

[Ś4: kākṣā] (MT_1,17.23) This body-house, crowded with the vessels and utensils of the array of sense-objects rich in impurities, and encircled by the brine of ignorance—this is not desired by me. MU_1,17.24
[It is] crowded with the vessels and utensils of the array of sense-objects abounding in impurity;
"viṣayīṇi" refers to the sense-faculties, and "kṣāra" refers to ashes. (MT_1,17.24)
This house of my body, with its high pillars of the knees resting upon the ankle-joints,
and made very firm by the timber of long arms— such a dwelling is not desired by me.
Guggulu is the stone that serves as the foundation for the pillar.

O Brahmin, this house of the body—whose windows are the manifest eyes, whose inner courtyard is the dwelling of the sporting Prajñā, and whose daughter is Thought—is not desired by me. (MU 1.17.26) [Ś4: guggu°] (MT 1.17.25)
This is clear.

(MT_1,17.26) That house of the body is not desired by me—its beautiful moon-chamber of the ears being covered by the thatch of the hair on my head, and its long-fingered porticoes being its protruding limbs. MU_1,17.27
"Covered" means enclosed.
A "candraśālikā" is an upper chamber or turret.
A "niryūha" is a wooden structure projecting outward.
This body-house, with its thick sprouts of hair growing upon all its walls, and its central chamber (the torso) utterly empty, is not desired by me. (MU 1.17.28) [Note:
"pīṭhapiṭhira" refers to the middle region of the body.]
With its seat and bowl-like belly,
with the hollows of its nails as its nave, and with winds that produce a whirring sound within its spokes,
this house of my body is not desired by me. (MU 1.17.29)
Regarding *āraṇitāntaram*: Ś4 reads *°arani°*.
*Nilayāḥ* means *ālayāḥ*. *Śāram* means variegated (*śavalam*).
This body-house of mine, with its windows and openings wide open, is not desired by me, as it is incessantly agitated by the force of the winds entering and exiting. (MU 1.17.30)
The wind is the vital breath (*prāṇavāta*).
This house of the body is not desired by me; it is terrifying with the door of the mouth overrun by the monkey-like tongue, and its fragments of teeth and bones are visible. (MU 1.17.31)
This is clear.

(MT_1,17.31) This house of the body, though smoothed with the plaster of the eyes and made restless by the movement of its mechanical parts, is dug up by the rat of the mind; it is not desired by me. MU_1,17.32
That which moves like a machine is therefore flickering;
for a moment, it shines with the light of a smile-lamp, beautiful with bliss.
For a moment, my body-house was not desired [as such], being pervaded by floods of light. (MU 1.17.33)
This body of mine is undesirable: it is an abode for all diseases, a city of wrinkles and grey hair, and a forest of deer that are all mental anxieties.
(In this context, "sāraṅga" refers to the deer-like anxieties.)

Their forest is the body. Uneven with the agitation of senses and wild beasts, empty, hollow and pithless, with the thickets of the heart shrouded in darkness—that forest of the body is not desired by me. (MU 1.17.34–35)
The senses themselves are the bears;
that which is their agitation makes [the path] uneven.
Darkness is ignorance and obscurity.
(MT 1.17.35) O Lord of Sages, I am unable to sustain this abode of the body, just as one of little strength cannot rescue an elephant sunk in the mud. (MU 1.17.36)
The "abode of the body" refers to the house known as the body.
(MT 1.17.36) What is the use of prosperity, what is the use of the body, what is the use of honor, and what is the use of worldly effort?
In just a few days, Time cuts away everything. (MU 1.17.37)
[It] cuts away; Ś4: *kṛtanti* is clear.
O Sage, this [body], consisting of blood and flesh, including both its exterior and interior—
Tell me, what beauty can there be in a body whose very nature is destruction? "Nāśaikadharmī" means that which has destruction as its sole property; [it refers to] that.
O dear one, what reliance can there be for a wise person upon those ungrateful things which, at the time of death, do not follow the life-principle from the body? (MU 1.17.39)
[What reliance can there be? Ś4:
*kaivā* [reliance?], clearly.
The body is as unstable as the tip of an intoxicated elephant's ear, and as fragile as a dangling drop of water.
"As long as he does not abandon me, so long shall I abandon him. The sense is that [the Self] is not grasped as an object of the notion of "I" (*ahantā*).
This sprout-like body is flickering with the movement of the wind, fragile, worn out, thin, and round; it is undesirable, being both harsh and sapless.
(MU 1.17.41) [Note: *naiṣṭo*] N11: naiṣṭo *yaṃ*; Ś4: naiṣṭo.

It is both slender and round; thus it is "slender and round. Having eaten and drunk for a long time—[food] as delicate as a young sprout—it becomes thin and, without effort, hastens toward destruction.
At first it attains a state of thinness;
thereafter, it pursues destruction without effort.
These very pleasures and pains, consisting of existence and non-existence, are what he [experiences].
For even after experiencing it further, the ordinary body indeed feels no shame.
(This is clear.
Having exercised sovereignty for a very long time and having enjoyed the glory of great wealth, [the body remains indifferent].
The body attains neither height nor stability; why, for what purpose, is it protected?
Why—that is, for what reason—is it guarded and preserved?

O knower of distinctions, at the time of old age one reaches old age, and likewise at the time of death one meets death; for the body, whether belonging to a wealthy man or a pauper, is exactly the same. (MU 1.17.45) O knower of distinctions!
The body of both the wealthy man and the poor man is exactly the same and without distinction:
at the time of old age, it undergoes aging; likewise, at the time of death, it undergoes death.
Therefore, the implication is that effort for the sake of the body and the means of enjoyment is indeed futile.
At the time of old age, [one encounters] decay;
for the sake of the body and the means of enjoyment,
within the belly of the ocean of *saṃsāra*, in the interior of the cave of craving— (MT_1,17.45)
This mute tortoise of a body remains asleep, its attachments released.
*Kuharaka* means a cavity or hole.

The logs of bodies, which are suitable for the single purpose of burning, are carried away in great numbers like [wood] in the ocean of saṃsāra; among them, they know some rare person to be a "hole" (randhra). (MU 1.17.47)
"Capable of a single purpose with burning": that which is called "burning" (*dahana*) is the one thing, the single objective (*artha* = *prayojana*). *N11*: *raha°*; *Ś4*: *kaś°*.
That which is termed "burning" is the single object or purpose.

In that context, "suitable" means something whose support is a living being known through what is to be known. The locative case in "among them" (teṣu) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
The sense is that others are like animals.
Thus,
for the discerning person, there is no purpose whatsoever in this physical body, which is characterized by long-standing wickedness, instability, and the fruit of its own downfall.
With the fruit of downfall and the fruit of destruction— for the discerning person who is engaged in self-inquiry—
having thus quickly reached old age while sinking into the mire of worldly existence; (MT_1,17.48)
It is not known where or how this "frog of the body" will go before long;
the body itself is the frog, the *bheka*.
Dardura [N11, Ś4: durāḥ] says:
Bodies, whose every undertaking is devoid of essence and which are like restless winds, are seen here by no one as they travel along the path of dust. *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 1.17.50.
"O Blessed One, the movement of the wind, of a lamp, and of the mind as they travel along a dusty road, a path of greed,
and a track of dust is perceived;
but the coming and going of our body and arrow is not known."
The meaning is: "belonging to us," that is, related to us.
Fie, fie again and again upon those who have their hopes bound to bodies and whose hopes are bound to the maintenance of the world—those who are intoxicated by the wine of delusion! MU 1.17.52
[Those intoxicated by the intoxicant of delusion] is clear; N11: *ma(c)iro°*, Ś4: *maciro°*. (MT_1,17.52)

"I am not the body, nor is the body mine; this [body] is not I, and likewise [I am not it]"—those whose minds rest thus, O Sage, are the supreme persons. "Tathā" means "likewise" or "in that same way."
This is the body; I am not it.

(MT 1.17.53) Those whose vision is clouded by defects—abounding in honor and dishonor, and finding delight in abundant gain—strike down the man whose attachment is bound solely to the body. (MU 1.17.54)
The perceptions of faults consist of passion and the like;
the state of being delightful due to abundant gain should be understood as occurring only at first sight.
[It is like] a female demon with graceful limbs who dwells within the attachment to the body.
We have been deceived by the artifice of egoism through this deception;
or, according to another reading, "in the lap of the body. This wretched wisdom has become entirely bound to the body by its attachment to it.
Alas, she has been deceived by the demon of false knowledge while all alone! For a demoness deceives only one who is solitary;
by that ruined soul, for whom there is not even the slightest truth, [she is deceived].
It is strange that people are deceived by a burnt body,
even though [it is clear] that it exists.
Ś3: "Of whom there is"; N10: "Of whomsoever there exists even the slightest thing that causes deception; [by that] one is deceived or cheated. (MT_1,17.57)
In just a few days, this withered sprout of a body falls away effortlessly, like a drop of water from a mountain stream. (MU 1.17.58;
MT 1.17.58) This is clear.
This body is soon to perish, like a bubble upon the ocean;
it vibrates fruitlessly and without result amidst the turning of worldly affairs— that is, within the cycle of saṃsāra.
"O twice-born one, I have no reliance for even a moment upon this body, which is a transformation of false knowledge— a city conjured by the delusion of a dream— whose destruction is most evident.
In the phrase "in a city conjured by the delusion of a dream," the meaning is "like a city seen in the delusion of a dream."
He who has determined stability in lightning flashes, autumnal clouds, and cities of the Gandharvas— cities resembling towns seen in the confusion of a dream—
he places his trust in physical conflict.
"He trusts" means he places his confidence.
With this verse at the end of the section on creation, he concludes the censure of the body:
"It is ever-victorious over a succession of constantly fragile effects, having achieved victory over those of deceitful conduct."
Having cast off this wretched body, which is full of every defect, like a blade of grass, I remain in happiness.
Regarding those successions of effects that are constantly fragile, he possesses victory over them; such is [the description].

That is to say, it is the means for accomplishing a succession of fragile effects. For this very reason, [it is] "born victorious" amidst the deceitful conducts and contemptible activities. May there be auspiciousness! (MT_1,17.62)
Thus ends the seventeenth canto in the Section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
[Chapter] N11, Ś4: Chapter [Number]. Having thus offered a censure of the body, he now introduces a censure of childhood, which is its first stage of existence.
N11: Oṃ; Ś4: Homage to Rāma.
Even having obtained birth in this ocean of saṃsāra, which is fickle in form and surging with the waves of worldly duties, childhood serves only for suffering. This is clear.
He explains the suffering caused by that [childhood] in detail:
"Incapacity, misfortune, craving, muteness, dull-wittedness, greed, fickleness, and wretchedness—all these prevail in childhood. (MU 1.18.2)
This is clear.
(MT_1,18.2) In states of anger, weeping, and ferocity, as well as those shattered by wretchedness, childhood is a bondage, like a tethering post for female elephants. MU_1,18.3
In the phrase "in the stages" (*daśāsu*), the locative case is used in the sense of a locus of experience (*vaiṣayika-ādhāra*).
That in which one is bound is called "bondage" (*bandhana*).
[It occurs] neither in death, nor in old age or disease, nor in misfortune, nor in youth.
Those anxieties which, in childhood, do not cut through the heart— [those same anxieties now] cut it asunder.
Old age itself is the disease; [it is] "the disease of old age," and therein [lies the suffering]. (MT_1,18.4) The undertaking of birth as an animal is despised by all;
the fickle conduct of the foolish brings suffering even beyond death. (MU_1,18.5)
He whose undertaking is like that of the animal species;
the meaning is that his undertaking is equal to that of the animal species. (MT_1,18.5)
To whom can childhood—merely a fragile reflection of dense ignorance consisting of various volitions, with the mind cut asunder and shattered—bring happiness? (MU 1.18.6) [Note:
*pratibimbaṃ* is found in Ś4 as *°mbe*.]
In what state is childhood? It is that in which the mind is cut asunder, shattered, and exceedingly fickle.
That is such [an example]:
a reflection is the illustration for those of dense ignorance who are utterly dull-witted.

What fear could there be in childhood, born of the intellect, which is constantly darkened by dullness and filled with dread at every step— [a fear] that would arise in what kind of calamity? [The phrase] "buddhyā bhayam" means "fear produced by the intellect."
Existence belongs to none whatsoever.
(MT 1.18.7) Amidst playful diversions, wicked amusements, evil pursuits, and base intentions, the fool incurs supreme delusion and powerful calamity. (MU 1.18.8)
In a wicked and contemptible mind;
what kind of delusion? That which arises because of a powerful calamity—such is it.
Of what nature is it?

It is a state of childhood that begins with the turbid onset of conceptual construction, characterized by wicked playfulness and a wretched foundation; it serves only for the subduing of the person, not for his peace.
For the sake of instruction and for the sake of killing;
for the sake of peace and for the sake of happiness.
Whatever faults, whatever misconducts, whatever evil courses, and whatever evil anxieties there may be—
all these are established in childhood, like owls in a ruined dwelling. (MU 1.18.10)
The *kauśikas*—according to N11 and Ś4:
the *kauśikas* are owls.
O Brahmin, fie upon those foolish men of ruined intellect who, like owls, proclaim with their vain minds that "childhood is delightful. (Śaṅkara ad Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.8)
This is clear.
(MT_1,18.11) Where the restless mind flickers amidst its fluctuations, how could even the sovereignty over the three worlds bring satisfaction there? MU_1,18.12
It bears— that is, it exercises power over— even the sovereignty of the three worlds, even that which takes the form of sovereignty over the three worlds.
For indeed, [it prevails] over all sentient beings and in all their states.
"O Sage, the mind attains tenfold restlessness in childhood. The word "tu" (but/however) is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. O Sage!
In childhood, however, the mind attains a tenfold degree of fickleness.
The mind is fickle by its very nature, and childhood is the height of fickleness;
when these two are joined together, my dear, by what means can there be an end to such extreme restlessness?
"Moving" (*calatā*) means the most excellent or primary; that is to say, "moving much. O Father!
While those two, the mind and the child,
remain closely joined,
by what means could there be an end or cessation within?
The meaning is: "by no one at all.
O Brahmin, has this fickleness been learned by women's eyes, by clusters of lightning, by garlands of flames, or by ripples of water, or perhaps from the mind since childhood? (MU 1.18.15)
The sense is that childhood is as fickle as the eyes of women and the like.
Furthermore, both childhood and the mind are observed to have a constantly shifting state, like two brothers in all their activities. (MU 1.18.16)
Of fragile existence and unstable state. (MT_1,18.16) All wicked beings, all defects, and all evil intentions depend upon childhood alone, just as men depend upon one who possesses wealth. MU_1,18.17
Those of evil intent are harsh;
they live off others and depend upon them. If a child does not find fresh and ever-new delight every day, he does not grow.
He attains that state and undergoes the swoon of the poison's onset.
[The mind] takes up ever-new, ever-fresh objects;
it comes under control with ease, yet it falls into a state of transformation with ease.

The fool delights in impurity alone, just like a dog; his face is constantly bathed in tears, and his mind is mired in the mud. (MU 1.18.19) This is clear. His heart is dull within the mire. (MT 1.18.19)
The child is like a heated plot of ground moistened by rain; he whose inner disposition is dull, being within the mud, that is, in the midst of the mud.
He is such that even a parched ground soaked by rain becomes exactly like this.
[The being] is wretched, intent on fear and food, and desires whatever it has seen.

A child with restless intellect assumes a body that leads only to suffering; his mind is tormented by failing to obtain the objects desired by his own volitions. (MU 1.18.21) This is clear. (MT 1,18.21) His intellect is distressed because he does not attain the states he craves through his own imagination.
The weak fool encounters suffering, as if his very heart were being cut away. (MU 1.18.22) [Note:
*abala* is clearly read as *ana* in Ś4.]
O Sage, those sufferings of a fool— which result from ill-conceived efforts and miss their mark, and which are intensified by many factions—
do not belong to anyone else.
[Those] with many factions and [characteristics] that are intense;
by means of "evil desires" (*durīhābhiḥ*), which are wicked actions (*duśceṣṭābhiḥ*) performed by them;
[those] by whom a target (*lakṣya*) or a foothold (*āspada*) has been gained.
Those [limbs] are *ulbaṇāni*, meaning hard (*kaṭhināni*), by virtue of that side which is one's own group (*svavarga*) and is numerous.
In this context, the fact that arrows serve as a point of comparison is suggested (vyaṅgya).
[The word] *tatkartṛkābhiḥ* [is written with] the Śāradā character *ta* for *tat°* by means of the Nāgarī character.
*ulvaṇāni*: N11, Ś4: *ullva°*.
"A child [was carried away] by a powerful horse that frolicked like a thought."
He is constantly tormented in his mind, as a forest glade is by the summer heat.
Regarding the word "aśvena," the reading here is "aśva eva.
A child who has entered the house of learning undergoes supreme suffering.
Like a great elephant at its tethering post, [the mind is bound] by that which is terrifying due to the imbalance of poisons.
This is clear.
It is a false conceptualization consisting of various mental desires.
Childhood, with its fragile disposition, leads to suffering that is exceedingly long-lasting;
"pelava" means dull-witted,
and it refers to that [childhood] in which such a disposition resides.
[The intention: N11: aśa°;
He [desired] to consume the frost and to seize the moon from the sky.
How could that which is desired by means of ignorance lead to happiness? (MU 1.18.27) [Note:
*tuhinam* as in N11;
*maurkhyeṇa* as in Ś4]
"Roasted" means fried.

(MT_1,18.27) O one of great intelligence, what difference is there between a child who is incapable of warding off cold and heat while situated within a funeral pyre, and a tree growing upon the earth? MU_1,18.28
"Within consciousness" (antaściteḥ) means within the unexpanded consciousness; it does not refer to expanded consciousness.
Consciousness (citiḥ) is the cognition of cold and heat.
[Within the consciousness] Ś4:
[of one whose consciousness has blossomed] Ś4: [of one whose consciousness has blossomed] (MT_1,18.28) those intent on eating desire to fly up with their two wings.

Fools, who possess the nature of birds, are constantly intent on fear and food. "Intent on fear and food" means those for whom fear and food are paramount. In childhood, there is fear of the teacher, as well as of the mother and the father.
Childhood is a house of fear for both the elder and the younger;
for it is said "from the elder and the younger," because an elder child indeed overcomes a younger child.

With a verse at the end of the chapter, [the author] concludes the censure of childhood: "Even one whose disposition is struck down by the state of every vice, who delights in the play of lack of discrimination, seeks refuge... [jyeṣṭhabālāc] N11: °lāś; Ś4: °laś (MT_1,18.30).
In this world, O Great Sage, for no one whatsoever does mere childhood provide sufficient satisfaction;
it is only non-discrimination that is truly playful,
and its refuge is the home.
The meaning is that it is the locus of non-discrimination.
The word "api" is for the purpose of completing the meter. Thus all is auspicious.
(MT_1,18.31) Thus ends the eighteenth canto in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus concluded the censure of childhood, [the author] introduces the censure of youth as it follows in sequence:
*Ś4: Homage to Śrī Rāma!; N11: Om!
Now, having abandoned the misfortunes of childhood, a person whose inner disposition is struck down...*
Youth ascends toward a fall, characterized by a treacherous agitation like that of a precipice;
it is such that there is an agitation within it similar to that of a chasm.
And here, "fall" should be understood as having the nature of the arrival of old age.
It should be known (*jñeya*). [In the manuscript N11, the reading *pāda* "jñeyaḥ" is partially illegible.
He explains in detail the particle occurring therein.
[In the manuscript Ś4, it reads *tatra* for *tatratyaṃ*.]
In that regard, the dull-witted person, following the fluctuations of his own restless mind which possesses infinite diversions, goes from one suffering to another; however,
it is not so for the wise one.
Helpless, one is overwhelmed by the demon of desire, which dwells within the hollow of one's own mind and causes manifold agitation; it overcomes one by force.
(The word *tatra* from the preceding verse should be understood as carrying over here as well.)
Here too,
as in the case of fickle women, he helplessly bestows his mind upon these thoughts that move restlessly on all sides, just as a son delivers his heart to the flames.

The summary meaning is that, just as a man in his youth directs his mind toward young women, so too does he direct it toward anxieties concerning the maintenance of his family and other such matters; "who," for instance, is like a young child? [He is] like a young child.
The meaning is: "just as he directs his mind toward the flames," so it is.
Those various faults, difficult to undertake, [arise] therein for one with such an intention.
O Sage, those things which are not even visible plunder the youth;
they plunder— that is, they deprive— the young man who is possessed by youth of his rest.
They are which ones?
O Sage,
they are yours.

The meaning is that those faults are not seen at all because [the self] has emerged from them; or else, it should be construed as: "those faults are not seen by anyone, nor by anything else. (MT_1,19.5)
Those people who have not been destroyed by youth— which, like the seed of the great hell, causes one to wander incessantly— have not been destroyed by anything else.
This is clear.
He who has crossed the terrifying realm of youth— which consists of manifold flavors and is filled with a multitude of mental fluctuations— is called steadfast.
This is clear.
Youth does not please me, for its form flashes like a blink, it possesses the thundering of restless clouds, and it is constantly illuminated by lightning.
This is clear.

Abounding in various whirlpools, mired in mud, with a dull bottom, and treacherous with its breaking waves, this formidable youth does not please me. (MU 1.19.9) Here, "whirlpools" refers to the impulses of desire.
Stuck in the mud, seized by evil; that in which the intention is dull—such [is it].
It is the leader of all men, charming for only a moment.
"Youth, which resembles a city of Gandharvas, does not please me"—
the singular number "of every man" (*sarvasya puṃsaḥ*) refers to the genus; the meaning is that it is the foremost and unfailing [desire].
Born as the foremost [of men],
for the flight of an arrow is indeed pleasant yet radiant with suffering.
"Youth, which constantly brings about the affliction of burning heat, does not please me.
"For the duration of an arrow's flight" means for a mere moment.
Sweet, savory, and bitter, yet corrupting and a source of defects.
"Youth, which resembles the surging waves of liquor, does not please me;
it is sweet at first, but bitter in its ultimate consequence."
Unreality appearing like reality, soon bringing about deception,
and equal to union with a woman in a dream— such youth does not please me.
This is clear.
Flickering and unstable like a flash of lightning, falsely constructed as a cycle,
my youth— resembling a whirling firebrand— does not please me.
This is clear.
Soft, expansive, and vast, yet empty within and destroyed in an instant—
this youth of mine, resembling an autumn cloud, does not please me.
This is clear.
"Youth does not please me; it is delightful only at first sight, yet its inner nature is devoid of reality, resembling union with a courtesan.
Here, *sadbhāva* means essence (*sattva*) and affection (*sneha*)."
Whatever misdeeds there may be, they all bring about every kind of suffering; they manifest in youth just as great portents appear at the time of destruction.
mahotpātā] Ś4: °ta iva] Ś4: ivā° spaṣṭam // (MT_1,19.17)
Even the Blessed One fears the night of youth, which brings darkness to the heart and possesses a terrifying form. "Hārda" means pertaining to the heart.
"She who creates darkness" refers to her of such a nature.
"The Blessed One, Śrī Mahādeva"—the intention of the word "api" (also/even) is that what need is there to mention others? (MT_1,19.18)

This delusion of youth causes extreme confusion, in which one's virtuous conduct is utterly forgotten and which brings about a failure of the intellect. (MU 1.19.19) [In this compound, "suvismṛtaśubhācāraḥ" means that in which virtuous conduct has been completely forgotten.]

In youth, a living being is consumed in the heart by the irresistible fire born of separation from a beloved, just as a tree is consumed by a forest fire. "Irresistible fire" refers to the unquenchable fire of desire (*kāma*).
For even an intellect that is expansive, clear, and pure may become turbid in youth, like a river during the rainy season.
This is self-evident.
A river, formidable with its dense waves, can be dammed;
but not so the thirst that agitates the inner self, made unsteady by youth.
By the phrase "unsteady by youth," this should be understood as a censure of youth.
"That beloved, those two full breasts, those charms, that face"—
through such thoughts as these regarding youth, a person reaches a state of decay.
"In youth" means in the prime of life.
In this world, the virtuous honor a young man afflicted by ever-surging thirst, and not one who is trivially desirous, like a withered scrap of grass. "Tarantī" means moving or becoming restless.
That which is flickering thirst—
by that he is afflicted and wretched.
For the sake of destruction alone [is this] for one blinded by intoxication, who wears the pearls of faults.
For youth is indeed the eternal tethering post for the great elephant of conceit.
"Defects" refers to passion and the like;
"conceit" is itself the "great elephant," meaning the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). Of that [elephant].
Thus, youth is a fresh forest for the trees of anger and weeping, which have egoism as their vast root and harbor the venomous serpents of the mental afflictions. (MU 1.19.26)
Those very tears shed out of anger become trees;
[the tree] is densely packed with sap and filaments, and crowded with petals of false conceptualizations.
Know that youth is the lotus-pond for the bees of evil thoughts;
"thou art youth," [and] "evil thoughts" refers precisely to those ill-conceived objects of enjoyment.
Cañcarīkas are bees;
their *puṣkara* is the lotus that serves as their support—
know this, understand it.
Of what nature is it?
The "pollens" (kesarāḥ) are the filaments, which are indeed the "flavors" (rasāḥ), meaning the tastes of sense objects.
"Confined by them" means crowded with difficulties;
likewise, "evil conceptualizations" refers to the petals that are indeed contemptible conceptualizations; "disturbed by them" means filled to overflowing with them.

Likewise: "For those who frequent the shores of the lake of the heart—those belonging to the factions of the done and the undone—the abode of the birds of mental anguish and physical disease is fresh youth. (Ś4: tayā; MT_1,19.27–28)
"Done and undone" refers precisely to what is prescribed and what is not prescribed; [the term refers to] those who possess such "bad sides" (kupakṣa).

Even that which is prescribed [as duty] is said to be "done or not done," because it causes one to deviate from the purity or impurity known as dharma. (MT 1.19.28) The ocean, whose full youth is its overflowing tide, disregards the boundaries of those insentient, restless waves whose number cannot be counted. (MU 1.19.29)
"Transgressing the bounds" means being devoid of restraint. (MT_1,19.29) Then, the uneven wind of youth stood ready to remove the dust—that is, the passion—from all the leaves of virtue. MU_1,19.30
He stands ready to remove everything, being by nature one who removes all;
he is covered with *rajas*, meaning the quality of passion (*rajo-guṇa*) as well as dust.
From that, he is pervaded.
The uneven wind of youth is skillful at stripping away and driving far off all the leaves of virtue.
Turbulent and fierce with dust, they turn the face pale.
The harsh dust of youth ascends to the highest peak;
the face is agitated and restless.
That which is refuse or rubbish— meaning dust gathered by a broom— is likewise "utkaṭa," that is, excessive or prominent.
Like a broom that sweeps away impurities, the youthful exuberance of men awakens a multitude of faults and cuts short the row of virtues; it is the very playfulness of the prosperity of evil deeds.
[It] cuts away the dust of the lotus-body and the flickering bee of the mind; this is clear. (Ś4: °kṛntanti spaṣṭam //) (MT_1,19.32)
Having bound him, this moon of youth deludes man;
[the dust of the lotus-body] is flickering.

The sense is that it is precisely by the power of youth that a person becomes attached to the body. (MT_1,19.33) The beautiful creeper of youth, having sprung from the thicket of the body, intoxicates the bee of the mind as soon as it has become attached and reached its full growth. MU_1,19.34
[They have gone] clearly:
the youth arising from the heat of the body-winds is but a mirage.
The deer of the mind, as they run about, fall into the treacherous forest;
the body itself is the desert.
In that regard, the body is a wilderness of heat arising from torment;
the objects of the senses, such as women and so forth, are a treacherous forest.
The moonlight of the body is the mane of the lion of the mind.
The youth of my ocean of life does not please me; it is clearly but a wave of the mind-lion.
This autumn of youth has indeed borne fruit within the wilderness of her body for only a few days; you should not place your trust in it.
"Borne fruit" means endowed with the fruits such as the enjoyment of a lover's embrace.
In an instant, this bird of youthfulness flies away from the body of one with little fortune,
just as a *cintāmaṇi* jewel slips from the hand in a mere moment.
This is clear.
Whenever youth ascends to its highest peak, sensual desires surge forth; at that time, they lead only to destruction. "Sensual" (sarasāḥ) means filled with the flavor of sense-objects.
Desires are longings.
Right then do the demons of passion and hatred leap about;
this entire host does not set until the night of youth has passed.
This is clear. (MT 1.19.40) O Youth, show compassion toward this wretched body, which is filled with various functions, perishes in an instant, and is dying like a son! MU 1.19.41
This is clear.
(MU 1.19.41) That greatly deluded man who, out of delusion, experiences joy because of youth which is momentary in its destruction—he indeed is known as a "human deer. (MU 1.19.42)
This is clear.
(MT 1.19.42) That person of very poor intellect who desires youth, which is intoxicated by pride, delusion, and arrogance, will before long be joined with remorse. (MU 1.19.43)
The meaning is: by means of remorse produced through that destruction.
Thus:
"By that destruction [of the body], those high-souled ones are righteous; they alone are the true persons on earth. (MT 1.19.43)
O virtuous one, those who have easily crossed over the peril of youth—
clearly,
the ocean, that abode of formidable sea-monsters, is crossed with ease.
It does not flash like a wave in a forest; it is full of defects and its youth is destroyed.
This is clear.
With this verse at the end of the chapter, he concludes the censure of youth.

Adorned with discipline, the abode of noble beings, radiant with compassion, and encircled by virtues—indeed, O dear one, such excellent youth is rare in this world, like a forest situated in the sky.
The meaning is that such youth is truly praiseworthy. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the nineteenth canto in the section on dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus completed the censure of youth, he introduces the censure of women by way of that same context.
*Śrī Rāmāya namaḥ*.
And in this woman, who is a puppet of flesh with a cage of limbs flickering like a machine, and who is adorned with sinews,
bones, and knots— what indeed is beautiful?
In that cage of limbs which is as flickering as a machine, belonging to a doll— that is, a puppet.
Even a doll remains a mere mechanical construct;
the underlying sense is that there is nothing at all beautiful about a woman.
Having separated the skin, flesh, blood, tears, and the watery moisture from the eye, [one sees only the void].
Behold this lovely thing; why do you become deluded in vain?
This is a description of all the limbs:
"Here are the hair, here is the blood"—such is the body of a young woman.
What can one of vast disposition do with this censured thing?
The sense is that it is not fitting for one of vast disposition to find delight in this.
Those [senses] which have been cherished again and again with garments and ointments...
Carnivorous beasts tear away those limbs of all embodied beings, even though they have been cherished.
Therefore, the sense is that even for women, the flesh-eaters will tear them apart.
"Removing [the pearls]" means:
On which breast the pearls of a shimmering necklace were seen to resemble the forceful current of the Gaṅgā water glistening upon the slopes of Mount Meru’s peaks. (MU 1.20.5)
In cremation grounds and at the ends of the quarters, that very same breast of a woman is devoured by dogs in time, like a small lump of food.
This is clear. A pair of verses.
Just as the limbs of a young camel in the forest are smeared with blood, flesh, and so forth, so too are the limbs of a passionate woman; for what attachment can there be even toward her?
This is clear. (MU 1.20.7) (MT 1.20.7)

It is merely imagined that a woman possesses a quality of being delightful at first sight; I believe, O Sage, that even this does not exist here [in the female body], which is the sole cause of delusion.
(MU 1.20.8) "Here" refers to the female body. (MT 1.20.8)
What distinction is there here between intoxicating liquor, which bestows expansive exhilaration by first agitating one's passion, and a woman who causes such transformation?
The word "madirāyāḥ" is in the ablative case.
(MT 1.20.9) O Sage, those elephants of pride that are tethered to the hitching post of women do not attain awakening, even with the long goads of tranquility. (MU 1.20.10)
This is clear.
(MT_1,20.10) Bearing hair like soot and sharp by nature at all times, women—flames of the fire of evil deeds—burn a man like straw. MU_1,20.11
This is clear.
(MT 1,20.11) They are to be revered, they are great-souled ones, and they alone are true men on this earth, who have easily crossed over the perilous strait of youth, O virtuous one. (MU 1,20.12)
From the peril of youth—that which is called a multitude of women—[one should flee].
For women, though burning even from afar and full of passion, are yet devoid of essence; they are both beautiful and terrible, like wood for the fires of hell. (MU 1.20.13)
"Even women who are full of passion become sapless wood"—this is an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).
