By him by whom living beings have thus been cast down;
by such a one.
The word "time" (kāla) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence].
The three words ending in the instrumental case are to be construed as adjectives qualifying the term "by one's own self" (svātmanā).
[piṣṭāḥ] Ś4: °ṣṭā pātitāḥ; [jantavo] Ś4: jantu°; [the three words ending in the third case] Ś4: °āṃta° (MT_1,22.43)
He is the doer, the enjoyer, and the destroyer; he is the rememberer who has attained every state. He performs all this, yet he does nothing at all.
Because it is of the nature of nothingness, no instrument of action is to be known.
With this verse at the end of the chapter, he concludes the censure of time:
"The entire body, though devoid of any internal parts, assumes forms both beautiful and ugly."
Manifesting and suddenly concealing itself here among men, it indeed sports through the power of Time.
Its bodily form— whether complete or incomplete— is to be understood according to the classification of its objects.
In the phrase "revealing and concealing," the addition of the augment *num*—even though there is no *sarvanāmasthāna* [case ending] present—is an archaic (*ārṣa*) usage. Thus all is auspicious.
(MT_1,22.45) Thus ends the twenty-second canto in the Vairāgyaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Having thus offered a censure of time (*kāla*), he speaks of the playfulness of time (*kālavilāsa*): Homage to the illustrious Rāma, whose sport is most formidable and from whom all calamities have been cast far away.
In this cycle of existence, of King Time,
whose power is immeasurable and whose play is most formidable.
In this world, which is like a tattered forest-thicket of the universe, the hunt is pursued by the wretched and deluded multitudes of living beings and wild animals.
The great ocean at the time of the Kalpa is a delightful pleasure-pool, wherein the beautiful submarine fire shines like a lotus in one corner. (This is clear.)
The daily sustenance [of the gods] is performed with those very worlds— abounding in pungent, bitter, and sour elements, and rich with oceans of curd and milk—
which have become stale. "Pungent, bitter, and sour" refers to those that are excessively tāmasika, tāmasika-rājasa, and rājasa respectively.
And those beings, both moving and stationary, which possess specific tastes such as pungent and so forth, as well as perfected substances— by means of these, being abundant and joined together,
and having been kept overnight, that is, having become stale.
But not with new ones; this is the meaning. "Kālyāvartanam" means the morning meal.
The word "asya" (of him), which appears in the first verse of the creation account, is to be applied everywhere.
Caṇḍī, who moves with fourfold gait and is accompanied by the entire host of Mothers,
is a she-wolf that drags away the human deer placed within the forest of *saṃsāra*.
Of this Time, Caṇḍī is the name of the Power (*śakti*).
The connection is that she becomes a she-wolf.
The group of mothers is well known.
Even a prince keeps a she-wolf for the purpose of hunting. (MT 1,23.5)
The earth is in the palm of his hand; the earth is a vessel for drink, filled with nectar, and adorned with garlands of swaying clusters of lotuses, blue lotuses, and white water-lilies.
The earth is vast.
Roaring, with a formidable lashing [of his tail], Narasiṃha is within the cage of his arms;
with a mane and broad, thick shoulders, he is the lovely play-bird.
*Narasiṃha* means *narasiṃha*.

Even for the sake of sport, a lion is kept in a cage for a prince. The god Mahākāla is indeed like a young cuckoo in play; he possesses the sweet sound of a gourd-lute and the stainless luster of the autumnal sky.
Mahākāla is a particular deity who holds authority over dissolution.
With a form of incessant radiance, he emits a shower of thunderbolts of suffering;
his bow is called Non-existence, and it flashes forth everywhere.
Vomited means ejected;
by which [the person], the arrows and thunderbolts are indeed sufferings.
That [bow] is both non-contemplation and a bow; thus it is the "bow named non-contemplation."
[The words] *vāntāḥ* [are glossed as] *udgīrṇāḥ* in Ś4.
He concludes the description of the play of time with a verse at the end of the canto.

Nourished by the unfolding of unsurpassed play, wandering, captivating, and sporting about while tearing asunder the world grown old—like a monkey agitated by age—he whose body quivers, Time, exerts himself here.
He exerts himself; he performs various kinds of activities. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-third canto in the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus described the play of time, he introduces the play of fate:
[Ś4: Homage to Śrī Rāma; N11: Oṃ.
Right here, there is another who is like a crest-jewel among those of wicked pastimes.]
"Destiny and time are spoken of by the world as 'it acts' and 'it exists.
"It acts" is a statement regarding activity;
"it exists" is a statement regarding being.
In this context, "time" (kāla) is intended to mean "fate" (kṛtānta), since the latter is a synonym for the former.
Thus:
"Apart from mere action, for that [agent] whose nature consists of its own vibration, no other form is perceived, nor is any desired object of action [perceived]. (MU 1.24.2)
Therefore, this entire succession of beings, eternally fragile,
has been brought to a state of extreme distress by suffering, like a garland of snow by heat.
Of that deity,
whose form is not perceived without mere action.
Nor is the intended object of action, which is sought after as the objective support of the action,
perceived.
For what reason?
Thinking "this one performs some action," by that [thought] this continuum of elements is brought into a state of disarray.
Whatever is seen here as the expansive circle of the world, that is his theater for dancing; herein he dances.
Regarding that deity:
with the intention of stating another name for him, he says:
"And bearing the third name, Kṛtānta, which is most terrible."
In this world, Fate, intoxicated and possessing the form of a Kāpālika, dances.
"Possessing the form of a Kāpālika" means being like a Kāpālika.
[The author] states that this very [Fate] is the substratum of all things.
O Sage, for Kṛtānta (Death) dances incessantly without ever losing his passion, while Niyati (Destiny) is his eternally beloved;
and Śeṣa, white as the digit of the moon, and the stream of the Gaṅgā— these two are his [two feet], making three in total.
Both the *upavīta* and the *avītābha* are upon the chest of *saṃsāra*. Which two? Śeṣa and the flow of the Gaṅgā.
They are *avītābhe*, meaning endowed with splendor.
Samsara itself is the chest; therein.
[On her] two wrists are the orbs of the moon and sun;
in her hands are a playful lotus and the Brahma-egg with its pericarp as the ear-ornament.
[The pericarp of the cosmic egg: *brāhmam* refers to the lotus that serves as the seat of Brahmā. *brahmāṇḍakarṇikam* [Ś4: *°rṇikām*; N11: *°rṇik(ā)am*] means the pericarp of the cosmic egg.
The pericarp of the Brahmāṇḍa; it is the pericarp because it is situated in its center.
The pericarp of the Brahmāṇḍa [lotus], strewn with stars as its filaments and possessing the flickering Puṣkarāvarta clouds as its petals.
The single sky is washed by the waters of the universal ocean;
"sky" (ambaram) means the ether (ākāśam).
Ambara means clothing. Before such a person as that, Niyati, the eternal woman of desire, dances with her efforts, her passion never subsiding. (MU 1.24.10)
By means of undertakings consisting of restraints and observances;
for indeed, in the presence of a male dancer, the female dancer also dances.
Within the hollow of the pavilion of the world, she who is fond of dancing— her form being unobstructed in its vibration— is flickering with coming and going through her various efforts.

With beautiful ornaments upon her limbs, she was a series of intermediate worlds of the gods; her vast circle of braided hair hung down as far as the netherworld (Pātāla) through the sky. The "intermediate worlds of the gods" refers to those regions belonging to the deities.
A row of them serves as a beautiful ornament upon their limbs.
Of what nature is the sky?
It reaches down to the netherworld; that is, as far as Pātāla.
It is long and pervasive;
and as she dances, her braid becomes long.
And Narakālī, with her garland of anklets, is filled with a tumultuous clamor.
Strung upon a thread of misdeeds, it wavers with its feet reaching down to the netherworld;
it is a garland of anklets and a string of tinkling bells.
A tilaka-mark of musk has been fashioned by her friend for the occasion.
It was recorded by Citragupta on the facial tablet in Yama’s domain;
"in Yama's" means in the realm related to Yama,
and "on the facial tablet" means on the tablet for the face.
That is to say, on the face in the form of the tablet of Yama’s decree,
it was "painted" (citrita)— meaning painted by Citragupta, or rather,
the script written by Citragupta.
The musk-tilaka comes into being;
of what nature? By means of the "friendship of action," that is, by means of the friend who is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
Having entered into Citragupta who had been prepared for the purpose, she composed it;
for a female friend indeed applies a tilaka to her friend.
Having assumed the form of Kālī, this goddess, who at the ends of kalpas performs the multitude of rites presided over by Citragupta,
dances once more with the loud roar of a mountain crashing apart.
Kālī is the power of time (*kāla-śakti*). Having assumed—that is, having resorted to—her form, the word "again" (*punar*) is used with reference to what occurred previously. (MT_1,24.15)
Furthermore, [he was surrounded] by those with dangling, wandering locks like the peacock feathers on a youth’s chariot,
terrifying with the great resonance from the vast cavities of their three eyes,
and whose hair was bestowed upon the head of Hara by the long, swaying autumn moon.
With beautiful, slow-moving white yak-tail fans made of the hair of fair-skinned maidens;
with Tumburu, who was delighted by Bhairava, whose form was like a mountain in a state of wild dance;
and with the begging bowls that were the skulls of Indra’s body, resounding from its thousands of apertures.
With its dry, skeletal frames and skull-topped staffs filling the sky,
it terrifies even itself, though it is already darkened by black clouds. (Kulaka) "Dry" means possessing the quality of desiccation.
Because it is the subject under discussion, this refers to *niyati* (destiny).
It makes even the self fear— that is, it causes the self to be overcome by terror— since the self has become "dense-black," meaning exceedingly dark.
The sense is: "What need is there to speak of others?"—
referring to oneself as being such that the parts of the body, meaning those components whose nature is like the breaking of the limbs of a bedstead (khaṭvāṅga), [are subject to decay].
The sky was filled by them;
by what kind of things? By the small *khaṭvāṅga* staffs of their bodies, as described in the passage beginning with "behind," and so forth.
Subsequently, being suspended [in mid-air], he was thus bewildered and wandering;
"Kaumāra" means belonging to Kumāra;
those for whom the peacock is the vehicle of their chariot.
By them;
the whistling sounds produced by the wind are to be known;
and that autumn moon which is both hanging down and flickering.
By him they were bestowed, that is, given; "kṛtā" (made) is the intended meaning.
Those whose hair is like that of Hara (Śiva).
By them;
the sense is that just as the hair of Hara is illuminated by the crescent moon,
so too is hers by the full autumnal moon.
Those for whom that very braid of Gaurī’s hair— showering lovely mandāra flowers and shimmering with lovely mandāra flowers—
is their fly-whisk.
By them;
he who is both in a state of wild dance and yet possesses the form of a mountain;
Bhairava, the Great Terrifier.
By those for whom he alone is the *ādaratumbaka*— the object of reverence, or a particular kind of musical instrument—
he whose thousands of apertures in the form of eyes resound; [he is] one who possesses thousands of holes in the form of eyes.
Such was that body of Indra;
it was by those for whom that very [body] served as an alms-bowl.
Likewise with black [forms].
And this external meditation has been described for the sake of those with coarse vision;
however, for those with subtle vision, it is taught by way of a different method in relation to youths and others.
Furthermore, the touch of necessity has been explained.

For those [beings], the great Bhairava is one who dances wildly (uttāṇḍava). [Ś4: omits "mahā"].

She whose form is the eye; with a beautiful garland of lotuses that are the wheels upon the heads of Viśvarūpa,
she shines as she dances through the great kalpas.
With the beautiful lotus-garland that is the wheel of the head of Viśvarūpa— the head-wheel of Virāj.
And that very [lake] is Cārupuṣkaramālā; by means of it.
With the terrifying sounds of the *ḍamaru* drums of the intoxicated Puṣkarāvarta clouds,
the *śiraścakra* [is such that] Tumburu and others indeed flee from it at the end of the eon.
*Ḍamaravas* are specific types of musical instruments;
*uḍḍāmaras* means formidable or fierce;
*tumburu* is a name for a *gandharva*.
At the end of the dance of Kṛtānta, who smiles with the orb of the moon, he wears as a crest the peacock-feather plume of the sky, beautiful with the moonlight of the stars.
Adorned with a crest of peacock feathers,
upon one ear there is a long earring like the Himalayas;
on the other, there is a beautiful golden disc like Mount Meru.
"At the beginning" means at the end of the eon;
"laughter" refers to the lunar disc itself, and [the term] belongs to that which is joined with it.
The moonbeams [...
that which is beautiful by means of them;
the sky itself is the plumage.
Of him who has that [ornament] with a hanging fringe as his head-ornament;
such is he. A *mudrikā* is a white, specific kind of ear-ornament.

*piñchaṃ* ] Ś4: *picchaṃ*.
(MT_1,24.22-23) Right here, the two dangling earrings are the sun and moon upon the orb of his cheeks.
The range of mountains from Lokāloka forms her girdle all around.
"Gaṇḍamaṇḍale" means on the surface of the cheeks;
a girdle situated at the waist is called a "kaṭimekhalā."
Moving here and there, like a circle of lightning, the girdle shines like a strip of silken garment upon the clouds, stirred by the wind. (MU 1.24.25)
She whose ornament—
a specific kind of decoration— is a circle of lightning, such that she possesses a circle of lightning as her ornament, is "one whose ornament is a circle of lightning. (MT_1,24.25)
With maces, spears, tridents, lances, barbed missiles, and clubs—
sharpened weapons gathered like the Destroyer himself to annihilate the multitude of living beings—
he stood within the long noose of worldly bondage cast forth by the hand of Time.
The garland shines upon his face, strung with the great threads of the remaining enjoyments;
it is for the purpose of binding him to saṃsāra,
completely on all sides.
"O Dīrgha!
Of this [Kṛtānta], which has just been mentioned and is synonymous with 'Fate' (daiva)."
Regarding "samanantaroktasya": Ś4 reads °anantaḥ ārokta°;
N11 reads °anaṃtaḥ*(ā)rokta°. (MT_1,24.26-27)

The row of bracelets formed by the seven oceans is his ornament, radiant with the brilliance of the jewels in the makara-heads shimmering with life. (MU 1.24.28) "Shimmering with life" means shining by means of the living soul (*jīva*).
"Containing living beings" means as many as there are; "makaras" refers to those [rivers] which possess them.
Even on bracelets there are figures of sea-monsters,
yet they are lifeless.
The great whirlpool of worldly activity is a succession of pleasure and pain.
Filled with passion (rajas) and dark with ignorance (tamas), his line of body hair shines forth.
That [line] is one in which there are great whirlpools of worldly activities and repeated returns.

Such a succession of pleasure and pain is his line of body hair (romālī), which shines forth; of what nature is it? It is full of dust (rajaḥpūrṇā), meaning it is filled with the quality of passion (rajo-guṇa).
Likewise, the line of hair (romālī) is dark as darkness, defiled by the quality of tamas;
it is possessed of curls, filled with dust, and dark as the night.
The great whirlpools of worldly affairs; the succession of pleasure and pain is its line of body hair. (Ś4 reads *°āvartā* for *mahāvartāḥ*;
Ś4 reads *°māvalī* for *romālī*.)
At the end of the aeon, Maheśvara, having withdrawn this dance of the world— which is of such a nature and fierce with the *tāṇḍava*— along with the process of creation,
again assumes his playful dance characterized by laughter, which embodies all forms.
She weaves this creation, which is full of laughter and adorned with the dramatic representations of old age, suffering, and grief,
together with Necessity (niyati).
Again, at the beginning of creation,
[he created] this world-form. He concludes this with the final verse of the section on creation.

Again he creates worlds, forests, other realms, and the arrangement of the web of living beings, as well as the beautiful fashioning of conduct and all that is moving and unmoving—just as a child tirelessly constructs figures from mud.
"Moving and unmoving" means extremely unstable. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth canto in the Section on Dispassion within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus described the play of destiny (*daivavilāsa*), he speaks of its fruition:
[Ś4: Homage to Śrī Rāma; N11: Oṃ!
And in this very context, O great sage, regarding these factors such as time (*kāla*) and so forth...]
"What reliance can there be here for those like me upon that which is called saṃsāra?"— the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied;
[this refers to] conduct (*carita*) or behavior (*vṛtta*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), fate (*daiva*) and the other factors are included.
(MT_1,25.1) "We remain as if sold by these [factors] such as fate;
like deluded wild deer, we are [tricked] by rogues who are clever in their deceptions. (MU_1,25.2)
This ignoble conduct is like Death itself, its mouth wide open, ready to swallow [us].
In this world, he incessantly casts the people into the ocean of calamity,
with his mouth ready to swallow them.
This is clear.
(MT 1.25.3) At the end, fate burns [the world] with cruel deeds born of evil desires, just as fire burns the world with flames that resemble flowers. (MU 1.25.4)
This is clear.

A single beloved wife, though possessing a beautiful form, causes constancy to falter because she is a woman, naturally fickle; likewise, destiny, though tending toward restraint, causes the law of necessity to waver.
It brings illness, it bestows disease;
it is not beloved for its beauty, but is beloved for its lack of form.
It incessantly devours the multitude of beings, as a serpent devours the wind.
Kṛtānta, whose conduct is harsh, having brought the body of the world to old age— he whose very body is the world— such is he.
That merciless king of Yama does not show compassion even for one who is suffering.
A person whose conduct is characterized by compassion for all beings has become rare. [The word] *ārta* means one who is miserable. O Sage, all classes of living beings have indeed meager resources.

The grounds of greed lead only to suffering and have a miserable end; they consist of meager wealth and are joined with essence-less possessions. Life is exceedingly fickle, while death alone is cruel.
Youth is exceedingly fickle, and childhood has been lost through dullness.
(This is clear.
The world is stained by the impurity of the arts; kinsmen are the bonds of worldly existence.
Sensual enjoyments are the great diseases of existence, and craving is a mirage;
one is stained by the arts known as the deception of others.
The enemies are indeed the very senses; truth has become untruth. (N11: marked as *kalaṅkitaḥ*) (MT_1,25.10) Śatravaś cendriyāṇy eva satyaṃ yātam asatyatām /
The mind itself strikes down the mind as its own enemy; the self, by means of the self, strikes down the self.
The self [is the agent]; by the self [is the instrument];
the self [is the object] that is struck down.
The word "by false conceptualizations" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Mind alone" means the impure mind alone;
it is not anything else.
The enemy of the mind is the enemy of the pure mind.
The ego is impure; the intellects are fragile and lead to blemish;
actions yield evil fruits; and pastimes have become centered on women.
Women have become delicate and lacking in sharpness;

they are made to possess the objects of desire along with aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*). Women have become banners of faults, and the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) have reached a state of flavorlessness.
And those women were objects of desire, modest, and charming at first sight; such were the women, full of aesthetic wonder (*sacamatkṛti*) and endowed with a sense of marvel.
They were made or fashioned;
that is to say, they were cultivated.
What kind of women were they?
They have the faults as their banners;
because they consist of the faults such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, they have passion and the other faults as their banners.
"Tastes" (*rasa*) refers to desires for objects such as the treatises and so forth.

They have become sapless and withered. The mind, having grasped a thing as a non-thing and surrendered it to the ego, is such that beings are obstructed by non-existence, and the end of existence is not attained.
[The state of being obstructed by non-existence] refers to us. A real entity is truly an entity;
however, by way of its non-substantiality—in the form of "I am the body"—it has been taken up and grasped as a non-entity.
Likewise, "the mind has been given over to egoism" means it has been seized by egoism. "Entities are obstructed by non-existence" means they are gripped by destruction;
the word "not known" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Therefore, the end of existence is not apprehended; it is not attained.
O virtuous one, the mind, its interior agitated, suffers in vain;
the serpent of passion plays there, yet it does not approach dispassion.
*Virāga* is the absence of passion (*rāgābhāva*).
He does not approach it; he does not go toward it.
[The absence of passion: Is this a textual corruption by the author?
(MT_1,25.15) When the vision is struck by the quality of *rajas*, *tamas* increases;
and *sattva* is not attained, for reality (*tattva*) is exceedingly far away. (MU_1,25.16)
Reality is the ultimate truth.
Stability has become instability; death is on the verge of arrival;
fortitude falls into despondency; and delight is constantly fixed upon that which is unreal.
Regarding the body and so forth, which are non-entities and have become non-entities:
through dullness of intellect, the mind becomes defiled; the body is destined solely for destruction;
old age blazes as it were within the body; and past misdeeds crackle forth. (MU 1.25.17–18)
Through sluggishness and dullness,
youth departs with effort, while association with the virtuous remains far away;
no path is found anywhere, and truthfulness does not arise at all.
Through the sign of youth, there is attachment to women.
(MT 1.25.19) The mind seems to become utterly bewildered within; joy has gone far away. Radiance does not arise, compassion does not dawn, and baseness approaches from afar. (MU 1.25.20)
This is clear.
(MT 1.25.20) People, intent on rising and falling, go from steadfastness to instability;
association with the wicked is easy to find, but the company of the virtuous is difficult to obtain. (MU 1.25.21)
Steadfastness turns into lack of steadfastness; the meaning is that it perishes.
[Steadfastness] N11, Ś4:
*°rata* (MT_1,25.21) Phenomena come and go; their cultivation binds one to existence.
This constant succession of elements is led nowhere at all. MU_1,25.22
"It is led away"—the word "by time" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
For even the directions are no longer seen, nor is any place left without a name;
even mountains crumble away—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
The directions are visible; they wither away. In one such as me, [the heads] are shattered. N11: °dṛśo. Ś4: dṛśyo; Ś4: śīrṣa°. N11: °dṛśe.
"Place" (*deśa*) would not partake of the designation "place," meaning that even for a place,
the name "place" would not exist by virtue of time.
Where such [things] are of such a nature...
Ten states will arise there; what reliance or what confidence can there be in a person such as I? This is the intended meaning.

"Even the oceans run dry and the stars perish; even the perfected ones (*siddha*) do not achieve perfection. What reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I? (MU 1.25.24) [Ś4 reads *bhava* for *bhajati*].
This is clear.
(MU 1.25.24) Even though it is non-existent, the sky is devoured and the world is shattered; even the earth falls into distress—what reliance can there be on a person such as I? (MU 1.25.25)
By its non-existence, that is, by its destruction,
even the sky is devoured— that is, swallowed.
Even the Dānavas are torn asunder, and even Dhruva has become one whose life is no longer fixed.

Even the immortals are slain; what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I? They are slain—by Time, it should be understood. Even Śakra is assailed by Śakras, and even Yama is indeed subject to restraint.
Even for the wind there is a state of non-wind; what reliance can there be on a person such as I? Even Soma attains the state of the sky, and even the sun suffers fragmentation.
Even fire falls into a state of ruin; what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
(agnir vyomatām / nāśam ity arthaḥ)
Even Parameṣṭhin, though he has not reached his final end, seizes Hari; even the Unborn (Aja) [seizes] Hari;
and even Bhava goes to the state of non-existence. What reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even Bhava, even Śrī Mahādeva,
attained the state of non-existence as Mahādeva.
Time undergoes fragmentation, and even Niyati is led away.

Even space is absorbed into the Infinite; what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I? [This refers to] some infinite, internalized reality, whose form is unknown through a system that is difficult to hear, difficult to speak, and difficult to perceive.
The worlds are being mimicked by some deluding agent.
[This] Tantra, which is difficult to hear, difficult to speak, and difficult to see, is a means of deception.
"Of whom," "by such a one," and "by anyone whatsoever" mean by one that is indefinable.

Having attained even a fraction of egoism, there is no one in the three worlds who is not bound here by that which dwells within all. Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is the sense of self-identity with the body and so forth.

That which brings about such [a state] is "tādṛśī" (of such a kind).
Likewise, "bhaṅguraḥ" means crooked like the outer corner of the eye;
it is crooked in its outer corners.
That which is noble in its conduct is therefore delightful;
likewise, lightning is flickering and exceedingly fickle.
Repeatedly extending light upon their own objects, knowledge, and the illumination of their own bodies—
those days were great, those were riches, and those were actions.
"Everything has become an object of memory; we too shall go [to that state] in an instant"—this is the connection with the phrase "those days.
By the word "that" (*tat*), there is a recollection of the days previously experienced.
It perishes day by day and is born again day by day;
even today there is no end to this burnt-out cycle of worldly existence for one whose form has been destroyed.
This is clear.
Men go to the state of animals, and animals even to the state of men;
gods likewise become non-gods. O Lord, what indeed is stable here in this world?
The transition of animals and others to the state of being human and so forth should be understood as occurring either by way of their inherent nature (*svabhāva*) or by way of birth (*janman*).
Weaving a web of rays again and again throughout nights and days—
Having caused the sun to pass through the body, it perceives the limit of its destruction. "Ativāhya" means having caused [the sun] to proceed.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all classes of beings alike hasten toward destruction, just as bodies of water do before the submarine fire.
This is clear.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—
all these are the fuel that has been completely dried up for the submarine fire of destruction.
"Completely withered" indicates that it is intensely scorched.
(MT_1,27.22) Wealth, kinsmen, servants, friends, and whatever powers one possesses—all these have become sapless for one who is terrified by the fear of destruction. MU_1,27.23

The word "mine" (*mama*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. (MT_1,27.23) These objects of experience continue to taste sweet for the wise man in this world only so long as the demon of destruction has not entered the path of his memory. (MU_1,27.24)
This is clear.
(MT 1.27.24) In one moment sovereignty arrives, and in a moment poverty comes;
in one moment freedom from disease, and in a moment the onset of illness. (MU 1.27.25)
This is clear.
(MT_1,27.25) By this great delusion of the world, which brings about error at every moment, who indeed—even among the wise—is not deluded? MU_1,27.26
This is clear.
(MT 1.27.26) For a moment the circle of the sky was smeared with the mire of darkness;
for a moment it was beautiful with a soft light flowing like molten gold. (MU 1.27.27)
Beautiful with a soft radiance like molten gold,
its hollow interior encircled for a moment by garlands of clouds as dark as blue lotuses;
at times emitting a tumultuous roar, and at other times remaining silent.
At one moment it is the play of the stars, at another adorned by the sun;
at one moment it brings delight through the moon, and at another it is entirely cast out. It exists through a state characterized by coming and going, and is subject to destruction.
Even a wise person does not fear this state of worldly existence; who indeed would fear it?
The sense is: what need is there to mention the case of one who lacks wisdom? Regarding "by this state," it means by the state of the world's persistence.
Calamities come for a moment; prosperity comes for a moment;
birth and then death come for a moment—O Sage, what indeed is not momentary?
The sense is that everything is indeed momentary.
In the past, O Father, one thing was here, and by these days it has become quite another.
Blessed One, is there anything at all that remains stable, even in its own form?
Father is Daśaratha;
other than another is "anyetaraḥ."
The nature of a cloth is seen in a jar, and the state of a jar is seen in a cloth. There is nothing that,
having been perceived, does not undergo reversal within cyclic existence.
In the cycle of existence (*saṃsṛti*),

what was seen as [true] at one time becomes perverted— that is, it undergoes reversal— through the medium of death and so forth at another time. A hero slain by a non-hero, even by a single person, is like a hundred slain.
Ordinary people have attained power, and the entire world revolves;
it revolves, that is, it undergoes cyclic change.
This multitude of beings constantly pursues error.
Like a series of waves arising from the perception of the movement of the insentient,
so too is the *janatā*— the multitude of people;
that which is the movement of the insentient.
Because of that perception, which is to say, because of contact—
that is, because of dullness—
there is the perception of the movement of water.
And thus:
"From that [infancy], in just a few days, comes the splendor of youth; then, old age.
Even in the body there is no single state of being; what then can be said of external objects? (MU 1.27.36)
This is clear.

In all things, toward all living beings—(MT_1,27.37) this rule applies: creating one thing from here, another from there, and yet another from elsewhere, he never grows weary, just as a child does not tire in play. MU_1,27.38
This is clear.
(MT_1,27.38) The Creator gathers this world that has arisen here, maddens it, devours it, strikes it down, and seizes it for himself through hundreds of calamities and upheavals. MU_1,27.39
It accumulates and increases;
it causes madness, making one possessed by insanity;
it devours and consumes.
It strikes down; it destroys.
It makes one's own, bringing under one's control. It smashes; it destroys completely. (MT_1,27.39)
In one moment [he creates] one thing, on another day another, and in the morning yet another;

What exists today does not exist tomorrow morning; what exists tomorrow morning does not exist today; and what exists at another time does not exist today. Everything revolves incessantly.
This is clear.
In this world, sufferings are continuous while pleasures are rare; they revolve around a person constantly, like nights and days. (MU 1.27.42) "Continuous" means uninterrupted.

for people subject to worldly existence, who partake in manifestation and disappearance, neither calamities nor prosperities attain stability. (MU 1.27.43)
"Of one who partakes in manifestation and disappearance" means of such a person as "one who undergoes manifestation and disappearance.

(MT_1,27.43) Stepping from one position to another, this wicked man, causing everyone to fall into calamity, stands like a moment of Time—a villain whose entire being is effortlessly turned upside down. (MU_1,27.44)

fall day after day from the vast trees of saṃsāra, blown down by the wind of time.

They are divided by that;

Like thorns,

(MT_1,28.8) "What use have I for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments, what use for wealth, or what use for undertakings?"
"By the power of egoism, this very [bond] has dissolved for me.

Indeed, this is the occasion: today, at a time endowed with all necessary conditions,

Now, one might ask: "Why does he become intent on medical treatment after abandoning the pursuit of sense objects? To this, it is said: Poison is the discordance of sense objects; poison is not called [merely] physical venom.

"Disparity caused by objects" means the disparity of objects.

Of one who is wise and endowed with discernment.

O Knower, free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, instruct me quickly in this manner.

This is clear.

That which is performed with malicious intent— uneven, harsh, destructive, and violent—
is indeed *āśāviṣavaiśasa*. (MT 1,28.17)
"This does not exist, this exists"—such is the delusion of worldly people;
this [wisdom] shakes the flickering mind, just as the wind disperses a mass of dust. (It "shakes" means it causes to tremble.)
The string of pearls consisting of the multitude of living beings, strung upon the threads of craving,
has as its permanent leader the mind, which is ever manifest through its nature as a part of pure consciousness.

for consciousness alone is the pure body, one's true nature.
That which belongs to someone; its state is "thatness" (tattā).
By her;
that is to say, by virtue of being composed of consciousness (cinmaya).

[Make it] free from impurity and tender.
O best among those who know reality, quickly dispel the mist in the forest of my heart and the darkness of my mind with some lamp of knowledge.
The heart is the lotus-heart itself, which is the forest;
therein is the mist.
The meaning is: "by someone," that is, by me who am incapable of speaking.

O Great-souled One, those mental afflictions do not even exist here for you; they do not reach destruction [of their own accord], yet they vanish through association with those of supreme mind, just as darkness vanishes by the moon. MU 1.28.22 O Great-souled One!

In this world, those difficult mental afflictions do not exist which do not reach destruction through association with the superior; the meaning is that by association with those of superior mind, difficult mental afflictions perish.
He concludes this with the final verse of the chapter.

Life is as fragile as water droplets hanging from a cluster of lotus petals shaken by the wind; enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds; and the rushing current of the waters of youthful indulgence is ever-tossing. Having realized this, I have swiftly applied a seal, firm as a mountain, upon my mind for the sake of lasting peace. *Life is as fragile as water droplets hanging from a cluster of lotus petals shaken by the wind; enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds; and the rushing current of the waters of youthful indulgence is ever-tossing. Having realized this, I have swiftly applied a seal, firm as a mountain, upon my mind for the sake of lasting peace.* [Note: *meghavitanamadhyavilasatsaudaminicancalah* is rendered as "flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds," following the variant *vilasa* found in N11 and Ś4.]
The *mudrā* itself is firmly placed upon the mountain;
*vitāna* means a collection,
and *lālanā* means playful charm (*vilāsa*).
Mudrā is silence;
that is to say, the non-perception of sense objects.
Of what nature is it?
"Like a mountain" means like a rock;
it is firm. May there be auspiciousness. Thus ends the twenty-eighth [chapter] in the section on detachment within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
The Chapter.

*Ś4: Homage to Śrī Rāma; N11: Oṃ!
Thus, [the world] is a hollow pit of the multitude of calamities that have arisen.*
Beholding the world submerged in the mire of mental constructs and reflections,
my mind seems to reel and a great agitation arises within me;
my limbs tremble like the leaves of an ancient tree.

"Abhyutthitaḥ" means having risen; "abhyudayaṃ gataḥ" means having come to prosperity. That which is a caravan of misfortune—that is, a multitude of calamities—by that [caravan] there is a crisis, a straitened condition.
That which has a hollow interior is "koṭaramadhyam.
That which is the mentalizing of the mind— that phenomenon called "mentalizing" (manana), which is synonymous with "volition" (saṅkalpa)— is [the meaning].
That very thing is the mud;
in that [mud],
there is agitation, which is to say, a state of distress.
The limbs are the members.
The intellect, its lap agitated by conduct that lacks supreme contentment and is devoid of true purpose,
fears in this world as one who has lost her support, like a child whose protector is weak.
"Empty of a locus" [N11:
*°spandā*] means unattained; it is the lap, the fold, of the practice and activity of supreme contentment.
By which;
that;
and it is such.
For this very reason, she is agitated;
even a young girl becomes agitated when deprived of the embrace of her beloved friend. Her husband is a lord of little power.
Of whomsoever;
she;
such as that.
Indeed, a child clearly fears that which has little strength, lacks a secure foundation, and is empty.
These fluctuations of the internal organ roll about amidst conceptual constructions,
like doeses deceived by a mere mirage in pits.

The meaning is that they roll about among conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); from one conceptual construction they go to another conceptual construction.
Or rather, they fall into delusion;
for what are the modifications of the internal organ like?
They are hollow, being devoid of substance because they are sweet only for a moment.
Those objects which are the focal points (*ālambāḥ*); by them they are mocked, that is to say, deceived, and turned toward themselves.
Deceived by delusion, fallen from the foundation of discernment, they have taken root in misery rather than in the state of the virtuous.
The wretched faculties, such as sight and the rest, have fallen like into a blind well;
the meaning is that they have entered a miserable and harsh state known as the sense-objects.
Thus,
thought— dependent upon the Lord of Life— does not remain in one place, nor does it go where it desires, like a beloved wife in the house of one who is unkind.
*Avasthitim* means stability. *Yathepsitam* means one's own desired object. *Jīva eva īśvaraḥ patiḥ* means the individual soul itself is the Lord and Master.
She is dependent upon him and subject to his will,
but not under her own control.
Having worn out all things, she who once gave and likewise sustained them— steadfastness has become distressed like a creeper at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having worn them out and become weary of them, she wears new ones; "she" is the understood subject.
*dhṛti* is, by implication, the intellect endowed with fortitude.
Having become disillusioned,
she cast aside all worldly objects and remained in a state of non-abiding;
having grasped and then released the self, she remained in a state of abiding.
That in which all objects have been cast aside, having passed from the hand.
The meaning is "useless.

"Abiding" (avasthiti) means "delight" (rati).

Discontent; my mind is [held] within by a support that is both moving and unmoving. (Ś4: *tira*; N11: *śithilā*) (MT 1.29.8)

for the poor have cut away its base, and thus the tree itself is severed.
By the root, that is, by the agent;
by the steady and unsteady, [meaning] for a moment unsteady;
by support, that is, by fortitude.
My intellect, which has become an object of action, is observed to be mocked—
that is, imitated. The sense is that my intellect is like the root of a tree that has been cut down, incapable of producing new sprouts.
Through fortitude, this mind— though flickering, expansive, and wandering through the worlds—
does not abandon its composure, just as an immortal does not leave his own celestial chariot.
It is expansive, endowed with the expansion known as conceptualization.
Therefore, what is that excellent state of stability— free from emptiness, effortless, unconditioned, and devoid of delusion— in which no doubt exists?
The word *sthitipada* means a state suitable for stability; *nāśaśaṅkā* means the apprehension of destruction.
All undertakings and great endeavors belong to virtuous people such as Janaka and others.
How is it that those who are solely devoted to worldly affairs have attained the state of excellence?
Those for whom there is an equal undertaking in all undertakings.
"Those who do everything" means as far as [possible]; "sujanas" refers to virtuous people.
In all undertakings, there is this very undertaking:
O bestower of great honor, how can a man here not be smeared by the mire of saṃsāra, even though it clings to his limbs? MU_1,29.13
In short, it is not defiled by the pleasure and pain produced through its own immersion, nor is it grasped by sins or merits.

The meaning is: "Tell that to me as well."
[He] says:
"Luring those who enjoy the experience of sense objects toward fear itself, how can these riches, whose nature is fragile, ever attain a state of stability?"
They lead only to fear and not to happiness.
"Objects" (viṣaya) refers to enjoyments (bhoga);

"Vibhava" refers to those for whom [the world] is the place of origin.
"Such as these":
"suitability" means loveliness by virtue of not giving rise to passion.
How can the lake of the intellect,
trampled by the elephant of delusion and its interior marred by stains,

In this context, "stain" (*kalaṅka*) should be understood as the pursuit of worldly enjoyments;
"intellect" (*śemuṣī*) means the mind (*buddhi*);
that [intellect] itself is the lake (*sarasī*).
Even while dwelling in saṃsāra and engaging in worldly affairs,
how is it that a person does not incur bondage, just as water on a lotus leaf?
This is clear.
How can one who creates this entire world—treating it as himself and yet as mere straw—attain supremacy without touching the mind’s own passion?
(MU 1.29.18) [uttamatām] N11: utuma°
"Producing" means generating;
by implication, it means knowing.
For the mind produces everything solely through the gateway of cognition.
The sense is that liberation occurs in either case.
Having followed the conduct of which Great Being who has reached the further shore of the ocean of existence, does this person proceed toward no evil deed? (MU 1.29.19)
This is clear from the following conduct and tradition. (MT_1,29.19)
What is that which is appropriate and beneficial? What would be that appropriate fruit?
And how indeed should one conduct oneself in this discordant and uneven cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)?
(In this context, "asamañjasa" means uneven.)
Therefore, O Lord of this world, tell me something by which I may understand the beginning and end of the Creator’s activity, which is not established as a whole. By that which is told...
"Pervading from beginning to end" means possessing both limits; "entire," that is to say, "complete. "Unstable state" means an uneven state.
Of what kind of world? Of the world whose activity is that of the elements—that is, whose form consists of the activity of Brahmā.
[Of what kind?
O Brahmin, act so that the cleansing of the impurity of my mind—the moon within the sky of the heart—may come to pass for me without obstacle. MU 1.29.22
The cleansing of impurity is the cleansing of the impurity known as doubt:
"What in this world should be accepted, what should be rejected, or what else?
How may the flickering mind attain rest, like a mountain? (MU 1.29.23)
Now, what else remains to be disregarded?
By what purifying mantra is this cholera-like plague of miserable transmigratory existence—
causing hundreds of labors— pacified without effort?
This is clear.
(MT_1,29.24) How may I attain that coolness within—the cluster of blossoms on the tree of bliss—which is like the full moon, undiminished even during the night of Rākā? MU_1,29.25
Having reached the fullness within on the night of Rākā, the full moon,
I no longer grieve;
may you, who are virtuous and knowers of reality, instruct me accordingly once more.
This is clear.
He concludes this with the final verse of the chapter:
"O Great-Souled One, the mind indeed finds rest only when it is devoid of anything other than the state of supreme bliss."
In this world, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) greatly torment [the mind], just as dogs in a forest torment a body with little life.
"They torment" means they churn [it]. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth [chapter] in the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Chapter.
Having thus described the state produced by dispassion (*vairāgya*), he introduces the inquiry regarding the means [to attain it]:
*Śrīrāmāya namaḥ*; *oṃ* [Salutation] to that which is as fragile as a drop of water hanging from a leaf moving on a high tree.
Upon a body as delicate as a digit of the moon, the lord of longevity,
fragile like a drop of water hanging from the trembling leaf of a lofty tree,
and as brittle as the throat-skin of a croaking frog in a field;
For a living being caught in the snare of the cycle of existence, amidst the gathering of friends and kinsmen,
the cloud of the dense mist of delusion thunders and flashes intensely— made manifest by the lightning of false hopes stirred by the winds of latent tendencies.
The fierce and fickle peacock of greed dances a wild dance;
the blossoming *kuṭaja* tree of misfortune bursts open with a crash;
and the cruel cat of Death seizes all living beings as its prey.
In this forest of life, where there is no hearing, no movement, and no passage, falling from somewhere above—
what is the remedy, what is the way out, what is the reflection, and what is the refuge? By what means might this wilderness of existence, which yields such inauspicious results, not come to be?
*aśubhodarkā*]: Ś4:
*°rko* [is] the digit of the cool-rayed moon belonging to Īśāna, residing upon the head of the illustrious Mahādeva;
the throat-skin of a croaking frog becomes exceedingly fragile.
Thus, she is apprehended by way of being a point of comparison. "Mihikā-meghe" means in a cloud accompanied by mist (nīhāra).
In what state [is the cloud]?
In one for whom that very evil hope, which is tossed about by the wind of latent impressions (vāsanā), is like a flash of lightning.

May this commentary on the chapter titled "Detachment," which honors the hearts of listeners whose minds are permeated by meditative cultivation, bestow excellent fruit.
Let this effort, which is determined by being an effect, belong to those entities whose capacity for action is established through the power of the penetration of their own potential.

Thus ends the chapter titled "Dispassion" (*vairāgya*) in the commentary on the *Śrī Mokṣopāya*, composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakantha, son of the illustrious Avatārakantha, grandson of the venerable Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha, the great devotee of Maheśvara and spiritual preceptor residing within the region of Śrī Kāśmīra. * [Scribe’s Colophon:]*
May there be auspiciousness for all the worlds.
2. Prakaraṇa: The Conduct of One Desiring Liberation (2,5.5–2,20.13) [Missing manuscript pages] Two human goals, equal and alike, fight like two rams.
Between one's own and another's, the exceedingly powerful among them prevails.
Because they produce results that are either beneficial or harmful, they are called "equal" and "unequal," or "even" and "odd.
One's own [force] is that which is contrary to the scriptures (*ucchāstra*).
"Belonging to another" means stated in the scriptures.
Two human goals fight like two rams; they engage in combat.
Even in that case, what is stated in the scriptures is equal.
The division is that one who is unequal [to the other] is "beyond the scripture" (*ucchāstra*).
In that regard, between those two human goals (*puruṣārtha*),
the more powerful one prevails.
A *huḍa* is a specific kind of horned deer.
Atibala says that very thing; thus he says:
"the meaning of 'bringing'..."

"Where misfortune is encountered even through effort prescribed by the scriptures, there one's own effort should be known as futile. (MU 2.5.6) Where a person encounters misfortune even through effort based on the scriptures, there one's own effort— meaning non-scriptural effort— is futile, that is, it produces misfortune.
The meaning is that it should be understood as "stronger" in the sense that one should know this misfortune arose solely from one's own powerful exertion upon entering into its midst. However,
by implication, where no misfortune is encountered, there the scriptural [authority] alone should be known as stronger.
And in all cases, there is a conjunction of two human efforts, because for one who is alone and without assistance, initiative is impossible.
It shows the supreme human effort that must be exerted by a man to produce what is beneficial,
relying on his own prowess while grinding his teeth against his teeth.
One who is diligent in the auspicious shall overcome the inauspicious through past human effort;
"supreme human effort" refers to the effort prescribed by the scriptures,
and "diligent" means endowed with exertion.
"Former human effort" refers to that which is called latent impression (*vāsanā*) from the past;
even if it is auspicious, it leads only to auspicious results.
Since it has been stated that only an auspicious latent impression bestows liberation, [the text] speaks of the "inauspicious. (MT 2.5.7)
"The thought that 'this past human effort impels me' must be forcibly cast underfoot;
for that [thought] is not superior to direct perception.
With the intention that the capacity to impel belongs to human effort alone—since this is observed through direct perception—it was stated that "it is not superior to direct perception."
To that same extent, one should strive with effort according to one's own human capacity,
until past karma spontaneously subsides.
One’s own human effort should be exerted by applying oneself to one's own domain in accordance with the scriptures.
"One must strive"—this is the usage stated with the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
(MT_2,5.9) "The former fault is undoubtedly pacified by present virtues;
for here, the example is the destruction of yesterday's fault by today's virtues. (MU_2,5.10)
"Decay" (*kṣaya*) means "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*);
this is clear.
Having cast aside false destiny, one should always apply a mind that is ever-exerted.

One should strive to instill within oneself that which leads to the crossing over of *saṃsāra* for the sake of prosperity (*bhūti*). Prosperity here refers to the sovereignty consisting of liberation.
One must not associate with those who lack effort, who are like donkeys among men, and who remain in a state of stagnation.
But exertion, according to the scriptures, is for the sake of accomplishing success in both worlds;
this is clear.
One must emerge from this cave of saṃsāra by one's own strength.
Relying on human effort, one must emerge from the cave of saṃsāra, that abyss of saṃsāra, just as Hari [did] from the cage of his enemies.
By a lion, that is, by Hari;
from the cage of enemies, meaning from the cage consisting of enemies.
Day after day, a man should examine his own conduct.
One should abandon what is equal to the behavior of beasts and take refuge in that which is appropriate for the virtuous.
One should examine it—make it an object of inquiry—as to what kind [of conduct] it is.
[One should consider] whatever is soft and abundant in the home, such as beloved food, drink, and so forth.
Like a worm tasting a wound, one should not reduce youth to ashes;
"kalila" means producing evil,
and "komala" means appearing tender at the outset due to its softness.
In a wound, there is an opening.
(MT 2.5.15) Through auspicious human effort, an auspicious result is swiftly attained;
through inauspicious [effort], an inauspicious one is always attained. That which is called "fate" is nothing at all. (MU 2.5.16)
This is clear.
(MT 2.5.16) He who, disregarding what is directly perceived, relies on inference alone, would flee upon seeing these two [objects] with his own eyes and thinking, "These are two snakes. (MU 2.5.17)
"By my two arms"—this is the ablative case.
"Fate impels me"—such is the mouth of those with deluded intellects;
seeing them whose vision is fixed on the unseen as supreme, Lakṣmī turns away.

The unseen, the most excellent, the supreme vision is called the vision of the Puruṣa; [it belongs] to those by whom it is attained. Therefore, one should fully rely upon discernment through human effort.
One should investigate those scriptures whose great purpose is the knowledge of the Self—
those for whom the knowledge of the Self alone is the supreme goal.
While contemplating the goal in the mind according to the scriptures, one should act toward one's own welfare.

Fie upon the wicked desires of those fools who do not accomplish [their goals] through their own efforts and personal exertions; "wickedly desired" means that which is sought after with a corrupt longing.
Human effort is not infinite, nor does it achieve its goal without exertion;
even with great effort, oil cannot be obtained from a stone.
"Infinite human effort" means effort that is without end.
And it does not come into being; rather,
it necessarily comes into being through human effort as its agent.
It does not desire effort, nor does it long for [effort] as its own producer;
that is to say, it does not transgress its own necessity through effort.
The sense is that even with great effort, a person is unable to transcend the human capacity fixed within himself.
He makes this easy to understand by means of an illustration; it is not [to be accomplished] through effort.
He clarifies the very meaning previously stated regarding "his own":
just as a jar is limited, and just as a cloth is limited.
"Likewise, for you, the purpose of human effort is fixed and limited in its scope.
The implication is that one should not strive for things such as traveling through the sky, which fall outside the domain of human effort.
And that [human effort] yields its own fruit through the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, and right conduct.
"This is the very nature [of the self] that it gives; otherwise, there would be the failure to achieve one's purpose.
(MU 2.5.23) "Otherwise" means in the absence of the study of scriptures, association with the virtuous, and right conduct.
This is the essential form of human effort; a person who acts according to destiny [yet exerts this effort]...
No one ever finds their human effort to be fruitless while acting with human exertion— that is, while acting under the designation "fate" (daiva),
though not actually believing in fate from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Even other supreme men, though afflicted by the suffering of wretchedness and poverty,
have attained equality with the lord of the gods through human effort alone.
This is clear.
Indeed, by means of those qualities— such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous— which have been practiced thus from childhood, one’s own goal is attained through human effort;
for "one's own goal" (svārtha) refers to the desired object known as liberation (mokṣa).
The word "by a person" (*puruṣeṇa*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The particle *hi* indicates certainty.
In the phrase "by those well-known qualities," the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
The word "yatnena" (with effort) indicates the reason. He provides the summary:
"that which is seen, experienced, performed, or heard through direct perception."
Those of evil intellect who think that what has been done, heard, and performed— all arises from fate— are mistaken. Everything arises from fate.
Those who think thus are of perverted intellect; they are slain and ruined.
If laziness did not exist in this world, who would not be wealthy or highly learned?
It is because of laziness that this earth, bounded by the oceans, is filled with human cattle who are destitute. (MU 2.5.28)

By human-beasts who are ignorant, by those without wealth, and by the destitute; therefore, the sense is that those desiring wealth or desiring liberation must exert human effort (*pauruṣa*) alone. (MT 2.5.28)
He describes the manner of human exertion:

"When childhood has passed—no longer restless with incessant imagined play—from the age of adolescence and its adornments onwards, a man, through association with the virtuous, should with effort bring his intellect to awakening regarding words and their meanings, and perform investigations into his own virtues and faults. (MU 2.5.29)
In childhood, which was fickle due to that play incessantly imagined through the examination of one's own virtues and faults.
When childhood has passed,
the man [attains] that age which serves as the ornament of the specific stage of development known as *paugaṇḍa*;
from that point onward means from youth onwards.
With effort—that is, with diligence—one should perform investigations into one's own virtues and faults. By means of what? By means of these [following] things.
"By association with the good" means by association with saintly persons (*sādhu-saṅgama*).
For in the absence of association with the good, the discernment of one's own virtues and faults is indeed impossible to perform. What kind of person [is he]?
One whose intellect is awakened regarding words and their referents: that is, one whose intellect is fully awakened with respect to both words and their meanings;
such a person.
The meaning is "one who knows the words and their referents."
Śrī Vālmīki describes the close of day at that place to Bharadvāja with a verse at the end of the canto:
"When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites."
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, it returned together with the rays of the sun.
Thus [it was] regarding the sage Vasiṣṭha.
So it is.
When she had spoken thus,
the day reached its end;
for the sun, the lord, [had set].
The assembly of the son of Daśaratha departed;
having performed salutations— that is, having offered obeisance to the sages— it withdrew.
She went to bathe for the sake of the evening rite, that is, for the purpose of the evening twilight prayer;
that assembly [remained] until the end of the night, at the waning of the darkness.

And he arrived together with the rays of the sun, the rays of Ravi. Thus all is auspicious. (MT_2,5.30) Thus ends the fifth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskara Kaṇṭha.

At dawn, the venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks to Śrī Rāma regarding the fruition of the matters described in the previous section: "Therefore, at dawn, human effort is primary; destiny is nothing other than that, so cast it far away."
One should forcibly rescue the living being by means of the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures;
there is no other [means] than that which was stated as the cause in the previous creation.
Past human effort— that is, human effort from a previous time—
becomes destiny (*daiva*).
Destiny is something distinct from, and separate from, [present] human effort.
It does not happen [that way].
Therefore, a person,
having cast that destiny far aside, should instead rely upon present, auspicious human effort.
By means of the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures acting as causes,
one should forcibly and by sheer effort cause the living being to cross over.
The word "from saṃsāra" is to be supplied as the remainder.
"In whatever measure there may be effort, in that same measure shall there be a swift result; thus human exertion alone exists—let that indeed be your destiny. (MU 2.6.2)
Exertion is human effort (*pauruṣa*); that which you have accepted as fate (*daiva*) shall belong to you alone. (MT 2.6.2)

Just as at a time of suffering one says, "Alas, what misery! (*hā kaṣṭam*), so too the expression "Alas, fate! (*hā daivam*) is a synonym for the word "misery. The meaning is that, like the exclamation "Alas, what misery!", the cry "Alas, fate! is uttered only by those who are wretched.
There exists no such thing as "fate" (daiva) that has a form other than one's own prior karma;
it can be overcome, as it were, by a fool through his own powerful effort, just as one might defeat a stronger man.
"Prior to one's own karma" means prior to one's previous karma.
There exists no such thing as "destiny" (daiva) apart from another form;
the meaning is that it possesses no separate existence apart from one's own prior karma.
Therefore, by a person, that destiny—
"By whom can he be conquered? means "just as a child can be conquered by a powerful man, so too [can he]. (MT_2,6.4)
Just as yesterday's evil conduct quickly attains purity through beautiful conduct today, so too does one's former misdeed [attain purification].
"By conduct today" means by the conduct performed this very day.
In that same way,
past misdeeds attain purity through present virtuous deeds.
Those who strive for victory over those [misdeeds] are not greedy for even a fraction of gain.

Those fools, common and wretched, remain dependent on destiny for the sake of conquering that [destiny]— that is, for the sake of conquering former inauspicious human effort in the form of evil tendencies—
for the sake of a mere fragment of gain, which consists of the acquisition of worldly objects.
The gluttonous are possessed by greed;
the common folk are base.
An action performed through human effort may be destroyed by fate.
In that case, it should be understood that the power of the destroyer is more potent than [the power] of the object to be destroyed.
"Of the destroyer" means of the agent of destruction, such as time and so forth.
For instance, even among two fruits on a single stalk, one may be hollow and empty inside.
In that regard, there is the vibration of effort, as well as the consciousness of its flavor. "Ekavṛntaphalau" means two fruits situated on a single stalk.
Of those two as well, that one which has a single fruit with a hollow interior and a coreless center—
meaning, the second one should be understood as having a center filled with essence—
is at that place.
The cognition of their flavor refers to that cognition which consists of the flavor of those two results;
"of that flavor" means of that [result]. "In that manner" means by that method.
Effort is the manifestation of human exertion; it is by such exertion that one acts with such passion that a single fruit results, though it may be devoid of essence.
The sense is that there is no power whatsoever here for destiny, which is merely suspected by others.
That all worldly phenomena, even when fully perfected, go to destruction— this should be understood as the great power inherent in the effort that causes their decay. (MU 2.6.9)
Of time, which causes decay and brings about destruction;
of that effort, which is human exertion.
(MT 2.6.9) Whatever is done by force against a beggar or a king by Maṅgalebha, [that is the fruit of such effort].
That was the great fruit of the efforts of the ministers, the elephants, and the citizens.
By means of Maṅgala, the auspicious elephant,
the mendicant became a king, a monarch.
Whatever is accomplished through exertion by ministers, elephants, and citizens— those who bestow the kingdom, namely the counselors, auspicious elephants, and the city-dwellers—
that is the fruit of human effort in the form of bestowing the kingdom; it is not the work of fate.
Just as a minister, by means of a lucky elephant,
crushes food with its tusks after overpowering it with its strength, so too is a small amount of strength crushed by a hero after he has overpowered it.
Just as food is crushed by the teeth after being seized and brought under one's control through human effort,
so too is it by a hero— a person endowed with present human exertion.

That which is small, being ancient and nearly worn out, is crushed after being overtaken by human effort. For the frailty of even great beings, despite their diligent exertion, has indeed been experienced.
For this reason— because they are employed by those [agents] in their activities like clods of earth, according to their will—
we [perceive] the lightness and dexterity of those great ones who are endowed with effort and human prowess.
"Experienced" means directly perceived or seen.
How is it experienced? To this, he says:
"According to their wish" means: because by those [beings] who possess effort,
those persons— by implication— devoid of personal agency [are brought about].
According to their desire, following their own will,
they are employed in tasks like lumps of clay.
Whatever human effort there may be of a capable person, whether visible or even invisible, [it is ineffective].
That [notion] was understood as "fate" by one who is powerless and lacks wisdom regarding the self;
however, for one who is capable and endowed with great human effort,
there is the visible— such as the person (puruṣa)— and the invisible— such as time (kāla).
Whatever may be human effort, whether visible or invisible,
performed by one who is unintelligent— meaning devoid of right knowledge—
and by one who is powerless— meaning lacking capacity in comparison to that [effort].
That is the human effort of one who is capable;
within oneself, regarding one's own object,
destiny is understood— that is, known.
Otherwise, one should not say, "This was done by fate for me."
"Known": "it is known," thus [it is said].
It is established that for living beings, the powerful exertion of the elements is destiny (*daiva*).
This mutual [striving] of those who are stationary yet possess presiding [deities] is evident;
it is the powerful effort of the elements over the minor elements.
It stands as "fate" (daiva).
For when a person is not capable [of acting], he says, "This was done by fate for me.
He says this to show that it is not only known by him alone, but by others as well.
Regarding the word "tasthuṣām" (of those standing):
the word "api" is used in the sense of conjunction;
"mithaḥ" means mutually or one another.
Even for those persons who remain as presiding deities, endowed with impellers and established [in their positions],
this meaning spoken by me becomes clear and manifest.
For they are the objects of governance, distinguished from one another by degrees such as being more or least insignificant;
whereas those who govern are distinguished by degrees such as being more or most excellent.
Furthermore, it is the presiding agent (adhiṣṭhātṛ) alone who is the destiny (daiva) with respect to that which is to be presided over (adhiṣṭheya).
Therefore, the meaning stated by me regarding these [terms] becomes perfectly clear; this is the intended sense.
In the section on "Collection":
[°u⟨ś⟩[c]ca° (MT_2,6.14)] Now, one might object that this principle does not apply to the case of a kingdom of mendicants. To this, the treatise replies:
"The natural wisdom regarding ministers, elephants, and citizens is beyond doubt."
She is the creator and sustainer of the kingdom of mendicants and the stability of the subjects;
she is the teacher of the scriptures, ministers, elephants, and citizens, and she is the priest.
He and the minister,
the elephant Maṅgala, and the citizens.
For them,
that cognition of intrinsic nature— which arises from intrinsic nature in the form of the intention to grant the kingdom to the monk—
is non-conceptual; that is to say, it is incapable of being destroyed.
Who is she?
She is the one who acts as the sovereign of the realm of monks,
and by means of that, she is also the sustainer of the stability of the subjects.
Therefore, the sense is that this same principle applies here as well; for this is the method: in whatever region there is a king...
He dies, and he has no son; thereupon,
the elephant Maṅgala bows down to that very king.
They perform [them].
The Teacher says:
The present [state] destroys the past, and the past forcibly destroys the present.
In this regard, the person who always remains unperturbed amidst the fluctuations of existence is the victor.
Human exertion is *pauruṣa*. Between those two types of human exertion,
he is "undisturbed," meaning free from agitation.
By way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the meaning is "possessing extreme power.

Now, one might ask: "In that case, which among the two is generally stronger? To this, he says: "Between the two, the strength of the present one alone would be evident through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
Therefore, destiny can be overcome through efforts, just as a child can be overcome by a youth.
This is seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):
indeed, one who practices auspicious conduct today is seen destroying the inauspiciousness of yesterday.
He states the conclusion:
"Fate" [is thus];
therefore, by means of present human efforts.
Destiny, which is past karma, and human effort can be overcome; by what means?
By what, as it were?
"Like a youth": the meaning is that just as a child can be conquered by a youth, so it is.
Or, "the harvest acquired over a year is carried away by a cloud. (MT_2,6.17)
"This man, Megha, triumphs as one who exerts superior effort.
The sense here is that even in this case, destiny possesses no power whatsoever.
Even when wealth acquired through gradual effort is lost, one should not feel dejected.
"Where my strength is not capable, what cause for lamentation is there?
[MU 2.6.19] "Strength" refers to human effort (*pauruṣa*).
The sense is that a person does not habitually engage in daily lamentation for the sake of attaining objects such as a kingdom when they are beyond one's power.
Engaged in lamentation:
"If I cause suffering for the sake of that which I cannot achieve, then my daily weeping is appropriate for one who has disregarded death. (MU 2.6.20)
Of one who has disregarded death—that is, one who does not even acknowledge the onset of death.
To that extent,
these [elements] flash forth by virtue of place, time, action, and substance, like the falling of death.
All worldly states indeed prevail for one who possesses superior effort.
"States" (*bhāvāḥ*) refers to entities such as death and so forth. [The author] now states the resulting conclusion.

Therefore, relying on human effort, having brought your wisdom to purity through true scriptures and the company of the virtuous, cross the ocean of saṃsāra. (MU 2.6.22) Purity means being free from the stains of passion and the like. (MT 2.6.22)
These two human goals—namely, that of the past life and that of this life—are like two fruit-bearing trees.
Of these two, the human goal pertaining to this life is superior in the world.
"Fruit-bearing trees" (*phaladrumau*) refers to trees that produce fruit.
The ignorant creature who does not destroy his meager past karma through auspicious efforts is not a master over the pleasure and pain of speech and mind;
this is the result of human action.
"Powerless" means incapable;
he is not even able to destroy speech, mind, pleasure, or pain—the point being that what need is there to mention the destruction of physical suffering? (MT_2,6.24)
But he who possesses noble wonder and dwells in the conduct of the virtuous emerges from the delusion of the world, like a lion from its cage.
"By good conduct" means by the conduct of the righteous.
One who possesses such a dwelling; that is, one who is like that.
The sense is that he alone is a vessel for auspicious human effort.
(MT_2,6.25) He who, abandoning what is perceived, stands in the useless and evil imagination that "someone is impelling me thus," is a base person who should be shunned from afar. MU_2,6.26

The visible is that human effort whose fruit is seen through direct perception. (MT 2.6.26) Among the thousands of worldly transactions that arise and pass away, one should conduct oneself according to the scriptures, having abandoned both pleasure and pain. (MU 2.6.27)
One should dwell according to the scriptures, that is, by not transgressing one's own discipline;
one should practice the religious life (*vihāra*) in such a way as not to abandon one's own unbroken boundaries of conduct.
All [these] attend upon him, like all the jewels of the ocean;
according to the scripture,
each follows its own kind.
"They attend" means they come into one's presence;
"all" means every single excellence.
The wise define [this state] as being solely intent on the effort toward that single task which accomplishes one's own welfare.
That [effort], when constrained by the scriptures, is called "human" (pauruṣa) for the sake of success;
it is singular and absolute regarding the task that attains one's own interest and accomplishes one's own purpose.
Devotion to effort, restrained by the scriptures and awakened by the scriptures, [is required].

The capacity of action—which is characterized by vibration—to accomplish its own purpose is inferred by one's own intellect through the sharpness gained from the company of the virtuous and the meaning of the scriptures. (MU 2.6.29–30)
Of the action whose nature is vibration— that is, of the action which has vibration as its essential character—
its capacity to accomplish its own purpose exists independently, without reliance on anything else.
The capacity to accomplish one's own welfare, which is connected to the association with the virtuous and the meaning of the scriptures through a sharp intellect, is inferred and discerned.
What is this capacity to accomplish one's own welfare?
It is auspiciousness.
The meaning is: what is established as "pure"? (MU 2.6.30) The wise know the infinite bliss of equanimity to be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Those from whom that infinite [bliss] is obtained—those scriptures and virtuous ones—are to be served. (MU 2.6.31)
Equanimity (*samatā*) is the state of seeing all things as equal.
Bliss (*ānanda*) of that nature is "equanimity-bliss" (*samatānanda*).
The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the supreme object to be attained.
That is Samatānanda;
he is to be worshipped by relying upon the human [means].
If that aforementioned human means is expressed by the term "fate" (*daiva*), [then it is as follows].
This is appropriate; we do not deny that this [result] does not exist in that [effort].
If that which was previously established as human effort is designated by the word "fate" (daiva), then it is so.
"It is being told" means "by you," which is the ellipsis;
that is the telling.
This is appropriate,
because this [state] is the means for attaining the bliss of equanimity;
that [other state] does not possess this quality.
Therefore, we do not censure it; we do not offer that criticism.
The intended meaning is that it is an object of equanimity.

[The means for attaining the bliss of equanimity: Regarding the bliss of equanimity (*samatānanda*), those fools who imagine that destiny (*daiva*) is something other [than one's own effort] have gone to their destruction.
Through one's own human exertion alone, there shall always be welfare in both worlds. (MU 2.6.33)
Anything other than past human effort results in decay—that is, destruction caused by a lack of exertion.
Just as yesterday’s misdeed attains splendor through a virtuous deed, so too does [neglect] reach ruin through diligence. (MT 2.6.33)
"Therefore, by means of such effort today, become one who performs good deeds. The word "today" (adyatanayā) is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
Just as by a good deed performed today, a bad deed of yesterday attains beauty.
In this way, [it is] so:
the past misdeed, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from a previous birth,
is [counteracted] today by a virtuous deed (*satkriyā*) consisting of the practice of true scriptures and the like.
It attains beauty and purity;
therefore, you should be one who maintains the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkāryavāda).
The evil deeds of previous births are seen as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand; whatever fruit arises from human effort alone, [it is seen thus].
The fool, having abandoned direct perception, sinks into the delusion of fate.
[utsṛjya] means having abandoned;
the fool is one who, due to destiny, asserts that results [arise from it] and is ignorant.
Having abandoned what is manifest— that is, the human agency established by the means of direct perception—
one sinks into the delusion of fate, which is an error consisting of the nature of fate.
Why is that?
Why is that?
Because we have seen and directly experienced the fruit as being due to human effort alone, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.
[It is] devoid of all causes and effects, yet imagined through the power of one's own conceptual construction.
Therefore, O one of auspicious intent, disregard that destiny which is composed of unreality and rely instead upon your own human effort;
for [destiny] is devoid of all those things which constitute causes and effects.
The meaning is that its nature is absolutely non-existent.
For this very reason, it is "fashioned" or produced by the power of one's own conceptual constructions;
that [world] consists of unreality, independent of fate (daiva).
O one of virtuous intention,
rely upon your own human effort;
the sense is that you should not be subject to fate.

When that fruit which has been conceived through the scriptures and the long-established local customs of virtuous conduct flashes forth in the heart, the mind does not turn toward anything else; thereafter, the limbs follow suit—they say this is "human effort" (pauruṣa). (MU 2.6.37) [Note:
*śāstraiḥ* means by the true scriptures.]
Of the virtuous ones, of the good people;
that which is practiced is conduct;
by means of that, he is engaged.
