Those regional customs (*deśadharma*) which have come down in an uninterrupted stream, and by which [a result] has become exceedingly well-rooted— meaning established from a very long time ago—
and for which a fruit has been conceived and determined as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
While that fruit throbs within the heart, manifesting as something to be accomplished,
there is another mind— that which is directed toward an object other than the aforementioned fruit.
It neither comes nor goes;
immediately following that,
"aṅgāvalī" refers to the series of limbs, such as the hands and other parts of the body.
Furthermore,
it does not come [to an end], but rather it becomes solely intent upon the means for achieving that.
The wise call this "human effort" (pauruṣa);
the meaning is that it is not merely the movement of the hands and so forth in whatever way.

Having understood that this state of manhood— which has been deeply rooted for an exceedingly long time— is the fruit of human effort rather than the result of what was previously taught, one must always exert oneself and remain devoted solely to personal effort.
Then, by serving true scriptures, virtuous people, and learned scholars, this [state] attains supreme fruitfulness.
This "puruṣatva"— the state of being a *puruṣa*— is to be personally experienced by the person himself.
"Pauruṣaphalam" means that which has as its fruit the human effort (pauruṣa) whose nature was described in the preceding verse.
Such [is it].
Having understood this very thing—
namely, the state of being intent on one's own effort and the accomplishment of human exertion— [one should act].
It must always be performed; immediately after that performance,
the person [should maintain] that state of being intent upon personal effort.
By serving true scriptures, virtuous people, and learned scholars, [this treatise] should be led to the highest excellence—
that is, to fruitfulness, which consists in being endowed with the fruit known as liberation.
The word *atha* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
[The state of being accomplished through human effort:

One whose mind is skilled in discerning between fate and human effort, and who has cultivated the conviction that "human effort alone always triumphs," should constantly apply himself to the endeavor of serving noble persons. MU 2.6.39
Men should exert themselves in serving noble persons.
Of what kind [of men]?
Those who possess discernment regarding destiny and human effort—that is, the investigation into their essential natures.
And by those which are beautiful;
furthermore, in what manner?
"By the mind," thus [it is said].
"By those that have been cultivated and ascertained.
Why?
Because the conduct has been practiced.

One's own human effort (*ātmapauruṣa*) always and eternally triumphs; because it produces all fruits, it exists in a state of supreme excellence. This very point is also stated by means of a concluding verse at the end of the section: *ātmapauruṣam evaikam sadaivātra vyavasthitam / sarvathā tad dhi kartavyam kim anena vicintitā //* "Only one's own human effort is established here as always present. Therefore, that alone must be performed in every way; what is the use of this deliberation? (MT_2,6.39)
Having understood that this disease consisting of the continuous succession of births is cured only by innate human effort in this life,
may the *jīva* lead itself to peace through the unfailing supreme medicine of serving the most excellent sages with a mind intent on contentment.
(MU 2.6.40) Here, *jīva* means the person (*puruṣa*).
Having understood that worldly human effort— which exists as something achievable in this life—
is for the sake of accomplishment;
then, by means of serving the supreme wise ones with contentment, practiced by relying upon that [effort].
Therefore, having been questioned by that very wise man;
[an answer] which is unerring and fruitful;
with the excellent medicine known as right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
May he lead to peace the disease consisting of the continuity of birth, which is of the nature of a stream of births. May there be auspiciousness! (MT_2,6.40)
Thus ends the sixth canto in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Because it is of the utmost importance to be adopted, he once again introduces the discussion of human effort:
"Having obtained a body free from disease and with few afflictions, one should thus compose oneself so that one is not born again. (MU 2.7.1)
The "slight affliction" (alpa-ādhi) is a mental distress caused by the means of livelihood and so forth; "pierced" by that means it has been subjected to striking.
One should compose oneself—that is, one should bring about composure within the reality of pure consciousness (cinmātra-tattva).
He who wishes to overcome destiny through human effort shall conquer both in this world and the next, with all his desires fulfilled. (MU 2.7.2)
"Divine" refers to fate in the form of lack of effort;
he is one for whom the desired objects, consisting of enjoyment and liberation, have been fully realized.

When their desires are fulfilled and their wishes realized, those who, having abandoned all effort, remain dependent on fate— those haters of themselves destroy their own dharma, wealth, and pleasure. (MU 2.7.3)
Their state of self-hatred should be understood as resulting from their destruction of the effects consisting of enjoyment and liberation.
Consciousness-vibration, mind-vibration, and sense-organ-vibration [are the causes].
These are the forms of the human goal; from these arises the emergence of the fruit.
"From these" means from these vibrations of consciousness and so forth.
He explains that the arousal of the human state arises precisely from the principle of consciousness (*saṃvit-tattva*).
Just as the mind moves according to the perception arising from the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), so it undergoes internal vibration;
in that very same way the body moves, and in that very same way there is the state of being the enjoyer of the fruit.
In whatever manner, by whichever mode,
there may be a cognition— that is, the manifestation of consciousness—
in that same manner, by that very mode.
The mind undergoes— that is, it moves toward— an internal vibration known as volition; that is to say,
precisely in accordance with the movement of the mind.

The body moves; it exerts itself toward actions consisting of the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. Consequently, it becomes the experiencer of the fruit precisely in accordance with that movement of the body.
The word "of the living being" (jīvasya) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
This internal vibration of the mind is well-established among even children, wherever and in whatever manner it occurs;
but fate is never seen anywhere, therefore human effort triumphs.
This which I have spoken is [true] from the beginningless up to the limit of the childish.
Thus he spoke regarding the result:
"By means of human effort, this Bṛhaspati became the teacher of the Lord of the Gods; and Śukra attained the status of teacher to the Lord of the Daityas through human effort. (MU 2.7.7)
The teacher of the Lord of Gods is "Deveśaguru.
O virtuous one, even those best of men who are afflicted by wretchedness, poverty, and suffering have attained equality with the Lord of the Gods through human effort alone. (MU 2.7.8)
"Equality with the Lord of Gods" means being equal to Indra.
(MT_2,7.8) Those who were great and rich in power, the abodes of various wonders, have become guests of hell solely through the fault of their own human [actions]. MU_2,7.9
"By a fault" means by a cause of fault; that is to say, by that which is contrary to the scriptures.

Through the cause of defects, the various classes of beings have evolved by the power of their own human effort alone, amidst thousands of existences and non-existences and in manifold conditions. (MU 2.7.10)
"Transformed" means having undergone a change of form;
that is to say, they have become possessed of existence, non-existence, and so forth.
(MT_2,7.10) [The state of] being established in three ways is through scripture, through the teacher, and indeed through oneself.
In all cases, it is the human effort (*puruṣārtha*) [that achieves success] and never fate (*daiva*).
"Success through three means" (*trisiddhitā*) refers to the attainment of results through three modes; "the result" is the understood remainder of the sentence.
"From oneself" means solely from one's own intuition, without [relying on] treatises and so forth;
for some are established through treatises, while others are [established] through a teacher.
Some [say] from themselves.
One should, with effort, cause the mind—which has entered into unwholesome things—to enter only into wholesome things; this is the summary of the meaning of all treatises. (MU 2.7.12)
In regard to impure activities consisting of the acquisition of enjoyments, the teachers stand firm and say:
"O son, practice with effort that which is beneficial, that which is not trivial, and that which is free from downfall. (MU 2.7.13)
"O son, O disciple, [we] stand"— the remainder [of the sense] being "as teachers. (MT 2.7.13)
"In whatever measure my effort is directed, in that same measure shall the fruit quickly appear.
Thus, one should be firm in the conviction: "I am the enjoyer of the fruit through human exertion alone, and not through destiny. This is the intended meaning.

Success is seen to arise from human effort; human effort is the method of the wise. Destiny is merely a consolation for those whose intellects are weak with suffering—those whose efforts are rendered feeble by misery and who cannot endure exertion.
In those who possess such intelligence,
the human sequence of means of knowledge, beginning with direct perception, is constantly observed in the world through its results, such as traveling to another country and so forth. (MU 2.7.16)
By us, "human effort" (*pauruṣa*) refers to the sequence connected with a person; that is to say, human effort consists of the form of moving the feet and so forth.
This is [inferred] from the result, such as going to another place.
A permanent means of valid cognition is seen to perform purposeful action;
from what kind of result?
From direct perception, that is, the means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception.

The meaning is: "from that which is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭa*)," of which the primary [characteristic] is its nature as a grasper (*grāhakatva*). Therefore, it is "human" (*pauruṣa*).
Thus it is fruitful; the sense is that it is not [dependent on] fate.
[That which performs purposeful action:
The enjoyer experiences satisfaction, not the non-enjoyer; the goer goes, not the non-goer;
the speaker speaks, not the non-speaker; thus human effort bears fruit for men.
This is clear.
(MT 2.7.17) Those of sound intellect cross over difficult straits by means of human effort without exertion, but not through this state of muteness. (MU 2.7.18)
By being mute, by being subject to fate, and by a lack of effort.
[In the form of being dependent on destiny:
Whatever effort a person exerts in whatever manner, he alone enjoys the corresponding fruit; for no one here obtains a result by remaining idle. (MU 2.7.19)
"Exerts himself" means likewise;
"remaining silent" means staying without exertion.
"By means of auspicious human effort, an auspicious fruit is obtained;
by means of inauspicious [effort], an inauspicious one, O Rāma. Do as you wish.
This is clear.
The attainment of the fruits of human effort here, occurring through the influence of place and time—
whether achieved after a long duration or quickly— is traditionally known as *daiva* (fate).
The expression "attainment is attained" (*prāptiḥ prāptā*) is a grammatical usage similar to "the effect is produced" (*kāryaṃ kṛtam*).
This is the attainment of the fruit that is the goal of human endeavor.
Destiny is not seen by the eye, nor does it exist in another world;
what is called "destiny" is said to be the fruit of one's own action in this world.
This is clear.
(MT 2.7.22) A person is born in the world, grows, and then decays again;
yet the divine principle is not seen therein as possessing childhood, youth, or old age. (MU 2.7.23)
In that person:
the reaching from one place to another, the holding of objects in the hand,
and likewise the activity of the limbs, proceed through human effort and not through fate.
This is clear.

(MT 2.7.24) The wise have declared that being solely intent on the effort toward the action that achieves one's goal is what is meant by the word "human exertion" (*pauruṣa*); by means of this, everything is attained. (MU 2.7.25)
Regarding that task which brings about the attainment of the goal,
there is one thing alone:
the state of being devoted to diligent effort.

But that which consists solely in being intent on actions for the sake of attaining what is harmful is called "the behavior of a madman," for nothing at all is attained by it. Regarding the phrase "in the attainment of the harmful": it refers to whatever action is performed for the purpose of attaining what is harmful.
In that regard, one [factor] is devotion to effort.

(MT_2,7.26) The capacity of action, which is characterized by vibration, to accomplish its own purpose is itself raised up by an intellect sharpened by the company of the virtuous and the study of true scriptures. (MU_2,7.27)
It is raised up; it is ascertained.
(MU 2.7.27) The wise know their own ultimate reality to be infinite and the bliss of equanimity.
Those virtuous teachers of the scriptures from whom that [reality] is attained through effort are to be served. (MU 2.7.28)
One's own ultimate truth is one's innate, supreme purpose.
(MT_2,7.28) Through the intellect, the qualities of true scripture and so forth [are acquired], and through those qualities of true scripture and so forth, the intellect [is refined];
these two increase mutually through practice, like a lake and the ocean over time. MU_2,7.29
The quality consisting of such things as authentic scriptures arises through intelligence (*mati*),
because one devoid of intelligence does not engage with authentic scriptures and the like.
Intelligence, in turn, arises from the quality of authentic scriptures and so forth.
Those two, possessing intellects characterized by the qualities of true scripture and so forth,
increase— that is, they undergo growth— through mutual practice.
Like two lakes;
like a lake and a cloud, as it were, a lake and a rain-cloud.
The meaning is that they increase mutually over time;
for sometimes a lake increases due to water rained down by clouds, while at other times it is the cloud [that increases].
"By means of the water taken from the lake."
Through wisdom [and] by means of wisdom— through qualities well-practiced from childhood, such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous—
the beneficial goal of one's own purpose is attained through human effort. (MU 2.7.30)
Through human effort— that is, through manly exertion— when practiced and cultivated,
one's own goal, namely liberation, which is one's innate purpose, is attained. By manly exertion, the Daityas were conquered and the activities of the world were established.
"The worlds here were fashioned by Viṣṇu, and not by fate.
This is clear.
With this concluding verse of the chapter, he teaches that human effort (*pauruṣa*) is what must be undertaken by Śrī Rāma.

O Raghunātha, in this world where human effort is the cause, exert yourself long and diligently so that you do not, O fortunate one, fall without doubt into the state known as that of trees and reptiles. In what kind of world? In this world where human effort is the cause.
That which has human effort (*puruṣakāra*) as its cause—
such [is the world]. For indeed, the world was produced from the human effort of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone.

"Effort" refers to human exertion (*pauruṣa*). "The state designated as trees and reptiles" means the condition of being a tree and so forth; for trees and the like experience suffering precisely due to their lack of human exertion.
Their [the senses'] grasping has been described. Thus all is auspicious.
(MT_2,7.32) Thus ends the seventh canto in the "Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation" chapter of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Oṃ. Furthermore, he refutes the doctrine of fate (daiva): Oṃ. Neither form, nor actions, nor a locus, nor prowess—what is this so-called "fate" that is asserted to be as substantial as false knowledge? MU 2.8.1.
The remainder [of the compound] is "of which the first half.

(MU 2.8.1) Those words which, regarding the attainment of the fruits of one's own actions, declare here "it is thus" or "it is so," have come to be established under the name *daiva* (fate). (MU 2.8.2)
The words "this is thus," or the speech "this has become thus."
The speech that "this is thus" is likewise a conviction held by those of deluded intellect that "fate exists"—
a conviction grasped through difficult comprehension, like a snake [imagined] upon a rope. (MU 2.8.3)
*Ātto* means *ārttaḥ* (afflicted);
*rajjāv* means *rajjuvā* (by a rope); *ātto* means *gṛhītaḥ* (seized).
By "difficult-to-comprehend ignorance";
the word *iva* has the sense of "as" (*yathā*).

Just as yesterday’s misconduct attains beauty through good conduct today, so too does today’s [misconduct] attain beauty through good conduct tomorrow; therefore, strive with effort to perform what is virtuous.
The meaning of this has already been explained.
(MT_2,8.4) That fool who believes that fate is established by the inference of the deluded should say to the fire: "Let there be burning from fate, or let there not be. MU_2,8.5
For that evil-minded and ignorant person for whom fate exists as something established by fallacious inference,
it exists as an ultimate reality;
by that evil-minded one.
Standing in the purifying fire,
one might say, "Let there be burning by fate, or let there not be"; however, in that case,
he is unable to say this, because his attainment is solely through burning— this is the sense.
If, in this world, destiny alone is the ultimate reality for a person, then what is the use of human effort?
Destiny itself will perform the bathing, giving, eating, and marriage.
The meaning is that bathing, giving, eating, and [taking] a wife are actions, which implies they are effectors of action.
And this is not possible for one who does nothing at all, because bathing and so forth would be untenable; such is the sense.
Or what is the use of the instruction of the scriptures? This person is supposedly mute;
he is merely moved by destiny—what can be taught to whom here? "Is moved" (saṃcāryate) means that which is of the nature of moving about is brought about.
"What?"—
the remainder of the question is "by whom? The sense is that if fate were the sole cause, no one would ever offer instruction to anyone else.
Moreover, no lack of movement is observed in this world except in the case of a corpse;
and movement is the attainment of results. Therefore, fate is useless.
This is clear.
"Now, is it not the case that a person performs action together with destiny? To this he replies:
"There can be no joint agency between the formless destiny and that which possesses form;
for even when the hands and other limbs exert themselves, nothing is ever accomplished by destiny alone."
By the formless, i.e., the bodiless divine [principle],
[the hands and so forth] of the embodied person are impelled— that is, they are set in motion.
Furthermore, there is no co-agency; therefore, an action performed by destiny— that is, having destiny as its agent—
does not occur in some cases.
Regarding the phrase "by that which is formless" (*mūrtirahitena*):

one might object, "Surely, even though the divine (*daiva*) is formless like the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*), it certainly possesses agency together with that which has form. To this, he replies:
"This divine [agency], like the mind and the intellect, is not experienced here [in this world]."
"Indeed, even down to the cowherds, the wise always regard destiny as non-existent (asat).
Since agency is not observed in a dead body, the mind and intellect are postulated;
and destiny has no utility here at all."
The meaning is that there is no occasion for such a conceptualization.

[Objection: But surely, since an effect is sometimes seen to arise from that very visible body and so forth, and sometimes it is not seen, the postulation of an unseen destiny (*daiva*) is indeed appropriate. To this, he says:
If the intellect were distinct from the object of perception, then that [object] would be something other; if it were the same, how could there be any difference between the two?
If conceptual construction is the means of valid cognition, why is human agency not also postulated as such?
Intellect (*buddhi*) is knowledge (*jñāna*). If it exists as something distinct, then the object would be other than that [intellect], meaning it would be a second thing separate from the first.
If that very same cognition exists and does not become distinct,
then what difference could there be between those two objects?
Therefore, the intention here is that the effect should arise from the body and so forth alone, due to their being purely similar [to the cause].
Now, one might object: "In this case, there is no utility for the distinctness of the intellect, because conceptual construction itself is the means of valid cognition."
Here he says:
"Conceptual construction.
If conceptual construction is not the first means of valid cognition, [then what is]?
If that exists,
why is it not conceived as being produced by human effort? It is possible through such conception, because the underlying principle is the same.

[From the word *kevala*: Furthermore, he again explains the impossibility of the co-agency of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), [stating]: "And there is no contact of that which possesses a body with that which is formless, just as there is none with space."
And since it is seen as a tangible form that has become attached [to the body], therefore fate does not exist.
"Of the embodied one" (vapuṣmataḥ) means of the one who possesses a body, of the one who has a material form.
There is no association— that is, no joint agency— with the divine, which is formless and devoid of material form. With what, then, [could there be such association]?
"Like space.
[Objection: "In that case, let the agent be indeed formless. To this, he says:
"And as for 'the embodied'":
we observe that it is precisely the embodied [body] that is conjoined with the moment of action (kāryalagna);
therefore, the sense is that agency belongs to that alone is appropriate.
It states that it bears fruit;
"therefore" means for that reason.
Fate does not exist,
because the conceptualization of it has been refuted.
Moreover, there exists another director of beings within these three worlds who is devoid of form;
let the multitudes of beings lie down, for Fate shall accomplish everything.
"Let them lie" means those who are impelled; the impeller is the agent.
One thing is called "fate," while the other is a distinct entity.
"Let them lie down; let them indulge in lack of effort toward their duties.
"I am thus appointed by destiny; what can I do while remaining in such a state?"—this is merely a word of consolation, for in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as destiny.
"Destiny" is thus [conceived] as such a state, such an occurrence;
it is imagined by the deluded. Those who are devoted to that have gone to their destruction.
But the wise, through human effort, have attained the highest state;
the wise are those devoted to that [effort], whereas others are devoted to fate as they themselves have imagined it.
They are deluded;
by means of human effort (*puruṣārtha*), that is, by human exertion (*pauruṣa*), [they fail to reach] the supreme state, the excellent station known as liberation (*mokṣa*). (MT 2.8.15)
"Those who are brave, those who are courageous, those who are wise, and those who are learned—tell me, by what means in this world is fate said to be proclaimed? (MU 2.8.16).
It is proclaimed; that is, it is spoken of.
The sense is that it cannot be explained by anyone.
(MT_2,8.16) If one whose long life has been determined by those who know time should live even with his head severed, then that is the supreme destiny. MU_2,8.17
By those who know the time, the astrologers.
O Rāghava, he whose scholarship has been determined by those who know the time is truly a knower of that [science] even without being taught; such is the supreme destiny.
One who knows that is a wise man.
O Rāma, by the sage Viśvāmitra, having cast fate far aside,
Brahminhood was attained through human effort alone, and not otherwise.
Brahminhood is clearly [attained] by these, O Rāma, and not by other men who have attained the state of sages. (MT 2.8.19)
She was attained solely through human effort and has long been traversed through the sky by these very ones endowed with human exertion,
and not by others who lack such effort— those ordinary beings.

They attained the sky, possessing the conduct of the supreme ether. Having eradicated the hosts of gods within the belly of the three worlds, the lords of the Dānavas established their empire through human effort alone. (MU 2.8.21)
Having destroyed— that is, having oppressed—
the hosts of gods, the multitudes of deities;
[these were] the lords of the Dānavas, such as Hiraṇyākṣa and others.
By their sheer power and through human-like effort alone, the lords of the gods forcibly seized from the Dānavas the world that was vast, mangled, and shattered. (MU 2.8.22)
Torn, shattered, and exceedingly fickle—O Rāma, water is held in a vessel for a long time through human effort and skill alone; it is not destiny that is the cause therein. (MU 2.8.23)
In a basket provided with holes and constructed from a specific type of wood,
water indeed remains by means of a certain application;
for [this occurs] amidst the stages of seizing, taking, agitation, confusion, and wandering.
O Rāma, the efficacy of destiny is not seen, just as that of a medicine [is not seen when one does not take it].
The mention of "taking away" (*haraṇa*) and so forth is an elliptical expression for all actions.
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"O you of auspicious intent, disregarding destiny— which is devoid of all causes and effects, imagined through the power of one's own conceptualization, and composed of unreality— resort to supreme human effort."
The meaning of this has been explained. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the eighth canto in the "Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa" of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Here Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, the time for the consecration has arrived.
O Brahmin, tell me that which is called 'divinity' (daiva) in this world. MU 2.9.1
O Blessed One,
O Brahmin Vasiṣṭha,
of what nature is he?
O Knower of all dharmas,
speak of that which is the divine power established and renowned in the world in this way.
It has arrived.
What, then, is it described as by the wise?
The sense is that an unestablished entity does not attain established status.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replies:
O Rāghava, human effort alone is the agent of all actions and not anything else;
it is the enjoyer of the fruit everywhere, and destiny is not the cause therein.
O Raghava, human effort is the agent of all undertakings; the other, such as destiny and so forth,
is not the agent.
It is not only the agent,
but also the enjoyer of the fruit; the sense is that this occurs through the medium of the person presided over by [the deity] itself.
In that case, destiny is not the cause;
therefore, the implication is that destiny does not exist.
Destiny performs nothing, enjoys nothing, and does not even exist.
It is neither seen nor respected; it is merely such a conceptual construction— namely,
of the form "Destiny alone does everything."
And the point is that conceptual construction lacks reality.
(MT_2,9.3) For those who possess fruits, the attainment of good or bad fortune here in this world, resulting from human effort, is designated by the term "fate" (*daiva*). MU_2,9.4
For the wise,

the auspicious or inauspicious attainment of a fruit that has been accomplished through human effort— that is, through meritorious or non-meritorious human action— is designated by the term "fate" (*daiva*).
The phrase "for the sake of the discourse of the ignorant" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
(MT_2,9.4) The constant attainment of desired or undesired objects, which results from the cessation of human effort, is designated by the word *daiva* (fate). (MU_2,9.5)
The wise hold that the cessation of human effort has reached its conclusion;
the attainment of desired or undesired objects is what is expressed by the word "fate" (daiva).
The particle "api" is for the purpose of completing the meter.

The attainment of a desired or undesired object— whether it be desirable or undesirable— is expressed by the word *daiva*. That future matter which is necessarily accomplished solely through human effort is what is expressed by the word *daiva* in this world-system.
"Bhāvī" means having the nature of coming into being.
"Puruṣārtha" refers to human effort; he is one for whom this alone is the single means of accomplishment.
Such is he.
In this world-system,
in this collection of worlds, O Rāghava, there is indeed nothing whatsoever belonging to anyone;
for destiny, which is like the sky, neither acts nor does not act.
The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because.
"Resembling space" means as utterly void as space;
the point is that the son of a barren woman neither accomplishes nor fails to accomplish anything for anyone.
The second word "hi" indeed expresses certainty.
When some established human purpose has been accomplished and the arising of its auspicious or inauspicious fruit occurs,
the expression "this stands thus" is called destiny (*daiva*).
He states the nature of the statement:
"this is established as being thus. "Siddham" means accomplished or perfected.
"This stands thus; it is established;
it is proven.
Such was my thought, for such was my certainty.
Thus, that method which exists for the attainment of the fruit of action is called destiny (*daiva*).
In this way, it consists of the means for accomplishing the fruit of action;
"attainment" (*avāptau*) refers to the reaching or acquisition of the fruit of action.
The sense is that destiny (*daiva*) is merely a matter of words.
(MU 2.9.9) In the attainment of desired or undesired results, the term "destiny" is used as a conventional expression for this;
it is called destiny simply as a word of consolation. (MU 2.9.10)
Of what nature is the speech that is merely consolatory? It is "thus" (evam), which means that which is the meaning.
The meaning is that its expression is the expression of a rule.
Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, regarding the karma previously accumulated,"
"How was this, which is called 'fate,' wiped away by you?
[This refers to] its state as a seed existing within the father previously;
"wiped away" means destroyed.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke this reply:
"Well said, O Rāghava! You understand; listen, and I shall tell you everything by which your conviction that there is no destiny will become firm."
This is clear.
He explains that very point:
"That latent impression (*vāsanā*) which previously existed indeed in great abundance, having been submerged..."
This very same [nature] has undergone transformation into the state of karma for human beings;
previously, it existed in the state of being a seed within the father,
in manifold ways (*bhūriśas*) and in many forms (*bhūriprakāreṇa*).
Whatever present latent impression (vāsanā), whether virtuous or non-virtuous, exists as a cultivation (bhāvanā),
it remains submerged in the seed; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
This very same [nature] has undergone transformation— that is, a change of form— into the state of karma, which is to say, into the form of action, for human beings.

The meaning is that all beings perform actions precisely in accordance with that [latent impression]. (MT_2,9.13) A living being becomes possessed of whatever latent impression it has; that it should have one action and a different state of being is simply not tenable. (MU_2,9.14)
The existence of one thing is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of another.
(MT 2.9.14) One who goes to a village reaches the village; one who seeks a city reaches the city.
Whosoever has the latent impression of whatever, that very person strives for that accordingly. (MU 2.9.15)
Furthermore, for one who intends to go to a village, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of going to that village is indeed manifest; otherwise, he would not go.
Whatever action was performed here in the past with intense urgency, that very thing is indeed designated by the synonymous term "fate" (*daiva*).
Here, in this saṃsāra which has two forms— namely, as this world and the next—
in the prior state of the seed existing within the father,
the performance of karma should be understood as occurring precisely through the medium of the father.
He provides this summary: "Thus, destiny is one's own actions; action is matured latent impression (*vāsanā*);
latent impression is nothing other than the mind; for the mind is traditionally held to be the person (*puruṣa*)."
In this manner,
one's own previously performed actions— namely, one's personal karma—
become destiny (daiva).
Mature latent impressions (vāsanā) become action (karman),
because it is precisely according to them that [the individual] is constituted;
latent impression is not something other than the mind.
The word "hi" indicates certainty:
the mind becomes the person (puruṣa).
Therefore, the sense is that there is no existence of destiny apart from the person.
Because it is the subject at hand (*prakṛtatvāt*), he speaks of this very same point once more: "That which is fate (*daiva*) are those actions; O virtuous one, action is indeed the mind."
"For the mind is the person; therefore, it is certain that there is no destiny.
In this [verse], the word "action" (*karman*) is to be supplied from the relative pronoun *yat*:
"that which is action."
That becomes the mind.
For whatever a single mind of a living being strives toward,
it surely attains that by its own nature, and not through destiny.
This is clear.
(MT 2.9.19) "Mind," "consciousness," "latent impression," "karma," "fate," and "one's own resolve"—O Rāma, these are the designations for the human resolve as proclaimed by the wise. (MU 2.9.20)
“Perceptions” (*saṃjñāḥ*) refers to the determination of a male, that is, the determination of a male form; in other words, it means "of a person" (*puruṣasya*). (MT_2,9.20)
O Rāma, just as a person of such a name exerts himself constantly through firm contemplation, he attains a corresponding result in full measure.
[This refers to one] designated by names such as "the mind" and so forth.
He offers this conclusion:
"O scion of Raghu, in this world everything is obtained through human effort alone and by no other means; therefore, may that [effort] grant you prosperity."
That is human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
It is "bestowing auspiciousness," meaning it grants the auspicious fruit known as liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*).
The word "those" (*te*) is an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The meaning is that, by him, may [this] become the bestower of auspicious fruit for all.
Śrī Rāma, who bestows the auspicious fruit known as liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*), asks: "How does the web of past latent impressions (*vāsanājāla*) impel me?"

"O Sage, I remain exactly as I am; what can I, a miserable being, do?"—the implication is that there is not even the slightest human effort (*pauruṣa*) possible. Thus Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks the following reply.

Therefore indeed, O Rāma, you shall attain eternal welfare through human effort alone, brought about by your own exertion, and not otherwise. [The word] *hi* indicates certainty; *ata eva* means "for this very reason," that is, for the reason stated previously.
By what kind of human effort? By that which is brought about through one's own exertion.
This is a grammatical construction similar to the expression "the head of Rāhu. (MT 2.9.24)

"O Rāma, the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—which is a collection of impressions—is twofold: auspicious and inauspicious. Of these two, either one or the other from the past exists [in you].
(MU 2.9.25) "Accumulation of latent impressions" means a multitude of latent impressions.
Alternatively, in another sense:
between two things,
one or the other is either auspicious or inauspicious.
If you are led there today by a stream of pure latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then through that very auspicious process you shall gradually attain the eternal state.
You are led according to your own [mental] inclination; thus, action is performed.
The "foot" (pada) is the state known as liberation.
[According to one's own inclination] (svānusāreṇa). Now, if an impure state should entangle you in distress, that former [state] must be conquered by you with effort and force. (MU 2.9.27)
An impure state or impure latent impression [arises] by force, that is, by compulsion.
[Objection: Is it not the case that some other entity, consisting of consciousness, impels me?
"How then can I myself do anything? To this he replies:
"O wise one, you are pure consciousness alone; you are not the body, which is insentient by nature."
If that very [Self] is perceived by another in the mind, then where indeed are you found?
*prājña*: *prājña* (the wise one) *cetanāmātra*: *cetanāmātra* (mere consciousness)
O wise one! You possess the fitness for this instruction that is about to be spoken in this verse: you are pure consciousness alone;
you are not the insentient body.
If that very thing, being nothing but mere consciousness,
were to act by means of another who serves as the cause and agent;
if [this were so],...
At that time, you do not exist; you are not present as the agent with respect to the act of thinking in the mind.
Because that alone exists; for it is not logical for two things to exist simultaneously, as it would be purposeless.
[The commentary on *tvam anyena*:
He explains once again the very meaning determined by the second half of the preceding verse:
"But if another causes you to perceive [objects], then who else could there be when you do not exist?"
Who would cause this [consciousness] to be conscious? Therefore, an infinite regress is not real.
If another were to cause you to be conscious, he would impel your status as the agent of the act of consciousness;
that being so, at that time—
"When you— who, by the reasoning previously stated, do not possess existence— exist,
who is this 'he,' and of what form?
[It is] you, the vibration of this-ness."
It would intend—that is, it would impel—toward the state of being the agent of the act of piling up;
for the impulse of that which is non-existent is not logical, such is the sense. Therefore, some other entity to be impelled must be postulated.
Since He, too, shares the same state of being and destiny as you, there would be no point of rest for Him anywhere as an object of impulsion;
therefore, with the intention that "you alone exist in the relationship of the impelled and the impeller," he provides this conclusion.
It acts; therefore means for that reason, from that cause. Infinite regress (anavasthā) refers to the lack of a final resting point in the series of impellers.
It is not real, nor is it ultimate; for it exists precisely through your own states of being the impelled and the impeller.
Therefore, the sense is that there is no other impeller for you whatsoever.
The agency of the act of consciousness; "it is the sword" [is the reading];
"he" [refers to the one who is thus];
what is its form? It is the form [of the sword].
The river of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), flowing along the two paths of the auspicious and the inauspicious, follows its own natural course, vibrating with the sense of "this-ness" (*idantā*).
One should be directed onto the auspicious path through human effort. "Should be directed" means one should be set in motion.
The sense is that one must constantly perform the contemplation of the auspicious, which consists of the renunciation of enjoyments.
O best among the strong, by means of human effort and power, one should cause one's own mind, when it has entered into impurities, to descend into the virtuous alone.
"Samāviṣṭam" means fully absorbed or settled therein.

One should cause it to descend; one should lead it. The mind of a living being moves from the unwholesome to the wholesome, and from that [wholesome] to the other [unwholesome], like a beast. Therefore, one should protect it by force. (MU 2.9.32)
From the unwholesome, which consists of attachment to the acquisition of enjoyments and the pursuit of the unwholesome;
and from that [which is] wholesome as well— one should protect, meaning one should guard against the unwholesome.
One should protect [it] quickly through the consolation of equanimity—not abruptly, but gradually;
one should protect the child of the mind with manly effort. (MU 2.9.33)
By "human effort" (*pauruṣeṇa*), [it means] by that consolation and encouragement consisting of an understanding of such a nature as: "All this is Brahman, it is equal. By that.
"Not abruptly" means not suddenly.
He explains the meaning of this in his own words:
"gradually, gradually," that is, through correct investigation.
But the meaning is not by means of *haṭha* (forceful methods) such as the suppression of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
"O Rāma, the flood of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—whether auspicious or inauspicious—which was previously made dense by you through practice, now make the auspicious one dense. (MU 2.9.34)
"Today"—the remainder of the sentence is "by my instruction.
(MT_2,9.34) "O crusher of enemies, know that when, through the power of prior practice, your latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arise, then the practice has borne fruit. (MU_2,9.35)
"O sinless one, even now your latent impression (*vāsanā*) attains density through the force of all that practice;
therefore, apply yourself to auspicious practice. (MU 2.9.36)
Now, in this present life, bring it forth; that is, bring it into manifestation.
For if your latent impression (*vāsanā*) had not previously attained density through repeated practice, [it could not arise now].

"But it will increase; therefore, my dear, be happy even now," [he says]. The intention is that one should strive for the supreme state which consists merely in the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Because of its effortful nature,
even when it is doubtful, gather only what is intensely auspicious;
for in this increase of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), no fault whatsoever arises from the auspicious.
Even while this increase of latent impressions remains doubtful— being an object of doubt as to whether it increases through practice or not—
you should intensely cultivate only that which is auspicious, making it the object of your practice;
for from the auspicious, no fault whatsoever arises.
In the *Sandehaviṣauṣadhī*,
he explains the irrationality of doubt [with the verse]:
"Whatever one practices in this world, one becomes composed of that very thing."
Thus, among the wise, this has been seen even from childhood as being free from doubt;
"in the world" means in the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra).
The word "by a person" (*puruṣeṇa*) is to be supplied as the subject.
O Bhava, endowed with auspicious impressions (*śubhavāsanā*), resort here to supreme human effort (*pauruṣa*) for the sake of your welfare, having conquered the five senses. (MU 2.9.40)
For the sake of prosperity, that is, for the attainment of the wealth known as liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
For the sake of attaining the state known as liberation while living:
"As long as your mind is unrefined and you do not know that supreme state, practice that which has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures. (MU 2.9.41)
"One whose mind is unevolved" means devoid of knowledge;

for this very reason, "one who has not known that state" (ajñātatatpada) means one who has not known the supreme station called Brahman. "The determination of that state" (tatpadanirṇaya) refers to what has been ascertained.

It is established that [the suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*). Therefore, having certainly understood the reality through the ripening of the astringent decoction (*kaṣāyapāka*), you, being free from affliction, must abandon even this auspicious flood of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). (MU 2.9.42)
Through the ripening of the astringent [meditation], by means of its characteristic attainment of the highest limit;

the flood of cultivation is a collection of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the form of a definitive resolution; "without affliction" means being free from mental distress known as unwholesome latent impressions. (MT_2,9.42)

With this verse at the end of the chapter, he instructs Śrī Rāma on what is to be practiced: "Following that auspicious path which is most beautiful and frequented by the noble, with a mind and intellect directed toward delightful states of being, attain the state that is forever free from sorrow; and having subsequently abandoned even that, remain perfectly established."
That which is exceedingly fortunate, and for that very reason cultivated by the noble ones,
is auspicious human effort (*pauruṣa*);
it is the intellect whose nature is agreeable and whose latent impression is auspicious.
By means of that [wisdom] acting as an instrument,
having led it to the state of being the object of constant practice,
one attains the sorrowless, which is free from suffering.
"Attain"— that is, reach— the "state," which is the condition of liberation while living; the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used here in its primary sense, as is characteristic of Vedic usage.
Thereafter, at another time,
having completely and perfectly cast off even that state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
"Remain in liberation from the body"—this is the meaning of "become firm. Thus all is auspicious.
"That is auspicious, that is auspicious" (MT 2.9.43).
Thus ends the ninth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Therefore, relying upon that supreme human effort which is an eternal kinsman for the sake of the highest good, make your mind one-pointed and listen to this which is spoken by me. (MU 2.10.1)
The instruction has been stated.
Quickly restraining the senses—which fall into intermediate objects and mount the chariot of desire—by means of human effort, bring them to a state of equanimity. (MU 2.10.2)
"In the intermediate states" means in the middle resting places consisting of enjoyments;
it does not mean in the supreme resting place which is the nature of the Supreme Self.
"Abhipātīni" means having the tendency to fall away.
*Manoratha* means the continuous flow of thought.
*Svārūḍhāni* means well-ascended.
*Indriyāṇi saṃyamya* means having restrained or withdrawn the senses.
Lead me to equanimity, which is the state of being free from attachment and aversion;
otherwise, you will not be heard [by me]. This is the intended meaning.
[She is] the bestower of the fruits of human goals for the sake of accomplishment in this world and the next.
"I shall speak the compendium (saṃhitā) consisting of the means to liberation, which is equal to its essence.
"Consisting of the means to liberation" means that which has as its essence the means to liberation—that is, that which expresses it. "Compendium" refers to the scripture.
Equal to the essence, comparable to the core;
having abandoned the latent impressions of saṃsāra so as not to grasp it again at the end, and having taken up perfect tranquility and contentment with a noble intellect— MU_2,10.4.
Having made the mind— which has been occupied with the investigation of the meaning of preceding and succeeding sentences— equipoised within the Self through continuous contemplation,
one attains that which brings about the destruction of pleasure and pain and is the sole means to great bliss.
"O Rāma, listen to this means of liberation that I am about to describe. Having done what? Having [listened]."
"Without re-appropriation," and so forth.
It is said "without re-appropriation" because a person might otherwise re-appropriate even that latent impression (*vāsanā*) which was abandoned during deep sleep.
"Within" means in the mind.
The sense is that otherwise you would not be able to hear.
"Having taken" means having grasped.
In what state is the mind?
It is of a single flavor, a flavor of equanimity within the self,
and not distracted by sense objects;
likewise, it is complete, possessing both prior and subsequent parts, which is the investigation of the meaning of the sentence.
That very object is the locus of movement;
therein it is honored.
Having heard this discourse on liberation, together with all those possessed of discernment—
"You shall go to that state free from suffering, where no destruction exists. [The word] *pada* means a place of rest.

Having thus taught the heroic prowess of Śrī Rāma as something to be taken refuge in, [the author] now provides the introduction for recounting the instruction spoken by Brahmā, which was remembered at the prompting of Viśvāmitra.
At the instigation of Viśvāmitra, this was spoken in a former age by the Supreme Brahmā:
it brings about the destruction of all suffering and is the supreme consolation for the intellect. (MU 2.10.8)
This which is about to be stated is the supreme consolation— that which provides the most excellent consolation— for the intellect (*dhi*), that is, for the awakened mind (*buddhi*). (MT 2,10.8)
Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Brahman, by whom was this spoken previously by the Self-born One, and how was it obtained by you? Tell me this, O Lord."
This is the knowledge that is about to be explained.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply: "There exists the Self of infinite manifestation, all-pervading and the refuge of all."
The sky of consciousness is the imperishable self, the lamp within all things.
"Sky of consciousness" means the sky whose name is consciousness;
that exists as the ultimate reality.
Of what nature? Infinite, meaning unbounded;
those manifestations (*vilāsāḥ*) which consist of the expansion, appearance, and contraction of creation.
He whose nature is the Self;
likewise, he is "all-pervading" because of his omnipresence, and is figuratively called a "goer everywhere," for actual movement to all places is not possible for him.
Because it is devoid of activity, it cannot be the locus of the action of going. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is [the locus] of all things, that is, of all entities consisting of both existence and non-existence.
He is the refuge, being the support by virtue of bestowing manifestation and bestowing existence.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is one whose self (ātman) is devoid of destruction—that is, a self which, by being the witness even of destruction and by bestowing existence upon it, is itself free from destruction.

For indeed, no one is able to create an obscuration for that which bestows its own manifestation and brings about its own existence; because if it were obscured, even itself would be unestablished. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is a lamp among all things because it illuminates them.
If one asks, "Where does it exist?
the answer is: no.
Because it is impossible to specify "where" for that which exists everywhere;
if one asks, "Even so, why is it not perceived everywhere?"—
This is incorrect;
for since that [self] is of a single nature as the seer, it is impossible even to say why it is not perceived.
Nevertheless, if it is asked, "Who is this? we reply: "It is he who asks.
If it is further asked, "But who is it that asks?"
Since that which appears with such extreme manifestness as the "I" should be investigated by oneself within one's own mind, enough with this disclosure of secrets.
Because he is not the substratum for the action of going (*gamikriyā*). To the question "What follows from that?", it is said here:
"From that [Prakṛti], which possesses the common form of both motion and non-motion, Viṣṇu was born."
Like a wave from the ocean filled with the essence of vibration,
[it arises] from that which possesses an identical form in both vibration and non-vibration— that is,
from that which is endowed with the common form called consciousness (cittva), despite the difference between the immersion in creation and indifference.
Then, from that space of consciousness (cidākāśa),
Viṣṇu— the specific deity known as Nārāyaṇa who effects the future creation and maintenance—
and the pure principle of intellect (buddhitattva) in its collective form (samaṣṭirūpa) were born.

The description of Rudra, who is of the nature of pure egoity (*śuddhāhaṅkāra*) and is the cause of reabsorption, was not provided because there was no desire to describe only the process of emanation.
Viṣṇu is like what? Like a wave.
The meaning is that it is just as a wave arises from the ocean when it is filled with surging fluid.
In the [states of] creation, absorption, and indifference;
[the one who brings about] future creation and maintenance was born.
Out of a desire merely to describe the process of creation:
from the pericarp of that [lotus] which is Mount Sumeru, from its petals which are the directions, and from its heart-lotus which possesses stars as its filaments, Parameṣṭhin was born.

From that Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is the pure intellect (śuddhabuddhitattva)— that is, from the lotus of his heart, which has Mount Sumeru as its pericarp and the stars as its filaments, and which consists of the cosmic egg situated within that heart-lotus; and also from a mere fraction of his essential nature, which is capable of being the future support for the entire world.
Parameṣṭhin— the specific deity known as Brahmā who brings about the production of future creation—
and the pure principle of the mind (manas) in its collective form,
were both born.
From a mere fraction of his own essential nature,
he— garlanded by the Vedas, the meaning of the Vedas, the lords of gods, and the circles of sages— created the entire creation, a flood of conceptual constructions, just as the mind does.
The entire world— that is, the whole universe appearing as something external—
[arises] from the pure principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*) which constitutes the cosmic totality (*samaṣṭi*).
Indeed, the entire world has originated from the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*) himself.
In this context, the state of being the standard of comparison should be understood as belonging to the individual (vyāṣṭi) mind,
because the collective (samaṣṭi) mind serves as the object of comparison.
In this corner of Jambūdvīpa, in the region named Bhārata, he created people through his sons, who were overwhelmed by mental anguish and physical disease. (MU 2.10.14)
"Janam" means the human race; he specifies this "jana" by means of the sons, who are the Prajāpatis, as well as ordinary people. (MT 2,10.14) He distinguishes the *jana*.

In this creation of the various classes of beings, it is the supreme means of nourishment for those beings— such as the gods and others— who have limbs dejected by existence and non-existence, and who are intent upon arising and destruction. (MU 2.10.15) "The various classes of beings" refers to the gods and so forth.
It brings nourishment and, by means of offerings to gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*), it provides satisfaction.
Seeing the suffering of those people, the Lord, the creator of all worlds, felt compassion just as a father does at the suffering of his son. (MU 2.10.16)
The Lord of those people— that is, of human beings— is Brahmā and the principle of the pure mind;
[he is] compassion, that is, mercy.
And here, compassion should be understood by one of pure mind through the entry of the mind into the creative visualization of the deity; enough with this disclosure of the secret.
Now, what did he do after that? To this, he says:
"Who could bring an end to the suffering of these whose hopes are destroyed and whose lives are forfeit? Thus the Lord of Beings reflected with one-pointed concentration for a moment.
"Whose hopes are destroyed" means those who have perished.
The end is the conclusion of those whose life-span is exhausted and who are subject to destruction.
[The text] concludes Brahmā’s reflection.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, created once again austerity, dharma, charity, truth, and indeed the sacred fords;
he himself created them.
The meaning is that, having composed the Smṛti scriptures, he regarded them as a duty toward people.
(MT 2.10.18) Having created this, the divine Creator of beings reflected again: "By this alone, there shall be no end to the suffering of men," [he thought] himself. (MU 2.10.19)
This is clear.
Furthermore, suspecting that one might ask by what means the end of all suffering for men will come about, he reflects:
"Nirvana is the supreme bliss, by which a person [is freed from rebirth]."
"It is neither born nor does it die; it is obtained through knowledge alone.
Having raised the doubt as to by what means that *nirvāṇa* might be attained, he reflects:
"through knowledge of that."
That is nirvāṇa;
it is obtained through knowledge alone— that is, through the knowledge of the reality of the supreme Self— and not from asceticism and other such means.
He himself establishes the propriety of employing the word "only" (*eva*):
"For knowledge alone is the means for a living being to cross over cyclic existence."
"Austerity, charity, and likewise pilgrimage—this is proclaimed as the subtle means (*aṇūpāya*).
(MU 2.10.21). "Subtle means" (*aṇūpāya*) refers to an intermediate means.
Then, raising the doubt as to how knowledge will be established for people, he reflects:
Therefore, for the sake of liberating these great-souled people from suffering,
I shall now quickly reveal a fresh and youthful means.
This reflection, however, should be understood as being prompted by the impulse of the thought concerning the composition of the instruction on the knowledge that is about to be produced.
Having thus reflected and withdrawn his supreme contemplation, the Blessed Lord Brahmā, born from the lotus,
formed a mental resolve and brought me into existence.

Among those who provide instruction on the source of the arising of my own inconceivable [wisdom], I am the foremost; I am Vasiṣṭha, the teacher of the treatise known as the *Mokṣopāya*, capable of generating knowledge in people such as yourself.
The expression "by me" (*mām*) is used in the manner of the phrase "the head of Rāhu."
"O Rāhu!
By what material cause have you arisen? To this he replied: "Having arisen from somewhere indeed very quickly, I have thus appeared here."
O sinless one, it quickly [arose] before that father, like a wave from a wave;
from some indefinable source, from a certain material cause.
"I have been born.
Then, he quickly appeared before and reached his father's presence. How was he born?

Just as one wave arises from another, in the investigation of ultimate reality, the arising of all things is invisible; thus, what is described here is merely a general arising. Enough with revealing this secret! [The questioner asks: "In what manner did you appear, and what did you do? To this, the Lord replied:
"I am the bearer of the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), together with my water-pot."

"Accompanied by his rosary, he bowed down and was greeted by him who was also accompanied by his rosary. The phrase "accompanied by his rosary" (*sākṣamāla*) is an adverbial modifier for the action performed at a previous time;
by this, his own state of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is expressed.
[With a rosary]—then, what was said and done by him to you? To this he replies:
"Come, my son," having said this to me, he [placed me] on the northern petal of his own lotus.
With his hand, he joined [her] to the moon-like [face], as one joins the cool-rayed moon to a white cloud.
Here, it is stated by way of a poetic turn that "the touch of the pure mind has arisen in me.
Clad in a deer-skin, with his own garment being a deer-skin;
My father Brahmā spoke to me, as a swan speaks to a crane:
"To me," that is, to me who am named Vasiṣṭha.
And in this context, the intervening reflection (*parāmarśa*) should be understood as the speech [of the father].
What did he say? To this he replies:
"O son, for a mere moment your mind has been as fickle as a monkey."
"May ignorance enter me as the hare enters the moon.
For indeed, for all beings, both ignorance and knowledge arise solely by virtue of the purity of the mind established through its internal state.
By this, his own state of being a knower is first illuminated.
He concludes the words of Brahmā:
"Thus, having been cursed by him immediately after my reflection, I, the twice-born, forgot my entire stainless true nature. (MU 2.10.29)
"I am a twice-born Brahmin named Vasiṣṭha; I have forgotten—indeed, I lost sight of—my own true nature. This is the connection [of the words]. (MT 2.10.29)

Then, having fallen into a state of dejection, I remained with an unawakened mind; tormented by suffering and grief, I became like a base person. (MU 2.10.30) "Unawakened" means devoid of certainty. (MT 2.10.30)
"Alas! How has this defect called 'saṃsāra' come to be?"—having thought thus within himself, he remained silent.
(MU 2.10.31) [Note: *cintitavān* is corrected from *saṃcintitavān*.]
The connection is that he thought, "I [am].
By this, it is indicated that immediately after his state of ignorance, detachment (*vairāgya*) arose within him.
Then that father said to me: "Son, why are you so full of sorrow?"
"Ask me about the destruction of suffering, and you shall be forever happy.
Thus he spoke;
by this, it was indicated that immediately following [his] dispassion (*vairāgya*), his inclination toward knowledge (*jñāna*) had arisen.
"Now, what did you do after that? To this he replied:
"Then, being questioned by me while I was seated upon the petal of a golden lotus, that Blessed One, the creator of all worlds, [taught] the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra."
By this, it is indicated that the investigation was carried out by me myself.
[Objection: But was he questioned by you, and what did he say? To this, he says:
"Was questioned" (*pṛṣṭaḥ*). What was asked? [End of fragment].
"How has this great suffering of saṃsāra come to be, O Lord?
And how is it exhausted for a living being? When he was thus questioned by me, he spoke at great length about that supreme purifying knowledge, knowing which [one attains liberation].
"I am, as it were, even superior to my father.
(MU 2.10.35) The superiority over the father should be understood as the attainment of pure consciousness (*cinmātratā*) by transcending the principle of the pure mind (*śuddhamanastattva*).
By this, his own self-established nature is declared.
For there are three kinds of perfected ones who possess progressive excellence:
through the guru, through the scriptures, and through themselves.

By transcending the principle of the pure mind (*śuddhamanastattva*), [one attains] self-establishedness (*svataḥsiddhatva*). Therefore, [I say]: "Know me, who have known all that is to be known and abide in my own nature."
The Creator of the world, the Speaker, the Cause of all, who has known all that is to be known, said:
"This has manifested within me"— such is the inner intention.
"What did he say? To this he replied:
"Having reduced him to a state of ignorance by means of a curse, you were made by me an inquirer, for the sake of the spiritual perfection of all people through this essence of knowledge."
The meaning is that [the son] thought, "This very ignorance has manifested within me," and thus it occurred to him.
Furthermore, what did he say? To this, he says:
"Now that the curse has been pacified, you have attained supreme awakening;
you stand as one with the Self, just as I do, like gold [is not distinct] from gold.
The sense is: "Now I too have become a man of knowledge"—such is my own realization.
Furthermore, what did he say after that? To this he replied:
"O virtuous one, go now for the sake of favoring the world to the great seat (mahāpīṭha) situated within Jambudvīpa, to Bhāratavarṣa."
[It is] clearly situated within Jambudvīpa.
Clearly,

my son, those of great intelligence who are devoted to the section on ritual action (*kriyākāṇḍa*) should be instructed by you, step by step, according to the sequence of the ritual section. *MU_2,10.40*
This is clear.

(MT 2,10.40) Furthermore, O virtuous one, those whose minds are detached, who possess great wisdom, and who are free from passion, should be instructed by you with knowledge that bestows bliss. (MU 2,10.41)
Then it occurred to me: "I shall give instruction through the door of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) for those devoid of dispassion,
but through the door of the knowledge section (jñānakāṇḍa) for those who possess dispassion."
The sense is that, otherwise, I would not even proceed to follow your instruction.
Thus he concludes the speech of Brahmā:
"Therefore, I have been commissioned by my father, the lotus-born one."

"O Rāghava, I remain here as long as the succession of beings exists. By the phrase "as long as the succession of beings," it is stated either by way of a general reference to the teacher being a knower of the elements or because of his own longevity;
however, the external object has not been explicitly stated at every step for the sake of clarity.
[Thus] the meaning [is established]. He concludes this with the final verse of the canto:
"Indeed, there is nothing at all left for me to do here; with the thought 'I must remain,' I am established upon the earth."
With a mental state that is utterly tranquil, as if my intellect were perpetually asleep, I perform my duties, yet I do nothing at all.
Indeed, this is certain for me, belonging to the lineage of all the wise known as Vasiṣṭha,
in this world.
There is nothing at all further to be done, because one has achieved the goal through the attainment of the reality of the Supreme Self;
nevertheless, I remain established here upon the earth.
In what state?

With the thought, "I must certainly remain here; I must remain in accordance with destiny"—thus having such a disposition, meaning one whose mind is intent upon it, or rather, one whose mind is resolved.

I perform my duty— whether it be work for the sake of maintaining the body or obligatory rites performed to avoid the fault of transgression— by means of a mental state that is thoroughly tranquil and free from the agitation of pursuing gain or loss.
By what kind of activity? By that intellect which is perpetually asleep; the meaning is: as if by one that is utterly tranquil.
Nevertheless, the meaning is that by virtue of the realization of the certainty "I do nothing at all" and "I am not the agent," [all is resolved]. May there be auspiciousness!
"Something [is] by way of the necessity of destiny.
Thus ends the tenth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Out of a desire to conclude what was stated in the previous creation,
he makes this reference:
"All this, the descent of knowledge upon the earth, has been told to you."
"And my own endeavor, as ordained by the Lotus-born.
"My own endeavor" refers to one's personal activity;
[it was ordained] by the Lotus-born, that is, by Brahmā, who is the essence of the pure mind.
"Conceived" means manifested;
the sense is that in this very manner, knowledge has descended here.
O sinless one, today you [desire] to hear this supreme knowledge.
"The mind of the Great One is intensely longing due to the dawning of his past merit.
This was spoken by Brahmā.
Śrī Rāma asks:
O Brahmin, how did the intellect of the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, proceed after the creation, for the purpose of introducing knowledge into the world?
"How" means "for what purpose."
For what purpose?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha gives the answer:
"In the Supreme Brahman, Brahmā himself, by the power of his own nature," [MT 2.11.3]...
Born eternally as one consisting of vibration, like a wave in the ocean,
[he arises] in the Supreme, whose nature is the most excellent pure consciousness alone; "consisting of vibration" means consisting of the limited self-reflective awareness of "I."
Having thus emitted this extended creation,
the Supreme Lord beheld all the courses of that creation, existing in the past, present, and future, within his own nature as supreme consciousness alone.
He beheld [it], with the words "with the eye of knowledge" being understood as the ellipsis.
When the destruction of the Kṛta and other ages—the time for the sequence of virtuous deeds—had arrived, the Lord, perceiving the delusion of the worlds, was moved by compassion. (MU 2.11.6)
The meaning is: "into a state of delusion.
Then the Lord, having created me and repeatedly endowed me with knowledge, dispatched me to the surface of the earth for the sake of pacifying the ignorance of the world. (MU 2.11.7)
Having joined me— who am known as Vasiṣṭha— with knowledge, that is, with the knowledge of the Supreme Self. (MT 2,11.7)
"Just as I was dispatched by him, so too were other great seers in great numbers,
headed by Sanatkumāra, Nārada, and others. By this, it is indicated that whatever teachers have existed or will exist in the future, this same method applies to them as well.
"By means of the sequence of ritual action and likewise by the sequence of gnosis,
[these teachings] were proclaimed in order to uplift the world, which is bound by the great disease of the mind.
(MU 2.11.9) "Proclaimed" (*īritāḥ*) means sent forth (*visarjitāḥ*).
To do what?
To uplift the world through the sequence of ritual action and the sequence of knowledge, according to the distinctions among those qualified [to practice].
In what manner is the world [to be uplifted]?
The mind alone is the great illusion, the great disease;
by it [the world] is propped up and bound.
Then, by those great sages, in the past when the Kṛta age had come to an end—
When the sequence of ritual action had gradually become pure and the earth had attained a state of attenuation,
kings were appointed according to the division of separate territories for the purpose of enacting the sequence of rituals and for the regulation of boundaries.
This is clear.

(MT 2.11.10–11) Furthermore, many treatises on traditional law (*smṛti*) and treatises on sacrifice (*yajña*) have been composed and proclaimed on this earth for the sake of accomplishing the goals of dharma, pleasure, and wealth. MU 2.11.12
They were fabricated and composed by the great seers (*maharṣi*); this is the ellipsis. The sense is that their instruction was not heard by the world.
The word "atha" (now/then) is to be connected with the following verse.
When this Kālacakra flows, then that sequence having dissolved, it is to be connected [to the following].
While people were intent on eating every day and devoted to the acquisition of rice,
the dualities of kings arose for the sake of sense-objects;
and living beings on earth fell into a state of being subject to punishment in great numbers.
"Dvandvāni" means dual combats;
"viṣayārtham" means for the sake of territory;
"daṇḍyatām" means the state of being subject to punishment or deserving of punishment.
The meaning is: "due to the commission of sins such as adultery.
Consequently, the kings gradually became incapable of protecting the earth without war; therefore, they, along with their subjects, fell into a state of wretchedness.
[The word] *bhūpā* [is] clear.
For the sake of removing their wretchedness and for the sake of the proper sequence of creation:
Therefore, these great perspectives on knowledge have been proclaimed by us and others. This science of the inner self (*adhyātmavidyā*) was previously described for those kings.
Thereafter, it spread throughout the world and is designated as "the royal science" (*rājavidyā*).

The meaning is that it is so called because it is treated with the term "royal science" in the *Gītā* and other texts, beginning with the words "the royal science, the royal secret" (*rājavidyā rājaguhyam*).
It is the royal science, the royal secret, the supreme treatise on the inner self (*adhyātma*).
Having known this, O Raghava, kings have attained supreme freedom from suffering.
*Rājavidyā* and *rājaguhya* are other names for the science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*).
Now, after many kings of stainless fame have passed away,
you, O Rāma, have been born today here on earth from this Daśaratha.
This is clear.
O crusher of enemies, this beautiful dispassion has arisen in your mind toward this exceedingly serene [being], and it is causeless— meaning, O dispeller of foes,
it is without such causes as revulsion or the like.
"Having the form of the loathsome and so forth" (*bībhatsādirūpam*).
[Objection: "But what excellence do I possess by means of dispassion that is without a specific cause? To this, he says:
"For indeed, for every fortunate person who is virtuous and discerning... (*sarvasyaiva hi bhavyasya sādhor api vivekinaḥ*)."
"O Rāma, dispassion preceded by a specific sign arises for one of rajasic nature.
This is clear.
However, this [state] which has arisen is unprecedented and causes wonder among the virtuous.
Your dispassion is causeless, characterized by sattva, and born of your own discernment.
This is clear.
Having seen the loathsome and the uneven, who indeed would not become dispassionate?
But for the virtuous, supreme detachment arises from discernment alone.
(MU 2.11.23) The loathsome [object] is a substance that serves as the objective support for the loathsome sentiment.
Indeed, those great ones of vast wisdom do so even without a [sensory] cause. (MT 2.11.23)
Only those in whom dispassion (*vairāgya*) arises possess pure minds;
for the sense is that dispassion does not arise without cause except through the state of having a pure mind.
[This occurs] through detachment resulting from the reflective awareness of the wonder of one's own discrimination (*viveka*).
For a person shines by means of wisdom, like a youth with a forest garland.
This refers to the reflective awareness of that wonder which is one's own discernment.
By her who was dispassionate— that is, free from attachment to external objects—
and not by one dispassionate through loathing;
having discerned this structure of saṃsāra through discrimination.
"Those who attain dispassion are indeed the supreme among men.
This is clear.
Having investigated this again and again by means of one's own discernment alone...
The magical illusion called saṃsāra— this "Indra’s net"— must be forcibly abandoned, both externally and internally. It must be brought entirely within the scope of renunciation.
Who would not become dispassionate upon seeing a cemetery, misfortune, and wretchedness? That dispassion which arises spontaneously is the supreme good. (MU 2.11.28) [This is clear. (MT 2.11.28)
You possess unartificial dispassion and have fully attained greatness;
you are a fit vessel for the essence of knowledge, just as soft soil is for a seed.
This is clear.
(MU 2.11.29) Through the grace of the Supreme Lord, the Master, the Supreme Self, a virtuous intellect such as yours pursues discernment. (MU 2.11.30)
The sense is that, however, no personal effort whatsoever prevails in this matter.
(MU 2.11.30) Through a great sequence of ritual actions, through austerity, through observance, through charity, through pilgrimages, and through long-term seclusion; (MU 2.11.31)
When evil deeds have reached exhaustion through long-term discernment and one engages in the investigation of ultimate reality,
the intellect of a living being proceeds [toward truth] by way of a chance occurrence (*kākatālīya*).
By the phrase "of the living being... by way of a chance occurrence" (*kākatālīyayogena*), the laxity of the sequence of ritual actions and so forth is indicated;
through a chance occurrence, there arises the application of the intellect toward the investigation of the Supreme Self.
Nevertheless, the sequence of ritual actions and so forth must necessarily be performed,
because even that serves as a means toward it to some small extent;
yet one should not become mired in that alone.
Since there also exists another primary means, such as the worship of a true guru, this is sufficient [for our purpose].
And as for the yoga of the intellect (*buddhiyoga*),
those devoted to ritual action have already had enough with their diligent rotations of the *cakra*.
People wander here in this world as long as they do not perceive the supreme state;
being intent on ritual action, they regard action alone as the means [to liberation].
The "supreme state" (param padam) is the exalted station known as pure consciousness (cinmātra).
Those devoted to ritual action (kriyāparāḥ), by means of the revolutions of the wheels, are those who repeatedly delight in activity; this is the meaning.
Having repeatedly seen this cyclic existence as it truly is through such means, one whose intellect is absorbed in that [realization],
Having abandoned [the world], they depart like elephants without their tethering posts;
having seen things as they truly are, having seen them as they exist,
[they abandon] that which consists of it— the world consisting of *saṃsāra*.
"Supremely transcendent" means the reality of pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātratattva*).
"They go" means they experience their own self as having that very nature.
O Rāma, this wandering in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsārasaṃsṛti*) is a difficult path of endless striving.
The great thread, which is the body, is not destroyed without knowledge. It is the path of saṃsāra, such that its endless activities consist of efforts taking the form of existence and non-existence.
The Great Tantra named Dehamuktā; Dehamuktā is the Great Tantra.
Knowledge is the knowledge of the reality of pure consciousness alone.

O scion of Raghu, it is by means of the boat of gnosis and reasoning alone that those of great intelligence have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to traverse; not by any other means. (MU 2.11.36)
The means (*upāya*) which is reasoning (*yukti*) in the form of knowledge (*jñāna*) is itself the raft;
by that [raft].
Listen with an attentive mind and with this constant vigilance to this method of knowledge which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. (MU 2.11.37) [Note:
*saṃsārāṃbhodhitāriṇīm* is corrected from *saṃsārāṃ⟨b⟩[bh]odhi°*.]
The sense is that you are unable to hear [this] without an attentive intellect.
For, O blameless one, these ways of suffering in the world, with their endless turmoil, burn within for a long time unless there is a means of liberation (*yukti*). (MU 2.11.38)
The reasoning called knowledge (*jñāna-yukti*).
O Rāghava, by what means other than the reasoning of knowledge can the sufferings of the pairs of opposites, such as cold, wind, and heat, be endured even among the virtuous? (MU 2.11.39)
[Regarding] "cold, wind, heat, and so forth":
by what other means?
By no means at all; such is the meaning.
