In this context, however, the consumption of black pepper by children and the elderly should be applied as an illustrative example.
In the young and the old, anxieties over suffering fall upon them at every step and burn them according to the time, just as a flame of fire consumes straw, O fool. (MU 2.11.40)
Anxious thoughts that give rise to suffering are "suffering-thoughts" (*duḥkhacintā*);
these should be understood as having objects of enjoyment (*bhoga*) as their domain.
For the wise man—who possesses realized knowledge and possesses right vision—such mental anxieties (*ādhayaḥ*) [do not arise].
They do not burn the wise man, just as the flames of fire do not burn a forest soaked by rain for years.
How is the wise man characterized?
That by which the known is experienced—
that is, that by which consciousness, the nature of consciousness, the reality of the self, is [perceived]— is [the means].
"Ādhayaḥ" means anxieties.
Of what nature was the forest? It was that from which clouds, raining down, issued forth.

Even when the desert winds of saṃsāra, which revolve as mental and physical afflictions, are stirred up like raining clouds, the knower of reality is not broken, remaining like a wish-fulfilling tree. (MU 2.11.42)
In the desert wind of *saṃsāra*, which is a whirlwind (*parāvarta*)— that is, characterized by repeated recurrence (*paunaḥpunyena*) of mental afflictions (*ādhi*) and physical diseases (*vyādhi*)—
it is thus agitated, possessed of the turbulence known as existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva*).
It does not break, nor does it fall under the sway of joy and sorrow;
this should be understood as occurring when the desert wind of saṃsāra is agitated.
Even the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) does not break when the wind is agitated.
The reversal of mental and physical afflictions;
thus,
for the sake of knowing reality, the wise person indeed exerts effort through wisdom.
One who is authoritative and whose self is awakened should be questioned with humility.
"Authoritative" (prāmāṇika) means one who speaks according to valid means of knowledge;
"awakened" (prabuddha) means one who has realized [the truth].
He by whom the self is realized as the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure consciousness, is one whose self is awakened.
"Filled with affection" means accompanied by a request.
The meaning is that, if questioned about something other than this, he would surely say something contradictory.
[Accompanied by a request:
When one who is authoritative has been questioned, the speech of that speaker of noble mind should be received with effort, just as saffron is taken up by a fine cloth. (MU 2.11.44)
With effort and with careful attention.
O best among those skilled in speech, there is no one more foolish than that man who questions a person ignorant of reality whose words are not to be accepted. (MU 2.11.45)
"Such a person" means one who does not know reality,
that is, one who conceives of a self in the body and so forth.
[This refers to] an authoritative speaker who knows that [reality], when questioned with effort.
There is no one more base than that person who does not carry out his word—
that is, who does not accomplish the purpose expressed by the words he has spoken.

Having first determined, through the effects [of his words], whether the speaker possesses knowledge of that or lacks it, the man who then poses a question is a seeker of great intelligence. (MU 2.11.47)

This is established by their actual conduct, and not by mere words; for by mere words, many people present themselves as knowers of Brahman. A fool who asks a question without having first examined the speaker— (MT_2,11.47) — [is like one who] asks about the color of a conch shell while standing on the shore of the ocean. ||| He who asks a question without having determined the character of the speaker is a fool. ||| Just as one standing on the shore of the ocean might ask about the color of a conch shell, so too does a fool ask a question without having ascertained the teacher. ||| Therefore, one should examine the speaker through his actions, and not merely by his speech. ||| For many people, even those devoid of knowledge, Such an inquirer would be inferior and not a fit vessel for the great purpose.
"Bāla" means a fool, like a child;
[he is unfit] for the great purpose known as liberation, which is the supreme goal.

When the intellect is blameless and capable of reconciling what precedes and what follows, a wise person should answer what is asked; it should not be told to one who is base and possesses the nature of a beast.
[This is] by a wise and intelligent teacher.

"Questioned" means the matter made the subject of inquiry. "O blameless one," likewise, regarding the preceding and following [parts], that is, the meanings of the preceding and following portions of the sentence.
That which is a resolution— the removal of mutual contradictions—
is "patience" (kṣamā) in the intellect;
it should be spoken to such an inquirer.
Therefore, one should not speak to an inferior questioner— one who follows the nature of a beast and is like a beast due to his delusion— because it would be useless.

Regarding the questioner: "Whether [the speaker] has considered the fitness of the questioner for the authoritative subject matter or not, the wise call that man here the most foolish who speaks [without such consideration]. (MU 2.11.50)
Because the questioner is more foolish, this [opponent] is the most foolish of all;
for among many who engage in a series of inquiries, the most foolish is he who is even more foolish than the questioner himself— the sense being, "What could such a person possibly say?"
"O descendant of Raghu, you are exceedingly a vessel of virtues, both as a seeker and as one most free from delusion;
I too know how to speak, and this is the union of us two."
The connection here is one of similarity: that you are an inquirer who possesses the qualities [to receive this teaching], and that I am a speaker of such [a nature].
(MT 2.11.51) O you who are skilled in words and their meanings, whatever I speak, you should determine with effort to be this very reality and hold it in your heart without interruption. (MU 2.11.52)
With effort,
he explains the nature of the determination:
"this" [refers to the following].
This matter spoken by the venerable Vasiṣṭha constitutes the ultimate truth;
previously, my word alone should have been accepted as true on the basis of devotion.
Consequently, its truth will become manifest of its own accord.
Otherwise, by means of subtle investigations based on your own conceptual constructions, not even the slightest bit of your undertaking will succeed; such is the intended meaning.
"Now, if what you have said does not apply to me, then what should be done? To this he replies:

"You are great, you are dispassionate, and you are a knower of reality regarding the condition of living beings; thus the truth takes root within you, just as saffron water adheres to a cloth. (MU 2.11.53)
For you are great and not base;
indeed, a base person is agitated even by a slight thing due to their baseness.
Likewise, you are dispassionate, being detached from the objects of worldly existence.
Otherwise, those [words] would not possess the fitness for a cognition permeated by word-meanings;
thus, you are skilled and proficient in the arrangement of the world's stability.
Otherwise, the instruction taught according to that analogy would not apply to you;
therefore, the reality of the ultimate truth as spoken by me applies to you.
In what way?
Like saffron water;
the meaning is: in the same manner that it clings to a garment.
Your wisdom— supreme in its focused attention on truth and discerning the ultimate reality— enters into the meaning of your words like the rays of the sun entering the midst of water. (MU 2.11.54)

"Devoted to attending to what has been said": [the compound] *uktāvadhānaparamā* means "that which is devoted (*paramā*) to the attention (*avadhāna*) toward what has been said (*ukte*), that is, toward what was spoken by me (*madukte*)."

That which has that very [reality] as its supreme object of apprehension is "of such a kind. Likewise, it refers to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the meaning of the other statements spoken by me.
Your discerning wisdom, being present, enters into the meaning of my words, which is near to the present.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "in water" (jalē). (MT_2,11.55)
"Whatever I say that is worthy of being accepted by you should be taken to heart with effort;
otherwise, I am not to be questioned by you here in vain.
Regarding "worthy of being accepted" (*ādeya*), the word "that [which is] worthy of being taken" (*ādānārham tat*) is to be supplied as the object.
"Surely there is no great effort required to take your words to heart, such that you speak thus. To this he replies:
"O Rāma, the mind is indeed fickle, like a monkey in the forest of saṃsāra;
having restrained it with effort within the heart, the song of the supreme truth should be heard. (MU 2.11.56)

For indeed, because the cessation of the mind necessarily involves effort, and without that, the taking of my words to heart is not possible; therefore, the sense is that there certainly is effort involved in taking my words to heart. (MT_2,11.56)

[Objection: "But how can I become devoted solely to your word, having abandoned my own kinsmen? To this he says: "Having kept for a long time at a great distance the person who lacks discernment, who is ignorant, and who finds pleasure in the company of the wicked, one must indeed honor the virtuous. (MU 2.11.57)
One who lacks knowledge is "ignorant" (ajñāna).
The sense is that turning away from wicked people and taking delight in the virtuous is the primary means for attaining liberation.
[Abstention] ... [°tiḥ].
Now, one might ask: "What will be achieved for me by honoring the virtuous? To this he replies:
"From constant association with the good, discernment arises."
"These two, enjoyment and liberation, are recorded as the fruits of the tree of discrimination.
This is clear.
[The question arises: "How can discrimination possess such power? To this, he says:
"Four gatekeepers are proclaimed at the door of liberation:
tranquility, inquiry, contentment, and fourthly, association with the virtuous.
The meaning is that without these—either individually or collectively—no one attains liberation; thus, discernment (*viveka*) possesses the power to bring about liberation.
[Without] these—whether four, two, or three—one should practice them with effort;
for they forcibly open the door to the royal palace of liberation. (MU 2.11.60)
[They] are to be served;
this is clear.
Or else, having abandoned one's life with every effort, one should take refuge in a single [teacher].
For when this one is brought under control, all four likewise come under control.
Regarding "this one":
here, in accordance with the subsequent verse, it should be understood as the single person who possesses discernment (*vivekin*).
[Objection: But how will the task be accomplished by this alone? To this he says:
"For one who possesses discernment is the vessel for the scripture, knowledge, austerity, and splendor—just as the sun, in its form as an ornament, is the vessel for all radiances. (MU 2.11.62)
One whose very appearance is an ornament—such is he.

[The author] explains how dullness of intellect, which is an obstacle to discernment, produces misfortune: "For in those who lack consciousness, dullness of intellect reaches a state of density. (MT_2,11.62)

"Water attains the state of being stationary, as if to the state of stone due to its dullness"; this is connected [in the commentary] as: "Intellect, having reached a density consisting of dullness, attains the state of being stationary."
"Now, if I am not fit for discernment due to the dullness of my wisdom, what should be done? To this he replies:
"But you, O Rāghava, are fit for discernment through your kindness, virtuous qualities, and insight into the meaning of the scriptures."
With an expanded inner self, you stand like a lotus at sunrise. O noble-minded one,
you are worthy to hear and understand this vision of knowledge,
just as one whose ear-insects have been removed is fit for the sound of a lute.
In the *Sanmati*, "sujana" means a good person; the state of being such is "saujanya.
Qualities endowed with that are "saujanyaguṇas" (qualities of goodness).
And they are those who have seen the meaning of the scriptures;
he is one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been expanded by them and is thus free from dullness of wisdom (*prajñāmāndya*). Likewise, it has been "extracted," meaning it has been drawn out.
He is one who has impurity residing in his ear;
such is he.
Therefore, the sense is that he alone is fit for discernment.
Regarding the qualities (*guṇāḥ*): how indeed is this so? To this he replies:
"By means of the yoga of the practice of dispassion (*vairāgya*), together with the perfection of equanimity and gentleness."
That state is attained, O Rāma, wherein no destruction exists.
"Practice" refers to the practice of the true scriptures;
"that state" is the station known as discernment (*viveka*).
He states the means for increasing discriminative discernment (*viveka*), which is the ultimate and primary goal:

"In the beginning, for the sake of liberation from *saṃsāra*, one should increase wisdom itself through the scriptures, through association with the virtuous, and through well-performed austerity and self-restraint. (MU 2.11.67)
"By those who have well-performed austerity and self-restraint":
austerity (*tapas*) is the restraint of the external senses; self-restraint (*dama*) is that of the internal [senses]. (MT_2,11.67)

One should strive to destroy folly— the poisonous tree of saṃsāra, the foremost watering for it, the abode of calamities, and the collyrium for the night of delusion. Delusion (moha) is cognitive inversion (viparyāsa).
"For by means of ointment, practitioners of mantras manifest night even during the day; thus it is called 'ointment'.
[The opponent asks: "But how is my foolishness destroyed? To this he says: "Know that this very thing is the supreme destroyer of foolishness."
This treatise which is being examined with a somewhat refined intellect—
*nāśanam* means the act of destroying;
"with a somewhat refined intellect" means by means of merely knowing some words and their meanings.
But it is not by means of the great net of knowledge of prophecies that causes agitation,
nor by that which is conditioned and associated with formative forces.

By the mere knowledge of a few words and their meanings, the mind undergoes contraction through folly— which, like a snake of false hope, leaps within the heart— just as leather placed in fire shrinks.
"By one who has gone into the serpent of evil desire":
evil desires are indeed serpents in the form of the longing for enjoyments; "by one who has gone" means by one who has entered into them.
The sense is that wicked desires arise solely from folly.
"Contraction" means the absence of the expansion known as the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cid-vimarśa*).
In a wise person, this perception of reality, which corresponds to the actual state of things, becomes serene.
Like the vision of the moon when its entire, stainless orb is free from clouds—
this "vision of reality" (vastudṛṣṭi), which is the "vision of the ultimate truth" (paramārthadṛṣṭi), will now be described by me.
"Is pleased" means she becomes serene;
the sense is that she does not find rest even in that.
She is endowed with the beautiful skill of investigating what precedes and what follows.
A person whose intellect is expansive is called a man.
An "object of prior and posterior investigation" refers to a matter that has been subjected to such investigation;
therein lies a certain charming cleverness.
Therefore, she is "Śālinī.
He tells her, "You too are such as this," with a verse at the end of the canto:
"With his blossoming white [splendor], which steals the mind, and whose cool radiance consists in the discernment of boons..."
You shine with a virtuous heart, just as the sky shines with the stainless moon;
it is blossomed, endowed with the expansion called discernment (*viveka*),
and white, being free from impurity.
With a mind-stealing, heart-captivating,
and excellent discerning mind— one whose very nature is cool— possessing such virtues as loving-kindness and the like.
You shine forth;
how so?
Like the sky.
The meaning is: "just as it shines by means of that moon which has become stainless, being free from the defilements of mist and so forth. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
"By one endowed with virtues such as loving-kindness," [and] "just as" (*yathā*)—
thus ends the eleventh [chapter] in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
The Creation.
In order to steady Śrī Rāma’s mind, he speaks once more of Śrī Rāma’s quality as a perfect questioner and his own quality as a perfect speaker:
"O Rāghava, you who possess a fully perfected mind and are worthy of honor, you know how to ask."
"You know what was said by him, and so I have proceeded to speak out of respect:
O Raghava, he whose mind is fulfilled and satisfied through the absence of desire for enjoyments."
Such as you are, you are indeed worthy of honor; you know how to ask questions.
What I have said has been stated, and you understand it;
therefore, out of respect for you, I have proceeded to speak further.
The intention is that I would not speak otherwise.
Having established the mind— free from passion and darkness and following pure being—
firmly within the self, remain steady to hear this knowledge.
Having correctly established— that is, having properly fixed— [the mind] which follows pure beings within oneself, and not upon external objects.
"In you exists the entire array of qualities of an inquirer,
and in me the series of qualities of a speaker, just as the splendor of jewels exists in the ocean.
This is clear.
O sage, you have attained through discernment a detachment born of worldly attachment, just as a moonstone attains moisture when struck by a multitude of moonbeams.
"Attained" means you have grasped; "you" refers to yourself.

"Since childhood, you have long possessed a pure cultivation of excellent qualities; for one who is pure, these qualities—such as detachment and the like—are as continuous and extensive as the fibers of a lotus stalk.
(MU 2.12.5) "Qualities" refers to detachment and so forth.
And by means of threads that are *atisaṃtatāḥ*, meaning exceedingly continuous (*atiśayenāvicchinnaiḥ*).
He states the result [of the practice] with the words "by means of threads" and "exceedingly uninterrupted."
Therefore, listen; I shall tell you a story, for you alone are its worthy vessel.
Indeed, without the moon, the pure night-lotus does not blossom.
[This] is a story spoken by Brahmā, or a discourse on liberation that has spontaneously manifested from within.
It should be understood that from this point onward, Śrī Vasiṣṭha imparts the very instruction spoken by Brahmā to Śrī Rāma.
He introduces the discourse on liberation spoken by Brahmā, which has spontaneously manifested from within.
Whatever undertakings there may be and whatever views there may be,
they all indeed go to complete rest when that state is seen—
that state known as pure consciousness alone.
When [the self] is seen— that is, experienced as one's own nature—
and when there is certainty (*vai*),
[one attains] peace, that is, tranquility.
Now, have these views reached peace for anyone today, or not? To this he replies:
If there were no resting of consciousness for one of noble mind, who could endure to bear such anxiety within this cycle of existence? (MU 2.12.8)
For a virtuous person of capable mind,
if there is repose in consciousness— that is, rest through the destruction of the vision of saṃsāra in consciousness itself, which is the self whose nature is consciousness.
It would not exist at that time,
in this state characterized by such suffering.
"In saṃsṛti," that is, in saṃsāra—who, being wise, could endure the anxiety of worldly existence, which never brings rest?
The meaning is: no one at all.
The phrase "like us and others" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The sense is that because he has attained rest, he has no anxiety at all, which is why he remains here.
"Like those of us [ordinary beings]," etc. (asmadādivat).
Now, one might ask: "Where does the thought of the fortunate one go? He says:
"Through the attainment of the Supreme, all mental fluctuations dissolve."
Like the rocks of the great mountain ranges [remaining unmoved] by contact with the multitude of suns at the end of an aeon,
all mental activities— the operations of the mind's thinking, that is to say, its reflections— [cease] through the attainment of the Supreme Self.
For one who is capable, [the afflictions] dissolve.
Regarding this, he states an analogy:
"At the end of the eon," etc. (MT_2,12.9).
O Rāma, this unbearable cholera-like affliction caused by the onset of the poison of saṃsāra is pacified by the purifying Garuḍa-mantra of yoga.
Saṃsāra itself is the cholera— a specific type of disease— caused by the onset of poison.
This cholera-like affliction caused by the poison of cyclic existence is destroyed by the Gāruḍa mantra.
Regarding the question of how that yoga is attained— which [is like] the cholera-like affliction caused by the poison of entering into cyclic existence— he explains it in prose:
"And that yoga is attained through the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures together with a virtuous person."
It is indeed obtained as consisting of the knowledge of the ultimate truth.
[The portion] ending with "is indeed obtained" by the good person (*sujanena*) is [to be supplied].
Commentary:

That yoga, which is the cause for the dissolution of the mental function of discursive thought, is indeed obtained through the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures in the company of virtuous persons;
it is certainly not unobtainable.
Of what nature is he? He consists of that knowledge which pertains to the ultimate reality, the principle of pure consciousness (cinmātra).
But it does not consist of the suppression of breath and so forth.
[Objection: If nothing at all will be accomplished even through inquiry, then what should be done? To this he replies:
One must understand that when inquiry is certainly performed here, there occurs the destruction of all suffering.
Up to the point "it must be considered," it is clear. He states the result:
therefore, those who possess the vision of investigation should not be viewed with contempt.

By the power of discernment (*vicāra*), the person who possesses right vision (*samyagdarśana*) casts off this entire cage of worldly existence (*ādhipañjara*), just as a serpent sheds its fully ripened skin; freed from the fever of passion and with a tranquil inner mind, he beholds the whole world as if it were a mere plaything. [Correction: *°hela°
By one whose fever has departed;
by one whose internal organ is cooled;
is beheld.
[The commentary] ends with "possessing right vision.
Regarding this, since the reality of the ultimate truth is obtained through investigation alone, the "views of investigation" are views known as "investigation."
"With disregard" means without respect;
they are not to be looked upon [in that way].
[Objection: "But what will be accomplished by such investigation?"
Here he says:
"investigates";
that is, by a person who possesses right vision and is endowed with right vision through the power of investigation.
The entire world, both external and internal,
is viewed as if it were a diversion or a play,
because he is free from joy and sorrow occasioned by its existence or non-existence.
By what kind of person?
By one who experiences this entire [world],
which is a cage called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), a cage consisting of a mass of mental afflictions (*ādhipañjara*).
Like a snake that has cast off its worn-out skin, he was free from fever, devoid of heat, and for that very reason possessed a tranquil inner heart.
By the power of reflection; [the reading is] *vicāravaśataḥ*;
by one possessing right view;
fully ripened.
Now, one might ask: what is the fault in possessing false vision such that one must rely on possessing right vision through inquiry? To this, he says:
for one who possesses false vision, this supreme suffering exists.
For the disease of saṃsāra is exceedingly treacherous;
like a serpent it bites, like a sword it cuts,
and like an arrow it pierces.
It entangles like a rope; it burns like fire; it blinds like the night;
and it renders one helpless like a harsh stone unexpectedly falling from above.
It carries away wisdom,
destroys stability,
and casts one into the blind well of delusion.
One is worn out by craving; there is no suffering in cyclic existence that one does not encounter. (MU 2,12.14) *harati* ] *hariya*°
The commentary [explains] up to the point "he attains";
it has reached the ultimate pinnacle.
Now, one might ask: "By whom was this suffering created for one who possesses right vision?
To this, he says:
"It is uneven."
It pierces, that is, it strikes.
Having realized that a detailed explanation is impossible, he speaks in general terms:
"not that."
A "saṃsārī" is one joined with *saṃsāra*.
Therefore, the meaning is that for one who possesses wrong view, there is indeed suffering produced by *saṃsāra* in this world.
[Objection: But surely this *saṃsāra*, being of the nature of sense objects, is exactly like that.
"What does this do for us? To this he replies:
"This is indeed a chronic cholera of the poison of the objects of the senses;
if it is not treated, it will result in nothing less than a succession of fruits leading to the multitude of cities of hell."
It performs this and that:
where there is the falling of a hundred cold swords, it becomes the striking with a blue lotus; where there is the burning of fire, it becomes the sprinkling of snow.
The carving away of limbs is the application of sandalwood paste;
the crushing within a whirling wind is the rubbing of the body.
The incessant falling of a multitude of yak-tail whisks and iron arrows shaken by the flames of unceasing fire is like the sprinkling of spray from a fountain-house for dispelling the summer heat;
the severing of the head is a pleasant sleep.
Silencing, dexterity, the seal, and great accumulation;
[ending with] "great accumulation" after "decapitation."
Commentary:
"Difficult to end" means impossible to destroy;
"objects" refers to the enjoyments of cyclic existence.
That itself is a severe cholera caused by poison;
if it is not treated,
then at that time—
The "mass" is the collection—that is, the multitude—of the cities of hell;
that itself is the "fruit. Its "consequence" is its continued operation through a continuous stream.
Because he exists in her, she is "such" (tādṛśī);
being such, she produces this or that corresponding suffering.
In response to the inquiry "What is that?", he says:
Regarding the phrase "wherein": "wherein" means when that suffering exists;
that is to say, having regard for which suffering.
The wind that whirls and throbs—
within its midst,
there is a thorough grinding, a state of being pulverized.
"Rubbing the limbs" refers to a massage that produces tenderness in the body parts;
the sense is that it is even more painful than being reduced to powder in the midst of a wind. "Unceasing" refers to those flames of fire.
In which [battle] there was the falling of such a mass of iron arrows (*nārāca-nikara*) as that whose yak-tail whisks (*cāmara*) were being shaken.
For the sake of dispelling— that is, for the sake of removing— the heat caused by the summer season; those which are the sprays from the shower-houses.
Their raining down occurs;
"seals of proficiency" refers to proficiency, which is skillfulness;
a "seal" (mudrā) is a contraction.
"Emaciation" refers to this;
there occurs a great accumulation, that is, an increase.
... as far as ... [ti] ... or wind ... for the purpose of dispelling ... [da]nā ... (MT_2,12.15)
It speaks of the fruit;
therefore, O Rāghava, one must not treat with indifference this wheel of saṃsāra, which is so unstable and dreadful with its thousands of painful efforts.
For this must certainly be investigated.
Up to the words "it must be investigated" is the end of the commentary (*ṭīkā*).
Therefore, for that reason.
O Raghava,
while this— which is of such a nature, bestowing the aforementioned great and harsh suffering,
and for that very reason dreadful with its thousands of painful exertions— is being experienced;
Samsara itself is a flickering machine; one must not show disregard for it— meaning, one should not harbor the contemptuous thought, "What can this do to me?"— but rather maintain respect.
Furthermore, what should be done?
To this he says: "Necessarily.
This [world] is necessarily this saṃsāra by the wise.
It must be investigated:
should one bring this into the scope of investigation by thinking, "What is this? This"? (MT_2,12.16)
"What else is to be done? To this he says:
"And it should be understood in this way: that indeed, through inquiry, there is the attainment of the highest good.
This concludes with the word "iti."
Commentary:
A person should understand and ascertain it in this way.
How so?
As it is said, in the case of certainty, there is the attainment of the higher good—that is, the attainment of liberation—through investigation.
Now, one might ask: does this discernment belong to anyone, or not? To this, he says:
Moreover, O moon of the Raghu dynasty,

if these great sages, great seers, brahmins, and kings did not have their bodies shrouded in the armor of knowledge, how could they endure even for a moment the torment of saṃsāra, which consists of suffering and is preceded by the activity of darkness?
Constantly experiencing [this], they remain with joyful minds.
This concludes the section ending with "they remain," according to the *Ṭīkā*.
"O Lord of the Raghu dynasty,
I [speak] and furthermore," such is the ellipsis: "I speak."
If these standing before us—
great sages, great seers, brahmins, and kings— have their bodies enveloped and covered by the armor of knowledge, that is, the armor known as discernment (*viveka*).
Such [beings]— that is to say, those endowed with knowledge—
do not exist;
that is, at that time.
How is it that these sages and others, though unable to endure suffering, [enter] this state consisting of suffering?
Likewise, it is preceded by the activity of darkness (tamas) and has the activity of darkness as its cause;
that which is the torment of saṃsāra is the affliction of saṃsāra.
Experiencing that [joy] constantly, and not merely occasionally through the attainment of their desired objects,
they remain with gladdened minds.
Therefore, the sense is that there certainly exists a distinction between these.
"Standing before them" (*puraḥsthāḥ*);
"of these very ones" (*evaiṣām*).
Here, he states the reason by means of a verse joined with a prose section.
For here, just as Hari, Hara, Padmaja, and the others remain free from curiosity and devoid of the disturbances of conceptual construction,
so too do those supreme among men— whose intellects are awakened and who have attained the lamp of the Self— abide in this world.
The end of the verse; the commentary (*ṭīkā*);
for (*hi*) because;
here in this world (*jagati*).

The "supreme among men" (narottamaḥ) means those who are the best or most excellent among all human beings; likewise, the "Self" (ātman)— which is indeed the Supreme Self (paramātman)— has been fully realized and perfectly experienced through the power of discernment (viveka).
Those for whom [the lamp] exists—
such awakened intellects, whose minds are endowed with discernment, namely the sages and others mentioned previously—
they remain in that manner.
Thus, in response to the expectation of how this is so, he says:
"free from curiosity" (*vikautukāḥ*).
"Free from curiosity" means devoid of longing for sense objects.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), Indra and the others are included. He states the result as follows: "And likewise... (MT_2,12.19).
When delusion is utterly exhausted, when the dense cloud of ignorance has dissolved, when reality is fully understood and the beloved Self is attained;

when, having deliberated with the noble ones, both existence and non-existence have been seen by the intellect as having lost their substance, and the true nature is perceived—this wandering through the world is a state of delight. [End of verse 20] / Commentary /
And that being so;
*vai* indicates certainty;
[one should dwell] together with the noble ones, the virtuous.
Having reflected upon saṃsāra and having reflected upon the reality of the self (ātmatattva),
when heedfulness regarding delusion— the effect of ignorance—
has dissolved, then [it becomes] dense and thick.
When the cloud of ignorance— that is, ignorance itself—
dissolves,
then [there is the cessation] of the two objects, existent and non-existent, which have become the referents of the cognitions of existence and non-existence.
When both [subject and object], whose forms have dissolved through the dissolving of the cognitions of existence and non-existence,
exist [in that state], then— in the Self, the reality known as the individual soul (jīva), which is the desired and supreme object of attainment— [the realization occurs].
When [the Self] has been fully known— that is, correctly ascertained as being distinct from the body and so forth—
not only when it is fully known, but also when it is attained, meaning when it is correctly experienced as one's own self through the renunciation of the body and other such things;
then, in that reality which abides as the witness of the individual soul (jīva) and the rest, the reality of pure consciousness alone.
By means of the intellect— that is, by the mind which is intent on grasping—
when [the Self] has been perceived as the bestower of the existence of the individual soul (jīva),
then this [action] is being performed.
*Jāgatam* means relating to the world (*jagat*).
*Aṭanam* is wandering about for the sake of maintaining the body's livelihood;
*ramaṇam* is sporting or play.
The meaning is that [the Self] is not subject to the touch of joy or sorrow produced by the presence or absence of objects.
At the end of the verse:
"And I shall tell you something else," he said:
"And another thing, O Raghava."

When the essence of consciousness has become serene within the heart, when the Supreme Being dances in His full majesty, when all perceptions of mental constructions have become fully absorbed, and when the activities of the internal organ subside within—when the Reality is beheld by the intellect with its flavor fully attained, this worldly wandering becomes a state of delight. (MU 2.12.21, end of verse;
commentary)
"O Raghava, I am he; furthermore, I shall speak.
What do you say? To this, he replied:
"In the serene" means when the Supreme has crossed over,
in the reality known as pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*).
When [the mind] is serene—being oriented toward self-illumination—and thus turned toward clarity;
when that supreme *cittattva* (consciousness-principle), which possesses majesty (*savibhava*) and is endowed with power (*śaktisahita*), abides in the heart in the form of *sattva*; [then...]
When it leaps and vibrates within the heart— that is to say, when it comes within the range of reflective awareness—
then, [it appears] amidst all perceptions of manifold creation, which consist of the perceptions of all living beings and so forth.
When they have become fully engaged;
when, by attaining the nature of all-pervading pure consciousness, they have become endowed with expansion even though they were previously devoid of it;
and then, within the formations of the internal organ—that is, within the structures of the internal organ—[the state arises].
Having attained the essence according to her own will,
she proceeded before her, toward peace— that is, dissolution into the nature of pure consciousness.
And then, when reality— reality known as pure consciousness alone— is seen, that is, experienced as the Self, by means of an intellect whose tendency toward obscuration has been dissolved; |||
This wandering through the world becomes a source of delight.
"Leaping in the heart" (*hṛdi valgati*) means it leaps within all perceptions of mental constructions (*akhilakalanādṛṣṭiṣu*).
Again, he speaks according to his previous intention.
Moreover:

"The chariot is the expansive body, the arrangement of horses is the movement of the senses, and the motion is from the wind; I am the unperceived, infinite, and incomparable one, whether as another or as the embodied self, wandering through the world"—when the reality is seen with such a stainless intellect, this wandering in the world becomes a source of delight.
First, the concluding verse of the chapter:
the commentary states that "body" refers to the gross body.
It is expansive, having the nature of vibrating everywhere;
it becomes a chariot.
The movement of the sense faculties and the arrangement of the sense faculties become the arrangement of the horses.
Because it acts as the driver of the chariot of the body by means of vision and other faculties for the sake of attaining what is desirable and avoiding what is to be rejected, there is movement.
The activity of the movements of the senses—which constitute the arrangement of the horses—and the capacity to impel the body, arises from the wind (*vāta*).
For it is by means of the wind that the senses, possessing the functions of seeing and so forth, move the body.
Or, in another sense:
the embodied one, the living being who identifies with the body,
becomes a horse (*arvan*).
Ultimately, because that [consciousness] alone is the mover of the body;
I, whose form is pure consciousness-only transcending the body and so forth, sport—that is, I move about—in the world.
How am I?
One who has not reckoned [the world] through the certainty of its being one's own self,
and by whom infinite and uneven perils— in the form of pleasure and pain— have not been determined as sources of suffering.
Such a person [is he].

For the king, being superior to the chariot and other such things, remains unaffected by infinite highs and lows; this is the certainty [of the matter]. By means of that which is "anagha"—meaning free from defects such as the sense of being bound within oneself—[he perceives].

Thus ends the twelfth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Having restated the view previously mentioned, [the author] describes the conduct of those of excellent intellect by means of its support:
"Supporting this view, the wise ones, their souls nourished, move about without arrogance, like great beings who have attained spiritual awakening. (MU 2.13.1)
*Asamunnaddhā*: [meaning] *ā-asamunnaddhā*;
having constantly relied upon this which was mentioned in the previous section, making it the object of deliberation.
"Those whose self is nourished":
"nourished" means having reached a state of extreme readiness for manifestation;
"those whose self"—that is, those whose self is called pure consciousness alone—is so described.
Such as they were— unconceited and free from pride—
they were like those who had risen up, as if having attained sovereignty.
Those who have attained sovereignty as described in the previous creation do not grieve, they do not beg, and they do not desire good or evil.
And they do everything, yet they do nothing at all.
They do everything that has come into their stream [of existence]; they act with the certainty that "this must be done."

They do nothing at all because they lack the conceit of being an agent with regard to themselves. They remain established in their own natural state; they act while remaining established in their own natural state, and they move while remaining established in their own natural state.
Free from the dualistic positions of rejection and acceptance, they abide within their own self.
"Healthy" (*svastham*) is an adverbial modifier in both instances, meaning "certainly.
The meaning is that they are free from the positions of what is to be rejected or accepted, and thus abide in the position of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
They come and yet do not come; they go to the forest and yet do not go.
They do not act, yet they act; they do not speak, yet they speak.

In all these cases, both the performance of action and its non-performance should be understood as occurring through the medium of the body and so forth, which are maintained by one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
As for non-performance, however—
Enough with this discussion regarding [the view that it is] merely impure consciousness.

Whatever undertakings there may be, whatever views there may be, and whatever perceptions of what is to be rejected or accepted there may be—they all perish once the state has been realized. (MU 2.13.5)
They are exhausted and dissolved;
that is to say, they manifest solely as the nature of the supreme state.

The mind, having abandoned all worldly attachment and possessing a sweet disposition, attains happiness from every side by its very nature as the state beyond [the relative], like the orb of the moon remaining [in the sky]. (MU 2.13.6)
Possessing a sweet disposition and endowed with friendliness,
even when free from the effort of mental construction and with all curiosity cast aside,
it does not fit within oneself, like an elixir of life within the moon.
The meaning is that it does not fit within, nor can it prevail within, the Self alone,
because it consists of absolute bliss (*atyantānandamayatva*).

The intention of the word "also" (*api*) is that even common worldly consensus holds that it is not logical for that which is devoid of the effort of thinking and devoid of curiosity to fail to measure itself within its own Self through bliss.
The elixir is the nectar of immortality.
It performs no magical illusions and does not pursue latent impressions;
having cast off childish fickleness, it shines forth in its full perfection.

Having cast off childish fickleness— the restlessness characteristic of a child— he does not pursue magical feats such as traveling through the air, which are accomplished through the power of mantras and the like; rather, he brings about their cessation.
It shines forth in such a way that it is full, accompanied by satisfaction.
[The author] explains in prose how the very perception of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) serves as the cause for the aforementioned mental states (*vṛtti*).
For such modes of conduct are obtained from the perception of the reality of the self,
and not from anything else; therefore, through inquiry, the self alone should be sought.
"He is to be worshipped and known by a person for as long as life lasts, and not otherwise"— thus ends [the passage]. This is the commentary (*ṭīkā*).
For indeed,
because such as these— the aforementioned modes of activity or functions— are [as described].
From that very perception of the reality of the self, which is the nature of the supreme self.
These are attained by the person,
not from anything else;
therefore, for as long as one lives, the person alone should be sought through inquiry.
One must investigate what its nature is;
thereafter, it is to be worshipped.
And here, "worship" should be understood as nothing other than making it the object of continuous, uninterrupted contemplation.
Therefore, it must be known;
distinct from the gross body and so forth, it must be known without doubt as the reality of the Self (ātmatattva), just like the gross body itself.
The "other" refers to the gross body and so forth.
"It need not be known.
The word "iti" marks the end of the prose passage.
[Objection: But have you not established that the contemplation of the self is something that ought to be performed?
"How will that contemplation be accomplished?
To this, he says in verse:
"The harmony between one's own experience, the excellent scripture, and the teacher."
Wherein the self is beheld by that continuous practice;
"one's own" (*svā*) means one's innate (*nijā*), which is experience (*anubhūti*); [the genitive] "of that" (*tasyāḥ*).
Of the three— namely, of the *suśāstra* (the excellent scripture), of the *guru* (the teacher), and of the *sadguru* (the true guru).
In which practice, that is, in what [form of] cultivation,
there would be syntactic unity— that is, by implication, a convergence— through a continuous, uninterrupted [stream].
By that practice,
by that means, the self is beheld by the person acting as the agent.

Even when fallen into dire calamity, one should not become equal to fools who disregard the meaning of the scriptures and show contempt for great men. (MU 2.13.11) [avajñātamahājanaiḥ] contains the correction: *ma⟨n⟩*h*ā°.*
"Alas!"—the intention of the word "api" is: "How could one who is healthy go [to such a state]?
In this context, he censures folly by way of this incidental remark.
Neither disease, nor poison, nor calamity exists upon the earth that causes such distress to men as the folly residing within their own bodies. (MU 2.13.12) [This is clear. (MT 2.13.12)
Just as this treatise is fit to be heard by those with some proficiency in refined language (*saṃskṛta*),
there is no other treatise whatsoever that removes ignorance in such a manner.
[The phrase] "those with some proficiency in refined language" means those who possess knowledge of words and their meanings.
"Worthy to be heard" means deserving of being listened to;
"this" refers to that which is called the means to liberation;
"dispelling ignorance" means it destroys ignorance, hence it is called "ignorance-dispelling."
This [work] is worth hearing, brings happiness, and is beautiful with illustrative stories;
it is entirely consistent with the meaning and structure of the words of the scriptures.
"Illustrative stories" refers to the examples that will be presented through the narratives.
By them, it is beautiful:
whatever is the meaning of the words of the treatise,
that alone is the kinsman.
Therefore, it is not contradictory;
the meaning is that it conforms to the purpose of the treatise.
[It addresses] those calamities which are difficult to overcome, as well as those empty and base rebirths.
Those various [women] give birth [to such offspring] out of folly, like thorns from a *khadira* tree.
This is clear.
Better [it is] for one with a bowl in hand [to wander] through the streets of the *caṇḍāla* dwellings;
O Rāma, wandering for the sake of alms is not a life lived by one overcome by folly;
it is merely wandering and roaming.
Having attained this light consisting of the means to liberation, a person [should not act thus].
No one again enters the blindness of the darkness of delusion;
[it is] light, because it illuminates the supreme reality, and its nature is that of light.
For so long does the dark night of craving cause the lotus of man to contract.
Until the stainless radiance of the sun of solitude has arisen. [This is] clear.
For the sake of liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra, together with kinsmen such as myself—
"Having known the true nature of the self through the authority of the teacher and the scriptures"—
this means by virtuous people such as myself.
"The authority" refers to that which is called the teacher and the scripture, which is the instrument of valid knowledge (*pramākaraṇa*).
Therefore, after the phrase "having known through the authority of the teacher and the scriptures," the word "one should remain" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
[The remainder: "Having known... [the remainder]. Those liberated while living move about here, such as Hari, Hara, and others; just like other Brahman-sages, so do you roam, O Rāghava. (MU 2.13.20)
Dwell in the monastery; perform your play by being free from joy and resentment.
(MT 2.13.20) In this world, sufferings are infinite, while happiness is like a mere moment or fraction of a second.
Therefore, one should not fix one's gaze upon pleasures that are followed by suffering. (MU 2.13.21)
"Among those things connected with suffering and permeated by suffering"—
to the question "What further should be done?", he says here:
"That state which is infinite and effortless is for the sake of attaining the essence."
This should be accomplished with effort by a discerning person.
It is infinite, being devoid of the three kinds of limitation;
it is effortless, because it is not to be achieved through exertion.

For the sake of attaining the essence— that is, for the sake of attaining the supreme human goal— it must be accomplished; it must be brought within the range of one's own perception by one who knows, that is, by one endowed with at least some knowledge, because a fool lacks the qualification for this.

These very persons are the supreme among men, the vessels for the goal of human life, whose minds—having abandoned all feverish distress—rest upon the unsurpassed state. "Unsurpassed" (anuttama) means that from which nothing higher exists; that is to say, it is the state beyond all excellence.
That which is such a state, one "takes hold of" that; thus it is "such.
Those [who are attached] to pleasures such as sovereignty and the like, which consist merely of the enjoyment of food and so forth—
Know those who are content while possessing wicked minds to be like blind *dundubha* snakes;
the meaning is that they are like blind *rājila* snakes because of their lack of correct vision.
Regarding "andhadundubhān" (in those who are wicked):
[it refers to] those who are deceitful, wicked, and characterized by the undertaking of evil deeds.

Those fools, whose intellects are dulled by delusion, go from enemy to friend in appearance, from devotee to enjoyer of pleasures; they pass from the difficult to more difficult, from suffering to suffering, from fear to fear, and from hell to hell.

Those whose intellects are sluggish with delusion and saturated with infatuation because they perceive enemies in the guise of friends and experience pleasure at their very face— such people as these never possess two [intellects] that are intent on destroying one another for the sake of their own welfare.
O Rāma, in this state of pleasure and pain, which is as fragile as a flash of lightning—
(this is clear)—
those great-souled ones who are detached and well-discerning like you [are not affected by it].
Know those men to be venerable who partake solely in enjoyment and liberation.
And their state of partaking in enjoyment should be understood as occurring only through the natural flow [of karma],
not as something achieved through effort.
Relying upon supreme discernment through the yoga of dispassion and practice,
one shall cross over this terrible calamity, the river of saṃsāra.
(MU 2.13.29) [vairāgyābhyāsayogataḥ] [°ābhyāsa°]

Practice is the study of the authentic scriptures. One should not sleep while in the midst of calamity— that is, while in a state of misfortune— nor indeed should one sleep here while knowing that this world is a mere illusion.

A person of discernment should not sleep during those [states] that cause fainting and delusion, nor should they treat them with indifference. Having entered this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), he who remains in it with indifference—
He lies within a blazing house made of straw.
"Made of straw" means constructed from grass.
That which, having reached, they do not return; that which, having attained, one does not grieve.
"That state is indeed attainable through intelligence; there is no doubt about this.
"Attainable through intelligence" means attainable through the intellect alone, and not attainable through external effort.
"Now, if that state does not exist, how can it be attained by the intellect? To this he replies:
"If it does not exist, what fault would there be for you in its investigation?
If it does exist, you will have crossed over the ocean of existence."
This is clear.
(MT 2.13.33) When a person’s inclination here is toward investigating the means to liberation, then he is said to be one who partakes in liberation. MU 2.13.34
This is clear.

(MT 2,13.34) A state of well-being that is imperishable, free from doubt, and devoid of delusion does not exist within the three worlds without the state of absolute isolation (*kevalībhāva*). (MU 2,13.35)

Well-being is the state of being healthy; it is the state of being alone, without duality, apart from the state of absolute liberation (*kevalībhāva*). Upon attaining that—the supreme attainment—no affliction (*kleśa*) is of use.
Neither friends, nor wealth, nor kinsmen provide assistance in attaining that state—
the attainment of absolute liberation (*kevalībhāva*).
Only physical suffering constitutes true affliction.
There is no movement of hands or feet, nor travel to another land; it is not accomplished through an excess of worldly afflictions, nor does it depend upon sacred fords or shrines.
In this matter, there is no movement of the hands, feet, and so forth.
And there is no journeying to another land;
this matter is not to be accomplished through an excess of afflictions,
nor is it dependent upon shrines or sacred sites.
That state, which is the refuge of sacred fords and shrines,

is attained solely through the conquest of the mind alone— a task accomplished by the singular purpose of human endeavor and whose activity is directed toward a single goal: the purification of latent impressions.
That state called "the state of absolute isolation" (kevalībhāva) is reached and attained by a person solely through the conquest of the mind alone. By what kind of conquest of the mind alone?

By means of human effort—that is, by personal exertion—alone and solely as the goal to be accomplished; furthermore, by what kind [of effort]? By that which has the same purpose and function as the latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Vāsanā means cultivation (bhāvanā);
these two have the same meaning.
It is by means of that action.
The meaning is: "by that which is to be accomplished through mere cultivation.
By abandoning the nets of suffering, a person attains that [state] which is to be accomplished by mere discernment and consists of the singular certainty born of inquiry. (MU 2.13.39)
By means of that investigation— that is, by means of discernment directed toward that object—
one whose certainty is singular, or absolute.
It is that which is to be ascertained through investigation; this is the meaning.
That is the state known as the state of absolute isolation (*kevalībhāva*).
By one who, seated on a comfortable seat, reflects upon that [Reality] for themselves,
no grief is felt once that state is attained, nor is one born again.
"Reflecting upon that" means being engaged in reflection on the state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).
That state is the state known as the state of absolute liberation (*kevalībhāva*).
The virtuous know it to be the ultimate limit of the essence of all happiness; they call that supreme elixir the unsurpassed outflow (*niṣyanda*) [of bliss]. (MU 2.13.41)
This is clear.
(MU 2.13.41) Because all states of existence are subject to decay, there is no happiness at all in either heaven or the human realm; it is like water in a mirage. (MU 2.13.42)
[This refers to] heaven and the human world, [that is,] the celestial realm and the world of men.
Therefore, the conquest of the mind should be contemplated, for it has tranquility and contentment as its means;
from that, infinite enjoyment of tranquility is attained, and thus bliss is obtained.
For this reason,
a person should contemplate the conquest of the mind.
Of what nature is it?
A person for whom tranquility and contentment are the means;
from that, [comes] the conquest of the mind.
The enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) of infinite tranquility is the wonder; that is to say, it is of the nature of the savoring of tranquility. Bliss (*ānanda*) is attained—that is, reached. (MT_2,13.43)
Whether living, moving, wandering, or falling,
and whether one is a *rakṣasa*, a *dānava*, a god, or a human—
having attained that supreme bliss born from the pacification of the mind, [one remains thus].
This is the fruit of the lofty tree of discernment (*viveka*), which has blossoming *śama* flowers; [it belongs to one] who,
though engaged in worldly affairs, does not accumulate a multitude of duties.
Like the sun situated in the sky, it is neither abandoned nor desired by one who lives,
goes, wanders,
or falls.
And this is an illustration; that is to say, while performing all activities—

whether by a *rākṣasa*, a *dānava*, a god, or a human— it is the fruit of the lofty tree of discernment (*viveka*), which is the flower of expansive tranquility arising from the pacification of the mind.
That supreme happiness called nirvāṇa is neither abandoned nor craved, like the sun situated in the sky; rather, equanimity alone is maintained toward it, as with the sun—this is the meaning.
By what kind of being [is this stated]? By one such as a *rakṣas* (demon), and so forth.

Even while engaged in worldly affairs, one who does not accumulate a multitude of tasks— that is, a collection of duties— does so because of the certainty that "I am not the agent," and thus does not experience them as being performed by oneself.
Now,
the ritual actions of the one whose flower of tranquility has blossomed.
The mind, having ascended the high tree of discernment, is profoundly tranquil, utterly clear, rested,
and free from delusion; being effortless and devoid of longing, it neither desires nor rejects anything.
"Free from effort" means devoid of the activity known as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
"Devoid of desire" means lacking the certainty that "this is what I desire.
The sense is that one acts through equanimity alone, as it arises spontaneously in the natural flow.
First, he introduces the determination of the gatekeepers of peace and the other qualities who have been mentioned:
"Listen to these gatekeepers at the door of liberation, as they are presented in their proper order."
By devotion to any one of these, one enters the gateway to liberation;
"by devotion to any one" means by the practice of any one.
Regarding "by attachment to one [of these]," it refers to the first mentioned [topic], tranquility (*śama*). He defines it thus:
"The cycle of saṃsāra is a long desert expanse, a state of suffering and defects."

The state of a living being, which consists of suffering and defects, attains coolness through the cooling water of tranquility (*śama*). Well-being is attained through tranquility, for tranquility is indeed the supreme state.
Tranquility is auspiciousness; tranquility is peace; tranquility is the warding off of delusion.
It is the supreme state, the most excellent station known as pure consciousness alone.
For the person who is satisfied by tranquility, whose self is cool and exceedingly clear—
For one whose mind is satisfied through tranquility, even an enemy becomes a friend.
For it is through hatred alone that one becomes an enemy;
since he has no such hatred, the sense is that his enemy attains the state of a friend.
For those whose inner disposition is adorned by the moon of tranquility,
their supreme purity arises like that of the oceans of milk.

Supreme purity is the state of being free from the impurity known as latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Those virtuous ones in whose hearts the lotus of tranquility has blossomed within the sheath of the heart-lotus are indeed like Hari, possessing two lotuses of the heart. (MU 2.13.53)
The lotus of tranquility is blossomed; this should be understood as the state of Hari’s two heart-lotuses, because of the presence of the lotus situated at his navel. (MT_2,13.53)
Those whose stainless moon-like faces shine with the beauty of tranquility—
these lords of their clans are worthy of homage, having surpassed the [celestial] moon in their loveliness.
Here, the very quality of being stainless (*akalaṅkitatva*) is the reason for their victory over the moon.
The splendors existing within the belly of the three worlds do not bring such joy as the manifestations of tranquility, which are like the perfection of universal sovereignty.
This is clear.

Whatever sufferings, whatever cravings, whatever unbearable anxieties there may be—all that perishes within those whose minds are peaceful, just as darkness vanishes before the suns. (MU 2.13.56; MT 2.13.56) [This is clear.]
For the mind of all beings follows after clarity;
it does not do so toward the moon as it does toward a person who has become tranquil and inspires wonder.
(MU 2.13.57) Clarity means serenity. (MT 2.13.57)

In a virtuous person who possesses tranquility and friendliness toward all living beings, the supreme reality manifests of its own accord. (MU 2.13.58) The "supreme reality" is the reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattva*).
"Of its own accord and without effort" means that it becomes serene; the sense is that it effects serenity known as the vision of its own true nature.
The uneven ones are harmful;
the soft ones are delicate.
Neither by drinking elixirs nor by the embrace of Fortune does a person obtain such happiness as that which comes from inner tranquility. (MU 2.13.60)
Within the mind—
O Rāghava, comfort with the sprinkling of the nectar of tranquility the mind that is enveloped by all mental and physical afflictions and overcome by the triple bond of craving.
Console and cool [the world] with the sprinkling of the nectar of peace for those overwhelmed by all mental and physical afflictions.

Whatever you do and whatever you eat with a mind cooled by tranquility, that is exceedingly sweet and delicious to you, and nothing else; for one whose mind is weary, it does not please. (The word *svadate* means "it pleases.")
That by which the mind is made to experience wonder— that is, to be struck with amazement— and is rendered languid, or filled with dejection.
O Rāghava, I believe that even those limbs which have been severed grow back again by means of that peace which brings such bliss to the mind bathed in the nectar-essence of tranquility.
O Raghava, I believe that the mind, bathed in the nectar-like essence of tranquility, attains a certain bliss; by means of that bliss—
Even severed limbs grow back again.
Neither Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Daityas, nor enemies,
nor tigers, serpents, and the like, harbor hatred toward one who abides in tranquility.
This is clear.
(MT_2,13.64) When all their limbs are well-armored with the nectar-like armor of tranquility, sufferings do not pierce them, just as arrows cannot pierce a diamond rock. MU_2,13.65
They pierce and strike him.
(MT_2,13.65) A king does not shine so much when situated within his honorable inner apartments as he does when adorned with tranquility through a balanced and healthy mode of conduct. MU_2,13.66
By way of function, that is, by means of activity.

People do not attain such satisfaction by seeing something dearer than their own life through worldly activity as they do upon beholding a person who is peaceful and of tranquil disposition. (MU 2.13.67)
[He is] one whose disposition is peaceful and whose mind is equanimous;
he who conducts himself well with a conduct characterized by tranquility and moderation.
He lives here in this world having attained joy, and not the other; the "other" is one who remains unpeaceful.
When one who is undisturbed in mind and tranquil performs a virtuous deed, all these beings rejoice in it;
they welcome and praise it. (MU 2.13.69)
He determines the nature of tranquility by means of defining the nature of the peaceful state:
"One who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled what is pleasant or unpleasant, neither rejoices nor desponds—he is said to be tranquil. (MU 2.13.70)
The sense is that equanimity itself is peace.
He who is equal toward all things, neither desiring nor rejecting,
having conquered the senses through effort— he is called "peaceful."
This is clear.
(MT 2.13.71) He whose mind is as pure as the orb of the moon and remains undisturbed even in the battles of death and festivals is called "peaceful. (MU 2.13.72)
This is clear.
(MU 2.13.72) Even when standing, he is as if not standing; he neither rejoices nor becomes angry.
He whose mind is in deep sleep and who is established in his own self is said to be "peaceful. (MU 2.13.73)
With a mind in deep sleep, he is devoid of the pursuit of joy or resentment.
One who is free from the pursuit of joy and resentment, whose vision— delightful with the flow of nectar— spreads toward all people with affection, is called "peaceful. (MU 2.13.74)
This is clear.
(MT 2.13.74) He whose actions are perceived with a clear and pure intellect to be exactly the same within as they are without—he is called "peaceful. (MU 2.13.75)
The meaning is: because of the absence of deceit.

(MT_2,13.75) Even in the midst of endless calamities, even at the end of eons when [the world] is burning, he whose mind does not consider this world to be insignificant is called "peaceful. MU_2,13.76
This world is hollow, devoted to hollow means.
(MT_2,13.76) He who has attained inner coolness, who does not sink into worldly objects, and who engages in daily affairs without being deluded—he is said to be peaceful. (MU_2,13.77)
One who has gone [on the path] does not sink; being unattached, one does not become overwhelmed by passion. One who engages in worldly affairs is a performer of worldly transactions.
He is neither deluded nor devoid of conventional discourse;
for in one who is devoid of conventional discourse, non-immersion is caused precisely by the absence of discourse, not by peace.

He whose mind, like space, is always free from stain while engaged in its own natural activity—he is said to be "peaceful. *Svaḥ* means "one's own"; *vyavahāraḥ* means "activity"; one who possesses such [activity] is described as *tādṛśasya*.
Among ascetics, the learned, officiating priests, and kings;
among the powerful and those rich in virtues—it is only the man of tranquility who truly shines.
(MU 2.13.79) This is clear. (MT 2.13.79)
For the great ones whose minds are absorbed in tranquility and who possess virtuous qualities,
bliss arises from the heart like moonlight from the cool-rayed moon.
This is clear.
Peace, the glorious one, shines forth as the limit of all multitudes of virtues, the exclusive ornament of manliness, and the place of fearlessness in times of distress. This is clear.
He concludes the description of tranquility with this verse at the end of the canto:

"Having relied upon that supreme state—tranquility, which is immortal, unassailable, and cherished by the noble—the great-souled ones have gone to the highest goal; O descendant of Raghu, follow that very same path for the sake of perfection."
O son of Raghu,
these men of great majesty are nectar, the very form of nectar.
Inviolable, indestructible, and cherished by the noble;
having relied upon tranquility— the nature of which was previously described—
one attains the supreme state, the nature of supreme consciousness, the most excellent station.
Just as those who have gone before have done, you should likewise maintain that same method for the sake of accomplishment. May there be auspiciousness! (MT_2,13.82)
Thus ends the thirteenth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. With an intellect purified by the stainless understanding of the scriptures and rendered supremely pure, one who knows the cause must constantly engage in inquiry into the self. MU 2.14.1
What is the use of one who knows the cause— that is,
a person who knows by what [cause] one is accomplished?
One must constantly perform an investigation of the self through the intellect.
"Now, what will be accomplished by inquiry? To this he replies:
"Having attained sharpness through inquiry, the intellect perceives the supreme state;
for inquiry is indeed the great medicine for the disease of long-lasting saṃsāra. (MU 2.14.2)
The supreme state is the great abode known as pure consciousness alone.
The forest of calamities, whose form is overspread with the blossoming of endless desires,
does not sprout again once it has been cut down by the saw of inquiry.
[The form] "anantehāparipallavitākṛti" [is explained as follows]:
those which are infinite *īhā*s, i.e., activities; by them, it is "paripallavitā," meaning it has become nourished or fully developed.
That which has its form.
O one of great wisdom, in delusions, the loss of kinsmen, calamities, and errors— in all such circumstances, discernment is indeed the refuge of the virtuous.
The path is the refuge.
(MT 2.14.4) Without inquiry, there is no means for the pacification of suffering.
Through inquiry, the wise abandon the unwholesome and their minds attain the wholesome. (MU 2.14.5)
This is clear.
(MU 2.14.5) Strength, intelligence, vigor, application, and the fruit of action—all these bear fruit for the wise man through discernment alone. (MU 2.14.6)
Practice is knowledge;
however, the meaning is that these [actions], when performed without discernment, produce only misfortune.

Relying on extensive investigation, one should cross the ocean of saṃsāra by means of this great lamp of what is appropriate and inappropriate, which accomplishes all that is desired and wards off misfortune. (MU 2.14.7)
The meaning is that this is the great lamp of what is appropriate and inappropriate, illuminating that "this is appropriate" and "this is inappropriate.
It is expansive and vast.
[It is] the one that has torn open the lotus-heart of the elephant of great delusion.
The noble lion of inquiry, being of pure self,
rends asunder— that is, destroys—
the deluded who, by the power of time, have reached the supreme state in this world.
This is the unsurpassed manifestation of the lamp of inquiry.
For even the deluded, in the course of time, attain the supreme state known as pure consciousness alone.
"Manifestation" (vijṛmbhita) means its playful unfolding.
It is unsurpassed and peerless.
Sovereign kingdoms, abundant prosperity, vast enjoyment, and eternal liberation—
these, O Rāghava, are the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree of discernment.
O Raghava,
it is clear:
those thoughts of the great ones here which delight in discernment—
They do not sink in adversity, like gourds in water.
They are called *vivekavilāsinyaḥ* because they possess this *viveka* (discernment). Those who conduct themselves with an intellect that captivates through the arising of inquiry—
For they are indeed the vessels for most exalted fruits;
through their charming and captivating discourse, which arises from discernment,
they obstruct the spreading of hope within the forest of the hearts of fools.
The flower-clusters of the *avicāra* and *karañja* trees are ways of suffering;
"hope" refers to the hope for liberation (*mokṣāśā*).
"Of those [trees] which obstruct its flow"— that is, of such *karañja* thorny trees that block the expansion of the quarters.
The ways of suffering, the constructions of suffering.
(MT_2,14.13) O Rāghava, may that sleep—which is as dark as powdered collyrium, which bears the fragrance of wine, and which consists of a lack of discernment—come to an end for you. MU_2,14.14
By means of soot-powder consecrated by mantra;
[the clouds are] dark and dense with soot-powder,
and they are as dark as soot-powder due to their extreme turbidity.
"Madirā" is so called because it maintains intoxication (*moda*);
even by the fragrance of wine, sleep becomes dense.
The sense is: "bring that very [sleep], which consists of non-investigation (*avicāra*)—that is, whose nature is non-investigation—to its end."
Even during great calamities and long-lasting hardships, a person devoted to right reflection does not sink into delusions, just as a mass of light does not sink into darkness.
Regarding such states as "What shall I do amidst delusions?"—
he in whose clear mental lake the multitude of lotuses that are reflection has surely blossomed shines like the Himalayas.
In the lake of the mind, known as the heart-lake or the Mānasa-lake— (MT_2,14.16)—
for one whose intellect has become devoid of inquiry and has fallen into dullness, a thunderbolt arises from the moon, like a phantom to a child. MU_2,14.17
*Mudhā* means lacking discernment (*vicāra*), being devoid of investigation;
it denotes dullness and stupidity (*jāḍya*).
From the moon—that is, from cyclic existence which is like the moon because it consists of the reflected images of consciousness and the sun—there arises a thunderbolt;

that is, the marvelous emergence of a thunderbolt in the form of joy and anger produced by the perception of existence and non-existence. This is the wonder of the production of a thunderbolt from the moon.
O Rāma, that lowest of men who lacks discernment must be abandoned from afar; he is like a thunderbolt, a pit of suffering, an anthill, or a springtime creeper that has withered.
What is the lowest of men? The ant-hill is painful for those who are eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍaka*),
for within the ant-hill there are clusters of thorns.
Furthermore, what is it?
Misfortune itself is a fresh creeper;
its honey is the spring season.

Whatever evil undertakings, misconducts, and anxieties there may be, they appear without reflection like *vetālas* [vampires] in the darkness. (MU 2.14.19) "Evil undertakings" (*durārambhāḥ*) refers to contemptible actions that are begun. (MT 2.14.19)
O scion of the Raghus, keep far away from him who lacks discernment, who is like a solitary, withered tree, and who is incapable of performing virtuous deeds;
[this refers to] a place in a secluded region devoid of people.
An old tree stands;
its state is similar to, or analogous with,
that [of the practitioner] regarding virtuous activities such as the cessation of the mind.
And through the giving of fruits, in auspicious deeds consisting of assistance to others.
In a place devoid of people, the mind of a living being, when secluded and freed from the helplessness of desire,
attains supreme bliss within itself, like the full moon. (MU 2.14.21)
"Secluded" means endowed with discernment (*viveka*);
"free from the helplessness of hope" is the reason provided by way of this qualification,
because the helplessness of hope itself is an obstacle to peace (*nirvṛti*).
Discernment, once arisen, thoroughly cools the entire body and adorns it exceedingly,
like the new moonlight adorning the world. "New" means pertaining to the autumn season.
For the intellect that is the banner of the ultimate truth, discernment shines like a white chowrie,
like the moon in the night for a living being.
[MU 2.14.23] "Of the ultimate truth" means of the ultimate reality known as the essence of pure consciousness alone.
By virtue of the common property of being a signifier, the cognition takes the form of a banner as its sign;
by virtue of bestowing beauty, it takes the form of a white chowrie.
Those entities, charming in their discernment and illuminating the ten directions,
shine like the sun, having shattered the disease of the fear of repeated existence.
"Entities" refers to things such as human beings and so forth.
Of what nature are these entities?
They are those by whom many fears of existence (*bhava*)—which are themselves like diseases—have been shattered.
The sun, too, illumines the ten directions.
Yet for a fool, the vampire conjured by the delusion of his own mind— which robs him of life—
dissolves through inquiry when it is night in the darkness.
This is clear. (MU 2.14.25) All worldly phenomena are beautiful when not investigated; they lack any real existence and fall apart under investigation. (MU 2.14.26)
When not analyzed,
all the states of the world— that is, all the entities of the world— do not exist as real entities.
By means of non-investigation— that is, by being devoid of investigation—
they become beautiful.
Of what nature are they?
Their existence is non-existent;
for this very reason, they are fragile under analysis because they cannot withstand investigation.
This [world], imagined by the innate delusion of the mind of man, bestows manifold suffering.
The long-standing vampire of saṃsāra dissolves through investigation.
This is clear.
It is equanimous and pure, free from affliction, infinite, and the refuge beyond thought.
Know that this state of absolute oneness (kevalībhāva) is the fruit of the supreme tree;
it is "even" (sama) and "clear" (svaccha), thus "even-and-clear" (samasvaccha).
It is "unassailable" (nirābādha), meaning it cannot be sublated by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

The "contemplation" (*manana*) is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the infinite and undivided reality of one's own self (*svātmatattva*); its "basis" (*āśraya*) is, by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), that which brings it about.
By him, through his unwavering state and his noble, manifest, expansive majesty,
he rises with dispassion like the coolness arising from the risen moon.
"Noble, manifest, and expansive" means possessing a formidable, manifest, and wide-reaching extent.
"Of whom there is splendor"—
by such [a person]. "Freedom from desire" (niṣkāmatā) is the absence of longing.
And this moon has risen; by it—[one might ask]—"But what will be accomplished by the absence of desire? To this he replies:
"By the great medicine for the fever of anxiety, which is well-established in the mind," (MT 2,14.29).
By means of that [state] which bestows supremacy, one neither desires nor abandons;
by that desirelessness,
the meaning is that one does not long for anything nor relinquish anything, but rather maintains equanimity toward all things.
Furthermore, what does it do? To this he says:
That mind, having its object as reality, becomes expansive and reaches a state of illumination;
it neither sets nor rises, like the sky with its exceedingly vast interior. (MU 2.14.31)
That which has that desirelessness as its constant object and support is "that which has that as its constant object"; likewise,
it is "vast," meaning it is of a nature to expand.
The meaning is that [the object] has come into appearance and become endowed with discernment.
(MU 2.14.31) It neither abandons nor acquires, it neither exerts itself nor ceases;
merely observing like a witness, it remains within the self as the world. (MU 2.14.32)
Seeing thus, he does not become weary, nor is he agitated;
he does not become stilled, nor does he abide within or without.
He neither clings to inaction nor is he submerged in actions;
the sense is that he conducts himself with equanimity toward everything.
He remains indifferent to what has passed and follows what has arrived.
Neither agitated nor excessively unagitated, he shines like a full ocean;
he follows along without attachment and proceeds with extreme intensity.
With such a mind, the great-souled ones of noble intent—
those yogins liberated while living— indeed wander about in this world.
This is clear.
Having dwelt for a very long time, as long as they desired,
those steadfast ones finally abandon the body and attain the pervasive state of absolute oneness (*kevalatā*),
which is liberation from the body (*videhamukti*).
By the phrase "as much as is desired," it is indicated that everything performed by the Blessed One is indeed desired by them.
(MT_2,14.36) Even in times of calamity, a wise person should diligently reflect with their own mind on the remedy for the question: "Who am I, and whose is this saṃsāra? (MU_2,14.37)
