The intention of the word "api" (even) is to suggest that it goes without saying that this applies even when there is success;
[it must be] accompanied by a remedy (*sapratīkāra*),
and not merely by thought alone.
And in this case, the remedy should be understood as the renunciation of enjoyment itself.
O Raghava, a king knows whether a difficult situation or a doubt regarding an action will be fruitless or fruitful only through deliberation, and not otherwise.
The sense is that even externally, the sovereignty belongs to inquiry alone.

(MT 2.14.38) The established positions of the Vedas and Vedānta, which are the cause of stability, are determined by inquiry, just as the features of the earth are discerned at night by means of a lamp. (MU 2.14.39)
The "Vedānta-sthitis" are the established positions in the form of the Vedas and Vedāntas;
they are the causes of stability, serving as the basis for the boundaries of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

The established principles of the Vedas and Vedānta [are as follows]: Discernment, like a beautiful eye, does not perish even in darkness; it is not distorted even by great brilliance, and it perceives even that which is concealed. (MU 2.14.40)

For when the eye is directed toward a brilliance that is not dimmed (*ajihmita*), it becomes "dimmed" (*jihmita*)—that is, turned away—due to the impact; and the meaning here is that such [impact] does not exist in this case.
Indeed, one who is blind to discernment (*viveka*), being born blind and evil-minded, is an object of pity for everyone. (MT_2,14.40)
He who possesses the divine eye and whose self is discernment triumphs over all things.
"Worthy of pity for everyone" means he is to be pitied by all.
"One whose self is discernment" (*vivekātmā*) means one whose primary essence is discernment; that is to say, one endowed with discernment.
"Victorious" means that she exists in a state of supreme excellence.
(MT_2,14.41) Consisting of the Supreme Self, to be protected, and the sole means to great bliss, this wondrous power of discernment must not be abandoned for even a single moment. MU_2,14.42
She is to be protected and guarded. A man who is skillful in discernment is pleasing even to the great, just as a fully ripened mango fruit is enchanting.
This is clear.
(MT 2.14.43) But those men whose minds delight in discernment, having known the upward path, do not repeatedly wallow in the various abysses of suffering. (MU 2.14.44)
Known means realized;
"above" means having transcended into pure consciousness alone; "going" means proceeding there.

Neither does a sick man nor one shattered by hundreds of misfortunes wail as much as the ignorant man whose soul is ruined by a lack of discernment; [in the phrase] "shattered by hundreds of misfortunes," the word *ca* (and) is to be supplied.

One whose self— its ultimate nature— is ruined and forgotten through lack of inquiry and lack of discernment, is such a person. Better is the state of being a worm in the mud, better is the state of being a thorn in a pit.
It is better to dwell in a blind cave than for a man to live without reflection.
(This is clear.
[He who lacks reflection is] the natural abode of all misfortunes and is despised by all virtuous people.
One should abandon that which is beyond the limit of all misfortune and is devoid of discernment. All those things which are harmful—
of these, this is the inherent, one's own [nature].
"Abode" means a locus for all misfortunes.
(MT 2.14.47) A great-souled person must always be engaged in inquiry;
for inquiry is the support for those falling into the dark well of worldly existence. (MU 2.14.48)
For "hi" has the sense of "because.
"Avalambana" means a support or basis.
[This occurs] for one who, by oneself and through oneself, supports oneself and investigates.
One should cause the deer of one's own mind to cross over the ocean of delusion that is saṃsāra; by means of the self (ātman) and the mind (manas),
[one should realize] the Self (ātmānam), which is the Supreme Self (paramātmānam).
"Having firmly grasped by means of cultivation" means having taken hold through meditative development.
He describes the essential nature of investigation:
"Who am I? How has this fault called 'saṃsāra' come upon me?"
"By means of reasoning"—this refers to *parāmarśa*, which is called *vicāra*. By "reasoning" (*nyāya*) is meant *yukti* (logical justification);
*parāmarśa* is continuous contemplation (*santatabhāvana*).
The heart of the evil-minded and unreflective person has long been made like a stone— utterly blind, noisy with delusion, and leading only to suffering. "Andhāndham" means exceedingly blind.
And that [speech] is both such and characterized by delusion;
the meaning is that it is joined with error through dullness.
It should be understood as leading to suffering for oneself and for others.
O Rāghava, for those here who perceive through the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence,
no reality whatsoever is properly known except through investigation. (MU 2.14.52)
Having known [it], one desists from grasping—that is, from apprehension. Renunciation is relinquishment. (MT_2,14.52)
Through inquiry, reality is known; from reality comes rest in the Self;
thence comes tranquility of mind and the complete destruction of all suffering.
Reality is that which is called pure consciousness, the supreme reality.
In the self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness alone,
he describes the essential nature of tranquility with the words "all," and so forth.
Because the destruction of all suffering is itself the nature of peace.
With this final verse of the chapter, he concludes the investigation and determination:
"The fruitfulness of actions bears fruit on earth when they truly attain manifestation from the Supreme."

May this [work], when examined with the very eye of clear discernment, shine forth even for you who are possessed of tranquility. (MU 2.14.54) [The reading] *gacchata* is indeed [used] in the sense of certainty (*niścaye*).
On this earth, the fruitfulness of actions bears its fruit through that very clear vision of discernment which is itself made manifest by clear discernment.
Especially from the highest [source], as discrimination alone is capable of making everything manifest as it proceeds toward clarity;
therefore, may this which has been investigated shine forth even for you who possess tranquility. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the fourteenth canto in the *Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. [The word *vicāritā* is thus established.]
Oṃ. Having thus determined the nature of inquiry, he describes the nature of the third [virtue], contentment:
"Contentment is the supreme good; contentment is said to be happiness. O destroyer of enemies, the contented person attains the highest rest. (MU 2.15.1)
A person who is contented is one endowed with contentment.
(MT 2.15.1) For the virtuous who possess the sovereignty of contentment and whose minds are long-rested, even an empire is like a blade of withered grass. (MU 2.15.2)
This is clear.
O Rāma, an intellect endowed with contentment regarding the conditions of worldly existence is never distressed, remaining unperturbed even amidst adversities. (MU 2.15.3)
He is not distressed nor does he suffer, being fully contented.
For those who have attained supreme satisfaction by drinking the nectar of contentment,
even incomparable wealth and luxury act as a poison to them.
They act like *prativiṣā* (an antidote); thus they are called *prativiṣāyante*. *Prativiṣā* is a specific kind of bitter substance.
These waves of the nectar-like essence do not satisfy in such a way [as those things].
For just as a sweet taste brings satisfaction and destroys defects— this is clear—
[the author] describes the nature of contentment by way of describing the essential nature of one who is content.
Having abandoned the desire for what has not been attained and having reached equanimity toward what has been attained,
he who is inwardly free from weariness regarding the unseen is said here to be "contented.
"What has been attained" means that which has come into his possession by the flow of events.
As long as the mind does not attain contentment within itself by means of the Self,
so long do calamities arise from the forest of the mind like creeping vines.
(MU 2.15.7) "By the Self" means by one's own [Self].
But not by means of enjoyments and the like.
A mind cooled by contentment attains full blossoming through the vision of pure gnosis, just as a lotus does under the rays of the sun. (MU 2.15.8)
The sense is that only one who is content possesses the qualification for knowledge.
When the mind is helpless under the sway of desire, devoid of contentment,
and withered, knowledge does not reflect within it, just as [an image] does not appear on a mirror whose surface is tarnished.
In the state of being overwhelmed by the helplessness of desire, it reflects and clings [to objects].
Due to the night of dense ignorance, the lotus of man does not close.
That lotus of man does not undergo contraction through the thick night of ignorance, in whom the sun of contentment has eternally risen. What is that? [It is the mind.]
He for whom that sun of contentment is perpetually risen—
though he may possess nothing at all— that person enjoys the happiness of universal sovereignty,
his mind being satisfied and liberated from mental and physical afflictions.
This is clear.
He who does not desire what has not been attained, and who enjoys what has been attained in due order—he, O gentle one, is of good conduct and is called "contented. (MU 2.15.12)
This is clear.
(MT_2,15.12) In the mouth of the great one who is fully satisfied with contentment and whose mind is complete—pure like the ocean of milk—the Goddess of Fortune shines resplendently. MU_2,15.13
This is clear.
(MT 2.15.13) Relying fully upon perfection within one's own self by means of the self itself, one should abandon craving everywhere through manly effort. (MU 2.15.14)
Fullness means contentment;
the meaning is that this comes through the self alone, and not through enjoyments.
For one who is filled with the nectar of contentment, a natural coolness arises within the mind;
it attains a stability as eternal as that of the full moon.
(MU 2.15.15) "Within" means in one's own mind.
Of one who is not empty but full.
(MT_2,15.15) With minds nourished by contentment, those of great prosperity attend upon him like servants, having entered into the state of servitude, as they do a king. MU_2,15.16
Just as servants who have entered into the state of servitude attend upon a king, so too do those of great supernatural power attend upon one whose mind is nourished by contentment.
When a person stands within their own self, which is pure and contented, with a mind nourished by contentment,
all mental anxieties are quickly pacified, like dust in the rainy season.
In that which is clear and free from the impurities of passion and so forth—
(MT_2,15.17)— the person shines with a pure state of being that is eternally cool, indeed free from blemish, and full like the moon. MU_2,15.18
The word *nāma* is used in the sense of certainty.
[She was] with one free from blemish, meaning devoid of the stain known as discontent. He concludes the analysis of contentment with the final verse of the chapter.

O descendant of Raghu, even the great sages who traverse the heavens bow down to that stainless king of men, who is adorned here by his equanimity and his wisdom, and who is possessed of virtuous qualities.
This is clear. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Oṃ. Having thus determined the nature of contentment, [the author] specifically describes the fourth [means], association with the virtuous (satsaṅga), for the crossing over of worldly existence by men: "In every respect here, O Great-Witted One, the company of the virtuous (sādhusamāgama) is beneficial for the transcendence of saṃsāra. (MU 2.16.1)
This is clear.
(MU 2.16.1) Those great-souled ones who protect the auspicious flower of discernment, born from the tree of association with the virtuous, are the vessels for the glory of its fruit. (MU 2.16.2)

Of the glory of the fruit—that is, of the splendor of the fruit known as liberation. (MT_2,16.2) The empty becomes crowded; even death acts like a festival; misfortune appears like prosperity in the assembly of learned men. MU_2,16.3
"Empty" refers to a deserted place;
"crowdedness" refers to a place filled with people. [He is] the frost for the lotus-pond of worldly existence, and the wind that disperses the mist of delusion.
Victorious in this world is the singular, auspicious meeting of the virtuous; "sādhu" means correctly or perfectly.
Excellent! Excellent!
Know that association with the virtuous is the supreme nourishment for the intellect, the destroyer of the tree of ignorance, and the complete expulsion of mental anxieties. (MU 2.16.5)
Expulsion is destruction.
(MT_2,16.5) Through association with the virtuous, the supreme lamp of discernment (*viveka*) arises—truly captivating and radiant like a cluster of blossoms from an *aśoka* tree. MU_2,16.6
This is clear.
(MT 2.16.6) The splendors of association with the virtuous bestow an unsurpassed, eternal, and ever-abundant bliss that is free from disease and free from affliction. (MU 2.16.7)
"Always plump" means always manifest.
Even by those who have reached an extremely painful state and have fallen into helplessness...
Human beings must not abandon association with the virtuous even for a moment.
This is clear.
In this world, associations with the virtuous are the auspicious lamps that illuminate the path of the righteous.
The rays of the sun of knowledge dispel the darkness within the heart.
This is clear.
He who has bathed in the cool and white Ganges of association with the virtuous—
What is the use of gifts for him? What is the use of sacred fords? What is the use of austerities? What is the use of sacrifices? (MU 2.16.10) [The reading *tapobhiḥ* is clear. (MT 2.16.10)
O sinless one, if there exist holy men who are free from passion, whose doubts are severed, and whose knots have been untied,
what is the use of austerities or visiting sacred fords?
Those whose knots have fallen away, whose knots called "desire" have been destroyed—
such holy men, whose minds are at rest, are indeed to be honored with supreme effort;
for the virtuous are to be beheld with longing, just as a poor man gazes upon jewels.
This is clear.
(MT 2.16.12) The intellect of the wise, possessing the beauty born of association with the virtuous, shines forever like a lotus amidst a host of celestial nymphs. (MU 2.16.13)
Kamalā is Lakṣmī. By that [Lakṣmī], the state of being a crest-jewel at the tip of the foot of Amalavilāsa was secured by that fortunate man who did not abandon association with the virtuous.
By that person;
of the state known as pure consciousness (cinmātra), which is the abode endowed with stainless play and pure radiance.
The state of having a crest-jewel is the ornament of the head;

by whichever fortunate person, whose nature is divinely ordained, association with the virtuous has not been abandoned—that very association with the virtuous must indeed be cultivated, for it shines in the state known as pure consciousness (cinmātra). This is the intended meaning.
The wise ones who have severed the knots of worldly attachment, the virtuous who are honored by all—
they must be served by every means, for they are the very means for crossing the ocean of existence. (MU 2.16.15)
"By every means" (*sarvopāyena*) is clear.
These [beings] have become like dried fuel for the fires of hell.
By those who have seen with ease the virtuous as the waters that extinguish the fire of hell—
this is clear.
The uneven delusion [consists of] such notions as "poverty is death" and "death is suffering."
It is completely pacified by the medicines of association with the virtuous;
this is clear.
One conceives of all the means [for its pacification].
Contentment, association with the virtuous, reflection, and likewise tranquility—
these alone are the means for humans to cross the ocean of existence.
This is clear.
Contentment is the supreme gain; association with the virtuous is the supreme goal;
reflection is the supreme knowledge; and tranquility is indeed the supreme happiness.
The intention of the term "supreme" (*parama*) is that there is no gain or anything else beyond this.
These four are the stainless means for the shattering of existence;
those by whom they have been practiced have crossed over the ocean of existence, which is filled with the waters of delusion.
(Regarding "mohavāreḥ": it means [the ocean] possessed of the water called delusion.)
O best among the wise, when even one of these has been practiced and its stainless arising attained, all four are indeed said to have been practiced.
This is clear.
Even a single one among all these is like the source of birth for all;
therefore, for the sake of complete accomplishment, one should diligently rely upon that one alone.
(The term *prasavabhū* means the place of origin.)
But contentment with the company of the virtuous and discernment proceed without deliberation in one whose mind is purified by tranquility, like the currents in the ocean;
"currents" here refers to the movements of the water.
It is beyond deliberation and free from doubt.

(MT_2,16.23) In a living being who possesses the company of the virtuous, discernment, contentment, and tranquility arise, just as fortunes appear in one who has taken refuge under a wish-fulfilling tree. MU_2,16.24
This is clear.
(MT_2,16.24) In a person endowed with contentment, discernment, tranquility, and virtuous association proceed, just as beauty and other qualities manifest in the full moon. MU_2,16.25
*Saundaryādyā* [is read as] *saundaryā°*;
this is clear.
Contentment through association with the virtuous and tranquility reside in one who possesses right reflection and a correct understanding.
Victories and glories proceed toward the best of ministers, as if toward a king;
[this refers to] the ministers who are knowers of counsel,
toward the "vara," meaning the most excellent.
He states the conclusion:
"Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, having conquered one of these—the mind, which is eternal—by means of human effort, one should diligently cultivate virtue. (MU 2.16.27)
Therefore, from among these four,
one should bring forth— that is, acquire— one quality, such as contentment or the like.
Relying on supreme human effort, one should conquer the elephant of the mind;
as long as even a single virtue is not attained, there is no higher state. (MU 2.16.28)
This is clear.
(MT_2,16.28) Grinding your teeth against your teeth with human effort, O Rāma, until your mind is firmly resolved upon the acquisition of virtue. (MU_2,16.29)
Whether you be a god, a yakṣa, a human, or even a tree—
O mighty-armed one, as long as this is so, there is no means whatsoever for you here [to attain liberation] through the acquisition of qualities, such as the acquisition of contentment and the like.
When even a single quality has borne fruit and attained strength,
all the defects of one with a poisoned mind quickly perish. (MU 2.16.31) [doṣāḥ] [de] [o]ṣāḥ.
The defects are passion and the like.
When the qualities increase, they grow and bring about the destruction of the defects;
when the defects increase, they grow and destroy the qualities.
This is clear.
For in this great forest of the mind, the swift river of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—with its vast banks of the auspicious and inauspicious—flows constantly among living beings. (MU 2.16.33)
This is clear.
For that [river], by its own effort, flows along whichever bank it is directed; therefore, act as you wish. (MU 2.16.34)
"Hi" signifies certainty. That river of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—he concludes this with the final verse of the chapter:
"By the speed of human effort, gradually fashion [the mind] so that it follows the auspicious banks within the forest of the mind."
O you of excellent resolve, for by this speed of human effort— the force of *puruṣakāra*— you are not carried away even slightly here by the river of your own nature,
that great river of your own latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Now, in response to the inquiry, "For what purpose do I place her on the bank?", he says:
"For here, indeed" (*iha hi*). For (*hi*) means because.
By following its auspicious banks, you are not carried away by that great river of your own nature, nor are you led hither and thither against your will;
for nothing at all is carried away by a river that remains within its banks. May there be auspiciousness.
Not so; not so.
Thus ends the sixteenth canto in the *Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskara Kaṇṭha.
He speaks thus as a fulfillment: "O Rāghava, you who have thus attained solitude are worthy to hear the words of knowledge, just as a king is worthy to hear the speech on statesmanship."
O Rāghava, you are great; knowledge is your voice. This being so:
That person who has attained discernment—
he—
Like you,
he is worthy to hear the words of knowledge.
Like whom?
Just as a king is worthy of hearing the words of policy—the utterances of statesmanship—so too [is he];
such is the meaning.
He is pure, possessing a great disposition for pure discernment.
Free from attachment to the insentient, he is fit, like the autumn sky for the moon;
he is pure (*avadāta*) through the practice of tranquility and other virtues, devoid of the impurities of passion and the like, and stainless (*nirmala*).
[The word *avadāta*] refers to that which is pure as the object of pure consciousness alone, and also to that which is white.

"Abandoned by the association with the dull-witted" means he has renounced them; that is, he does not engage in [worldly activity]. Alternatively, by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇayā*), it means he is abandoned by the association with the "dull," namely the clouds. (MT_2,17.2)
You, who are supported by this unimpaired splendor of virtue,
listen to these words about to be spoken, which remove the delusion of the mind.
This is clear.
This treatise belongs to that person for whom the wish-fulfilling tree of merit stands bowed under the weight of its fruit,
and who strives to hear it for the sake of the liberation of living beings.
This is that very scripture.
One who is fortunate becomes a vessel for words that are purifying, sublime, and grant the singular realization of the Supreme; the base person does not. (MU 2.17.5) [bhavyo] [bhavyo]

The fortunate one possesses a divine nature. This compendium, equal in essence to the *Sāra*, which declares the means to liberation, consists of thirty-two thousand [verses]; when known, it bestows nirvāṇa.
The *saṃhitā* is the scripture;
it is equal to the essence, that is, equivalent to the core meaning;
it has been understood, meaning it has been thoroughly investigated. (MT 2,17.6)
"Now, what will be accomplished by this? To this he replies:
"Just as when a lamp is lit for one who is awake, light proceeds even against his will, so too shall nirvana come about through this. (MU 2.17.7)
[Of one who is awake: *vini°* means as when a lamp is lit;
even for one who does not desire it, that is, even for one who has no longing for the light.
For one who is half-asleep and half-awake,
light manifests;
in this same way, it proceeds through this conjunction.
Nirvāṇa is the absolute dissolution into Brahman.
Whether known by oneself or heard from another, it bestows happiness precisely through the cessation of delusion;
described as the word of the authoritative one, it is immediately like a wave of nectar.
"Described by the words of a trustworthy person"—this is the reason for the term "heard," expressed by way of its qualification.
(MU 2.17.8) Just as the delusion of a snake in a rope perishes through inspection, so too does the suffering of saṃsāra come to rest through this contemplation. (MU 2.17.9)

The examination (*prekṣaṇa*) of this compendium (*saṃhitā*) is "this-examination" (*etad-prekṣaṇa*); [the work proceeds] from that. (MT_2,17.9) In it, there are six chapters (*prakaraṇa*), consisting of sentences whose meanings are joined with reasoning, composed separately, and containing the essence of illustrative examples and well-spoken verses. (MU_2,17.10)
I have composed and arranged six treatises within this [work].
Of what nature are they?
They are sentences accompanied by their meanings, that is, meaningful sentences.
In which [verses] there are meaningful statements endowed with logical reasoning;
furthermore, of what nature are they?
Those [teachings] in which the most excellent essence is expressed through illustrative examples.
Regarding the "logical" [sections]:
he specifically points out the six sections beginning with the one called "Detachment," which is proclaimed as the first.
"By which dispassion increases, like a tree in the desert through irrigation.
To the question, "What is accomplished by that?",
he says here:
Regarding the term "dispassion" (*vairāgya*):
in response to the inquiry as to how much [of it] has been accomplished, he says:
"That in which one thousand and five hundred verses have been contemplated within the heart."
When [the self] is investigated, its purity arises like that of a polished gem.
Regarding "vicārite," the singular is used in the sense of the genus (jāti) with reference to the treatise.
That section on detachment consists of one thousand five hundred verses of the text.
What is it?
It is that which, when reflected upon in the heart, [leads to liberation].
It is luminous and manifest;
its purity, which is the absence of stains such as passion and the like, arises. Like what?
"Like a gem when polished and purified":
the meaning is that just as purity arises in a gem when it has been thoroughly cleansed, so it is here.
Thereafter, the chapter titled "The Conduct of One Seeking Liberation" was composed;

it consists of approximately one thousand verses and is beautiful due to its composition of well-spoken words (*sūkti*). [MU 2.17.13] That which is the work in the form of *sūkti* refers to the prose statement (*vākya*).
Therefore, it is "beautiful";
the meaning is that it is appropriate.
[An objection: But what is being stated there? To this, he says:
For when the nature of men who seek liberation is described, it is understood that one possessing such a nature is fit for liberation. [Objection:
But what will be accomplished by this description?
To this, he says:
"having such an intrinsic nature."
[Of such a nature]—thus [it is].
Now follows the section on origination, consisting of parables and narratives;
it comprises five thousand verses and is a presentation of consciousness.

The meaning is that "the presentation of consciousness" (*vijñānapratipādanam*) refers to that which presents consciousness (*vijñānapratipādakam*). (MT_2,17.15) The splendor of the world (*jāgatī śrī*), consisting of the forms of "I," "you," and so forth, which comprises the seer and the seen, is described as being where it is neither arisen nor yet arisen. (MU_2,17.16)
This is clear.
(MU 2.17.16) When that [Veda] is heard, this entire world—including ourselves, you, all its expansions, the worlds, space, and the mountains—is understood within the interior of the ear. (MU 2.17.17)
Free from the grasping of a solid mass, without foundations and without mountains,
devoid of the primary elements such as earth and the rest— it is like a city created by mere imagination, in whatever context of origination it may appear.
(MU 2.17–18) In whichever [context] of origination...
That [cognition] is associated with "I," "you," "we," and "you.
Regarding the phrase "it is cognized," the term "hearer" (*śrotr*) is to be supplied as the agent.
In response to the inquiry, "Of what kind is it cognized?", he says:
"The grasping of a mass," and so forth.
For a city appears as being exactly like this within conceptual construction; thus, it is adduced as an illustration.

Furthermore, of what nature is that which is awakened? To this he says: It is like an object perceived in a dream, spread out like a kingdom of the mind, resembling a city of the Gandharvas—an apprehension devoid of any real object. (MU 2.17.19)
The meaning is that it resembles the appearance of entities perceived in a dream, similar to objects seen in a dream.
Gandharvas, for the sake of their own dwellings, imagine a city in the sky through conceptual construction.
That very city of the Gandharvas is empty of objects; it is devoid of real, existent objects such as jars and the like,
yet it is that in which there is perception— that is, cognition.
It appears like the delusion of two moons, spread out like the water of a mirage,
resembling mountains seen from a moving boat, and is utterly devoid of any attainment of reality.
This is clear.
Resembling a demon that causes the mind to wander, yet seedless and radiant;
resembling the inspired eloquence regarding the meaning of a discourse, it is like a string of pearls in the sky.
"Seedless" means devoid of a cause.
The meaning of the discourse is the subject matter to be described;
the eloquence regarding that is its manifestation as if shimmering before one's eyes; that which possesses such radiance [is the discourse].
For in a narrative, the subject matter to be described appears as if standing right before one.
"The sky," it is said.
For indeed, due to delusion, a string of pearls is seen in the sky.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, as the state of being a wave exists in water,
and as blueness appears in the sky— though it has arisen as something non-existent— so too is this [world].
Just as bracelets and the like, though non-existent, arise within gold, so too the world, though non-existent, is perceived as having arisen; this is to be connected with what was stated previously.
Likewise,
that which has arisen as non-existent— without walls and devoid of colors, yet captivating to the mind—
is like a painting in a dream or in the sky, produced without effort and shining for a long time.
"Citraṃ" (variegated) or "vā" (or)— the two words "vā" indicate an alternative position:
one either perceives what was seen in a dream as variegated, or [perceives it otherwise].
Or, a painting seen through delusion in the sky is perceived;
how is the painting?
It is "without a wall," meaning devoid of a wall.
Likewise, it is devoid of color, meaning it is devoid of colored substances.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is without action and without creation.
And likewise, "long-lasting" means radiant for a long time;
by these qualifiers, the supramundane nature of the variegated [painting] has been stated.
The variegated: "The variegated" occurs throughout (MT 2.17.23).

Just as non-fire itself assumes the state of fire in the case of a variegated flame, so too [the Supreme Being], assuming the nature of the world consisting of words and meanings which are unreal in essence, [assumes that state]. (MU 2.17.24)
"Likewise" means in that same manner.

"Consisting of the non-existent" means having the nature of the non-existent. The term "the world" refers to both sound and its referent; this is an expression where the abstract state (bhāva) is the primary focus.
That which has the form of the word "world" (jagat) is perceived as bearing the nature of its referent;
how so?
Just as a painted fire is not a fire and lacks the power to burn, being no fire at all.
It possesses, that is, it maintains, the nature of fire, which is non-existent [in that context].
[The state of being non-burning:
Like a stone leaf rich with a garland of waves and blue lotuses, it has arisen;
like a heap of impurity produced from the powder of a whirling wheel's roar, it has emerged. (MU 2.17.25)
"Rich with garlands of wave-lotuses, stone-leaf": it is understood as having arisen like that stone-leaf (śilāpattra), which is rich with garlands of wave-lotuses.
For on a stone slab there appear lines in the form of waves and in the form of lotuses; these alone are to be understood here as the "garlands of waves and lotuses.
And the objects [of cognition] are to be understood here as standing in the place of those waves and lotus garlands.
Furthermore, as to how it is awakened,
he says here:
"By the wheel" (cakre).
Of a wheel being spun— that is, of a wheel—
one perceives what is like a rising mass of impurity, namely the powder produced by the whirring sound.
For as the wheel revolves, the dust of the earth rises with a whistling sound.
Like a forest in summer— withered of leaves, fallen and lost, devoid of sap—
it resembles a dance frantic with death, yet provokes laughter from the stone-women.
It brings laughter like the smile of a stone woman;
it is the dancing of a single person in a house of darkness, yet the conduct of one who is no longer mad.
It is the autumnal sky of pure consciousness, from which the mist of ignorance has been cleared away.

The intention here is that one perceives the dancing of each individual within a house of darkness as having such a form, yet it is perceived as being entirely more unreal than that. Beyond this, with the intention that one perceives [the dancer] as consisting of pure consciousness and residing in pure consciousness, he says:
"Tranquil":
when this section on origination has been heard by the ear, one understands that this autumnal sky of knowledge has the mist of ignorance completely stilled.
It is as if carved upon a pillar, or like a painting applied to a wall.
Like something fashioned from mud, whether sentient or insentient, it is perceived as if carved out within the pillar known as pure consciousness (cinmātra).
In the pillar [of consciousness],
it is understood as if it were engraved.
Likewise, it is perceived as being placed like a painting upon the wall called pure consciousness (cinmātra). Here, "mud" (paṅka) should be understood as the very nature of pure consciousness itself.
It is conscious because its essence is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*);
it is unconscious because it is an object of apprehension.
Therefore, the fourth section, concerning persistence (*sthiti*), has been formulated.
"Three thousand verses consisting of well-spoken narratives (*ākhyāna* and *ākhyāyikā*).
Here, "well-spoken" refers to *ākhyāna* and *ākhyāyikā* that possess beautiful names; [the text] consists of those.
Now, one might ask: what was stated in the section on the maintenance of the world? To this, he says:
Thus, the world has come to abide in the form of the sense of "I," fully developed through the sequence of the seer and the seen; this has been described here. (MU 2.17.30) [Note:
*draṣṭṛdṛśyakramaprauḍham* is corrected from *dṛṣṭyā* to *draṣṭṛ*.]
The sense is that, as described [in the preceding], it is primarily the very existence of the world in the form of the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) that is determined here.
This delusion of the world shines forth, filling the expanse of the circle of the ten directions.
It is said there that [the self] has long been thus arrived at growth; "long" (*cira*) means for a great length of time—
that is to say, for the most part.
Then follows the Upaśāntiprakaraṇa, consisting of five thousand [verses];
this fifth section is declared to be purifying and beautiful through the lineage of the sages. (MU 2.17.32) [Upaśāntiprakaraṇa] °śānti⟨ḥ⟩.
"By the lineages of sages" means by those lineages of sages who will be mentioned as examples.
"Beautiful" means lovely. In response to the inquiry, "What indeed is being described here?", he says:
"This world, I, and you—that delusion has arisen;
thus it is pacified"—this is what is stated in this compendium of verses.
"This world, I, and you."
Thus,
such a delusion has arisen;
it exists as a reality.
"It is stilled"—
thus it is said in this chapter on pacification.
In what kind of [work] is this?
It is in that which contains a compendium of verses;
such is it.
The word "that" (*sa*) refers to the supreme cause.
[Objection: But what will be accomplished by hearing this? To this he replies:
"When the section on tranquility is heard, the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*) comes to rest."
How is saṃsṛti (the cycle of existence) characterized? It is clearly manifest through *vibhrama* alone—
that is, through erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*)— and its perception is only slightly attained.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is that which has some slight degree (*leśena*) of being obtainable (*labhya*), that is, of being perceived (*upalambhana*) or touched (*sparśa*).
The sense is that otherwise the section on *nirvāṇa* would be purposeless.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*) remains thereafter, he says: "It remains as a hundredth part, consisting of the nature of subsided delusion."

Residing in the mind through another's conceptualization, it is unreal, like the splendor of a city [in a dream]; it is clearly unattainable, like the cries of a battle occurring in a dream while standing by one's own side.
It is like the sound of a terrifying thunderbolt from a cloud intoxicated by its own volition;
"the cloud intoxicated by volition" refers to the cloud seen within volition,
and that which has become stilled is the "stilled cloud intoxicated by volition."
It is like that terrifying sound of a thunderbolt. (MU 2.17.36) It is comparable to a city created by the construction of forgotten dreams and mental fabrications;
it is like a dark-limbed woman at a festival in a future city’s garden. (MU 2.17.37)
That city which has as its creator those two— dream and mental construction— which have been forgotten.
That woman whose likeness is such—
namely, the dark-complexioned woman named Śyāmā— who was full of festive joy and passion in the garden of the future city.
In the same way, that [state] in which the limb is its own essential nature (svarūpa) is such.
[Samādanā] is like the experience of the meaning of a fierce discourse being uttered by a tongue that has vanished;
it is like a wall-surface pervaded by a painting whose colors have not yet been applied, remaining fixed within the mind.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is with a tongue that is perishing, but not with a tongue that has already perished.
That which is spoken as a fierce discourse; its meaning;
and the experience thereof.
That wherein there is such a comparison; that which is like that.
Like what?
And those paintings which are not drawn by hand but exist within the mind of the painter—
by them, [the world] is pervaded like a wall-surface covered with murals.
[Unscratched]—
[scratched]— resembling a city of imagination being scrutinized,
its excellent form unmanifest, like a dance that has not yet arisen in all seasons. (MU 2.17.39)
It is being made to be seen clearly,
but not forgotten;
it is transparent and without a wall.
A city of imagination;
its likeness is similar to it.
For all those who have reached puberty, there is the crushing—that is, the destruction—of the unborn bridegroom.
In the same way, that [woman] whose form is indistinct;
the phrase "of those who are menstruating" is stated in order to indicate that she has entered into the mind by virtue of being nearby.
Among all women of childbearing age,
it is the future menstruation that colors the spring-like season with the form of the approaching flower;
it is like a river of calm water in which the flood of waves remains submerged within.
She whose coloring is like that of the essence of spring, which possesses a beautiful form destined to be called "flower."
The meaning is "resembling that.
That which has a multitude of waves submerged within it is "antarlīnataraṅgaughā.
Such is this gentle-water river—a river possessed of gentle water.
She is equal to and identical with that [reality].
By these qualifiers, it is indicated that immediately after hearing the section on tranquility (*upaśānti*), the creation exists as a nature that is merely an ascent into the intellect (*buddhi*).
The multitude of waves is submerged within;
[the reading] *saumyavāriyuktā* is [to be understood as] *saumyavārisadṛśī*.
Then, the sixth chapter, titled "Nirvāṇa," is proclaimed.
The remaining portion of the text should be known as its extent, which bestows great meaning.
Thus, after the section on tranquility (*upaśāntiprakaraṇa*),
the extent of the remaining text is sixteen thousand five hundred [verses].
[Objection: "But what will be accomplished by hearing that? To this he says:
"When that [Self] is realized, the hearer becomes one who has attained Nirvāṇa, with all conceptual constructions stilled;
his nature is the light of consciousness beyond the object of thought, the essence of pure awareness, free from all affliction. (MU 2.17.42)
Nirvāṇa is merged in Brahman;
the conscious self has the nature of pure knowledge;
it is free from affliction, being devoid of the affliction known as the visible world.
Transparent as the treasury of the supreme ether, with all wandering through existence stilled,
having brought the journey of the world to its conclusion, he remains well-established,
having accomplished what was to be done.
He by whom the course of the world has been brought to an end— that is, terminated—
is such a one. "Kṛtam" means completed or finished.
He is one by whom that which was to be done has been accomplished;
he is such as this,
and for that very reason, he is well-established.
A diamond pillar for all extensive undertakings, resembling the sky,
he is supremely satisfied, having swallowed the entire web of the world exactly as it exists.
(MU 2.17.44) "All" refers to those which are "extensive undertakings."
Among these, "vajra-pillar" means immovable. "Resembling the sky" means being like space because of being unstained even by those actions performed for the sake of maintaining the body.
"Swallowed" means dissolved within one's own self, which is the nature of consciousness.
The meaning is that he is completely satisfied with and indifferent toward the entire web of the world.
Having become like space, his mental engagement with all forms and perceptions has entirely vanished.
It is devoid of the states of cause, effect, agency, that which is to be abandoned, and that which is to be acquired.
Form is the object;
light is the means for its apprehension.
*Manaskṛtiḥ* is *manaskāraḥ*;
it means the mental application (*anusandhāna*) toward a form perceived by light. (MT_2,17.45) Possessing a body yet bodiless; though within saṃsāra, not transmigrating.

Consisting of consciousness alone, he is like the interior of a stone that has been struck; [he is] "with body" (sadehaḥ), because the body still remains as the residue of the vital principle (sattva).

"Without body" (nirdeha) because of the absence of ego-identification with the physical body; "consisting of consciousness" (cinmaya) because of the certainty that "I am of the nature of consciousness";
[and] "the interior of solid stone."
That which is his belly—
by that he is compared;
such is he, because he consists of pure consciousness beyond the reach of thought.
The sun of consciousness, though shining in the world, is like the interior of darkness;
although its nature is that of supreme illumination, it has, as it were, entered into a state of supreme blindness.
"The sun of consciousness" means that which has the nature of the sun of consciousness.
For this very reason, even while manifesting in the world,
no entity whatsoever is possible that is devoid of contact with consciousness; for if it were so, it would follow that it lacks the nature of being an existent thing (*sattva*).
It is like the interior of darkness; it is that which has the interior of darkness as its simile, because it is devoid of the differentiation of categories of objects. It is not [perceived].
For within the belly of darkness, there is no discernment of objects;
even that which has the nature of another's light, or even that which has the nature of the transcendent light of consciousness,
becomes as if it has reached supreme blindness, because it does not see anything at all.
Because he is a witness to something [beyond], his wicked play of saṃsāra is restrained; the cholera of his desires is destroyed;
the vampire of his egoism has perished; though possessing a body, he is bodiless.
This is clear.
(MT 2.17.48) This splendor of the world rests upon a single tip of one of his body hairs, like a bee upon a flower somewhere on Mount Mahāmeru. (MU 2.17.49)
In some [place], so subtle as to be impossible to describe—in the remainder of the phrase, it is "like a dream.
For in a dream, the world of the dream resides within some part of a person.
Within the hollow of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) in every single atom—(MT_2,17.49)
It sustains thousands of world-lakṣmīs and, having created them, beholds them—
[this occurs] within the hollow, situated in the midst of the sky of consciousness, which is the very nature of the space of pure consciousness.
In every single atom, he creates and sustains thousands of world-glories;
not only does he sustain them,
but because he abides as their witness, he also beholds them.
Now, one might ask: "How is it that he contains thousands of world-glories within himself?
To this, he says in the final verse of the chapter:
"He contains [them] within" (*antarvartayati*). [The manuscript reading *vartayatīty* is corrected to *vartayatīty*].

O Mahāmati, even by hundreds of thousands of Hari, Hara, and the lotus-born Brahmā, the expansion of the heart of one who possesses liberation cannot be measured; alas, there is surely no such expansion for that which is non-existent.
(The word *bata* expresses certainty.)
O Mahāmati, for a person who possesses liberation— that is, one endowed with liberation through the gateway of hearing the discourse on Nirvāṇa—
there is an extensive exposition concerning the heart, primarily emphasizing its essential nature.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is "extensive within the heart.
That [expansiveness] cannot be brought within the scope of measurement or comparison even by hundreds of millions of Viṣṇus, Śivas, and Brahmās;
for it is the vastness of the multitude of entities consisting of Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, and so forth, which are themselves non-entities (avastu).
"Certainly" (*nūnam*) indicates certainty.
It does not exist;
moreover, it is not logical for a non-entity (*avastu*) to become an entity (*vastu*).
And thus, there is no contingency of the aforementioned location; this is the intended meaning.
May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the seventeenth canto in the *Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskara Kaṇṭha.
Oṃ. For the sake of engaging the listeners, he explains that this treatise, being distinct from others, serves as a means for others toward right knowledge:
"Upon merely reciting this, supreme awakening arises."
Since, like a seed sown, a good fruit necessarily arises from it—
in this Saṃhitā which sets forth the means to liberation—
what is "awakening" (bodha)?
Because from that awakening,
the auspicious fruit called liberation— the excellent fruit—
inevitably comes to be.
From what [is it like]? It is like from a sown seed.
[Objection: Having abandoned other treatises composed by the Great Sage, why do you accept this very treatise?
To this he replies:
"Even a human-authored treatise is to be accepted if it teaches through reasoning;
however, anything else must be rejected even if it is of ṛṣi-origination, by one who relies solely on logic. (MU 2.18.2)
If human effort— that which is produced by man—
is to be accepted, it must be grasped.
That which makes reasoning known is that which makes sound logic known;
the other is that which does not make reasoning known.
"Ārṣa" means composed by the sages (ṛṣis).

And here, those endowed with intuition should understand a certain intention, which we have stated at the very outset: that for those possessed of intuition, [this matter] is to be known by themselves, whereas for those devoid of it, it is not to be explained.
"A statement endowed with reason is to be accepted even from a child;
anything else is to be rejected like a blade of grass—even so it was said by the Lotus-born One. (MU 2.18.3)
In this case as well, those possessed of intelligence (pratibhāvat) should personally understand the meaning stated at the outset as something to be known by oneself;
nor should they show disregard for this treatise because of their understanding of it, for that would result in the loss of their intelligence.
This applies likewise to what follows hereafter.
In this regard, one should infer for oneself.
Furthermore, he explains this very same point by way of another method: "He who would drink from a bitter well, thinking, 'This is the well of my father's water'—"
Who would instruct that person who, having abandoned the water of the Ganges standing right before him, pursues one possessed by passion?
That person who, having abandoned the water of the Ganges standing in front of him...
"This well belongs to my own father, my father"—
for this reason,
it is called *kaupam*, meaning "pertaining to a well."
Who would instruct— that is, advise— that passionate man, who is possessed of the defect known as attachment toward his father, by making him drink bitter water?
The sense is that he is not worthy of instruction;
this is the intended meaning here:
"the person who..."
Even a human statement endowed with sound reasoning is rejected on the grounds that "this is of human origin";
yet a statement of the ṛṣis, even if devoid of such reasoning, is accepted.
One accepts [the text] merely on the grounds that "it is of the Ṛṣis"; no further instruction regarding it need be given.
"For one who is passionate" (*rāgiṇam*);
"his instruction" (*tasyopadeśaḥ*) follows the very subject at hand.
Just as when the dawn has begun, light will inevitably arrive; so too, upon this being recited, one's own discernment will surely come. [In the verse,] "uṣasi" is an archaic (ārṣa) feminine form.

Self-discrimination (*svaviveka*) is discrimination regarding the Self (*ātmaviveka*). When the teaching has been heard from the mouth of a wise person, or when it has been understood by oneself, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) arises in the intellect through gradual inquiry. (MU 2.18.6)
First, there arises within him a highly refined command of speech—
pure, liberated, and lofty like a climbing vine— which serves as the ornament for the assembly hall.
This is clear.

"Now, for me who am dispassionate, what is the purpose of refined speech? To this he replies: "A supreme dispassion arises, endowed with the quality of greatness, by which even kings and even pythons are moved to affection. (MU 2.18.8)

For even kings, when they encounter those who are dispassionate, come to feel affection for them as if they were pythons. A man who knows what precedes and what follows becomes wise in all matters, just as one with good eyesight and a lamp in hand [discerns things] in the night. (MU 2.18.9)
In all matters and in every worldly transaction,
defects such as greed and delusion gradually diminish sufficiently,
just as the mist over the quarters of the sky vanishes in the approaching autumn. (MU 2.18.10)
What are greed, delusion, and the rest?
The meaning is that they become attenuated, just as mists over a direction where autumn is near— that is, during the approaching autumn season— become thin.
Just as mists [disperse],
so too do the intellects depend solely upon the practice of discernment;
no action whatsoever bears fruit without its own repeated practice.
Now, one might ask: for what purpose do they require the practice of discrimination?
To this, he says:
The mind attains clarity like a great lake in autumn;
it achieves supreme equanimity like the ocean when the Mandara mountain has ceased its churning.
Clarity (*prasāda*) refers to purity due to being free from the impurities of passion and other afflictions.
It acquires— that is, it maintains— the quality called equanimity (*sāmya*), which is supreme and unsurpassed.
In this case as well, agency belongs to the mind alone.
With its darkness dispelled, like a vajra-tip that has cast down the veil of gloom,
wisdom blazes forth intensely, discerning the true nature of things.
"Nirasta" means gone far away;
"kālimā" means turbidity; she is one who possesses that [turbidity].
(MT_2,18.13) Views such as dejection, poverty, and faults have been shown to have their internal [nature] revealed.

They do not cut into the vital points, as arrows [do not pierce] one who is clad in armor. "Shown" means analyzed; those [words] whose internal portion, known as the essence (*sāra*), has been revealed.
The meaning is that they are known to be devoid of essence.
Terrifying fears of cyclic existence do not seize the heart of the wise man, even though they stand before him, just as rats cannot gnaw through a great boulder.
Of what nature is the heart?
Even though it stands before one, even though it is situated in front;
furthermore, of what nature is it? It is wise.
"How might there be a primacy of destiny or of human effort regarding birth and action?"—
such a multitude of doubts is pacified just as darkness is dispelled by the sun.
(MU 2.18.16) "Of destiny and human effort" means of fate and personal exertion.
Primordially, it is the state of being the cause.
In every way, the attachment to all things subsides when the light of wisdom has dawned, as when the night has passed away.
In all things— namely, all entities that are fit for relinquishing or acquiring—
the connection consisting of relinquishing and acquiring subsides in every way.
Under what condition does this occur?
When the light of the vow had arrived,
as if the night of the moonless dark had already passed.
The meaning is that equanimity alone prevails everywhere.
Like the depth of the ocean, like the stability of Mount Meru,
and like the internal coolness of the moon, it arises in the one who investigates.
This is clear.
(MU 2.18.18) That state of liberation while living gradually reaches its full fruition, entering into the yogi whose every conceptual construction has been stilled. (MU 2.18.19)
That [state] is well-known to the yogin; "having entered" means having effected an entry.
Cool toward all objects, pure, supremely illuminating, and wise,
it attains supreme radiance like the full lunar moonlight.
[This occurs] regarding all objects— whether existent or non-existent— which comprise the totality of things.
"Cool" means free from the afflictions known as joy and resentment;
"pure" means free from passion and the like;
she is such because she bestows the supreme light, which is the light of pure consciousness alone.
It is both beautiful and wisdom, thus "excellent wisdom" (*sudhī*);
it belongs to the moon, thus "lunar" (*aindavī*).
In the stainless space of the heart, where the sun of discernment shines with the light of tranquility—(MT_2,18.20)
The banners of the Kali age, which bring about a multitude of misfortunes,
do not rise against one who possesses such tranquility (śama) as their light; for "kali" here refers to strife and agitation.
The *ketus* are the defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which serve as signs;
and at the rising of the sun, the *ketus*, namely the comets (*dhūmaketus*), do not rise.
They are pacified, they attain purity, and they remain gentle when [the mind] is well-elevated.
Cravings that are unsteady and dull are like rows of clouds in autumn;
they are not unsteady and dull [in the case of the wise]. Cruel vulgar behavior, which produces whatever it may, ceases.
With dejected faces, she was like the sport of the *piśācas* at the arrival of day;
acting as she pleased and doing what was improper,
for through vulgarity a man does whatever comes to mind.
When the intellect is firmly fixed upon the wall of the Dharma and has taken up the yoke of fortitude,
mental afflictions do not ravish it, just as winds cannot destroy a painted creeper.
Dharma alone is the wall; she was clinging to it, and for that very reason had ascended the burden of fortitude— that is to say, she was endowed with steadfastness.
For one who is endowed with the Dharma becomes steadfast;
"citrarūpā latā" means a variegated creeper—[he destroys] that.
An embodied being endowed with fortitude does not fall into the pit consisting of attachment to sense objects;
for who indeed, knowing the path, would run headlong into a chasm?
In that which consists of attachment to sense objects, i.e., in the form of addiction to enjoyments; he supports this very point with the second half of the verse: "Who indeed... and so forth.

In action that is free from attachment to sense objects, consistent with sacred scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous, his intellect delights in whatever comes to him, like a noble woman in the courtyard of the inner apartments.

Those whose conduct and behavior are virtuous through immersion in the true scripture known as the *Mokṣopāya*; for such persons, [the teaching is] according to what has been attained, that which comes by the natural flow.
But not without effort:
"In the millions of worlds, however many atoms there may be, one whose mind is free from the notion of creation perceives the creations situated within each and every one of them. (MU 2.18.27)
He is one whose intellect is free from the notion of creation;
it is a marvel that, despite such an intellect, he perceives creation in every single atom through the knowledge of the pervasion of pure consciousness, which is the seed of creation.

The vision of creation should be understood as occurring within every single atom. (MU 2.18.27) For a person whose inner organ has been purified by the realization of the means to liberation, the flood of enjoyments neither causes distress nor brings delight at any time. (MU 2.18.28)
The meaning is that he maintains equanimity toward enjoyments.
He beholds the multitudes of creations falling and rising in every single atom without restraint, like waves upon the water. (MU 2.18.29)
They fall and become latent;
they leap up and manifest. He does not hate what has arisen, nor does he long for what has ceased.
"Even though he is awakened, he performs his duties like an unawakened tree.
His state of being unawakened with respect to himself should be understood as his state of being unawakened within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Now, one might ask: "What kind of excellence does he possess? To this, he says:
An excellence is seen that is common to the world, following what has been attained; yet,
in the attainment of desired or undesired fruits, his heart is not defeated.
It is common to the world and not something extraordinary;
it is a continuation, a following along, with respect to what has been obtained as it arrives in the natural flow.
He who possesses [it] is one who follows according to what has been attained;
[this occurs] in the heart, that is, in the mind.
He was not defeated, for he was no longer subject to joy or resentment.
(MU 2.18.31) Having studied this entire treatise and having discerned it, one experiences this directly; it is not merely a matter of spoken words like a boon or a curse. (MU 2.18.32)
"You certainly experience this aforementioned fruit.
Anticipating the question, "Indeed, how can we be capable of experiencing this due to the fear of transgression (pratyavāya)? he says:
"But it has not been so stated."
The phrase "like mantras and so forth" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Now, one might ask: "Since this is difficult to understand, how can we engage with it? To this, he says:
"This treatise is indeed easy to understand, being adorned with various ornaments."
Poetry is dense with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), beautiful, and instructive through examples.
The phrase "instructive through examples" serves as a reason, by way of a qualification, for its ease of comprehension.
One who knows even a few words and their meanings understands this [poetry] quite naturally on their own.
But he who does not know this himself must hear it from a wise person;
[the phrase] "one who knows even a little of the words and their meanings" means that such a person understands and comprehends.
"Now, what is to be done by one who lacks knowledge of the words and their meanings?
To this he says: "By himself" (svayam).
"But what will be accomplished by hearing this? To this he says:

When this has been heard, reflected upon, and known, then for the attainment of liberation, no further practice such as austerity, meditation, or recitation is of any use here. "Heard" means having been brought within the range of hearing.

When the Self has been brought within the range of mental reflection— that is, when it has been known and meditated upon— for one who has thus engaged in hearing and the other stages of practice; (MT_2,18.35)
For a person who has repeatedly examined this scripture through intense study,
preceded by scholarship and the refinement of the mind,
the formidable demon of the seer and the seen— the notions of "I" and "the world"— is destroyed.
Like a *piśāca* [ghost] that subsides by itself at sunrise, the *piśāca* of the seer and the seen ceases without obstacle. By this,
it has been stated that both the external purpose and the internal purpose will be accomplished.
The delusion that "the world exists" and "I exist"—though it remains present—subsides;
like a dream-delusion once fully recognized, it no longer delights us at all. (MU 2.18.38)
It remains as it is; it has not entered into a state of absorption by means of the application of mantras and so forth.
[An objection: "But how can there be pacification of that which is already established?
To this, he says: "The delusion of a dream."
The meaning is that even for one who is devoid of flavor (*arasa*) and remains [in that state], peace alone is to be known, because of the absence of anything that causes agitation.

Just as joy and dejection do not afflict a person within a city of imagination (*saṃkalpanagara*), so too [joy and sorrow] do not afflict one internally when the delusion of the world (*jagadbhrama*) has been fully understood.
"Within the mind" means when it has been thoroughly understood and correctly ascertained;
the phrase "joy and dejection do not afflict [one]" is drawn forward by the word "tathā" (thus).
Just as a painted snake, once fully recognized, does not cause fear of a snake,
so too a visible snake, once fully recognized, does not bestow pleasure or pain.
When this [visible snake] is fully recognized and correctly determined to be "this is a painted snake," it no longer causes fear.

The snake called "visible" is the visible snake. (MT 2.18.40) Just as the state of being a snake in a painted snake perishes through thorough knowledge, so too does cyclic existence, though it remains present, become pacified. (MU 2.18.41)
This is clear.
(MT 2,18.41) Now, one might object: "The attainment of the ultimate truth is indeed extremely difficult for us;
and thus, for the sake of attaining it, there must be this immersion into the treatise."
"It is indeed improper. To this he replies:
"In the touching of a *sumana* blossom, some degree of contact may occur;
but in the attainment of the state of ultimate reality, for us there is no contact whatsoever. (MU 2.18.42)
In the phrase *sumanaḥpallavāmarśe*:
*sumanaḥpallavāmarśe* means "in the crushing of flower-buds"; *vyatikaraḥ* means "effort."
The meaning is: [this applies] to us who know the reasoning, but not to you who do not know the reasoning.
In "sumanaḥpallavāmarśe," *amarśe* means the crushing of flowers and sprouts; in "°marde," *mardde* [is used].
This expresses precisely the absence of contact.
In the crushing of a flower petal, there occurs a vibration of its parts;
here, however, there is only the cognition of the mere intellect, not the cognition of the limbs or parts of the body.
"Gacchati" means it becomes engaged or operative.
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *gam* here functions in this sense [of "awakening"]. "Limbs" refers to the parts of the body;
"awakening" means setting them in motion. (MT_2,18.43)
Seated on a comfortable seat, eating as is appropriate,
never remaining engaged in activities contrary to good conduct,
and reflecting at ease according to the occasion and the place.
By encountering this scripture or another, as may be possible, through association with the virtuous,
one attains the awakening of great knowledge which brings peace to saṃsāra; by means of that,
one does not again undergo the torment of the machine of the womb.
This occurs according to possibility, and not as something achieved through deliberate effort.

For it is said that one should "not remain" in actions contrary to virtuous conduct (*sadācāra*), because remaining therein leads to the fault of engaging in rejection or acceptance [of what is improper]. "According to the moment" means at every instant.

"Sukha" means that which bestows happiness; "yathāsambhavaḥ satsaṅgaḥ" means where there is association with the virtuous as far as possible; "idaṃ śāstram" refers to this treatise called the "Means to Liberation" (mokṣopāya) which I am about to proclaim.
"Other" refers to another scripture similar to this one.
"Great knowledge-awareness" (*mahājñānabodha*) is awareness whose nature is great knowledge.
This [term] is connected with the first half-verse.

Those beings who, having obtained enjoyments, remain fixed upon their taste for this much alone— they are not even to be mentioned as the lowest, being like worms in the excrement of their own mothers. (MU 2.18.47)
"In such a limited amount of rasa,
the *bhūtas* are ordinary beings.
Having thus stated the greatness of the scripture, he brings Śrī Rāma face to face.
Listen now, O Rāghava, to this expansion of knowledge being told by me, which is the innermost essence of the intellect—
possessing an interior more essential than the intellect itself.
The meaning is that it surpasses the intellect.
Regarding the phrase "surpassing the intellect" (*buddhyatiśāyī*),
having anticipated the objections raised by Śrī Rāma in the middle [of the text],
he says: "Listen in detail to her by whom this scripture is heard."
This meaning is investigated by means of that very technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*) and reasoning (*yukti*) through which this scripture is heard.
Listen to that in detail; and listen also to that by which it is investigated—this is the connection with what precedes. (MT_2,18.49)
He explains the definition itself:

"The wise know that to be an example (dṛṣṭānta) by which there is an understanding of an object not yet experienced here through the observation [of another], which yields the fruit of assisting comprehension. (MU 2.18.50)
The comprehension of an object through what has been seen: by means of that which has been seen,
there arises a cognition that is the comprehension of an object not previously experienced.
The wise call that an illustration; of what nature is it? It is the benefit known as awakening.
That very fruit; that which bestows it is "of such a kind. To the question, "What is the purpose of providing an example? he says here:
Without an illustration, O Rāma, a novel matter is not understood,
just as at night in a house one cannot perceive the vessels and utensils without a lamp.
"Vessels and utensils" (*bhāṇḍopakaraṇa*) refers to the collection of articles.

O Kākutstha, by whichever examples you are made to understand here by me, all of them indeed possess a cause; however, that which is to be attained is without cause. "Prāpyam" means that which is to be reached.
Existence (sat) is the reality known as pure being (sanmātra).
Regarding the phrase "called the six measures" (*sanmātrākhyaṃ*),
in response to the inquiry— namely, whether all these examples (*dārṣṭāntika*) are exactly like this or whether there are others—
the author says "all" (*sarvāṇi*).
Furthermore,
other instances where the relationship of cause and effect is declared between the object of comparison and the comparison exist for all things indeed, with the exception of the Supreme Brahman.
Excluding the supreme Brahman, among the examples and the things illustrated,
there exists the nature of arising and the relationship of cause and effect.
The meaning is that Brahman has neither an effect nor a cause;
therefore, the intention is that not all illustrative examples (dārṣṭāntika) are similar to Brahman.
[The example of the instruction on "hm" is indeed told here for him.
Therefore, he states the result.
For when an illustration from the instruction of Brahman is indeed mentioned here, it is therefore accepted as having a common property with only one part [of the subject].
"Hi" signifies certainty; "ataḥ" means for this reason.
In this world,
when an illustration of Brahman is spoken of, or when an illustration of Brahman is mentioned therein,
"having a common property in one respect" means being similar in one respect.
It is accepted [as a partial similarity],
but not as total identity; for the Brahman under discussion (the *dārṣṭāntika*) is unfit to be both cause and effect,
whereas the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) exists precisely as both effect and cause.
Such is the intended meaning.
[Of the Dārṣṭāntika:
Whatever example is given here for the realization of the reality of Brahman, each and every one of them should be understood as belonging to a world seen in a dream. (MU 2.18.55)
The meaning is that this world, perceived in a dream, is of the nature of an illusion. He states the conclusion: [text follows].
This being so, how can there be an example possessing form for Brahman which is formless? Thus, the conceptual utterances of fools do not arise;
"do not arise" means they do not emerge.
The intended meaning is that this has already been refuted by us for that very reason.
Therefore,
in the refutation of examples, no other [fault] such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) or contradictory (*viruddha*) arises, because the world is like a dream. (MU 2.18.57)
What is "other" than the aforementioned view?
None at all.
This statement—such as "this is established," "this is contradictory," and so forth—is a view consisting of [assertions like] "this is established" or "this is contradictory."
Because the world is like a dream, when a critique of an example is raised, it does not arise for the purpose of critiquing the example itself.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the view that "this is established" or "this is contradictory" [only] in a partial sense;
for in a world comparable to a dream, one cannot say "this is established" or "this is contradictory."
The meaning is that speaking [of it] is not logical, because everything is illogical.
"Perceiving what is established, contradictory, and so forth" means "he knows" (*veti*);
[this is the sense]. (MT_2,18.57)
That which is non-existent in the past and the future is examined as being present;
just as waking is, so is dreaming—this is established, unimpaired, even for children.
(MU 2.18.58) [siddham] °ddha[m]
Regarding the two objects of the past and the future,
the term "non-entity" (*avastu*) is a designation emphasizing their ontological status;
that is, their lack of substantiality (*asattva*), which is established through an investigation of the present.

For in the present, that which has already passed is non-existent because it has gone, and that which is yet to come is non-existent because it has not arrived; thus its lack of reality enters the path of investigation.
Since it is non-different from those two, the unreality of the present as well is unavoidable—this should be understood by oneself.
Therefore, [this applies] from children up to the very foolish.
"Just as a dream, so is waking"—
this is unimpeachable and is thus established as correct.
The unreality [of things]:

"Those objects which appear through dreams, mental constructions, meditation, curses, medicinal herbs, and so forth, serve as examples here, because the state of the world possesses that same nature. (MU 2.18.59)
Regarding the phrase "those objects," the word "seen" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Because they have that nature—that is, the nature of objects such as those in dreams—and because of this partial similarity (*ekadeśasādharmya*), the relationship of exemplifier and exemplified (*upamānopameyabhāva*) exists here between unreal entities and the real Brahman; this is the intended meaning.
"Regarding those points [which are established] by similarity in one respect"—
if you ask, "What is the status of the other treatises composed by you?", he says here: [they are established] by similarity in one respect.
Whatever other treatises have been composed by the author for the sake of the means to liberation, in those as well,
this alone is the singular method for the awakening to that which is to be known.

The meaning is: "by me," the author who has composed this work as a means to liberation; "of the object to be awakened," that is, of the reality of Brahman which is to be made known; "in awakening," that is, in its exposition.
"Vyavasthā" means the established order.
Now, one might ask: "In what way does the world possess a resemblance to a dream? To this, he says:
"And that the world has the appearance of a dream will be understood from the sacred scripture (*śruti*) and the authoritative treatise (*śāstra*)."
"It cannot be spoken quickly, for speech indeed proceeds in succession.
[The word] *avabhotsyate* means "it will be understood" or "it can be known."
"In that case, please explain the entire treatise all at once.
To this, he replied:
"Swiftly."
The sequential nature of speech is indeed evident;
for it is not possible to utter a second or subsequent sentence without having completed the first sentence.
One will realize that the world is like a dream, a mental construction, a meditation, a city [of the gandharvas], and so forth;
since these alone are the examples, therefore they appear here and no others. (MU 2.18.62)
Regarding the examples:
since the world consists of those cities and so forth which are seen in dreams, mental constructions, and meditative concentrations.
The analogy for them is such that it becomes like that; therefore, those very things— the city of *sudhyāna* and so forth— appear as examples, manifesting within our intellect.
Other things, such as cities and the like, though real,
do not appear [in that way], because they are illogical [in that context].

Therefore, those very things such as the city of Sudhyāna and so forth— which are compared to awakening by means of their causes— are not the actual causes. In those cases of illusory comparisons, complete similarity is not possible.

Brahman is without cause, being devoid of any causal factor. It is compared through illusions of similes—through errors consisting of forms that lack any commonality whatsoever with other things seen as similes. (MT_2,18.63)

The wise person, being free from dispute, must accept that the object of comparison shares a common property with the standard of comparison in at least one respect, for the sake of understanding. It is the wise person who does so, not the unwise.
The sense is that he remains intent on dispute from the very outset.
Now, one might ask: "How can an analogy through a single similar property bring about the cognition of the object of comparison?
To this, he establishes an illustrative example.
Indeed, when perceiving an object, apart from the mere light [emitted] by a lamp,
nothing at all— such as the vessel, the oil, or the wick— is produced. (MU 2.18.65) [sthālatailavartyādi] [vartyā°]
"From mere luster" means from that which has the nature of mere light.
"Sthāla" means a vessel.
This very point is stated in connection with the illustrative example.
"O dear one, through its similarity in one respect, the means of comparison brings about the cognition of the object compared,
just as a lamp reveals an object by means of its light— that is, by its single part called radiance.
(MU 2.18.66) [The phrase "by means of its light" refers to that single part known as radiance.]
When the awakening of understanding regarding that which is to be known arises through even a mere portion of an illustration,
the determination of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) should be grasped as something to be adopted;
the sense is that one must not remain at the mere illustration alone.
One must not, by falling into the state of a fallacious logician, destroy awakened consciousness through impure conceptual constructions that deny direct experience. (MU 2.18.68) [Note:
*anubhūtyapalāpāt* is the corrected reading.]
Awakenedness is the state of being a knower (*jñānitā*).
For sophists, by raising objections at the very outset, destroy this awakenedness.
By what kind of conceptual constructions?
Regarding what has been experienced, there is denial (*apalāpa*), which is concealment (*nihnava*);
by that [denial], they are "seized" or taken hold of.
(MT 2,18.68) Now, one might ask: "Why should we abandon the ancient scriptures and treatises to accept the scripture spoken by you? To this, he says:
Even if it arises from deliberation and produces experience, a body of words that has come down through tradition among people like us—
even if spoken by a woman— nevertheless, any other Vedic statement is merely the babbling of words and not *āgama*.
(MU 2.18.69) [The phrase] "among people like us" refers to those who are authoritative.

"Even that spoken by a woman" means even the incoherent prattle uttered by a woman; "the state of being a discourse on the treatise" (vāṅmayaprasaṅgatām) means the state of being a discourse on the scripture (śāstraprasaṅgatām),
which is to say, the status of being a scripture (śāstratvam).
It has approached.
Of what nature is it?
It brings about experience through investigation.
Now, in the alternative case:
even Vedic speech is merely *pralāpa*—that is, mere babble;
it does not constitute *āgama* because it lacks the capacity to produce direct experience (*anubhava*). This is the meaning.
He expresses this very point with the final verse of the chapter:
"O dear one, we possess the conviction that this is so; therefore, the unification of all scriptures into a single statement has borne fruit.
Consequently, for us, there is no means of valid cognition other than the self-awareness nourished by the intrinsic limbs of the scripture consisting of the apparent reality. (MU 2.18.70)
"O friend, we possess this understanding;
for that reason,
by means of that intellect of ours."
Because the unification of all treatises into a single voice has borne fruit;
for this reason,
for us.
There is no means of valid cognition other than experience, that is, knowledge;
in every treatise, we have observed that experience alone is the means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the sense is that for us as well, that very [consciousness] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
From what kind of consciousness? From that which is characterized by self-awareness (*saṃvedana*).
The "conventional" (prātītika) is that which has come from cognition;
it is not, however, the imagined (kalpita).
This is the meaning.
That treatise which consists of that [knowledge] is itself its own limb because it is beneficial; thus, "from that nourished" means from that which has attained growth.
