[The meaning: Thus ends the eighteenth canto in the section on those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu-prakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. *Arthaḥ*. *Arthāḥ*. (MT_2,18.70)
Oṃ. He clarifies once again the very point previously stated:
in similes, it is the possession of common characteristics in specific respects that is grasped;
for if there were complete similarity between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, what difference would there be? (MU 2.19.1)
"By a distinguished part" means by a part that accomplishes the effect.
"Similarity" (*sādharmya*) means resemblance.
The meaning is that because the effect is established even by a single part, there is no [need for further proof]. (MT_2,19.1)
From the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures concerning the realization of the one Self through the Buddha as an illustration,
and through the direct realization of the meaning of the Great Sentence (mahāvākya), peace is called Nirvāṇa. "One" means absolute.
That treatise in which self-knowledge is presented as the subject to be established— of such a treatise, there is a meaning.
Through his realization and reflection,
by means of the arising of the comprehension of the meaning of the great sentence,
which encompasses the determination of the meanings of both the intermediate sentences and the great sentence.
Accomplished peace is the absence of mental agitation;
it is called Nirvana by the wise.
From what kind of sensation?
By means of examples known from the Buddha—that is, established [authorities].
Having determined the meaning of the great sentence by internalizing the meanings of the intermediate sentences, he provides the conclusion:
"Therefore, enough with these outbursts of conceptual constructions regarding the example and the thing exemplified."
By whatever means possible, one should quickly take recourse to the meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*).
"Enough; there is no need for these"—this is the meaning.
Know that peace is the supreme good; one should be diligent in attaining it.
"Rice is to be eaten; it has been obtained. What is the use of these conceptualizations regarding supernatural powers (*siddhi*)?

Peace (*śānti*) is the absence of agitation caused by mental conceptualizations. "By conceptualizations regarding supernatural powers" means by such thoughts as, "How was this accomplished? (MU 2.19.4).
That which is without cause is compared by those seeking awakening to things that possess causes,
using similes that resemble the object of comparison in certain respects. Here,
"that which is without cause" refers to Brahman, which is devoid of any cause.
In one respect, by means of a single quality:
one should not remain here amidst enjoyments with a soul devoid of discernment,
like a blind frog that has grown fat within the belly of a well.
This is clear.

(MT 2.19.6) Through examples and reasonings, one should strive to abandon what is contrary [to the goal] and desire the other; one who possesses discernment should be devoted to the meaning of the treatise on peace. (MU 2.19.7)

"Vāñchita" means desired; "itarat" means other than that which is subject to deliberation. "Śānti" is peace and "śāstrārtha" is the meaning of the treatise; he who shines by means of these two is [described] as such. (MT_2,19.7)
From time to time,
he engaged in the practice of acquiring wealth for righteous purposes through the study of scriptures,
tranquility, amiability, wisdom, and association with those who know them.
The wise person should investigate until they attain rest within themselves—
that peace called the fourth state (turyapada), which is beyond further destruction.
Scripture, tranquility, gentleness, wisdom, and association with those who know that [reality]— these are the means.
He was characterized by these;
that is, he acquired, from time to time— that is, repeatedly— in the midst of matters consistent with the Dharma, meanings that do not deviate from the Dharma.
One who possesses such actions—
such a wise person should reflect for as long as it takes until [attaining] that which is not subject to further destruction, being devoid of annihilative non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).
It attains that which is designated as the fourth state— that which has "the fourth state" as its name—
the peace characterized by repose within the Self, which is repose in the Self.
From the dharma,
of that; of that, as long as there is no further destruction.
"Now, what will be accomplished by resting in the Self? To this he replies:
"For one who is joined with rest in the Fourth state (turya) and has crossed the ocean of existence—whether living or dead, whether a householder or an ascetic. (MU 2.19.10)
He has no concern with what is done or left undone, nor with the delusions of the Vedas and Smṛtis;
like an ocean without Mount Mandara, he remains as he is.
[This applies] to one who is living—that is, liberated while living (jīvanmukta)—and to one who is not living—that is, liberated after death (videhamukta).
"Artha" means purpose.
Now, one might ask: "How does it remain? To this, he says:
"Nirmanthara" means that it is endowed with rest.
In one respect, there is a commonality of properties between the objects of comparison and the subject of comparison.
One who desires awakening for the sake of realizing what is to be awakened should not remain fickle in their questioning;
"cañcu" by means of "codya" means one who is known as, or is famous for, being such [a person].
"Thus, one whose beak is [sharp] for challenging" means one who has the habit of posing challenges.
Whatever is to be understood must be understood by you quickly through whatever means possible; that leads to liberation. Yet those who are agitated and eager for debate do not perceive this.
The word "te" (they) is a genitive case used in the sense of the agent; "tvām" (you) is the understood object; "vyākulāḥ" means agitated and eager to raise objections.
At that time, they do not even see you; what need is there to mention that they might attain you? This is the sense.
"Agitated and eager for inquiry":
he describes the characteristic of one eager for inquiry [as follows]:
"When [the mind] has come to rest in the heart, which is the space of consciousness, in the nature of experience..."
He who asks about what is not beneficial regarding the vast reality is called one who is prone to frivolous objection.

Even when [the mind] has come to rest in the heart— that is, in the *manas*, within the sky of consciousness (*saṃvidākāśa*), the sky of awareness (*cidākāśa*) which consists of experience— [it remains so].
One who, regarding a matter, poses a question that is useless in the form of a doubt,
is called by the wise a "readily provoked querist."
The sense is that he who repeatedly raises objections even regarding a matter already established by his own experience is called "skilled in caviling" (codyacañcu).
The questioner:
The ignorant person, conceptualizing through portions of conceited discrimination, defiles his internal awakening, just as a snake defiles its own stainless mouth. (MU 2.19.15)

By means of the conceit "I am one whose nature is to correctly admonish," that is, by means of conceptual fragments produced through such conceit; by means of conceptual fragments in the form of admonitions;
internally, within oneself.
The ignorant one, conceptualizing his own cognition— that is, making it endowed with conceptual construction—
defiles awareness; he renders it corrupted by the impurity of duality.
Therefore, the sense is that you should not entertain futile conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
He now introduces the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that are useful for this instruction.

O Rāma, just as the ocean is the single locus for all existing waters, so too is perception the sole means of valid cognition here; listen to that. [MU 2.19.16] Of all existing means of valid cognition, which are divided into various types such as inference and the rest—of them all.
Just as the ocean is the place and support of the waters,
so too there is only one means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in this world, namely perception (pratyakṣa).
For inference and the other [means of knowledge] cannot exist without perception.
O Rāma!
Listen to that which is called direct perception (pratyakṣa), the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The place [sthānaṃ]— he declares it to be indeed direct perception:
"The wise know that the essence of all objects is direct perception, which is sensation."
"Indeed, that which is established with respect to that [object] is declared to be direct perception (pratyakṣa).
The 'supreme' means the most excellent;
because it bestows accomplishment by way of revealing the essence of all objects, the realization that constitutes the essence is indeed knowledge."
They know it as *adhyakṣa* because the word *adhyakṣa* denotes the essential substance;
O Rāma, "nūnam" signifies certainty.
That which is established as being directly perceived with respect to the nature of sensation— that object is designated as "perceptual" by the wise.
Based on the etymological derivation that "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is that which is established in relation to the sense faculty (*akṣa*),
and because the word *akṣa* denotes the "supervisor" (*adhyakṣa*)— just as in the case of the word *bhāma*—
what follows from this? To this, he says:

Because it is the experiencing, the feeling, and the comprehension of things as they truly are, it is given the name "direct perception" (pratyakṣa) here; and that very thing is the living being (jīva). Therefore, by the wise...
Of experience, which is of the nature of experiencing; of realization, which is of the nature of realizing;
and of feeling.
In this world,
that which exists as it is and not otherwise conceived is given the name "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
Since only that which is feeling is established as being with respect to feeling, and because everything else is absorbed into it, that alone becomes the living soul (*jīva*).

Since anything other than feeling, such as the body, is like a stone and thus incapable of being the living soul, one should understand that the distinction between them is made by the clarity or lack of clarity in experience and cognition. (MT_2,19.18)
He explains that this very nature belongs to all objects:
consciousness itself is that [Self], which consists of the notion of "I-ness. That consciousness by which an object arises is known as the "object" (*padārtha*). (MU 2.19)

That very same living being (jīva) is consciousness (saṃvit) during the state of ascent; that same being becomes of the nature of the notion of "I" (ahaṃtā-pratyaya-ātmaka) during the state of descent.

That individual soul (jīva), whose nature consists of the notion of "I-ness," arises— that is, it manifests— in the form of that consciousness by which, or through that perception of a jar and so forth,
it emerges.
That consciousness is what is remembered by the wise as the "referent" (padārtha);
for indeed, apart from consciousness, the referent has no separate intrinsic nature of its own.
Even if it exists, it is non-existent because it is a mental construction;
for without consciousness, that which exists does not truly exist.
In the state of ascent, it is ascent; in the state of descent, it is descent.
It is non-existent; it is non-existent. (MT_2,19.19)
It describes how the world-nature of objects arises through delusions consisting of various successions created by conceptualization, discursive thought, and so forth;
it manifests as a world just as water manifests as waves and the like.
That object,

having its various sequences constructed by conceptualization, discursive thought, and so forth— namely, by those erroneous cognitions such as conceptualization and discursive thought which reside in the subject.
It manifests as the world. How so? Just as water.
The meaning is: "in such a way that it manifests as waves and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "How has pure consciousness come to possess such a form? To this, he says:
"At the beginning of creation, through the play of creation, it was suddenly without cause."
Having manifested itself within itself as its own direct cause, it is direct perception;
it is of the nature of direct perception,
prior to creation.
Being indeed without cause,
at the beginning of creation, at the time when it is oriented toward emanation,
it vibrates through the play of creation.
In the Self, which is of the nature of emanation, within its own self;
by itself, through its own sovereignty;
it has become the cause.
The sense is that it is not appropriate to raise the objection "how [is this so]? regarding that which is established by its own independence.
At the time of the emergence of creation (*sargonmukhatā*), [the text reads] *sargonmu* (MT_2,19.21).
Now, one might ask: what is the nature of the causality belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*), whose form is that of sensation? To this, it is said:
"The causality of this soul, though non-existent, remains as a state of deliberation (*vicāra*)."
It is as if the perfection of the world-form has attained manifestation within this [consciousness]. "In the perfection of the world-form" refers to the investigation or reflection;
"of this" refers to the living being whose nature is pure awareness.
Or it becomes a cause; what kind of causality is it?
Even though it is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate truth, even though its own nature is non-existent.
It exists as if real;
furthermore, of what nature is it?
It has attained manifestation, that is, clarity.

Now, does the causality of that living soul (jīva) perish once again, or does it not? To this, he himself says: "But inquiry, having destroyed its own form which is the meaning of the negative particle (nañ), quickly brings about the supreme state as a matter of direct perception. (MU 2.19.23)
Discernment itself, being devoid of the meaning of negation and endowed with its own inherent nature,
destroys its own form— that which is called its own discernment—
and [attains] the supreme state, its own true nature, which is unconditioned by causality.
It makes [the soul] perceptible; by the force of investigation alone, the sense that the soul is a cause perishes once again—this is the meaning. (MT_2,19.23)
Now, in response to the inquiry as to how investigation brings the supreme state into direct perception, he says:
"When even the investigating mind, while investigating, does not perceive itself, then that which is beyond all description remains as the Supreme alone. (MU 2.19.24)
Only this remains:
deliberation (*vicāra*) and reflection (*vimarśa*).
Reflecting upon oneself—that is, making oneself the object of reflection by considering "What is my nature?"—one engages in this investigation.
When one does not perceive a self— because it has no form whatsoever— and thus finds nothing,
then there is the supreme state, the unsurpassed essential nature known as pure consciousness alone, which is beyond all description and devoid of reflective thought.
The meaning is that it remains thus because there is nothing further to be investigated.

[Investigating the self: While investigating, [one asks] whether or not the person performs the functions of the intellect, the senses, and the organs of action in this state. To this, he says: "The person... [nanu].
When the mind is desireless and tranquil, there is no purpose served here by those actions of the cognitive senses, whether they are performed or not, because of the absence of mental cultivation.
[In this context,] "in the mind" refers to the mind whose nature is inquiry.
When [the self] is desireless and does not perform its own activity,
it is therefore peaceful; for the person, by means of those well-known [qualities], [liberation occurs].
Through certain actions performed by the faculties of cognition, no purpose is achieved; and through those not performed, no purpose is achieved either.
Why?
Because of non-cultivation, that is, due to the absence of cultivation;
in other words, because of independence.

By some [it is said]: "by means of the intellectual faculties and actions. [The opponent asks: "In that case, what is the status of the organs of action? To this, he says: (MT_2,19.25) *nanu tadā karmendriyāṇāṃ kā vārtety* / *atrāha*.
Then,
when the mind is desireless and tranquil, those organs of action do not engage at all in action and the like, like a machine that is no longer being operated.
In that state, there is no activity of the organs of action at all;
what, then, can be said of their functions?
Such a state is indeed difficult to attain even for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
For they do not remain here forever;
however, those who are liberated while disembodied (videhamukta) are always identical with this [reality]. Enough of further elaboration.
"Thus" (evam):
with the intention that the peace of the mind will come about precisely through the pacification of the investigation into the nature of sensation (*vedanā*), he says:
"The wise know sensation to be the cause for the movement of the mental machine."
Just as a rope is inserted inside a wooden ram,
so too the wise know that the movement of the mind-mantra (manomantra) has sensation alone as its cause.
For the mind moves immediately after sensation;
the life-channel is the rope within this mind.
Of what [is it the rope]?
The meaning is this: just as in the case of that wooden ram,
the mind is like a wooden ram.
The channel of the vital breath is like a rope;
sensation is like the one who seizes the rope.
This is because sensation alone is the cause for the activity of the mind.
"It is logical that through the pacification of that [feeling],
there is the pacification of that [mind].
Now, let it be granted that there is peace of mind through the pacification of feeling.
When the mind is disturbed by the agitation of sensation, from what does the world emerge? To this, he says:
the world is agitated by form, light, mental attention, objects, and so forth.
Just as there is an internal vibration within the wind, so too [feeling] exists within sensation.
The meaning is that "entities" (*padārtha*) are substances (*dravya*) which serve as the substrata for form (*rūpa*) and the rest;
therefore, the world, in the form of form and so forth, emerges from sensation alone.
"But how can this [limitation] exist for consciousness (*vedana*), which is pure by its very nature? To this he replies:

"Pure consciousness, which perceives all things as its own self, arises in such a way that it manifests itself as consisting of the external forms of space and time, as well as the internal body. (MU 2.19.29)
Pure, it is not established in any particular form;
for this very reason, whatever universal self-awareness arises, it shines and vibrates as being of that very nature.
The sense is that the world does not exist within it like a stain.
Of what nature is that sensation?
It is that which consists of direction, time, the external, and the internal;
that is "direction and so forth."
"Extended" means having attained expansion;
that whose body— its own form— is characterized by the directions and so forth is "that which has as its bodily form the extended external and internal directions and time."
*Digādi*: that whose nature (*svarūpa*) begins with *di*;
he explains that very same point again and again by means of another verse (*ślokāntareṇa*).
[The reading *ślokān ta°* is likely a scribal error for *ślokāntareṇa*.]
The seer alone remains, maintaining his own nature while appearing as the visible object;
just as his own form appears there, so indeed is it.
(MU 2.19.30) [yathā] [ya]thā.
The seer alone is the very nature of sensation; the seer alone appears as the object of vision. Thus, he remains abiding while maintaining such a nature.
In that context, the word "of him" (tasya) is to be understood as "of that [seer]. His own form is how it appears and manifests;
that is his own form.
It is exactly so, and not otherwise; the remainder [of the thought] is that it is like a dream.
Wherever the Self, as it were, has attained the state of volition, all things become that very thing.
It remains there quickly and shines as if it were of that very form.
Everything becomes the Self;
therefore, wherever and in whatever manner that Self abides, there it shines as if it were of that very form.
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, it does not shine, because it remains exactly as it is in its own nature; thus the word "as if" (iva) is employed.
In what manner is the self "as if"?
The meaning is that it has attained the nature of volition and the state of being volitional;
otherwise, its possession of various forms would not be logical.
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*),
how could it be possible for the seer to possess the nature of the seen, as if by virtue of being the self of all? This is not tenable.
The state of being a seer exists only when there is a real seer; however, for that which is non-existent,
there is no object of sight.
Because the seer exists as the pure self of all through its being the nature of everything,

its state of being an object of sight seems plausible; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is not plausible because [the seer] does not deviate from its status as a seer— this is why the word "seems" (iva) is employed.
For that which is non-existent, being non-existent by its own nature,
there is no status as a seer of the visible; for if it were conceived as a seer in relation to itself, it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya) due to its dependence upon itself.
The state of being the seer of the visible [is explained];
by way of being the seer, he states the result.
Therefore, this world remains as the Brahmakalpa, being indeed without cause;
it is directly perceived as the Creator itself, while its parts are without limiting adjuncts (anupādhi).
Thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is without cause because the pure Brahman is not an agent, and is therefore devoid of any causal instrument.
This world remains established as being like Brahmā, resembling Brahmā.
Of what nature is the world?
It is indeed perceptible and manifest;
it is devoid of a creator or a knower, because pure Brahman cannot possess the status of a knower.
Otherwise, the consequence would be impurity.
Now, let it be that Brahman possesses neither causality nor motherhood.
"Let that [non-existence] belong to its parts"—
to this he replies:
"its parts."
But in the other alternative,
the portions (aṃśāḥ) of that Brahman are without limiting adjuncts (anupādhayaḥ), meaning they are devoid of such adjuncts as the nature of being a cause.
Otherwise, it would follow that by way of that [intermediary], the latter too would possess a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Free from creator, [creator], and knower;
the state of being a mother.

Thus, having abandoned this digression, he follows the subject at hand: "O virtuous one, that supreme state, which consists of nothing other than one's own effort alone, is far removed from the meaning of the word 'destiny' (daiva); for it is attained within by a hero through his own human exertion (pauruṣa) alone. (MU 2.19.34)
O virtuous one, having cast far away that which is designated by the word "fate"— which is merely one's own effort imagined as being of another form— [understand this].
That supreme state is attained by the hero through his own inner manly effort— that is, through mental prowess.
With this verse at the end of the chapter, he states the limit of investigation according to the truth and the pure tradition of the lineage of teachers.
Until you yourself attain that supreme state which is pure, awakened, and of infinite forms— by means of truth that is white and free from fault,
according to the doctrine of the lineage of teachers and following their wisdom.
Investigate for as long as it takes until you attain the state of consciousness that has transcended otherness. What is this state of otherness like?
"Purified" means free from the stains known as "cetya. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "self-awakened," meaning awakened by itself.
Furthermore, of what nature is she?
She is "of infinite form," meaning her essential nature is unlimited. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
(MT_2,19.35) Thus ends the nineteenth [chapter] in the *Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
The Chapter.
Gathering together the worldly conduct of one who seeks liberation, he says:
"In the *Āryasaṃgamayukti* and other works, one should forcibly increase wisdom;
from that comes the state of a Great Being through the marks of a Great Being. (MU 2.20.1)
At the outset, by means of association with the noble— through the method known as "association with the virtuous"—
a person should lead their intellect toward growth and the capacity for discernment.
Thereafter, through the marks of a great being accomplished by that intellect, the state of a great being shall arise.

Now, in response to the inquiry, "How can the status of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣatā) be established without the qualities of a Great Being?", he states that one must indeed acquire those very qualities: "Whatever person shines forth here by whichever quality...
[siddhyati].
Thus, for whatever quality a person excels in this world...
Therefore, for the sake of increasing one's intelligence, one should quickly train in each and every one of those [virtues].
There is also a reading, "buddhyā vivṛddhaye," which means "by means of an intelligence increased through association with the noble ones (ārya) and through right reasoning (yukti)."
Otherwise, in the absence of the growth of the intellect, how could there be the capacity to perceive the virtues of others?
[Objection: In that case, since the perception of virtues would be very easy, the state of being a great person (*mahāpuruṣatā*) would also be easily accomplished. To this, he says:
"Indeed, it is well; indeed, it is excellent.

But this state of being a Great Person (mahāpuruṣatā), which is endowed with qualities such as tranquility (śama) and so forth—O Rāma, no one attains perfection without right knowledge (samyagjñāna). (MU 2.20.3)
Therefore, the intended meaning is that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) alone must first be established through association with the noble ones and through reasoning.
[Objection: But what will be accomplished by right knowledge? To this he says:
"From knowledge, tranquility and the other qualities increase through the succession of virtuous persons. (MT_2,20.3)
They are praiseworthy on account of their inner fruit, like fresh sprouts of rain;
from what kind of knowledge?
From that which proceeds from the lineage of holy men (*satpuruṣa*).
But not through the succession of an unworthy person.
"Succession" (krama) means sequence;
by the word "etc. (ādi), self-control and so forth are included.
The word "vṛṣṭeḥ" is in the ablative case.
Now, in response to the inquiry, "What might result even from tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities?", he says:
"From the qualities such as tranquility (*śama*), the supreme knowledge increases."
Like an excellent rain of rice from sacrifices that consist merely of material food, [this knowledge] is the highest;
it is the most excellent because its object is the Supreme Self, being superior to all other forms of knowledge.
He states the result [of this knowledge]:
The virtues, such as tranquility and the rest, arise from knowledge, and likewise, knowledge arises from tranquility and the rest;
these two mutually increase, just like a lake and its waters.
Therefore, from knowledge come tranquility and the other virtues;
from tranquility and the others comes knowledge,
just as a lake arises from the clouds and the waters.
The summary meaning is that the clouds are full of sap.
Furthermore, he explains this very point again:
from knowledge comes the conduct of a true person; from knowledge comes the path of a true person.
Both the sequence of knowledge and the conduct of the virtuous man increase when they proceed reciprocally;
that is to say, [knowledge increases] from the conduct of the virtuous man, such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth.
Now, one might ask: once knowledge and tranquility are perfected, by what effort on the part of the person is the attainment of the supreme state achieved? To this [it is said]:
He provides an answer with an illustration:
"Just as the joy of song is accomplished by Kamalarakṣiṇī through her far-reaching, high-pitched melody, accompanied by the scaring away of birds. (MU 2.20.8)
Accompanied by the far-reaching and lofty [vision],
together with the true person of knowledge, by means of the non-agent who possesses the form of an agent.
In the same way, a man free from desire attains that state by means of such a song as was performed by the cowherd girl Kamalarakṣiṇī—
the song which was both extensive and sublime.
The destruction of birds, which is the removal [of them] from the grain,
is accomplished together with the joy of singing;
for she has no effort toward that end.
For by the mere act of singing, the joy of the song and the destruction of the birds are accomplished;
for it is the very nature of deer that upon hearing a song, they abandon even their food.
Likewise, the agent [says]: "I am not..."
By the "agent"— that is to say, by the Puruṣa who, though free from the taint of agency, appears as if he were an agent due to the certainty [of being so];
and by the two instruments, namely knowledge and the exertion of a true person (jñāna-śatpuruṣa-īhā), which consist of knowledge, tranquility, and so forth.
Without effort— that is, entirely free from exertion—
the supreme state, known as pure consciousness alone,
is reached; that is, it is attained.
The meaning is that the means here consists solely of this—namely, knowledge and tranquility (śama) and so forth—and nothing else whatsoever.
By what kind of person? By one who is a man (puruṣa).
"By one who is desireless" means by one who is devoid of longing even for the attainment of the state [of liberation], due to being full of knowledge, tranquility, and so forth;
the point is that otherwise, because the agitation in the form of desire would persist, there would be no fullness.

He concludes the subject matter of the chapter titled "The Conduct of Those Seeking Liberation" (*mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa*), [referring to] the birds of the bliss of song (*gītānandakhaga*) and the deer (*mṛga*). *gītānandakhagotsādayoḥ*: *da⟨sya⟩* *kha* *go* *mṛgāṇām*: *gā⟨n⟩[ṇ]āṃ* (MT_2,20.8-9)
"O descendant of Raghu, this sequence of right conduct has been declared by me;
now this sequence of knowledge is being correctly taught.
(MU 2.20.10) The sense is that only one who is established in this [conduct] possesses the qualification for the sequence of knowledge that is about to be described.
Now, in response to the inquiry, "What are you doing now?", he says:
"It is taught as follows."
Likewise, just as there is a sequence of right conduct (*sadācāra*),
there is a sequence of knowledge (*jñānakrama*), which is the method for the perfection of self-knowledge taught by Brahmā.
[The author] now describes the greatness of this treatise (*prakaraṇa*).
"This [work], which bestows fame, longevity, and the fruits of human goals,
should indeed be heard by the wise from a trustworthy person who has mastered the meaning of the scriptures.
This section, called "The Conduct of One Seeking Liberation," is intended both to attract those with an external outlook and to grant them long life.
It bestows the fruit of the goals of human endeavor and grants liberation. From what kind of person? From one who is authoritative (*āpta*), meaning one whose knowledge is correctly ascertained.
"Of the self-treatises" means of the treatises on the inner self (*adhyātma-śāstra*).
"By which" refers to their meaning; therefore [it is said].
Now, one might ask: what would come of hearing this? To this, he says:
But having heard this, by the power of the purity of your intellect, you will go to the state of the virtuous,
just as water involuntarily attains clarity through contact with the *kataka* nut.
Having heard this, you—
Through the perfection of the purity of the intellect, by the power [of that purity], you will go to the state of the virtuous without any effort at all.
Here, he provides an illustration with the second half of the verse,
beginning with "yathā" (just as).
*Kataka* is a specific substance that clarifies water.
Now, one might ask: "How does a person attain the supreme state by hearing this?
To this, he provides the answer with the final verse of the chapter:
[the person].
O Sage, once the knowable has been known, this mind indeed goes helplessly to the supreme state;
for that which is realized as the indivisible, supreme [reality] never again abandons the state of realization. (MU 2.20.13) [Skt.
*mune*] → [Skt. *mune*] (corrected from *muner*)
"O Sage, O Śrī Rāma who possesses the form of a sage because you are endowed with the deeds of a sage;
for (hi), because..."
The mind, having known that which is to be known, goes to the supreme state entirely of its own accord.
Therefore, the sense is that for one who has realized the knowable, the attainment of the true state through the hearing of this scripture is indeed logical.
Now, one might ask: even if the mind has known the knowable, if it should ever abandon that state of having known the knowable, what then should be done?
To this, he says:
"That which" (yat). It refers to that object which is supreme in the mind, and not an inferior object consisting of sense-pleasures.
It is perfectly understood and firmly ascertained;
that is the mind.
It refers to the state of awakening to that supreme reality.
For that which is awakening,
it certainly does not abandon its state.
The intended meaning is that one who has known what is to be known never, at any time, loses the state of having known what is to be known.
Thus, "Auspiciousness! Auspiciousness! Auspiciousness! ||| Śivaṃ śivaṃ śivam ||| iti |||1||
The attainment of the six states;
the state of having known that which is to be known.
Thus ends the twentieth canto in the *Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
May this exposition of the conventional discourse of those seeking liberation, intended for listeners whose hearts are graced by the immersion in meditative cultivation, yield excellent fruit.
Let this effort, which is determined by being the effect of those entities, be the capacity of things directed toward an action by virtue of the penetration of their own power.
May this conduct of one seeking liberation, which contemplates the fitness for the noble fruit of attaining one's own true self, manifest within my mind.
Thus all is auspicious.

Thus ends the chapter on the Conduct of those Seeking Liberation in the *Śrī-Mokṣopāya-Ṭīkā*, composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Avatārakaṇṭha, grandson of the venerable Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha—the great devotee of Maheśvara and spiritual preceptor residing within the region of Śrī-Kāśmīra. May there be auspiciousness!
Homage to Śrī Rāma. Oṃ, homage to Śrī Rāma. [Śrī Rāma].

Having subdued the dense darkness of delusion by fixing the mind on the recollection of one's own awakening, and having remembered the sandals of the venerable Guru— which bestow knowledge and possess most exalted power— and having meditated upon that sinless Śrī Gaṇeśa, the son of Śiva and lord of the gods who destroys all obstacles, this commentary on the section concerning the "Manifestation" (utpatti) is being composed by Bhāskara.

Thus, having established the conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*)—which is destroyed by the recollection of one's own awakening—in this chapter called "The Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation" (*mumukṣuvyavahāra*), for the purpose of qualifying [the disciple] for the instruction to be expounded; and having contemplated that Śrī Rāma has attained the fruit of its practice merely by hearing it;

and having determined that the knowledge of the non-arising and the true nature of arising of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is the fundamental cause for attaining liberation, which is the goal to be acquired; [he proceeds].

Commencing the section on origination (*utpatti-prakaraṇa*) which establishes that [reality], and setting aside the impossibility of the relationship between teacher and disciple by resorting to the unity of Brahman that is about to be taught, the author— anticipating an objection raised by another regarding the existence of instruction for a disciple distinct from oneself— first describes the experience of the knower of Brahman, which perceives the distinction between objects even within the unity of Brahman, using the analogy of a dream as the means to resolve that objection.
For the purpose of establishing the qualification for the instruction to be explained:
[having meditated upon] the section on generation (*utpattiprakaraṇa*).
In the absence of the state of instructing disciples distinct from oneself,
first,
the knower of Brahman shines as Brahman within himself through the powers of speech, like a dream.
"That which is this—let him who knows it by means of its own words know that. The word "knows" (vetti), which occurs in the subsequent sentence, should also be construed with the preceding sentence;
thus, this is the meaning.
The knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*) is one who possesses knowledge of Brahman;
he "knows" (*vetti*), meaning he experiences it.
When there is an expectation for the object (*karman*)—as in the expression "see, the deer runs"—the sentence itself is stated as the object.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the splendors of speech": Brahman is some subtle reality expanded (*bṛṃhitam*) into the form of various objects; it shines, that is, it manifests.
It vibrates;
by what does it shine?
By these very words and their meanings.
By means of those entities which are denoted by words such as "the first" (yad-ādi) among the pronominal stems;
that is to say, in their form.
The instrumental case here denotes a state of being (itthambhāve).
Furthermore, when the denotability of things by the first set of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) serves as a characteristic mark of a real entity (*vastu*),

that object where a pronoun is employed is called a "substance" (*dravya*); for it is recorded in the tradition of the learned that "that object is intended to be expressed as something to be differentiated."
It is to be known: in what substratum does it shine? In the Self, upon its own wall, because there is no second entity distinct from it.
And this manifestation should be understood as pertaining to the waking state by implication,
because the dream state is taken as an illustration and because deep sleep is the locus for the manifestation of mere emptiness.
By which [words] are the meanings of "this," "that," and "self" [expressed]?
"By means of the manifestations of speech" (*vāgbhābhiḥ*):

here, "speech" is intended as a conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) by virtue of having the same object. Therefore, the meaning is "by means of those whose nature is the manifestation of conceptual differentiation."
For these appearing objects are indeed of the nature of conceptual construction, like the objects in a dream;
because that which exists as their essence— pure consciousness alone— is in reality the true object.
In what does it appear? Like in a dream;
as in a dream.
Brahman is expanded as the objects within its own dream; within the reality called the Self, that is,
within the Self as its own ground.
By means of the manifestations of speech, which consist of the appearance of conceptual constructions—
that is, by means of their own words and referents— it shines forth; such is the meaning of "tathā" (thus).
For it is witnessed by all that Brahman, which exists as the self-nature (*ātmabhāva*) in a dream, appears as the nature of objects (*padārthabhāva*).
Now, one might object: "But other schools, such as the Buddhists, deny the existence of objects altogether."
To the question, "How then did you say this?", he replies with the words "yo yad" (whoever... whatever).
Whosoever—be they a knower of Brahman, a Buddhist, or anyone else—who knows or experiences whatever state of affairs, such as the absolute non-existence of things, in every respect.
Let him know that; let him experience it. What is the use of our knowing that?
The sense is that our intent lies solely in the knowledge of Brahman.
And here, because the word *yat* is seen to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with the triad beginning with *idam*, it is established as referring to the universal (*sāmānya*).

The remaining three, beginning with *idam*, refer to particulars (*viśeṣa*). Even among those, the word *idam* refers to that which is known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, since the inclusion of all categories of objects is accomplished by these four pronouns alone, [the subsequent terms] are of no further use.
It should be understood that this means "not speaking to others.
Alternatively, the term "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*) is used as a form of address to indicate Śrī Rāma’s distinguished qualification for the knowledge of Brahman;
thus, the meaning is quite clear.
Nor does there arise the fault known as "difficulty of application" (duryojakatva).
Located in the subsequent sentence;
strengthened;
where there is a pronoun.
pertaining to the time of waking;
by which [what kind of] things?;
in reality.
By means of his own being— that is,

by resorting to the experience of the knower of Brahman as described— he refutes, through this reasoning, the objection raised by others which had become a subject of doubt, [only] when the entire creation exists within the ether of Brahman.

"By this logic"—that is, by this reasoning consisting of the experience of the knowers of Brahman, which establishes the difference [of things] despite their being composed of Brahman—[the opponent] who was eager to challenge with the question "What is this? Of what do you speak? has been refuted;
but not by the reasoning of the Buddhists and others, which effects the total denial of all things.
When the creation— the multitude of entities that are the objects of the act of creating—
exists within the Brahma-ether, which is the nature of the Brahma-space; when [this is so].
What is your form? What is this? What is the form of this treatise? For what disciple, and of what form is that disciple?
"You speak" means you declare;
because everything has the single nature of Brahman,
it is of such a form.
An objection (*codya*) is a challenge (*ākṣepa*); by that, one is known as "cañcu. This means, in effect, one who raises objections of such a nature.
He is refuted and rejected;
by that, the suffix *cañcup* is applied to form *vitta*,
meaning "renowned" or "famous."
Now, how is this objection refuted by this?
It is said:
by the knower of Brahman.

Even though there is oneness with Brahman from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), it is entirely appropriate to provide instruction in that [dualistic] form by resorting to the maxim "as is the yakṣa, so is the offering" during the state of conventional practice (vyavahāra)— for one accepts the world as being like a dream, just as for a disciple who is like a dreamer.
In every respect, this objection is appropriate only for the Buddhists and others who deny the existence of categories of reality.
[The suffix -cañcu-] see Pāṇini 5.2.26.

(MT_3,1.2) Having thus dispelled the objections raised by doubt, he addresses the listeners toward his own instruction: "I, for my part, [shall speak] according to my knowledge, according to the reality, and according to the sequence."
"O wise ones, listen to all this as I speak it according to its true nature.
The word *tāvat* signifies totality;
I am the teacher named Vasiṣṭha.
I shall now speak— that is, I shall relate— in its entirety this treatise entitled "The Means to Liberation."
How do I speak? According to my knowledge, following after knowledge; likewise, according to the reality, following after the reality.
In that same way, "according to sequence" means in accordance with the order;
furthermore, how?
"According to intrinsic nature" means in accordance with the intrinsic nature.
For it is only the four qualities beginning with knowledge that serve as the grounds for the engagement with this treatise;
therefore, for that reason,
O wise ones!
"Listen to all of this; let it be brought within the range of your hearing.
The address "O wise ones" (*budhāḥ*) indicates that only the wise possess the qualification for listening to this treatise.
By the word "all," he implies that by hearing this entire work, the attainment of the supreme goal will occur; therefore, one should not rise from one's seat midway.
It has been indicated that one must go.
In accordance with the subject matter,
having brought before him the assembly of wise ones worthy of hearing, he summarizes the intended meaning of the *Utpatti-prakaraṇa* (the Chapter on Origination) in a verse.
He says:
"One perceives the world as if in a dream, consisting of consciousness and the void, free from the body;
for the analogies of the dream and the cycle of existence are fully contained right here within. (MU 3.1.4)

It is called *cit* because it causes the group of organs—which are like stones—to act as agents of conscious activity through its own penetration; thus, *cit* is some pure reality inherent within all things.

Alternatively, it is called *cit* because it cognizes (*cetati*); it is some reality that constitutes the agent of the act of cognition. That very [reality] is the sky (*nabhas*), because of its all-pervasiveness, [like] space (*ākāśa*).
That consciousness-space, the *cidākāśa*, perceives the world— the manifest proliferation of the visible which is by nature mobile—
as being like a dream; having itself conceptualized it as a dream, it experiences it as such.
What is the world like? It consists of the cognition of the body.
"Cognition of the body" is the knowledge: "I am the body."
"Ahankara" means egoism; its modification is the nature of the body-ego (dehātmamaya), which is the very form of egoism,
and not the pure [sattva]— this is the meaning.
Now, one might ask: "Why is a dream given here as an illustration? To this, he says: "In a dream...
A "dream-world" (*svapna-saṃsāra*) refers to the worlds perceived within a dream.
These very examples are the points of determination.
These examples of dreams and saṃsāra are fully contained right here, within this very waking world.
But they are not connected—
that is, related—
merely upon their appearance, because they are established by conceptual construction alone.
Therefore, the intention is that the dream has been stated as an illustration.
Having placed the illustrious Rāma— who is himself omniscient— at the center, [the author] sets forth this meaning stated in brief for the sake of introducing it to those of dull intellect.
After this treatise consisting of the discourse on the conduct of those seeking liberation,
I shall now fully expound this subsequent section concerning Origination.
That in which the discourse on the conduct of those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) is extensively presented is "consisting of the discourse on the conduct of those seeking liberation";
[it is] from such a treatise.
That is to say, from the section known as the "Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation" (*mumukṣu-vyavahāra*); "furthermore" (*param*) means something else;
"is fully explained" (*parikathyate*) means it is correctly explained.
He undertakes the commencement of the section as previously promised:
"This bondage is the existence of the visible; in the absence of the visible, there is no bondage.
Listen now in due order to how this visible world does not truly exist."
This is the bondage currently being experienced: it is attachment to the visible,
[which arises] from the existence of the visible— that is, from the multitude of objects that constitute the domain of the act of seeing.
Existence (sadbhāva) means the attainment of its own nature;
that is to say, its manifestation toward the observer. Of which [nature]? Of that [object].
He becomes such [a person]. When there is an absence of the visible, bondage— that is, being bound—
does not occur.
For binding is never observed in the absence of a rope.
[Objection: But how can the non-existence of that which exists and is perceived be established?
Regarding this, it is said: "It is not possible.

The word *tu* (but) indicates the distinction of the object of perception (*dṛśya*) from the pure seer (*śuddhadraṣṭṛ*), who is the one for whom [the possibility] exists. The object of perception is not possible; that is, it does not possess the status of being the agent of the action of coming into existence.
Because it is established as a mere cognition by way of the analogy of a dream. [The opponent asks:
"But how is this so?
To this, he says: "Just as this..."
This is the impossibility of the perceptible;
listen now to how it occurs, in due order.
Now, in response to the inquiry, "For what purpose do you speak of the section on origination first?", he says: "Only that which is born in this world indeed grows;
it is that alone which attains liberation, or heaven, or hell. (MU 3.1.7)
The distinction is as follows: by transgressing both dharma and adharma one attains liberation;
by dharma one attains heaven; and by adharma one attains hell. (MT 3.1.7)
"Now, what follows from that? To this he replies:
"Therefore, for the sake of awakening to them, I shall first describe how and by whom one enters into transmigration. (MU 3.1.8)
Since origination and the other [stages] share a single substratum,
therefore, for the sake of understanding— that is, for the sake of your knowledge— [I shall explain] among those stages of origination and so forth which occur in succession.
In this present context,
I shall first of all relate that.
What is that? It is the person; "in what way" means by which manner.
In *saṃsṛti*, which has the nature of wandering through cyclic existence; "even before," that is, at the very beginning of creation;
it "undergoes birth," meaning it assumes existence as something distinct from Brahman.
The meaning is that immediately following this, I shall also explain the stages of increase and so forth at the beginning of the section on "Abiding" (sthitiprakaraṇa).
The word *hi* is used for emphasis.
For this very reason, it should be understood that even the name of this treatise is "The Chapter on Origination."
In the middle: *madhye* [of] *tava*. This is the elision of the original explicans *tava*, which corresponds to *te* in the *Mūla* (MT_3.1.8).
Therein, he first promises a concise exposition.
[The summary: O Rāghava, listen briefly to this statement regarding the meaning of this treatise;
thereafter, I shall explain it to you in detail according to your desire.
O Raghava, listen briefly to this subject matter of the section on origination— the meaning of the section concerning the nature of the origin of this world.
Then, immediately after the summary,
I shall explain the detailed exposition according to your desire. Without a summary, your doubts would not arise, and thus a detailed explanation would not be possible.
The sense is that this is because the detailed account would fall within the scope of doubt.

Intending to describe the origin of the world briefly as previously promised, and recognizing that it would be improper to state the nature of the fundamental cause through a positive injunction (*vidhimukha*) to a disciple whose intellect is overwhelmed by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), [the author] resorts to the maxim of "driving in the post" (*sthūṇānikhanananyāya*) by way of the destruction of the world.
He begins to explain the nature of the fundamental cause—
that which is seen as this entire world, both stationary and moving.
Like a dream during deep sleep, that which we perceive as this present reality perishes at the end of the kalpa.
The world— consisting of the stationary and the moving, O you whose nature is both stationary and moving—
is seen and experienced as a collection of perishable entities.

That [world] perishes at the end of a kalpa—specifically during the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*), which consists in the cessation of all that is visible when there is a desire to express an internal object, and also in the state beyond that; but according to the view that it refers to external objects, it perishes at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) occurring at another time. It "perishes" means it is destroyed thoroughly, from its very root known as latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and from its substratum.
Because it abides as the fundamental cause, it goes to non-perception;
like what? Like a dream.
The meaning is: "just as a dream perishes in deep sleep.
Now, one might object: since the world exists in deep sleep in the form of a seed, otherwise its re-emergence would be impossible.
If it is asked, "How is this relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison established? [the answer is]:
No, because the common property called stillness exists in both cases.
For the relationship between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison arises precisely by resorting to a mere common property through its persistence;
thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
[occurring at another time] ...
commencement ... from the support ... from the root, the support ... it goes ... [to] ... it goes.

By relying merely on a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), he states the fundamental cause as a supplementary detail for the purpose of revealing its true nature (*svarūpa*), for which this effort was made: "Therefore, it is motionless and profound; it is neither light nor pervasive darkness."
"Whatever remains is inexpressible and unmanifest. (MU 3.1.11) This means that after the destruction of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*),
there remains some subtle entity that cannot be designated by any name whatsoever.
It remains as a residue;
even upon its destruction, since the perceiver of destruction would be absent, the destruction of conceptual proliferation (prapañca),
though accomplished, would be merely non-existent— this is the intended meaning.
[Objection: "But why is that entity not stated by name? [Response:
To this, he states the reason by way of a qualification:
"it is 'inexpressible' (anākhyam). Because it exists as the agent of expression, it cannot be reduced to the status of the object of expression.
[Objection: But how can that which is inexpressible exist?
[Response: To this as well, he states the reason by means of a qualification:
"unmanifested. It is unmanifested because of its extreme subtlety.
The meaning is that it has not been perceived by the sense faculties existing as either external or internal.
And it is quite clear that what is not perceived by the external or internal sense faculties is indeed "inexpressible" (*anākhyatva*).
Because the faculty of speech is also inaccessible [to it], one might ask:
"How can it also possess non-manifestation?
To this as well, he states the reason by means of a qualification: "neither light nor darkness."
Pure consciousness (cinmātra) is light when not conjoined with an object of cognition (cetya);
that object of cognition is darkness.
Alternatively, light refers to the sun and other such luminous bodies.
"Darkness" (*andhakāra*) means "obscurity" (*tamaḥ*); the sense is that its essential nature is distinct from that [light].
And thus, it is precisely its non-manifestation (*anabhivyaktatva*) [that constitutes darkness], as between light and darkness...
This is because [the object] is the domain of manifestation.
Nevertheless, fearing the consequence of [the self] becoming void, he provides the qualification "pervaded" (tataṃ).
The meaning is that its essential nature is stretched out everywhere.
The thought is: "If it is empty, how could there be suchness? [The questioner asks: "By what essential nature does its state of being woven exist?
To this, he replies: "Still and deep."
It is both "stimita" (immovable) and "gambhīra" (profound), hence "stimitagambhīra.
Because it consists of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), there is an absence of any expansion that takes the form of an object of cognition; thus, it is "niḥspanda" (motionless).

Because it is without support (*nirālambana*), there is an absence of anything distinct from itself that could plunge into it; thus, it is "duravagāha" (difficult to fathom)—this is the meaning. And for this reason:
The sense is that it exists as woven together in the form of pure consciousness alone, which is without support (*nirālamba*). Although it does not remain in a state of non-creation,

according to the principle to be explained by the word "supreme" (*param*), there is always indeed a vibration (*spanda*) of that reality toward the manifestation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

For one who abides in purity, its perception is never possible at all; nevertheless, according to the principle to be explained later— such as that a place is distant from another place— its perception is always possible for those acting with moderation, and thus one should not turn away from it.
But for those who are liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamuktas), even the state of being eternally identical with That is possible;
for such is the very majesty of this reality of pure consciousness (cinmātratattva).
It is so; that which is at all times identical with the universe is also transcendent—there is nothing contradictory in this.
By way of qualification;
that which is unnameable;
by those who are established.
"Motionless" (*niḥspanda*) [is explained] by the method to be stated in 3.1.12a and so forth;
[it is explained] by the method to be stated in 3.7.17a. (MT_3,1.11)
Now, if that reality is indeed inexpressible, how is it that the wise have assigned designations to that reality such as "the Real," "the Self," and so forth? To this, he replies:
"The Real, the Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Truth"—these and other such names for that Great Soul have been devised by the wise for the sake of conventional usage. (MU 3.1.12)
"By the wise" means by those who have realized that [reality].
"Constructed" means brought forth through conceptualization. "For the sake of conventional usage" means for the purpose of accomplishing the conventional usage known as instruction for disciples.
The point is that no designations such as "season" (*ṛtu*) and so forth function there by taking up any basis for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*).
[Objection: Let it be so;
what of it? To this he says:
Let it be so: that very Self, though remaining as it is, shines forth as if it were something else;
it seems to enter into the state of living beings, undergoing the indignities of future existence.

Remaining exactly as it is from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), never deviating from its declared essential nature (*svarūpa*), that Self (*ātman*) is the reality known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which— being characterized by the aforementioned attributes— is the agent of the action of constant movement due to its perpetual manifestation. It is also the state of being a living being (*jīvatā*), which is the state of a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) acting as the sustainer of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), whose inherent nature is contrary to the action of constant movement.
It approaches as it were, it goes as it were;
what is that Self doing?
Shining forth as if it were something else.
By attaining its own objectivity by itself,
it manifests as if it were a form of the cognizable distinct from itself;
for indeed, through the mere act of self-reflection, the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) and so forth arises as a form of the cognizable within pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
The phrase "being such" (*tathābhūta*) expresses the suitability of the two words *iva*.
For it is not logical that that which is "such" in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) should be "not such.
Indeed, even when water—which has never fallen away from its state as water—attains the condition of being a wave, it does not, in an ultimate sense, become non-water.
He was intent on [preventing] what kind of future torment for those who are living?
That which is to come in the future.
The name "bhavanaśīlā" means that which lives by the torment of name-and-form (nāmarūpa);
it refers to that [name] whose torment is defilement (mālinya).
The meaning is that [the name] is fit for being uttered;
and the state of having been manifested by the name should be understood as occurring upon the manifestation of *vaikharī*.
Now he describes the state of the mind that arises immediately after that very state of being a living soul (jīva):

"Then, having become agitated by the conceptualization of the meaning of the word 'living soul,' it becomes the mind (manas), becoming sluggish through the act of thinking, while its nature remains silent. (MU 3.1.14)
"Mantharībhavan" means becoming sluggish;
"tataḥ" means after that, following the state of being a living being (jīvabhāva);
"saḥ" refers to that self (ātman).
The mind comes into being.
What kind of mind? The self of silence.
Silence is the incapacity for the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the innate nature (*sahajasvarūpa*).
From what does that state arise? To this, he provides a qualifying attribute containing the reason:
Regarding the phrase "becoming sluggish": the meaning is that he becomes sluggish, that is, he becomes indolent.
To the question "from what does he become sluggish?", he says:
"Because of cogitation" means because of the dharma called the cogitation of being a living soul (*jīvatva*).
For it is precisely through the state of being intent on cogitation that the self becomes sluggish toward self-reflection.
From that, it becomes the form of the mind.
Of what nature is it? It is the state of being agitated by the conceptualization of the meaning of the word "living soul" (jīva).
The word that denotes the individual soul (jīva) is the "jīva-word. Its referent is the individual soul in its subtle form;
the "conceptualization" (kalanā) of that [referent] is the reflective awareness of it as one's own essential nature.
He has fallen into that agitation which was produced by her;
such is the meaning.

In every respect, consciousness (*cinmātra*), whose nature is non-different from the object of thought (*cetya*), first performs a self-reflective awareness as "I" through the state of the mind (*citta*).
In that process, the aspect that exists as the subject (*grāhaka*) is named "consciousness" (*cit*).
But for that which exists as the object of apprehension, there is the state of being a living soul (*jīva*);
consequently, that living soul has the reflective awareness of its own atomicity (*aṇutva*). That...
And thus, it possesses the nature of mind.
Immediately after the state of being a living being,
becoming sluggish,
he declares that the fruit has ripened.
By that [means], the mind arises from the Great Supreme Self (mahat-paramātman),
which is perfectly stable, assuming an unstable form like a wave from the ocean.
"By that" means for that reason.
The mind, which is of the nature of the subtle atom (*aṇu*),
comes into being— that is, it manifests— from the Great, the Pervasive Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Like what? Like a wave;
just as [a wave arises] from the ocean, the very stable sea.
The wave becomes unstable in form;
that is the meaning.
And in this context, stability is to be understood in relation to the wave.
Having stated the arising of the mind from the well-stabilized [state], he describes the arising of the world, which is its effect,
[beginning with the word] "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*).
That [mind] itself constantly and spontaneously conceives [objects] at its own will;
by that means, this splendor of the magical net (indrajāla) is spread out as if it were extended.
Here, "that" refers to the mind, which has been called the supreme self (paramātman).
By oneself;
that is, not having made anything else one's intermediary.
At will; by one's own desire.
But not by the instigation of another;
he intends, that is, he forms an intention. Therefore, by means of that mind.

This being experienced is the splendor of a magical illusion (*indrajāla*); because it appears as something false, like a magical illusion, it is a creation consisting of the array of the sensory networks (*indriyajāla*). It is "spread out," meaning it is expanded.
In what manner is it?
It is as if expanded, as if broad;

however, because it abides in the mind whose nature is atomic (*aṇu*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is devoid of expansion—the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed for this reason. (MT_3,1.16)

He states the fruit of explaining that the emergence of the mind arises from the Supreme Self, just as the emergence of the creation [arises from it]: "Just as the referent of the word 'bracelet' has no separate existence apart from gold, so too the referent of the word 'world' does not exist apart from the Supreme. (MU 3.1.17)
Just as the referent of the word "bracelet" is a particular configuration that constitutes the denotation of the word "bracelet," it is not capable of being separate;
that is to say, in reality, it is not fit to be distinct from the gold.
In what sense does the word "bracelet" (kaṭaka) reside? It resides in a golden bracelet; that is to say, in a bracelet made of gold.
In the same way, the status of being the referent of the word "world" (jagat) belongs to the Supreme.
By the phrase "in that same way" (tadvat), everything pertaining to the illustrative example is invoked;
by this, the meaning is as follows:
"tadvat" means "in that manner."

The meaning of the word "jagat" (world) as it applies to that which is established as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)— which, according to the principle previously stated, transcends [the world] while existing as the world— is as follows: [it refers to] others.
It is not subject to separation from another.
[Kanakāt] °kā⟨n⟩[t] (MT_3,1.17):
For the sake of leading those of deluded intellect, he states this very same point once more:
"In Brahman alone exists this world, non-different from it, as it truly is."
The world does not exist as a distinct object from the Word, just as bracelets and other ornaments do not exist apart from gold;
it exists precisely in this manner as it is,
and not by attaining any other mode of being.
This world exists as non-different in essence— that is, non-different in nature— from Brahman, which is expanded and pure consciousness;
therein lies the meaning of the word "world."
The meaning— the denotable object— of the word "jagat" (the world),
which consists of the arrangement of categories distinct from Brahman,
does not exist.
Because the world, which is considered as such [as the effect], is established as being Brahman,
what indeed is the meaning of the word "world"?
It is like the state of being a bracelet and so forth.
The meaning is: just as the state of being a bracelet or the like does not exist in gold [when it is not fashioned into such], so it is here.
[The meaning of the word "world" (*jagat*)]:
For this very reason, [the author] restates the arising of the world from the mind—which establishes its non-existence and thereby strengthens the aforementioned point—by means of a simile:
"Just as a wave in a mirage is insubstantial and flickering."
The splendor of the world, like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), is extended forth by the mind alone—and not by anything else.
"By the mind alone" means that it is not by any other means;
"worldly" means pertaining to the world.
"Of the nature of the world" means, in short,
the splendor of a magical illusion;
it is being fully displayed.
In what manner? Precisely as non-existent, that is, with a non-existent nature itself;
for there is no separate existence of the mind apart from Brahman.
Of what nature was the splendor of that illusory net?
It was unreal, having an unreal nature like the mind which serves as its own cause; by what kind of mind? By [the mind] of the one who perceives it.
A river that appears in the heat is a "heat-river";
like that [river],
just as by means of an unreal heat-river an unreal, flickering wave is manifested.
The meaning is "so it is.
Now, one might ask: how is it that in the previous verse the golden bracelet was used as an illustration, whereas here it is the waves of the river Tāpanī? This is true.
In the preceding verse, the example of a golden bracelet was given for the purpose of stating that the world is, in its ultimate sense, of the nature of Brahman;
in this verse, however, it is for the purpose of stating that it does not exist apart from Brahman, thereby removing any objection regarding that very point.
The river of heat serves as an illustration; thus, because they both accomplish the same result, there is no disparity between the two examples.
For if the world were not a mental construction, it would follow that it possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*);
and in that case, [the world] would possess a distinct ontological status.
To say that this [world] is Brahman would be improper;
for it is not proper to say of a jar, "This is a cloth. This verse is introduced in order to remove such an untenable objection.
Thus, even the example contained within that [argument] is appropriate for that very purpose.
[The splendor of a magician's trick]: How [does he describe] the worldly splendor of a magician's trick? "Ignorance, cyclic existence, bondage, illusion, delusion, and the great darkness."
"Those whose names are designated as 'imagined' by those who know all"—
that is, by the omniscient ones.

Now, having recognized that the disciple desires liberation from the splendor of this "magical illusion" (*indrajāla*) that has been described, [the author] provides a definition of the nature of liberation.

Considering that it is impossible to define the nature of liberation without knowing how a disciple attains it, and further considering that even the definition of the nature of liberation is impossible without knowledge of the nature of its opposite— bondage— he promises to define that [nature of bondage] with the words "of bondage."
"First, listen to this description of the nature of bondage being told;
thereafter, O moon-faced one, you will understand the true nature of liberation.
Regarding "bondage": it is the state of attachment to the visible world, which has the splendor of a magical illusion (*indrajāla*).
With the words "tataḥ" (thereafter), he consoles the disciple who has become perplexed by the promise to define the nature of bondage that is not subject to further acquisition.
"Tataḥ" means immediately after the description of the nature of bondage.

The sense is that after defining what is to be abandoned (*heya*), it is logical to define what is to be adopted (*upādeya*); liberation (*mokṣa*) is independent of the visible world (*dṛśya*). He now describes the nature of bondage (*bandha*).
"O dear one, the existence of the object of sight for the seer is called bondage;
the seer is bound by virtue of the object of sight, and through the absence of the object of sight, he is liberated. (MU 3.1.22).
O dear one, "the existence of the object of sight" means the actual presence of the object of sight.
"Of the seer," meaning of the agent of the act of seeing;
"bondage" is what is being designated.
The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is for the purpose of completing the meter.
This very point— that the seer makes [the mind] fit for the yoga of tranquility through positive and negative concomitance—
is explained as being "by virtue of the seen" (dṛśyavaśāt), that is, by the power of the seen,
meaning by the power of the existence of the seen.
Because of the absence of the visible, that is, through the non-existence of the visible;
for when the object exists, the subject also exists,
and when that [object] is absent, that [subject] is also absent.
The two reasons are to be applied by oneself to the two statements.
Therein, he describes the nature of the visible:
"the world, you, I," and so forth; that which consists of creation is called the visible.
As long as this [world] exists, liberation is not found.
The world, which consists of emanation, is the cause of bondage; it is the manifold expansion of the visible.
In that regard, you are the disciple desiring liberation,
and "I" am the teacher;
by the word "etcetera," liberation is included.
Because for that [Self] as well, the state of being an object of sight (dṛśyatva) does not cease;
the wise call the world, "you," "I," and so forth—the visible—the object of the act of seeing.
When the question arises, "Why so?", he states the reason by means of a qualification.
"Of the nature of creation" means having the form of that which is being created;
and the fact that what is being created is an object of perception is quite evident, since it is preceded by the act of seeing.

Furthermore, that creation is preceded by seeing (darśana) is to be understood from the force of such scriptural passages as "It thought" (*tad aikṣata*). He restates its being the cause of bondage with the words "as long as" (*yāvad*).
As long as this world, which is perceived as beginningless, exists— that is, as long as it possesses existence— liberation does not occur.
Because the cause of bondage remains present,
and because the object of perception possesses, by its very existence alone, the intrinsic nature of being a cause of bondage.
On account of the force of such scriptural passages as "That [Being] thought" (ChU 6.2.3),
[the Teacher] spoke to the disciple— who was endowed with the conceit that the visible world and so forth had ceased to be seen— merely by stating the words, "This is not this."
"This is not it, this is not it"—the disease of the visible world does not subside through such futile ravings that give rise to conceptual constructions; on the contrary, it increases.
(MU 3.1.24) "This" refers to that which is being experienced.
"This is the visible world;
it does not exist.
This visible world does not exist"—those who remain in such a state [of thought] are futile, being devoid of the fruit known as the pacification of the visible world.
Likewise, by means of "prolixities"— that is, the utterances of a madman that generate conceptual constructions (saṅkalpa), specifically those conceptual constructions known as prohibitions—
the "visible disease," which is the affliction called the visible world, [is cured].
It does not become pacified because it remains in the form of a negation;
on the contrary, it increases, that is, it grows,
because it acts as an augmenter of the conceptualization known as negation.
But how can negation be an object of perception? True; because it is an object for the perceiver, even negation appears to the perceiver as distinct from himself.
Because it is an object of the seer (*draṣṭṛviṣayatvāt*). [Objection:
Surely, the cessation of the visible (*dṛśya*) does not occur by this mere statement;
let it be so, but we shall establish its cessation through reasoning (*tarka*) and other means. To this, he says:
Not by mere words,
nor by the crushing weight of logical reasoning, nor by the observances of other sects and the like, [is the world refuted],
because these are merely investigators of the existing, perceptible world. (MU 3.1.25)

Because the collections of arguments (*tarkas*)— those groups of reasoning that, being primarily characterized by differentiation, result in the appearance of reality in the visible world— their analytical investigations (*kṣodas*) do not pacify the disease of the visible.
Likewise, the visible disease does not subside through pilgrimages, religious observances, and the like;
for these, such as the weight of logical reasoning (*tarka*), are investigators of the existing visible world, becoming investigators of its reality.
In that regard, logical reasonings possess the capacity to establish the nature of things directly.
For sacred fords and the like result in fruits such as heaven;
indeed, it is not logical that they should have non-existence as their ultimate goal.
[Regarding the proof of the existence of the objects of the visible world:
Is it not the case that reasonings (*tarka*), even though the world exists, declare it to be non-eternal in its ultimate part; thus, they too [establish it] only partially?
"It is indeed possible that the visible world may be brought to cessation. To this he replies:
"But if the visible world exists, it can never cease;
for there is no coming into being of what is non-existent, nor the ceasing of what is existent. (MU 3.1.26)
[The existent] BhG 2.16ab:
"The visible" (dṛśyam) means that which has become the object of the act of seeing;
"the world" (jagat) refers to the collection of entities whose nature is perishable.
If it exists, if it is ultimately real,
then at some place or at some time— wherever or whenever.
It does not subside and does not attain peace,
because that which is non-existent does not partake in the agency of the action of existence;
"bhāva" means being or existence.
It does not exist;
thus, for that which exists and partakes in the agency of the action of being,
non-existence is the state of non-being.
It does not exist; the meaning is that it would entail the loss of its own essential nature (svarūpa).

Regarding the state of being an object of the act of seeing, he states the fault in the case of the ultimate reality of the visible (*dṛśyaparamārthasattva*): "Wherever this [consciousness], whose nature is consciousness that is beyond being an object of thought (*acetya*), abides... (MT_3,1.26).

There, the splendor of its object of vision arises for the seer even within the interior of an atom. [The self whose nature is consciousness that is not an object of thought]; "not an object of thought" (acetya) means that the collection of entities made manifest by consciousness itself and brought within its own range is the "object of thought" (cetya).
That in which there is no object of cognition (*cetya*) is "without an object of cognition" (*acetyā*);
that is to say, it is distinct from the objects of cognition whose nature has been previously described.
Such is the consciousness;
its very nature (*svarūpa*) consists of that, being composed of it (*tanmaya*). He whose self (*ātman*), that is, whose essential nature, is such [is the subject].
He is the Self whose nature is consciousness yet is unperceived by the intellect;
wherever— in whichever place—
and in whatever state— this is what is meant.
He remains;
even in a minute belly, even in an extremely subtle belly;
there, in that place.
For this seer, the splendor of the visible world arises—that is, it manifests.
Now, one might ask: how can such an elaborate manifold (prapañca) abide in a space so exceedingly subtle?
It is possible;
it is true that its manifestation occurs therein through a memory produced by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a coarse object of perception.
It is indeed established because of its being the nature of reality.
[The Self whose nature is both non-conscious and conscious: *The Self whose nature is consciousness* (MT_3,1.27).
Now, he speaks to those who are seized by the conceit of having attained peace regarding the reality of what is seen through means such as austerity and meditation:
