"Through austerity, meditation, and so forth, manifestation is indeed accomplished—because [the Self] is of that very nature. // 2(6)[7]//

Now, [thinking], "The world that was visible to the seer through asceticism, meditation, recitation, and so forth—that has been wiped away by me; it has been abandoned by means of asceticism, meditation, and chanting," it is like being satisfied with a mere measure of sour gruel. *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 3.28.
"Polished away" (*pramṛṣṭam*) means wiped clean for the seer (*draṣṭuḥ*), that is, for the agent of the act of seeing.
The world (*jagat*), as the visible object (*dṛśyam*), becomes the objective domain of the act of seeing by virtue of being distinct from [the seer].
That visible world-form has been abandoned by me through austerity, meditation, and recitation, and brought to a state of peace;
such is the meaning.
It is like the statement, "I have become satiated by the substance of vinegar," which is made upon being satisfied by vinegar;
for just as hunger is instead produced by the substance of vinegar consumed for the purpose of satisfying it, so too is this case.
Likewise, the point is that even through austerities and other such practices performed for the sake of propitiating a deity distinct from oneself, only an increase in the perceptible world occurs.
The object of the act of seeing (*dṛśikriyāviṣaya*).
[Objection: Let the visible (*dṛśya*) be real.

But what does this visible world do for the extremely subtle *jīva*, who has departed from the visible at the stage of liberation and has consequently become incapable of perceiving specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*)?
For indeed, no agitation caused by the external world is observed in one who is asleep. To this, he says: "If, having emerged from that [state], there is a visible world, then it is reflected."
Within this mirror of consciousness, even in the interior of a single atom, there is no doubt that the entire world— the collection of perishable, visible things— exists,
whether it be nominally real or ultimately real.
Then, even within the interior of an atom, even in its extremely subtle center—
while this [reality] abides as the self,
in the mirror of consciousness, in the polished surface of awareness.
"It reflects" means it transfers by way of being a reflection.
How is this so? To this he says:
"O Rāma, just as [an object] situated here or there reflects in a mirror."

"O Rāma, for this reason— because, just as an object situated here or there appears within the mirror of consciousness (cid-ādarśa), so too do mountains, the earth, rivers, directions, and so forth. (MU 3.1.30)
It reflects and is reflected in a mirror;
"just so" means in exactly that same way.
"Mountains, sky, earth, rivers, oceans, and so forth" refers to mountains, the sky, the earth, the rivers, and the oceans.
Those who are the lords of mountains, heavens, earths, and rivers;
those who are the beginning of this world— that is "the one whose beginning consists of mountains, heavens, earths, and rivers."
Such a world is reflected in the mirror of consciousness, in the polished surface of the intellect.
Because it is impossible to abandon intrinsic nature.
This is the point:
for existence itself is indeed radiance.
If that which is visible exists in the ultimate sense, then it consists solely of radiance because it is pure consciousness;
since it is by its very nature self-radiance, it can never be separate from it, and thus the mirror of consciousness can never be devoid of the reflection of the visible.
It reflects;
it vibrates; consisting solely of vibration.
And thus, with the intention that there would follow the consequence of the non-existence of liberation, he says:
"Therefore, therein again arise suffering, old age, death, and birth;
the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence; and the gross and subtle, the moving and the unmoving. (MU 3.1.31)
Therefore, if the mirror of consciousness were again and again joined with reflections due to the existence of the visible world,
then suffering would arise once more within that very pure consciousness.
In that same way, old age would occur; likewise, death and birth would occur;
and similarly, the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence, as well as appearance and disappearance, arising and ceasing, would come to be.
Because this is the very nature of saṃsāra.
Of what kind are suffering and the rest?
They are gross and subtle, moving and unmoving.
In this regard, the distinction is that those [elements] belonging to the waking state possess grossness and immobility,
while those belonging to the dreaming state possess subtlety and mobility.
Because there is no manifestation of suffering and so forth during deep sleep;
thus, the implication is that since the individual soul (*jīva*) would be seized by saṃsāra in the form of gross and subtle suffering and the like, liberation could never occur for it. (MT_3,1.31)
Now, one might object: "Granted that the visible world exists as ultimate reality;
nevertheless, what power does it have to produce harm for those devoted to meditative concentration? To this, he says:
"This visible world has been wiped away by me; I no longer abide within it.
This very [realization] is the inexhaustible seed for the recollection of cyclic existence within meditative absorption.
By means of the method of meditative absorption, this visible world has been wiped away—that is, destroyed—by me.
For this reason, I am not one who is "established" (āsthita) here in the sense of being attached (āsthā-yukta).
This very point is the subject matter stated in the first half [of the verse]:
in *samādhi*, which has the nature of the cessation of the visible (*dṛśyoparama*).
From the recollection of saṃsṛti— that is, from the recollection of the visible object—
it would become an inexhaustible seed.
It should be understood that the term *saṃsṛti* is applied figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to the visible object which is the domain of saṃsṛti.
This is the meaning:

for one who has been transformed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), does the purification of the visible world and the lack of attachment to it manifest as established realities or not? If not, then even if these two have been accomplished, they are simply non-existent.
Because, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the very nature of existence is nothing other than vibration;
and if it vibrates, then the memory of saṃsāra remains exactly as it was,
because its seed— vibration— is present.
But surely this same fault applies even to the absolute non-existence of the perceivable (dṛśyātyantābhāva) which you accept:
if the absolute non-existence of the perceivable manifests, then the perceivable is already established,
because its seed— namely, manifestation— is present.
If it is argued that this [state] is simply the non-existence of the visible object—that is, the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the visible—[we reply:

no. For the proponent of the absolute absence of the visible does not intend for samādhi, which is by nature the cessation of everything, to be the absolute absence of the visible; if it were so intended, the aforementioned fault would indeed follow.
However, only the ascertainment of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible object is useful for that [knowledge];
for it is not appropriate to recite a mantra for the purpose of warding off a snake in a rope.
Rather, it is only the ascertainment of the absolute non-existence of the snake— namely, "this is not a snake"— that is useful in that context;

and this ascertainment of absolute non-existence arises solely through the knowledge of the pure consciousness that serves as the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), which is produced by association with a teacher and the scriptures.
It is accomplished; it is not by means of meditative absorptions that reduce one to the state of a stone—enough with this elaboration.

In the case of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible (*dṛśyātyantābhāve*), it is established that meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—whose nature is the cessation of the perceptible as accepted by those who assert the reality of the world—is not merely the substratum for the seeds of the perceptible. (MT_3,1.32) *sidhyati* [is corrected from] *siddhyati*; *dṛśyā* [is corrected from] *dṛśyāṃ*. Not only does it serve as the support for the seeds of the perceptible, but it is also the very state of the cessation of the perceptible.
Indeed, it exists; however, with the intention of showing that there is also an incapacity for performing causal functions, he says:
"But while this visible world exists, neither the state of imperishable deep sleep nor the fourth state (turya) is possible through non-conceptual meditative absorption. (MU 3.1.33)
But in the alternative case:
while this world-appearance exists, while the nature of the world exists as an object of perception, while it exists as ultimate reality.
By means of non-conceptual samādhi, which is a state of composure whose essential nature is the cessation of all [mental activity],
neither inexhaustible deep sleep nor even the fourth state (turya) is possible or established.
Inexhaustible deep sleep refers to the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is the domain of the disembodied liberated one (videhamukta).
The fourth state is the domain of those liberated while living; it is the state of *turya*.
It is established;
[it is] the sphere of those liberated while in the disembodied state (*videhamukta*); [it is] the Fourth (*turya*) or the Void (*viśuddha*).
It proves precisely the impossibility [of its existence].
For upon emerging from meditative absorptions, just as at the end of deep sleep,
this entire world of suffering appears in its true state, unbroken and whole.
For this reason:
because emergence from meditative absorptions (samādhi) is inevitable;
that is to say, at the stage of emerging from meditative absorption.
"Remaining as it was" means remaining just as it was before;
for that very reason, it is "unimpaired," not deficient in any respect,
and "entire," meaning complete.
This world-appearance, which manifests and vibrates as suffering, appears as if within deep sleep.
This is the meaning:

just as for a person who has fallen into deep sleep at night— and for that very reason has forgotten the entire phenomenal world (jagat-prapañca)— the phenomenal world again manifests exactly as before upon waking in the morning.

Likewise, for a person who has attained the samādhi whose nature is the cessation of everything by whatever means possible, at the inevitable time of emergence from that state, the phenomenal world necessarily manifests once again just as before;
otherwise, it would follow that the absolute non-existence favored by us would result.

And thus, just as in the case of eating one's maternal uncle's wife, it is not logical that through a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which effects the cessation of the world for a mere moment, there should be the attainment of the Fourth State (*turya*)— whose nature is the perpetual non-existence of the world— or that which transcends it.
[The meditation on] the nature of the cessation of all [phenomena] leads to the undesirable consequence of absolute non-existence as we define it;
by this, he states that such meditation would result in fruitlessness.
O Rāma, what indeed is attained by means of meditative absorptions? For even when there is a momentary equanimity, what happiness is there if one subsequently falls back into misfortune?
What indeed has been attained?
The meaning is that not even the slightest thing is attained.
To the question "How is this so?", he says: "For" (bhūyaḥ), which means "because" (hi).
"Again, there is the occurrence of misfortune":
again, the occurrence of misfortune means the occurrence of misfortune in the form of schism;
[it refers to] that in which [this occurs].
Even in such a momentary equanimity, even in that state of balance which flashes forth for a single instant—
what happiness is there?
For equanimity that appears only momentarily does not bestow true happiness.
Therefore, the sense is that even by attaining that [equality], nothing at all is truly attained.
The word "api" (even/also) illuminates that equality is undoubtedly a locus of happiness.
Now, one might object: "If he is constantly absorbed in samādhi, how can there be the reappearance of old age and suffering due to the absence of emergence from that state? To this, he says:
"Or even if he should attain a state of stability in non-conceptual samādhi..."
I consider that state to be like an imperishable deep sleep, that stainless station;
it is the station where the Person (puruṣa) is absorbed in non-conceptual meditative concentration (nirvikalpa-samādhi).
I think that he might either remain constantly in a state of withdrawal or perhaps depart.
That even then—
that non-conceptual meditative absorption—
is the stainless state, the great abode known as pure consciousness alone, free from the impurity of dullness.
It does not exist,
because the impurity called "insentience" (jāḍya), which consists in the incapacity for seeing what is visible, remains as if in a state of sleep.
Of what nature is that?
It appears like an inexhaustible deep sleep, resembling the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta),
yet it is not its true nature,
because emergence inevitably occurs at some point in time.
Because it is established [in that state],
and because an emergence from the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is never possible,
due to its absolute dissolution into pure consciousness (cinmātra). (MT_3,1.36)
For one who asserts that the visible world is real, even non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) is impossible;
what then can be said of remaining or moving? With this intention, he says:

When this visible world exists, nothing at all is truly attained; for it is only through the delusion of the mind that the error of the world appears here and there. (The word *nāma* is used in the sense of certainty.)
While this world is being experienced, while the ultimate reality exists, by someone— that is, by any person whatsoever— ...
That non-conceptual meditative absorption is not attained by a person,
whether he is situated in the place of meditation or in any other location whatsoever.
"By mental delusion":
delusion residing in the mind is the error that the world is real; this is "mental delusion. By means of that, there is the delusion of the world.
*Kila* signifies certainty; the sense is that it "comes. This is the intended meaning.
Just as a person who is certain of the reality of what is perceived sees that very object even while sleeping at night,
so too one who has entered meditative absorption (samādhi) would surely see it as well, because the principle is the same.
And thus say those who maintain the reality of the perceived.
Even non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*) itself is not possible;
what then can be said regarding remaining or moving within it? [Objection:

Surely, even for one who has ascertained the reality of the perceptible object, nothing in the form of a manifestation arises through the application of any means of mental retention (*dhāraṇā*), however it may be employed.
"Non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*) is indeed accomplished. To this, he says:
[Regarding] non-conceptual meditative absorption, if the observer then forcibly cultivates the nature of a stone, [he will become one].
Even at the end of that [state], it remains as if trembling, and yet its visibility arises once more.
The "seer" (draṣṭṛ) is the knower (pramātṛ).
This occurs even if [the state] is forcibly brought about by some kind of violent practice (haṭhayoga).
He remains, staying while contemplating the state of being a stone;
even then, at that time,
for this observer who contemplates the nature of a stone within himself.
At the end of that— necessarily at the end of its state as a stone—
the state of being visible, having cloth and so forth as its object,
arises and manifests.
For it is not possible for one who is alive to constantly cultivate the state of being like a stone;
thus, the meaning is that if [the object] is perceived as something determinate, a stable, non-conceptual samādhi cannot be accomplished at all. (MT_3,1.38)
He explains the impossibility of attaining the state of being like a stone:
"And yet, non-conceptual meditative absorptions, which are equal to the state of being a stone, do not remain for some [practitioners] in such a way that it is experienced by all. (MU 3.1.39)
"Equal to the state of stone": [the compound] *pāṣāṇatātulyāḥ* means equal to the state of stone (*pāṣāṇatāyās tulyāḥ*).
The meaning is that they are free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The very cultivation of the state of being stone destroys the state of being stone for that observer;
for it is impossible for a stone to cultivate its own stoneness—this is the sense.
Thus, even though the state of being stone is established as it is, it is not logical for it to be the supreme state, because its insentience has not departed.
He says that the meditative absorptions (samādhis), though not having attained a firm rootedness like a stone,
become the supreme, peaceful state, which is the nature of consciousness— unborn and imperishable.
The transformation [of the stone] into its established state;
this is the meaning:
because its insentience is never lost due to its incapacity for seeing the visible, the state of being a stone lacks the nature of pure consciousness (cinmātratva).

This is incorrect. For pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is always inherently capable of both cognizing and being cognized. However, if it does not occasionally exercise that cognition independently, it does not thereby fall into the state of insentience (*jāḍya*).
For it is not appropriate to say that a person is incapable simply because he does not perform an action independently;
thus [the author] concludes what was stated previously.
Therefore, if this existent were visible, it could never cease;
that it might cease through austerity, recitation, and meditation is merely the imagination of the ignorant.
This is because of the reason already stated.
If the visible object were existent,
it would be impossible for it to be known by another [consciousness], because of its own substantiality.
That very thing is nothing but mere nirvāṇa; it is the pure mind, abiding as the state of Mind-Only in the form of the Lotus-Born. It remains.
That [realization] is mind-only;
it does not reach the state of earth and so forth, nor the ultimately real nature of earth and other elements.
Because it consists of the pure awakening that is the very nature of nirvāṇa;
for this very reason, the intention is that Padmajā lacks a material, elemental body.
[Regarding the term] *paramārthasantaṃ*:
Is it not the case that there exist various kinds of minds, since a distinction of mind exists for every individual soul?
Therefore, how [can it be said to be] from the form of Padmajā?

It has been stated that the origin of the world proceeds from the mind alone. To this, he says: "Of all beings endowed with minds who engage in the cycle of transmigration, this first one is a reflection, a body of consciousness, arising by itself. (MU 3.3.14)
Among all those beings whose minds are engaged in worldly affairs within saṃsāra,
that lotus-born one is the first reflection— the first manifestation that serves as the cause for the future creation of the mind.
The word "of pure consciousness" (cinmātrasya) is to be supplied [as the possessor].
Of what nature is this? It has a body of mind; that is, its form is pure mind.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "arising by itself," that is, by its own nature.
But not as something else;
it is that which has an arising, meaning a new manifestation.
The meaning is that even after its arising, it remains precisely in its prior state;
therefore, the intention is that its production is described from this very [state] alone.
This establishes its initial state of desirelessness (*prathama-pratīcchandatva*).
From this primordial prototype, this creation has issued forth as non-different from its own nature,
like the perception of movement [arising] from the wind. From this one called Padmaja.
From the first,
from the previous reflection;
this is what is being experienced.
Emission;
it has spread forth, having reached expansion.
Of what nature is it?
She is non-different from this, not separate from it;
for this very reason, she has its own nature and consists of it.
Like what?
Like the vision of vibration; just as vision has the nature of vibration— meaning,
it is simply vibration.
It proceeds from the wind;
that is the meaning.
Therefore, it is logical that this alone possesses the quality of being the primary desire-to-act (*prathamapraticchanda*).
This is the intended meaning.
He provides a summary:
"From this form of creative intuition, [the Lord] assumes the nature of mere creative intuition."
Thus this creation shines forth, existing as if it were a real experience.
This being so, from this lotus-born one, who is of the nature of manifestation— that is, whose very essence is manifestation.
This creation— this visible sphere which is the object of the act of creating—
is indeed of the nature of mere manifestation; it possesses only the form of manifestation,
but does not possess a form composed of gross elements.
It shines forth; it manifests.
For a wave devoid of the quality of fluidity cannot arise from water that possesses the quality of fluidity.
Of what nature is this creation?
He is established.
How?
Like the experience of truth, he is one whose experience is true.
That is a true experience;
"like that" means similar to it.
However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), it is merely an appearance like a dream—this is the purpose of including the suffix *-vat*.
Regarding this, he provides two examples:
"In this context, the examples are a city in a dream and likewise sexual union with a woman in a dream;
though non-existent, they shine with the experience of reality through the fulfillment of their purpose. (MU 3.3.17)
"Radiant with the experience of truth" means in this place;
that is to say, in the state where the manifestation of creation consists of nothing but a mere appearance (*pratibhāna*).
A dream-city is a city seen in a dream;
likewise,
sexual union with a dream-woman is sexual union with a woman seen in a dream.
There is an illustration.
Of what nature is it?
Although non-existent, its essential nature is non-existent because its core consists merely in being perceived.

"By the fulfillment of the purpose" means by the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). "Radiant with the experience of truth" means having the nature of appearing like an object endowed with the experience of truth.

By means of accomplishing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), [the text] states that even in the absence of a body for the Lotus-born One (*padmajasya*), there is the manifestation of a body, which is radiant with the experience of truth.

Not composed of earth and the other elements, the Lord of Beings, who is his own self, shines with the form of space and is bodiless; yet he appears as if embodied, having the form of a person. "Not composed of earth and the other elements" means his essential nature is distinct from earth and the rest.
For this very reason, he has the form of space (vyomākṛti), that is, the form of the ether;
and for this very reason, he is bodiless (adeha), being devoid of a material body.
He is self-existent (svātmabhū) and lotus-born (padmaja).
It shines and vibrates as if possessing a body,
because it is the agent of the manifold proliferation of various effects that constitute a body.
Of what nature is this one who has become his own self?

Bhūteśa is the lord of all beings by virtue of being the progenitor of all beings. Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is *puruṣākṛti*, meaning one whose form (*ākṛti*) is like that of a person (*puruṣavat*).
He is such;
otherwise, he would not have formulated the conception of having four faces in the scriptures—this is the meaning. (MT 3.3.18)
It explains its arising, its subsiding, and its absence:
that consciousness, because it consists of conceptual construction, arises and then subsides;
but because its own nature is self-dependent, it neither arises nor subsides.
He is consciousness from the perspective of ultimate reality; his nature is consciousness.
He is the lotus-born one.

Because his nature is volition (*saṅkalpa*), he arises—that is, he manifests—by way of having the nature of volition consisting of the self-reflection (*svaparāmarśa*) which rests upon pure consciousness alone.
Then, immediately after its arising, it subsides and even attains peace,
because conceptualization has as its fixed basis both arising and subsiding.
Likewise, that lotus-born one [is so called] because his own nature— known as pure consciousness (cinmātra)—
is under his own control, and because that very nature is the object of the reflective awareness "I am that."
It neither arises nor ceases;
for arising and cessation are not possible for pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which—being synonymous with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—is eternally manifest.
The sense is that these two [arising and cessation] are not possible even for the Lotus-born [Brahmā], whose very nature is certain within that [consciousness] as his own self.
Because it is dependent on itself;
because its own nature [is such].
Now he explains that this very [Self] is the cause of the world.
Brahmā is devoid of volitional construction (saṅkalpa), his form is free from earth and the other elements;

he is the absolute self consisting of mind alone, the cause of the existence of the three worlds. "Devoid of volitional construction" means being without a subtle, transportable body (ātivāhika-deha).
Likewise, his form is devoid of earth and the other elements, being free from the gross body;
for this very reason, he is "alone," meaning non-dual, which is to say,
his nature is pure consciousness alone.
Even so, he is essentially mind-only (*cittamātra*), whose nature is that of a pure mind consisting of pure volition (*saṅkalpa*).
Brahmā is the lotus-born one;
[he is the cause] of the existence of the three worlds, that is, of the reality of the three worlds.
It becomes the cause.
[Thus: "Even though [he is] of the nature of form" (MT 3.3.20).
Now, one might ask: by whose impulsion does the lotus-born Brahmā, who is of the nature of a pure mind, arise from the non-dual pure consciousness? To this he replies:
"This very volition (saṅkalpa) shines forth, as it were, being its own source."
This [world] shines as having the nature of space, like a mountain of one's own volition (*saṅkalpa*); this is the certainty. Just as this volition is experienced by everyone.
"Arising from oneself" means originating from oneself,
and not arising from another;
it shines and vibrates.
Likewise, this lotus-born one, whose form is pure mind and who is self-arisen,
shines and vibrates.
How?
It is like a mountain of your own volition (*saṃkalpa*). A mountain seen in a volition is a "volition-mountain" (*saṃkalpa-śaila*);
your volition-mountain is a "volition-mountain of yours" (*bhavatsaṃkalpa-śaila*).
"Like that" means like your mountain of resolve (*saṅkalpaśaila*);
the sense is: "just as your mountain of resolve appears as its own manifestation."
And since the self-manifestation of volition (saṅkalpa) is well known in all cases,
that very [volition] appears twice, by way of both its general and particular aspects.
He is taken as the object of comparison.
[The author] explains, with three verses and their underlying reasons, that this lotus-born one is devoid of a material body (*adhibhautika-deha*).
[Regarding "the lotus-born one's lack of a material body"]: *°kāyadeharā°*.

Because of a deeply rooted and singular forgetfulness of its subtle, transportive nature, the state of being material appears in vain, like a ghost, to one whose great consciousness has been awakened by this very first effort. (MU 3.3.22) For one whose great consciousness has been fully awakened by this initial exertion...
Because of his state of pure consciousness, the forgetfulness of the subtle body (*ātivāhika*) does not arise;
therefore, the demoness of materiality (*ādhibhautikatā*) does not arise for him—that false delusion of dullness which, like a mirage, produces falsehood. (MU 3.3.23–24)
By which cause, from whence;
by means of a firm-rooted, fully developed,
and absolute forgetfulness of the subtle spiritual body (ātivāhika).
Of the state of being *ātivāhika*, that is to say,
of the nature of the subtle body;
"that which is absolute forgetfulness" means total oblivion.
By that [term],
"ādhibhautikatā" means the state of being related to other beings;
that is to say, grossness.
Like a piśāca, the unreal appears and manifests in vain; the remainder of the sentence is "of the impure mind."
Therefore, for that reason,
this Piśācikā— a false form of a Piśāca— appeared before this lotus-born one, who is of the nature of pure mind.
The state of being material (ādhibhautikatā) is the condition of being material;
that is to say, the state of grossness.
It does not shine forth, it does not manifest.
What is the nature of materiality?
It is the delusion, that is, the vastness, of dullness— that is, of insentience.

It is so called because it bestows [this state] pre-eminently; for by the attainment of materiality (*ādhibhautikatā*), the dullness of the mind increases. Furthermore, of what nature is this materiality?
The meaning is that the unreal appears as unreal.
Like what?
Like a mirage.
The meaning is "just as a mirage is unreal.
Now, one might object: is it not the case that the state of being material (ādhibhautikatā) and the state of being subtle (ātivāhikatā) are caused by forgetfulness?
"Let it be so; but how is it that she does not exist within him in the form of a pure mind born from a lotus?
To this, he states the second verse—situated among three verses—as a supporting argument, beginning with "this."
For the first time, that which was previously [unawakened] is now fully awakened by means of that exertion directed toward self-reflection; thus, it is endowed with self-reflection.
That which is the great consciousness (mahāciti) is pure consciousness (cinmātra);
[the word] "of that" means "of its own nature."
Of this lotus-born one, whose form is pure mind—
due to his being pure consciousness (*śuddhasaṃvit*), that is, by virtue of possessing a consciousness unadulterated by the stain of duality—

there is a "forgetting of the subtle body" (*ātivāhikavismṛti*); by resorting to an expression where the state (*bhāva*) is the primary referent, this means the non-forgetting of the state of being a subtle body (*ātivāhikatā*).
It does not arise, nor does it manifest;
therefore, the sense is that its state as a purely transportive (ativāhika) body, caused by the absence of forgetfulness, does not become a state of materiality (ādhibhautikatā).

For it is observed that for one whose consciousness is stained by duality and whose mind is impure, it is the mind itself that appears in the form of gross cities and so forth; thus, no effort need be made here [to prove this].

[Kā]kā eva [eva]: By means of the fact that the Lotus-born One consists of mind alone, he metaphorically extends (atidiśati) this to his effect, the world, by way of fitness, such that the world also consists of mind alone.

When Brahmā consists of mind alone and is not composed of earth and the other elements, therefore the universe is mind alone; for whatever that [mind] is, that indeed is this [universe]. The word *yadā* (when) is used in the sense of *yataḥ* (because).
When and from what [source]:
Brahmā, born from the lotus,
becomes nothing more than mind, that is, pure mind alone.
Therefore, the universe is merely mind; for whatever object there is—
From which, that is, from whatever entity;
it comes into being,
that is, it assumes the state of being an agent of existence.
That entity remains that very same thing;
for we observe that a jar, while partaking in the existence and agency of the clay, possesses the nature of clay.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that the arising of the world is in reality non-arising, just like the mind.
[Regarding *mṛdaḥ*:

MT_3,3.25] Now, since the Lotus-born [Brahmā] lacks any auxiliary cause distinct from his own material cause, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), let it be that he consists solely of the mind (*manomātra*), having the nature of nothing more than the grossification of pure consciousness.
If the world arises from that [unborn], how is it logical for it to consist of mind alone, given the existence of auxiliary causes such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)? To this, he says:
"For that which is unborn, there are no auxiliary causes."
Even for that which is born from them, those [causes] do not exist at all; however, certain [other] auxiliary causes (*sahakārīṇi*) exist for the Unborn One (*ajasya*), that is,
for the Lotus-born One (*padmajasya*).
Because, for whatever reason,
there are no auxiliary causes;
"tu" (but) indicates certainty.
Therefore, for that reason,
of that world which is born from it— that is, produced from it—
certain things are its auxiliary causes.
They do not exist at all,
because it is impossible for unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) and other effects of the mind to act as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) with respect to the mind;
for that which arises from something [cannot be its auxiliary cause].
That very [entity] ought to be the cooperative condition for that [effect],
because at the time of its own production it is itself non-existent with respect to others.

Thus, if one accepts [the self] as a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*), it follows that it must depend on other cooperative causes for its own production; otherwise, it would be impossible for it to function as a cooperative cause even for others. To the question, "What follows from that?", he says:
Because there is no diversity of effects arising from a cause, there is nothing whatsoever here [of that nature];
for whatever the pure cause is, such is the effect established here.
By this, since there are no auxiliary causes for the world, [the effect is of the same nature as the cause].
Therefore,
in this context regarding the world born from the Lotus,
there is a diversity of effects— that is, a distinction among effects— arising from their causes.
There is not even a slight [portion] remaining;
for it is observed that the diversity of effects called "pot" arises from clay only when there is the presence of auxiliary causes such as a stick and so forth.
Therefore, in this case, whatever kind of pure cause exists,
the effect remains of that same kind,
because of the absence of auxiliary causes that would produce differentiation.
Therefore, the underlying sense is that the world is indeed nothing but pure consciousness.
Regarding the auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*):

he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that has borne fruit concerning the world born from the Lotus (*padmajajagat*). *Padmajajagadviṣaye*: "In the domain of the world born from the Lotus. (MT_3,3.27)
In this regard, no relationship such as cause and effect is tenable;

for the three worlds are exactly as the Supreme Brahman is. This is because, here, there is no distinction between pure consciousness and the Lotus-born (Brahmā), nor between the Lotus-born and the world.
The relation of cause and effect, such as causal dependence and so forth—
not even in the slightest degree— is not tenable.
Beyond this is Brahman, pure consciousness alone;
such is its nature.
The three worlds consist of forms such as that of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] and others; these are the three worlds.
It becomes such because it is precisely the relationship of cause and effect and so forth that brings about difference.
[Objection: Granted that the Lotus-born [Brahmā], who is of the nature of pure mind (*cinmātra*) and arises from pure consciousness, may indeed possess the nature of pure consciousness.
But how is it possible for the three worlds to arise from a lotus born of a pure mind? To this he replies:
"The world is stretched out by Brahmā, who has attained the state of mind;
it is not other than his own pure self, just as fluidity is not other than water. (MU 3.3.29)

He attained a state of pure mind, which possesses the alternative name "Padmajā," as if by Brahmā— who has expanded into the form of all objects and consists of pure consciousness alone— having arrived or having entered it.
From the pure Self, from its own [nature],
this world— which is non-different and not separate— is stretched out, that is, expanded.
That is to say, it is made manifest within one's own self; by what? Just as by water—that is, in the same manner as by water.
The quality called fluidity (*dravatva*), which is non-different from the self and serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the initial motion,
is extended;
such is the meaning of "likewise" (*tathā*).
Even regarding the mind (*manas*), because its nature as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) does not depart from it in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that since the world also arises from pure consciousness, it is logical that it too is nothing but pure consciousness.
"But if that is so, how does this diversity appear? To this he says:
"All this that is spread out is stretched forth by the mind alone; it is entirely unreal, like a city of the imagination, like a city of the Gandharvas. (MU 3.3.30)
With the mind well-known as "lotus-born," that is, with a pure mind;
it is extended, meaning it radiates everywhere;
this is the body, which is shining.
This entire world is stretched out—
that is, manifested— by the Supreme Brahman through its distinct existence (*sattā*). Of what nature is all this?
It is indeed non-existent, having the very nature of non-existence; it does not have the nature of existence.
How so?
It is like a city of imagination;
the meaning is that just as a city of imagination is non-existent, so too is it.
Furthermore, how is it so?
It is like a city of the Gandharvas;
just as a city of the Gandharvas [is illusory].
The meaning is "just as": it is just as a city of the Gandharvas exists even though it is real [only in appearance].
For the Gandharvas, for the sake of their own dwelling, construct a city in an empty space through mental imagination.

That very thing is called a city of the Gandharvas; it is this [world] that is expanded out as something distinct by the mind alone, which has arisen from pure consciousness (cinmātra). Otherwise, for what purpose would the mind arise? This is the intended meaning.
*tanuḥ* [or *tanus*] (MT_3,3.30):

By means of absolute certainty, he further declares the unreality of the elemental nature (*ādhibhautikatā*): "The elemental nature does not exist, just as the state of being a snake does not exist in a rope."
"But how could Brahmā and the others, being fully awakened, remain there?
Regarding the phrase "Brahmā and the others," by the word "others" (ādi), Viṣṇu, whose nature is pure intellect, and Rudra, whose nature is pure egoity, are included.

The awakened ones (*prabuddha*) are those endowed with an excellence of awakening due to their absolute purity. By the logic of the "stick and cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), he states once more that for one whose mind is awakened, the material body (*adhibhautikatā*) is unreal; indeed, only the subtle body (*ātivāhika*) exists.
"How and why could there even be a discussion here regarding the physical body?"—
the word "kila" indicates certainty; [this refers to] a person whose mind is awakened, that is, one whose understanding is perfectly certain.
The subtle body alone— which is of the nature of the *ātivāhika*, characterized by its capacity for transporting [the self]—
does not exist,
because of the knowledge that one's own nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
In this state of awakened intellect,
how could there even be discussion— that is, talk— concerning the physical body? Why would it be so?
How could it be so?
[The text] declares the unreality of the world, which has arisen from the lotus-born [Brahmā] who is devoid of a physical body,
by means of the human being named "mind" (*manas*), which assumes various forms.
"The world is a kingdom of the mind," appearing as if it were real—
thus [it is said] of that which bears various forms, namely of that which is called by the name "mind" (*manas*),
belonging to the human being known as Padmaja, who is devoid of a physical, material body.
A kingdom of the mind is a mental construction;
it exists as the world, established in the form of the world.
It comes to be so.
In what manner is the world?
It is as if it were of the nature of reality (*satyarūpa*).

However, because in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) it consists of nothing but conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), it is not of the nature of reality; thus, the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed.
And since the dream serves as a clear illustration in this context, no further effort has been made here.
The expression "the kingdom of the mind" (*manorājya*) for the person named "mind" (*manas*) should be understood as being like the phrase "the head of Rāhu.

Now, an objection may be raised: in the scriptures, it is stated that the status of being born from a lotus belongs only to a specific deity, such as the four-faced Brahmā; how then can that [apply here]?
"How is it that you have spoken of that as being the pure mind alone? To this he replies:
"Know that the mind itself is Viriñca, consisting of volition; having expanded its own form, this world is spread out by the mind. (MU 3.3.34)
You are the mind, whose nature consists of conceptualization and whose essence is the self-reflective awareness described as pure consciousness; you are the pure mind,
Viriñca, the lotus-born.
Know, that is, understand;
for one's own body is one's own true nature,
which is expansiveness, that is, vastness.
Having led this world with the mind,
it is stretched out— that is, it is expanded.
That is to say, it is produced. For this alone constitutes the nature of Viriñca: that the world is produced, and that it is produced clearly by the mind alone, according to the analogy of a dream.
Thus, it is logical that he alone possesses the nature of Viriñca; the conceptualization of him as a specific four-faced deity, however, is intended only for those of coarse vision—this is the sense.
[The author] states the absolute non-difference between Viriñca and the mind.
Viriñca is the form of the mind, and the mind is the body of Viriñca;
earth and the other elements do not exist here [independently], and therefore earth and the rest are merely imagined.
Viriñca is the one born from the lotus.
Of the pure mind, of the mind,
its form— that is, its essential nature—
comes to be.
The mind is pure; it is the mind of Viriñca, the lotus-born;
it is his body, his very nature.
It occurs because they perform the single function known as "production";
here, [it refers] to these two, Viriñca and Manas.
Earth and the other elements do not exist,
because, having arisen from pure consciousness alone, they do not deviate from being pure consciousness alone;
therefore, for that reason.
Earth and so forth, beginning with the ground,
are imagined— that is, they become conceptualized through mental construction—
just as in a dream; this is the implied sense.
[In the case of conceptualization:
Is it not the case that the mind, having the form of Viriñca, how could it produce the world without a material cause?
For even for one who is skillful...
[The opponent argues: "The potter possesses the power to produce a jar even without the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) known as clay. To this, [the author] replies:
"Even for the potter, let it be seen that within his heart there exists a lotus, beautiful to the mind, like a lotus in a pond. (Padmākṣe padminīvāntar manohṛdy asti dṛśyatā).
The mind and the vision of what is seen are never, in any way, distinct.
Here, the suffix *bhāva* is used in its own sense according to Vedic usage;
thus, this is the meaning.
Let the visible be seen within the heart of the mind;
it exists, it abides.
Because it arises in that very same way from pure consciousness (cinmātra) endowed with all powers;
otherwise, its manifestation as the visible world would be impossible.
Like what? Like a lotus pond.
Just as there is within a lotus plant— that is, a lotus stalk— the seed of a lotus, which is the lotus-germ.
The meaning is "so it is.
Furthermore, the fact that the lotus-eyed one was within the lotus pond is to be inferred from her emergence from it;
for that which does not exist within something cannot emerge from it.
Like water from a waterless jar;
therefore, the "mind-seen" and the "vision of the seen" consist of the vision of the mind and the vision of the seen.
At any time whatsoever.
Not even in the slightest degree do they become distinct,
because they exist in the relationship of material cause and its effect.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no dependence here upon a material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) that is inherently distinct [from itself].
"It remains" means it persists;
this very point is further strengthened by another illustration.

It is thus confirmed: "In this regard, your own dream and mental construction, whose nature is the sovereignty of the mind, serve as the very illustration through personal experience; therefore, the ground of the visible world exists within the heart. (MU 3.37)
And here it is clear: "In this case, it is clear.
Therefore, just as a piśāca dwelling within the conceptual construction of the mind [frightens] a child, [so does the imagined nature appear].
In this way, she who takes the form of the visible destroys the internal seer— the seer who is of the nature of the mind—
just as a sprout situated within a seed [destroys it] according to place and time.
Thus the intellect perceiving the visible creates and indeed expands a radiant body;
for these three verses occur at the end of the first section of the creation, and thus have not been laboriously explained again here.
[End of section] See YV 3.1.45–47.
(MT_3,3.39) He states the established conclusion with a verse at the end of the chapter:
"If that visible suffering does not subside at any time while the visible world persists, then the state of isolation (*kaivalya*) cannot belong to the witness (*boddhari*)."
When the object of perception is impossible, the state of being a perceiver ceases even while the perceiver remains; for they call this liberation.
This suffering of the perceived—which is currently being experienced—is suffering in the form of the perceived.
That which is real is ultimately real; if it exists,
then it never ceases.
The meaning is that this follows the principle that "the non-existent does not exist within the existent. When the object of perception has subsided, [it remains] in the cognizer, the seer.
Isolatedness is the state of being isolated;
that is to say, it is the nature of being a non-cognizer.
It does not exist.
Because that which is distinct from oneself exists as an object of perception and cognition,
having explained the manner in which liberation would be impossible, he now describes liberation itself.
Regarding the word "dṛśye" (in the visible):
it refers to the alternative position;
that is, when the visible object is impossible.
According to the logic already stated, when there is the non-arising of intrinsic nature and the arising [of phenomena],
the state of being a cognizer— that is, a seer—
would be stilled; it would reach peace.
For there is no such thing as the status of a seer for one who is devoid of an object of sight,
regardless of what state the object of sight may be in,
even if it remains present.
Because it is appearing, it also partakes of persistence.
[Objection: But what will be accomplished by that pacification of the state of being a cognizer?
To this, he says: "For that belongs to him."
"Hi" indicates certainty.
"The wise" refers to those who have pacified the state of being a cognizer; "of this" refers to that cognizer.
They say— that is, they declare— liberation to be the distinguished release,
because liberation consists precisely in the absence of orientation toward the visible world. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the third canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Śrī Vālmīki speaks to Bharadvāja:
While the leader of sages was thus delivering this lofty discourse, and while the assembly remained as if silent, intent on hearing him with single-minded devotion—MU 3.4.1.
When the entire royal assembly had been seated as if depicted upon a painted wall,
the day became sweet with its warmth, having only a moment remaining; all worldly activity, along with the rays of the sun, began to fade away.
To the leader of sages, Śrī Vasiṣṭha; "thus" means in this manner;
"exalted speech" refers to words whose meaning is profound.
He speaks when there is an occasion; for this very reason, he remains as if in silence, as if endowed with the vow called "silence," amidst the assembly of people.
When [the state] has arisen that is of a single flavor and endowed with exclusive savor;
likewise, without vibration— that is, without the vibration produced by women and others who serve as one's own support.
The meaning is: by being devoid of movement caused by women and others who serve as one's own support.
While the sounds of networks of small bells were present, likewise, there were green parrots and parakeets situated within cages.

Thus, when the entire assembly hall of the king— the whole royal palace—
was as if fixed upon a painted wall, as if depicted in a picture;
[it was] with sweet sunlight, with mild light.
The day had [only] a *muhūrta* remaining, that is, two *ghaṭikās* remaining;
likewise, worldly affairs— that is, the conduct of the world— [had ceased].
Along with the rays of the sun, it attained thinness.
In response to the inquiry, "What else occurred at that time, [characterized by] the absence of movement caused by women and others who were its own support? he says:
"The winds blew, rich with the intoxication of clusters of blossoming lotuses."
The winds blew with a sweet, gentle movement, as if they had come for the sake of hearing.
The winds blew— that is, they were blowing— with a sweet movement, meaning a soft movement.
Of what nature are they?
They are blooming clusters of lotuses, groups of lotuses; within them, they are intoxicated—meaning their forms have emerged due to the closing [of other flowers]—and they are also fleshy.
Such were the winds;
of what kind were they? As if for the sake of hearing—the hearing of the words of the sages.
As if they had arrived;
even he who comes for the sake of hearing [the teaching] blows with a sweet vibration alone.
Those of exalted form,
for the sake of hearing,
reflect upon what has been heard, like the sun moving through the succession of day and night.

The sun, Bhānu, abandoned its solitary path and went to the empty slope of the sunset mountain; "the wandering for the arrangement of days" refers to the revolution for the purpose of creating the day.
He abandoned it, having relinquished it;
likewise, it was empty,
and for that very reason, solitary and devoid of people.
He went to, that is, reached, the slope of the sunset mountain;
as if to do what?
To make the multitude of the sages' words the object of his hearing—that is, to hear them.
"To contemplate" means, as it were, to make it an object of reflection;
for even one who wishes to contemplate some teaching or instruction they have heard must likewise abandon the delusion that consists in [clinging to] the form of action.
And he went to a solitary place.
(MU 3.4.6) A misty darkness arose over the forest lands, as if they had become cooled within through the hearing of consciousness, like states of tranquility. (MU 3.4.7)
In the forest lands, those darkened by the onset of mist—darkened by the onset of frost—arose; they became manifest. For at the close of day, mists arise.

What are they like? They are dark with the onset of mist; they are like states of tranquility because of their freedom from agitation, just as things that are cool possess a cool nature by virtue of destroying heat.
Peacefulness;
through hearing the consciousness— that is, by hearing the consciousness as spoken by Śrī Vasiṣṭha—
within the minds of the listeners.
They rose up;
that is the meaning of "so be it.
People became scarce in their movements even in the ten directions.
As if to listen with full attention, they abandoned all movement;
at the close of day, the natural stillness of people's wandering was poetically imagined as a cessation of motion undertaken for the sake of listening.

By abandoning their movements, the shadows assumed the long form described by Vasiṣṭha, as if they had extended their necks to hear the entire sequence of descriptions concerning all things. (MU 3.4.9)
"For at the time of evening, shadows indeed lengthen;
even he who wishes to hear something becomes long-necked. This is a statement regarding two natural properties. The doorkeeper, bowing low before him, spoke to the lord of the earth:

"O King, the time for bathing and the worship of the twice-born has indeed passed by. Having become humble and bowed down, [the sage] says "What did he say?"—anticipating the action—the second half of the verse states the object of that action as "deva" (O King). The particle *hi* indicates certainty.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha, having thus withdrawn his sweet speech, said:
"Therefore, O Great King, let this much be heard by you for now. (MU 3.4.11)
Having said, "I shall speak something else tomorrow morning after withdrawing [my mind]," he became silent.
Having heard this and replied, "So be it," the king [acted] for the increase of his prosperity.

"Vadiṣyāma" [means] "we shall speak"; "astūktvā" means "having said 'so be it'"; "having heard this and said 'so be it'," [he performed worship] by means of the offering of flowers, water for the guest, water for the feet, honors, and the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
He respectfully honored the celestial rishis,
the sages, and the brahmins with offerings of flowers, water for the hands, water for the feet, marks of respect, sacrificial fees, and worship.
Knowing that the listeners were eager to hear, he said, "In the morning"; that is,
immediately upon hearing [the request],
and not by way of providing a reply.
He was Daśaratha.
Upon merely hearing it, the king, having engaged in conversation, [uttered] a reply.
Then the entire assembly, including the circle of kings and sages, rose up;
their faces were encircled by a halo from the mass of rays radiating from their earrings.
"Assembly" (sabhā) refers to the multitude of people.
He qualifies the assembly hall with the word *kuṇḍala*:
a mass of rays, a collection of light-beams, which is strewn and diffused on all sides from the earrings.
Its "pariveśa" is its circumference or orb; by that, the faces of the people—that is, the faces of those in the assembly—are surrounded in which [assembly]. That [is the assembly].
"Kuṇḍaleti": *kuṇḍale*...
"Sabhāsamukhāni": *°sa⟨da⟩mu°*.
With armlets, bracelets, and anklets jingling as they struck one another's shoulders.
With the spaces between their chests filled by golden bands pressed down by the weight of necklaces,
they met one another as their shoulders brushed against each other.
Therefore, it is that [city] in which armlets and bracelets are jingling;
and it is that [city] in which the spaces between the chests— the middle parts of the chest-slopes— which possess the luster of golden bands, are struck by the weight of necklaces.
Their golden-ribboned garments were struck by the weight of necklaces;
with swarms of bees awakened and resting upon the removal of their crests,
the upper parts of their heads resounded with humming, as if with hair falling down.
Upon the crests— that is, upon the flower-crests of the members of the assembly—
by means of emission, that is, by the exhalation of fragrance;
they were rested, meaning they possessed rest.
Likewise, by the swarms— that is, the multitudes— of those honey-drinking bees who are awakened and skillful in smelling fragrances.
With the regions of their heads filled with a humming sound— that is, possessing the head-regions of people accompanied by the sound of humming—
by what [beings] was this like? By swarms of bees, that is,
by those whose nature is to fall.
Because they were black in color, they were like the hair grown from a crown;
their faces in all directions were turned to gold by the brilliance of their golden ornaments;
and the activities of their senses were completely stilled through the meaning of the Sage’s words held in their intellect.
The quarters of the sky were turned golden by the radiance of their golden ornaments;
the activities of their senses were completely stilled by the meaning of the words of the Sage dwelling in their intellects.
The sky-dwellers went to the sky and the earth-dwellers to the circle of the earth;
everyone performed their own daily activities in their respective homes.
(The light) was the radiance, the brilliance, of those wearing golden ornaments.
By him, golden forms were fashioned;
those by which the faces of the quarters [were illuminated] were of such a kind.
Likewise, "situated in the intellect" means having the nature of manifesting within the intellect,
and not being forgotten;
this refers to the meaning of the Sage's speech.
By that [means], the functions of the senses— the activities of the sense organs— which have become thoroughly stilled and have attained a state of non-orientation toward their respective objects,
are of such a nature.
The sky-dwellers, moving through the atmosphere,
went into the void;
the earth-dwellers went to the circle of the earth.
Then all those beings, including the sky-dwellers and others,
performed their respective daily routines within their own abodes and private dwellings.
In the meantime, the dark night appeared like a young woman in a house empty of the crowds of people. (MU 3.4.19) [Note:
*bālāṅganā* = *bālā-aṅganā*]
In this interval, at this time,
the night was dark,
a nocturnal night joined with its watches.
Free from the throngs of people, abandoned by the masses of men,
the leader of the day departed to illuminate another region;
for the duty of a noble man is indeed to provide light everywhere.
The state of being a maker of light, the nature of being a creator of illumination, [is] the quality of a true person (*satpuruṣatvam*).
Belonging to a virtuous man—that is, connected with a noble person.
(MT_3,4.20) The twilight arose on all sides, bearing a multitude of stars, like the splendor of spring appearing when the forests of *kiṃśuka* trees are in full bloom. MU_3,4.21
She appeared; she became manifest.
(MT_3,4.21) Birds settled within the mango, *nīpa*, and *kadamba* trees, at the tops of village shrines, and inside houses, as if their minds were fixed in a state of motionless stillness. MU_3,4.22
In the mind— [in the] heart—
the birds, the winged creatures, settled down; they became hidden.
Where?
In the mango trees, the *nīpa* flowers, the tops of the *kadamba* trees, the village shrines, and the interiors of houses;
that is, the mangoes, the *nīpas*, the tops of the *kadamabas*, the village shrines, and the interiors of the houses.
In that regard:
what are the "birds" (khagāḥ)? They are like [the birds]. What are the "modes of activity" (vṛttayaḥ)? They are like those [birds].
The meaning is: just as those mental activities (*vṛtti*), which are the operations of the minds of the Śrāvaka followers, dissolved into the mind (*citta*), so too [did they dissolve].
They vanished; at that time, those mental states (*vṛtti*)—as stated in 3.4.22d in Ś1 and Ś3: *tadā tā vṛttayo yathā* (MT_3,4.22)—describe the manifestation of the twilight glow.

Adorned with fragments of clouds tinted by the light of the sun, as if with a slight hue of saffron, the western mountain— clad in yellow garments and joined with the sky— is united with the beauty of the star-necklace emerging from the ocean of darkness. (MU 3.4.23) [kuṅkumacchāyayeva] °y⟨ai⟩[e]va.
[The mountain] with its final peak,
as if by the hue of saffron— meaning by the splendor of the sun, which resembles an arrangement of saffron— with the light of the sun.
By small fragments of clouds— meaning by bits of cloud that have been slightly adorned and brought to a yellowish hue.
The western mountain, the setting peak (astaśaila), was observed;
[there] Śrī Nārāyaṇa, clad in yellow garments, appeared upon the ocean of darkness known as Tamas.
And he was clothed in yellow garments,
for even the fragments of clouds adorned by the radiance of the sun take on the form of yellow clothing,
and [he was so] because of the yellow garment of the ocean.
It is indeed fitting that he is joined with the illustrious Nārāyaṇa.
Of what nature is the western mountain?
It is endowed with the beauty of a necklace of stars.
He whose necklace is Tārā herself is Tārāhāra;
[he is so called] by virtue of his splendor or beauty.
Endowed with; endowed with glory;
he who is both the necklace of stars and endowed with glory is the "Nakṣatramālāśrīyuta."
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He has gone to, or entered into, space, which is the sky.
The meaning is that it pervades space;
otherwise, its nature as a necklace of stars would be impossible,
[as it belongs] to Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, its possession of a necklace of stars, its endowment with Lakṣmī, and its equality with space through the penetration by Bālī are indeed established.
This is the reality (*tattva*) of the *khasama* [state].
Having first performed the twilight peace-rite (*sandhyā-śānti*), he describes the arising of darkness;
having taken up the worship, when the twilight has passed, he departs as he came.
And the darknesses arose like circles of vetālas;
[vetālavalayā] is clearly [the reading].
A cool breeze blew, shimmering with droplets of dew, shaking the tender sprouts with ease, soft, and suggesting the presence of night-lotuses;
for "suggesting night-lotuses" means by way of the fragrance of night-lotuses.
Even the quarters of the sky, though their stars were clearly visible, fell into utter darkness,
like widowed women with long,
hanging tresses of hair.
Those whose hair was long and exceedingly extended... (MT_3,4.26).
He arrived, filling the world with a flood of the milk of splendor; his form composed of elixir, he was like the ocean of milk and the moon filling the sky. (MU_3,4.27)
The world (*bhuvana*) is indeed the flood of milk that is the splendor (*tejas*) of *Bhuvas*;
by that [flood].

It had the appearance of an elixir and the appearance of nectar. Masses of darkness fled and vanished somewhere, like the ignorance of kings' minds when the words of scriptural knowledge are heard. (MU 3.4.27–28)
From him by whom the words of knowledge spoken by Vasiṣṭha— that is, the utterances of wisdom— have been heard;
from such a person as that.
The ignorance—that is, the follies—of kings beginning with Daśaratha;
as well as the sages, protectors of the earth, ascetics, and likewise the brahmins. (MT 3.4.28)
Like various meanings within the mind, the manifold meanings associated with the words of the illustrious Vasiṣṭha came to rest in their own respective abodes.
"Manifold meanings" refers to the diverse senses connected to the speech of the illustrious Vasiṣṭha;
"in their own abodes" means in their own homes.
They rested; they took rest.
In their own homes, [there were] things of various meanings...
In their own homes, the thick darkness, dark as a female elephant, departed;
there, for them, the dawn slowly arrived, appearing like mist.
Like the body of Yama, resembling the form of Yama;
this refers to the dawns of those sages and protectors of the earth.
The bright stars in the sky became imperceptible, like showers of saffron dust swept away by the morning breeze.
(MU 3.4.31) This is clear. (MT 3.4.31)

Behold, Viveka-vṛtti (the faculty of discernment) has arrived, her eyes opened by the light of the sun, like a new-born dawn in the minds of the great. (MU 3.4.32) [ājagāmārkaprabhonmīlitalocanā] °bho⟨r⟩[n]mī°
The function of discrimination (*viveka-vṛtti*) is the mental operation known as discrimination (*viveka*).
(MT_3,4.32) Then the sky-dwellers and the earth-dwellers again approached the assembly hall, having performed their morning rites in the same sequence as the previous day. (MU_3,4.33)
The connection is that those who move through the sky and those who move upon the earth arrived at the assembly hall in the very same order as the previous day.
That vast assembly hall entered [the narrative] with its former arrangement;
it became motionless in appearance, like a lotus pond when the wind has ceased.

The assembly’s state of motionlessness is to be understood as resulting from its former arrangement and configuration, and from its eagerness to hear the instruction of the venerable Vasiṣṭha. Then, taking advantage of the occasion, Rāma spoke with a sweet voice:
He spoke to Vasiṣṭha, the tiger among sages and the best of speakers, having found an appropriate occasion;
the implication is that otherwise there would be the fault known as impudence.
In response to the inquiry, "What did he say?", [the author] says:
"O Blessed One, tell me clearly what the nature of the mind is, since by it this entire cluster of defects is spread out. (MU 3.4.36)
"What is the use of describing the form of your mind?
To this, he says: "Because by that mind... [referring to] by that mind.
This is the form of creation.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply:
O Rāma, not even the slightest form of this mind is perceived.
"Just as there is nothing other than the mere name of the sky, which is empty and insentient by nature," O Rāma, "apart from the mere name of this mind— that is, excluding the mere name—
not even the slightest form is perceived."
The meaning is that there is only the name of the mind, but no form.
Of what kind is this mind?
It is empty (*śūnya*), being of no nature whatsoever because it cannot withstand analysis.
"Insentient" (jaḍā) means endowed with the quality of insentience because its establishment depends upon being apprehended by a witness;
"whose form" (ākṛtiḥ svarūpaṃ yasya) refers to that [which possesses such a form].
Of what such [thing] is it like?
It is like space;
just as space has the nature of being empty and insentient.
The meaning is "so it is."
[It] exists;
[it] exists by virtue of having its establishment dependent upon the apprehension of a witness. This very point he confirms.
The mind exists as a real entity neither externally nor within the heart;
know, O Rāma, that it is situated everywhere, just like space.
The mind does not exist as a real entity externally, because it is not perceived by the external senses.
Even in the heart, that is, even in the region of the heart,
no real entity exists;
for indeed, nothing called "mind" is found in the region of the heart.
O Rāma,
you [are] this mind.
Know— that is, understand— that it exists everywhere, both externally and within the heart;
for its effect, known as conceptualization (saṅkalpa), manifests both externally and within the heart.
For even volition (saṅkalpa) takes as its object external things such as a jar, as well as internal things such as pleasure;
how is it that the mind (manas) is not like this?
"As the sky":
the meaning is that just as the sky is situated everywhere, so it is.
[Objection: "Even so, its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) must be stated;
for it is not logical that something absolutely non-existent should be present everywhere. To this, he says:
In every way and in every respect, this which has arisen for him is non-existent, resembling the water of a mirage.
But hear the nature of form in brief: it is like the illusion of a second moon; you, O mind, have arisen from the unreal, having manifested falsely.
Therefore, this which is being experienced is like the water of a mirage and likewise comparable to the delusion of a second moon.
Form is its own nature; listen briefly. (MT 3.4.39) This explains the very nature of the mind.
O virtuous one, know that this which has become manifest as the appearance of an object— whether it be existent or non-existent— is the mind and nothing else. (MU 3.4.40) O virtuous one,
[it refers to] an object or thing, whether it be existent or non-existent.
This "inspiration" (pratibhāna) is a flash of intuition;
that is to say, it is the mental synthesis [of an object] as a thing.
"Manifestation" (prathā) means firmness.
That has passed away;
know that to be the mind.
The other, conceptualized by logicians and others as being composed of atoms and so forth, is not it.
"The mind does not exist, whether as being or as non-being"— this was stated by resorting to the distinction between various philosophical disputants. He repeats this very point again and again.
That which is the manifestation of an object is designated as "mind" (*manas*);
there is never anything else whatsoever that exists by the name of "mind.
The manifestation of an object is the appearance of the object-nature within objects.
"Know that the mind is volition; it is not distinct from volition. Just as water [is not distinct] from fluidity, so too is movement [not distinct] from the wind.
This is clear. (MU 3.4.42)
Where there is volition, O dear one, there the mind likewise resides;
volition and the mind are never, for anyone, distinct from one another.
(MU 3.4.43) "Where" means in whichever state.
A conceptualization occurs:
"O friend!
there, in that state."
That is well known:
the mind thus remains established in that form called conceptualization.
In some cases, [the terms] *anirvācya* (ineffable) and *saṅkalpamanasī* (conception and mind) [are used];
at any time, indeed.
They do not exist as distinct,
because they possess a single nature. Whether it be real or unreal, that which appears as an object— [is this appearance itself the object]?
Know that the mind is of just that measure; it is Brahman, this Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
Whether real or unreal, that which is the appearance of an object—the manifestation of an object—exists.
That appearance of an object is merely that;
it is the mind (*manas*) or consciousness (*citta*).
Know— that is, understand—
that this mind, whose nature is the manifestation of objects,
is what is described in the treatises.
Brahmā is another synonym for Pitāmaha; he is called Pitāmaha because he is the cause of all creation,
for it is stated in the scriptures that the very cause of creation possesses the nature of Brahman.
It describes the mind as having the nature of a subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), which is experienced by all during dreams and so forth:
"The mind is designated as the self of the subtle body;
the material intellect (ādhibhautika-buddhi), however, is the long-enduring consciousness. (MU 3.4.45)

By the wise, the self (ātman) or essential nature of the body— which is of a transporting nature, clearly characterized by reaching a destination within a moment that would otherwise take a year to reach, and which appears as a body in dreams, mental constructs, and so forth—
is designated as the "mind" (manas).
But it is not the atom as conceived by the logicians;
for it is not tenable that its aforementioned nature should be capable of excessive movement,
since such [movement] is not observed in the gross body composed of those [atoms].
In this context, he establishes that the firmness of the intellect (buddhi-dārḍhya) consists in its being a physical body (ādhibhautika-dehatva), using the word "ādhibhautika" [as the reason].
The particle "tu" indicates a distinction.
By the wise, "ādhibhautika-buddhi" is understood as the intellect having the form of a physical body.
That is to say, it refers to the nature of the physical body (*ādhibhautika-deha*).
"Long-enduring cognition" (*cirasthiti-dhī*) means that the intellect (*buddhi*) regarding the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) has attained firmness;
this is what is always being described.

For it is the intellect itself—having as its object the subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*) whose nature is the mind—that manifests through the state of solidity as the material (*ādhibhautika*). There is no such thing as a separate "material" entity consisting of flesh; for even if such a thing were to exist, it would be like a non-entity without being an object of the intellect.
However, when it is an object of the intellect, its nature as intellect does not depart.
For that alone is called an object (*viṣaya*) which appears as if situated at the tip of the subject (*viṣayin*);
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpāta*) that even a yellow substance would become the object of the cognition of blue.
The second particle *tu* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
The state of the body being material (*ādhibhautika*) [results from] the firmness of the intellect; the intellect being material [results from] the firmness of the mind.
Someone—namely, someone.
Because it is an unreal construction (*asatkalpa*).
[The term] *viṣayyagrastha* is a corruption for *viṣayyagra-stha*.
He states that the mind is synonymous with the "visible" (*dṛśya*) in order to prove its visibility.

"Ignorance, transmigratory existence, mind, intellect, bondage, impurity, and darkness"—the supreme ones know these to be synonyms for the object of perception (*dṛśya*). Therefore, the mind is indeed the object of perception; otherwise, it would not possess the status of being a synonym for the object of perception.
[Objection: But how is it logical for the mind, which appears as the grasper of objects, to be synonymous with the "visible"?
[Reply: To this he says:
"For there is no form of the mind whatsoever apart from the visible."
Furthermore, I shall state again that this visible world has indeed arisen, yet it is not [ultimately real].
I shall state this because of the following reason.
Apart from the visible, there is nothing whatsoever distinct from the visible; for the nature of the mind is indeed [of that same character]. This is certain.
It does not exist.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is logical for the mind to be synonymous with the "visible" (dṛśya).
[The opponent asks: "But what follows from that? To this, he says:
And as for "the visible":
this visible object has not arisen,
because it was stated previously.
Therefore, the sense is that the mind, too, is indeed unarisen. Now, one might object:
"Previously, no certainty arose in me regarding the non-arising of the visible"; to this he replies:
"I"—this very [term] signifies the non-arising of the visible.
I shall speak further;
the intention is that [the subject] is difficult to understand.
He explains precisely the non-arising of the visible object.
Just as the lotus bud exists within the lotus seed,
so too does the visible world exist within the atom of supreme consciousness.
Just as the lotus bud is within the lotus seed, the eye of the lotus.
It remains within;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that its emergence at the forefront would be impossible.
Likewise, the "visible world" is the world that has become the object of the act of seeing.
It extends down to the ultimate atom of great consciousness.
Great consciousness is consciousness that is undivided;
it is called an "atom" precisely because of its extreme subtlety.
It remains within—that is, in the middle of it.
The implication is: otherwise, from where could its emergence occur?
Therefore, because the visible world lacks any separateness from the Great Consciousness, its very non-arising is the ultimate reality.
This is precisely what he states again and again.
Just as light is to illumination, just as movement is to the wind,
and just as liquidity is to water, such is the visibility of the Seer. (MU 3.4.49) "Light" is a specific quality that is the cause for the manifestation of objects.
Heating is vibration;
the meaning is that there is no existence of an object of perception distinct from the perceiver.
Just as there is no bracelet apart from gold, just as there is no water in a mirage,
and just as there is no wall in a dream-city, so too is the perception of the visible object within the seer. (MU 3.4.50)
This is clear.
By this principle, he declares that even the fact established—that the seer consists of the seen—is to be wiped away as an impurity:
"Thus, the state of being the seen, which exists in the seer as if it were non-different [from him]," [is to be removed].
I shall quickly wipe away even that impurity from the mirror of your mind.
This being so, [it is] non-different— that is, not distinct— from the seer, the agent of the act of seeing, according to the reasoning already stated.
That which is the state of being visible— the state of being the object of the act of seeing— is as if it were established [in the form]: "I."
Impurity exists as impurity;
that too is non-different from the seer, as is the state of being an object of vision.
From the mirror of your own mind—that is, from the reflecting surface of your own mind.
I cleanse [the mind],
so that in every way there may be no appearance of the visible in your mind;
even that which appears as non-existent, the visible, [is cleansed] in its slightest part.
The sense is that it results only in suffering.
Now, one might object: how can that which is non-different from the seer be considered a stain (*mala*), given that only that which is distinct [from the seer] can be a stain? If this is argued:
True.
Even though the observer determines the objectivity [of the seen] as non-different from himself, he also brings about its difference from himself;
that which is called "difference from oneself" [is thus established].

Since self-identity cannot be established without a counter-correlate (pratiyogin), it is clear that the visible world (dṛśya), which brings about the appearance of difference from oneself, is indeed a stain (mala); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

[The Seer] — [ṣṭ⟨r⟩ā (MT_3,4.51)] But for what purpose do you effect the removal of the state of being an object of sight even for that which is of the nature of impurity, while remaining non-different from the Seer? To this he replies:
[non-differentness] — [°ya⟨t⟩tve°]

Know that the state of being a solitary one (*kevalībhāva*) is that which, by force, becomes the non-seeing of this seer when there is no object of sight; [it belongs] to this [Self] which exists as the Self, precisely because of the non-existence of the unreal.
(MU 3.4.52) "Of this" refers to that which abides as the Self.
Of the seer, that is, the agent of the act of seeing;
when there is an absence of the visible object;
by force, that is, by power.
That is to say, "without its own effort.
For that which would be "non-seeing"—
indeed, there is no such thing as the state of being a seer for a seer apart from an object to be seen.
Even though it exists in the state of power (*śakti*), its essential nature (*svarūpa*) does not depart; therefore,
[you are] "thou" (*tvam*).
Know— that is, understand— that state of being a non-seer to be isolation (kaivalya), which is liberation.
Because liberation consists solely in the seer’s lack of orientation toward the visible;
