of what kind of seer? Precisely because he is neither non-existent nor existent.
With respect to the state of being a seer, it is non-existent;
with respect to its state of absolute isolation (*kevalībhāva*), it is existent. For the absolute isolation of that which is non-existent is not logical.
Thus, the meaning is "of that which is inexpressible.
Therefore, the sense is that for the sake of attaining the state of isolation (kaivalya), the complete eradication of the object of vision must indeed be accomplished in every respect.
Therefore, [it is] precisely because of the non-existence [of the object]... [that the state of being a witness is established].
Now, one might object: "Even if the state of being a non-seer is established through the power of the absence of the visible, the state of being solitary (*kevalībhāva*) is not yet established;
for, as in deep sleep, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and so forth directed toward visible objects persist. To this, he says:
When an entity has attained its perfected state (*siddhatām upagate bhāve*), the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion, hatred, and so forth,
subside— just as the agitation caused by movement ceases when the wind is stilled.
When one has attained the state of reality within the internal state—
that is, the state of being a non-seer produced by the absence of the visible— then...

The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of attachment, aversion, and so forth— namely, the residual traces (*saṃskāra*) of attachment, aversion, and so forth toward previously perceived objects of the visible world— subside, that is, they reach a state of peace,
because of the absence of both the substratum and the object.
In deep sleep, however, because the substrate and its objects persist in the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),

there is likewise the persistence of attachment, aversion, and so forth, which follow those [substrate and objects] in the absence of latent impressions. For in deep sleep, there is no destruction of the seer and the seen along with their roots.
For if one were to arise from that state again, it would follow that there is still a basis for attachment;
indeed, attachment is not appropriate when something has been destroyed along with its very root.

However, for those who have ascertained the non-existence of the visible object, no attachment arises at any time even when the visible object appears; in this matter, one's own mind alone is the witness—enough with this elaboration.
What, then, is the latent tendency (*vāsanā*) of passion, hatred, and so forth?
Just as there is agitation through vibration;
or, when the wind is not vibrating,
the agitation produced by the wind— which is of the nature of vibration— is the state of being agitated.
It perishes;
that is the meaning of "thus.
Therefore, [the state] of non-perception caused by the absence of the object of perception—
The sense is that it is indeed logical for there to be the state of being a Kevalin.
Regarding the seer and the seen:
because this very point is extremely difficult to understand, he explains it again and again:
"When everything consisting of the directions, the earth, and space is impossible... (MT 3.4.53).
Just as the stainless form of light remains when that which is to be illuminated has vanished,
so too, when the visible world— consisting of the three worlds, yourself, and me— has attained non-existence,
there arises for the pure-souled seer that state of absolute isolation.

When the collection of objects— which possess the nature of the directions, the earth, and space, and which consist of the very essence of the directions, the earth, and space— is such that it cannot possibly exist, yet is [erroneously] perceived as something to be illuminated and made manifest.
When it does not partake in the agency of the act of origination,
the purity of light— that is, of the sun's radiance—
is such that it is stainless and pure.
It would follow that form exists even beyond the reach of the sense faculties;
for light that has departed from the solar disc and has not fallen upon a wall cannot be perceived by the eye.
When the three worlds and "I" have attained non-existence— that is, the absence of reality— within the visible world,
[there remains] the seer, who stands as the illuminator of the visible.
Such a state of isolation (kevalībhāva), which is the nature of purity,
would belong to the seer; of what kind of seer?

Otherwise, for one whose nature is pure consciousness yet stained by the impurity of the object of thought (*cetya*), a state of stainlessness— which is synonymous with the state of absolute isolation (*kevalībhāva*)— would be impossible.

For just as the nature of a mirror— consisting solely of its own essence— appears in a mirror when there are reflections of infinite mountains and all other things from the solar orb, so too is it here.
When the delusion of the visible world— such as "I," "you," and "the universe"— has subsided,

there arises that same state of absolute oneness (kevalatā) while the Seer remains established, no longer looking outward. The word "subsided" (praśānte), which pertains to the subject of the illustration, should also be applied to the illustrative example itself.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
for "hi" signifies certainty;
those which are infinite and entire, such as mountains and so forth.
When that reflection has become stilled—
that is, when it has ceased to assume the state of a reflection within the mirror, being apprehended as the illustrative example—
it exists in the mirror as having the nature of the mirror alone, consisting solely of the essential form known as the mirror.
It would be like the nature of a mirror;
that is to say, in the delusion of the visible—such as "I," "you," and "the world"—which is the delusion regarding the form of the visible.
"In the visible" means, in short, within the object of perception.
When [the mind] has become tranquil, then,
while the observer remains inactive— performing no act of seeing—
the seer stands [as he is].
Such would be that state of absolute isolation (*kevalatā*).
The sense is that just as only the pure mirror remains when there is no reflection, so too only the pure seer remains when there is no object of sight.
Thus is the meaning. Thinking that the non-existence of the visible object was impossible, Śrī Rāma asks about the meanings [of the verses].
If this [fault] does not subside, or if there is no non-existence of that which exists,
we do not perceive non-existence in this visible world which bestows defects;
the word "vā" (or) has the sense of "yataḥ" (since/because).
This visible object is existent; if it is so, that is,
if it possesses existence.
Then it does not cease;
for as long as something exists— that is, as long as it possesses existence— non-existence is not found.
Because it would entail the loss of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Otherwise, even fire would suffer the loss of its capacity to burn.
[Objection: In that case, then, it must be non-existent (*asad*).
"Let it be so.
To this he replies: "And non-existence," meaning [non-existence] which bestows defects—that is, which bestows the defects inherent in passion and the like.
The sense is that it is not logical for that which is non-existent to be a source of defects, because otherwise even the son of a barren woman would possess that quality.
*sattābhajataḥ* [is] *satt(ā)bhajataḥ*;
*bhavatv* [is] *bhavatv*;
*na* [is] *na*.
He states the conclusion:

"Therefore, O Brahmin, how can this cholera of the visible world be pacified—it which causes confusion through the arising of manifoldness and bestows a continuous succession of suffering? (MU 3.4.59)
"Arising from various things" means the production of diversity.
That which is "delusion" is false cognition;
she is such that she produces that. (MT 3.4.59)
To bring his vow, "I shall wipe it away," to fruition, Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks this reply:
"Listen to this mantra for the pacification of this demon of the visible world."
O Rāma, because of this [consciousness], you will utterly perish and go to death before that which shines forth before you. O Rāma, you! [This refers to] him who manifests before you.
For the pacification of the visible piśāca,
listen to this mantra, which consists of the collection of words that will be spoken hereafter.
By means of which mantra this visible piśāca [attains] absolute death— the non-existence of the three times.
It comes and goes; from that, it perishes and passes out of sight. And it is fitting that for a piśāca there should be death by means of a mantra and its disappearance.
The visible piśāca says this very mantra:
"O Rāghava, that which exists can never be destroyed."
Because that [object], even when it has perished, remains as a seed within the heart;
O Rāghava, whatever object possesses existence...
Its destruction never occurs at any time;
for that is a real entity.
Even if it has perished— perished by some other factor accepted by opponents, such as the destruction of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa)—
it remains as a seed within the heart, that is, within the mind.
It exists either as a seed-state, which is to say, it exists in the form of a latent potential;
for even a thing that has perished is seen to recur again and again within the mind.
[By the destruction, etc., of the inherent cause] ... by the destruction, etc. ... in the form of existence ... "existence" ...
thus.
[hi] °ya(ti)*te hi* (MT_3,4.61).
[Objection: "But what fault is there in that? To this he says:
"The cognition of the visible world, having arisen again in the space of consciousness from the seed of memory..."
It spreads forth a vast defect that takes on the form of the world, the mountains, and the sky;
[the term] *smṛtibījā* means having recollection as its seed, that is, having recollection as its cause.
The "cognition of the visible" (dṛśyadhīḥ) is cognition having the form of the visible;
that is to say, the visible itself.
Having arisen—that is, having manifested—in the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).

Furthermore, it expands— that is, it specifically spreads out— the fault, which is not minute but vast, taking the form of the world, mountains, and sky, by way of subtle conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
because it is seen in dreams.
"Surely, what follows from that? To this he replies:
"In this way, there would be the fault of the impossibility of liberation, and yet its partial occurrence is not possible;
for gods, sages, and seers are seen to be recipients of liberation. (MU 3.4.63)
This being the case,
there would be the fault of non-liberation— a fault consisting in the undesirable consequence that liberation does not exist.
Because liberation is precisely the absence of the visible object, which is twofold by way of being gross or subtle.
[The opponent objects: "Let that fault be;
what will it do to us?"
To this he says: "And not... That defect of non-liberation does not occur even in part.
Because gods, sages, and seers are seen to be recipients of liberation.
Furthermore, he explains this very point again:
if this world had a beginning, then there would be no liberation for anyone.

Whether it be situated outside or within the heart, the visible world is merely for the sake of destruction. If this world and so forth were to possess existence, then [it would belong] to some particular perceiver.
Liberation is release from the visible;
it would not occur. For even if the destruction of the visible were somehow brought about, the visible would manifest again in a subtle form due to the power of memory.
For whether the visible object be of a gross form situated externally, or of a subtle form situated within the heart,
it serves for destruction— that is, for the purpose of producing the destruction known as bondage.
The meaning is that there is no difference in their quality as agitators.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), deep sleep, torpor, and so forth are included, because those too are objects of perception (*dṛśyatva*). (MT 3.4.64)
"If that is so, then what should be done? To this he says:
"Therefore, O Rāma, listen to this most terrifying proposition, which you will surely understand through the subsequent text. (MU 3.4.65)
And the extreme terrifying nature of the proposition should be understood as arising from its engagement with the impossible.
He explains the subsequent text itself for the purpose of awakening Śrī Rāma:
"I am characterized as being of the nature of space, the elements, and so forth."
"Indeed, O Rāma, there is no meaning whatsoever for the word 'jagat' (the world) [other than you]. O Rāma! Indeed (*nanu*) signifies certainty;
it refers to that which has the nature of space, the elements, and so forth."

Thus, that which is characterized as "I" and so forth is determined to be the meaning—the referent—of the word "world. From the perspective of ultimate reality, it does not exist at all; it simply does not possess existence.
But it does not perish after having become a part of existence;
and this being so, there is no consequence of the fault of non-liberation,
for it is not observed that what is non-existent can act as a binder— this is the sense.
Although space is an element (*bhūta*), it is mentioned separately because of its preeminence;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the effects of the elements are included.
[Objection: But how is it logical for the world—consisting of the "I" and so forth—which appears before us, to be real in every respect? To this, he says:
Whatever web of objects is seen here before us,
all that is indeed Brahman alone— undecaying, immortal, and immutable.
This "web of objects" (*dṛśyajāla*) which is present before us consists of the collection of visible things whose forms are blue, pleasure, and so forth.
It is seen and experienced;

all that is ageless and immortal because it is devoid of a body, being free from old age and other such states inherent in the subtle elements (tanmātra). Likewise, it is imperishable, meaning it is devoid of destruction.
Brahman alone is expanded as the world; it is the pure reality of consciousness itself that becomes the world in this manner. For it is observed that water exists in the form of waves.

And this being the case, it is indeed logical that the world, even while appearing, is non-existent; for the point is that the existence of a wave, even while appearing in water, has never been observed.
By means of the state of being waves, he further confirms that the visible world is nothing but Brahman alone:
"In the Full, the Full expands; in the Supreme, the Supreme remains as peace."
In the sky alone has the sky arisen; Brahman abides in Brahman.
In the full, the supreme.
In the full and independent [state],
it flows forth and performs its movement;
it is situated in its own nature within the transcendent Supreme.
In the term *brahmaṇi*,
meaning "in the expanded reality," the pure consciousness (*śuddhacittattva*) is described here by means of locative endings,
while it is described by means of nominative endings [in the following].
That is the object of knowledge for the world which has that nature.

[Objection: But how is it logical for the pure consciousness (*cittattva*)—which is endowed with qualities such as fullness—to abide [within itself]? For we observe that what is deficient abides within what is superior.
It is true that there is no abiding here in the sense of being something to be placed [as a substratum], by which the aforementioned fault would follow.
However, because of the absence of that state of being merely that, there is no consequence of fault here; enough with these elaborations.
There is neither the visible object nor the seeing, neither the seer nor the act of seeing.
This pervasive reality is neither empty, nor inert, nor consciousness; it is simply the tranquil.
It is not the visible object of the act of seeing.
There is no being, nor does it partake [in existence];
seeing is the act of seeing;
there is none that exists.
The seer, the agent of the act of seeing,
does not exist; nor does seeing, which is the fruit to be accomplished by the act of seeing.
And it does not exist, because the essence of all these is mere cognition.
[Objection: In that case, does this non-existence itself exist? To this, he says:
It is not "empty.
Emptiness is the absence of visible objects and so forth;
yet that [emptiness] does not exist either.
For it is not logical for that which is absolutely non-existent to appear, since that would entail the appearance even of things such as a rabbit's horn. [Objection:
In that case, there would simply be insentience (jāḍya).
For in the case of insentience (*jāḍya*), there is indeed non-existence for all;
regarding this, he says "not insentient" (*na jaḍam*).
This is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant; thus, "insentient" (*jaḍam*) means "the state of being insentient" (*jaḍatvam*).
It does not exist;
for if it were real, the manifestation of the visible and so forth would be untenable.
[Objection: In that case, would it not then be simply consciousness (cit) alone? To this, he says:
"Not anything" (no cit): "cit" means pure consciousness (cinmātra).
It does not exist, because it exists only in dependence upon that which is objectified (cetya).
And because, according to the reasoning already stated, such a thing is impossible;
for if that is so, what then exists?
Indeed, absolute non-existence cannot be presented to the intellect.
Regarding this, it is said: "Peaceful" (*śānta*) means that which is extended and whose essential nature vibrates everywhere;
"all this" refers to the visible world and so forth.
It becomes peaceful;
it becomes pure consciousness alone, free from the agitation of mental objects.
[Asattā] *asattā* (MT 3,4.69).
Failing to reach certainty in this matter, Śrī Rāma imputes to the sage the quality of propounding an impossible meaning:
"A mountain is ground by the son of a barren woman; a rabbit's horn is perceived."
"Stretching out its mass of arms, the rock performs the *tāṇḍava* dance;
the sands drip oil, and the stone figurines recite; the painted clouds roar"—such, O Lord, was this speech. (MU 3.4.70–71)
The word "thine" is understood [as the subject].
O Lord,
this is thy speech.
Thus it comes to be;
it becomes of such a form. What is this?
"By the son of a barren woman," and so forth.
The meaning is that "people perceive a rabbit's horn"—that is, they begin to perceive it.
The verbal form *pramāyate* is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
The sense is that your statement is in every respect expressive of a completely unrelated meaning.
The address "O Lord" is intended to dispel the lack of discipline manifested through the attribution of the capacity to convey an impossible meaning.
The world consists of mountains, space, and so forth, characterized by the suffering of old age, death, and the like.
"What is this 'it does not exist' that even you say to me? (MU 3.4.72).
The meaning is that it is not reasonable to deny the multitude of entities—such as old age and so forth—which are directly perceived and experienced.
The word "api" (even) is intended to indicate that Śrī Vasiṣṭha is unfit to be a proponent of impossibility.
By the word "mine" (mama), he demonstrates his own status as a true disciple.
[The denial of the class of entities] ...
"just as" this is indeed true, then you should speak appropriately; with this intention he said.
"O Brahman, tell me how this universe is neither established, nor produced, nor exists, so that this may become certain for me. This refers to the absence of establishment and the other states.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply:
"I am not one whose speech is inconsistent; listen, O Rāghava, as this is being told:
how this unreal world appears, like the son of a barren woman or the light of a sunless sky."
I am the one named Vasiṣṭha;
he whose speech is "asamanvitā," meaning unconnected or incoherent.
I am not such a person as that,
O Raghava.
Listen: this world,
in whatever manner or by which means.
The non-existent appears;
it flashes forth before you;
thus I speak.
What is this like? It is like the son of a barren woman;
it is like one who utters the sound "āra," yet it is like the son of a barren woman.
The meaning is: "in such a way that it appears, though it is non-existent. He explains that very point:

This was unproduced from the very beginning; therefore, it is not substantial. For this visible world appears by means of the mind, just like a city in a dream and the like. (MU 3.4.75) This refers to the visible universe.
In the beginning, that is, at the primordial stage;
at the commencement of creation, which consists in pure consciousness becoming oriented toward an object of thought,
[the world] was unmanifest.
From the perspective of ultimate reality, because it does not deviate from the state of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*),
it was not supported by an existence distinct from that [consciousness].
For even in the external world, no existence distinct from clay is observed in a jar being produced from clay.
Therefore, for that reason,
this world is sufficient;
there is no need for anything further.
It has no existence and does not partake of it, because its existence is obtained merely through being the witness of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-sākṣitāmātra*), like a city in a dream.
[Objection: "If that is so, then how does this appear? To this, he says:
"Idam" means "this"; "hi" indicates certainty; "this" refers to the visible world; "by the mind" means by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
It shines; it manifests as an object of sight.
Like what?
Like a city.
The meaning is: just as a city appears to the mind in dreams and the like, so it is here.
Regarding the word *mṛdaḥ*: [it means] "from clay" (*mṛdaḥ*).

Now, one might argue that it is indeed logical for the visible world, which appears to the mind through its own existent nature, to possess existence. To this, he replies: "And the mind itself, at the beginning of creation, was unproduced and of a non-existent form."
Listen likewise, and I shall explain how this is experienced:
"unborn" [means] at the beginning, at the commencement of creation, in the state described as the very start of the world-process.
The mind itself is unarisen;
for this very reason, it has the nature of non-existence, its own-being being unreal.
Listen!
"I shall speak of this in such a way that it may be experienced by you just as it is. [Objection:
"Is it not improper to abandon the discussion of the non-existence of the visible object under consideration and instead discuss the non-existence of the mind? To this, he says:
The mind spreads this defect consisting of the visible world, which is of the nature of decay;
it is indeed unreal, appearing in an unreal form, just as one dream follows another.
The mind [spreads] this [world] appearing before us.
It extends— that is, it expands— the defect consisting of decay, which has a perishable nature; the defect consisting of the visible, which has a visible form.
In what state is the mind?
It is non-existent, because its nature is merely a manifestation; thus, its very essence is non-existent.
In what state is this defect consisting of the visible world?
It has the aspect of the non-existent and the nature of the non-existent,
because it is expanded by that which is non-existent;
for that which is expanded by the non-existent cannot possibly become existent.
Otherwise, even a web of words spread by the son of a barren woman would attain existence.
How is it like the mind?
It is like a dream.
The meaning is: just as a dream, which is unreal in its own nature, extends another unreal dream-form;
for it is indeed observed that one dream occurs within another dream, and there is no dispute on this point.
It further states that this very [consciousness] is the cause even with respect to the body, which serves as its own substrate:
"It itself, by its own free will, quickly conceives a body; by that means, this splendor of a magical illusion is expanded out by what has been expanded. (MU 3.4.78)
That mind; this physical body, appearing as the self; quickly—that is, rapidly;
by itself, without depending on the assistance of another.
"According to her own will" means by her own desire; "she brings about" means she accomplishes it through mere volition;
furthermore, he speaks again of the very subject at hand with the words "by her."
By that mind—
this [world], which appears as an object of perception—
he states the aforementioned meaning by summarizing it in a verse at the end of the chapter:
The mind flashes, moves, leaps, begs, exists, sinks, withdraws, and by itself assumes the state of another; it merely vibrates due to its flickering power.
This is merely an illustration.

Therefore, whatever action occurs here, it is produced solely by the mind; this is the summarized meaning. May there be auspiciousness! Thus ends the fourth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus heard that the determination regarding the mind must necessarily be made, Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, what indeed exists here in this mental delusion? How has the mind, consisting of illusion, arisen, and from where?"
O Blessed One, tiger among sages, O Blessed One, best of sages:
in this delusion that takes the form of the world,
what indeed exists as the mind, and of what nature is it?
Likewise, how has it arisen? In what manner has it manifested?
From where does the mind, which consists of illusion and has the nature of illusion, come to be?
With the intention of explaining its very origin first in that regard, he says: (MT_3,5.1)
"Speak!
O Lord, best among speakers, tell me in brief first how [this world] originated; thereafter you shall explain the remainder of what is to be said."
"You shall proclaim,
O Lord;
you [shall proclaim] to me the arising that culminates in the mind."

What remains after my questioning shall be "leftover" (*śiṣṭa*); you will proclaim—that is, explain—that very remainder yourself, because it has been left over. This is the intended meaning. (MT 3.5.2)
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
When the great dissolution has occurred and all that is visible has attained non-existence at the beginning of creation, only the tranquil remains.
When [it] has arrived—
that is, when there is the attainment or fulfillment of the specific state known as the fourth (turya), which is the great dissolution, or the time of the end of the great aeon (mahākalpa).
At the beginning of creation, when the entirety of the visible world— which consists of all created things, their destruction, and their residual impressions—
has attained non-existence, that is, has become invisible; at that time.

Only the Peaceful remains—gradually, step by step, as the witness of creation and destruction; having emerged even from agitation, that certain reality which is ineffable alone remains as the residue.
Here, "creation" refers to the witness toward the multitude of objects within its own domain.
Destruction (saṃhāra) is the non-existence of the object to be accomplished;

refinement (saṃskāra) is the refinement of the object and the non-existence of the object. The distinction between these two—namely, the refinement of the object and the refinement of the non-existence of the object—should be understood.
He clearly explains what remains after [all else] has subsided:
"The unborn, undecaying, and stainless God, the Sun, remains without having set."
The Supreme Self, Maheśvara, is at all times the creator of all and is everything.
The Supreme Self is, in the ultimate sense, a certain internal reality that exists and abides as the object of the "I-notion" (*ahantā*) for all beings.
Because it first exists as the witness to the great dissolution, and subsequently remains as the witness to the inherent natures being conceptualized in whatever manner they may be,
the statement regarding the existence and presentness of the Self— which is eternally established here— is not a source of error, as it is employed from the perspective of the knower.

In response to the inquiry, "Of what nature is this Supreme Self?", the author states the qualifying attributes, beginning with "unsetting" (*anastamita*). He is "unsetting" because, unlike the imagined individual self (*svāstha*) which remains as a subject of perception, he is in effect free from setting. He is "radiant" (*bhāsvān*) because, by virtue of being the witness, he illuminates everything and is thus of the nature of the sun.
And it is a marvel that the Radiant One does not set; for he is unborn, being devoid of birth,
since manifestation indeed constitutes birth.
And that [non-arising] is not tenable for it,
because it has always manifested as the self;
for it is never tenable that the self is non-manifested.
Because he exists as the grasper even prior to the manifestation of his own dream;
the Lord is one whose nature is play,
for otherwise, how could such a world come into being?
For one whose nature is not to play becomes averse even to the mere movement of the hands;
he is free from ailment, having emerged from the disease called illusion.

Otherwise, because he would be seized by the disease known as *māyā*, it would be illogical for him to be the impeller of *māyā*; for one who is seized by a disease does not become an impeller of that very disease.
He is the maker of all at all times, in all places, and in all circumstances.
Otherwise, it would be illogical for everything to arise at all times from everything;
[for] everything would possess the nature of everything else. Otherwise, what would constitute the essence of entities?
Maheśvara is the supreme controller;
otherwise, all things would not be determined by their respective natures.
Thus, [it is said] "from the disease called illusion" (*māyākhya-rogāt*);
he further qualifies that very same [disease].
From which words turn back, which is realized by the liberated,
and for whom designations such as "self" and so forth are merely conceptual constructs and not born of intrinsic nature.
It is understood that all words— both worldly and Vedic—
proceed from the Supreme Self, because [they originate] from Him.
They turn back;
for speech proceeds toward an object by placing convention (saṅketa) at its forefront, and it is impossible to establish a convention regarding the Supreme Self.

It is impossible [to establish a convention for it], because it is not within the range of either external or internal sense-faculties. It is observed that the making of conventions occurs only with respect to an object that is within the range of the senses, by way of direct apprehension (*hastagrāhikā*). Therefore, [if it is beyond the senses], it does not exist.
Regarding this, it is said: "by those who are liberated. This means precisely by those who are liberated—those whose minds are unattached to objects of perception—and not by worldly people.
That which is understood as the self— that is, known as the self—
for liberated beings indeed know some pure reality as the self,
since otherwise liberation would be impossible.
Thus, the point is that its non-existence is not tenable.
[Objection: But surely, it is improper to state that words turn away from it, because words such as "self" (ātman) and so forth denote it.
Regarding this, he says: "And for whom...
The words "by those who know reality" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Imagined" means established through conceptual construction, without depending on any basis for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), just like names such as "oil-drinker" (*tailapāyikā*) and so forth.
[Like the notion of a "tail-eater" (tailapāyika), etc.
Now, if that [Self] is indeed one alone, how is it that the Sāṅkhyas and others have spoken of "puruṣas" and so forth? To this he says:
"The person who is for those with the views of the Sāṅkhya, and Brahmā for the Vedāntins..."
For those who know consciousness, there is consciousness alone, which is absolutely stainless.
For the followers of Sāṅkhya, who delight in the Sāṅkhya philosophy,
the Sāṅkhyas indeed describe the Puruṣa— also known as the Jīva— as the sole remainder, distinct from Prakṛti.
And when that [self] is investigated, it finds its rest only in the nature of the aforementioned Supreme Self;
thus it is rightly said: "the person for those who hold the Sāṅkhya view.
This should be applied everywhere in the same manner.

The intention is that since the distinction between names remains as it is, the aforementioned fault does not follow. Now, if one asks: "Upon what philosophical system (darśana) did the venerable Vasiṣṭha base this scripture?"—the answer is: True;
he composed this scripture by relying upon the essence of all philosophical systems.
Otherwise, the acceptance of all philosophical systems would be untenable;
for here, the discussion of the Vedānta scriptures is seen to predominate.

In comparison with that, even the Śiva-śāstra—which is a great secret—is [superior] by only a small degree; so, enough of this digression from the subject at hand. Brahman is the tranquil essence of consciousness (cittattva), which has become both the locus and the object of ignorance.
Cognition-only (vijñānamātra) is formless knowledge whose objects are things such as jars and cloths.
He who is the life-force, another synonym for whom is the "knower" (*jña*);
he who is the emptiness of the proponents of emptiness, and the illuminator of the splendors of the sun;
he who is the speaker, the rememberer, the truth, the enjoyer, the seer, and the agent at all times.
That which is the illuminator is the state of non-existence (*na kiñcittvam*), the emptiness experienced in deep sleep.
And this is an illustration;
by it, one should understand that for all philosophical systems (*darśana*), that which serves as the point of rest for all entities is precisely this [reality].
Furthermore, what is its nature?

Regarding the phrase "it becomes," it is said here: "the illuminator. That which is the illuminator of the splendors of the sun—that is, of the splendors whose essential nature is the sun and so forth—becomes the manifester by means of its resting upon a specific locus called the eye.
Likewise, that which is always, indeed eternally,
as *ṛta*— that is, by way of truth,
in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
He becomes the speaker, the rememberer, the enjoyer, the seer, and the agent, because he exists as the self of all these— speaker and the rest. "Ṛtam" is an adverbial modifier of the action.
That which exists yet appears as non-existent in the world, which, though residing in the body, is far away—
this is indeed the light of consciousness, for it is like the radiance of the sun. (MU 3.5.8)
That which is the Self— though it exists and, because it remains as the substratum for this entire delusion of the world, possesses the nature of being real—
it nonetheless becomes unreal.
Because it is not within the range of external or internal sense organs;
that which is the Self,
although residing in the body— since it is impossible for a body of stone-like nature to be the locus of such movement otherwise— even while situated therein.
It reaches far;
otherwise, there would be no perception of the sun and other celestial bodies situated in space. Indeed, this is certain.
This light of consciousness is the light whose nature is the sentience of objects;
from what does it arise? Like what?
Like light;
just as light is the seeing of objects from the shining sun.
It occurs; that is the meaning of "tathā."
Moreover,
from whom the gods, such as Viṣṇu and others, emerge like rays from the sun,
and from whom the infinite worlds arise like bubbles from the ocean; MU_3,5.9.
The deities are to be known as twofold: internal (ādhyātmika) and celestial (ādhidaivika). Among these, the celestial ones are well-known;
the internal ones are as follows:
The mind is Brahmā;
the intellect is Viṣṇu;
the ego is Rudra.
The senses and so forth are the deities;
likewise, the worlds should also be known as being of two kinds,
and they too are well-known as belonging to the divine realm (ādhidaivika).
But the internal ones should be understood as mental intentions.
The [objects] beginning with the senses,
as well as those mental [states],—
all these multitudes of visible things enter into it like waters into the great ocean.
That which illuminates both itself and objects like a lamp;
the meaning is that the multitudes of the visible dissolve into it— that which is the form of the seer— and become absorbed within it.
He who is the nature of pure consciousness;
he [who perceives] the Self— the Self which is the nature of pure consciousness—
as well as objects (padārtham), where the singular number is used in the sense of a genus (jāti).
And it illuminates and makes manifest the objects of experience, like a lamp.
The form of the seer:
that which is in the sky and in the body, in visible things, in waters, and in creepers.
The Self which is situated in dust, in mountains, in winds, and in the netherworlds; likewise in space and in the body,
as well as in visible stones.
He is established in the waters, in creepers, in dust, in motes, in rocks, in mountains,
in winds, and in the netherworlds (pātālas).
And this is an illustration;
by it, one should understand that [the deity] resides everywhere in the stationary [objects]. Among the stationary things...
If it is asked how the existence of the self as something stable is possible:
it is true;
for when all stationary things are investigated, [they are likewise found to lack such stability].
They rest precisely in ineffability (*anirvācyatā*);

and since ineffability alone is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the self (*ātman*), there is no contradiction whatsoever. Alternatively, stationary beings (*sthāvara*) are either endowed with a self (*sātmaka*) or devoid of a self (*nirātmaka*).
If they were devoid of self (*nirātmaka*), what form could they possibly have? But if they possessed a self (*sātmaka*), then it must be understood that the self clearly resides within them.
(MT 3.5.11) That which causes the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*) to overflow, agitated, here and there—
By which the deluded are rendered mute, remaining as if fixed in meditation upon a stone;
that which is the Self (ātman)— the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka), whose nature consists of the three internal organs and the five subtle elements—
[constitutes] the group of sentient beings.
It causes them to float here and there, leading them wherever; that is to say, it makes them perform various movements. "Mūḍhāḥ" means the dull-witted.
By means of that essence which remains as the self,
[they] have been rendered mute, having been made incapable of reflection; "meditation like stone" means meditation that is like a stone.
They become as if paralyzed;
that is to say, they become as if utterly inert,
because even the deluded, from the perspective of ultimate reality, possess the nature of pure consciousness alone.
The employment of the word "iva" (as if).
[Its own nature:
by whom the sky was made empty and by whom the mountains were made solid; [from the sense: from the sense. (MT_3,5.12)
By whom the waters were made to flow, by whose power the sun blazes,
and by which Self, through its omnipotence, the sky— having assumed a form beyond the principles (nistattvarūpa)—
exists as that which pervades space.
It was made empty, its nature devoid of reality;
likewise, by that self which resorted to the state of clay or stone.
The mountains are the peaks that pervade themselves; they have been made solid and rendered dense. Likewise, by that [element] which has attained the state of liquidity, and by its own nature.
The waters (āpaḥ) are the liquids pervaded by themselves;
they are "fluid" (drutāḥ), meaning endowed with the quality known as fluidity (dravatva);
they are "made" (kṛtāḥ).
Likewise, Ravi— the Sun— is situated by way of pervasion;
by whose power— that is, by the influence of that Self which has attained the state of luminous, illuminating splendor—
it becomes radiant.
And this is an illustrative indication.
From which flow forth the various showers of the essence-less cycle of existence, like rains from a cloud filled with inexhaustible nectar— those mountains [of the Dharma]. (MU 3.5.14)
Inexhaustible means devoid of destruction;
that which is immortal is the essence of bliss.
From that, [it is] full, meaning replete.
For from which [source], from the Self,
the showers of the sapless rain of saṃsāra— showers in the form of the torrential downpour of worldly existence—
spread forth and flow along.
Like what?
Like rains;
just as [they fall] from that which is filled with inexhaustible nectar—that is, filled with imperishable water.
From the cloud— that is, from the rain-cloud—
showers flow forth;
such is the meaning.
In whom the waves of the three worlds, consisting of manifestation and disappearance,
vibrate incessantly like rays of light from the sun. "Consisting of manifestation and disappearance" means endowed with appearance and concealment.
The waves of the three worlds, which incessantly surge within that which is, by implication, the ocean.
What is it like? It is like mirages,
as they appear in the heat of the sun.
"Marīcyaḥ sphuranti" means "they flash like mirages. Thus is the meaning.
The waves of the three worlds [are like those of the ocean].

That which is of the nature of destruction yet has an indestructible essence, which abides within all things, which is hidden though distinct, and which is established within all existents; [that is the Self].
Just as its nature is indestructible, so too, because it stands as the witness even to the destruction of that which is imagined [to perish], the Self is devoid of destruction;
for the Self does not take the form of destruction.
This is because it exists even as the state of destruction;

otherwise, how could destruction—which is devoid of a self—be manifest in any form? Likewise, although it is distinct [from objects], its nature transcends all categories of things by virtue of being pure consciousness alone.
That which is the self (ātman) is established within all phenomena,
because it exists as their essential core (sāra).
Furthermore, it is contradictory for that which is indestructible to possess the nature of destruction, and for that which is distinct from all entities to reside within all entities.
Of what nature, then, is this self?
He resides within all things;
he stands within as the controller.
For this very reason, he is hidden and invisible from without. (MT 3,5.16)

By what wind does that creeper of primordial nature (prakṛti) dance— the creeper born in the sky, bearing the great cosmic egg as its excellent fruit, with the mind as its root and the senses as its leaves? *Prakṛti* is a certain principle that constitutes the fundamental cause of the world.
That very creeper is the *vratati*;
by which wind— that is, by which wind in the form of the Self—
it dances, meaning it assumes agency through transformation into the state of an effect.

Otherwise, since it would be impossible for that which is insentient by nature to exist as an effect, it would be illogical for such an insentient entity to possess agency with respect to its transformation into the state of an effect.
Of what nature, then, is the creeper of primordial matter (prakṛti)?
In the sky— that is, in the nature of space, which is pure consciousness (cinmātra)—
she was born,
having manifested; likewise, she for whom the very universe is her excellent fruit.
Such is she; thus,
she is one for whom the mind alone is the root.
She is such;
she is one whose petals are the very sense-faculties (indriya).
That [nature],
being such,
is said to be established merely as a matter of conventional cognition by virtue of its having the mind as its root.

Thus, it should not be questioned how it is said that *prakṛti*, which is the root cause of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), has as its root the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) of the *puruṣa* contained within it.
The creeper of primordial nature (*prakṛtivratati*) is that jewel of consciousness which shines within the casket of every body;
within that moon, these rays of the web of worlds quiver. (MU 3.5.18)
The "jewel of consciousness" (*yaś cinmaṇiḥ*) means that consciousness itself is the jewel;
it is a gem because of its luminosity.
The Self, which has that as its essential nature, shines forth— that is, manifests— as the individual soul (*jīva*) within every casket of a body, that is, within all the bodily caskets.
Otherwise, what would be the nature of the living beings residing within the body? And it is logical that jewels should shine forth from a casket;
these are the ones being seen before us.
The rays of the world-web flash forth within that moon;
otherwise, what support would they have for their manifestation?
For the manifestation of a world-web that is without a substratum does not enter the intellect; moreover,
the world-web possesses the nature of a mirage because it is an object of the light of consciousness, and thus its status as the light of consciousness is never lost.
It should be known that what is insentient by nature is not capable of being an object of consciousness;
because of their mutual opposition, it is impossible for the latter to be present when the former is present. (MT_3,5.18)
In that dense mass of tranquil consciousness, which rains down nectar,
all beings flash like streams of water and clear visions like lightning bolts.
"Raining down nectar" means raining down bliss.
In that [Self], which is a tranquil mass of consciousness, whose nature is like a cloud called pure, independent consciousness— in that Self,
all beings, that is, all objects,
are like drops of water.
Views are cognitions having those as their objects;
they flash forth clearly and manifestly,
like lightning.
And it is fitting that when a cloud pours forth rain, there is the flashing of lightning along with the streams of water; so too,
one's own state of being a showerer of bliss should be understood through the fact of being the object of supreme love for others.
For one who does not shower bliss does not become an object of supreme love;
since we observe that only those such as sons, who shower bliss, are objects of love.
Furthermore, the fact that the self is the object of supreme love is self-evident to everyone, so no further effort is required to prove it.
[As the locus of supreme love] °āspanda°;
[the locus of supreme love] °āspando°;
[the state of being the locus of supreme love] °āspanda° (MT_3,5.19)
When objects marvel at one another through the vision of that [consciousness],
by which the non-existent has been born as non-existent and the existent has attained its state of being existent.
Objects are the various classes of entities consisting of the nature of the enjoyer and the enjoyed;
"mutually" means in one another; "by the way of perceiving" means by the seeing of that [object].
"Insofar as it is by the state of seeing that" means:
they experience wonder, that is, they experience bliss;
the meaning is that the very act of seeing that is the cause of their wonder. False.
Thus it was stated by way of a general objection. This is the intended meaning:
first of all, enjoyers, having experienced desired and undesired objects of enjoyment, become indifferent toward other objects of enjoyment.
Otherwise, the enjoyment of the object of experience being taken as an object at that time would never reach its conclusion;
furthermore, their state of independence from other objects of experience at that time cannot be established without the experience of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) therein.

Indeed, it is precisely through the wonder experienced in a single object that a person becomes indifferent toward other objects. And when that wonder is investigated, because it is the cause of indifference, it is found to be the very nature of the Self.
Since it is the Self—whose nature is the state of supreme rest—that is the cause of indifference, it is entirely logical for the enjoyer [to be the Self].
Regarding the nature of perception which serves as the cause of aesthetic wonder amidst objects of enjoyment,
since this matter is accessible only through direct experience, those possessed of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) should strive for it themselves; enough with further elaboration.
Likewise, by that very self which stands as a witness,
the non-existent was born from the non-existent;
likewise, by that such-like self.

Being has attained reality, because without a witness there can be no conceptualization of existence and non-existence— that is, of being and non-being— regarding what has gone toward the existent and the non-existent.
Desirable and undesirable;
of the object of enjoyment;
is accomplished.
The cause of wonder:
In whose presence this inert body moves even though he has no desire for it—
[the presence] of that supreme jewel who remains tranquil within himself.
Because it is devoid of the basis for desire, it belongs to one who is free from desire;
therefore, it pertains to one who abides in a peaceful self, remaining free from the agitation known as the desire to move.
In the presence of which supreme jewel this iron— known as the body (*kāya*) or physical frame— is dull, consisting solely of the nature of being an object of perception,
and yet it moves and performs activity.

Since even *prāṇa*, which is considered the cause of bodily movement, is endowed with the power of the self (*ātman*), it is logically impossible for it to be the ultimate cause of bodily motion. The term "supreme" (*parama*) is employed to indicate the absence of insentience found in external jewels.
And it is logical that iron moves when in proximity to the gem known as the magnet.
Because of being devoid [of it];
this body [is such] because of being endowed with the power of a self.

In the presence of the jewel known as the magnet, [the iron] moves, vibrates, and acts; such is that which has attained existence through its approach to all beings, [determined by] destiny, place, and time. (MU 3.5.22)
*Niyati* is a specific power that brings about restriction among entities.
*Deśa* is a particular entity that serves as the substratum for entities.

*Kāla* is a certain particular entity whose nature consists merely of calculation (*kalana*), which is inferable from the movement of the sun and other phenomena, and which acts as the cause of the transformation of entities.
Movement (*calana*) is general motion;
vibration (*spandana*) is activity directed toward an object;
and action (*kriyā*) is an act such as cooking and so forth.
And this is an illustration;
that is to say,
by that which goes toward all sentient beings— that is, by that which pervades the objects and categories within the entire domain of existence.
By which self it has attained existence;
for the pervaded attains existence only through the pervader.
Necessity (*niyati*) is vibration (*spandana*);
because it consists of pure consciousness, that which is space arises through the awareness of the void.
The state of being the knower of objects remains unestablished because it consists of pure consciousness;
being pure, it has not reached a final conclusion in any form whatsoever.
That which is consciousness is the act of cognizing;
because it has that as its very nature,
it is "unestablished," meaning it has not reached a finality through any form whatsoever.
He who,
by virtue of knowing the sky— that is, being endowed with the consciousness "I am the sky"—
is the void, the ether.
It comes to be;

the meaning is that it becomes of the nature of the non-existence of categories (padārtha). This is by virtue of being endowed with consciousness in the form "I am a category" through the state of cognizing categories.
"Arthatvam" means the state of being the meaning of a word (*padārthabhāva*).
It "abides in" or "resorts to" [that state]. Due to the force of the prefix (*upasarga*), the root *sthā* (to stand) has the sense of resorting.
"A jar established in its nature as a jar does not become a cloth"; thus it is said that [the Self] is "not established" [in any particular state].
With the final verse of this section, he concludes the description of the greatness of the Self:
"Even while seemingly performing the infinite activity of the great worlds, He never does anything at all."
He alone remains, having abandoned the notion of arising and abiding, established in his own self which is changeless consciousness that never sets;
"he" is the subject to be supplied.

He is the Self who, although—as it were—performing an infinite vibration regarding the great universe (mahājagat), since the manifestation of the world would otherwise be impossible, performs an infinite vibration as if toward the great universe.
At no time does he perform anything whatsoever, because of his utter purity and the absence of the conceit of agency;
otherwise, the use of the word "as it were" (iva) would be inappropriate.
Of what nature is he?
In consciousness that is without setting:
just as [the sun] does not set, so too, because it abides as the witness even of the imagined setting of itself, that consciousness is ultimately devoid of setting;
in its own nature.
Likewise, he remains established in his own self, in his true nature, which is changeless and free from transformations such as passion, hatred, and the like.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is one by whom the mind has abandoned the notions of arising and persistence regarding the world, as well as the notions of arising and persistence regarding himself.
He is such;
that is to say, he is indifferent toward the arising, the maintenance, and by implication, the destruction of the world.
Thus all is auspicious.
(MT_3,5.24) Thus ends the fifth canto in the Chapter on Origination within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Having thus established the true nature and majesty of the Supreme Self, and perceiving that Śrī Rāma was eager for its attainment, [the author] describes the easy means for attaining it:
"Of this Supreme Self, the highest God beyond all gods..."
Supreme perfection arises from knowledge alone,
and not from the exhaustion caused by ritual performance;
[this refers to] one whose true nature has been explained as such.

Of the God beyond gods, whose nature is unsurpassed play, who is radiant by nature, the unsurpassed Supreme Self; from knowledge alone— that is, from the means called knowledge alone— comes *siddhi*, which is attainment in the form of perfection.
There is his accomplishment, which consists of the exhaustion resulting from practice;
that is, the weariness caused by the performance of the practice.
That which gives that [result] is "such-like"; it does not exist [otherwise]. Now, one might ask: "How can there be propriety without performance? To this he says:
"In this case, knowledge is the performance; nothing else is required."
That [attainment] consists in the experience of the cessation of the delusion of water in a mirage.
Here, in this attainment whose nature is the realization of the Self,
"knowledge" refers to the practice— the exertion that accomplishes the goal of attainment.
There exists another [form of] practice called "knowledge," distinct from the practice known as bodily activity;
that [bodily] practice is not required.
That is knowledge:
the cessation of the delusion of water in a mirage.
By which; that; such is the feeling.
In the same way, it possesses form; thus it becomes "of such a kind. The meaning is that it becomes the nature of right knowledge.
"Now, where does such a Self abide? To this he says:
"It is neither far away, nor in space; it is not unattainable, nor is it difficult to reach.
Having the nature of the radiance of its own bliss, it is attained from one's very own body. (MU 3.1.3)
This self has the nature of the manifestation of its own bliss; it is not far away,
because it exists within one's own body.
By this, the suspicion that [the Self] might reside in a great sacred site located at a distance is dispelled.
This is the Self; it does not exist in space.
By this, the suspicion that it might reside in the worlds situated above is dispelled.
This self is unobtainable; it is impossible to obtain;
it does not exist.
Because it is always obtained;
otherwise, it would be unfit to be the self.
By this, the doubt regarding its difficulty of attainment is dispelled.
This self is uneven and harsh, and yet it does not exist.
Because it is the locus of supreme love;
for indeed, it is not logical that hardness should be the locus of love, since [love] is qualified by being directed toward another.
What need is there to speak of love?
By this, the suspicion of cruelty—like that of kings and others who are seized by the intoxication of even a fraction of power—is dispelled.
For the Person (Puruṣa) is of the nature of the manifestation of his own bliss, whose essence is the appearance of self-arisen bliss independent of objects such as enjoyments.
That Self is obtained from one's own body alone;
by the phrase "having the nature of the radiance of its own bliss," any notion of inequality is dispelled.
By the phrase "from one's own body," the [objections] of being at a distance and being situated in space are refuted;
by the word "is obtained," the objection of its being unobtainable is refuted.
[She is] restrained;
[she is] whose form is the radiance of her own bliss;
from her very own body.
Now, it may be objected that some claim the attainment of the Self is achieved even through austerity and the like; to this he replies:
"In this regard, austerity, charity, vows, and so forth do not contribute anything at all.
Apart from resting solely in one's own true nature (svabhāva), there is no means here. (MU 3.6.4)
In this regard, with respect to this accomplishment consisting of the attainment of the self,
asceticism, charity, vows, and so forth do not assist it in the slightest; they do not provide even a fraction of assistance,
because they function as external limbs that contribute only remotely.
For through austerity and the like, there is indeed the purification of the inner being (*sattvaśuddhi*), but not the attainment of the Self (*ātmaprāpti*).
In this regard, it refers to this attainment of the Self.
Apart from resting in one's own nature— that is, apart from resting in one's true form—
there is no means of accomplishment.
Regarding "assistance" (*upakāra*),

for those who are incapable of resting in the true nature (*svabhāva*), he explains the means: "In this matter, there is solely dependence upon the scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and the excellence of true yogis."
The means is that which is uncontrived, the awakening from the snare of delusion.
Here, "in this" refers to this attainment of the Self.

The scripture is the treatise on the inner self (*adhyātmaśāstra*); and that [is attained by] those who possess both the company of the virtuous and the practice of yoga—namely, those who possess the company of the virtuous and the practice of yoga.
In this context, "supremacy" means single-minded devotion.
It is thus;
however, asceticism and the like are not the means— that is, the method.
What is the means?
It is that which [destroys] the net of delusion in the world— that is, the manifold expansion of false knowledge known as the ignorance of the true nature of the world.

By implication, for the person in the world who is bound by the net of delusion known as the cognition of "worldliness," there is an uncreated, innate awakening [to the truth] that "this is indeed Brahman."
In this way, it becomes an awakener.
And except for the scripture, the company of the virtuous, and true yogis,
this is indeed Brahman.
He explains the primary nature of the means for attaining repose in the Self— which is the fruit of being intent upon the scriptures and so forth—
as follows: "Merely by the thorough recognition that 'this is indeed that God'..."
Suffering does not arise for such a person, and he attains the state of liberation while living.
This cycle of worldly existence—consisting of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth—is characterized by its tendency to manifest before one as "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*).
It is well known because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it exists as the very nature of the Self for all beings.
The Lord is the reality of consciousness (cittattva) characterized by luminosity and playfulness;
this is so simply by means of this much alone—
by the mere thorough comprehension, that is, by right knowledge alone.
Suffering does not arise for the living being,
because even suffering that arrives through the stream of existence is known to be nothing but pure consciousness.
That living being attains, or reaches, the state of liberation while alive.
"Because [the Self] is liberated even while in proximity to the body.

(MT_3.6.6) Śrī Rāma, unable to accept that austerity and other such practices— which are well-known as means— are not actually means, and doubting whether the Self is easily attainable or merely nearby, asks:
It is said that by the mere thorough comprehension of this [Self] within the Self,
faults such as death and the like will never again afflict one.
(MU 3.6.7) "Within the Self" means within one's own self.

By the mere thorough comprehension and right ascertainment of this Self as the foundational substratum of the world beginning with the "I," defects such as death and so forth no longer afflict one. For indeed,
once one has attained the state of pure consciousness (*cinmātratā*), the afflictions pertaining to the body, such as death and the like, are not capable of causing any harm.
"In that case, since the object of knowledge has already been known, you should simply maintain silence. To this, the God of gods replied: "How is this Great One obtained from afar?
By what intense austerity, or by how much hardship?"

From what distance, or from how great a distance, can this God of gods be attained by us? Likewise, by what intense austerity is he attained, or else by what degree of hardship consisting of the restraint of breath and so forth?
It is attained;
for it is not logical that such a God of gods could be attained without austerity and the like, or the restraint of the vital breaths and so forth,
because otherwise it would follow that everyone would attain him.
For it is not observed that all [beings] possess its attainment;
nor is it logical for that which has not been attained to be an object of knowledge.
The point is that only a jar or the like, once it has been reached [by the sense organ], is observed to have that status of being an object.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha provides the answer: "By means of one's own human effort and through expanding discernment... [jñānaviṣayatvaṃ]... he speaks.
O Rāma, that deity is not known through the acts of austerity and ritual bathing; rather,
[it is known] by one's own human effort, which consists in the nature of effort called mental prowess.
Likewise, by means of expanded discernment— that is,
by means of discernment endowed with expansion in the form of such discrimination as "Who am I? and "What is this world?"—
that God is known by that person.
It is not known [to be attained] through the acts of austerity and ritual bathing,
because those are intended solely for the purification of the mind and so forth.
By the word "is known," it is indicated that here only knowledge itself is to be accomplished as the means.
There is no attainment [of the object].
For indeed, in the case of one who perceives a mother-of-pearl shell standing before him as silver and who desires the attainment of that shell, the attainment of the shell cannot be established.
It is indicated that what is to be established is merely the cognition in the form "this is indeed mother-of-pearl"; for this reason,
no answer is given to the question "from how far away?", as it would be utterly irrelevant.
[The reason for not stating a further response is its absolute irrelevance: (aṃ)syā° (MT_3,6.9).
For one possessed of passion and the like, asceticism and so forth are clearly not a means [to liberation].
However, even if they were a means for one devoid of those [passions],...
With the intention that the very absence of passion and so forth is what constitutes the means [to liberation], he says:
"O Rāma, the abandonment of passion, hatred, delusion, anger, pride, and envy—without these, austerity and charity are merely affliction and not real [dharma]. (MU 3.6.10)

Austerity and generosity constitute "austerity-generosity" (*tapodāna*); it is genuine, performed with a natural disposition. When the mind is afflicted by passion and the like, one deceives another and takes their wealth.
Whatever is acquired from that gift, its fruit belongs to him who has need of it. "From that" (*tataḥ*) means from that wealth;
the suffix *tasil* is used here in the sense of all case endings (cf. Pāṇini 5.4.44, vārttika 1).

When vows and the like are performed with a mind afflicted by passion and other defilements, that is called hypocrisy; its fruit is either slight or non-existent. The word "vā" (or) indicates an alternative position.

Since it declares that [the fruit] has been attained, one should therefore, through human effort, take the primary medicine for the destruction of the disease of saṃsāra: association with true scriptures and virtuous people. (MU 3.6.13)
One should acquire or earn;
that is to say, one should perform it—
for the sake of destroying the disease called saṃsṛti (saṃsāra), meaning for the purpose of destroying the disease known as worldly existence.

For the sake of destroying the disease called saṃsāra: "In this regard, apart from one human effort, no other means whatsoever is found to lead to the attainment of the destruction of all suffering. (MU 3.6.14)
In this regard, regarding this attainment of the Self,
human effort— consisting of the investigation of authentic scriptures and so forth—
is the "course," meaning the means.

Regarding the attainment of the destruction of all suffering, which consists in the attainment of the destruction of every single form of suffering: [the opponent asks], "Well then, what kind of human effort (*pauruṣa*) is that? To this he replies: "Listen to what kind of human effort it is for the sake of attaining self-knowledge."

Hear from me what kind of human effort leads to the attainment of self-knowledge, by which the cholera-like diseases of passion and hatred are entirely pacified. What is that [effort] like? It is as follows.
By which manly effort the cholera of passion and hatred is entirely pacified;
otherwise, the sense is that it would not serve as the cause for attaining self-knowledge. (MT_3,6.15)

With a mind satisfied by contentment, abandoning greed for enjoyments, he proceeds to fulfill his promised description of the nature of the Puruṣa by means of an exposition that is as appropriate as possible and not in conflict with worldly convention or scripture. (MU 3.6.16)
According to one's capacity, through diligent effort and with a mind free from agitation,
one should first resort to devotion toward the company of the virtuous and the study of the true scriptures.
(MU 3.6.17) [śrayet] [°vam(i)]
One should apply oneself with diligence,
relying on whatever [practice] is possible, in accordance with one's capacity.
But not by means of a livelihood or subsistence achieved through strenuous effort; nor should one harbor greed for enjoyments— that is, craving for sensory pleasures.

One who is content with whatever wealth has been obtained, who disregards what is censurable, and who delights in the company of the virtuous and in the true scriptures, is swiftly liberated. (MU 3.6.18) "Censurable" refers to wealth and such things acquired through unjust means. (MT 3.6.18)
"Now, how is he quickly liberated? To this he says:
"For the one of great intelligence whose own nature is fully known through investigation, these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara—become objects of compassion. (MU 3.6.19)
By means of investigation— that is, by an inquiry established through the power of association with the virtuous and so forth—
the intrinsic nature (svabhāva), which is one's own essential form, has been fully known and ascertained as being distinct from the body and other such things.
By which [means]:
for such a person of great intelligence endowed with wisdom.
These—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara—are to be pitied. In what way?
They become objects of compassion because they possess a calamity consisting in their being intent upon activities such as the creation of the world.
What need is there to mention how his swift liberation might be achieved? Such is the sense.
These—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara—are to be pitied;
what kind [of beings] are they?
Indeed, first of all, you yourself stated that association with the virtuous alone is the means.
"Who indeed would be a true virtuous person with whom one should associate? To this, he replies: "One whom people call a 'virtuous person' because he is for the most part composed of good qualities."
He would be distinguished; he would be virtuous—one should resort to him with diligence.
"Consisting mostly of good people" means for the most part good people;
by the word "mostly," it is implied that even if there is some lack of virtue [in them].

When a person is declared to be a good man by relatives due to some specific purpose, yet is described as being of bad character by wicked people who take pleasure solely in censuring others, there arises a need to eliminate both the notions of goodness and badness regarding that person. Having thus established the determination of what constitutes a good person, he now proceeds to establish the determination of the scripture.

Among all branches of knowledge, the science of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā) is the foremost; they call that treatise which relies upon its discourse a "true scripture" (sacchāstra), and one who investigates it is liberated.
(MU 3.6.21) [vidyānām: BhG 10.32c]
Among all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), that is, among all forms of cognition,
the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), which is the knowledge of the self (*ātmajñāna*),
is preeminent.
Therefore, the wise call that treatise which takes as its basis discourse on those [topics] and expounds the science of inner self (adhyātmavidyā) a "true treatise" (sacchāstra).
A person who possesses such inquiry is said to be one endowed with inquiry into the true treatise.
He is released from the bondage created by saṃsāra; he becomes liberated.
Therefore, the meaning is that only the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra) is applicable here.
Having clarified with the final verse of this chapter that discrimination arising from the study of authentic scriptures and the like is the primary means [to liberation], he declares:

"By means of discriminations born from the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures, impurities are forcibly destroyed, just as the turbidity of waters is removed through contact with *kataka* nuts, or as the dullness of those who are ignorant is dispelled by the consumption of the *abhaya* herb. (MU 3.6.22)
Impurities consist of passion and the like;
in the context of people, they consist of dust. *Kataka* is a specific substance that clarifies water.
He tells the second illustration:
"Just as for the dull-witted.
This means for those who are dull-witted, lacking their own discernment.
Because of the employment of fearlessness; that is, because of the employment— known as consolation— of the fearlessness granted by someone.
Therefore, the impurities— which take the form of fears caused by [misconceptions such as] a rope-snake and so forth—
perish;
that is the meaning of "likewise."
It has been said that for the dull-witted, fearlessness arises through their own reflection upon the discerning; thus all is auspicious.
"Abhayaṃ" [is] "fearless";
"vinaśyanti" [is] "they perish.
Thus ends the sixth canto in the section on Origination within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Considering that the attainment of the Self cannot be achieved without traveling to a distant land and employing a web of means, Śrī Rāma again poses the very same question as stated before:
"Who is this deity who has been described, by knowing whom one is liberated?"

"Tell me, where does that god reside, and how may I attain him? [He replied: "That god who was described by you—he does not abide far away; he is eternally established within the body, renowned as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). ...In whom...
this very god was described by you.
Likewise, when that deity is known, a person is liberated; that is, liberation is attained.
You speak:
"Where does that deity reside?
I [know] this deity over there."
"How? By what means? How may I obtain or attain it?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply.
This deity who has been described by me does not abide at a distance;
he is eternally established within the body, renowned as pure consciousness alone (cinmātra).
This deity who has been described by me—
This [Self] does not abide far away in a distant land,
since it is renowned and well-known as pure consciousness (cinmātra).
This [Self] is eternally situated within the body;
otherwise, even though the body is like a stone, it would not possess the capacity to be the locus of movement, just like a dead body.
Furthermore, it is not logical to say that what resides within the body is located at a distance.
The sense is that even in the case of one's own two hands, there is no conjunction because they are situated at a distance from each other.
[Because of being situated at a distance and because of the absence of conjunction.
[tv⟨aa⟩[ā]saṃ° (MT_3,7.2)] But in that case, would it not follow that this [self] must have the same dimensions as the body?
And thus, like the body, it too would be subject to impermanence.
Regarding this, it is said:
"This [Self] is all this universe, but the universe is not this;
for this alone exists as one, but there is no perception of a designation called 'the universe'. (MU 3.7.3)
This Self is this entire universe, this entire world;
it becomes so because everything exists as its essence.
But in the alternative view,
that [Self] is all-pervading because it exists as the essence within all things; thus, this [universe] does not exist [independently].
For indeed,
because this one alone exists—
the vision that names all, the sight that possesses all names.
The phrase "the universe" (viśvam) means that it does not exist;
for even though the universe appears, from that perspective its nature as such [unreality] is never lost.
For indeed, when water is overtaken by waves, the perception designated as "waves" does not arise;
for even while the waves appear, from the perspective of one possessing discernment (*vivekijana*), the nature of the water does not depart.
This entire world is the world;
by that vision, it belongs to the All-born.
[Objection: But surely Śaśibhṛt and others are also the very nature of Mahādeva;
so why have you said, "For he alone exists"? [Response: To this, he says:
"Because of his desire" (tat).

This moon-bearer is pure consciousness alone; the one whose banner is Garuḍa is pure consciousness alone; the sun is indeed pure consciousness alone; and the lotus-born Brahmā is pure consciousness alone.
This is the illustrious Mahādeva, known as the bearer of the moon, who is renowned as the agent of creation and dissolution;
he is pure consciousness alone.
If it be asked, "How can this be so?"—
it is true;
does the moon-bearer exist as sentient or devoid of sentience?

If it were insentient, being of the nature of stone, its security and vulnerability would be exactly equal to that of the lowest things in the world. But if it is sentient, then clearly it is pure consciousness itself that manifests in that form.
[Objection: In that case, how is there a difference between the moon-bearing [Śiva] and a worm?
If it is argued that there must indeed be equality [between cause and effect],
who has said that [the effect] does not exist?
Is it not the case that difference is postulated because one perceives the effect to have characteristics distinct from [those of] the cause?
This is indeed an improper assumption;
for it is not reasonable to postulate a difference between a spark of fire and a great mass of fire based on a difference in their effects.
Is it not the case that there is no difference in the effects of a spark of fire and a great mass of fire, since they both possess the single effect known as burning?
If it is argued that [the distinction is known] from the observation of their effects,
then what kind of difference in effect exists between the moon-bearing mountain (Śiva) and a worm?
Because the action of knowing and the action of the instrument are one and the same;
as for the distinction based on their being greater or lesser,
that exists in the illustrative example.
Since it also exists, there is no contradiction whatsoever;
this should be applied similarly elsewhere as well.
He who has the garuḍa as his banner is the presiding deity of stability.
*Tapana* is the sun, who effects the ripening of all things within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
*Kamalodbhava* is the venerable Brahmā, whose office is creation.
When the internal meaning is intended, *Śaśibhṛt* refers to the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
Garuḍadhvaja is the intellect (buddhi);
Tapanas is the vital breath (prāṇa);
Kamalodbhava is the mind (manas)—thus they are to be applied.
Because one observes that it is distinct from its effects, [it is] not an effect;
by way of its distinction from effects— [there exists that single thing called "burning"]—
Śrī Rāma asks.
Even children say this: if the world were merely consciousness, what indeed would there be here for instruction?
(MU 3.7.5) If the world were merely consciousness...
It occurs thus:
"This alone is the truth," and so forth;
even children say this at that time.
For all indeed declare that the world consists of life (*jīva*), which is synonymous with consciousness (*cetanā*).
Therefore, what could there be here called "instruction" (*upadeśatā*)?
For instruction consists precisely in making known what was previously unknown.
Here, by the term "the ignorant," the Buddhist Vijñānavādins are intended;
for they alone assert that consciousness—of which "volition" is another synonym—is the self. (MT_3,7.5)
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
That which you have understood— that the universe is mere consciousness and sentient—
is not at all that knowledge which brings about liberation from existence.
The conscious one is pure consciousness; that which is called consciousness is pure consciousness.
Thus, the universe comes to be.
So it is.
You are indeed that; for you have understood this,
even in its slightest degree.
The means of crossing over from saṃsāra, which is the deliverer,
has not been understood because of a lack of familiarity with the reality that is pure consciousness alone.
Indeed, the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) perishes through the mere knowledge of the reality that is pure consciousness alone.
How is this so? To this, he says:
"That which is called 'sentience' is the cycle of worldly existence; this individual soul (*jīva*) is known as a bound beast (*paśu*)."
From this very [name] emerge the waves of old age and death;
indeed, consciousness becomes the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
