For one who abides in pure consciousness alone, the very orientation toward the object of thought (*cetyaunmukhya*) constitutes consciousness itself, and that same orientation toward the object of thought constitutes transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
Indeed, transmigratory existence is said to be wandering; and wandering is rising up from one's own natural state.

And at the moment when pure consciousness (cinmātra) is oriented toward an object of cognition (cetya), there indeed occurs an emergence from its own state, which consists of pure consciousness alone; otherwise, what would "orientation toward an object" even mean? This very cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is of the nature of consciousness, is thus described by the wise.
The individual soul (jīva) is said to be like a bound animal (paśu) because it is devoid of knowledge of its own true nature. Indeed, that which performs the activity of living is called the jīva.
And consciousness itself is life;
therefore, by metaphorically attributing that [life] to what possesses it, the state of being alive belongs to consciousness alone.

The recourse to such metaphorical attribution here is for the purpose of eliminating the notion of any means of living other than the activity of living, insofar as the jīva is, in the ultimate sense, of the nature of pure consciousness alone.
It has been done. [The opponent asks: "But what follows from that?
To this he replies: "Precisely because of this.
The waves of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa-vīcayah*) are the ripples of old age and death pertaining to the body and so forth.
From this very volition alone;
they emerge, they go forth— that is to say, they manifest.
The meaning is that for the dreamer, there are no waves of old age and death pertaining to the dream-body.
Regarding the dreamer:
it says this once again—
that the individual soul (*paśu*), though ignorant and formless, is indeed a vessel for suffering alone.
Because it possesses consciousness, it perceives this; yet, remaining itself, it is utterly devoid of purpose.
It is formless, distinct from both the gross and subtle bodies;
likewise, it is [the witness] of suffering itself, which takes the form of the manifold world being produced by itself.
He is a vessel, one who has become a fit recipient;
this is because he arises from pure consciousness alone in such a form,
for otherwise even his arising would be purposeless.

Likewise, this individual soul (jīva), though being like a bound beast (paśu) because it is ignorant— lacking the reflective awareness of its own true nature called pure consciousness— is nevertheless [the subject].
Because it is conscious— that is, because its essential nature is pure consciousness—
this world, consisting of the ego and so forth, which manifests its own nature at the outset,
perceives; that is, it makes [the world] the object of its own manifestation.
For this indeed is the "consciousness" of consciousness—that it cognizes whatever [object] there may be; thus it is said, "because of consciousness.
[An objection: "But what is accomplished by that consciousness?
To this, he says: "it cognizes" (*cetati*).
Then, a great calamity in the form of the world arose— meaning it appeared and became manifest by itself, without his will.
And in this context, the fact that a dream serves as an illustrative example is perfectly clear, so no further effort has been made [to prove it].
[Regarding the passage beginning with] "from egoism" (*ahaṅkārādikaṃ*): [The text reads] *ahaṅkā°*.
Now, one might ask: "Could this suffering of this conscious being ever possibly cease? To this, it is said:
"That which would be freedom from consciousness, or rather, the state of being turned away from consciousness."
That is its state of fullness; having known it, one does not grieve.
First, there is freedom from the object of thought (*cetya*); then, through independence, there is the turning toward the object of thought; then, by means of discernment, there is emergence.
Or rather, it is the state of being turned away from the object of thought, which is precisely the absence of turning toward the object of thought.
That which belongs to this volitional agent is its state of being filled,
its state of fullness.
It exists as such because it is full by virtue of its own nature, which is pure consciousness alone;
[it refers to] that state of being filled.
Having known and ascertained [the Self] as the nature of ultimate reality, one does not grieve— that is, one does not become a partaker of the suffering called saṃsāra—
due to the state of being filled by the consciousness that abides within oneself.
Because of the knowledge of its unreality, there is also the knowledge of the unreality of the suffering spoken of therein.

Here, one should understand the distinction: the state of being free from the object of cognition (*cetya-nirmuktatā*) occurs in the stage of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*), whereas the state of being directed toward the non-objective (*acetyonmukhatā*) occurs in the stage of liberation after death (*videhamuktatā*).
[Regarding what was said there:
"But then, what will be the state of this conscious being? To this he says: "The knot of the heart is broken; all doubts are severed."
And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.10) [The knots are severed;
the high and the low.]

When that which is well-known as abiding as the self of all is seen— meaning when it is realized as the ultimate reality through its nature as the self— in the Great Pure Consciousness (*mahācinmātra*), which consists of both the supreme and the non-supreme, that is, the supreme form of pure consciousness and the non-supreme form of the conscious self-nature; and when this has been determined as one's own being.
"When this state of fullness is known" means when it is realized;
"of this conscious being" refers to the "knot of the heart," which consists of objects such as enjoyments and the like.
It is split asunder and destroyed because of being fully satisfied;
likewise, all doubts— that is, all uncertainties concerning the true nature of things— are eliminated.
They are severed by the certainty that the essence is pure consciousness alone;
likewise, the karmas— those actions performed for the sake of maintaining the body— are severed.
They perish,
because they do not take up any defilements.
"It would then be divided.

[The opponent replies: "In that case, I shall establish that 'I' is precisely the state of being turned away from objects of thought (*cetyonmukhatva*), which is absolutely to be accepted. To this, he says:
"But its state of being turned toward objects of thought cannot exist without the non-existence of objects of thought."
The object of sight, which is the object of consciousness, cannot be obstructed; how indeed can it be stilled?
For that conscious subject, the state of being directed toward the object of consciousness—that orientation toward the object—is what constitutes its consciousness.
Without the non-arising of the object of thought (*cetya*), it is impossible to obstruct [the mind].
For fire that has fallen upon a bundle of cotton does not become extinguished [by itself]. [Objection:
In that case, do you not simply destroy the object of thought?
Thus, it is said here: "the object of thought" (cetya). The visible, which is the very nature of the visible, is the object of thought.
How could it be stilled?
That which exists does not cease to be, because its destruction is impossible.
This is the meaning:
if an object of cognition exists, how could it ever cease?
If that [object] does not exist, then the absence of any orientation toward an object (cetyānaunmukhya) is established by itself; therefore,
in the case of its apprehension, effort apart from mere cognition is not appropriate.
For indeed, no one ever entertains the thought of the destruction of the son of a barren woman.
[Regarding the word *cetyam*:
Here Śrī Rāma asks:
"By means of the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures, one is a crosser of the ocean of saṃsāra."
"O Brahmin, tell me, what is that Supreme Self like which is seen, the one who carries [one] across the ocean of saṃsāra? [The answer:
"By means of association with the virtuous and the true scriptures, O Brahmin..."
Samsara itself is an ocean because it is difficult to cross;
the Savior is that Supreme Self who is perceived within it.
"You speak;
what is he like?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha, disregarding Śrī Rāma’s question, explains the very same matter as previously stated.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Those who desire this consciousness— the individual soul— which is shattered in the wilderness of birth, are ignorant even though they are wise.
This conscious being, which is born in the wilderness of worldly existence, becomes fragmented and attains a state of limitation;
those who desire this as the Self are wise, even though they investigate it only slightly more than those who identify the body with the Self.
They become ignorant because they perceive a living soul (*jīva*) as a self where there is no self. To the question "How is this so?", he says here:
The living self (*jīva*) alone is here [in this world] the transmigrator, due to its consciousness and the continuity of suffering;
when this is known, nothing remains unknown anywhere.
The transmigrations (*saṃsāra*) are those distinguished by the divisions of waking and so forth;

because they consist of a continuity of suffering, and because one experiences that continuity of suffering pertaining to the transmigratory states as residing within oneself, they belong to the living being (*jīva*) alone.
Therefore, when this individual soul (jīva), which is the substratum of saṃsāra, is known— that is,
when it is attained through its defining characteristics— then [the following occurs].
Nothing whatsoever has been cognized—that is, made an object of knowledge—or attained through figurative indication. It does not exist.
If it is asked, "In that case, by whose knowledge is something attained regarding the continuity of suffering? he says here:
"O Rāma, if the Supreme Self is known, then that continuity of suffering [is ended]."

O Rāma, if the supreme reality of the Self—which exists as the essence of the individual soul (jīva) that has been described—[is realized], then [the notion of being a limited self] comes to an end, just as cholera ceases when the onset of poison is pacified. 3.7.15. If... [it is so].
It is known;
it is attained through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā);
that [is so] at that time.
The continuity of suffering is the form of saṃsāra; it goes to, that is, reaches its destruction or end.
The meaning is that at that very moment, something is attained.
Like what?
Like cholera.
The meaning is: "in such a way that it comes to an end upon the subsiding of the onset of the poison.
Śrī Rāma was disregarded by Śrī Vasiṣṭha because he was unfit for instruction due to being so overwhelmed by his intense longing to hear about the nature of the Supreme Self.
He asks again about the nature of the Self: "O Brahman, tell me truly the form of the Supreme Self,
by seeing which a person shall cross over all delusion."
From the whole:
*samyaṅ* means form (*rūpa*) or essential nature (*svarūpa*); it is according to reality, correctly.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha, having ascertained Śrī Rāma’s fitness for instruction by virtue of his intense longing, speaks the reply: "The form of consciousness that exists in the interval when it has traveled from one distant land to another in the mere twinkling of an eye—that is the nature of the Supreme Self. (MU 3.7.17)
From one location, which has been made an object of cognition and consists of a perceptible form; "far" means extremely distinct;
another location, being taken as an object of cognition, is called "another perceptible," namely, a different location.
"In a mere instant" means in just a single moment; that is,
without experiencing any confusion in the interim,
as she has attained [the state] by grasping it as an object of focus.
Of consciousness— that is, of the intellect (*cit*) which is oriented toward grasping the object of perception—
in its intermediate state, which is uncolored by the passion for the previously perceived or the subsequently perceived,
that form which arises, that ineffable essential nature which exists.
That very [Self], and not something else similar to it—
the reality of the Supreme Self (paramātmatattva), which is the essence of all individual selves (jīvātman).
It takes on form, because even while consisting of all things, it transcends all. Now,

when consciousness makes the subsequent object of awareness its support at the very moment it has made the preceding object of awareness its support, what is this so-called "middle" wherein it resides?

The nature of consciousness as the supreme self has been stated; it is now explained: [it is] the own-nature of consciousness, which was colored by a previous object of cognition, [once that object has ceased]. It is stainless.

Since it is illogical for passion to arise toward that which is yet to be experienced after the form has been reached, one must know that this intermediate state, consisting of a stainless intrinsic nature, necessarily exists;
just as in the case of a cloth dyed with indigo, when it is washed with the desire to apply a yellow dye, the intermediate state consisting of the pure cloth becomes manifest.
Otherwise, it would be impossible for one who intends to act otherwise to produce a cognition characterized by yellow color.
But surely, the cognition whose object was previously experienced has already perished?
But now, a new object of cognition has arisen;
thus, that which is called the "middle" exists as nothing but emptiness. Does it mean, then, that the self exists in the very form of emptiness?
If [it is argued that it does], no; because at the time of apprehending a subsequent object of cognition, the recollection of a previously cognized object would be impossible.

Indeed, without a single consciousness that exists in its pure form in the interval—remaining present both at the time of apprehending the previous object of cognition and at the time of apprehending the subsequent one—a recollection having the previously cognized object as its domain cannot be established.
By this, the principle of consciousness (saṃvittattva), when free from the coloring of objects of cognition and untainted by insentience, is declared to be the Supreme Self (paramātman).

For those who practice here, the attainment of the Supreme Self will occur before long and without effort. This very state is known by the name "entry into the central channel" (madhyadhāmāveśa); enough with further revealing of secrets.
And in this context, because it is extremely difficult to find something intermediate between two similar objects of cognition, it is described as "distant."
[By way of being an object:
that form which becomes [the object],
having been made into an object (*ālambanīkṛtya*).
Because of the desire to produce a yellow coloration;
because of the object being experienced as posterior; because of the impossibility of recollecting a previously experienced [object].

In that great ocean of consciousness, which is the supreme self, there exists only the absolute non-existence of the world-process and the state of transmigratory existence, as previously experienced objects. MU 3.7.18
In that great ocean called awakening, within that vast sea known as enlightenment,
[is found] the existence of the world— that is, the nature of the world's being—
and saṃsāra.
Absolute non-existence alone— non-existence throughout the three periods of time, like a bubble— is indeed that which exists;
it becomes the very nature of the Supreme Self.
This is the intended meaning: the seeker of liberation, first ascertaining through the scriptures and other means— by means of the analogy of the rope and the snake,

and subsequently by the analogy of the gold and the bracelet— that the visible world lacks existence apart from Brahman, and having attained certainty regarding the identity with the pure reality of consciousness (*cittattva*), perceives through the power of practice that everywhere there is only the pure reality of consciousness.

Just as a goldsmith perceives the nature of gold in bracelets and other ornaments, so too, when one experiences that which is the very nature of knowledge, that alone is the nature of the Supreme Self.
Now, it may be objected that an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) relative to the world is not possible.
If it is argued that because the world existed previously,
even for one who has ascertained the absolute non-existence of the world, it must have appeared as a world in the past— this is incorrect.
For a prior false appearance does not negate the fact that an object, once ascertained at a later time, is the counter-positive of an absence existing in all three periods of time.
For if the rope had previously appeared as a snake, it would entail the contradiction that the rope is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence;

however, when the rope was previously perceived as a snake, everyone clearly perceives that the snake is indeed the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence existing throughout the three periods of time—
thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
The absence of existence apart from Brahman;
the nature of the Supreme Self;
the state of being the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence throughout the three periods of time.
In that [state],
where the sequence of seer and seen has utterly set even while remaining present—
[that state] which is not space, yet is space, is the form of the Supreme Self. (MU 3.7.19)
Even while remaining present and appearing directly before one's eyes,
this sequence of seer and seen— consisting of the form "this is the seer" and "this is the seen"—
exists within which object.
"Enough" means "excessively";
"properly" is the intended sense;
"astaṃ" means "dissolution."
[The state of] "gone" has occurred.

But surely, since the sequence of seer and seen remains established, how can its dissolution into something else be possible? And if it is argued that, for this reason, it is altogether improper to describe the nature of the Supreme Self by means of this [analogy], then [we reply]: [it is not so].
No.
To begin with, do the seer and the seen appear to some witness or not?
If they do not, then how can they possess the status of being the seer and the seen?

If they are established in whatever manner, even when that [reality] is established, how can their distinction—that "this is the seer" and "this is the seen"—be established? If they appear as such, then their dissolution into That is indeed easy;
for one cannot transcend the witness of a dream while remaining within the appearances of the dream.

There is no contradiction whatsoever in the possibility that the seer and the seen are endowed with some intrinsic nature; likewise, that entity which is not space— because it lacks the state of being an object of cognition due to its exclusive nature as a subject— is indeed distinct from space, which has the singular form of being an object of cognition.
It becomes space;
the meaning is that by means of qualities such as pervasiveness and transparency, it becomes denotable by the word "space.
That very thing remains that same reality.
But there is nothing else whatsoever that is similar to it;
such is the nature of the Supreme Self.
In the case of an object, the seer and the seen are established.

Space:
That which is empty yet as if not empty, in which emptiness the world is situated;
that which remains empty even when the flood of creation exists—that is the form of the Supreme Self. (MU 3.7.20)
That entity which is empty because it cannot be grasped by the external or internal faculties has no form whatsoever;
yet it appears as if non-empty, as if it were something.
It exists; otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be the substratum for the delusion regarding the form of the world. For a non-existent thing cannot serve as the substratum for anything.
Otherwise, it would follow that even the son of a barren woman could serve as the locus for the delusion of friendliness.
Thus, in the void— that is, in that which has the nature of emptiness according to the logic already stated— [in that] wherein...
The world, being existent, persists like a jar or other objects made of clay;
otherwise, what would be the nature of the world? This is the intended meaning.
Likewise, while the flood of creation— that is, the entire mass of emanations— exists, abiding as that which is to be presided over or as an effect;
that which is empty, being devoid of any entity distinct from itself.
It is so;
for it is not possible to conceive that a rope possesses a distinct entity by virtue of its state as a snake, nor that clay possesses a distinct entity by virtue of its state as a jar.
That becomes the form of the Supreme Self.
[Thus] indeed, when it abides in that state, that which is empty—devoid of any entity distinct from itself—and which, though consisting of pure consciousness, remains like a massive stone;
yet which is insentient within while being truly sentient—that is the form of the Supreme Self. (MU 3.7.21)
Whatever object there may be,

even though it consists of great consciousness and, by the very impossibility of otherwise accounting for its being the witness of the entire world, exists as the very nature of the radiance of great consciousness,
it remains like a massive stone.
It becomes as if utterly inert,
because, due to its extreme tranquility, it is averse to independent self-reflection even when there is such reflection. But what is it like?
The meaning is that, within its ultimate essential nature,
it is indeed non-inert;
whereas that which is inert appears as if it were inert.
These two qualifiers should be understood as supporting the meaning stated in the first half [of the verse] by way of transcending their respective order;
that is the nature of the Supreme Self.
By transcending the sequential order,
that which, having attained union with everything— both external and internal—
reaches the state of its own essential existence, is the form of the Supreme Self.
The entire world, including everything external and internal— that which exists as both outside and inside—
is that by which, as the witness (sākṣin), it stands; [the world] has a connection, a relation, with that reality.
"Having attained" means having reached the state of being an object;
"intrinsic existence" (svarūpasattā) refers to the existence of the specific individual form.
It is attained.
For, in the absence of manifestation through the perception of a witness, the existence of even such things as blue or pleasure—though they exist—is seen to be as if non-existent;
that [manifestation] is the nature of the Supreme Self.
Just as light belongs to illumination, and as emptiness belongs to the sky, so is this established wherein; that is the form of the Supreme Self. [MU 3.7.23] "Of illumination" means of light.
Just as light is a specific quality called luminosity that serves as the cause for the manifestation of objects,
or as emptiness is the state of being empty,
so it is in the sky, that is, in space.
It exists;
likewise, in that same manner,
this world exists.
In whatever invisible object it resides,
that becomes the form of the Supreme Self.
This is the intended meaning:
just as light, while appearing, is not described as being primarily itself, because otherwise it would be impossible to describe it as having the quality of illumination.
Furthermore, when light is investigated, it is found to be truly indefinable (*anirvācya*).

Likewise, this world, as it appears, should be understood as resting upon some indefinable, essential, and primary principle (*pradhāna*). That in which it rests is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
But surely, by these [arguments], the status of the Supreme Self has been established for some entity accessible through inference;
and thus it should be understood that this Supreme Self is merely conceptualized.
If it is argued that this is because what is accessible through inference is merely conceptualized,
whereas only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is accessible solely through non-conceptual direct perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*),
possesses ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*).
This is incorrect;
for although the nature of the Supreme Self— which is to be taught— manifests at every moment through its own essence during the intermediate states, it remains unknown as the Self.
"Your self is like a long-forgotten kinsman standing before you"— regarding this, there is no touch of inference for those possessed of intelligence;
as for those lacking intelligence,
they have no authority here at all, so enough with deliberating upon the faults and virtues of others.
Like a long-forgotten kinsman standing before one,
Śrī Rāma asks:
"How indeed is this Supreme Self to be understood everywhere?"
How could there be the non-existence of this visible world called "the universe" by us? This Supreme Self is of a nature distinct from the universe.
"From all sides" means everywhere;
that is to say, in all circumstances.
How indeed does one awaken?
Since this visible world— which pervades both the external and the internal— is of such magnitude, how could its non-existence possibly occur? For in the waking state, the gross universe manifests.
In the dream state there is the dream-world;
in deep sleep there is insentience;
and there is no state apart from these.

And this question was posed by Śrī Rāma— who always desires to attain the state of being identical with the Supreme Self— without relying on the intermediate stages that flash forth every moment in his waking consciousness and consist of the nature of the pure Supreme Self.
"It does not exist" [is the end of the quote].
"Consisting of the nature of the pure supreme Self" [is the reading];
Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply.
If there were a firm realization of the absolute non-existence of this worldly delusion— which has arisen like the color of the sky—
that would be the known form of Brahman, and not by any other action.
But apart from the absolute non-existence of the visible, there is no other auspicious state;
[this refers to] that which has been born, manifested, and is now shimmering before one, like the color of space.
"Of the world" means as far as [the world extends].
"The realization of absolute non-existence" is the knowledge of absolute non-existence;
it is not, however, what is called "destruction."
That in which there is power endowed with established accomplishment.
Such would it be; if it were so,
then at that time.
The form— that is, the essential nature— of Brahman, the Supreme Self,
would become known.
It would not arise through any other action distinct from this, such as austerity and so forth;
for [it cannot exist] apart from the absolute non-existence of the perceptible— that is, without the absolute non-existence of the perceptible.
There is no other auspicious state or auspicious means;
moreover, the absolute non-existence of the perceptible is established solely through the gateway of knowledge.

This is a statement regarding the means for realizing absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), because that which is brought about by effort is a non-existence consisting of cessation (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); it is like the realization of the absolute non-existence of silver in mother-of-pearl, or the absolute non-existence of a jar in clay.
The term *jagata* [of the world’s delusion? is established as *jagataḥ*;
it is like the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar.

Now, one might ask: how can the absolute non-existence of the world, characterized by its visibility—which is established through the gateway of right knowledge—serve as the means for attaining the Supreme Self? To this, he says:
"In the attainment of absolute non-existence, [there is the realization] of this visible world as it truly is..."
That ultimate reality remains; it is thus awakened to and known by one who exists in such a state as it truly is,
and not by one whose [existence] has been destroyed through effort.
Upon the attainment of the absolute non-existence of this visible world-form— that is, upon the attainment of its absolute non-existence—
just as there is the absolute non-existence of silver perceived in mother-of-pearl, or the absolute non-existence of a jar perceived in clay.
Or, when [all else] has been established,
that which remains— being the substratum of the visible or the essence of the visible— is the ultimate reality; that is the supreme self (paramātman),
which "remains" (śiṣyate) by virtue of being the residue.

Just as in the cognition of the absolute non-existence of silver there is "mother-of-pearl," or as in the cognition of the absolute non-existence of a jar there is "clay," since nothing else exists apart from that [Prakṛti], it is perceived by the Puruṣa;
its existence is determined through indirect (parokṣa) cognition in the form "it exists."
Then, immediately after that, it is known;
it is ascertained through the direct perception of "I."
[The Supreme Self:

"But surely, let the absolute non-existence of the perceptible not be established through the means of knowledge; rather, the knowledge of the Supreme Self will arise simply through forgetfulness produced by the web of means such as the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). To this he replies:
"[produced by the web of means such as the restraint of the vital breath]... the vital breaths..."
There is no consciousness anywhere that exists without a reflection, apart from the absence of an object of perception;
for where indeed does a mirror remain without a reflection?
Consciousness (*cit*) is the essence of mind (*cittattva*) existing in the state of being the witness.
Apart from the non-existence of the visible— which is established as its own witness—
[the mind] is without reflection, meaning it is devoid of the reflection of the visible;
that is to say, it does not act as a witness to the visible.
In some cases it does not exist,
because that would entail the abandonment of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Here, he states an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to support this point.
"Where does it disappear?"—the sense is that an actual mirror is never seen devoid of a reflection while the existence of the original object (*bimba*) persists.
[Objection: But surely, even when the original object is located in another place, the mirror remains devoid of the reflection despite the continued existence of the object.
If it is argued: "Let there be the existence of external objects as they are perceived;
nevertheless, by means of breath-restraint (prāṇarodha) and other methods, consciousness (cit), not extending outward, will become devoid of contact with the perceptible."
This is incorrect;
for without the cognition of absolute non-existence, it is impossible to destroy the seed of the perceptible.

Otherwise, there would be no manifestation of the manifold of dreams within one who is asleep. If it is argued that such a person does indeed have dream-manifestations because they lack means such as the restraint of breath (*prāṇarodha*),
then [the same applies to] those who are devoid of the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible.
Ask only those who are free from deceit and capable of such acts as stopping the breath;

ask them whether you possess a dream-appearance or not. But have we not already asked those who are free from deceit and endowed with the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible? By them—
It has also been stated that one is the perceiver of one's own dream;
let it be so stated—what loss is there?
It appears just as it does in the waking state.
In this very way, they possess the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the world, even in a dream;
for they do not perceive the visible object as something merely appearing as a visible thing,
but rather as Brahman— enough with this elaboration.
Regarding them:
"But even so, do we not perceive the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*) even without the absolute non-existence of the visible? To this he replies:
"Without the possibility of the existence of this visible world called 'the universe' (*jagat*..."
The supreme reality is never perceived by anyone at any time. The "arising of existence" refers to the supreme existence (*parāsattā*) of this [reality] which shines forth before one.
Of that which is called "the world"—
that is, of the collection of entities consisting of the visible objects that are the domain of the act of seeing—
there is no possibility of existence, meaning there is absolute non-existence, without [the Self].
By a certain person;
at some time;
the supreme reality, the reality known as the Supreme Self (paramātman).
It is not perceived, nor is it known;
therefore, the meaning is that the absolute non-existence of the perceptible must be established by means of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Śrī Rāma, doubting the non-existence of the perceptible, asks:
O Sage, how can there be non-existence for this vast web of the visible—the cosmic egg and the stability of the world? Where is Mount Meru within the interior of a mustard seed?
This is the description of its vastness.

Just as when someone says, "Mount Meru exists within the interior of a mustard seed," the statement ultimately rests upon the fact that it expresses an impossible matter; such is the sense [of your claim] regarding you, who likewise propound that the existence of the world does not exist.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
"O Rāma, if you remain for a few days with an undaunted mind,
intent upon the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures, then I shall [bring about] that [liberation] in an instant."
"I wipe away your perception of the visible world, which is like a mirage;
when the visible is absent, the state of being a perceiver also subsides, and pure awareness alone remains.
O Rāma, you—
If, for some days— that is, for however many days—
he remains with an untiring intellect, meaning one whose mind is undisturbed,
up to the point that he possesses direct perception.
At that time, you abide devoted to the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures; therefore,
at that very moment, I [shall appear] before you.
"Towards you" means as far as you;
"the visible" refers to the world in its visible form;
"I wipe away" means I destroy.
The meaning is: "I shall bring about the state of being endowed with absolute non-existence by means of knowledge.
What is it? Like what?
Like awakening.
The meaning is: "just as" correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) clears away the water of a mirage, so too [does this].
By this, it is stated that association with the virtuous and so forth serves as the primary means for the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible.
[An objection is raised: "But what will be accomplished by the removal of the perceptible?"

Regarding this, it is said: "In the absence of the visible. When the absence of the visible is established by means of knowledge—that is, when the non-existence of the object of perception is proven—the state of being a seer (draṣṭṛtā) is stilled and undergoes dissolution.
"In that case, would it not follow that only non-existence remains?
To this, he says: "Awakening" (bodha).
Awakening is the pure reality of consciousness (cittattva), which serves as the witness to the absolute non-existence of both the seen and the seer.
It remains, that is, it is what is left over;
otherwise, even the absolute non-existence of a perceptible object, though established, would be equivalent to a mere non-entity.
"Akhinnadhīḥ" means one whose intellect is undaunted.
[The phrase] "being endowed with absolute non-existence by way of knowledge" means [being endowed with] absolute non-existence through the gateway of gnosis.
Now, one might ask: how is it that the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtā*) reaches pacification solely through the absolute non-existence of the seen? To this, he says:
The state of being a seer exists when there is this object of sight; the state of being an object of sight exists when there is a beholder.
Indeed, unity exists when there is duality, and duality exists within the perception of unity. (MU 3.7.33) [In this world] which has the nature of manifesting before one.
When the visible— the collection of objects that are the domain of the act of seeing—
exists and possesses being, then,
from the perspective of ultimate reality, the state of being a seer would belong to the seer whose nature is pure consciousness alone.
Because the status of being an agent with respect to the action of seeing is possible when the object exists;
for indeed, when rice and so forth exist, [one is the agent] with respect to the action of cooking which has them as its object.
Agency belongs to the person alone who engages in action, just as the state of being a cook belongs [to one who cooks];
it is not the case that the seer possesses the status of a seer merely through the existence of the object seen.
Moreover, with the intention that the visibility of the object of sight exists even by virtue of the existence of the seer, he says "visibility. "Avekṣake" means in the observer;
that is to say, in the seer.
When existence exists, it partakes in being;
in the ultimate sense, the state of being an object would have as its substratum the object that is pure consciousness alone.
For [an object] does not [exist] by means of a cook.
Rice and other such items, when made the object of the act of cooking, assume the state of being cooked, which has "the state of being boiled rice" as its synonym.

Therefore, the sense is that because they are seen as mutually dependent, and because there is an absolute absence of [any separate] visibility, the status of being a seer as an object of seeing perishes. In the context of explaining the mutual dependence of the state of being a seer and the state of being seen, it follows that their unity and duality [are likewise untenable].
He describes mutual dependence as "oneness.
Oneness is primarily that oneness residing in the observer who is first fit for counting; duality is that inferiority residing in the objects of sight which are subsequently fit for counting as two.
When there is existence, one resorts to the being;
it would exist,
because in the absence of duality, counting itself does not occur.
For calculation indeed proceeds by observing duality and so forth in order to establish it;

but in the absence of duality and the rest, for what purpose would its operation occur? Moreover, if the establishment [of calculation] were to proceed by itself, then the non-establishment of oneness—which constitutes its very first component—would be manifest.
Likewise, "duality residing in the object" refers to duality [perceived] in the cognition of unity—
that is, in a cognition having the form of unity—
meaning in the unity residing in the perceiver.
If it were so,
then having counted one, the second would indeed enter the range of counting; thus, it is clear that [the second] cannot exist without oneness.
The occurrence of duality is untenable.
Even by the existence of the seer;
existence;
the state of being cooked.
It depends upon;
[the reading] *dvitvādikaṃ* is [corrected to] *dvitvādikaṃ*;
[the reading] *anupapattiḥ* is [corrected to] *anupapattiḥ*.
It declares the result:
when one [of the two] is absent, the accomplishment of both occurs; for here there is no such thing.
When the duality of subject and object, as well as the state of being the seer and the seen, has ceased, the Real remains.
"hi" signifies certainty; "ataḥ" means therefore; "atra" means here, between these two—namely, oneness and duality;
"ekābhāve" means when there is an absence of one, that is, the absence of either oneness or duality;
"dvayoḥ eva" means of both of them, namely of both duality and oneness.
Success does not occur.
[Objection: "But what will be accomplished by that?
To this, he says: "By duality and unity."
The destruction of duality and unity, as well as of the seer and the seen, is the "destruction of duality, unity, seer, and seen.
When that [destruction] occurs, that reality called "Being" (sat), which exists as the witness of duality and so forth, remains;
it is what is left over.
Having interrupted the discourse concerning the "Real" (*sat*), he makes his vow once again to cleanse away the visible world:
"I shall cleanse for you the entire visible world, including the ego and all else."
Through the perception of absolute non-existence, the impurity [arises] from the mind as the primary source;
all that is "I," beginning with the ego-sense (*ahantā*) and headed by the state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*).
The impurity is that which has become impure:
the entire visible world. From the mirror of your mind—that is, from the reflecting surface of your own mind—[it appears].
"By the cognition of absolute non-existence," that is, by the knowledge of absolute non-being;
in other words, by the production of the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the object of perception.
"I shall wipe away."
And it is appropriate to wipe away the dirt from a mirror.
[The opponent asks: "But how can you possibly effect the wiping away of this entire visible world? To this he replies:
"The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being."
But as for that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), what affliction is there to be wiped away?
For that which is non-existent cannot possess the agency of existence;
"existence" (*bhāva*) here means being (*sattā*).
It does not exist; for even a rabbit’s horn would then incur existence,
since it would follow that existence acts as the agent of its own existence.
Non-existence is non-being;
it does not exist,
because that would entail the loss of its own nature.
Furthermore, the loss of its own nature is not logical,
because it would entail the undesirable consequence that even fire would lose its quality of being fire;
for that which does not exist by way of its own nature [cannot be said to exist].
What difficulty could there be in wiping that away?
Indeed, no one's effort is ever seen directed toward breaking the horn of a hare.
If it is asked, "Even so, what follows regarding engagement (*pravartana*)?", he says here:
"regarding engagement" (*pravartane*).

Regarding this, he says: "In this regard, he says: That which was unarisen at the beginning of the world, and that which is seen spread out here, is Brahman itself, expanded by its own consciousness within its own stainless self. (MU 3.7.37)
At the very beginning, first of all, the world, though seemingly augmented by its own nature,
remains unarisen.
Therefore, the sense is that there is no difficulty in wiping away the world.
Now, one might ask: "If the world has been unarisen from the very beginning, then what is this that appears?"
Regarding this, he says: "And as for this... That is to say, "and as for this"—whatever is seen here has its nature extended and expanded.
That very Brahman, the reality known as Brahman itself,
within its own stainless self— that is, upon its own wall which is the nature of pure consciousness alone—
becomes intensely expanded (*bṛṃhita*) by virtue of its consciousness.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be Brahman; for Brahman is defined precisely as that which is characterized by expansion (*bṛṃhā*). Furthermore, it cannot be said that the "expansion" of a real entity consists in the arising of some other entity.
Furthermore, because it arises from the fluidity of water, there would be the undesirable consequence that its swelling as a wave is the production of a separate entity;
yet even a fool does not admit that waves are distinct from the water.
Similarly, [the objects of a dream] are merely the self, whose nature is consciousness, appearing in the form of dream-objects.
It has been observed that [the self] is nourished; this is stated because [the self] possesses consciousness.
It becomes;
because of its nature as consciousness (*cittvāt*), it is well-nourished (*svabṛṃhitam*);
in the water (*jale*). (MT 3.7.37)
Again and again he says this very thing:
that which is called "the world" has never arisen, does not exist, and is not perceived; just as the state of being a bracelet and so forth exists in gold, why this effort to polish it?
The word "name" (nāma) is used in the sense of determination; thus,
the world is neither produced nor does it exist.
And yet it is not perceived,
because it exists as the very form of Brahman itself.
What, for instance, is the world like?
It is like the state of being a bracelet and so forth;
for example, the state of being a bracelet and so forth does not exist in gold,
because it exists only as gold in that form.
The meaning is "so it is.
Therefore, what effort is required for its cleansing?
For it has been cleansed by the mere knowledge of Brahman itself.
For the state of being a bracelet or the like appearing in gold is not something that cannot be wiped away;
it is wiped away by the mere knowledge of its being gold. (MT_3,7.38)
Having recognized that the disciple is thus devoid of consolation, we shall here explain at length through many logical arguments how to provide him with consolation,
so that it may indeed be experienced by him personally as something uncontradicted. (MU 3.7.39)
"Uncontradicted" means that we have [already] refuted it;
this refers to the matter previously stated,
which has been [refuted] here in this treatise at length through many logical arguments.
We shall explain:
"certainly" (*nūnam*) indicates certainty;
that is, just as this is experienced by you yourself without contradiction.
He speaks precisely on the subject at hand: "For how can there be existence here for that which has never arisen from the very beginning?
How can there be a river of water in a desert, or a planet in the second moon? (MU 3.7.40)
How [could there be] figurative status? For how could there be certainty regarding that entity which does not even arise at the very beginning?
Its existence here is its being (*sattva*). From what does this arise? To this, he states two examples beginning with "from what" (*kutaḥ*) and so forth. (MT_3,7.40)
Just as the son of a barren woman does not exist, just as there is no water in a desert,
and just as there is no tree in the sky, so too does the delusion of the world not exist.
The "delusion of the world" (*jagadbhrama*) is a delusion whose form is the world;
that is to say, it is the world itself. [Question:
If so, what is this that appears? To this, he says:
"O Rāma, that which is seen here is indeed the untainted Brahman itself.
We shall explain this to you later through reasoning, and not by mere words. [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6] "That which is seen here by us..."
That which is free from affliction, devoid of the affliction known as existence and non-existence,
becomes Brahman itself; we [become that].
This [was stated] previously, at the outset;
by means of logic, that is, through arguments;
for you, meaning for yourselves.
We shall explain it;
we shall not explain it by means of speech alone.
The suffix *tasil* here has the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). (Pāṇini 5.4.44, Vārttika 1).
With this verse at the end of the chapter, he declares that the rejection of reasoned speech is to be abandoned:
"O noble-minded one, it is improper for a person of exalted intellect to show contempt for that which those who know the truth proclaim here through reasonings.
They know him to be truly ignorant who, with a deluded mind, disregards what is consistent with reason; such a person brings about his own misery. (MU 3.7.43)
"Those who know it" (tajjñāḥ) refers to those who have certainty;
"contempt" (avahelanam) means neglect.

It brings hardship and bestows suffering; the ellipsis "of oneself" refers to [efforts] through impossible exertions. Thus all is auspicious. (MT_3,7.43) Thus ends the seventh canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Śrī Rāma asks: By what reasoning is this known, and how is it established?
Once this principle has been experienced, nothing remains to be known.
This is the unreality of the perceptible.
Now, one might ask: "For what purpose do you inquire after the reasoning here? To this, he says: "By means of logic (*nyāya*)."
For when this principle has been realized through reasoning, nothing remains of that which is to be known.
Because everything is known through hearing the reasoning.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha, intending to fulfill his promise to speak in detail, says the following:
"For a long time, this cholera of false knowledge has been established."
The world, known by that name, does not cease through anything other than the mantra called "investigation.
When it has ascended into the intellect and manifested as real,
the nature of the world must be understood as being false knowledge, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
And the destruction of cholera is accomplished through the mantra.
[The author] strengthens Śrī Rāma’s resolve regarding the hearing of the instruction to be spoken:
"O Rāma, I shall tell these narratives for the sake of attaining awakening."
If you hear them, O virtuous one, you are indeed liberated and wise.
"Narratives" (*ākhyāyikāḥ*) are instructive stories;
they are for the sake of attaining awakening, that is, for the sake of establishing the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible world.
"Released" means untouched by the visible.
He states the penalty for not listening:
"If you do not [listen], because of your habit of agitation, you shall rise from the midst and depart."
Therefore, for you who follow the ways of animals, not even a fraction of that will be accomplished today.
If you do not listen to us,
or if, out of a habit of agitation, you rise from your seat and depart,
then at that time—
For one who possesses the nature of an animal, being equal to a beast,
they will not achieve even the slightest success.

[Objection: "But if nothing at all will be accomplished even by listening with firm resolve, then what should be done? To this he says: "Just as one who desires a certain object strives for that object, he necessarily attains it, provided he does not turn back out of exhaustion. (MU 3.8.5)
Whatever person desires whatever object— that is, makes whatever thing the object of their desire— [attains it].
In that way, and according to its secondary method,
he exerts himself; but not otherwise.
He will certainly attain that,
provided that he does not turn back when exhausted.
In accordance with that [method], [one thinks]:
"Now, what kind of effort shall I make regarding this desired object? To this, he says:
"O Rāma, if you are devoted to the company of the virtuous and the study of the true scriptures..."
Then, in days or indeed in months, you attain the supreme state:
in days if you possess unsurpassed intuitive insight;
otherwise, in months.
Such is the division.
(MT 3.8.6) Śrī Rāma, having become certain of the excellence of Śrī Vasiṣṭha, asks for a scripture as a means to awaken self-knowledge:
"O best among those who know the scriptures, [teach] a scripture for the awakening of self-knowledge."
What indeed could that primary thing be, by knowing which one does not grieve?
[The word] *jñāte* [is used] for the sake of awakening to self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), for the purpose of the manifestation of self-knowledge.
"One does not grieve; the kind of grieving that consists of attachment to the visible world is no longer experienced. Śrī Vasiṣṭha replies:
"O Mahāmati, for those whose primary focus is the knowledge of the Self, this alone [is the case]."

Those for whom the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna) is the primary subject matter and constitutes the essential core of the scriptures— the supreme scripture among all scriptures known as the Mahārāmāyaṇa.
Of such [persons].
This is the history named *Rāmāyaṇa*, this which is called the *Mahārāmāyaṇa*.
Now, in the *Śrīmahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the venerable Vālmīki himself—

In the context of narrating the life-story of Śrī Rāma, the instruction bestowed by Śrī Vasiṣṭha upon Śrī Rāma has been composed; yet, since this was extracted by some compassionate person from the *Śrī Mahārāmāyaṇa*, how could Vasiṣṭha have referred to the *Śrī Mahārāmāyaṇa*— which exists subsequent to the time of that instruction— by using the demonstrative pronoun "this" (*idam*)?
If you argue that by this [verse] the fact that the glorious Mahārāmāyaṇa was composed by Śrī Vasiṣṭha is illuminated, we have already reached this conclusion at the very beginning;
why do you ask again and again?

For it has been stated therein that those possessed of creative intuition (pratibhā) have the capacity to understand this meaning by themselves, whereas it has been stated that those devoid of it lack such qualification.
Thus, ask your own intuition; if there is no intuition, then, due to a lack of qualification, one should simply observe silence—enough with this prolixity.
Extracted: *uddhṛtaḥ* [corrected from *dhṛtaḥ*].
Regarding the beginning: N11, fol. 3r, lines 3–5. (MT_3,8.8) He praises the *Śrīmahārāmāyaṇa* itself.
From this supreme history, a higher understanding proceeds;
this is declared to be the essence of all histories. (MU 3.8.9) [That is,] from this work called the Rāmāyaṇa. (MT 3.8.9)

Since the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatva*) arises spontaneously upon hearing this verbal scripture, therefore this alone is supremely purifying. (MU 3.8.10) [In the verbal scripture, i.e., the treatise. (MT 3.8.10)
The world of appearances, though already existing, comes to an end through inquiry,
just as the mental impression of dream-objects vanishes once the dream is recognized.
It is "already existing" in the sense that it has not been destroyed by the blows of a hammer or other such means.
Regarding this, he states an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as).
"Bhāvanā" means the cultivation of reality.
The particle "eva" is for the purpose of completing the meter.
The meaning is this: just as in a dream, when the waking state is recognized as unreal,
joy and resentment are no longer experienced toward the presence or absence of things encountered therein.
Otherwise, just as with past objects experienced while awake, there would be the arising of joy and resentment due to the presence or absence of objects belonging to that [dream] state. Likewise,
when the unreality of the visible world is known through the investigation of the *Mahārāmāyaṇa*, joy and resentment would arise from the presence or absence of objects within the field of vision.
"It is not known.
[Objection: "But surely there are other treatises as well;
why then do you assert that this alone is the unique cause? To this, he says:
"What exists here exists elsewhere; what does not exist here exists nowhere else.
The wise know this to be the treasury of all the sciences of consciousness.
Whatever exists here in this Rāmāyaṇa, found in its entirety,
that [is found] elsewhere in other treatises.
The meaning is that it exists as something distinct.
That which does not exist here does not exist anywhere at all in any scripture.
Therefore, the wise, who know the essence of all scriptures,
regard this glorious *Mahārāmāyaṇa* as the treasury of all sciences and the storehouse of all spiritual treatises.
They know; they understand. He describes the fruit of hearing the *Śrīmahārāmāyaṇa*, whose characteristics have been stated:
"He who would hear this constantly, for him of noble wonder..."
"Even for a child, the intellect attains supreme awakening; of this there is no doubt.
The meaning is "even for a child, that is, even for a fool";
the implication is, "what need then to speak of a learned man?"
This is said for one who is averse to this [teaching], for it does not please the unworthy due to the arising of their own misdeeds;
let such a person investigate whatever treatise exists composed of the language of knowledge. (MU 3.8.14)
"To one who is unfit" means to one endowed with a demonic nature.
"Consisting of knowledge and speech" means filled with the words of knowledge.
[Objection: "But for me, who desires liberation, what is the use of hearing this? To this, he says:

But when this [text] is heard, liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva) is experienced by oneself, just as freedom from disease is experienced when a potent medicine has been drunk. (MU 3.8.15) [Note: jīvanmuktatvam] [Correction: °kt(i)a°]
When it is drunk— that is, when it is absorbed by oneself— it occurs quite spontaneously and without effort.
For when this scripture is being heard, the listener understands this within his own self.
This which has been stated by us is exactly as it is, and not like a boon or a curse.
This is the matter spoken by me.
Now, one might object: if there were some transgression or the like for one who exerts effort toward hearing this, then—
"What is to be done?"—
to this he says,
"this," meaning that which is accompanied by a boon and a curse (*varaśāpa*).
The word "mantravat" (like a mantra) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

With the final verse of the chapter, he declares that the investigation of one's own self (*svātmavicāra*) is the unique cause for the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible world (*dṛśyātyantābhāva*): "This suffering of worldly existence (*saṃsṛtiduḥkha*) is stilled by the great discourse of the investigation of one's own self alone."

Neither by wealth, gifts, austerity, nor Vedic learning—nor by hundreds of efforts devoid of discourse on that [Reality]—is this nature of the visible world [comprehended] for you. *Note:* "te" refers to "tava" (for you). "Idam" refers to "this nature of the visible world" (*dṛśyasvarūpam*).
The suffering of saṃsāra is the suffering called birth;
[it is overcome] by the great discourse on the investigation of one's own self—
that is, through the investigation of one's own self.
That great discourse, the vast mutual conversation—
it is by that alone that [the mind] is stilled.
This suffering of saṃsāra is not stilled by wealth, charity, austerity, learning, or the Vedas.
Therefore, "it must be so" is the ellipsis;
for this reason, by a person,
[there should be] that inquiry into one's own self.
That which is conversation with the virtuous— that is, mutual discourse—
for that purpose, hundreds of efforts have been abandoned; that is, hundreds of efforts other than conversing have been relinquished.
By that [means],
he must become such a one. May there be auspiciousness!
O you, that which has the nature of the visible belongs to you; it is for the sake of the investigation of one's own self.
Thus ends the eighth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. He clearly explains the meaning of the verse at the end of the previous section:
"Those whose minds are fixed on Him, whose life-breaths are absorbed in Him, who awaken one another, and who constantly speak of Him—those people find contentment and delight. (MU 3.9.1)

For those who are solely devoted to knowledge, through the investigation of self-knowledge, that state of liberation while living arises—which is indeed liberation from the body. Their minds are fixed on that: on this very inquiry into one's own Self.
Those whose minds are such— such are they.
Likewise, in that investigation of one's own self,
those whose vital breaths— that is, their external senses— have reached their final end (niṣṭhā).
They,
being such as they are,
[performed] that investigation of the self in that manner.
Those virtuous ones who, while mutually awakening one another, likewise discourse upon that investigation of the self;
They are satisfied and become endowed with contentment;
likewise, they delight others and bring them to a state of being endowed with contentment—
those who are solely devoted to self-knowledge and solely intent upon the investigation of the self.
For those persons,
through the investigation of self-knowledge, that state of liberation while living arises and manifests;
it is indeed the very same as liberation after death.
Completely, due to the absence of identification with the body.
[Endowed with contentment] (tuṣṭiyuktāḥ):
Śrī Rāma asks: "O Brahman, what are the characteristics of one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and one who is liberated after death (videhamukta)?"
"Tell me so that I may likewise strive with an intellect guided by the vision of the scriptures.
Regarding the phrase "of one liberated while living," the word "ca" (and) is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. "I strive" means I exert effort.
A characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is a property (*dharma*) that establishes its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). By what kind of intellect? By the mind (*buddhi*). How characterized [is that intellect]?
She whose eyes are the very scripture itself.
"Of such a kind" means "in accordance with the treatises."
To her,
Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply as it truly is: "This [world] belongs to one who, though engaged in worldly activity, remains as he is."

He for whom the sky has set and remains as the sky—even while engaged in worldly affairs and performing transactions among the objects of the universe—is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). MU 3.9.4. "Even while engaged in worldly affairs" means even while performing transactions among the various things of the world. Of such a person...
It exists exactly as it is, in this very manner; its essential nature has not been destroyed by any effort whatsoever. This is the world, which is characterized by manifesting before one.
Having set and having gone to destruction,
it therefore becomes the void, which is of the nature of emptiness;
he is called by the wise one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
The meaning is that the characteristic of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) is the perception of the appearance of the world as unreal, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Having reached a state of exclusive devotion to awakening, he remains as if in deep sleep even while awake;
he who continues to engage in worldly affairs is called one liberated while living.
In *bodhi*, which is the knowledge of the self preceded by the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible world;
he whose *niṣṭhā*— that is, his delight— is in that alone, being solitary.
He is solely devoted to awakening;
his state is thatness (tattā);
he has attained—that is, gone to—that state.
The person who,
even while awake— that is, precisely in the waking state—
and even therein, is merely a worldly agent, engaged only in the business of worldly activity as it arises in the stream of existence.
He remains as if in deep sleep, as if entered into deep sleep; that is to say,
he remains without any mental synthesis.
He is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta) by the wise.

Moreover, it is observed that even for a man who remains engaged in worldly activity during the waking state—such as one intent upon women and the like—his state of being is like that of deep sleep; thus, no further effort is required.
For a person,
for one who engages in worldly activity, neither the radiance of the face nor pleasure and pain arise or pass away.
He who remains established in whatever state has been attained is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
[Regarding "in happiness": for one who remains established in whatever has been attained, that is, one whose steadfastness follows the natural flow [of events].
He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets in pleasure or pain, due to being free from elation and resentment—
he is called by the wise one liberated while living.
He who remains awake while standing in deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists,
whose consciousness is free from latent impressions— he is called liberated while living.
This refers to the person.
It remains awake; that is, it maintains awareness directed toward external objects. Of what nature is it? It is as if it were remaining in deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
Such a person is one who,
through the certainty of pure consciousness alone, is devoid of any mental connection with external manifoldness.
Thus, for such a person...
The waking state of the world is the waking condition;
it does not exist [as such] because [the liberated one] consists of the fourth state (*turya*).
For the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), seeing everything in the waking state as consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), is established in the state of the fourth.
Thus it is:
likewise, for one whose awakening is free from latent impressions— that is, devoid of the impressions of the forms of "I" and "mine"—
there is the knowledge of external objects such as the body and so forth.
He is called by the wise one who is liberated while living.
He for whom there is no latent desire (*nirvāsana*),
who, even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like,
remains internally as utterly pure as the sky— he is called one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
That person who,
even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like,
and even while indulging in attachment toward those such as sons who are the basis of passion;
Even when turning away from an enemy who is a vessel for hatred,
or even when moving out of fear of lions and the like;
Within the mind,
it becomes as utterly transparent and exceedingly pure as the sky,
because the flow of attachment toward objects such as sons and the like is rendered free from subsequent mental connection through the force of [this practice].
For it is only through investigation that impurity ceases in the mind;
by the wise, such a person is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta).
By the word "etcetera," the inclusion of the body and other objects, as well as egoism and so forth, is intended.
Because of acting without subsequent attachment;
of the body, sense objects, and so forth.
He whose state is not characterized by egoism, and whose intellect is not defiled—
Whether acting or not acting, that person is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta), whose state of egoism—
that mental modification consisting of the sense of "I"— has ceased.
It does not exist,
because Brahman is seen to be the creator in all cases;
such is the case for whichever person [it may be].

The intellect, though associated with attachment, is not defiled; that is to say, it is not stained by sins in the form of passion and so forth. By the wise, such a person is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Of what kind of person?
Of one who performs actions for the sake of maintaining the body, or who performs actions that have come forth in a continuous flow;
likewise, or of one who does not perform them for some reason.

In this regard, one should understand that there is an absence of the stain of the notion of "I" because, at the time of action, one acts without subsequent mental attachment, and at the time of non-action, one remains established in the reflective awareness of pure consciousness alone.
And he [is the one] for whom the creation and dissolution of the cosmic order occur through the opening and closing of his eyes.
He who perceives the three worlds as being equal to the sky is called one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). "Equal to the sky" (*khasama*) means similar to space (*ākāśa*).
That person [is he] who,

by means of the opening and closing of his eyes, [governs] the three worlds of the cosmic order— the external triad of worlds beginning with the earth (bhūḥ), and the internal triad of worlds beginning with waking— and likewise [the three states] beginning with waking.

That is to say, through the unfolding (*unmeṣa*)— the manifestation known as the non-orientation toward objects— of the consciousness-principle (*cittattva*) which is determined to be the Supreme Self;
and through its closing (*nimeṣa*)— the concealment of its own nature known as the orientation toward objects—
he perceives dissolution and origination, that is, withdrawal and emergence.
Likewise, he perceives concealment and manifestation;
by the wise, he is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta).
Alternatively, "unmesha" is the self-reflection [of consciousness].
In that regard as well, equanimity is the closing of the eyes;
likewise, manifestation occurs through opening,
and dissolution through closing.
Thus, one should establish the connection precisely by disregarding the order of enumeration.
[Regarding the arrangement of the three worlds external to the *bhū* group:
He who is the enjoyer yet does not appear as an enjoyer, having attained oneness with pure consciousness;
who remains within like one asleep—he is called liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). (MU 3.9.11)
The person who has attained oneness with pure consciousness— that is, unity with pure awareness— like an enjoyer.
The Buddha, being endowed with awakening,
remains as if asleep within,
because he is free from all discursive mental activity.
Of what nature is he? He is as if a non-enjoyer (*abhoktā*), even while being an enjoyer— that is, even while possessing the agency of the act of enjoying—
because, through the knowledge of his own pure consciousness, he lacks the conceit (*abhimāna*) that "I am the enjoyer."
He is called "liberated while living" by the wise.
Always a seer yet appearing as a non-seer, alive yet like one who is dead, engaged in worldly affairs yet as immovable as a mountain— he is called liberated while living.
He who, while being a seer and indeed maintaining the agency of the act of seeing, does not remain like one blind,
becomes a non-seer.
Likewise, he who, even while living and indeed while engaged in the activity of living,
becomes like one dead—
that is, becomes similar to the dead.
Like one who is dead, because of the absence of desire for enjoyments and the like;
likewise, he who is a worldly agent, even while performing worldly activity,
becomes like a mountain.
Because he is, in reality, free from agitation,
he is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta) by the wise.
In reality:
because the world does not tremble before him, and he does not tremble before the world; being liberated from joy, resentment, and fear, he is called one liberated while living.
The world is the common world;
because it does not tremble, due to the absence of any cause for trembling, it does not undergo agitation.
Likewise, that which does not tremble before the world, because it is devoid of purpose.

For one who is solely intent upon his own purpose indeed becomes agitated toward those from whom he perceives no benefit for that purpose. Of what nature is such a person? He is liberated from joy, resentment, and fear—that is, devoid of joy, resentment, and fear.
Because of the knowledge of the oneness of pure consciousness within oneself,
he is called "liberated while living" by the wise. With the mental constructions of saṃsāra stilled, though possessing parts, he is partless.
He who, though possessing a mind, is as if mindless, is called liberated while living;
he for whom the fluctuations of worldly existence have been stilled.
He is one for whom the fabrication of worldly existence has become quiescent, having dissolved through the vision of pure consciousness within the self.
Such is the person;
even though he is possessed of *kalā*, that is, endowed with the faculty known as knowledge (*jñāna*).

He becomes "partless" (niṣkala), having emerged from all parts, through the knowledge of his own nature as pure consciousness alone. Likewise, even he who possesses a mind— that is, one endowed with a mind whose essential nature is pure being— [is liberated].
Being without mind, he has emerged from the mind due to the absence of a defiled mind;
by the wise, he is called "liberated while living. (MT 3.9.14)
He who, though engaged in all kinds of worldly affairs, remains cool as if toward the interests of others, and whose self is full— that one is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
"Full-souled" (pūrṇātman) means one whose self is satisfied by being pure consciousness alone, which is peaceful and independent.

Regarding all categories of objects that arrive in a continuous flow, and regarding the entire multitude of purposes, he becomes cool—free from the fever of anxiety—as to whether this will be accomplished or not. In what way is he like? [He is like one who is unperturbed by the outcome.]
"As in the case of others' interests":
the meaning is that it is just as a worldly person becomes cool toward the interests of others.
"He is called by the wise one liberated while living" (MT 3.9.15).
Having described liberation while living, he now speaks of disembodied liberation (videhamukti), which follows in due order.
[The reading is] *kramaprāptām* [not *kramaḥ prāptām*].
Having abandoned the state of liberation while living when the body is destroyed by the power of time,
consciousness attains disembodied liberation, just as the wind [loses] its vibration.
One who has attained the state of consciousness through the secondary sense (lakṣaṇā) is a *jīvanmukta* (liberated while living).
[This occurs] in the body (*deha*), that is, in the physical frame,
by the power of time (*kāla*), that is, by the force of destiny (*niyati*).
When the wound has been destroyed and healed,
having abandoned the state of being liberated while living— that is, the condition of *jīvanmukti*.
He attains the state of liberation while embodied and the condition of liberation beyond the body.
Like what, having abandoned what?
Like the wind [leaves] trembling;
just as the wind abandons the trembling, that is, the performance of movement.
The meaning is "so it is.
Alternatively, there is a reading: "pavanaḥ spandatām iva" (like the wind's movement).
He describes the characteristics of this [state] briefly, as if they were those of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
The one liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta) neither rises nor sets, nor does he cease;
he is neither existent nor non-existent, neither far away, nor "I," nor anything else.
The "one liberated while in the disembodied state" is the person who has attained liberation from the body through the absence of the sense of "I" and the consequent disappearance of the body itself.
It does not arise, because it abides as the nature of pure consciousness that is eternally risen;
likewise, it does not set,
because whatever is imagined as having set arises from that very source.
Because it cannot be otherwise;
likewise, it does not cease, for that would entail the non-existence of the appearance of saṃsāra;
nor does it exist.
Because it is not within the range of external or internal sense faculties,
it is likewise not non-existent;
for if it were so, it would follow that there is no manifestation at all due to the absence of such phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*).
For a rabbit's horn cannot manifest in any form whatsoever;
likewise, it does not exist as something distant.
Because it exists as the essence of "I-ness" (ahantā) for all,
it is not thus;
it does not become a limited subject (pramātṛ).
Because it exists as the infinite subject (*pramātṛ*),
the other— the limited object of knowledge (*prameya*)—
does not exist.
Because it exists in the state of being immeasurable and beyond limit.
Having stated his transcendence of the universe (*viśvottīrṇatā*), he briefly describes his being composed of the universe (*viśvamayatā*):
"Becoming the sun, he blazes; as Viṣṇu, he protects the three worlds."
Rudra withdraws all, and the lotus-born Brahmā creates all; that [Self],
having attained the state of pure consciousness alone, being liberated from the body (videhamukta), becomes the sun, and having reached the nature of the sun, it blazes,
assuming the agency of the act of heating.
Likewise, having become Viṣṇu, he protects and guards the three worlds;
this should be applied everywhere in the same manner.
It should be understood that these [deities], beginning with Sūrya, possess a twofold nature by way of being both external and internal.
For that which is seen as the sun in the external sky is the internal vital breath (*prāṇa*),
because, like the sun, it effects the maturation of the body.
Likewise, Viṣṇu is the intellect (buddhi),
because he likewise causes the persistence of volition (saṅkalpa);
likewise, Rudra is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
In the same way, the lotus-born [Brahmā] is the mind (*manas*), because he likewise causes all volitions (*saṅkalpa*) to dissolve into himself,
and because he produces volitions.
In this manner, it should be applied everywhere according to what is possible.

Now, one might ask: how can one who is liberated in the disembodied state (videhamukta), having assumed the nature of moving and non-moving entities such as the sun and so forth, perform all the activities inherent in them?
True.
In that regard, the vital breaths (*carāḥ*) are clearly observed to be presided over by the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) and the pure consciousness (*śuddhacittattva*);
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even when they have entered the state of death, they would still serve as the substratum for activity as before.

[Objection: Is it not observed that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is the impeller in that action? For it is seen that lifeless bodies, such as those of inanimate objects, are devoid of activity. [Reply:
This is incorrect.
For the vital breath (*prāṇa*), though it appears here like some conscious agent capable of impelling, is not actually so;

rather, it acts as if performing exit and entry through the impulse of some other independent conscious being, like a ball propelled by Devadatta. Thus, it is the pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*) that, by acting as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the body, is the agent of the actions belonging to the body.

It is understood as follows: even in non-moving things (acarāḥ), the action of remaining (avasthitikriyā) which is observed must be known as being produced by that [motion], because it is an action, just like the action belonging to moving things (caragatakriyā). For, where there is an incapacity for their own action in moving things that appear directly as conscious, what need is there to mention non-moving things that appear directly as insentient in their capacity to perform action? Therefore, just as...

It should be understood that just as pillars and other objects remain standing because they have been established by Devadatta acting as their presiding agent, so too do these immobile things remain standing because they have been established by some reality residing within them.
In that case, since Devadatta's existence outside of those objects is directly perceived, one does not postulate his being contained within them.
In this case, however, since no gross entity whatsoever is perceived externally, its being contained within [the body] is postulated;
yet, let it be granted that its external existence is not contradicted either.
And thus, agency in all actions— which culminates in pure consciousness alone— is indeed established even in that [consciousness] when it has attained identity with it,
just as a drop of water merged in the ocean is characterized by the qualities of the ocean. The remainder—
Even a dead body should be understood as being impelled by the wings [of the vital breaths].
