Now, even so, it is only established that the one liberated while in the body (videhamukta) performs all actions;
however, it is not established that he becomes everything.
If it is asked, "What is the news regarding that?"—
it is true;
this is the news concerning it.
When one investigates what the nature of moving and non-moving entities consists of, their true form—being ungraspable by the hand—rests in nothing other than ineffability (*anirvācyatā*).
And this very ineffability is the essential nature of pure consciousness (*śuddhacittattva*); thus, [one realizes] its state as pure consciousness.
For one who has departed and attained liberation from the body (videhamukta), it is entirely logical that all states of being are unified; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Furthermore, this very nature of the pure reality of consciousness (śuddhacittattva) is established by direct perception for those who experience it.
But this effort has been made for the sake of those who do not know; enough with further elaboration.
The rites are empowered by the reality of the inner guide’s pure mind;
[the rites] of those with immovable bodies.
capable;
like a ball being propelled by Devadatta;
they remain.
Being situated outside;
indeed, [it is] just so; implied by the alternative; (the conduct) portion.

Having become space, it supports the masses of wind together with the stars, gods, and asuras; having become the range of the principal mountain ranges, it serves as the abode for the cities of the world-protectors,
along with the stars, gods, and asuras— that is, together with the lunar mansions, deities, and titans.
The connection is that, having become the range of the principal mountain ranges (*kulācala*), it becomes the abode of the cities of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
(MT 3.9.19) Having become the earth, it sustains this unbroken stability of the worlds;
having become grass, shrubs, and creepers, it yields a continuous succession of fruits. (MU 3.9.20)
This is clear.
(MT 3.9.20) Bearing the appearance of water and fire, it blazes and becomes liquefied;
as the moon, it exudes nectar, and as the *hālāhala* poison, it brings death. (MU 3.9.21)
Bearing the form of water, it flows, being endowed with the quality of fluidity; bearing the form of fire, it burns— so it should be applied.
"Having become the moon, having become the *hālāhala* [poison]"—thus it should be connected.
The Hālāhala poison manifests its fiery energy; hope spreads blinding darkness.
Being empty, it becomes like the sky; being a mountain, it utterly obstructs.
He obstructs; he performs obstruction.
He makes the mobile [world] when he is in the state of consciousness, and being stationary, he takes a stationary form.
Having become the ocean, he encircles the woman Earth, just as a bracelet encircles the wrist.
"Abiding in the state of consciousness"— that is to say, having become endowed with the nature of consciousness—
he makes the moving immobile while being in an immobile form, and he makes the immobile moving.
Having become an ocean, it encircles—that is, it surrounds and covers on all sides—the woman who is the earth; "the earth itself is the woman. Like what? Like a bracelet.
Just as a bracelet [adorns] a woman; that is to say, a bracelet [adorns] a woman's arm.
It encircles;
that is to say, "so it is."
Being in the form of a stable entity (*san sthāvarākṛtiḥ*),
having assumed the body of the supreme sun, he spreads his light within and remains perfectly tranquil, [pervading] the mass of motes in the three worlds.
Having become the supreme solar body, the body of the sun of consciousness,
[he shines] upon his own wall, which is of the nature of light.
Spreading out— that is, expanding— the mass of atoms known as the three worlds,
he remains entirely tranquil, for being established in the state of a witness, he is free from any agitation caused by that [expansion].
And it is logical that in the light of the sun there should be the spreading of a stream of motes and their coming to rest;
having realized that specific differentiation is impossible, he speaks in general terms:
"Whatever this appears, has appeared, or will come to appear."
Whether it be that which is visible throughout the three periods of time, or indeed all of this entire world— this is what he [the yogin] perceives in the alternative case.
It shone previously, it flashes forth; likewise it shines today, it flashes forth;
likewise is its radiance, its flashing forth.
"He will attain" means he will come forward;
thus, one who perceives all that is visible throughout the three periods of time is called "liberated while in the body" (*videhamukta*).
Here, Śrī Rāma asks:
"How can you speak thus, O Brahmin? For my vision is indeed obstructed; it is my firm conviction that this [vision] is difficult to attain and hard to traverse."
O Brahmin, you speak; tell us:
how is it that a person endowed with such qualities as these becomes one who is liberated from the body (videhamukta)? How is he established [in that state]?
For indeed, because of this reason,
my certainty is thus.
It occurs.
What [is it that] occurs?
It is uneven and harsh.
This aforementioned vision,
which takes the form of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*),
is difficult to attain and difficult to master.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply:
"O Rāma, this is called liberation; this is declared to be Brahman;
this is described as nirvāṇa. Listen now: how is it attained?"

O Rāma, the wise call this state "liberation while disembodied" (videhamukti); for liberation while living (jīvanmukti), because it rests upon the mind whose nature is *sattva*, is considered as if it were not yet final liberation.
This is called "Brahman" by the wise,
because it possesses the quality of expanding (*bṛṃhaṇa*) through the existence of all things. This is called "Nirvāṇa" by the wise, because of the dissolution of all limited egoity in every respect.
Listen, how this is attained by a person:

that which is seen here as the visible world, joined with "I-ness," "you-ness," and so forth—this is attained through the intellect by means of the non-arising of even that which exists. (MU 3.9.27–28)
By us— this visible world, which is joined with notions such as "I" and "you," is seen and experienced—
even though it exists in this very manner.
Of this world;
by the cognition of its non-arising— that is, by the very knowledge of the absence [of the world] in the form "this is indeed unarisen"—
meaning by the knowledge that this world, as its object, is unarisen.
Up to this point, the state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti), characterized by the aforementioned qualities,
is attained— that is, reached.
The two particles *api* and *vā* have the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.
By this, it has been stated that the absolute non-existence of the perceptible is the cause of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*).
Śrī Rāma asks again: "When those who have attained disembodied liberation enter the three worlds, then—"
O best among those who know what is to be known, I think that when you have attained the state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti), you have indeed reached the very nature of creation itself,
should you then enter the three worlds.
O best among those who know what is to be known,
I think that at that time they have indeed reached the state of creation; they have indeed entered into the condition of being created.
Because it manifests only as the existence of objects contained within creation,
Śrī Vasiṣṭha gives the following reply:
"If the three worlds exist, then let them attain their true nature."
Where not a single referent for the term "the three worlds" exists,
how can there be a cognition of the meaning of the statement "Brahman has become the three worlds"?
Therefore, no other conceptualization of the referent of the word "world" is possible for us.
If the creation of the three worlds exists—
that is, if it truly comes into being— then [so be it].
That [is] then;
they are those liberated while disembodied;
that-ness [is] the state of the three worlds.
"May they proceed together," meaning may they go correctly; "where," meaning in whichever place;
"whatever is the referent of the term 'trilokya'," meaning whatever object is associated with the word 'trilokya'.
The meaning of the term "trailokya" refers to both the word known as "trailokya" and its referent;
[such a thing] is not possible in that context.
"Cognition of the meaning of the statement" means a cognition whose form is the form of the meaning of such a statement;
that is to say, [the cognition] that "the statement is of such a form and the meaning is of such a form.
From what does it arise?
Because the referents of the words "the three worlds" are impossible;
the meaning is that they do not exist.
What [is this referring to]?
Thus, by means of the characteristic of Brahman, one becomes disembodiedly liberated (videhamukta);
that which has gone to the state of the three worlds becomes the state of emanation (sarga).
He provides the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*):
therefore, for that reason;
[the nature] of Brahman is one thing, and [the nature] of others is another.
The conceptual construction of the word "world" and its referent—that is, the conceptual construction whose nature consists of the word "world" and its referent—does not exist.
If [it be so], by this same consequence he repeatedly declares the very identity of the world and Brahman:
"It is non-different, peaceful, a mere appearance, as pure as space."
For those who have realized the truth, the truth is simply that the world is Brahman alone;
the world is the creator,
non-different [from Brahman] because it exists as its very form, being devoid of any entity distinct from itself.
It is peaceful, resting in its own nature;
it is a mere manifestation, having the nature of being merely a manifestation;
it is as stainless as space, clear like the sky.
"He becomes Brahman indeed"—
this is precisely what that means:
for one who has awakened to truth, who is endowed with the knowledge of reality.
It becomes true.
Regarding this, he tells an illustration:
"For just as [gold] is not seen even when a gold bracelet is examined."
The state of being a bracelet can never exist anywhere except in pure gold;
the phrase "just as" (yathā hi) serves to indicate that this is an illustration,
[as stated] by us.
Regarding a golden bracelet or a golden bangle—
even after investigating and scrutinizing it thoroughly—
nowhere is the state of being a "bracelet" seen apart from stainless gold.
Just as a bracelet is nothing but gold, so too the world is nothing but Brahman; this should be applied by way of the analogy seen in the preceding verse, as well as the following two verses.
He now states the second analogy:
Apart from water, I do not perceive anything at all in the waves of the ocean;
for that which is seen as "waviness" by those like you does not exist there at all.
"In the expanse of water, amidst the waves, I see nothing other than water; there is nothing else in the expanse of water.
Thus he tells the third illustration.
The state of vibration is never, at any time or anywhere, other than the wind;
the wind is always nothing but vibration. Therefore, no world exists apart from that.
(MU 3.9.35) "At any time" means at any point in time; "anywhere" means in any place.
In some place or other,
the state of vibration (spandatva) is not different from the wind (pavana),
because the wind is indeed vibration itself.
"He says that the world has borne fruit" means:
since there are three analogies for the world being Brahman, therefore the world does not exist. And thus, the sense is: how can one who is liberated while bodiless (videhamukta) undergo rebirth?
In another place, he again explains the very same point previously stated by means of an illustration:
"Just as emptiness is space, so heat itself is water in the desert."
"Just as light is nothing other than radiance, so the three worlds are nothing other than Brahman.
This is clear.
Śrī Rāma asks:

O Sage, teach me that supreme method by which liberation from the world of appearances arises through the attainment of its absolute non-existence. O Sage! [This refers to] the world of appearances—that which is perceived in the form of the universe.
By means of that method, through the attainment of absolute non-existence— that is, by the accomplishment of absolute non-existence—
liberation arises; you [attain] for me the supreme, unsurpassed state.
Teach that reasoning:
what is the logical justification for how the absolute non-existence of the world-objects serves as a means to establish liberation? Please provide the reasoning on this point.
The intended meaning is "please tell."
"Unsurpassed" (*niratiśayām*).
[The text reads: "Is it not the case that you ask for logic again and again? To this, he poses another question preceded by an answer:
"When the seer and the seen have mutually perished and there is a single cessation..."

When one has come to abide in the non-existence of duality, Nirvāṇa remains. Therefore, tell me how Brahman, which is thus established in its own nature, is understood as the absolute non-arising of the world of the visible.
Because, according to the principle already stated, this has been said by you yourself—this is the ellipsis.

Since it was stated by you alone regarding the seer and the seen, which are mutually established—that is, mutually proven—according to the aforementioned principle, between these two: the seer and the seen.
When there is the destruction of one [of the two],
and consequently, when both have reached the state of non-existence,
that is nirvāṇa, which is absolute isolation.
It remains;
therefore, for that reason,
of the visible world— that is, of the world whose nature is visible.
"Absolute non-arising" is the nature of absolute non-existence, which is absolute non-origination;
it is understood— that is, known— by means of such reasoning.
Likewise, Brahman— the pure reality of consciousness—
is expanded into the form of the world; thus, it exists in the form of the world while remaining established in its own nature, established in its essential self.
Tell me and explain how you understand it; speak thus to me.

[He spoke] like one intoxicated by the penetration of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), once again regarding the logical proof for the absolute non-existence of the perceptible and the logical proof for the abiding nature of Brahman.
And he asks: "By what reasoning is this known, and how is it established?
But once this is established, O Sage, nothing remains to be proven."
This is the absolute non-existence of the visible world, and this is the abiding of Brahman in its own such nature.
Now, why do you ask these questions again and again?
Regarding this, it is said: "In this [case]"; O Sage, when this has been established.
That which is to be accomplished (*sādhyam*) is that which ought to be proven; it "remains no longer" means that nothing remains.
This is because only liberation is desired, and that has been established by this very [treatise].
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
"This chronic cholera of false knowledge, having been rooted for a long time,
will surely be extinguished at its very root by the mantra of inquiry."
"Nūnam" signifies certainty.
This "cholera of false knowledge"— a specific kind of cognition consisting of the thought "this visible world exists in pure consciousness alone"—
has taken root and appears as true within the mind.
And the pacification of cholera by means of a mantra is appropriate;
and here, the investigation should be understood as being of the form: "What is the nature of this visible object?
One might object: "But at that time, I have already performed an investigation, albeit in brief."
How then is this visible world not peaceful? To this he says:
"It cannot be utterly eradicated all at once in a single moment."
For on a mountain where the ascent and descent have equal effort,
[one acts] to completely cut off— that is, to destroy—
this; he establishes this with the second half of the verse by saying "he attains" (sameti).

Just as someone who has climbed to the summit of a mountain and wishes to descend from it cannot descend all at once, so too the perception of the reality of the visible world, having been firmly established for a long time, cannot be removed instantaneously; thus, the sense is that one must engage in inquiry for a long period.
[The author] declares that the statement of reasoning results in this conclusion.
Therefore, by means of the yoga of practice, through reasoning and logical justifications, so that the delusion of the world may be stilled, this is being told; listen.
"Therefore" (tasmāt) means for that reason.
By the yoga of practice, through the method of practicing investigation;
likewise by reasoning, that is, by reasoning produced by one's own intellect;
and likewise by logical justifications, that is, by the arguments stated in the treatises on logic (*nyāya*).
The delusion of the world— the worldly illusion consisting of the nature of the visible—
would be pacified in what manner, by what means?
In that manner, in that way;
this web of speech which is about to be spoken is being told by me.
Listen to that; bring it within the range of your hearing.
"By means of the practice of reflection," [it is said].
Now, one might ask: "What will be achieved for me by hearing that? To this he says:
"O Rāma, I shall tell you this narrative for the sake of attaining awakening."
If you hear that, O virtuous one, you are indeed liberated and wise.
(This is clear.
Fulfilling the promise made immediately prior, he proceeds with the detailed exposition promised at the beginning of the treatise.
Now I shall introduce this Section on Origination, which I am telling to you:
O Rāma, he who indeed originates becomes liberated by that very act.
The word "atha" (now/then) signifies immediate succession; it indicates that this follows immediately after the brief exposition.
For what purpose is the section on origination (*utpatti-prakaraṇa*) explained first?

To this he says: "He who indeed... The sense is that since we have set out to explain liberation, we must first explain the section on origination; otherwise, it would be improper to speak of liberation without a basis.

"In this matter, what do you say when this section on origination (*utpattiprakaraṇa*), which begins with the words 'He who indeed...', is being explained in detail? To this, he replies: "It is afflicted (*pīḍyate*) and delights (*ramati*). (MT_3,9.45)
"This world-illusion, though unborn and of the nature of space, appears in this manner"—
this is what is now being explained by me in this chapter on origination;
"this" refers to that which has the habit of manifesting before one's eyes.
The delusion of the world is the error that takes the form of the world;
thus, by this reasoning,
they are indeed unborn and unarisen.
Therefore, being of the nature of space (*khātmikā*), having the form of the sky (*ākāśasvarūpā*), it shines; that is to say, it manifests.
Thus [it is said].
I shall now speak on this section concerning origination.

(MT_3,9.46) Intending to explain the section on origination itself, and in accordance with the maxim of "driving in a post," he first describes the dissolution of the phenomenal world— which veils that [reality]— in order to reveal the pure consciousness alone, which is the fundamental cause of origination.
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving—
everything, rich in all its various forms, including gods, asuras, and kinnaras.
When that great dissolution arrives, which brings about the transformation of Rudra and the other deities,
it becomes non-existent and invisible; it goes somewhere or perishes—
its nature being inexpressible.
Rich in every aspect, endowed with all modes such as existence and non-existence;
during the great dissolution known as the fourth state (*turya*), and at the time of the end of the great aeon (*mahākalpa*);
transforming into Rudra and others, and characterized by the absorption (*laya*) of Rudra and the rest.
Here, Rudra is to be understood as the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), the Lord Mahādeva who holds authority over dissolution.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of Viṣṇu and others who hold authority over the creation and maintenance of the intellect (buddhi) and the rest. "Invisible" means beyond the range of the external senses.
Now, one might ask: "How does it become invisible? To this he says: "Somewhere.
It goes somewhere—that is, it attains oneness with that indefinable reality which is the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*).
That is to say, it manifests as something other;
for this very reason, it perishes, that is, it goes beyond the range of perception.
For the total destruction of that which is appearing is not logically tenable.
For it would follow that even the silver in the mother-of-pearl would be subject to total destruction;
yet the silver in the mother-of-pearl is not destroyed in every respect.
Rather, it manifests in the form of mother-of-pearl.
What remains when this manifest world is destroyed?
Is there anything remaining for those who hold authority over creation and maintenance? Indeed, what is left when this world that appears before us perishes?
For when the silver that appears in a mother-of-pearl shell is destroyed, the mother-of-pearl remains; regarding this, he says:
"Therefore, there is neither light nor pervasive darkness, but something still and profound."
Something remains that is inexpressible and unmanifest.
Thereafter, following the destruction of the visible, there remains something— namely, by implication, the very nature of the witness to the destruction of the visible— an indescribable reality.
That which remains is what is left over (*śiṣṭa*).
Otherwise, where would this entire world, appearing as it does, abide? For the destruction of that which is appearing is not logical, unlike the destruction of the intrinsic nature of a jar.
Because it consists merely in appearing in another form— just like the disappearance of silver in mother-of-pearl—
appearance in another form is not possible without predominance.
Of what nature is it? It is "stilled and profound.
"Stilled" means devoid of the vibration called directedness (*unmukhya*).

It is profound because it cannot be fathomed—both due to its nature of plunging into its own domain and because it lacks being an object for the act of plunging. And such is it, and such is it. Furthermore, of what nature is it?

The meaning is that light (*tejas*), by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*), is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) and other such worldly sentient beings. Likewise, darkness (*tamas*) is not distinct from insentient objects; this is the meaning.
Alternatively, by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness alone, it is distinct from light and darkness which are external to the nature of the object of cognition (*cetyasvarūpa*).
Thus it should be known. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is that which is woven throughout everything.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?

The meaning is that it is "inexpressible" (anākhyam) because, while existing as the agent of expression, it lacks the status of being an object of expression and thus cannot be expressed. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is "unmanifest" (anabhivyaktam), its true form not being revealed because it is beyond the range of both external and internal organs.
Furthermore, the connection of these qualifiers as a chain through the relationship of cause and effect has already been established previously; therefore, no further effort is made here.
Moreover,
(i) even preeminence (*prādhānyam*) is pervading everywhere; here, it is the vigor of all.
Because it abides as the agent of expression (*ākhyākartṛtvena*), the subject matter that was declared as remaining is further qualified in detail:
"It is neither empty nor space; it is neither the visible object nor the act of seeing."
Nor is there a flood of real entities that exists by way of infinity; that is,
whatever object exists as infinity, by way of being infinite.
It is not empty;
for if it were [empty], its status as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the world would be untenable.
Indeed, an empty thing is never observed to be the substratum of anything.
In that case, because the peacock-feather whisk and other such objects appearing therein are supported by the rays of the eye,
so too is that object which is not space.
Because, according to the stated principle, it is distinct from emptiness,
and because space consists solely of emptiness,
that which is visible does not exist.
Because its essential nature is that of the pure seer,
there is no perception of that which is a [mere] thing.
Because its establishment does not depend upon a seer or a seen object,
that which is the flood of real entities would indeed be insentient [if it were otherwise].
Indeed,
even from a peacock-feather whisk and the like,
there arises something whose nature is indefinable, yet which possesses a form more full than the full.
It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; it is neither a non-entity nor a becoming.
It is of an indefinable nature, its form being more perfectly full.
From that which is considered full, such as space and so forth,
there arises a reality whose form is even more full, possessing a more complete configuration.
It is something whose nature is indefinable, something whose essence is inexpressible;
likewise, it is that which does not exist as a being (*sat*). [...
[Is this an explanation of the preceding passage, with the *pratīka* "nāsat" lost due to haplography?]
Because it is impossible for it to be the substratum of the world;
likewise, that which is neither existent nor non-existent [cannot be so],
because both faults would follow.
Likewise, that which is not non-existence persists even as the absence of its opposite;
for pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), devoid of objects of thought, is infinite, undecaying, and auspicious.
That which is without beginning, middle, or end, which is beginningless and free from affliction— being such as this,
in response to the inquiry "What is that which is of such a nature?", he says "pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*) and so forth.
It is pure consciousness alone, whose very nature is consciousness;
therefore, it is devoid of any object of cognition (*cetya*), yet it is not stained by objects of cognition.
It is infinite, because it exists as the witness even of one's own mind.
For therein, because it illuminates space and time—which establish the distinctions of beginning, middle, and end—it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end;
because there is no mind from the outset, it is devoid of the afflictions (*ādhī*) that depend upon it;
and it is free from corruption, being devoid of the diseases consisting of the intrinsic natures of existence, non-existence, and so forth. (MT_3,9.52)
In whom the world vibrates like a swan amidst pearls of vision—
he who is both this and not this, the God whose nature is both being and non-being. (MU 3.9.53) [yaś] ya⟨c⟩[ś]
In which object the world vibrates— that is, manifests— by way of being the basis for empowerment.
How?
Like pearl-geese in the gaze.
Pearl-geese shimmering in the gaze are "pearl-geese in the gaze."
"Like those two" means in that same manner;

for, by the power of disease, the rays—which constitute the components of vision—flash in the sky in the form of pearls and in the form of swans. "Consisting of being and non-being" means having the nature of both being and non-being.
That is to say, "ineffable.
He is the God who is characterized by playfulness and whose nature is luminosity.
This collection of entities becomes objectified as "this," because it exists by way of its essential nature;
whereas that which is not "this" is a deity.
Because it exists with the ego-sense as its core.
[Because of the essencelessness of the ego:
He who, though without ears, tongue, nose, skin, or eyes, hears, tastes, smells, touches, and sees everywhere and at all times; [MU 3.9.54]

"Without nose, skin, or eyes" means being devoid of the sense-faculties of hearing and taste; likewise, "without nose, skin, or eyes" means being devoid of the sense-faculties of smell, touch, and sight.
He who, everywhere— that is, in all places—
and at all times— that is,
at all moments— hears, performs the act of hearing all sounds.
He relishes; he performs the act of relishing all tastes.
He smells;
he performs the act of smelling all odors.
It touches; it performs the act of touching all objects. It sees; it performs the act of seeing all forms.

Because it abides as the essence of all the sense-faculties and all clarity pertaining to all places and times, it possesses the state of being all subjects throughout all places and times who are seized by the conceit of being the agents of acts such as hearing.
Or because it remains [as such]; and for this [mind],
which exists as the essence of the faculties, dependence on other faculties is not logical, given that the faculties [themselves] exist [in dependence upon it].
Because it is illogical for that essence itself to require those [other factors] just as they do, independently of other sense faculties; furthermore,
even if those [factors] were postulated, they would result in having no nature at all without this being their essence.
But insofar as this [consciousness] is the essence, it exists even in the form of that very [object];
and even when it exists in the form of all subjects, there is no dependence on other sense organs.
For that very reason, due to being intoxicated by the senses, the other senses become useless.
[One whose tongue has no ears] (ā)a° performs [ā]° ...
[the activity of tasting all flavors] ā(r).
[he] touches the activity of tasting the eight flavors; having touched [them], ... svā° ... sam(e) astās[v]ā[dā]svāda⟨ś⟩[na]kri° spṛśati ] sp⟨a⟩[ṛ]śa°
The action of touching through the contact of all [senses]; by virtue of being the essence of all faculties and all clarity pertaining to all places and times;
that very [light] by which the nature of existence and non-existence is characterized.
The painting of creation, which is without beginning or end, is his own nature, and it is also devoid of coloring.
Being that very one whose nature is pure consciousness (cinmātra), he has attained the state of the seer;
he alone, and no other whatsoever.
By which light and by which essential nature— that is, by the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*)— the variegated picture of creation, the form of the world,
is perceived and seen.
Since it is impossible for a seer to perceive the world without the light of consciousness,
in what manner is this variegated creation?
It is of the nature of both being and non-being.
Consequently, it is indefinable as either existent or non-existent.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is without beginning or end; the meaning is that it is devoid of beginning and end because its essence is nothing but beginningless and endless pure consciousness.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is of the nature of solidity; the meaning is that, by virtue of being of the nature of mere appearance, it is of the nature of space, like a dream.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is "without passion" (*arañjana*), meaning that although it appears through the passions of existence and non-existence, it is ultimately liberated by virtue of its purity.
The word *api* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
The painting of creation; the painting;
the painting of creation.

He who perceives the world—[which, like the pupil in the center of the brows when the eyes are half-closed, appears as if colored by the notions of existence and non-existence]—as being always of the nature of space, as a mere appearance whose true form is the Self; [he is liberated]. (MU 3.9.56)
He who perceives— that is, brings within his own range— the essential nature called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as his own being, and the world as its perishable object-form.

Of what nature is the world? In ultimate reality, it is of the very nature of space; because it lacks the form of a world, it is indeed of the nature of nothing at all. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
"Appearing as existent" (*sadābhāsa*) means it appears as if it were existent;
the meaning is that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it is not existent.
How does one see this?
"Like the pupil in the middle of the brows of one whose eyes are half-open":
that by whom the eye is half-open is "one whose eyes are half-open."
The two eyebrows themselves are the location of the *bhūḥ* [syllable];
the middle of that is the "middle of the brow-ground" (*bhrūbhūmadhya*).
It is the star (pupil) shining in the middle of the brow-ground for one whose eyes are half-open.
In the same way;
just as a person with half-opened eyes perceives the very ray of his own vision in the middle of his eyebrows in the form of a star—
such is the meaning.
And the meaning is to be understood through dramatic gesture.
The intrinsic nature [of the state] of one whose eyes are half-open;
with eyes half-open.
For that Lord, there is no other cause, like the horn of a hare;
and this world is his effect, like a mass of waves from water.
The meaning is that for that Lord, there exists no [other] cause.
But how is it that this has no cause?
True;
its cause is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa) and of the nature of non-consciousness (acidrūpa).
Nor the latter, because it is impossible for that which is of the nature of non-consciousness (acid-rūpa) to be the cause of that which is of the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa).
As for the first case, how could that very same thing of the nature of consciousness be the cause of itself, which is also of the nature of consciousness?
Thus, by the phrase "of whom this [is the effect]," he declares that the entire world is its effect.
It should be understood that the world is an effect of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), like a dream-world.
[It arises] from that which blazes perpetually on all sides and resides within the cauldrons of the mind.
By the light of that lamp which is pure consciousness alone, the three worlds shine.
Regarding "that lamp which is pure consciousness alone":
its status as a lamp is to be understood through its quality of being illuminating.
By means of speech— that radiance of consciousness emerging through the doors of the senses—
the three worlds, manifesting in the three states as the threefold proliferation,
shines forth; it vibrates with light.
Of what nature [is he]?
"From everywhere" means in all places; "blazing" means capable of making everything manifest.
Furthermore, of what nature [is he]?
He is one who abides within the vessels of the mind— that is, within the forms of the mind— remaining there as their essential substance.
And it is appropriate for a lamp to remain within its receptacles;
likewise, although the mind indeed dissolves during deep sleep, it is said to be so because it remains there in the form of seeds.
Even externally, the three worlds known as Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ appear by the mind alone.

Without which even these luminaries such as the sun are like darkness; but when it exists, the three worlds proceed like a mirage. (MU 3.9.59) [emended from *indriyadvāranirgatayā* to *indriyadvāranirgatayāṃ*] (MT 3.9.58)

Without which [the eye] these visible objects— such as the sun and so forth— would remain as if devoid of the essence of the visual faculty; without it, they too would be like a cataract, resembling darkness.
They exist; for the sun and other luminaries, when not illuminated by the eye, are clearly just like darkness itself.
As for the word "satī" (being): it is just as mirages arise when the sun is present.

Likewise, the meaning is: in whose proximity the three worlds—whether vibrating, they seem to arise, or being motionless, they seem to have entered within him—in whom this splendor of the world exists like the circularity of a whirling firebrand. (MU 3.9.60)
When that [consciousness] vibrates— possessing the vibration known as the orientation toward the visible— the splendor of the world seems to arise;
when it is without vibration, it does not.
It is as if it enters within, and as if it enters into that;
yet in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it neither arises nor enters—this is why the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed.
In what is it as if? It is as if in a firebrand (*alāta*).
Just as when a whirling firebrand is spun rapidly,
the state of being a wheel— the form of a circle—
arises.
When there is no movement,
it becomes as if contained within a firebrand;
such is the meaning of "tathā" (thus).

The Great Pervasive One, whose nature is both vibration and non-vibration, is pure and inexhaustible; His essence consists of the play of the creation and dissolution of the world, joined with the vibration known as the orientation toward the visible. (MU 3.9.61)
The play of the creation and dissolution of the universe— the play of the emanation and withdrawal of the world—
whose nature is imperishable, meaning free from destruction,
and stainless, meaning untainted by the impurity of duality.
"Great" means endowed with greatness;
for this very reason, it is all-pervasive.
"Intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) means the essential form itself.
It exists, but not otherwise.
How so?
Whether the play of creation and dissolution is being perceived or not being perceived,

since this [play] is like something unreal, there is no need for concern regarding it; for, because it is an object of consciousness and is contained within consciousness, it is of the very nature of consciousness itself—
thus there is no contradiction.
Of what nature is it? It consists of both movement and non-movement; its essential character is that of movement and non-movement.
Among these, the play of emanation consists of movement.
The play of withdrawal consists of motionlessness.
Thus,
his existence— which consists of both movement and stillness and is all-pervading like the wind—
is differentiated only by name for the sake of conventional usage, but not in reality. (MU 3.9.62)
That whose existence consists of both vibration and non-vibration:
existence joined with the orientation toward the object of thought is "consisting of vibration," while that devoid of it is "consisting of non-vibration."
"By means of conventional usage"— that is, by means of the name itself which has been established for the sake of conventional usage—
as if they were distinct.
In what state are they?
All-pervading and universal, it has entered its own nature which transcends that [world];
of what is it like? It is like the wind.
The existence of the wind consists of vibration, by which trees and other things tremble;
[the existence] consisting of non-vibration is the very nature of space.
But how is this so?
The oneness of existence, which consists of both vibration and non-vibration,
is real; just as the oneness of water, whether in motion or still, is determined by those who are skillful, so it is here as well— thus there is no contradiction.
[āspandamayī] there [ta]dra°; [spandāspandamayyāḥ] °mayyā[ḥ];
[niḥspandasya] ni[ḥ]spa° (MT_3,9.62).
He who is always awakened, yet always asleep;
he who is neither deeply asleep nor awake, being everywhere and at all times—
in all states whatsoever, he is always thus.
The awakened one is indeed endowed with supreme knowledge because he abides as the witness;
yet he is also always as if asleep,
for he has entered a state of sleep due to being devoid of any reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that [awakened state].
He who, everywhere indeed— in all places,
at all times, and in every particular state—
does not fall asleep.
Because its nature is eternally that of awakening,
it does not become a Buddha;
for even when there is self- and other-apprehension, it remains turned away from them through equanimity.
"That which is motionless is Śiva, the peaceful; that which is movement is the existence of the three worlds.
He who is the single one of full form, whose nature is the play of both movement and stillness"—thus [it is said].
"That which is motionless" means the absence of orientation toward objects of thought (*cetya*).
It is peaceful, free from agitation;
it is auspicious, which is to say, blissful.
It comes to be.
That which is vibration and that which is the orientation toward objects of cognition—
this is the existence of the three worlds; it constitutes the state of the three worlds.

He who is the one whose nature consists of the play of vibration and non-vibration, whose essential form is both endowed with and devoid of the orientation toward the object of thought (cetya); how is he?
[Thus it continues: He exists.
How is he? [Thus it continues:]...
"Bharitākṛtiḥ" means one whose form (ākṛtiḥ), that is, whose essential nature (svarūpam), is full (bharitā) and consists of everything (sarvamayī).
Such is the nature of that One:
its simultaneous possession of vibrancy brings about manifold variety;
like fragrance in flowers, it does not perish even when those flowers perish.
Even though it is present before the eyes, it is ungraspable, like whiteness in white cloths.
That which does not perish even when perishable objects perish, because it persists in a subtle state as their material cause (*upādāna*).
For even when a jar has perished, its subtle essential nature as clay, which serves as its material cause, does not perish;
it is just like a fragrance.
The meaning is as follows: just as when a flower has perished, its fragrance continues to waft through the air for some time without vanishing; so it is here.
That which is "ungraspable" (agrāhya) means it cannot be apprehended by any external or internal sense faculty.

Of what nature is it? Even though it is situated in direct perception—that is, even while existing within direct perception—no one's own self is not directly perceived; for no one thinks, "I am not here."
What is it like?
It is like whiteness. Just as the quality of whiteness existing in a cloth, though perceptible, cannot be grasped by the hand; so it is.
The meaning.

One who is like a mute yet speaks, one who is like a stone yet thinks, one who is an enjoyer though eternally satisfied, and one who is an agent yet possesses nothing— such a person is to be grasped. (MU 3.9.66)
*Mantā*: He who is the speaker;
for he exists in the form of every speaker.
Of what nature is he?
Even though he is like one who is mute, his state of being like a mute is due to his freedom from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
He is the thinker and the knower.
For without that [consciousness], there could be no other so-called "thinker.
It is like a stone,
because, being of the nature of pure consciousness alone, it is devoid of the taint of thinking.
He who, though eternally satisfied— being always satisfied by himself alone due to his nature as supreme bliss—
is still an enjoyer;
for the state of being an enjoyer does not depart from one whose nature is that [of bliss].

He who, although being the creator of all creators by virtue of bestowing capacity upon them, has nonetheless attained the state of being a non-doer; here, one should know that he is the "something" (kiñcana) who is the true agent.
The meaning is that it is therefore not an agent. And its state of non-agency is to be understood precisely through its being nothing at all (nakiñcanatva),
because agency consists in having some specific form.
He who is the agent—[is he] the agent? There is nothing here; [there is] no agent from that.
He who, though bodiless, possesses all limbs and has a thousand hands and eyes;
he by whom this entire world is pervaded, even though he does not abide anywhere.
Though he is "bodiless" (*anaṅga*), meaning devoid of limbs because he consists of pure consciousness alone.
He possesses all his limbs.
Of what nature is he?
He has a thousand hands and eyes.
In this context, the word "thousand" signifies infinity;
therefore, the meaning is "one whose eyes perform infinite deeds.
This refers to the state of having eyes that perform infinite deeds.
And it should be known as being his own self-nature within his infinite bodies;
the word "thousandfold" serves as a qualification that indicates the reason.
Likewise, by which all this is pervaded.
Otherwise, the sense is: "Of what nature would this be?"—
by which [nature],
even though it has not been established, nor is it existing anywhere.
How so?
The meaning is: "not even in the slightest degree.
This is because its lack of established existence cannot be apprehended.
He whose sensory functions are entirely complete even though he is devoid of sense organs and power;
he for whom these modes of mental emanation exist even though he is without a mind. His sensory functions are all present.
Of what nature is he? Even though his sensory faculties have lost their power,
he possesses the function of all the senses because he is the very essence of the faculties.
For one whose mind is even "mindless" (*nirmanasa*)— meaning that even that which has the form of the mind exists as non-conceptual pure consciousness (*nirvikalpacinmātra*)—
the modes of mental emanation (*manonirmāṇarīti*) occur;
otherwise, from what source could these [appearances], manifesting in this or that form, arise?

Because it is the very essence of the senses, the terrors of the serpent of saṃsāra appear due to its non-perception; yet when it is seen, all these afflictions flee in every way and for all time. (MU 3.9.69)
Because of non-reflection— that is, due to the absence of correct knowledge regarding their objects—
the fears arising from the serpent called saṃsāra, which originate from that serpent,
appear and manifest.
Just as there is trembling due to the fear of a snake arising from the absence of correct knowledge regarding a rope— this is the intended meaning of the word "uraga" (snake)—
so too, it is solely through ignorance of the Supreme Self that this cycle of transmigration and the fears thereof appear within that Supreme Self.
When [the Self] has been seen— that is, experienced as its own true nature—
then "calamities" (ītayaḥ), meaning afflictions, exist in every way, that is, in all their various modes.
"At all times," that is, at every moment;

"they flee" means they go far away. The fleeing of calamities (*ītayaḥ*) is nothing other than the knowledge of the nature of the Supreme Self, which is the reversal of their appearance as calamities.
Because even those [appearances] are, from the perspective of ultimate reality, of that same nature.
When that witness—the expansive, stable manifestation—is present, like a lamp, all activities proceed within it;
for it is when that [Self] exists that the various desires, preceded by movement, come forth. (MU 3.9.70)
In the witness (sākṣin), which is the subject that perceives all states of stillness and movement;
in the expansive (sphāra), which is all-pervading;
in the manifestation (ābhāsa), whose sole essence is radiance.
When the *dhruva* (the stable) is indifferent— meaning,
when it remains merely present—
there arise various mental activities (*citrehāḥ*), that is, manifold operations of the mind.
Of what nature are they?
Bodily movements proceed preceded by vibration.
The meaning is that they are accompanied by that [consciousness].
The implication is that in the absence of some internal principle of consciousness (cittattva), the arising of conceptual constructions and bodily movements would not be possible.
Like what?
Like an action, that is, like a worldly activity;
just as a lamp provides mere presence, while worldly activities proceed by themselves.
The meaning is "so it is."
In all of them,
various mental activities (*manovyāpārāḥ*) proceed.
Because bodily movements are like hundreds of rows of objects in the form of pots and cloths,
just as the waves, droplets, surges, and billows are of the ocean. (MU 3.9.71)
From which [source] as their material cause (*upādāna*) arise the waves, droplets, surges, and ripples;
from which arise the hundreds of series of objects in the form of jars and cloths— that is, the collections of hundreds of entities whose nature consists of jars and cloths.
They exist;

for even though others have stated that only atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth possess the nature of a material cause (*upādāna*), nevertheless, because those [atoms] lack the nature of a material cause with respect to conscious beings, there must be some entity whose nature is both conscious and unconscious.
There is no dispute that appropriation (*upādāna*) is to be conceptualized;
what is it like?
It is like ripples, droplets, surges, and waves.
The meaning is: "in the same manner as they arise from the ocean."
That very same thing arises as something else through the delusions of hundreds of categories,
just as gold appears as bracelets, armlets, neck-ornaments, and anklets.

That very one called consciousness, while existing in its own unprecedented form, arises—that is, goes forth—as something else, by means of another nature; the meaning is that it assumes, as it were, the nature of another. By what means?
"By the delusions in the form of a hundred categories" means: delusions that take the form of a hundred categories; by those [delusions], which is to say, by the hundred categories.
And here, "hundredfold" refers to the ultimate infinity;
what is it like?
It is like gold.
Just as gold manifests itself in the form of bracelets,
armlets, neck-ornaments, and anklets—
such is the meaning.
You who are the self-luminous essence, I who am this, and these people here;
and that which is not you, O unawakened soul, nor I, nor these people, nor that [which is other].
O you who are not yet awakened in nature, who have not yet realized the reality of the Supreme Self,
who are of the nature of a single manifestation and whose very essence is pure knowledge—
you who exist as one fit to be instructed.
The meaning is that it appears as "you";
the meaning is that I, who am the teacher,
appear as "I."
And as for the phrase "these people exist" (yaś ca ya ete janāḥ asti), the meaning is that they appear as such;
this is because [the Self] abides as the essence in all things.
"Is it not then the case that this [Self] is indeed limited? To this he says, "And which...
The meaning is that, in reality, it exists as the nature of pure consciousness alone, free from conceptual constructions such as "you-ness" and so forth.
Not having the nature of an awakened one;
having the nature of appearing as a single [entity];
by way of that reality; it exists by way of that reality.
Because it is established, it is both distinct and non-distinct, both existent and non-existent, and yet fragile;
in that [reality], the world of appearances flashes forth like a series of waves upon the water. (MU 3.9.74)
"Bhaṅgurā" means having a perishable nature;
"dṛśyabhūḥ" refers to the realm of the visible,
which is the collection of entities that are the objects of the act of seeing.
That very [reality] is *bhūḥ*; it is the ground (*bhūmi*) because it is the support for various arrangements.
It is that in which [all things] manifest and shine forth as the foundational substratum.

The fact that the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*) serves as the substratum for the visible world is to be understood through the analogy of a dream. In what manner? As being non-different from it; that is, without having undergone any separation from it, just as one thing appears as if it were another.
The meaning is "appearing.
For that which is non-different, the appearance of otherness brings about variety,
even in the absence of actual difference.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a lack of identity between the universal and the individual—just as there is between them in other cases—he states "that very [consciousness]" to express their identity. That very [consciousness] is not even in the slightest degree of a nature other than that;
it does not appear as something other than itself.
Like a series of waves;
for even though a series of waves exists within water in that very form, its appearance as if it were not that form is established by universal experience.
The visible object is not distinct from the very nature of consciousness itself.

Because it is devoid of that nature; because from it comes the reckoning of time, from it the visibility of the visible, by it the mental construction, and by it the manifestation of lights. (MU 3.9.75)
Since the reckoning (*kalana*) or conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of time— which is devoid of adjuncts such as the present and so forth— occurs with respect to an object,
the sense is that the conceptualization of time is not tenable without an internal conceptualizer.
For the visibility of the visible occurs only when there is a seer;
indeed, without a seer, the visibility of the visible is not possible,
by means of which mental conceptualization arises.
For even the mind is not established without a witness (sākṣin),
by which there would be the manifestation— that is, the flashing forth— of cognitions such as those of jars and other objects.
It exists; for cognitions do not arise without a knower.
Even without vibration, the mind is accomplished.
Whatever you perceive—action, form, taste, smell, touch, sound, and consciousness—that is the God; and that by which you perceive, that too is He. (MU 3.9.76)
By the phrase "even by that [means] having obtained that action," the word "you do" (*karoṣi*) should be connected in place of the word "you know" (*vetsi*).
Therefore, this is the meaning:
you perform an action.
That is the instrument;
moreover, he is the aforementioned god who performs play.
It exists;
that by which you act through the faculty of action is the faculty of action.
That deity also exists;
likewise, whatever form, taste, smell, touch, or sound you perceive—that perception is that deity. It exists.
That which you perceive by means of the five faculties of the intellect— that too is that deity; likewise, the consciousness consisting of volition and so forth—
whatever you perceive, that is that deity.
By whichever internal organ you perceive,
that too becomes that very deity;
by this, the identity of the fruit of the action and its instrument is stated.
But that [agency] of the agent is indeed established beyond dispute.
Having thus stated its essential nature by means of its qualifiers, he speaks of the means for entering it:
"having spoken," [meaning] having stated its nature.

O virtuous one, worthy of awakening to the Supreme Self, among the seer, the seeing, and the seen, that which exists as the act of seeing— you shall realize your own self through focused attention upon it. (MU 3.9.77)
By means of that attentiveness— that is, by bestowing attention upon that—
you perceive, that is, you know, your own self, which is the Supreme Self constituting your true nature.
In that regard, where?
Among the triad of the seer, the seeing, and the seen.
Whatever view remains established— this is the conclusion here:
all conventional discourse is accomplished only within the threefold structure.
In that context, the seer is the agent;
seeing is the action;
and the visible object, serving as the focal point, is the object of action.
That toward which an action arises is the object;
however, the instrument, being the nature of the uncommon cause, is not distinct from these [other factors].
Because the causal efficiency belongs to the totality alone,
there arises in the seer— who is seized by the conceit "I am the seer"— a vision whose object is the visible, which has the single form of the graspable.
Otherwise, the relationship of seer and seen between those two would be impossible.
Because the seer is seized by the conceit of "I," it cannot be purified instantaneously;
however, the seen, due to its utter insentience, [can be].
Therefore, since its security and vulnerability are identical to those [of the cognition], one should set those two aside and apply attention solely to the perception (*darśana*).
But is it not the case that perception, too,
is corrupted by defects in its basis (*āśraya*) and its object (*viṣaya*)?
It is true that it cannot be purified while remaining in the seer.
The removal of egoity, which resides in the object of perception, and of insentience is indeed impossible;
however, for a vision that is tainted by even a slight touch of both, it is quite possible to remove the two defects existing as constituent parts through partial means.
In this regard, the method is as follows:
my form is not perceived,
because it is clearly distinct from me.

Furthermore, because it lacks the nature of a seer, it does not possess the form of the seen, which is distinct from me; because it possesses the nature of a grasper, nothing other than those two can be grasped. Therefore, it is impossible to apprehend anything that is distinct from them.
Since there exists an ineffable vision, it is established that vision is the nature of the Supreme Self; consequently,
the identity of the seer and the seen is all the more firmly established,
for the existence of the seer and the seen is not possible once the connection with vision has dissolved.
Because the seer possesses the status of a seer precisely by being the locus of seeing,
and because the seen possesses the status of the seen by being its object;
or alternatively, "seeing" here should be understood as the state of desiring to see.
For at that time, it manifests as pure indeed, due to the absence of any coloring by a substrate or an object; but subsequently, it attains grossness.
[The supreme self (paramātman)] because of the absence of being a seer;
[of the seer and the seen] because of being a seer.
[Regarding the seer and the seen: because of being the seer (*draṣṭṛtva*) [and] because of being the seen (*dṛśyatva*). (77) (MT_3,9.77)
He summarizes what was previously stated with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"The unborn, undecaying, non-inert, eternal, constant Brahman—auspicious, stainless, beginningless, and beyond reproach because its objects of knowledge are barren; devoid of all mental constructions, the cause of causes, experience itself, unknowable, yet the very act of knowing—the state of consciousness within. (MU 3.9.78)
"Having known" means "he knows," up to the point where it becomes the end;
that is, it becomes the final limit of the entire range of all that is visible.
That is to say, it remains at the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). Of what nature is it? It is unborn (aja), because it exists at all times.
It is undecaying because it is distinct from the body;
it is non-inert because it is distinct from the mind;
it is eternal because, although it is the self of the universe, it does not deviate from its own essential nature.
Brahman, because it expands in the form of the universe;
eternal, because it does not perish throughout the three periods of time; auspicious, because its sole nature is bliss.
It is stainless (*amalam*) because it is devoid of the impurity of differentiation (*bhedamālinya*). It is beginningless (*anādyam*) because nothing exists as its beginning.
By "those with barren objects of knowledge" (*vandhyavedyaiḥ*), [it is meant] those for whom objects of knowledge are futile.
It is irreproachable and unafflicted,
because it is not corrupted by the existence or non-existence of those [phenomena] residing within it;
it is devoid of all conceptualization, because its essential nature is free from discursive thought.
It is the cause of those causes— namely Brahmā and the others—
who are considered to be causes; for even they possess form and are therefore themselves caused.
Experience is the very nature of experiencing;
for experience alone is possible for the previously mentioned specific qualities.
Even though its nature is that of experience, fearing that it might be sullied by the object of knowledge, he says "unknowable" (avedya).
It is unknowable, untainted by contact with the knowable, and pure consciousness; that is to say, it is of the nature of non-objective consciousness. Thus all is auspicious.
"Knowing the state of being known" means that for one who is born, it constitutes the final form; [it is] "that which remains at the great dissolution"—this is the extent of the meaning.
By those [who abide] in that state, it is devoid of all mental construction (*kalpanā*).
[Regarding] "in its nature as experience" (*anubhavasvarūpatve*),
thus ends the ninth canto in the chapter on Origination within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! Here, as if having fallen into delusion, Śrī Rāma asks: "Regarding that which remains when the great dissolution has occurred—let it be called 'formless'; of this there is no doubt. (MU 3.10.1)
Regarding this, there is no doubt;
this is the matter.
"Formless" means devoid of form;
the sense is: "Let it be so; I too have confidence in this matter."
What is this?
It is that which is the existent reality when all things have perished at the occurrence of the great dissolution.
"It remains" means it persists as something remaining.
He explains that it is not tenable to deny its nature as a real entity—such as emptiness—which is devoid of any externally perceived form:
"How could it not be empty? How could it not be luminous? (MT 3.10.1)
Or how could it not have the nature of darkness, or how could it not consist of space?
How then would that not be empty?
The meaning is: let that very thing be so.
This should be applied everywhere in the same way.
"Luminosity" (*prakāśa*) refers to the luminosity of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). "Consisting of space" (*khātmaka*) means having the nature of space (*ākāśa*).

Or how could it not be of the nature of consciousness? Or how could it not be the individual soul (*jīva*)? How could it not be the principle of intellect (*buddhi*), or how could it not be the mind (*manas*)?
This was stated because even the nature of being consciousness is there negated from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Or how could it be that nothing exists, or how could everything exist?
By this turn of phrase, a kind of delusion has arisen in me:
"Nothing exists" does not mean that anything exists in any form whatsoever.
Because even "nothingness" is refuted,
how could it not also be "everything"? To this,
the venerable Vasiṣṭha gave the following reply:
"This question posed by you is extremely difficult;
yet I shall split it apart without effort, just as the sun dispels the darkness of night.
Here, the word *ati* is displaced in its syntactical order.
This question posed by you is extremely difficult and most hard to understand;
however, it has been specifically set forth.
"I shall split this with ease and without effort. Because the question takes the form of a mental knot, he says, "I split it."
Who is like the sun? Like the sun,
which is full of rays (aṃśumān), just as it destroys the darkness belonging to the night (naiśaṃ tamaḥ).
The meaning is "so it is.
He resolves the very question:
that which remains as the existent (*sat*) at the perfection of the end of a great eon (*mahākalpa*).
Therefore, O Rāma, listen as this is being told: how it is not empty.

This is well-known—whether at the occurrence of the end of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*), in the fourth state (*turya*) or that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*), or at the completion of the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)—and it cannot be denied by anyone.
O Rāma! That which is denoted by the word "That" (tat) is the existent reality;
"yathā" means in whatever manner.
It is not empty;
it is that very same mode,
which is being explained immediately hereafter.
Listen,
for that which is being told by me is precisely what is being explained.

Just as a carved figure remains on a pillar even though it has not been carved out [separately], so does the universe abide therein; therefore, that state is not empty. (MU 3.10.7) [anutkīrṇā] → *anutkīrṇā*
It has not been carved out by a woodcarver, nor has it been revealed by being hewn;
its state of remaining within the pillar is due to its manifestation at the forefront of the world’s true nature.
Its state of being established is due to its manifesting even this very day;
such is the distinction.
That "pada" is the station known as the Supreme Self (paramātman).
If that [consciousness] were empty, then where would the world exist? The point is that an error without a substratum is untenable.
It is said to be "uncarved" because it appears precisely as differentiated.
Having been carved out,
may there be stability;
may it become abundant.
He explains this in detail as follows:
"This world, known as the universe, appears thus with its great abundance;
whether it be real or unreal, where in that could there be emptiness? (MU 3.10.8)
Wherever this expansion is being experienced,
let it be real; let that which is called "existence" (bhāva) be of the nature of the existent.
He whose name is "the World," who possesses great enjoyment and great expansion— may he be real; may he be of the nature of reality.
Whether it be unreal or of an unreal nature,
that [cognition] appears— that is, it manifests— in whatever object serves as its substratum.
In that case, where is emptiness?
The sense is that it is not tenable.
The one whose nature is existence is called Bhava; his nature is that of the Real.

Just as a pillar that has not been carved with a female figure is not empty of such a figure, so too, my dear, the world is Brahman; therefore, that state is not empty of it. (MU 3.10.9) "Anutkīrṇasālikaḥ" means one in which no female figure has been carved.
He applies this to the case under discussion with the word "so too" (*tathā*).
O father, O venerable one!
By the word "so too," the two words "not" (*na*) and "empty" (*śūnya*) found in the preceding sentence are drawn in.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
likewise, Brahman does not become empty of the world. He states the conclusion with the words "therefore."
In the case of the illustration:
likewise, O gentle one, Brahmā is like a wave in the water; it neither exists nor does it not exist.
In this same way, this world has entered into Brahman, having reached the state that is both void and non-void,
just as [the reflection] enters into the water of the moon when the water is free from agitation.
And it does not exist,
because at that time it is unobtainable;
yet it is not non-existent.
Because it will become manifest later on,
he states the application to the example with the word "likewise" (*tathā*):
because it is appearing, it has reached the state of being non-empty.
Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it has no form whatsoever, it should be understood that it has reached the state of emptiness (*śūnyapada*).
[Objection: "In that case, does not the existence of the world in Brahman become established through its similarity to a puppet (*putrikā*) and so forth? To this, he says:
"Because space, time, and so forth are stilled, the fashioning of a puppet occurs within a tree. (MT_3,10.10)
But in the non-sentient realm, by what means is one not deluded within?
(In the phrase "within the tree," *drume*, it refers by indication to a pillar.)
The fashioning of a daughter occurs according to the influence of place, time, and the agent and so forth; however,
this is specifically regarding the primary cause called Consciousness (cit), which, within the non-born element (aja-dhātu), is devoid of any new manifestation.
Within the mind;
by what person?
By one who is not deluded—that is, one who does not become possessed by delusion.
Rather, the meaning is "by everything indeed.
Why is one deluded?
Because space, time, and so forth are quiescent.
By the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of the agent and so forth is intended;
the meaning is "due to the cessation of place, time, agent, and so on.
Furthermore, this cessation should be understood here as being nothing other than pure consciousness alone (śuddhacinmātratā).
And delusion (moha) should be understood as being of the nature: "How does the world appear within Brahman, which is devoid of contact with space, time, and so forth?"
By virtue of the agent and so forth: *kartrādi* [is the reading];
of the agent and so forth: *kartrādīnām*;
because of the quiescence of place, time, agent, and so forth: *deśakālakartrādiśānteḥ*.
He states the conclusion:
"That [world] consisting of pillars, statues, and so forth, is a simile that resembles the ultimate state of the world only in part, not in every respect. (MU 3.10.12)
For it is appropriate to fashion a figurine within a pillar by means of the occurrence of place, time, and so forth;
however, that is not appropriate within the element of consciousness (ciddhātu), which is characterized by peace.
Therefore, for that reason,
immediately after this was stated, [the examples of] a pillar, a statue, and so forth were given;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), waves and water are included.
In the ultimate sense, regarding the state of the world,
a similar illustration exists merely by way of excluding emptiness with respect to one part of it.
"Not at all" means not in every way; the meaning is that it does not exist.
Having refuted its emptiness by virtue of being the support of the world, he now refutes it by demonstrating its true nature: "This [world] never arises from another, nor does it ever cease."
This form is merely the existent Brahman abiding within its own self, [derived] from the supreme Self. Now, one might ask: "If the world neither arises nor ceases, then what is this that appears?"
Regarding this, it is said:
"This" refers to that which is solely non-dual,
the existent, whose very nature is existence.
Brahman is the expanded reality;
it remains established within its own self, that is, within its own essential nature.
Of what nature is this form?
This world, accompanied by both peace and arising;
"form" (rūpa) means one's own essential nature (svarūpa).
Of which; that;
such.

The state of Brahmanhood of the world, together with its quiescence and emergence, is to be understood as being the object of the expansion that has Brahman as its locus; for the object of such expansion is indeed the very nature of Brahman. And thus, the emptiness of Brahman [is established].
The sense is that this is not tenable.
He states the refutation of emptiness on the grounds that non-emptiness is impossible:
"The conceptualization of the meaning of the word 'empty' is dependent upon [the existence of] the non-empty."
Since non-emptiness is impossible, how could there be emptiness and non-emptiness?
The meaning is: "in dependence upon that" refers to the dependence of non-emptiness—which is a certain positive form—upon non-emptiness;
[it is] the conceptual construction of emptiness.
The conceptualization— that is, the imagining— of emptiness, which is the state of being nothing whatsoever,
occurs.
To the question "What follows from that?", he replies here with the words "because of non-emptiness.
This means because of the impossibility of non-emptiness, due to the impossibility of having any form whatsoever according to the reasoning already stated.
Emptiness and non-emptiness, nothingness and non-nothingness—
from where [do they arise]? The meaning is that they do not exist.
The sense is that when one of two dependent things perishes, both perish.
Furthermore, the absence of any specific form should be understood as pure consciousness alone, which is without support (*nirālamba*).
Emptiness and non-emptiness,
nothingness and non-nothingness;
having excluded emptiness, it excludes the nature of luminosity.
Indeed, this light, which is perceived by the eye, cannot arise from the elements within Brahman;
for how could there be the sun, fire, moon, stars, and so forth in that imperishable [Brahman]?
(MU 3.10.15) This [light] is what is seen with the eye.
"Born from the elements" means produced from the elements such as fire and so forth;
"illumination" means light;
"hi" (indeed) indicates certainty.
It is not possible within Brahman, the all-pervading reality,
because [the self], being pure consciousness, transcends it.
Regarding this, he states the latter half as the reason, beginning with "sūrya-".
The word *kila* serves to indicate the nature of the reason.
*Avyaye* means "in that which is devoid of destruction."

The meaning is that since the sun and other such things are subject to destruction by virtue of having a physical form, their persistence here is not logical; what, then, can be said regarding their possessing that very nature [of being formless]?
It refutes the state of being of the nature of darkness (*tamas*).
The absence of the luminous great elements (*mahābhūta*) is called darkness.
"But because it is not produced from the primary elements (mahābhūta), there is no darkness here [in consciousness] at all.
The sense is that proponents have established that darkness is merely the absence of light. He states the conclusion with the words "mahābhūta... and so forth.
But in the specific sense [of "produced"],
it is produced from the absence of the great elements (mahābhūta) by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇayā), because of the absence of the manifestation of the great elements;
that is to say, it is of that nature.
"Darkness" here refers to that which exists as a real entity; by that reason, namely, because it is an absence of the illumination of the great elements.
It does not exist.
Where? In any part whatsoever, in the locus where the great elements abide.
Since an absence that is the counter-correlate of the great elements is impossible, darkness also is not tenable here;
what then to say of its color? This is the intended meaning.
[Because of the absence of the manifestation of the great elements: *apra* [for *aprakāśa*].
[In the phrase "the abiding-place of the great elements": *ayata* [for *āyatana*]. (MT_3,10.16) Now, one might ask: "In the absence of fire (*tejas*), how can that manifest? To this, he says:
The manifestation of its own experience belongs solely to this reality whose form is space;
that which exists within it is experienced by that alone, and not by anything else.
Of this existent reality, whose form is space and whose nature is nothingness—
Self-experience (*svānubhūti*) is that experience which constitutes one's own essential nature;
it is *anubhava*. That very self-experience is the light (*prakāśa*), the radiance that effects manifestation.
The meaning is that this [light] shines by its own direct experience alone, and not through external light.
To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says here: "That which is within."
Whatever exists within [the self],
it is experienced by that very person through that same [self] acting as the instrument;
it is brought into the sphere of one's own direct cognition.
But not by another,
because it is impossible for another to enter therein;
this experience itself is the experiencer, the experiencing, and the object of the experience.
And thus, the meaning is that there is no dependence on anything whatsoever in that regard.
[The word] *anyasya* [is corrected to] *anya*; it connects with the subject under discussion:
"that which is liberated from darkness and light" is this undecaying state (*ajara-pada*).
"Know this very one to be the sheath of space, the sheath of the world's existence"—
in this manner,
that which is being described as the remainder is stated.
"Ageless" means free from the defect of old age;
"the state" (pada) means a place; "by darkness and light" means by means of both darkness and light.
It is liberated.
He begins to refute its nature as space with the words "ākāśa" (space).
You [are] this Supreme Self;
indeed the sheath of space, that is, the very midst of space;
the sheath, the treasury, of the world's existence.
Know; understand.
[The text] confirms this very point by means of an illustration: it confirms it.
*dṛḍhayati* [is corrected from] *d⟨ra⟩[ṛ]ḍha*.

Just as there is no difference whatsoever in the case of the *bilva* tree and that which is called the *bilva* fruit, so too here there is not even the slightest distinctness between Brahman and the world.
(MU 3.10.19) [The word] *bilvasya* refers to the *bilva* fruit.

Of the object that is the basis for the application of the name "bilva"— that is, the entity which is the cause for the occurrence of the designation "bilva"— in whatever manner, by whichever means, some [person]...
There is no difference;
likewise, in that manner, here in these three worlds,
there is not even the slightest distinctness between Brahman and the world.
The sense is that Brahman is indeed the world,
and the world is indeed Brahman;
the reading may also be "of the wood-apple" (bilvasya) or "of the interior of the wood-apple" (bilvamadhyasya).
"In this [world], in this Brahma-world" (*ehāsmiṃl... brahmajagatoḥ*).
One might ask: "Even so, what is relevant to the present context? To this, he says:

Just as a wave exists within water, and just as a jar exists within clay, so too the existence of the world resides therein; how then could that [reality] be of the nature of empty space? (MU 3.10.20) "In water" means in the liquid.
"In such a way" means in that manner, so that there is no interval (*vīci*).
"In which" means in whichever [thing] that has become the basis of appropriation (*upādāna*).
The existence of the world is that entity;
it is of the nature of space, having the character of the ether.
How could it be so?
To prevent [the misconception] that [consciousness] is of the nature of consciousness alone, he begins the systematic exposition:
"The beauty of the analogies such as clay and water is not equal here [to consciousness], for that [analogy] possesses form."
Brahman is as pure as space, and that which resides within it is likewise so;
this is the beauty of the analogies such as clay and water regarding this subject of Brahman.
It is equal, that is, appropriate;
it does not [occur].
To the question "Why?", he says:
"Having an aspect" (*sākāra*) means that it possesses an aspect (*ākāra*).
To the question, "In what sense is earth, water, and so forth fit to be compared by virtue of having an aspect? he says here:
"Brahman" [is used]; "tu" (but) indicates a distinction;
it becomes formless, as clear as the space of Brahman.
The sense is that it is not appropriate for formless Brahman to have the status of an analogy with respect to clay and the like, which possess form. He states the conclusion:
"Of that," etc.
Therefore, for that reason,
the world situated within— that is, existing inside— that [reality] likewise becomes formless; this is the meaning.
*tuḥ*] Only here. *sthitaṃ*] *°anta(vya)re *sthi*(jñe)taṃ* (it should be understood as ending in *vya* and situated there).
[The world:
Again, under the guise of a summary, he establishes the formlessness of the world:
"Therefore, such is the space of consciousness that it is even purer than [physical] space."
That which resides within it is likewise the very same as that which constitutes the meaning of the word "world.
The purity of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), even more so than that of physical space, is to be understood from its lack of insentience (*jaḍatva*).
Within that [space] resides the world.
It remains exactly as it was, indeed formless;
and of what nature is it?
It is that which possesses the portion of the meaning of the word "world."
This is an indication where the abstract state (bhāva) is predominant;
