therefore, the meaning is that it also possesses the status of being the referent of the word "world" (jagat), by virtue of appearing in the form of the world.
Just as the pungency within a peppercorn is not perceived in empty space apart from an eater,
so too the state of pure consciousness in the supreme ether is not perceived without the element of the object of thought.
Just as the pungency and bitterness residing within a peppercorn, amidst other peppercorns,
is neither perceived nor seen by anyone except the eater; so it is here.
The meaning is that when there is an enjoyer, [consciousness] is characterized by that very [enjoyer].
Likewise, in the supreme space, which is the Supreme Self,
resides pure consciousness alone (cinmātratva).
Without the object of thought (*cetya-kalā*) and the portion of the object of thought,
it is not perceived;
for it is precisely through the relishing of the object of thought that the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is known as pure consciousness.
He states the conclusion:

"Therefore, even though consciousness is by nature non-conscious, because it is not distinct from itself, this world-existence is exactly like that, by virtue of being essentially nothing but that. (MU 3.10.24)
"From that" means for that reason;
"in the Self," which is one's own essential nature called pure consciousness (cinmātra), by virtue of being devoid of objects of thought— that is, through the absence of anything to be thought.
Even consciousness (cit) becomes non-consciousness (acid),
because, according to the previous reasoning, there is the capacity to firmly establish the object of cognition (cetya) as pure consciousness (cinmātra), and because that [object] is absent here.
Its absence here is to be understood as being Brahman itself, by virtue of its existing within Brahman.
He extends the lack of mind even to the world that is non-different from Brahman,
[saying] "the state of being the world";
this too is the state of being the world.
In that very way, by virtue of being non-different from Brahman whose nature is consciousness, it becomes of the very nature of the insentient;
as the reason for this, he provides the qualification:
"by the power of having such a nature alone."
For [the world] is dependent (*vaśā*) upon that very nature— that is, upon the essential nature of Brahman alone which is insentient;
the meaning is that it has the essential nature of insentient Brahman.
By this, the absolute non-difference between Brahman and the world is also established;
nor does it follow that Brahman is merely insentient in nature,
since that [point] will be proven later as well.
[Due to the capacity for strengthening the state of pure consciousness alone] ... [the state of being nothing but the nature of non-consciousness]. [The state of being nothing but that] (MT_3,10.24).
Now, if the world is entirely non-different [from consciousness], what is the nature of form, light, and mental attention? To this, he says:
Form, light, and mental attention consist of that very [reality] and nothing else;
therefore, the universe as it truly exists is either deep sleep or the fourth state (turya).
Form, light, and mental attention.
Form (rūpa) refers to blue, yellow, and so forth.
Light (āloka) is the vision thereof, or the illumination that serves as the instrument.
Mental attention (manaskāra) is mental apprehension.
These [cognitions] have that as their object and are composed of that alone.
He states the meaning of the word "alone" by saying "not anything else.
And their being composed of that [object] is because, without having that as their object, they would be as good as non-existent.
He states the conclusion with the word "yathā" (just as);
for this reason,
the entire world (*viśvam jagat*).
Existing in this very manner, as it truly is,
and not having been rendered invisible by any power whatsoever,
it becomes deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
Anticipating the objection that there might be a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of duality even in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he says "the fourth" (*turya*).
The meaning is that it becomes one with the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which is the very nature of the fourth state.
He further describes the state of being permeated by Brahman (*brahmamayatā*) even during the yogi’s worldly activity, by virtue of the world having the nature of Brahman as the fourth state.
For that reason, the yogi—though engaged in worldly affairs—is one whose self is as if in deep sleep and whose intellect is tranquil;
he abides in Brahman, which is without appearance and the source-container of all appearances.
(MU 3.10.26) "For that reason" refers to the cause previously stated.
The yogi, concentrated on the unity of the world and Brahman,
remains as Brahman, which is the very nature of Brahman.
How much less could such a person remain [disturbed]?
For even while engaged in worldly affairs, though performing conventional activities,
his intellect is tranquil, being free from agitation.
How can such a state even exist?
Because the self in deep sleep has its internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) dormant with respect to the phenomenal world;
for it is logical that one whose mind is dormant with respect to the phenomenal world possesses a tranquil intellect.
Thus. Of what nature is that Brahman?
It is "without appearance" (nirābhāsa), meaning it has emerged from various appearances;
the sense is that it transcends them.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is the casket— the source of emergence— for all manifestations, that is, for all cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth.
[Regarding] "all sounds" (*sarvabhāṣāṃ*),
he once again explains the very non-difference between Brahman and the world that is under discussion: "Just as the process of fluidity resides within calm water that possesses form."
Likewise, the universe remains in that formless [state], similar to it, within the Supreme; [the Supreme] which is formless,
yet possesses a nature graspable by the external senses,
and which is serene and free from agitation.
In water,
the process of flowing is the sequence of specific qualities that constitute the non-inherent cause of the initial vibration;
it occurs just as it exists [in its natural state].
Likewise, the universe exists within the Supreme Brahman, which is formless;
in what manner does it exist?
The meaning is that it is similar to that, yet without form (*anākṛti*).
Just as in gentle water, the quality called fluidity—which, though capable of being something distinct because it is about to become manifest—is composed of that [water];
so too the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), though capable of being distinct because it appears as such, is composed of Brahman.
Such is the intended meaning.
Having stated non-difference as "the universe" (*viśvam*) and "whatever" (*kiñcit*), he speaks of reality (*tattva*) itself as "worthiness" (*arhaḥ*) and "consciousness-ness" (*cinmātratva*).
From the Full, the Full flows forth; from the formless, the formless.

The universe has appeared from Brahman, yet that universe is devoid of any objective reality. *Note: The manuscript reading *pūrṇāt* is corrected to *pūrṇāt* (Full) as per the context and the critical apparatus.*
Formless [is that which arises] from the full Brahman;
the world is of a full nature.
It spreads forth and shines;
and here, "spreading forth" refers to its application toward a disciple whose intellect is overcome by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
[It proceeds] from the formless Brahman.
The world is formless;
it expands.
Therefore, that which is the universe appearing from Brahman has come into manifestation.
That [space] becomes devoid of all objects—that is, devoid of all objects such as jars, cloths, and so forth;
the meaning is that it becomes one with Brahman alone.
That which is devoid of a mind overcome by conceptual proliferation is abandoned [of existence];
from the Full, the Full flows forth, yet that remains established as the Full alone.
Therefore, the universe is unproduced; and that which appears produced is indeed that very same [Brahman]. From the full Brahman comes the world, which is itself of a full nature.
It spreads and shines forth;
its expansion becomes established,
yet by that expansion no fragmentation whatsoever arises for it— this is the meaning.
The result is stated as follows:
"Therefore," meaning for the reason previously mentioned,
"the universe is unarisen."
Because he is always established in the state of Brahman; and with regard to one who cannot tolerate the non-arising of the universe, he says "And that which... and so forth.
And whatever has arisen,
that very thing becomes Brahman alone.
The meaning is that even for that which has arisen, there is no contradiction with its being Brahman.
[The refutation:
By this much of the analysis, it has been established that Brahman is insentient in nature;
thus, since [sentience] is impossible in that state, how could there be any sense of "something" (cit-arthatā) in that term?
"Since there can be no experiencer [of it], what is the sharpness of black pepper?"—
the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be supplied; that is,
for this reason.
Because of the impossibility of the object of consciousness;
that is, because of the impossibility of the world, which is the object of consciousness (cit).
In that state, which is the very nature of Brahman,
what possibility is there for the existence of any objectivity— that is, for the word "consciousness" (cit) to have a basis for its application?
It does not exist.
The meaning is "nothing at all.
For it is only by not making anything an object of consciousness that it is appropriate to call consciousness "consciousness" (cit).
But in the absence of an object of cognition, that [cognition] is not tenable;
and the absence of an object of cognition has already been established in detail.

And here, the negation of its being for the sake of consciousness should be understood as being due to its transcendence of that [consciousness], not due to its insentience. To provide a supporting illustration for this, he says "āsvādakā" (the taster);
the meaning is "like what? Like nothing at all."

The meaning is: "due to the impossibility of a taster" means "by virtue of the impossibility of a taster. Furthermore, he explains this very point: "Whether this [world] exists or does not exist, it has arisen from the mind for the sake of another mind. (MT_3,10.30)
Since the reflection does not exist [as a separate entity], how can there be the capacity for reflection?
The "capacity for reflection" refers to the consciousness (*citi*), which is the state of being consciousness belonging to the mind (*citta*). It is the nature of consciousness itself.
In the Supreme Self;
though non-existent— having a non-existent nature from the perspective of ultimate reality— it appears as existent,
like something truly real.
Regarding this, he states an example: "Because of the absence [of it]," with the word "of the mirror" being understood as the ellipsis.
Just as the mirror's capacity to receive a reflection is known only by means of the reflection itself.
But in its absence, that [cognition] is not known. Likewise, another's mind is known only by means of an object of cognition; the point is: in the absence of such an object, how could it be known?

In order to exclude [the notion of] having the nature of a living soul (*jīva*) and so forth, even while it exists, he qualifies the reality of the Supreme Self: "That is subtler than the subtlest, even beyond the atom. (MT_3,10.31)
It is pure, subtle, supreme, and more tranquil even than the interior of space;
that is Brahman. It is subtler than even an atom, exceedingly minute.
From what kind [of cause] as well?
Even from that which is more minute (*aṇīyas*), that is, even from that which is subtler than a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth;
and its subtlety consists in its being ungraspable by the external sense faculties.
That which is to be known is Brahman. Of what nature is it? Pure, being undefiled by the dust of passion and the like.
Subtle,
supremely transcendent,
peaceful, and empty of all mental activity.
From whatever [source],
even from the interior of space;
because its nature is unconditioned by direction, time, and so forth, it is exceedingly vast.
That manifestation is without beginning or end and is devoid of anything to be manifested;
that Brahman becomes exceedingly vast, extremely expansive.
Why? Because—
Because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of "substance" (vastu) is intended, meaning that it is devoid of the three kinds of delimitation.
Now, how is this [so]?
If it is argued that [space] is the state of being devoid of delimitation by directions and so forth,
yet remains extremely vast even in that state, we reply:
Is direction, first of all, something cognized or not?
If it is not so, then being itself unestablished, how could it determine another?
If it is being cognized, then it is determined by consciousness alone; how then could it determine that [consciousness]?
The same should be understood for time and the other factors as well.
It is only when delimited by directions and so forth that it becomes limited; in the absence of those, however, it is exceedingly vast— thus its state of being non-exceedingly-vast is established.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?

It is without beginning or end (*anādyanta*), for even when a beginning and an end are conceptually constructed in such a manner, it remains devoid of beginning and end because it is the witness (*sākṣitva*) to them.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
The meaning is that its nature is knowledge devoid of what is to be manifested, being free from both appearances and objects of cognition.
Its extreme extensiveness; [the word] *ativistṛ* should be read as *ati[vi]stṛ*;
of the two being conceptualized; [the word] *māna* should be read as *māṇa*;
the nature of gnosis devoid of appearing objects of knowledge; [the word] *saṃjñe* should be read as *saṃjñe*. (MT_3,10.33)
By relying on the aforementioned qualifications, he negates its nature as a living being (jīva) and so forth:
"Wherein only the form of consciousness (cidrūpa) is found, there how could there be the state of a living being?
How could there be the form of mental impressions (vāsanā), which are like the wind? (MU 3.10.34).
In that Brahman which is thus distinguished by such qualities,
the very nature of consciousness— this being an expression emphasizing the state (*bhāva*) rather than the substance—
is not obtained; that is, it is not experienced according to the logic previously established.
In that case, how could there be the state of being a living soul (jīvatā) within such a Brahman?
Of what nature is it?
It has the form of consciousness (*cittatākārā*); that is to say, it is the state of being consciousness (*cittatva*) entered into the bed of the object of cognition (*cetyaśayana*).
The meaning is that it possesses that very form.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It has the form of the wind of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Latent impressions are the cultivation of the notion of an object of thought (*cetya*).
That very [consciousness], by virtue of its movement, is the wind;
it takes that form.
The implication is: "What talk can there be of 'living-ness'—which is the state of pure consciousness devoid of any object of thought—when it has entered the bed of objects?"
In this very way, according to the previous reasoning,
the nature of mind is the aspect of mind.
Regarding the phrase "entered into the state of being perceived" (*cetyaśayanāviṣṭāyā*):
by the very absence of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*), it simultaneously refutes the status of being a living being (*jīva*) and so forth;
for precisely because the nature of consciousness does not arise there, the state of being a living being (*jīvatā*) simply does not exist.
There is no intellect, no state of consciousness, no sense organs, and no latent impressions;
this is solely because of the non-arising of the form of consciousness— that is, because the essential nature of consciousness has not emerged—
and not due to any other cause.
The non-arising of that form has already been explained. Furthermore, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the contemplation of "I" (*aham-bhāvanā*) abiding in a subtle form.
[Objection: But how can there be the state of being a living soul (*jīvatā*) and so forth here through the non-arising of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*)?

It is true that there is no [such thing as a soul]; for since the swelling of consciousness itself does not arise in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, it is entirely logical that the state of being a living soul and so on is non-existent—
thus, there is no contradiction.
He states the conclusion:
"Thus, although this state is established as full of the commencement of dissolution, it is an undecaying ground;
from our perspective, it remains peaceful, empty, and more vast than space."
The state characterized by the supreme self is established as full of dissolution yet free from decay, being devoid of the bodily attributes known as old age;
it is a place more tranquil than space, that is, superior to space from our perspective.
In that way, the void remains as having the nature of nothingness. How so?
The meaning is: "in this way," by means of the reasoning previously stated.

Having realized that the nature of the Supreme Self is difficult to comprehend, Śrī Rāma asks once again: "What is the form of the ultimate reality, which has the appearance of infinite consciousness?"
Furthermore, explain this skillfully for the increase of understanding.

"You, moreover, [explain] skillfully and correctly" means for the increase of knowledge regarding the Supreme Self, that is, for the expansion of wisdom concerning the object that is the Supreme Self.
Explain this; tell me what it is. Of what?
Of that well-known one whose form is infinite consciousness—that whose essential nature is consciousness undivided by space and the other directions.
"What is the nature of the Supreme Self, which is the ultimate reality and the very essence of truth? To this,
the venerable Vasiṣṭha gave the following reply:
Listen as this Supreme Brahman, which remains as the cause of all causes when the great dissolution has occurred, is now described.
"When the great dissolution has occurred" means at the time of the fourth state (*turya*), the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), or at the time of the end of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*).
The cause of causes is the root cause;
it is that supreme Brahman, the reality characterized as the Supreme Self, which has expanded into the form of the world.
It remains, meaning it persists as the witness of the great dissolution.
Therefore, listen as I describe this very nature of the Supreme Self. (MT 3.10.38) He thus describes the essential nature of the Supreme Self.
Having destroyed one's own self through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind,
that which is the form, that which is inexpressible— that is the form of that reality;
[of] that reality, which is the Supreme Brahman, another synonym for which is the Supreme Self (paramātman).
That is form.
What is that? That which is form.
That which remains is called the "residue" (śeṣa). It remains because it persists as the witness to its own destruction.
Of what [does it remain]?
Of the mind.
Having done what?
Having destroyed its own self, having brought it to dissolution in pure consciousness alone.
When what exists?
The meaning is: when there is the cessation of activity, that is, the destruction of activity.
What is its nature?
That which "cannot be described" means that, due to its extreme purity, it is not fit to be described. This is the intended meaning: [it is known] by the mind alone.

According to the maxim "having cut through the mind," the pure mind— which has emerged slightly from the fluctuations of saṃsāra by means of right knowledge— destroys its own mixed nature (of both pure and impure) through the power of contemplation (*bhāvanā*), which serves as the cause for the cessation of both pure and impure mental modifications (*vṛtti*).
Thereupon, that mind becomes merged in some indescribable, exceedingly pure state, and thus itself becomes indescribable.
And this state of being is experienced by everyone in deep sleep;
however, it is mixed with a state of delusion.
And when that mind becomes such as that, then its state of being the Supreme Self occurs;
in that very state, the yogi should remain attentive.
"Having cut through" means having destroyed;
"destruction" refers to the destruction of existence (*bhava*).
There is no visible world and no seer, for in the absence of the visible, [the seer] has dissolved.
That which is "shining" (bhāti) is the manifestation (bhāsana); that is the form of that reality.
Of that reality—of the reality characterized as the Supreme Self—that is its form.
It becomes that form.
What is that?
It is this very manifestation,
which is a radiance or a flashing forth.
What is this "thus"?
Thus, the visible world— the object of the act of seeing—
does not exist, because it is established as mere cognition.
The seer is the agent of the act of seeing;
because of the absence of anything visible, he appears as if dissolved,
as if merged.
This is the meaning:
first, the absolute non-existence of the perceivable must be ascertained through reasoning by means of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Thereafter, by virtue of that absolute non-existence of the perceivable, the perceiver also becomes, as it were, dissolved.
Consequently, it flashes forth that neither the seer nor the seen exists;
and because that flashing forth is of the nature of nothingness, being devoid of any taint of seer or seen, it becomes inexpressible.
And that very thing is the nature of the supreme self;
therefore, the yogi should remain attentive toward it.
bhāsanaṃ ] °sa⟨mā⟩naṃ;
līna ] lī⟨l⟩[n]a;
samyagjñānena ] °ya⟨k⟩[g]jñā°
If that which is the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*)— the essence of consciousness— is oriented toward the object of cognition due to the absolute non-existence of the visible world,
then that pure, stainless, and tranquil consciousness alone is the cause of all causes.
The intrinsic nature of the living being (jīva) is well-known;
that is pure consciousness (cinmātra).
The cause of causes, which is the nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman) as the fundamental cause, exists.
What is that pure consciousness (cinmātra)? It is the consciousness (citi) which serves as the material cause (upādānakāraṇa) of the individual soul (jīva).
The body is the true nature;
for consciousness has the nature of pure awareness alone. Furthermore, of what kind is it?

It is "stainless" (vimala), meaning it is not defiled by the impurity of the object of cognition (cetya). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "quiescent" (śānta), meaning it is free from the agitation caused by the injury of the object of cognition.
What is that pure consciousness?
It is that which constitutes the intrinsic nature, the very form, of the individual soul (jīva).
The masculine gender of the word *yat* is used in relation to the word *svabhāva*.
To the question, "When, then, does this become the nature of the living being (*jīva*)?", he says:
"If..."—that is, "if it should be directed toward the womb."
Because it is consciousness itself, when oriented toward an object of cognition, that constitutes the state of being a living soul (jīva).
This is the intended meaning:
that which is pure consciousness, when directed toward an object of cognition—
That very [reality] which exists becomes fully manifest through right knowledge; having ascertained its non-substantiality (asattva) and purified it, it becomes inexpressible.
And that indeed is the form of the Supreme Self.
In this regard, the yogi must remain vigilant.
Furthermore, consciousness (citi) exists in two forms: by virtue of its being the agent of self-reflection and by virtue of being the object of reflection.
Among these, the name of the first is "pure consciousness" (cinmātra), while that of the second is... [the object of reflection].
It is called "consciousness."
Furthermore,
by means of right knowledge,
the form of the supreme self [is realized]. (MT_3,10.41)
Now, when there is contact with wind or other elements by means of the thumb or a finger,
that form of the mind which belongs to the living person is the supreme Self.
(MU 3.10.42) [jīvataḥ] = [jīva]taḥ
"Form" is the understood subject;
that supreme,
most excellent reality is the form of the Supreme Self.
What is that? It is whatever form belongs to the mind, to the consciousness.
Of what kind of mind?
Of one who is living, that is, capable with respect to its own function;
but not of one who is incapable therein, such as in states like fainting.
For at that time, there is only his state of delusion,
not his nature as the Supreme Self.
Under what condition does this occur?
Or by means of the thumb or a finger;
this is an illustration [of the principle],
for it applies to all parts of the body when there is no contact with wind and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), fire and so forth are included.
"Non-touching" (*asparśana*) means the absence of touch.
This is the intended meaning.
If there were no contact with any substance whatsoever in any part of a person's body, then that consciousness pervading that limb would be entirely without a support;
at that time, for one who is intent on attending only to that specific limb—
Even though the mind is capable of grasping external objects, it remains as the Supreme Self alone, which is pure, without support, and of the nature of non-objectifying consciousness;
at that very time, having abandoned all mental fluctuations, the yogi should examine with full attention.
Like states such as fainting;
of fire and so forth; fire; without support.

[The form of the Supreme Self, which is pure, without support, and of the nature of consciousness alone: O sinless one, that form which remains after long contemplation—of that state which is dreamless, infinite, non-inert, and firmly established—is what is left. (MU 3.10.43)
of the non-inert [ajaḍāyā],
of the long-pondered [ciracintāyās],
it remains [śiṣyate].
O sinless one, free from defects such as passion and the like—
that reality—
at that time, during the moment of the dissolution of the Great Self.
It remains.
What is that? It is whatever constitutes form.
Of what? Of long-standing reflection;
"long" meaning throughout the entire night.

The "thought" (*cintā*) that has been performed is the contemplation (*ādhyāna*) directed toward a desired object already attained. Regarding that thought, he states its specific qualifications, beginning with "of one that is not sleep" (*asvapnāyāḥ*), meaning [a thought] that has not transformed into the state of sleep.
A thought being formed while awake transforms into the state of a dream;
and since it has transformed into a dream, it may—due to its lack of control over the subject—concern other objects as well. Thus, it is rightly said that [the cognition] "is not of a dream."
"Of the infinite" means of that which proceeds with an uninterrupted continuity;
the meaning is that no other thought enters into its midst.
For some thought, when performed without interruption by one who is not insentient, brings about a state of swoon.
To exclude that [possibility], the qualification "of the non-inert" (ajaḍāyāḥ) is employed.
"Dense abiding" (ghanasthitiḥ): "dense" (ghanā) means compact (nibiḍā).
Even when being contemplated, she does not admit entry;
this is her state, her abiding.
Of her [who possesses such a state].
That;
of such a kind;
meaning, of that which is without support.

This is the intended meaning: when performed while awake, thought—which is severed [from its objects], free from the defect of dullness, and untainted by the touch of that which is being contemplated—attains the very state of being the non-objective consciousness (acinmayatā) consisting of awakened awareness (bodha). And since the supreme self-nature is precisely this non-objective consciousness, the yogi should remain attentive therein.
Thus [it is said].
Free from defects such as passion;
at the time of the dissolution of the Great Self;
by way of not being dependent on other objects.
Fainting—
that which is the heart of the sky, or of stone, or of the wind—
is the form of that consciousness-space, the unperceivable Supreme Self.
Of that well-known, non-objectifiable, and untainted by contact with objects— the sky of consciousness, whose nature is the space of manifestation.
The form of the Supreme Self is its essential nature; that is what it is. What is that?
That which is the heart of space, known as the void; or else, that which is...
Regarding that which is the heart of both stone and wind:
therein, the heart of the stone consists of extremely subtle particles that are impenetrable to anything else.
When the heart of Pavana is sought, it comes to rest in emptiness alone.
If it is argued that by this his insentience (jaḍatva) follows, we say no; for that objection is refuted by the declaration of his name, "the Sky of Consciousness" (cidvyoman).
When investigation is performed, the heart of space and the other elements is found to be, respectively, of the nature of emptiness and unfit for the entry of anything else;
and such indeed is the form of the Supreme Self. Therefore, the yogi should cultivate that state with focused attention.
The state of one who is worthy, who is beyond thought and without mind, yet possesses life and action—
that is the supreme, peaceful existence of that primordial reality.
Of that primordial reality,
the other [state] is supreme, excellent,
peaceful, and free from agitation.
The persistence of existence;
that [persistence] would belong to that primary reality, the reality characterized as the supreme self.
What is that? It is the state of abiding, which would be existence.
Of what?
Of a living person, that is, one endowed with life;
but not of one who is dead.
Of what kind? Of one who is "acetya" (unconscious).

Because through right knowledge there is certainty regarding the non-existence of the object of thought; therefore, it belongs to one who is devoid of the object of thought, and for that very reason, to one who is without mind—that is, devoid of mental activity.
Furthermore, of what nature is such a person?
"Of one who possesses action" means one who performs actions such as moving; the sense is this:
not performing mental activity toward an object of thought, and for that very reason, entirely devoid of mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*).

Just as the individual person (puruṣa) is the performer of actions such as moving and so forth, even so is the supreme reality of the Self (paramātmatattva), which performs the activities of creation and the rest;
in this regard, the yogi must remain attentive.
By means of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*):
therein, that which is the middle of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) and of the dense light; (MT_3,10.45) [that is the state].

And that which is the middle of vision, the wise know that to be the form of Brahman. "Of Brahman" means of the Supreme Self (paramātman), who has expanded through the state of being various entities;
"they know" means they understand that form.

What is that? It is the middle, the intermediate state, of the light that has arisen from consciousness— which is itself a slight manifestation— and which consists in the manifestation of the object of cognition.
It is so for that which is dense and compact,
and for light such as the solar orb and the like that has arisen.
That which is the middle is the intermediate state;
likewise, it pertains to the act of seeing that has arisen for the seer.
That which is the middle is the middle state;
this is the meaning of "existence" (bhāva).
There are three states of the light of consciousness, the external light, and vision:
the initial state, the intermediate state, and the final state.
In that regard, at the time of the rising of external light such as the sun, there is an initial state which is defiled by contact with the sun;
and there is a final state at the time of the illumination of objects.
That [state] is defiled by contact with objects;
however, the intermediate state consists of the nature of pure light and is called *anākhyā* (the Inexpressible).
And such indeed is the nature of the Supreme Self.
In that regard, the yogi should remain attentive;
this same principle should also be applied to the perception of the light of consciousness.
The distinction between consciousness-light (*citprakāśa*) and vision (*darśana*) should be understood as being based solely on their limited and unlimited nature.
This applies likewise to sensation (*vedana*), light (*prakāśa*), the visible (*dṛśya*), and darkness (*tamas*).
That sensation which is without beginning or end is the form of the Supreme Self.
That is the form of the Supreme Self;
what is it?
That which is the continuous connection of feeling;
of what nature is it?
It is without beginning or end and proceeds uninterruptedly; for only that which has intervals can repeatedly possess a beginning and an end in its middle. Of what?
Of illumination, which has the nature of illuminating objects;
of sensation, that is, of cognition;
and furthermore, of what?
Of *tamas*, which has the nature of being solely graspable;
of some particular deity imagined as an object of sight (*dṛśya*) that must necessarily be seen. This is the intended meaning.

The concentration on gnosis (*jñānadhāraṇā*) and the concentration on the deity whose form is identical with the object of knowledge (*jñeyaikarūpadevatādhāraṇā*), proceeding without interruption, become transformed through their nature as consisting solely of gnosis and their nature as consisting solely of the deity; thus, they become the single-natured form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
In this regard, the yogi must remain attentive.
Or rather, [is it] of the perceiver— the instrument of cognition,
the illuminator—
[or] of the visible object, which is like the appearance of light?
It should be understood that [this refers to] darkness graspable by the eye of one who has attained vision, specifically "external darkness.
This is because some have stated that there are meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) upon external light and external darkness.
Of the specific deity, [of] the god,
[who is] perceivable by those with purified vision; since the world arises as if from that which, though its nature is eternally unarisen, possesses [the quality of] light.
That supreme self-nature, though non-different, appears as if it were different.
That "supreme self-nature" is a form belonging to the Supreme Self.
What is that?
From which, because of which, the world seems to arise, as it were; it goes toward emergence, as it were.
Because it is manifest.
Of what nature is it?
Even though its form is eternally unarisen, it is eternally unarisen.
In the ultimate sense, it possesses a form that has not manifested in the form of the world because its nature is pure consciousness alone;
even so,
furthermore, what is its nature?
It is undivided and consists of that;
furthermore, how is it?
The word "abiding" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
It is "situated," meaning present;
how so?
"As if divided," that is, as though it were divided.
The use of the suffix *-vat* is for the purpose of negating any ultimate difference [between the world and its source].
This is the intended meaning: because this world arises from a subtler reality, just as a mass of waves arises from water.
It emerges; that indeed is the form of the supreme self.
In this regard, the yogi should practice with vigilance.
Even for one intent on worldly affairs, there is a state of sitting like a stone.
The state of being space belongs precisely to that which is not space; that is its form, pertaining to the Supreme Self (*pāramātmika*).
That form pertains to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). It is the form belonging to the Supreme Self.
What is that?
It is sitting and remaining like a stone, even for one who is intent on worldly affairs and even while performing such affairs.
What is that seat?
It is precisely that which is distinct from the nature of space, because it possesses qualities such as insentience (jaḍatva) and is thus devoid of the attributes of space.
The state of space (*vyomatva*) is the nature of space (*vyomabhāva*).
This is the sense:
even while engaging in worldly activity, a person remains devoid of concern for success or failure therein.
"One becomes the very form of the Supreme Self;
therefore, the yogi must remain attentive therein.
Furthermore, this triad consisting of the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower—
Whatever arises and whatever sets there— each of those is the supreme,
the highest.
"Each of those" refers to what is well-known [in the world].
It becomes the supreme, most excellent, highest, unsurpassed reality characterized as the Supreme Self (paramātman).
What is that?
In which [place]— that is, in what [place]—
this [world] is being experienced.
The object of knowledge is the domain of the act of knowing; the act of knowing is the process of cognition; and the knower is the agent of the act of knowing.
Their state is the condition of being the object of cognition, the act of cognizing, and the cognizer.
That which is called the threefold form—the triad consisting of the object of cognition, the act of cognizing, and the cognizer—arises and passes away.
This is the meaning.
The triad beginning with the object of knowledge (vedyādi) arises and dissolves within some reality called pure consciousness (cinmātra) by virtue of being perceived as an object;
that alone is the nature of the Supreme Self.
The yogi should remain attentive there.
The agent of the act of knowing;
form;
that in which this state of being the knower of the object and the act of knowing is reflected.
In the great mirror of the unawakened state and so forth, that form is remembered by the wise as supreme. That "supreme" means most excellent;
"form" refers to the essential nature characterized as the Supreme Self.
It is taught:
what is that?
It is that wherein, in the great mirror, there is the state of the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower—the triad beginning with the object of knowledge.
It reflects; it manifests as a reflection.
In what state?
In that which is devoid of intellect and so forth—namely, in the intellect and so forth when they are free from [the conceptualization of] intellect and so forth.
And it is logical that a mirror is devoid of cognition and so forth;

for while a mirror is devoid of cognition and so forth due to its insentience (*jāḍya*), this [mirror-like nature of the Tathāgata] is devoid of them due to its transcendence— this is the distinction.
This is the meaning:
the triad beginning with the object of cognition (vedya) flashes forth in a single moment and dissolves in that very same moment;
by its own manifestation, it does not impart any impurity whatsoever to its substratum, existing solely as a reflection.
It shines; for even a reflection flashes forth only for a moment and dissolves only for a moment, and it does not impart its own turbidity to its substratum, such as a mirror.
Your [consciousness], which is distinct from the triad, serves as the substratum for the reflections of the triad consisting of the object of cognition and so forth.
Some entity must necessarily be admitted;
otherwise, the reflection of the triad would be impossible.
And such an entity, being thus admitted, [is established].
It becomes truly inexpressible,
and that indeed is the reality of the supreme self;
therein, the yogi must be attentive.
"It must be meditated upon.
(MU 3.10.51) That form of the Great Consciousness which transcends the mind and the six senses—whether in the moving or the stationary—remains at the end of creation. (MU 3.10.52)
That reality, which transcends the six sense organs with the mind as the sixth and transcends even the source [of manifestation], remains at the end of creation, during the great dissolution.
What is that?
It is that which would be the form of the Great Consciousness, of pure consciousness alone.
Of what nature is it?
It is beyond the six sense faculties,
including the mind as the sixth among them.
Those are the six [senses] with the mind as the sixth;
those are the faculties, the six faculties with the mind as the sixth;
those are the past, the past six faculties with the mind as the sixth.
The meaning is that it is beyond their range.
Where?
Whether in the moving or in the stationary.
This is the meaning:
the state of possessing consciousness in mobile beings is indeed beyond dispute;
it is likewise the case even in stationary things such as grass and even in mountains.
It is not determined by the emergence of grass and so forth;
for it is not logical that anything should emerge from that which is insentient.
Because hair and other such things are not seen to emerge from a dead body;
and thus, that form in which consciousness exists everywhere is indeed inexpressible (*anākhyam*).
And that alone is the reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattvam*).
Thus; in this regard, the yogi should remain attentive.
For if the form of stationary beings (*sthāvara*) were composed of consciousness, then one would not observe the emergence of body hair and so forth from it.
Freed from the mind, intellect, and so forth, that [Self] becomes equal to the Supreme.
The inclusion of the word *hi* (twice) is for the purpose of filling out the metrical foot.
That would be equal to, or the same as, the Supreme Self (paramātman). It would be so.
That, at that time;
when?
That which consists of awakening, whose very nature is the act of awakening.
If it should exist,
what would it be?
It would be the form that belongs to stationary beings.
This is the intended meaning:
the form of immobile things is necessarily devoid of agitation, yet it is corrupted by insentience (*jāḍya*).
Therefore, having abandoned insentience, one must make one's own reality of consciousness (*jñānatattva*) free from agitation simply by not contacting the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Thereafter—
And thus the attainment of the supreme self occurs;
in this regard, the yogi must practice with vigilance. These are the concentrations (dhāraṇās).
It has been clearly demonstrated that each one is a means for attaining the Supreme Self.
For the purpose of completing the meter: *°opādānaṃ pādapū°...°rtha⟨ḥ⟩[ṃ] paramātmanā* ] *°nā (iti)*;
*tadā* ] *[tat] tadā* (MT_3,10.53).
He concludes what was previously stated with a verse at the end of the chapter:
"Upon the cessation of Brahmā, Arka, Śakra, Hara, Viṣṇu, Sadāśiva, and the rest, this one supreme Śiva alone remains here;
he is the taught, the undecaying, the effortless, the desired, neither mixed nor unmixed, not dependent on the atom, yet dependent by those who have taken refuge. (MU 3.10.54)
Not dependent on atoms (*aṇvanāśritam*): this [reality], abiding as its own self-nature,
is Śiva, whose essential nature is supreme bliss.
The supreme, most excellent reality remains in its own essential nature; it abides exactly as it is.
But it does not perish;
under what condition?
When there is the cessation of Brahmā, Arka, Śakra, Hara, Viṣṇu, Sadāśiva, and the rest.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of all beings from the gods down to the grasses.
Regarding Brahmā and the others who are the lords of their respective worlds:
when the time of the end of the great aeon (mahākalpa) has arrived in the form of a peaceful dissolution; [then...]
Hara is the performer of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Sadāśiva is the bringer of bliss by bringing everything into his own nature.
Alternatively, [he is so called] because he brings about the arising of the volitions (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth of the minds and other faculties of Brahmā and the rest.
The meaning is: "when [the state] called the fourth (turya) has become quiescent.
Of what nature is it?
It is "remaining" (śiṣṭa), which means it is declared as the residue, being taught as the witness of all quiescence.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is undestroyed, not being within the sphere of destruction.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is effortless and easy to understand.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is desired, meaning most beloved by all.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is mixed, having the essential nature of various existents and non-existents. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is not mixed, but is of the nature of pure consciousness alone.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It is that which is resorted to by the world—which is atomic, limited, dependent, and of the nature of an attribute—and which has been grasped as its substratum. Thus all is auspicious.
"The supreme [and most delightful] Brahmā, Arka, Śakra, Hara, Viṣṇu, Sadāśiva, and so forth, in their state of peace" (MT_3,10.54).
Thus ends the tenth canto in the "Section on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Śrī Rāma asks:
This form, this visible world named the "shining," O Brahman—where indeed does it go upon the occurrence of the great dissolution?
This world, which manifests before one,
the visible object that is the domain of the act of seeing,
is called "jagat"— the entity known as the world.
It exists in the ultimate sense (paramārtha) alone; otherwise, its appearing in such a manner would be impossible.
Of what nature is this form?
That which has this as its own nature— this nature consisting of the presence and absence of what is being experienced— is "that which has this as its form" (*idam-rūpa*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says here: "O Brahmin, [it is] the great dissolution... and so forth.
Where does this very world go when the great dissolution occurs?
The meaning is: to what region does it go?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha also asks something similar to this.
From where does he come, or what is the son of a barren woman like, and where does he go?
Tell me, where does it go, from where does it come, or tell me of the forest of the sky?
From where does it come?
The meaning is "at the time of arising.
Of what kind, or what nature, does it go?
"Where does it go?
means "at the time of its destruction.
The sense is that your question is similar to this.
Śrī Rāma gives the following reply: "The son of a barren woman and the forest of the sky do not exist, nor will they ever exist.
What kind of visibility could he have, and what kind of non-existence?"
By the negation of the present and the future, the negation of the past is also implied.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of what kind?"
"Visibility" means the state of being fit for perception;
that is to say, existence by way of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha, taking the answer spoken by Śrī Rāma as an illustrative example, gave his own reply.
Just as the son of a barren woman and the forest in the sky never exist at any time,
so too the entire visible world, beginning with the universe, never exists at any time.
By the word "beginning" (*ādi*) in the phrase "beginning with the universe," dissolution (*pralaya*) is included.
"Kadācana" means "at any time whatsoever. He states the conclusion:
"That which indeed did not exist at the beginning is neither produced nor destroyed."
What kind of arising could there be for it? What talk can there be of the word "destruction"?
[The word] *kila* indicates certainty (*niścaye*).
That entity which,
at the beginning— that is, previously—
has not yet arisen.
Nor does it perish;
it does not even partake of destruction.
Likewise, it does not exist, nor does it enter the sphere of stability.
Of what kind and of what nature is its arising?
And in the absence of arising, what talk can there be of the word "destruction"?
The sense is that it is not even proper to speak in this manner.
Śrī Rāma asks again:
"Indeed, there exists the conceptualization of the son of a barren woman and a tree in the sky."
Just as that [void] is characterized by destruction and birth, why should this [world] not be exactly like it?
The word "tāvat" indicates the absence of any disagreement;
"hi" expresses certainty.

The sense is that if the conceptualization of a barren woman’s son and so forth did not exist, even the mere mention of "the barren woman’s son" would be untenable. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "That [is the case]."
That is a conceptualization such as the son of a barren woman;
although it is unreal, it is nonetheless characterized by destruction and birth, that is, it is possessed of destruction and birth,
just as it occurs.
Likewise, why should this visible world not be characterized by birth and destruction, even though it is unreal?
The meaning is: let it be so.

And thus, the sense is that the question "Where indeed does it go? is entirely appropriate. In response, Śrī Vasiṣṭha stated by way of a different turn of phrase that while the conceptualization of a barren woman’s son is appropriate through the superimposition of a son seen elsewhere upon [the barren woman], here the conceptualization is not appropriate because there is no existence whatsoever even for that which is perceived, as to where it might be.

Just as a statement devoid of logical sequence is meaningless, so too is the existence of the world; therefore, O incomparable one, properly perform the churning with your locks of hair upon that which has blossomed.

The word *phulla* [is used] in the sense of "without equal" (*atula-bhū*); indeed, the particle *hi* indicates certainty. The existence of the world (*jagat-sattā*) is likewise (*tathā eva*), by that very same manner;
it is *niranvayā*, having proceeded without aiming at any specific object whatsoever.
It is, that is to say, futile; and how so? Thus: [the text continues].
The statement beginning with "of the flower" and ending with "the knitting together" is such that it becomes without a logical connection (*niranvaya*).
He demonstrates this very lack of connection through other examples:
just as, for instance, even though it is clearly visible in a golden bracelet...
But the state of being a bracelet does not exist at all, and likewise the state of being the world does not exist in the Supreme.
Just as in a golden bracelet, although the state of being a bracelet is clearly perceived, it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality because it consists solely of gold;
so too in the Supreme, which is pure consciousness alone.
The meaning is that, in the same way, the state of being the world does not exist.
And just as emptiness does not exist in space as something distinct,
so too the state of being the world does not exist at all in Brahman, even though it is perceived.
The word *ca* (and) is used for conjunction.
"Possessing a negative concomitance" (*vyatirekavat*) means being endowed with a negative concomitance; the meaning is that no negative concomitance is perceived between space and emptiness.
He states the illustrative example: "the state of being the world.
This means the nature of being the world.
In that manner, in that way;
in Brahman, the all-pervading nature of consciousness,
it simply does not exist.
The meaning is "because it cannot withstand analysis.
"Of what kind even?
means "even though it possesses perception," that is, even though it is perceived by way of appearing.
Just as blackness does not exist apart from collyrium, nor whiteness apart from snow,
so too the world would not exist as something separate from the Buddha; it does not exist in the supreme state.
Just as blackness, which is the state of being black,
cannot exist apart from soot,
so too whiteness, which is the state of being white [cannot exist apart from its substrate].
Just as [the world] cannot exist apart from Him,
the Buddha is determined to be, in the ultimate sense,
the world itself.
In the supreme state, in the Supreme Self;
thus, in that manner,
there is no separate existence.
The two locatives "pare pade" should be understood as standing in the place of two ablatives.
Just as whiteness and the state of being white do not differ from snow, and just as coolness does not differ from the moon,
so too the creation does not exist as something distinct from Brahman.
The word "ca" (and) denotes conjunction;
for example, "coldness" means the state of being cold,
[derived] from "himāt," meaning from that which is cool.
It does not differ from, nor is it superior to, the moon; likewise,
the creation does not possess difference from, nor is it distinct from, Brahman.
In the section on "Conjunction" (*samuccaya*):

Having stated the identity [of the world] by way of demonstrating the relationship between the possessor of qualities and the qualities, he now declares that this identity is established through the delusion of the world.
[The unity through the illustration of qualities and the qualified:

Just as water in a mirage and the lunar nature in a second moon do not exist at all, so too the world does not exist within the stainless Self, even though it is perceived. *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 3.11–12.
The Dārṣṭāntika says "thus" (*evam*):
in the stainless self, in the Supreme Self whose nature is pure consciousness;
"thus" means in that manner.
The meaning is that the world, though seen and though appearing, does not exist.
Now, an objection is raised: "Is there not a discrepancy, since previously bracelets and the like were employed as examples, whereas here it is desert water and so forth?"
If it is argued that this is an undesirable consequence,
we say no;
for by means of the previously cited analogies, the monolithic nature of Brahman as the world has been established.
In this regard, there is no lack of truth;
however, as for the result, all the examples have their purport solely in the oneness of Brahman, so there is nothing contradictory whatsoever.
(MT_3,11.12) He further confirms this very point by means of another example.
Firmly established,
this light of the eye of consciousness shines in the sky of consciousness,
like a string of pearls in the stainless firmament called the world. (MU 3.11.13)
This light of the eye of consciousness stands as the self in direct perception; "consciousness" (saṃvit) means consciousness itself, that is,
pure awareness (cit).
The "eye" (*vilocana*) is the organ of sight by virtue of its similarity as an illuminator;
its "light" (*āloka*) is its ray.
It "shines," meaning it manifests as the nature of objects.
Where? In that which is called the world— that is, in the world named [the world]—
in the sky of consciousness, the space of awareness.
How is it?
It is like a string of pearls;
just as that [string] exists in the stainless sky, the elemental space.
It flashes forth;
"tathā" means in that manner. This is the intended meaning.
Just as rays emerging from the eyes are seen shimmering in the sky in the form of strings of pearls,
so too are the rays called the "lights of consciousness" (cidāloka) that arise from the consciousness (cit).

They appear in the sky of consciousness known as the world, manifesting in the form of various objects. (MT_3,11.13) In the space of consciousness, that which shines by itself through its own consciousness is understood to be the very self in the form of the world. MU_3,11.14
That which is the sky of consciousness, within the sky of consciousness— on its own wall called the sky of consciousness—
by virtue of being consciousness, through the state of consciousness.
It shines and vibrates;
that is to say, it becomes the object of the self-reflective awareness as "I.
For in the absence of such reflective awareness, its [existence]—
Otherwise, consciousness itself would not exist;
by means of that various space of consciousness,
its own nature— which is called "shining forth"— [is manifested].
The world is thus perceived and known,
precisely because the world has the nature of a reflection.
The space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) follows the subject at hand: for that which does not exist from the very beginning cannot [arise later], because its cause is impossible.
Even in the present, that [world] does not exist; what kind of destruction could there be therein? (MU 3.11.15).
Indeed, whatever thing is called the "world" does not exist by itself from the very beginning, because its cause is impossible.
That [destruction] does not exist even in the present;
in that regard, with respect to that entity,
destruction is suspected by means of the example of the son of a barren woman— [that is,] destruction.
Of what kind? Of what form?
The meaning is: it might not exist because of its unsuitability due to the absence of an object.
[Objection: But since the cause characterized as the Supreme Self exists, how can the impossibility of a cause arise? To this, he says:

How could the insentience belonging to the elements— insentience observed in the elements such as earth and so forth— be capable of being the cause of that [consciousness], just as sunlight cannot be the cause of a shadow?
(MU 3.11.16) "Insentience belonging to the elements" (*bhūtajāḍya*) refers to the insentience perceived within the elements.
That in which the dullness of the elements is impossible—
that is "asambhavadbhūtajāḍyam.
This refers, by implication, to the reality known as consciousness (cit).
Where is the insentient entity, such as earth and so forth, capable of being the cause [of consciousness]?
The meaning is that it is not capable. He states an illustration for this: "of a shadow," and so on.
Since sunlight is clearly incapable of being the cause of shadow because it destroys it, its status as an illustrative example is untenable.
[Regarding the word] *chāyāyā*:
"But surely the world might exist even in the absence of a cause? To this he says:
"Due to the absence of a cause, this effect is not something that has arisen at all."
That which is indeed the cause exists as such; it is established in this manner.
[Because of the absence of a cause: "This is not [so]. *kāraṇābhāvataḥ*: °taḥ; *nedam*: n⟨ai⟩[e]dam.
That is because of the previously stated reason;
that is, due to the absence of a cause, from the non-existence of a cause.
This is what is being experienced.
The effect called the world— the effect—
has arisen; it does not exist.
How so?
The meaning is: "not even in the slightest degree.
Furthermore, why is this seen?
To this he says: "That which... It is that very same entity which, existing in this manner as the form of the world, is present.
What is that very thing? It is the entity which is suspected to be the cause of this world, by virtue of being its cause.
The meaning is that it exists in this way alone, and nothing else whatsoever.
That which appears as unarisen is indeed the manifestation of consciousness itself.
That world which is perceived in a dream is merely the manifestation of consciousness;
whatever object appears, though it is indeed unborn,
that is [the manifestation] of consciousness, that is, of knowledge.
"Manifestation alone" means that it is precisely the radiance [of consciousness] that appears as suchness;
this occurs.
Regarding this, he states a corresponding illustration with the words "that which... (yad).
By the word "that" (tat), there is a reference to the world;
since the nature of dream as the manifestation of consciousness is established by all experience,
it is taken as an illustrative example.
Just as the delusion of the dream-world is nothing but the internal manifestation of consciousness,
so too at the beginning of creation, the manifestation of the world is extended within Brahman;
"within" means in the mind.
The delusion of the dream-world is a delusion having the form of a dream-world;
that is to say, it is what is called the "dream-world" [superimposed] at the beginning of creation, at the commencement of the world's manifestation, by means of the intellect.
By the word "tathā" (thus), the manifestation of consciousness is implied;
"ātatam" means expanded or extensive.
The delusion of the dream-world:
whatever is seen here at the beginning of creation exists as the very reality abiding within the Self.
Nothing whatsoever in this world ever sets or rises;
that is, whatever object is being experienced here.
It is perceived;
that is indeed real,
for it is a real entity within its own self, which is of the nature of consciousness, its very own form.
It remains.
He states the result: "it does not set.
The word "therefore" (ataḥ) is to be supplied [as the subject].
The sense is that it exists eternally in the form known as pure consciousness alone.
Just as liquidity is water, as movement is wind, and as light is appearance, so too the three worlds are Brahman alone. (MU 3.11.21)
The meaning is that no one is able to demonstrate "appearance" (*ābhāsa*) as something distinct from fluidity and so forth in water and the like;
"illumination" (*prakāśa*) refers to the light of the sun and other such sources.

Appearance (*ābhāsa*) is the manifestation of an object. (MT_3,11.21) Just as the internal knower exists as if it were a city within the consciousness of a dream, so too does one's own self alone appear as if it were the world within the Supreme Self. (MU_3,11.22)
Just as in the consciousness of a dream— that is, in dream-cognition,
meaning during the state of dreaming—
within, that is, within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Consciousness alone shines forth and manifests like a city;
likewise, one's own self alone [shines] within the Supreme Self.
The meaning is that within its own substrate, which is designated as the Supreme Self (paramātman),
the world appears as if it were real;
however, there is no such thing as a "world" other than this.
"Just as in the consciousness of a dream" (*yathā svapnasaṃvidi*).
Here Śrī Rāma asks:
"If it is so, then O Brahmin, tell me how there can be such a solid conviction?"
"This visible world has arisen like the experience of an unreal dream;
O Brahmin, tell me this,
if such is the manner previously described."
In that case,
this which is being experienced is the visible object.
The visible object itself is poison— that is, a poisonous substance— because it produces delusion; it possesses a very dense conviction,
meaning that within it there is a very dense conviction or consolation.
That;
such;
how? By what cause?
"Born" means arisen;
how so? Like the experience of a non-existent dream.
Just like an unreal experience of a dream— an experience having the form of a dream,
that is to say, a dream— so it is [with this].
Not considering liberation possible without the absolute non-existence of the visible world, he asks about that very point in detail.
"When there is an object of sight, there is indeed a seer; when there is a seer, there is the state of being an object of sight.
When both exist within a single reality, there is bondage; when one ceases, both are liberated.
The word "kila" indicates certainty.
The existence of the seer occurs when there is the existence of the seen; and the existence of the seen occurs when there is the existence of the seer.
This is because it is by you yourself [that this has been stated]. Such is the meaning.
He states the result with the words "in one being": between two [beings], there would be bondage for one being;
between two, upon the destruction of one, there would be liberation.
Therefore, the sense is that for the sake of liberation, only the destruction of one [defilement] needs to be accomplished.
Regarding "the existence of the seer" (*draṣṭṛsattā*):
"by you alone" (*tvayaiva*). See MṬ ad 3.9.38–39.
(MT_3,11.24) Now, one might object: "Even there, why do you ask again and again about the absolute non-existence of the visible? To this, he says:

As long as there is no absolute impossibility— that is, as long as the visible object has not reached its exhaustion— so long can the state of the seer being a non-seer, which bestows liberation, not occur. (MU 3.11.25) [adraṣṭṛtvaṃ] ad⟨ṛ⟩[ra]ṣṭṛ°
The Buddha is perfectly known;
he is inexhaustible and uninterrupted. Non-seeing is the state of being a non-seer.
The meaning is "pure consciousness alone.

Since the absolute non-existence of the object of perception is easily established, whereas the negation of the status of being a perceiver is difficult to achieve without that absolute non-existence of the object, the point is that the question regarding the absolute non-existence of the object is raised again and again.
Non-seeing: *adraṣṭṛ* [the state of being a non-seer]:
*adraṣṭṛbhāvaḥ*. Of the exclusion of the state of being a seer: *draṣṭṛtānirāsasya*.

"Surely, what purpose do you have in the absolute non-existence of the perceptible? For the goal is accomplished even by the destruction of the perceptible. To this, he says: "If the perceptible were possible at first and subsequently underwent destruction..."
Then that bondage, which consists of the uselessness of recollecting the visible world, does not perish.
[Regarding the phrase *dṛśyasmaraṇānartharūpaḥ*: "the uselessness of recollecting the visible world" means that the very recollection of the visible world is itself the uselessness.]
That which has such a form— that kind of bondage—
does not perish; it does not go to destruction.

For the recollection of an object that was previously known as real and subsequently perished is indeed unavoidable, just as in the case of one's mother and so forth; such is the intended meaning. When does that occur?
If,
at first— that is, previously—
the visible object were possible, meaning it existed as a reality established by valid reasoning;
Thereafter, it comes to destruction and ruin; therefore, the meaning is that non-existence must be accepted here as pertaining precisely to all three times.
"Subsequently, [there is] destruction; indeed, what memory can there be of a visible object that has perished? To this he replies:
"Wherever it may be situated, the movement of consciousness is like that of one's own mirror."
Indeed, this reflection, consisting of the memory of creation, truly adheres.
The word "hi" (indeed) is used for emphasis; "this" refers to what was just mentioned;
"consisting of the memory of creation" means having the nature of recollecting the creation.
The reflection necessarily adheres; it adheres inevitably.
To what?
To a certain movement—that is, to a particular mode of consciousness.
Like what? Like a mirror.

Just as a reflection appears on a mirror situated anywhere when there is proximity of objects, so too a reflection appears on the movement of consciousness (cidgati) situated anywhere due to the proximity of the perceived object, because of its subtlety.
The meaning [is as follows]. (MT_3,11.27) If that is so, when does liberation occur? To this he says:
"For if the visible world was never produced from the very beginning and does not exist by itself,"
Liberation is possible because of the absence of the delusion of the seer and the seen.
The "visible" refers to the collection of entities that are the objects of the act of seeing;
from the very beginning— that is, right at the outset—
it is itself unarisen, being unborn by its own nature.
If it is so that [it] does not exist at all,
then at that time—
Liberation is possible; it becomes logically established.
Why?
Because of the absence of the delusion regarding the seer and the seen.
This is the meaning:
when there is the absolute non-existence of the visible, the delusion that "this visible belongs to the Puruṣa" subsides; upon its subsidence...
And even the delusion that "I am the seer" subsides;
consequently, only that which is the nature of pure consciousness remains,
and that alone is liberation.
Because of the absence of the delusion of seer and seen,
he concludes the question:
"Therefore, since liberation is impossible for me, [I shall proceed] through the method of encouragement."
"O best among the knowers of the Self, declare the absolute impossibility regarding that which is perceived.
O best, most excellent among the knowers of the Self;
therefore, for that reason.
Because liberation, which is impossible without the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible, would otherwise be unaccountable for me;
[therefore,] the absolute impossibility residing in the visible [is established].
"Speak! From where? means: by means of the method of encouragement, having exerted supreme effort. (MT_3,11.29)
The venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke this reply:
"Just as that which is non-existent appears as the entire universe,
listen, O Rāma, as I relate it to you through a long discourse."
"In that way" means: listen; I shall explain that manner to you.
By what?
By means of a discourse— a continuous succession of sentences— that is long and detailed.
Likewise, how so?
The world is composed of all things, having the nature of the totality of all that is perceivable.
"In whatever manner" means by which mode.
"The non-existent alone shines" means that it manifests as bubbles due to its lack of reality.
[Objection: Why do you speak with such a long discourse? To this, he says:
As long as that [deed] has not been fully described through words recounting your resolve,
so long does it not rest within your heart, like dust in a lake.
(MU 3.11.31) "Through words recounting your resolve."
A "discourse of determination" (*vyavasāyakathā*) is a discourse that produces a specific determination or ascertainment;
it consists of sentences that express such [determination], namely "sentences of discourse of determination.
That [refers to] the non-existence of the perceptible.
As long as it has not been described in detail, so long will it not find rest in your heart nor take its place there. How is this so?
Just as dust,
just as fine particles do not settle in a lake.
The meaning is "so it is."
"Just as with dust [in the eye], will anything be accomplished for me by the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of what is perceived? To this he replies:
"You [must know] the absolute non-existence of this state of delusion regarding the creation of the world."
"Having realized that the self is established in one-pointed meditation, you shall carry out worldly affairs.
You shall carry out the worldly affairs consisting of kingship that have come down through tradition; you shall carry them out like the transaction of counterfeit coins.
But you shall not be turned away from it as one in the state of dispassion (vairāgya),
nor attached to it as one in the state of delusion (mūḍhatva).
Of what nature are you?
One whose self is established in single-pointed meditation:
on the meditation, that is, the contemplation, of that one reality called pure consciousness alone.
He whose self (ātman) is such— that is, whose mind (manas) is of the nature of pure being (sattva)—
is he.
Such a one:
the meaning is that you shall be single-mindedly devoted to meditation on pure consciousness within,
even while participating in external worldly affairs.
Having done what? Having [realized] this state of the delusion of the world's creation which is currently being experienced.
"Having the form of the world's creation" means having the form of the world's manifestation;
"the state of delusion" means the firmness of delusion;
its "absolute non-existence" means its non-existence throughout the three periods of time.
"Buddhvā" means having known; such is the meaning.
[transmitted through tradition] ... by means of the knowledge of the state [of being] ... externally ...
of that which is being experienced ... experiencing.
Regarding the phrase "absence throughout the three times," in response to the inquiry "What follows from that?", he states another result:
"The grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence, the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving."
But perceptions will not pierce you, any more than arrows pierce a great mountain.

When there is knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible, perceptions—whether grasping or rejecting existence and non-existence, gross or subtle, moving or stationary—will not pierce you; they do not inflict the "wounding" that consists in the production of joy or resentment.
Here, "existence" (bhāva) means manifestation.
Non-existence is disappearance;
grasping is seizing;
relinquishing is abandonment.
Since even entities and the like are perceived as being absolutely non-existent, no beating caused by them will happen to you;
for it is not the case that anyone has ever been beaten by the son of a barren woman— this is the intended meaning.
What are they like?
They are like arrows;
just as arrows do not pierce through a great mountain.
The meaning is "so it is.
He declares his thesis regarding the absolute non-existence of the perceptible:
"This is that very Self alone; there is no second conceptualization."
O Raghava, I shall explain to you how this world has arisen here;
it is well-known,
existing as something directly perceptible to all.
There is only one;
he clarifies the meaning of the word "only" with the word "not.
The second conceptualization is the conceptualization consisting of the visible.
It does not exist;
and thus, the absolute non-existence of the perceptible world is indeed manifest—this is the intended meaning.
If that is so, how is it that the world appears?
Regarding the word "exists," it is said here: "the world. Herein, in this non-dual Brahman, I shall explain to you how the world arose.
The sense is that by this very means, the absolute non-existence of the visible world will become manifest.
He summarizes this with the final verse of the chapter:
"Therefore, all these manifestations have unfolded; for he, O dear one, is the Great-Souled One who is the Whole within the whole."
It itself arises and dissolves, having as its locus the sheath that illuminates the observation of forms and the mental deliberation [upon them].
From that material cause, which is characterized as the Supreme Self (paramātman), [it arises].
These are being experienced;
they are the manifestations, the visible forms, the playful displays—
meaning that they emerge like pots from clay.
Therefore, from what? Indeed, for the sake of certainty;
O friend!
He who, having become the entire manifold of all that is perceivable,
arises by himself and through himself alone, reaches manifestation and likewise undergoes dissolution and reaches absorption.
What is that Great Self?
It is the observation of form, the mental reflection, and the mental attention.

It is the manifestation within the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which acts as the witness, through the gateway of mental reflection upon the form perceived by the sense organ; it is the radiance of these [three].
The treasury is the form, the abode, the place;
the meaning is that these [elements] abide right there and emerge from right there. May there be auspiciousness!
In that very place, these [verses]: "tatraivaita" (MT 3.11.35).
Thus ends the eleventh canto in the Chapter on Origination within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! He fulfills his promise, having declared, "I shall speak":
from this supreme, peaceful state, which is supremely purifying.
Listen with the highest intelligence to how this universe has arisen from that Supreme,
which is the most excellent, and whose true nature has just been explained immediately following this.
From the "Peaceful" (śāntāt), which is free from the agitation of conceptual proliferation (prapañca);
from the "Supremely Purifying" (paramapāvanāt), which is the unsurpassed purifier because it purifies even those things that are themselves purifiers;
from the "Abode" (padāt), which is the locus characterized as the Supreme Self (parātman).
In whatever manner this entire universe, being experienced,
has arisen— that is, has become manifest.
That refers to that manner;
by means of the highest— that is, the most excellent—
intellect.
Listen.
By this, it is stated that only one of supreme intelligence possesses the qualification [for this].
He explains that very point:
Deep sleep appears like a dream, and Brahman alone appears like a creation;
all is one and that is peaceful—listen now to the sequence regarding that.
"Deep sleep" (suṣuptam) means the state of deep sleep (suṣuptiḥ).
Like a dream, it appears— that is,
it manifests—
just as a dream arises for one who has awakened from deep sleep.
Brahman alone— the reality known as pure consciousness— is expanded through the state of creation; it appears as if it were the creation itself.
[Objection: In that case, surely Brahman, being the material cause of the world, must be insentient just like the world;
for we do not observe a cause to be endowed with the same defects as its effect.
Regarding this, it is said: "All. That is Brahman;
it becomes all.
And it becomes one;
and it becomes tranquil.
The sense is that this is indeed a marvel in every respect.
Now, one might ask: "How does it arise? To this, he says:
"In that regard" (*tatra*). The word *tāvat* signifies totality (*sākalya*). He explains the sequence itself as follows:
The incessant manifestation, by its very nature, which consists of mere existence, belonging to that pervasive jewel of consciousness whose essence is infinite light—
that [manifestation] itself appears within the Self as if it were something to be perceived.
That manifestation is ungraspable in nature, yet it indicates desire, impatience,
and inquiry;
it is something slight, appearing only as a trace.
The word "as it were" (iva) is employed because [the mind] appears as if it were going toward the object of cognition, whereas in ultimate reality it does not go.
How so?
By itself, through its own nature.
But not by the instigation of another,
because another is absent there;
in what [is he absent]?
In the self, whose nature is consciousness known as "manifestation" (sphuraṇa),
at that time there is nothing else whatsoever existing apart from it.
What then?
Whatever flickering there is—
namely, the reflective awareness "I"—
is constant and continuous.
By its own nature, that is, by its very essence; of what? Of [the Tathāgata].
Of that [Self], which is well-known as appearing as "I" in all [things] and whose nature is infinite light, the term "infinite" (ananta) means unconditioned;
its essence is that light,
and its own-being (svabhāva) or essential nature consists solely of that.
He [is the one] of that gem of consciousness which is spread out, meaning, of that whose nature is infinite light.
Of that jewel of consciousness which is extended and pervades everywhere—
of what nature is its radiance?

Its essence is pure existence (*sattāmātra*), its nature is the form of pure existence; for the conventional usage of "existence" occurs only within the manifestation that is the nature of radiance. This is the point: it is pure.
In the ultimate sense,
apart from that, whatever there may be— none of it exists.
And the state of being an object of cognition is the state of being an object of consciousness.
And that [connection] would have to be a connection with consciousness (*cit*).
However, a connection between consciousness and that which is of the nature of the non-conscious (*acid-rūpa*) is not tenable because they are contradictory;
for a connection between light and darkness is never observed anywhere.
And the tranquility of the mind is established by the aforementioned reasoning precisely through the impossibility of there being an object of cognition.
The connection [is as follows]:
Brahman alone shines forth, pure, in this manner, by means of itself within itself;
