because of its nature as consciousness, like water because of its fluidity, it manifests within itself in the form of whirlpools.
Thus, in the form of the world;
clear and free from the stain of the object of thought;
by itself, through its own nature.
When the self, which is one's own essential nature,
has become the foundation, Brahman alone— which is the self of all— shines forth and manifests.
Why?
Because it is consciousness (*cittvāt*), that is, because its nature is consciousness (*cidbhāvāt*).
The point is that if it were not manifest as the world whose form consists of objects of consciousness (*cetyarūpa-jagat*), it would not possess consciousness itself.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "due to fluidity. Just as water, because of its fluidity, vibrates in the form of whirlpools within its own nature called "water."
The meaning is "so it is."
In this regard: "This which appears here is indeed non-existent, yet it is experienced here as if it were existent;
in the end, it perishes as something non-existent, just like one's own death in a dream. (MU 3.13.52)
This world appears and shines forth as if it were real, though it is indeed unreal; by us, it is perceived as if it were real,
here within the nature of the Supreme Self.
It is experienced;
at the end,
in dissolution, that which is non-existent perishes.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "as in a dream" (MT 3.13.52).

Having explained at length the absolute non-existence of the world, he declares its nature as consisting of Brahman, which is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [The word *brahmamayatvam* contains the correction *madhya*.]
Alternatively, because its nature is pure consciousness (*vāja*), this world is eternally free from affliction,
undivided, without beginning or end, and has the interior of the sky of mere cognition as its belly.
Or rather, this [is] the world.
Because it is eternally of the nature of the unborn and because its nature is pure consciousness devoid of birth,
it is "free from ailment" (anāmaya), meaning it is free from the diseases such as being a substratum or a superstratum mentioned previously;
however, it is not characterized by non-existence.
And that absence [of duality] was stated with respect to those who, despite having cognitions pervaded by it, do not see its true form;
what is this [absence] like?
Unbroken, its nature is complete; without beginning or end, it is devoid of beginning and end;
its interior is the mere expanse of consciousness.
It is merely known;
it is not destroyed by blows from hammers or other such instruments.
For when the world is scrutinized with perfect knowledge, it becomes nothing but the interior of space.
He summarizes what was previously stated with a verse at the end of the chapter:
"In the supreme ether alone, the first Lord of Creatures shines forth eternally by himself, identical with emptiness;
for he possesses a subtle, transportable body and not a form composed of the elements such as earth; therefore, that which has not been born does not exist as a reality. (MU 3.13.54)
The first is the primordial one;
Prajeśa is Brahmā;
"in the supreme" means in that which transcends all.
In the sky, that is, in the sky of consciousness;
eternally, at all times;
by itself, by its own very nature.
It shines and vibrates;
thus, the meaning is that the entire process previously described applies only to one whose mind is dissatisfied, even without the commencement of creation.
Of what nature is it?
It is equal through emptiness, that is, by way of its empty state;
it is equal to that through its purity.
But he is not of that nature, because that would entail insentience (*jaḍatva*);
for "hi" indicates certainty;
he is the Lord of Creatures (*prajeśa*).
The *ātivāhika* body consists of a subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*); it is not, however, composed of the gross elements (*bhūta*).
But in the case of the specific [object],
it does not have the form of gross elements such as earth; therefore, by that reason known as "not having the form of the elements," [it is established].
Earth and the other elements do not exist as real entities.
[Objection: Since the Lord of Creatures (Prajeśa) does not have the nature of earth and the others, how is it that earth and the others do not exist as real?
To this, he says: "When... [etc.]
The word "yataḥ" has the sense of "from which.
That from which [something] was born or produced does not exist.

If the Lord of Creatures (prajeśa), whose form is pure mind, were to assume that [material] form, then the earth and other elements would be produced; however, it is not possible for the Lord of Creatures to assume such a form according to the previously stated principle.
Therefore, the earth and other elements likewise cannot be produced.
The meaning is that it is not possible. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Oṃ! Having thus repeatedly stated that the world is absolutely non-existent and consists solely of the one Supreme Self, and having understood that only that much remains to be established, he speaks once more of that very point: "In this way, the world—the visible objects such as the sense of 'I' and so forth—has arisen as nothing at all."
And because it is unborn, that which exists is indeed only the Supreme;
[that which begins with] "I-ness" (ahantā) and so forth does not exist at all.
In this way, according to the aforementioned method, the visible world has not arisen even in the slightest degree.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says here: "Because the world is unproduced. This means because the world has not been born.
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of completing the meter.
[It means] "it does not exist at all.
Now, one might object: "How do you establish the non-existence of the world by its being unproduced, given that it exists because it appears?"
Regarding this, it is said: "And that which...
That is precisely the supreme, transcendent, pure consciousness alone;
so it is.
But not the world. What is that?
The meaning is: that which exists, which cannot be negated because of its manifest appearance.
[If you say: "But surely it was previously established that [the self] exists as a living being; how then can it be so? To this he replies:
"This very supreme space itself perceives by itself among the living beings."
Within the belly of the motionless ocean, the water seems to quiver;
this [state] previously mentioned is indeed the supreme space, the very space of pure consciousness.
By itself, through its own nature,
it perceives— that is, experiences— the state of being alive among those who live.
What is it like? It is like water; as [water] within the belly of the motionless ocean, that is, in the midst of the motionless sea.
The water that was still begins to vibrate;
here, by the word "vibration" (spanda), that which is possessed of vibration is indicated—
namely, the state of being endowed with vibration.
One intends; and in this context, volition is merely the capacity for that [action],
for there is not even a partial quality of motion in water therein.
It is logical. Likewise, in the case of Brahman as well, there is merely the fitness for being a living soul;
however, there is no such thing as "living-soul-ness" (jīvatā) existing therein.
Just as in the case of water, the knowledge of fitness arises because it is logically connected with the capacity for movement in the future.
The distinction is that [Brahman] appears in the form of the individual soul (jīva).
In the belly of the motionless ocean;
in the midst of the motionless ocean;
there.
[Gre] 'g⟨n⟩[re] (MT_3,14.2): He demonstrates this very point through various modes of expression:
"Let it be seen that [the mind], without ever abandoning its nature as space, seems to perceive."

Like a dream, a mental construction, or a mountain [in the mind], this internal activity of consciousness is the supreme space; it perceives, as it were, and experiences, as it were, the state of being an object.
Of what nature is it?
Its form is that of space; its form is called the space of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). It is indeed never abandoning [that nature].
The sense is that upon the abandonment of that [ego], there would be no awareness of it;
for the "I-reflection" (aham-parāmarśa) is essentially the function of consciousness (cid-vṛtti) as conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa),
just as [the reflection of] a face in a mirror is essentially the function of consciousness as conditioned by the mirror.

In dreams, mental constructs, mountains, and so forth— namely, within dreams and mental constructs that have been made one's own objects, such as mountains that are one's own essential nature— one perceives the state of being visible,
thinking, "This is a mountain."
The meaning is "so it is."
That body which is the visible state, devoid of earth and the other elements, belonging to the Great Virāj Self—
that is indeed the subtle body (*ātivāhika*), consisting of pure consciousness and like the clear sky.
Devoid of earth and the other elements, yet not defiled by contact with gross earth and the rest;
[this refers to] the Virāṭ-Ātman—the Supreme Self who exists in the form of the Virāṭ; "Mahān" means the pervasive one.
Whatever body exists, it is indeed subtle and of a transportive nature.
Here, he states the qualification by way of the reason: "consisting of pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*). For [the Self] has the nature of the stainless ether called pure consciousness.
The subtle, transportable nature (*ativāhikatva*) of the body consists of pure consciousness.
"It was seen in a dream"—thus one does not exert oneself [over it].
It is like a mountain in an inexhaustible dream, comparable to a city in a stable dream;
its form is like an army of figures situated in a painting within the mind of a painter. (MU 3.14.5)
It is like a multitude of statues on great pillars that have not been fixed in the ground;
it is like a *sālabhañjikā* statue on a firm pillar, its self unanchored within the space of Brahman. (MU 3.14.6) [Note: *putrikau* is corrected to *putrikāu*.]
Sālabhañjaka:
The first Prajāpati was formerly renowned as Svayambhū;
because of the absence of his own prior actions, he was without a cause.
Renowned as the primordial cause,
he is celebrated as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū).
He was known by the name Svayambhū,
the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati),
at the beginning of the previous creation.
It occurs without a cause, being devoid of a cause. Why?
This is because of the absence of former actions— that is, the deeds performed in previous kalpas as one's own past works—
and it is well-established in all the scriptures that karma is indeed the cause of birth.
The absence of his activities should be understood as arising immediately from pure consciousness (cinmātra).
What is its nature?
"Imperishable," and so forth:
"imperishable" means free from the defect of momentariness, like a dream-mountain that is other than [ordinary] ones; that which has an appearance like such a dream-mountain is [the object].
He is like a mountain of imperishable dreams;
he is comparable to a city of stable dreams.
By contrast with other dream-cities, he is stable and possesses a stable form.
That for which the city of a dream is the simile;
he [is the one].

By these two qualifiers, its stability even in its state as a *ativāhika* (conveying) body is stated. "The mind situated in a painted creation" (*citrakṛtsthitacitta*) refers to the mind located therein; that which is the army in the painting (*citrasainya*), the painted army appearing before one's eyes.
Therefore, he whose form and nature were such— that painter possessed a form identical to the painted army stationed within his mind;
he was neither dug in nor carved out.
That which is like the mass of figures on a great pillar that has not been fixed in the ground is "like the mass of figures on a great pillar that has not been fixed in the ground. He is like that.
In the firm pillar of the Brahma-ether, he is one whose self is not fixed and whose true nature is not carved out;
"Sālabhañjikā" means a large doll.
This is an explanation specifically of the qualification "not fixed."
By these two qualifiers, its state of being solely composed of Brahman is expressed.
[He has the appearance of an army stationed within a painting, with his mind fixed upon that which is situated in the painting.
At the end of the great dissolution, it is said that even the primordial Grandfathers are liberated; since they are all [liberated] from this [state], what role does prior karma have for them?

All the primordial Grandfathers (Pitāmahas) are liberated— that is, they dissolve— into their own essential nature called pure consciousness at the conclusion of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Here, the word "conclusion" (*paryanta*) is intended to signify the culmination or final limit.
The result is stated as "ataḥ" (from this);
for this reason,
in all those aforementioned primordial ancestors (pitāmahas).
What becomes of past karma? The meaning is that it becomes nothing at all;
and so it is said:
The meaning is that all of them are indeed devoid of agency.
The nature of the wall must be released; it exists as both visible and invisible, and yet it is neither the visible, nor the seer, nor the creator, and indeed everything is so.
This very one is the *praticchanda* (the conforming desire) of all objects; from this arises the series of living beings, just as a row of lamps arises from a single lamp.
This is that very same Prajāpati mentioned previously.
It exists as the reflection and collective totality of all objects,
because it is the essential nature of all appearances.
Of what nature is this? It is that which is precisely capable of being released, and indeed capable of passing through the middle;
it is of the nature of a wall.
For a wall, by virtue of its nature as an obstruction, cannot be passed through in the middle;
however, this wall is indeed unprecedented, and it must be abandoned.
Because it possesses the magnitude of entry and exit for all movements of the visible,
its nature as a wall is due to its being the support of everything.
Furthermore, what is it like?
It exists as the visible, established in the form of the visible;
and it exists as the invisible, established in the form of the seer.
This is because the seer and the visible consist of Prajāpati, whose nature is the pure mind appearing as mere consciousness (cinmātra).
Furthermore, what is it?
It is neither the visible object nor the seer; it is neither the creator nor the agent of the act of creation, because its nature transcends everything.
Furthermore, what is it?
And indeed all this.
Now, how is it that this reflection exists?
To this he says: "from this."
For from this Prajāpati, the series of living beings arises—that is, it manifests.
Now, one might object: does the series of jars not arise from clay, or the series of snakes from a collection of ropes? In that same way, [the world] arises.
"It is not observed that those two possess the nature of the imitated and the imitator.
To this, Dīpālī says:
"In this case, there exists a distinct mode consisting of the imitated and the imitator, which is different from [the modes of] evolution (vivarta) and transformation (pariṇāma)."
Existence.
In the form of the seer (*draṣṭṛrūpeṇa*); [the word] *draṣṭṛ* [is used for] *draṣṭṛ*;
"of the seer and the seen" (*draṣṭṛdṛśyayoḥ*);
[the word] *sarpālīnyaṃ* [is used for] *sarpālīnyam*.
"By means of volition alone, he indeed proceeds from volition, devoid of earth and the other elements,
yet appearing as if possessing earth and the others— like one moving from one dream to another dream without walls.
The word "kila" is used here in the sense of certainty.

"Devoid of earth and the rest" means being free from gross earth and so forth because it exists in the form of a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*). "As if possessing earth and the rest" means appearing as if accompanied by them due to its mode of appearing. "Without walls" means being devoid of mountains and the like that appear in the form of walls.
The world is called *saṅkalpa*; it arises— that is, it manifests— from Brahman, whose form is pure *saṅkalpa* (volition) consisting of the mind.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "from a dream," meaning from a dream consisting of conceptual construction;
"another dream" means another dream consisting of conceptual construction.
"Just as it goes," means "in that manner. From this very reflection, these individual souls (*jīva*) emanate forth.
And because of the absence of auxiliary causes, that very [state] belongs to you; therefore, from this one named Prajāpati—
From the appearance of their respective inclinations,
these living beings manifest as direct perception.
They spread out, meaning they undergo movement.
In that case, by virtue of being produced from that [cause], they would necessarily be distinct from it;
to this, he replies: "the auxiliary cause" (sahakārī).
Those living beings are that very thing;
they are not distinct from it.
Why?
Because of the absence of auxiliary causes, that is, because of the absence of those auxiliary causes which consist of prior karma.
For it is a well-known principle that in the absence of auxiliary causes, the effect is of the very same nature as its cause.
(MT_3,14.12) In the absence of auxiliary causes, the effect and the cause are one; therefore, this creation is not something other than the Supreme. MU_3,14.13
The "effect-and-cause" refers to both the effect and its cause;
from Prajāpati, who is superior to others in relation to the visible world,
there arises the "delusion of creation," which is the playful manifestation of creation.
Brahman alone is the primordial Virāj-self; the state of emanation is the Virāj-self itself.
It exists in this way as the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa), since the earth and other elements are unreal.
Brahman alone— that is, the very reality of Brahman— is the primordial Virāṭ Self, the Supreme Self in the form of Virāṭ.
The state of emanation is indeed the emanation of that very Virāṭ Self.
It occurs; the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is for the purpose of completing the meter.
He provides a summary with the word "jīva."

That which was previously mentioned is indeed the *jīvākāśa* (the space of the individual soul); because it is enveloped by everything from the state of being an object of consciousness (*cetyatva*) up to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), it is called "pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*), yet it remains the *jīvākāśa* itself.
It is in this manner that [the world] takes on the form of the creation of Prajāpati and the rest.
He remains [there].
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because of the earth, etc."—that is, from which cause.
Earth and the other elements become non-existent.

The Virāṭ Ātman itself is the state of emanation; having heard [the term] "jīvākāśa," Śrī Rāma, having fallen into some doubt, asks: "jīvākāśa. (MT_3,14.14) jīv⟨a⟩[ā]kā° (MT_3,14.14) jīvākāśa. Thus, having heard "jīvākāśa," Śrī Rāma, having fallen into some doubt, asks.
"Could the mass of living beings (*jīvarāśi*) be limited, or is it infinite?

Or rather, does there exist an infinite aggregate of souls (*jīvapiṇḍa*), immovable like Mount Meru? This "mass of living beings" refers to what was called the "space of living beings" (*jīvākāśa*), that is, the collection of souls.
Is it limited, or rather infinite?
Is it immeasurable, or perhaps an infinite self, a mass of life like a mountain, resembling a peak?
It exists.
A *rāśi* is a collection of things existing as distinct entities;
a *piṇḍa*, however, is like a lump of clay—a single, unified mass consisting of living beings—such is the distinction.
[The aggregate of living beings: [°ñjaḥ] (MT_3,14.15).
Anticipating the objection, "Why do you ask about 'aggregate' and 'mass'? he says: [of aggregate and mass: °śi⟨ḥ⟩pi°.
Why do the *jīvakas* emerge like streams from a rain-cloud, like spray from the ocean, or like sparks from heated iron? (MU 3.14.16) [Note:
*kaṇās* is corrected to *kaṇāḥ*.]
"Dhārā" refers to streams of water;
"śīkarāḥ" refers to droplets of water;
"taptāyasaḥ" refers to iron heated by fire.
"Particles" (*kaṇāḥ*) refers to minute fragments consisting of fire.
Why? The meaning is that if the mass of living beings (*jīvarāśi*) or the aggregate of living beings (*jīvapiṇḍa*) is not admitted, their departure (*niryāṇa*) would be impossible. (MT_3,14.16)
He concludes the question:
"O Blessed One, tell me this: the definitive determination regarding the net of living beings.
This has been mostly understood by me; please make that very thing manifest."
"O Blessed One, you are [the one];
thus it was asked:
'Tell me the definitive determination regarding the net of living beings.'"
Having said this much, [the opponent asks], "Was this not heard by you?
To this, he replies, "It is known.
By me, that is, for the most part, in its abundance.
"It is known; however, it is not known in its entirety. Therefore, reveal that very thing so that I may know it completely"—this is the intended meaning.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"There is no such thing as a single living soul; how then could there be the arising of aggregates?"
"Your words are like saying that a hare's horn has flown up and departed;
for in ultimate reality, there is not even a single living being—
how then could there be the existence of the multitudes you have asked about?"
He states that this question is irrelevant by saying "the hare's horn":
your statement is like the words, "The hare's horn flies up into the air."
In the first place, a rabbit's horn does not exist at all;
what talk can there be of its flying?
Likewise, the living soul itself does not exist.
The sense is: what need is there to mention their heaps and so forth?
There is no [obstacle]; there is indeed no [obstacle] at all. What is there for its soaring? Its soaring.
All this that has been asked is refuted [by the following]:
"O Rāghava, there is no individual soul (jīva), nor are there multitudes of souls;
nor does there exist any single mass of soul resembling a mountain. (MU 3.14.19)
From the perspective of ultimate reality, because everything consists solely of pure consciousness, the individual soul (jīva) does not exist.
O Rāghava,
there are no multitudes of individual souls.
Furthermore, there is no single, mountain-like mass of living beings;
therefore, the implication is that this question of yours is not appropriate.
By means of this form of benediction, he declares that this certainty must be established by living beings.
Let your firm conviction be this: that there are no conceptualizations whatsoever— neither those consisting of the notion of the meaning of the word "jīva" nor any other conceptualizations—
that exist at all.
"This certainty that it is yours— let this certainty be immovable and firm."
What is this?
This refers to the conceptualizations of the meaning of the word "jīva.
These, accompanied by all conceptualizations—that is, joined with all conceptualizations such as the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) and so forth—do not exist.
[With the conceptualizations of the sense of "I" and so forth:
"But surely, since the jīva and other [entities] manifest through direct perception, how could this determination be appropriate? To this he says:
"It is not appropriate."
Indeed, there exists here the pure, stainless, and all-pervading Brahman, which consists of consciousness alone.
Just as it attains whatever aspect it wills by virtue of its omnipotence,
so too, through the very sequence of pure consciousness, it unfolds like a fully blossomed creeper.
Indeed, one quickly perceives that very [reality], whether it be embodied or formless;
for "hi" indicates certainty. It is pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*), whose nature is pure consciousness alone;
therefore, there exists the stainless Brahman.
Of what nature is it? It is all-pervading, meaning it extends throughout all places and times.
What follows from this?
Regarding this, he says "that":
that is Brahman;
because it possesses all powers, since it has all power.
Then, in whatever manner, that portion consisting of the individual soul and so forth— the act of conceptualization— [arises].
"By oneself" means by one's own self,
and not through dependence on another; "he finds" means he makes it the object of his own perception.
Of what nature is that digit? It is like a creeper, by means of the sequence of pure consciousness— that is, through the progression of pure consciousness.
"Fully blossomed" means opened;
for this is the very sequence of pure consciousness alone, that it causes conceptual constructions to unfold.
"Nanu" signifies certainty.
That conceptualization—
whether embodied or formless, gross or subtle— he perceives instantly; at that very moment, he sees it as already fully accomplished.
And thus: in ultimate reality, the living being (jīva) does not exist as something established in itself; the sense is that for what could there be a state of being a heap or a mass?
[By the sequence of pure consciousness alone] ... this [is] the coarse and subtle [form] of that very [consciousness].
Now, if Brahman perceives the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, then would it not follow that these are indeed distinct from it?
"Because only that which is distinct from itself falls within the range of perception," to this he replies:
"The individual soul, intellect, activity, vibration, mind, duality, and even unity."
The intellect (buddhi) directs that well-known Brahman, which is manifesting its own existence, toward cognition.
It directs its own existence and its own radiance toward sensation; it makes sensation its object,
which is to say, it perceives.
Of what nature is its own existence?

It consists of the living principle (*jīva*), cognition (*buddhi*), the vibration of activity (*kriyāspanda*), the movements for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and the mind (*manas*).
"Duality and unity" means both duality and oneness;
[she is] shining and vibrating in this very form.
And thus, the sense is that even though it is within the range of vision, it is not logical for the living being (*jīva*) and so forth to be distinct [from the body].
[Regarding] its own radiance (*svasphurattā*):

"But how does the existence of Brahman (*brahmasattā*) manifest as the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth? To this, he says: "That [existence] is indeed consciousness; thus it becomes [the world], for it is Brahman itself through the power of awareness."
Ignorance perishes through discernment, yet it does not realize this; for that [ignorance],
though awakened by the awareness of the reality of Brahman, remains unknown as the reality of Brahman.
It is exactly so; it indeed manifests in the form of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth.
Through awakening—that is, through the knowledge that exists as the reality of Brahman—one becomes Brahman itself.

Because there is no difference between existence (*sattā*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*). Now, one might object: although the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth are identical with Brahman due to the absence of any existence other than the existence of Brahman, that ignorance (*abodha*) which previously existed as the object of the existence of Brahman remains exactly as it was—just like a jar or other objects—since it is known as being ignorance. Thus...
And thus, the state of being composed solely of Brahman is not established;
to this, he says:
"non-awakening" (*abodha*), meaning [it is removed] by means of awakening through discernment.
It goes to destruction; however, in the other case,
that is ignorance.

The object of awakening is not perceived, nor is it realized, because of its contradictory nature; for at the very moment it is to be awakened, it has already perished. The point is that darkness cannot be the object of light.
"It is accomplished" [is read as] "it is not awakened";
he confirms this very point by means of an example.
Just as darkness perishes when observed by means of a lamp,
yet its true nature is not known [as a substance], so it is indeed with non-awakening.
Just as darkness, when observed— that is, when the act of seeing has begun— by means of a lamp...
It perishes;
[it is] the reality, the essential nature, of this darkness.
And it is not known [by whom];
the word "by a person" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He applies this to the case under discussion (the *dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "of one who lacks awakening."
"Hi" signifies certainty;
the meaning is that the true nature of ignorance (*abodha*) is not known in this very way.
[The author] concludes the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman.

Thus, Brahman alone is the individual soul (jīvātman), undivided and continuous, possessing all powers, without beginning or end, and bearing the form of the essence of the Great Consciousness (mahācitsāra). "Thus" means in the manner previously described.
The individual soul (jīvātman) becomes none other than Brahman.
He states its qualifying attributes that bring about this state of being Brahman with the word "nirvibhāga.
"Nirvibhāga" means devoid of division (vibhāgarahita).
For there is no division whatsoever in the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), because it is partless;
it is continuous, being filled with light, and devoid of any internal space.
It possesses all powers, and its possession of all powers is indeed perceived directly in states such as dreaming.
It is without beginning or end; and its being devoid of beginning and end is established precisely by its being the delimitation of beginning and end.
For that which is delimited cannot effect the delimitation of its own delimiter.
He who assumes the form of the essence of great consciousness;
"great consciousness" is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*),
and its "essence" is luminosity (*prakāśa*).
He assumes his form as the one who bears the essence of great consciousness;
the meaning is that he is of the nature of luminosity.
Being without beginning or end, he is not able [to perceive];
in every respect, he utterly rejects the conceptualization of difference.
However, because this [Brahman] is entirely infinite, no conceptualization of differentiation exists;
for whatever conceptualization there may be, it is that very [Brahman] itself due to its being experienced.
(MU 3.14.27) "Of this" refers to Brahman. In the case of a specific distinction, [the following applies].
"By way of all-infinity": it is both "all" and "infinite," thus "all-infinite";
its state is "all-infinity";
by that.
There is no conceptualization of differentiation— that is, no conceptualization in the form of differentiation;
in other words, there is no "differentiation."
Because it is impossible for there to be a distinction between that which possesses all forms and that which is infinite;

for it is not logical that clay or the like— which, in relation to a jar and so forth, possesses all forms such as jars, bowls, and the rest, and is thus infinite— should have a distinction from the jar itself.
But surely, being all-encompassing (*sarvatva*) and being infinite (*anantatva*) are precisely what distinguish [the whole] from that which is not all-encompassing and that which is finite;
thus, its distinction from those two is established by them alone.
To this, he replies: "It exists."
For "hi" has the sense of "because"; that which exists is the mental construction (*kalana*), namely, the construction of duality (*bhedakalana*).
She becomes that very Brahman itself. Why? Because:
"From experience" means from the very nature of experience.
The point is this: whatever conceptualization exists, is it experienced or not? If it is not...
How could that which is itself unestablished bring about difference in Brahman?
If it is experienced, then, being of the very nature of experience, and since experience is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), its identity with Brahman is already established.
"She would indeed become Brahman."
Regarding the [passage] "sāntāc ... kalanā," here Śrīrāma asks:
"It is so. O Brahmin, how is it that all the living beings of the world do not act according to the will of a single soul, given their subjection to the unity of the Great Soul?
"O Brahmin, this is what you have said."
"It becomes thus" means that it truly becomes so;
that is, all living beings there come to conform to the will of a single being.
He raises an objection: "How so?
[The answer is: "All living beings of the world.
Living beings residing in the world are "living beings of the world" (*jagajjīvāḥ*).
"By virtue of the oneness with the Great Life (mahājīva)" means:

by the Great Life known as pure consciousness (cinmātra), which is enveloped by the manifold expansion (prapañca) beginning with the state of being perceivable and ending with the subtle elements (tanmātra).
"Oneness" (ekatā) refers to unity (aikya).
"By its power" means by the influence;
"by the will of a single living being" means by the will of any one ordinary living being.
How is it that [these things] are not tenable?

The meaning is this: since all individual souls (jīvas) consist of the one Great Soul (mahājīva) whose nature has been described, it is logical that when a desire arises in one soul, there is a union with all souls.
"By virtue of the oneness with the Great Life" (*mahājīvaikatāvaśāt*);
"in the state of being composed solely of the Great Life whose nature has been described" (*proktasvarūpamahājīvaikamayatve*). Śrī Vasiṣṭha spoke this reply.
That Great Soul, which is Brahman, consisting of all powers, remains here according to its own will— undivided and continuous. "Mahājīvātman" means the Great Soul.
That Brahman remains here according to its will, in accordance with its own desire.
Of what nature is that Brahman?
Consisting of all powers:
that whose self (ātman) consists of all powers— that is, which is filled with all powers.
That;
such is the nature of Brahman as consisting of all powers, because all powers arise from it alone.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is "without division" (nirvibhāga), meaning it has transcended all divisions by virtue of its indivisible essential nature. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is continuously filled with the essence known as light.
[The Great Living Being: "Let Brahman indeed remain as it pleases; what follows from that? To this, he replies:
Whatever that Great-Souled One desires comes to him immediately;
yet first his desire perishes, for from consciousness (cit) that duality arises.
That is Brahman. Whatever he desires, he makes it the object of his will.
That alone,
and nothing else,
belongs to that Great-Souled One, Brahman, whose nature is all-pervasive.
"Quickly" means at that very moment of desire; "comes to be" means it is accomplished.
By this, he explains that duality arises from the destruction of oneness, as stated previously.
*Cit* means desire.
It should be understood as a desire qualified by consciousness (*cit*), just like the expression "a blue lotus.
And here, being qualified by consciousness means having consciousness as its object.
It is to be understood; the word "since" (yataḥ) is to be supplied.
Therefore, the meaning is this:
since consciousness itself is desire.
"I shall become of the very nature of consciousness"—such is the singular desire. "Previously" means at the beginning of the first creation;
"in this" (ataḥ) is used in the sense of the locative case, meaning "in this Brahman."
The word *tu* has the sense of *iva* (as if). It "perishes," meaning it undergoes a destruction consisting in the state of not being an object of clear manifestation;
however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it does not perish, because it is all-pervasive.
Thus, the word "tu" (but/however) is employed.
Furthermore, the destruction of desire for consciousness as an object is to be understood as occurring precisely through the arising of desire for the objectified [phenomenon].
Therefore, for that reason.
"Duality" (*dvitva*) refers to the state of being divided, existing in the form of the object of thought, the individual soul (*jīva*), and so forth;
it "arises," meaning it manifests.
The sense is that duality arises precisely through the desire for duality, as this desire serves as the cause for the destruction of the desire for oneness (*ekatā*).
[Regarding the arising of duality:
...the form of being beyond the object of clear manifestation...
[he] explains the sequence of power, action, and instrument immediately following the emergence of duality.
Subsequently, by means of his own powers divided into duality, he fashioned the sequence of actions in this manner: "By this, it becomes thus. By him—that is, by Brahman.
Of those divided by duality; that is, of those divided— that is, established— by way of duality, which is a state of being twofold.
In this manner— that is, by way of this method— the sequence of ritual action has been conceived for one's own powers.
"Hi" signifies certainty;
"how" means "in this way"; "anena" means "by this," [and] "sampadyate" means "is accomplished."
[The sequence of ritual action:
By this [word "hi," meaning certainty],
he declares that his desired goal has been accomplished.
The restriction established by that power of Brahmā, beginning with Śakti, cannot arise without it; rather, it is the will of Pradhāna alone that comes forth. (MU 3.14.32) [taṃ] [t(a)aṃ]
By that well-known primordial power, which serves as the fundamental cause and is of the nature of Brahman— that is, related to Brahman.
That rule which has been established as a destiny corresponding to one's own will—
that rule.
Without [them], that is, apart from them, there would be no arising of the other stations of consciousness.
The word "therefore" (ataḥ) is to be supplied [from the context].
Therefore, the desire of the Pradhāna alone arises— that is,
the desire of Brahman, who is the Pradhāna and the Great Soul of all living beings.
Desire alone grows; it transforms into the form of the individual soul's desire.
Thus, it is simply the state of following the primary desire, not its capacity for restriction.

It has been stated [elsewhere]. If it is argued that here, however, it is "due to its capacity" (*tacchakteḥ*), we say no; for there is no difference between the capacity and that which possesses the capacity (*śaktitadvatoḥ*).
He explains this very point through various formulations:
that desire of the power called *jīva* bears fruit, but not without the performance of the regulations of the primary power (*pradhāna-śakti*). (MU 3.14.33)
Of that [power] called *jīvā*;
of which power called *jīvā*, and of which living being (*jīva*) whose nature is that power;
that desire bears fruit, meaning it becomes endowed with its result.
The word "of her" (tasyāḥ) is to be supplied [in the text]. This desire belongs to that power;
[it exists] without the performance of the regulation of the primary power.
Without the performance of the observances— that is, the practice of the rules— of the power of Pradhāna, which is the power of Brahman, [the goal] does not come to be.
The sense is that it does not even attain its own essential nature;
what, then, can be said of its fruit?
This would be the case if the regulation of the primary power (*pradhāna-śakti*) were not well-established.
Therefore, due to the presence or absence of capacity, that fruit would not arise anywhere for those things that lack volition.
[This refers to] the power of *pradhāna* and the power of *brahman*;
the "restriction" is the restriction of the power of *pradhāna*.
"Supratiṣṭhaḥ" means well-established;
"na cet" means if it were not so; "tat" means then.
The fruit of the *rohitaka* trees would not exist anywhere, in any place or at any time.
Why?
Because of capacity and incapacity;
by capacity means by the power of Brahman;
by indication means by its restrictive rule.
That which is capacity is the efficacy toward a result;
the absence of that is incapacity.
Therefore, it is because of this capacity and incapacity.
Since the fruit of various kinds of red actions exists, it is inferred that there is some rule by which these actions possess the capacity to produce a fruit; this is the intended meaning.
[The author] now returns to the subject at hand.
Thus, the Great Soul, Brahman, exists, devoid of end and beginning; it becomes millions upon millions of individual souls, or else it is nothing at all.
The beginningless cycle of existence is devoid of end and beginning; it consists of millions upon millions of living beings, yet it is empty of a self.
In this way, according to the manner previously described,
there exists the Great Life (Mahājīva), which is devoid of Brahmā and the others, and free from end, middle, and beginning.

He provides the answer to the previously mentioned question, "From where do the individual souls (jīvakas) emerge? with the words "the peak of the individual souls" (jīvatkoṭi). That is Brahman; it is the great peak of the individual souls.
Of those living beings who are the agents of the activity of living,
in a number amounting to ten million times ten million,
he himself becomes of that very form.
The meaning is that living beings do not emerge from it;
nevertheless, even so, nothing at all exists.
Because it remains exactly so within its own nature, which consists of consciousness.
Regarding what was stated previously [in 3.14.16d], "numbering in the millions and tens of millions," one might ask: "By what means does the Brahman enter into living beings? To this, he says:
Through the non-perception of the object of thought, the living being comes into existence and enters the cycle of transmigration;

through the non-perception of that [object], form attains peace from transmigration. (MU 3.14.36) "From the non-perception of the object of thought" means from the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the multitude of entities that have become objects of consciousness (*cidviṣaya*).
The individual soul (jīva) becomes Brahman;
from that, it enters into transmigration and becomes a partaker of saṃsāra, characterized by the taint of pleasure and pain.
But surely, at some point, its transmigration must cease?
"Or does it not? To this he replies:
"That," because there is no awareness of that, meaning there is no reflective awareness (*aparāmarśa*) of it.
The word "of this" (*asya*) is to be supplied [from the context].
The form of this living soul, of the cycle of existence— that is, of saṃsāra— attains peace, that is, tranquility.
"He undergoes transmigration" (*saṃsṛtiṃ yāti*);
[the word] *vyā* is to be supplied, and [the word] *ādhyā* is to be supplied.
Now, one might ask: "What is accomplished for the living being (*jīva*) by the cessation of transmigration? To this, he says:
Thus, through the sequence of activities of the superior living beings, the state of being the primordial living being arises for those who are inferior, just as the state of gold arises from copper.
This being so, when there is the cessation of saṃsāra...
Of the eldest living being, that is, Brahmā; by the sequences of actions of the eldest living being, meaning by the sequences of actions of the eldest living being;
the state of being the primordial living being and the state of being Brahmā for the youngest living beings.
It arises; it manifests.

Here, the sequences of ritual action (*kriyākrama*) performed by Brahmā for the sake of the life-force (*jīva*) should be understood as the "oldest" (*jyeṣṭha*). This is because only the sequence of ritual action performed by Brahmā has the power to bring living beings to the state of Brahmanhood. In this regard—
He provides an illustration with the words "of copper":
just as the state of being gold arises from copper through the successive processes of a goldsmith's work, so it is; this is the meaning.
"Regarding the phrase 'the sequence of rites' (*kriyākramā*),
[the author] says 'thus' (*iti*) to recall what was stated previously."
In this infinite supreme space, even though this multitude is non-existent,
it arises as if existing, being essentially the void itself and consisting of the wondrous play of consciousness.
Thus, in this infinite, well-known supreme space— the immeasurable sky of consciousness (cidākāśa)— according to the sequence previously described,
this aforementioned multitude, which is the phenomenal expansion (prapañca) consisting of the nature of the objectified (cetyatva) and so forth, [is subsumed].
Though non-existent, it arises as if existent.
Of what nature is it? It is the self alone, whose very form is nothingness.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is of the nature of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkaraṇa*). The "wonder" (*camatkaraṇa*) of consciousness is the act of tasting through its own power.

That whose nature is that [consciousness] is "consisting of the wonder of consciousness" (*ciccamatkaraṇātmaka*); for independent consciousness cannot be directed toward an object of cognition (*cetyonmukhatā*) without such a wonder.

[Consisting of the nature of the wonder of consciousness. Regarding the phrase "nanu camatkaraṇārtham anyāpekṣāyā avaśyambhāvāt kuto 'syāḥ svatantrāt" (Surely, because there must necessarily be a dependence on something else for the sake of the wonder [of consciousness], how can this [consciousness] be independent?), he says in response:
"anyāpekṣāyā" (of the dependence on something else).
Regarding the phrase "independent and so forth":
that which is experienced as a spontaneous wonder by consciousness itself—namely, the future name, body, and so on—they know that to be the contemplation of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāvanā). (MU 3.14.39)
That wonder which is encountered by consciousness itself, together with its own object and its support, without any effort—
[that wonder] itself becomes the object of that encounter—
the wise call that the state of "I-am-ness," namely, the ego (ahaṅkāra).

The wise know that even egoity (ahaṅkāra) is merely the wonder of consciousness; what need is there to mention the individual soul (jīva)? This is the intended meaning behind the apprehension of the sense of "I."
Of what nature is it? It is that which has a future name, body, and so forth; that is, that which possesses a future name and a future body, etc.
That [is] the designation "I-ness" (ahaṃkāra);
the body is of both gross and subtle form.
The designation of [the self] as both object and agent (*karmakartṛ*) is used to indicate its independence from anything else.
[The state of being the object of union] ...
[he] speaks at great length about the subject at hand, the unity of consciousness (*cidaikya*). Unity of consciousness.
That which is consciousness (*cit*) is the light of consciousness (*cidāloka*), and because it consists of that, it is infinite.
This very expanse of the worlds is reflected within it.
[This refers to] the light of consciousness, whose nature is infinite.
That light which is the cause for manifesting entities is a specific nature;
it may exist. Of what kind is it?
Because it consists of that [Brahman] and because it consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), it is infinite; like consciousness, it is immeasurable.
And this immeasurability of consciousness arises from the absence of a measurer, since it is impossible for consciousness itself to be a measurer with respect to itself.
And this should be understood: it is this aforementioned light of consciousness (*cidāloka*) regarding an object distinct from itself;
[it is said] "of that consciousness" (tasyāś citeḥ), meaning "this expansion of the world" (*bhuvanābhoga*), that is, the vast extent of the universe.
It reflects; that is, it manifests as a reflection by virtue of not taking up impurity.
That which is light; of that [light], this is... (MT_3,14.40)

By means of words such as "transformation" (pariṇāma) and "modification" (vikāra), that very same immutable consciousness, though indivisible due to its uniform nature, becomes aware through its own power alone. By its own power— that is, by its innate power which manifests as the subject (pramātṛbhāva)— the immutable [consciousness], which is devoid of destruction, acts as the agent.
That very consciousness (cit) is understood—that is, cognized—by means of words such as "transformation" (pariṇāma) and "modification" (vikāra).
It is well-established that a word functions as the cause for the cognition of its meaning; therefore, no further effort is required [to prove this].
Of what nature is it?
Because of its being of such a nature, that is, because it is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Although it is indivisible—that is, incapable of being differentiated—[one might ask]:
"If it is non-different from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), how can it be designated by terms such as 'transformation' (*pariṇāma*) and so forth?"
If it is argued that this [is not the case], we reply: True.

Just as water, though non-different from its own nature, is designated by the term "transformation of water" and the term "its modification" once it has attained the state of a wave, so too is this [consciousness]; thus there is no contradiction.
That very consciousness, having attained [the state] through words such as "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) and "modification" (*vikāra*),
is the self of uninterrupted play; it is the inherent savoring of consciousness itself.
This world exists as nothing other than that non-objectifiable light— that is,
consciousness whose nature is a light devoid of any stain of objectivity;
[it exists] spontaneously, without effort.
That which is the tasting is the relish of one's own power;
of what nature is it?
It is characterized by an uninterrupted playfulness.

That whose nature (*ātman*) consists of uninterrupted play (*avicchinnavilāsa*), meaning it is endowed with a vibration (*sphuraṇa*) free from interruption or fragmentation— that is "that which has an uninterrupted-play nature."
That very tasting exists as the world itself, abiding in the form of the world.
This power of consciousness, which is spread out, is subtler even than space.
By its very nature, it perceives this non-duality;
for that which is even subtler than space, indivisible,
and spread everywhere, pervading all.
The consciousness has power, which is its capacity; that is consciousness.
By its very nature, that is, by its own existence alone.
But it does not do so through effort or the like; rather,
it perceives this aforementioned specific "I-ness" (ahantā) and cognizes it as the state of ego-grasping (ahaṅkāra).
That which is subtle and undifferentiated flashes forth within the self by the self alone like water;
he perceives that very [substance], extending to the end of the universe, as the atom of egoity.
Of this *citi*,
the self (*ātman*) is its essential nature (*svarūpa*) known as "vibration" (*sphurattā*). Within the self, that is, within its own essential nature known as vibration.
By its own nature, not by effort;
that which throbs and shines.
How?
Like water, like a wave;
that very vibration is this consciousness (cit).
He perceives the atom of egoity; he grasps it in the form of limited egoity.
Of what kind is this atom of egoity?
It is that which reaches the end of the world, extending to the very limits of the universe.
That very [consciousness],
by virtue of its form as limited egoity (*parimitāhaṃtārūpatayā*),
is beautiful and produces wonder, insofar as it causes the consciousness (*citi*) to marvel.
This world, which is spread out as a mere name within His own self,
is that very [Self] which produces wonder for the one who produces wonder.
*Tataṃ* means expanded or extensive. *Jagannāma* means that which is named "the world" (*jagat*).
It has been made.
The word "by that very [consciousness]" is to be supplied as the remainder.
O Rāghava, the consciousness-nature of the intellect is egoism; that itself is conceptualization.
Since even the subtle elements and so forth are consciousness alone, where then can duality and unity reside? (MU 3.14.46)
When [the mind] has ceased,
the state of consciousness (*cittva*) becomes the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*);
the meaning is that this occurs through the transformation of the very state of consciousness into the form of the ego-sense.
O Raghava,
that very thing is indeed the ego;
it becomes conceptual construction.
Feminity depends upon the categories of conceptual construction;
therefore, that which arises from the *ahaṃkāra*— the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth—
is nothing but consciousness itself.

Since the ego (ahaṅkāra), which has the subtle elements (tanmātra) as its cause, is of the nature of consciousness (cittva), where could duality and unity reside? The meaning is that they do not exist.
If it is argued: "Let there be no duality;
but how can unity not exist?"—do not say so, for without its opposite, duality, even unity is not established.
For indeed, without shadow, light does not become manifest,
because it is inexpressible.
Having thus established that everything consists solely of consciousness (*cit*), he enjoins upon the disciple the practice of abandoning duality.

If you do not renounce even that which is the cause of life, then renounce both "you" and "I. Remain as the remainder in the middle between being and non-being, and become one whose nature is the ultimate goal.
The person (*puruṣa*) has the nature of the meaning "it exists" (*bhavati*); that is, he has the nature of the meaning [of the word].
That is, he has the nature of the meaning of the sentence of the teacher's instruction as implied by the word "thus" (*iti*).
"Be intent upon that"—this is the meaning. He states the instruction of the Guru implied by the word "iti": "Abandon both 'you' and 'I'."
The sense is that by means of which, while living, one goes far away. Furthermore, as to what its form is when one stands still, he says here: "the remainder."
Abide between existence and non-existence, indefinable as either being or non-being;
remain as pure consciousness alone, the witness that remains even when all conceptual proliferation has been sublated.
"Abandon both 'you' and 'I'.
Having thus instructed the disciple regarding non-duality as that which is to be practiced, out of compassion for him, he speaks again of non-duality alone:
"Just as consciousness first conceived its own existence, so it has arisen."
I perceive that existence and non-existence are seen as non-different from the void; thus do I know them at the beginning of creation within consciousness and the like—
my own innate existence, which consists of the manifestation of my own being.
"In whatever manner" means by which form, such as that of a living being (*jīva*) and so forth;
"of this [world]" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The being of this consciousness is such that,
having arisen and become manifest in that form,
it is seen as non-different from the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
The word "by the knowers" (*jñānibhiḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
By the word "I" (*aham*), the subject (*pramātā*) who is the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*) is expressed.
Then [the text] says: "I perceive and know both existence and non-existence."
But the meaning is that it does not exist in that way.
Thus, the sky of consciousness, the void, the activities of the world, the void, the oceans, the gods, and the mountains—
because they are of the nature of the wonder of consciousness in the form of the void, there is indeed nothing else that exists.
*citkhaṃ*] is to be composed based on Bhāskara’s interpretation of *jagadīha* as a compound:
*citkhaṃ* means that the sky (*kha*) is the ether (*ākāśa*).
The activities of the world— meaning the efforts of beings for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful—
become empty.
The oceans, the gods, and the mountains—even these become space itself.
Regarding this, he states the second half of the verse as the reason: "having the form of space" (khākāra).
For "hi" has the sense of "because";
"khākāraḥ" refers to that which is the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*);
it is that very thing which constitutes its form.
That;
its state is reality (*tattva*);
therefore, because it has the nature of the wonder of consciousness in the form of space.
There is nothing else;
the meaning is that everything, being of the nature of its own form, becomes solely the wonder of consciousness.
The wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāraḥ*)— that which is the wonder of consciousness—
is never at any time separate from that which is its own playful manifestation (*vilāsa*).
If even that which possesses parts is a reality, what talk can there be of that which is partless?
That which is a manifestation (*vilāsa*) of something, its very pulsation (*sphuraṇa*), is that [reality].
That [entity] is never, at any time, not distinct from that very reality which possesses parts; for no one asserts that a wave is distinct from water— this is the intended meaning.
The meaning is that even in a dream, that [object] must be described as being without parts, devoid of constituent members.
Because it possesses parts;
"he speaks" means [he speaks]; that is not so. (MT_3,14.50)
Now, one might object: "Even if consciousness (*cit*) has the world as its form, since there exists another consciousness that perceives it, it cannot consist of non-duality. To this, he replies:
There is no other consciousness that is eternally unperceived, for consciousness is by nature never unmanifested.

Whatever is the form of the world, that is the form of the manifestation of that very [consciousness]; it belongs to the eternal consciousness (*cit*), which is unperceivable and incapable of being made an object of thought, yet is consciousness itself, grasping its own self.
The sense is that there is no loss of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpatva). Of what kind of consciousness?
Of that whose form is unconstructed (avitatākṛti).
She whose form is subtle, pervasive, and does not abide anywhere in any shape;
of her.
But is this not unestablished, because [the self] is endowed with the nature of the cognition "I am manifesting"? To this, he says: "That form... and so forth.
Whatever form there is—
such as "I am vibrating" and so forth—
that becomes form.
The word "that" (tat) must be supplied [from the previous context];
that is the form of the world alone, but not of consciousness (cit).

Primarily, consciousness (*cititva*) belongs to that very consciousness which apprehends "I am manifesting"; however, for that which has the form of the object of apprehension— "I am manifesting"— consciousness, though present only in a secondary sense, does not deviate from its nature as the world (*jagattva*).
Of what kind of world? Of that which has the nature of various manifestations;
these various manifestations are such as "I am manifesting" and so forth.
That which is the form of something belongs to that [thing], which consists of the manifestation of this or that.
Whatever comes within the range of being perceived, all that is indeed the world; this is the meaning.
To intend;
having intended; the state of intending;
[of that which has the nature of the radiance of this and that]; [of the radiance of this and that].
"Mind, intellect, ego, the elements, the mountains, and the directions"—
this arrangement of synonyms for the world's existence arises from the reality of consciousness.
This series of terms, beginning with "mind" and "intellect," has been spoken [in this manner].
The arrangement of synonyms for "citta" is as follows. Why? Because of the existence of the world, which consists of mind, intellect, and so forth—that is, because of the existence of the world.
Because it is the reality and because its nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), the meaning is that all words denote consciousness alone.
Know that the world is the consciousness-ness of consciousness; for there is no world-appearance that does not possess the nature of consciousness.
Since it is not non-worldly, it would be conscious; since there is no difference in its nature as being, how could there be a world?
[The reading *nājagac* is corrected to *nājaga(c)*.
Consciousness (*cittvam*) belonging to the conscious (*citaḥ*) is the state of being consciousness (*cidbhāvam*).
Know—that is, understand—that this world is that certain principle by which it becomes fit for the name "consciousness" (cit). That is to say: know that very thing.
He states the reason for this with the word "not" (na), because (hi) for that reason,
consciousness (cittva) is not the world (ajagat), being distinct from the world (jagato vyatiriktam).
It does not exist;
for in the absence of the world of objects and forms, it is evident that consciousness, being inexpressible, lacks the capacity for sentience.
This is the intermediate conclusion.
He says, "not the world.
The word "therefore" (ataḥ) is to be supplied;
that is, for this reason.
Because of the reason that consciousness is non-worldly, it would be insentient;
it would not be fit to be called "consciousness.
If the world did not exist, even consciousness—which is otherwise indefinable—would lack its nature as consciousness.
This is the intended meaning. He states the ultimate conclusion: "Because there is no difference in being" (*bhāvābhedāt*).
Because there is no difference in the nature of things (*padārthābhedāt*), which is established by the previously mentioned principle of the non-difference between consciousness and the world;
[therefore] from where and how could the world [arise]?
It may be so;
for when there is no difference between consciousness and the world, since consciousness consists solely of the one Intellect (*cit*), it is Intellect alone that exists in every way—
this is the sense in which the world does not exist.

[The state of being] conscious: that innate wonder within the seed of consciousness (*citi*) which is the Marīci-seed, is itself this world, established as nothing more than the mere subtle element of the individual soul (*jīva-tanmātra-mātra*). (MU 3.14.54)
Within— that is, in the middle of— the seed-syllable *marica*, which is called *citi*;
that which is the "wonder" (*camatkṛti*), meaning the aesthetic thrill known as the relishing of one's own power, which stands in the place of pungency.
She herself exists as this world; she remains in the form of the world.
In what state is the world?
It consists solely of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) of the living being; its nature is exclusively that of the five subtle elements of the individual soul, and not composed of gross elements.
Because grossness is unreal, according to the analogy of a dream.
Because it is consciousness, that very [consciousness], appearing as the world, manifests through its own power as the "I-sense" (*ahaṃbhāvanā*) of the Intellect;
this is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature consists of vibration and action, and which is designated by future names. (MU 3.14.55)
The manifestation of its own power, which consists in the flashing forth of its own power—
that which exists as the sense of "I"—
from whence does it arise?
Because of its nature as consciousness, due to the cause known as the state of consciousness; for "hi" indicates certainty;
this is the manifestation of its own power.
It becomes a living being (*jīva*).
Its masculine gender is used in relation to the living being.
What kind of living being is it?
That which is action, having the nature of vibration and consisting of a slight pulsation—
that is the self, its own essential form.
The meaning is that for whom [the self] consists of the activity of vibration, it is of the very nature of the vibration of consciousness. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
The meaning is that the manifestation of *vaikharī* speech is designated by the term "the future" (*bhaviṣyat*).

That which is the mental apprehension (*kalana*) as consciousness (*cittva*), having successfully accomplished the direction of the object of expression (*abhidhārtha*), is differentiated by exclusions (*vyavaccheda*) and modifications (*vikāra*); therefore, [in its true nature] it does not exist [as such].

Regarding *vyavacchedavikārais*: the elision of the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhīlopa*) after *citaḥ* is appropriate here as an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). The reading *°vikārais* is correct; the variant *°vikārais* is also acceptable. The word *antaḥ* is understood.
That which is reckoning— that is, circumscription— by way of being consciousness, by way of the nature of awareness,
occurs.
Of what nature is it?

It is that by which the direction of the meaning of the expression—the mere essence of the meaning of the names—is easily accomplished, that is, capable of being achieved with ease; thus, it is "that by which the direction of the meaning of the expression is easily accomplished."
For it is only of a delimited object that a name and its state of being denotable by that name can be established.
That [object] is differentiated; it exists as distinct from consciousness. By what means?
This means that the mind is not touched by the transformations of exclusion;
let there be the production of distinctions from insentient things.
These are indeed the modifications;
by them— meaning,
because of being endowed with those.
If [the self] is distinct from the body, what is the loss?
To this, he says: "Therefore... [etc.]
Therefore, because it is distinct from consciousness (*cit*),
it does not exist; for that which is distinct from consciousness cannot logically be an object of cognition (*cetyamānatā*).
And even when that [object] is not present,
because it is of the nature of consciousness, it is devoid of conceptual construction.
Due to the absence of temporal succession (*kalanā*), there is also the absence of consciousness (*cittva*) which is devoid of purpose;
and with the absence of consciousness, there is the absence of the world. And when that [world] is absent, there is the sovereignty of pure consciousness alone—this is the intended meaning.
May the transformations be easily accomplished; may they come to pass. (MT_3,14.56)
Now, one might object: "Granted that everything consists of the one consciousness;
nevertheless, the mutual distinction between the agent and the object, which are its constituent parts, is difficult to avoid. To this, he says:
There is no difference between the agent and the action, for both consist of the vibration of consciousness;
the action is merely vibration, and that alone is known as the Person (puruṣa).
There is no distinction between the agent and the object, both of which consist of the vibration of consciousness and possess the form known as the manifestation of consciousness.
How is this so?
To this, he says: "It is vibration. Action would be mere vibration, because it is observed that only external vibration constitutes action.
"He alone is remembered as the Puruṣa"— the words "by the wise" are to be supplied.
This is the intended meaning.
When investigated internally, nothing whatsoever is found apart from consciousness;
whereas jars, cloths, and so forth exist externally. Therefore, [consciousness] is distinct from them.
The pure knowledge that "there is no relation whatsoever" is what remains;
and that alone is the vibration of consciousness known as its manifestation (sphuraṇa),
which is itself action (karma).
Since even external actions, such as the movement of the body, are preceded by that [consciousness],
it is indeed that reality itself.
And that very [self] is the person (puruṣa),

because nothing else is perceived within, and because it is impossible for the external body, which is like a lump of clay, to possess the nature of a person; thus, it is established that action is the person.
*Antaḥ*:
being examined within;
*eva*: indeed.
*Tattvam* [thatness]: it establishes the unity of the entire class, beginning with the individual soul (*jīva*).
Consciousness is the vibration of men; and that very consciousness is the mind.
But the mind, while possessing the nature of a sense organ, moves indeed in various ways.
"Jīva" means in the state of consciousness (*cit*), that is to say, in its essential nature as consciousness (*citsvarūpa*).
There is vibration;
for men, that very [vibration] is the mind, which is another synonym for karma,
and it is indeed vibration itself.
Because there exists no individual soul (*jīva*) or mind (*citta*) apart from the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*), it is specifically the mind itself,
in its nature as the vibration of consciousness, that is the *citta*.
The form of the sense faculties exists;
it does not undergo various diversities.
Of what nature, then, is the mind?
It is indeed non-different; because it is one from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is devoid of multiplicity.
This is the intended meaning here.
The living being (*jīva*) is, first of all, merely the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*);
that mind (*citta*) is likewise of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
and that very same mind [manifests] in the form of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
It undergoes transformation;

and then, having gone outward through the doors of the sense organs which have themselves been transformed, it assumes the form of objects consisting of the fivefold nature of visible form and so forth.
Thereupon, it attains the state of the fivefold group that serves as its substratum.
And thus, because it transforms into the state of being that effect, the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*) itself exists in the form of gross and subtle entities;
and since that [vibration] is non-different from consciousness, everything [is consciousness].
It remains as nothing other than the very nature of consciousness.
Indeed, the world is a flash of the light of consciousness, wherein all distinctions have been stilled;
therefore, nothing other than that exists as cause, effect, or the like. (MU 3.14.59)
For this reason:

the entire world without exception is a manifestation of the radiance of consciousness (*citprakāśacchaṭā*), because it consists of a series of established objects within the radiance of consciousness; thus, it becomes a series of the radiance of consciousness.
Of what nature is it?
It is that in which all distinctions have been stilled;
"stilled" means they have dissolved into pure consciousness.
That of which all existents (bhāvas) without exception— that is, in their entirety— are the specific qualities (viśeṣas).
Therefore, for that reason,
the state of being cause and effect and so forth does not exist as something other than pure consciousness, separate from it.
For even the relationship of cause and effect and so forth, insofar as they constitute the world, do not lose their nature as a radiance of consciousness.
Because the radiance of consciousness never departs [from me], it is established that: "I am uncuttable, I am unburnable, I am indeed unmoistenable and undryable;
I am eternal, ever-moving, fixed, and immovable. (MU 3.14.60)
It is established that this is so because the entire world, beginning with living beings, consists of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśamaya*).
This very certainty becomes firmly established.
Why is this?
I am of the nature of the light of consciousness;
I am indivisible, for, like that which has no body, I am not subject to being cut.
In this same way, the phrase "this is not combustible" and so forth should also be connected [to the preceding].
"I am eternal. Regarding this eternity, he states the reason by way of a qualification: "ever-present" (satataga), which means existing at all times.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is *sthāṇu*, firmly established in his own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Here too, he states the reason by means of the qualification "immovable" (*acala*).
For the meaning is that he is unshakable.
[He is] of the nature of the light of consciousness;
[he is] indivisible.
(MT_3,14.60) Now, if all is of the single nature of consciousness, for what reason do disputants argue? To this, he says:

"For just as they dispute here, so do they wander in delusions; we, however, are not wandering, for we have become free from delusion. The word "disputants" (*vādinaḥ*) is to be supplied [as the subject].
The proponents are the logicians and others; here, in this light of consciousness,
"in what way" means by whatever manner.
They dispute; they engage in contention.
Likewise, they dispute with delusions, that is, with false cognitions.
Because there is no dispute among those who have realized the truth. For instance,
the logicians [assert] the self to be characterized by the quality of cognition and subject to transmigratory existence.
And they say:
the Sāṅkhyas [hold it] to be the form of knowledge, yet indifferent; the atomists [hold it] to be the form of atoms; and the Cārvākas [hold it] to be the form of the primary elements.
The Buddhists [regard it] as having the nature of emptiness;
the Vedāntins, as having the nature of peace;
and others likewise [regard it] as something else entirely—if [this were so].

Even though these [disputants] argue out of mere concern for their own respective offices, nevertheless, the delusion of the disputants— those established in various positions who, for the sake of moving from a lower station to a higher one, abandon their respective levels— is described.
If the disputant acts through such delusion...
"If you are thus disputing, how then do you stand? To this he says: "Wandering," which serves as a distinction.

We have become free from delusion; we have become such that false knowledge has been cast far away, because we accept pure consciousness alone, which transcends the various qualities described in the Veda. In what state have we become?
The meaning is that they do not wander.
Now, one might object: "But did not Śrī Vasiṣṭha, intent on refuting that doctrine, engage in a formal debate?
Not so.
Even when refuting that doctrine for the sake of awakening [the opponent], since all doctrines are already accepted by the mere admission of pure consciousness (cinmātra),
for everyone indeed accepts pure consciousness alone.
However, they dispute regarding its specific particulars.
Furthermore, he explains that it consists solely of consciousness alone:
"In the visible, material world, which is firmly rooted in the ignorant, modifications and so forth appear as distinct."
In that which is formless, reflected in the consciousness of the knower, within the sky of consciousness whose nature is both being and non-being;
[and] in the formed, the gross, the visible, the collection of entities that is the object of the act of seeing.
In what state? Deeply rooted among the ignorant; that is, among fools.
"Saṃrūḍhe" means having become firm;
that is to say, known by the ignorant.
"Vikārādi" refers to transformation and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth are included. The sense is that the gross, perceptible [entity] possesses the fitness to be the substratum for properties such as modification (*vikāra*).
In the formless and subtle;
in that which flashes forth within the consciousness of those who know it, among the knowers of reality; in the sky of consciousness, the space of the intellect.
Modifications and the like would not exist separately.
In what kind of space of consciousness?
In that which has the nature of both being and non-being, whose very essence is both existent and non-existent.
The meaning is that if the transformation and so forth are existent, then it is still composed of that very [substance];
if they are non-existent, then it is likewise.

In the void of consciousness (citkha), the essence of the mind (cittattva), through the savor of the object of thought, expands its own clusters of blossoms— pure as the sky— which are the powers named Time and the rest; this is the glorious honey of consciousness.
The splendor of the honey of consciousness, the beauty of spring known as Consciousness,
expands— that is, spreads— her own clusters of blossoms, which are the powers (śaktis) designated by names such as Time and so forth, and thus endowed with the names of time, place, and the like.
Why?
Because it is endowed with the flavor of the object of thought— that is,
it possesses the savor of what is perceived— and the blossoming of flower-clusters is indeed joined with the essence of the beauty of spring.
What are the powers?
The reality of consciousness (cittattva) consists solely of pure consciousness (cinmātra),
because there is no difference between the power and that which possesses the power.
Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are as clear as space; they do not possess a manifest, gross form.
It is indeed logical that he describes the manifestation of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) by its own nature as having the form of the object of cognition (*cetyarūpatayā*).

The unstruck sheath of consciousness itself flashes forth in manifold variety; the jewel of consciousness itself shines in manifold variety without a cause. [The term *citkañcuka* means "the sheath of consciousness."]
"Kañcuka" (bodice) here signifies, by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), "cloth";
the cloth known as consciousness (*cid*).
By itself, that is, by its own nature.
"It manifests as manifold" means that it becomes possessed of variety, like a variegated cloth;
and this manifoldness should be understood as being produced by the object and the cognizer.
Likewise, the jewel of consciousness itself shines forth in its own manifoldness.
And the polishing of a gem is indeed appropriate;
he himself explains the meaning of "by itself" as "without a cause.
The conscious wind (*cidvāyu*), which is non-inert by nature, possesses an intrinsic vibration that is distinct [from ordinary movement].
The water of consciousness itself possesses a manifold movement that is not buried;
its vibration is of a distinct character, endowed with a movement different from that of external air.
Regarding this, he states the qualifying attribute "consisting of a non-inert self" as the reason.
The sense is that the movement of the inert and the non-inert must necessarily be distinct;
while the water remains buried underground,
it undergoes various writhings and various throbbings.
But consciousness, when it has entered into the depths,
does not undergo various fluctuations.
It exists and yet does not exist;
it is itself a lofty peak of consciousness fashioned from various elements;
it is itself the radiance of consciousness, a moonlight of awareness that is eternally risen, overflowing with manifold aesthetic delights.
The high peak of consciousness (*cic-chṛṅga*), fashioned from various elements (*vicitra-dhātu*) and yet devoid of fabrication (*nirmāṇa-rahita*), is lofty.
Various elements.
"Variegated" means of various kinds;
"elements" refers to the causal substances known as the primary elements (bhūta) in which [they reside].
That [horn] also becomes possessed of various minerals; it becomes endowed with various minerals such as red ochre and the like.
But rather, it is an emanation:
consciousness itself, a moonlight of awareness, radiant with the flavor of manifold wonders, and endowed with the radiance of the flavors of various objects of cognition;
by means of that, it is perpetually arisen.
Even the external moonlight possesses the splendor of various nectarean flavors;
however, it arises only during the bright fortnight.
The various causal substances are themselves always manifest as the stainless, pure light of consciousness.
