When the ignorant person has himself set as it were, consciousness (citi) arises in the knower through knowledge;
the sense is that this is because light possesses the quality of manifestness.
Regarding the word "himself" (svayam): [it refers to the ignorant person].
In the ignorant fool, consciousness itself becomes as if set;
and its state of being "set," even while it remains present, is simply its not becoming an object of knowledge— hence the employment of the word "as if" (iva).
Consciousness itself arises from knowledge in one who knows and is endowed with knowledge;
just as the sun, though blazing in the sky, is not risen for the blind.
But with respect to that which is accompanied by the sense-faculties, it has been stated; the meaning is that this [case] is also like that.
This very [consciousness],
though itself inert, has by its own inertia reached the state of deep sleep within insentient things;
yet, because it is consciousness, it is itself both vibrating and non-vibrating, like the great sky of pure awareness.
Consciousness [is present] in insentient things such as stationary objects;
by means of insentience, that is, by way of being insentient,
it itself is the state of deep sleep, the locus of *suṣupti*.
It has arrived;
it is the great sky of consciousness, the great space called consciousness.
It spontaneously vibrates, endowed with the quality of throbbing radiance.
In that manner, it becomes motionless, endowed with tranquility;
for external space, however, there is motion in the form of wind, while its own essential nature is motionless.
The great sky of consciousness is endowed with radiance; it is endowed with quiescence. (Conformity with the explicans, MT_3,14.68)
In the virtuous one who possesses qualities, consciousness declares the existence and non-existence of the world;
for the world both exists and does not exist as the manifestation of the light of consciousness.
The world both exists and does not exist within the singular emptiness of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). This is certain (*hi*). It is the illumination of the light of consciousness;
that is, the illumination of the light of consciousness known as *cit*, which is the radiance called consciousness.
Light (*prakāśa*) is a quality known as illumination.
The world both exists and does not exist;
the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that existence and non-existence are of equal importance.
The meaning is this:
just as in the case of light, which is the substratum possessing the quality, there exists a quality called "illumination" because it appears as distinct [from the substratum].

Therefore, because it cannot be apprehended apart from that [consciousness], it does not exist. Likewise, the world also exists because it appears within the substrate called consciousness, which is its substratum;
yet, because it cannot be apprehended apart from that [consciousness], it does not exist.
The same should be applied to what follows as well.
Regarding "the space of consciousness" (*cidākāśa*):
the single emptiness of the space of consciousness is the quality known as emptiness (*śūnyatva*).
The state of being the singular void of the space of consciousness.
The letter *ca* [is used].
In the term *cidākhye*, it is written as *°ākhy⟨o⟩[e]* (MT_3,14.69).
The world, which is the great form of the light of consciousness (*cidāloka*), both exists and does not exist.
The world exists and yet does not exist as the dense vibration of the wind of consciousness.
The great form of the light of consciousness is radiant, characterized by the quality known as white.
Regarding "cinmāruta" (the wind of consciousness):
it is well known that vibration (*spanda*) is indeed a quality of air.
The world, which is black with the darkness of the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), both exists and does not exist.
The world exists and does not exist on the day of the light of the sun of consciousness (*cidarka*).
Furthermore, blackness is the quality of darkness.
Regarding the term "sun of consciousness" (*cidarka*): [it refers to the illumination of consciousness].
Because the day conforms to the light of the sun, it possesses that quality.
[In order to confirm what was stated previously, he speaks in every way to establish that the world indeed possesses the quality of consciousness.
To establish [this], he says: *dṛḍhayituṃ*.
The delusion of the world is a single atom of the mountain of consciousness-ink;

the world-line is the heat of the fire of consciousness; and the whiteness of the world is the whiteness of the conch of consciousness. Consciousness itself is the mountain of ink, the mountain of collyrium.
Its [the world's] ultimate constituent is the atom (*paramāṇu*).
It should be understood that the mountain possesses the quality of being the atom because it is metaphorically designated as such by virtue of depending upon it.
The "form of the world" (*jagadākāra*) refers to the delusion of the world (*jagadbhrama*).
"Jagat" means as much as "the world.
"Jagallekhā" is the row or series of worlds.
The world is the interior of the mountain of consciousness; the world is the fluidity of the water of consciousness.

The world is the sweetness of the sugarcane of consciousness; the world is the oiliness of the milk of consciousness; the world is the liquidity of the water of consciousness. The "interior of the mountain of consciousness" refers to the portion within that exists as its essential nature.
Fluidity is *dravatva*;
viscidity is the quality (*guṇa*) known as *sneha*.
The world is the coldness of the frost of consciousness; the world is the blazing of the flame of consciousness.
The world is the oiliness within the ghee of consciousness; the world is the wave in the river of consciousness. (MU 3.14.74) [Note:
ciddhimaśītatvaṃ ] °ma⟨h⟩[ś]ī°]
The "blazing flame" is the crest of fire called consciousness (*cid-ākhyāgni-śikhā*). Its "blazing" is the act of flaming.
Because vibration (*vīci*) consists of a structural arrangement, it possesses the quality of water.
The world is the sweetness of the honey of consciousness; the world is the golden armlet of consciousness;
the world is the fragrance of the flower of consciousness; the world is the fruit at the tip of the creeper of consciousness.
Its quality is its nature as form.
The creeper is metaphorically attributed the quality of being the fruit because it is dependent upon it.
He states the result:
"The existence of consciousness alone is the existence of the world; the existence of the world alone is the body of consciousness."
In this regard, differentiation, modification, and so forth do not exist [in consciousness], just as impurity does not exist in the sky.
Therefore, the very existence of consciousness is the existence of the world; the very existence of the world is the body of consciousness.
The meaning is that the existence of the quality is not different from the possessor of the quality, nor is the existence of the possessor of the quality different from the quality;
this refers here to the distinction, modification, and so forth, between consciousness and the world.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), transformation and so forth are included.
It does not remain as it is.
What is it like?

In the sky, like a stain. [The text] concludes that the world consists of both the existent and the non-existent: "Thus, this triple world, being composed of both the existent and the non-existent, exists as something made of the existent."
"Because it is of the nature of that which is beyond conceptualization, it is either existence, non-existence, or that very [Reality] itself"—
this is according to the manner previously stated.
"The three worlds" refers to the triad known as Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar, or alternatively, the triad of states beginning with waking.
"By being composed of Being" means by being a modification of consciousness whose nature is Being;
thus it "becomes both existent and non-existent.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a distinction between the root cause, consciousness, and its effects based on their respective status as the substratum of existence or non-existence, he says:
"Without conceptualization":
the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative position;
"that very same" refers to these three worlds themselves.
Existence exists in what is non-existent;
why?
Because its nature is not subject to conceptual construction.
"Non-conceptual" means being unfit for the conceptualization of existence or non-existence.
That which is its self is the conscious self;
its state is "reality" (*tattva*).
Therefore,
the meaning is this:
the two words "existent" and "non-existent" denote the agent of the actions of being and non-being.
And thus, the conceptual distinction between agent and object is difficult to avoid;

however, when [the scriptures] speak of existence and non-existence as pure, objectless expressions of the acts of "is" and "is not," they describe nothing other than the nature of consciousness itself, which is free from conceptual construction.
Since the three worlds are non-different from that [consciousness], their status as existence and non-existence is likewise [non-conceptual].
Thus it is logical that there is neither existence nor non-existence.

[Regarding the expression for the action of existence or non-existence that is pure and without objective support: "Indeed, let there be a relationship of part and whole between the world and Brahman. To this, he replies:
"The meanings of the words 'part' and 'whole' are like the horns of a hare."
Fie upon those dull-witted people who have imagined the meanings of the terms "part" and "whole" in order to deny direct experience!
(MU 3.14.78) [Regarding the phrase *avayavāvayavitāśabdārthau*: *yaiḥ* refers to those dull-witted ones.]
In order to deny experience— that is, to deny the experience known as the identity of the world and consciousness—
the term "part-and-whole-ness" (avayavāvayavitā), meaning the relationship designated as the state of being part and whole,
[is employed]; its referent (artha) is the specific relation expressed by that term.
Those two—the meanings of the words "part" (avayava) and "whole" (avayavin)—are conceptualized;
they are imagined through one's own conceptual construction. How are they conceptualized?
Like a rabbit's horn;
the meaning is that it is just as someone might imagine a rabbit's horn, even though it does not exist externally.
"Fie upon them" means that they are indeed objects of reproach;
and their being objects of reproach is due to the cognition of the whole as distinct from its parts.
The point is that there is no such thing as a "whole" distinct from its parts.

(MU 3.14.78) Where the world—including mountains, heaven, the earth, rivers, and lords—does not exist because of the oneness of consciousness, what occasion for error regarding anything else could there be? (MU 3.14.79)
In that place called the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), there exists the world together with its mountains,
sky, earth, rivers, and oceans— that is, accompanied by mountains, space, land, and seas.
Because of the oneness of consciousness, because of the unity of consciousness;
it does not exist.
In this context, regarding the delusion of "otherness," the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
What possibility is there for the other [type of] error, which consists of that effect?
[Including mountains, space, earth, and oceans]—
he explains the state of being composed of everything through the analogy of a stone:
"Though dense as the heart of a stone, consciousness is as clear as its own space."
Just as a stone contains within it its entire tranquil configuration,
so too does consciousness (cit) contain everything in its entirety, being tranquil in the ultimate sense and free from the agitation of existence, non-existence, and the like.
And it maintains a specific arrangement called "sanniveśa" within its own interior.
Of what nature is she? Though "thick" like the *śilāhṛdaya*—
that is, though she is thick like the *śilāhṛdaya* because she is filled with the essence known as "light."
It is indeed as clear as space;
it is truly as clear and stainless as the sky,
but it is not capable of containing the world within itself.
Regarding this, he states an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as):
just as a stone, though filled with its internal essence, contains within it a structural arrangement called a multitude of lines;
such is the meaning. (MT_3,14.80)
[Objection: "But even so, I, the questioner, am indeed distinct [from you], for otherwise a question would be impossible. To this, he says:
"In the space that is the collection of all things, you are like a mere fragment of space."
In the space of the multitude of objects, there are no delineations of "you," "I," "this," "that," or "self," for you are like a mere fragment of space.
The "collection" (*nikara*) of objects is their aggregate;
that very aggregate is the "space" (*avakāśa*) because it is of the nature of nothingness.
In that [space].
The meaning is "in the midst of that.
You are the questioner;
you are like a mere fragment of space.
He states the result with the words "tvattā" and so forth.
Therefore, for you— the questioner—
there are delineations of "being-you-ness," "not-being-you-ness," "the self," and "the delineation of being-you-ness and not-being-you-ness."

The "expressions" (ullekha) exist as the state of being you and the state of not being you, by virtue of having the nature of your existence and my existence. These expressions of "being you and not being me" are the conceptual constructions (vikalpa) of your being and my being.
Conceptual constructions of "thou-ness" do not exist as they abide in the nature of "Thou";
conceptual constructions of "I-ness" do not exist as they abide in the nature of "Me."
Because it has the nature of space.

By means of the simile of the sprout, he explains the subject at hand— the fact that consciousness consists of everything— as being pervaded like the arrangement of a multitude of lines within a sprout, by virtue of its having the nature of your own being.
This consciousness, by its very nature, internally maintains that which consists of both difference and non-difference;
"consciousness" (cit) refers to the subject, and "this" (idam) refers to the object of cognition (cetyam).
Within, that is, in its own midst;
it maintains [itself]. From where?
By way of intrinsic nature.
But surely, with regard to some purpose, of what kind is it?
It consists of both identity and difference.
"Other" means different by its own nature; "not other" means not different by its own nature;
that which has such a self.
That [reality] consists of both difference and non-difference;
furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is extended, meaning endowed with expansion.
How does it bear [the marks]? It is situated within the sprouts, that is, in the midst of the sprouts;
like the arrangement of a multitude of lines within the sprouts, that is, similar to the arrangement of a multitude of lines within the spaces between the sprouts.
And since it is impossible to separate the multiplicity of the mass of writing from its appearance on the sprout— because they cannot be distinguished—
and since their non-difference is clearly established, it serves as a simile.
Where [is it] clear? It is indeed clear:
the primordial grandfather of the entire multitude of causes, being the cause of the causes and so forth.
Know that consciousness is, by its very nature, devoid of causality;
for you are consciousness, the state of being conscious,
through your own experience— that is, by way of your essential nature and your own direct realization.
But it is not so merely by my saying; for the Self is without cause—
that is, its very nature (svarūpa) is devoid of any cause.
Know it to be such; that is, understand it to be so.
Of what nature?
The Grandfather (Pitāmaha) who is the primordial source by virtue of his name as the Cause—that essential nature is the "Cause-Grandfather" (Kāraṇādipitāmaha). Of which causes? [Of all causes.]
Of all the multitudes of causes, that is,
of all the multitudes of causes for the entire range of the perceptible.
Regarding them,
the meaning is this:
the causes of everything that is perceived are the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
The cause of those is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); the cause of that is the principle of consciousness (cittva).
Of what nature is it?
[It is] beginningless (*anādi*).
Now, one might object: "Let consciousness (*cit*) also be unreal, just like the world. To this, he says:
Nor can the non-existence of the inconceivable consciousness be established even by words;
for it is observed that only that which exists arises, like a sprout from a seed.
[The term] *acetyāyāḥ* means "of that which is not defiled by the impurity of the conceivable."
The meaning is that the non-existence of the accumulated [elements] cannot be established even by speech; it is not even fit to say this.
He states the latter half of the verse as the reason for this: "That which...
because whatever exists arises, appearing as something distinct.
"This has been seen by us"—this is the ellipsis.
Here he states an illustration: "from a seed.
This is the intended meaning.
Just as a sprout, existing in the form of a seed, arises from the seed,
so too does the object of cognition exist in the nature of pure consciousness;
and thus, by the impossibility of the object of cognition otherwise [existing], [pure consciousness is established].
"It is not logical that pure consciousness alone should be unreal.
With this verse at the end of the chapter, he summarizes what was previously stated:
"O dear one, within this Great Consciousness there exists the three worlds, possessing distinctions just like the utterly empty sky."
"O dear one, through experience you have become certain that this entire visible world consists of the supreme state;
for the three worlds are within the interior of this Great Consciousness, which is pure consciousness alone."
"Suśūnyabheda" means that whose differentiation (*bheda*) is "suśūnya"— that is, one who is exceedingly *suśūnya*, having the nature of nothing whatsoever.
That [is] "in every way devoid of difference in its own nature"— this is the meaning.
It exists.
What is it like?
It is like the sky;
just as the sky is devoid of differentiation.
The meaning is "so it is.
He states the result with the word "paramam" (supreme):
therefore, being one who possesses such certainty, you are indeed "tvaṃ" (you) endowed with this conviction.
Existence;
from what?
From experience—that is, by means of one's own direct experience.
But it does not happen merely through faith based on what I have said.
Why?
Because the entire visible world is composed of the supreme state; it is indeed the very nature of consciousness, transcending all. It becomes so.
"Of no-thing-form" means one who possesses the certainty that "it is nothing. The venerable Vālmīki informs Bharadvāja of the day's end with a verse at the conclusion of that canto.

When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites; the assembly, having offered salutations, went forth to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun. (Thus ends what was previously stated. *Munimatālaṃkāra* 3.14.86.
When the sage Śrī Vasiṣṭha had spoken— that is, while he was speaking—
then, immediately after the instruction mentioned in the preceding verse.
"Day" (divasaḥ) means "a day" (dinam). "Went" (jagāma) means "passed away" (gataḥ). Regarding this, he states the reason: "to its setting" (astam).
Since the sun, the lord, has set;
"sabhā" refers to the assembly of listeners.
She went to bathe for the sake of the evening rites, such as the evening *agnihotra* sacrifice,
because there is no entitlement to perform any ritual whatsoever without bathing.
That assembly [was held] at the end of the night when the *śyāmā* had ceased— that is to say, at the beginning of the day— by the rays of the sun, that is, by the sunbeams.
Together with her, she returned;
the word "to hear" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
"Snānam" means "to bathe.
Thus ends the fourteenth canto in the *Utpattiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. The venerable Vasiṣṭha offers praise at the beginning of the day to that which is being described:
"Just as a pearl shines within the pure sky, so too does this world, which is of the nature of space, shine within the sky of consciousness. (MU 3.15.1)
This world, as it is being experienced,
becomes nothing but space.
Regarding this, he states a sentence supported by an illustration as the reason, beginning with "yathā hi" (for just as).
The word "hi" is used in the sense of "yasmāt" (because);
because [it is so], the world exists within the stainless *cidgagana*, the space of consciousness.
It shines forth in such a manner;
in what state?
As the self alone, that is, as the very nature of the space of consciousness.
How is it so? Just as in the sky, that is, in the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*),
there is a pearl, meaning a collection of pearls.
It shines.
This is the meaning:
just as a pearl seen in the sky through the vision of an error is actually the sky itself, so it is in the sky of consciousness.
Even the world that is being perceived is nothing but the sky of consciousness.
In the sense of "because":
The puppet of the three worlds appears as if carved, even though it is not carved upon the pillar of consciousness;
yet it is neither carved there, nor is a carver to be found.
In the pillar of consciousness, known as the pillar of *cit*,
the statuette of the three worlds— though not actually carved—
appears as if it were carved.
But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), it does not appear; thus, the word "as it were" (*iva*) is employed.
Now, one might ask: for what purpose is it not said that "it is carved out"? To this, he says: "And not... [and so forth].
That daughter named Jagat is not carved [in stone];
here, the meaning for the sake of conviction must be understood by oneself.
It is not fit to be cut away,
because it has no form whatsoever;
nor is there here a cutter, that is, an agent of cutting away.
It exists because of the absence of duality.
Just as within the ocean there are no stirrings of water, even though they do not deviate from their own nature; (MT_3,15.2) so too [is this].
Just as those who know the supreme become as if they themselves are the objects of knowledge, so too do those who know the visible [world].
The word "yathā" (just as) is to be supplied [to complete the comparison].

"Situated within the ocean" means existing in the interior of the ocean; "the waters' lack of movement" refers to the waves. "Though not fallen from their own nature" means that although they have not deviated from the essential form known as water.
Just as in the case of cognition (*vidi*), with respect to an object (*viṣaye*),
things that are to be known (*vedyāḥ*)— that is, capable of being known by way of being objects of perception—
seem to come into being.
However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), they do not exist; this is why the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed.
Likewise, when the other [the subject] has transcended the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), there are no knowers of the visible, that is, no knowers whose form is the visible.
That is to say, they appear as if they were visible objects.
Even the arrangements of the lattice-like reflections of the sun within water— which appear as gross forms to the world— are, with respect to the subtle atom, like immovable mountains. (MU 3.15.4)

Regarding "the arrangements of lattices of the sun's radiance within the water" (*jalāntargatasūryābhājālakāracanāni*): the sun's radiance that has entered into the water is "the sun's radiance within the water" (*jalāntargatasūryābhā*). The "arrangements of lattices" belonging to that [radiance] are "the arrangements of lattices of the sun's radiance within the water."
And this is its nature: the solar radiance within the water takes on the form of a lattice;
those [reflections] appear so gross to the perception of the world that they are like immovable mountains.
With respect to the subtle, they become gross.
"Contained within the water" [refers to] the "arrangements of lattices";
this confirms the previously stated grossness of the example.
It confirms that the appearance of the world has no appearance of its own, because it is non-different from Brahman;
whereas the reflection of the sun’s rays in water gives rise to the experience of difference.
The appearance of the world becomes non-appearance;
why?
Because it is not distinct from Brahman, meaning that its nature is Brahman.
But in the case of separation (*vyatireka*), the mass of rays from the sun reflected in water provides an experience of separation and brings about the manifestation of duality;
therefore, the sense is that grossness (*sthūlatva*) is appropriate here. (MT_3,15.5)
Even these things— earth and the rest— which have been experienced in this world that has the nature of space, do not exist at all, just as in dreams and mental constructs.
[In the phrase] "having the nature of space," it means having the essential nature of the void of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
In the world;
like what two? Like a dream and a mental construction.
The meaning is that just as the earth and other elements, though experienced in dreams and in mental constructions, do not exist, so it is here.

The grasping at a solid mass (*piṇḍagrāha*)— the notion that "this exists"— is not possible anywhere in this consciousness, which has the nature of space, just as water is not possible in a river of air.
Here, *graha* means grasping.
Grasping like a lump is "lump-grasping" (*piṇḍagrāha*).
The notion that "it exists" is lump-grasping; it is lump-grasping because it is the cause for the conventional usage of "existence.
This occurs while this [object], which consists of consciousness and space-form, is being experienced.
It occurs;
in some place or other, it exists even in a slight degree.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "In a mirage-river," and so forth.
"‘Being’ is the grasping at a solid mass.
[Question: But how does the appearance manifest in this world whose nature is non-existent? To this, he says:
"In this world, which is devoid of grasping at a solid mass and is like a city of imagination..."
In that which lacks the grasping of a solid mass— wherein even what appears as a solid mass is non-existent— it shines like a river in a desert, appearing in the form of an illusion.
In this world, which is like a city of imagination and resembles a city sketched by the mind,
the state of being an object of perception is of the nature of delusion,
consisting of false cognition.
It shines, it gleams;
like what? Like a river in the Maru desert, in the region of Maru.
He explains that because the world is unreal in nature, being of the form of an illusion, it does not fill the scales of a balance, just as in a dream:
"Just as in a dream, there are no two scales whatsoever filled by the mountain of the dream-world."
Freed from mental construction, they are filled with the splendor of the visible world, which is nothing but the void;
like a dream-mountain,
they do not become objects of comparison with the world.
Because weight is of an unreal nature, there is no filling of the scale;
because extension is of an unreal nature, there is no filling of space.
And since this is established by universal consensus in cases such as dreams, it serves as a valid example.
He states the conclusion with the words "kalanā" (calculation/conceptualization): "Free from calculation" means free from the conceptualization known as the state of being an object of perception.
Excluding this cultivation of the meaning of the words "world" (*jagat*) and "omniscient" (*ajña-vijñātṛ*),
there is indeed no difference in the meaning of the words "world," "Brahman," and "ether" (*kha*). (MU 3.15.10)
Regarding the words *jagat*, *brahma*, and *kha*:
"by the ignorant" (*ajñaiḥ*) means by those devoid of knowledge of the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*).
"Known" (*vijñātā*) means made the object of one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*).
The cultivation of the meaning of the word "world" (*jagat*): that is, the continuous contemplation of both the word "world" and its referent.
Having set aside and abandoned that mental cultivation regarding the meaning of the word "world" as understood by the ignorant,
there is indeed no difference or distinction whatsoever among the meanings of the words "world," "Brahman," and "space."
The meaning is that these words are merely synonyms.

Since the world's nature as space is not established for the ignorant person because they do not know the true reality, the abandonment of the conviction regarding the reality of the world and the cultivation of that [conviction] has been stated.
[It] does not exist at all; rather,
this manifestation of the sun of pure consciousness, which is beyond the object of thought, is toward the sky just as subtle as the cloud of volition is toward a [physical] cloud.
But in the case of the specific distinction: for that which shines as pure consciousness alone, whose solar intellect is undefiled by objects of thought, "appearance" (bhāna) means manifestation;
this refers to this world.
"Towards the sky" means in comparison with external space;
"in that manner" means it becomes subtle in that way.

Just as a cloud perceived while awake is subtle compared to a cloud seen by one who is dreaming, so too is a cloud created by one's own conceptualization— sketched forth by one's own mental construction— subtle when compared to a cloud in the waking state. Just as a dream-city is transparent when compared to an excellent city in the waking state...
In this way, this world is transparent with respect to the imagined world,
just as the dream-city is transparent with respect to the excellent city of the waking state according to worldly cognition; it exists as a mere appearance, free from the impurity known as grossness.
It is so from the perspective of the Knower;
this is what is experienced while awake.
The world:

with respect to the imagined world, it is pure, being of the nature of pure consciousness alone, free from the impurity called conceptualization (saṅkalpa); thus it is stainless, even though [it belongs] to the knower.
Even a city in a dream is exactly like that; nevertheless, this was said solely for the purpose of awakening the ignorant.
Therefore, the world, whose nature is consciousness and which cannot be an object of cognition, is nothing but the void alone.
Know that the words "void" and "world" are synonyms, both consisting of pure consciousness.
"Non-objective, conscious form": *acetya* means from that aforementioned reason;
"non-objective, conscious form" refers to the form of pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*).
The world becomes nothing but empty space. He states the conclusion: "they are void."
Therefore, they are empty because of the absence of grasping at a solid mass, having no form whatsoever;
they are composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), having the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*).
Know that the words "space" (*vyoma*) and "world" (*jagat*) are synonyms, as they denote the same meaning. (MT 3.15.13)
With the desire to explain the events that are about to be described, he concludes what was previously stated with three verses:
"Therefore, nothing whatsoever has arisen here in this world of appearances; it remains as it is, unnameable and unmanifest. (MU 3.15.14)
Therefore, because it consists solely of consciousness,
not even the slightest portion of any visible object, such as the world and so forth,
has ever arisen.
Of what nature is it? It is "inexpressible," meaning unworthy of a name.
He states a qualification as the reason for this: it is unmanifest and beyond the range of the senses.
For it is indeed improper to apply a name to that which is not manifested in another form.
Anticipating the objection that "in that case, the world would be something previously non-existent," he provides the qualification "abiding" (avasthitam).
It remains as it is; how? Just as it is situated.
The meaning is: "just as before, so it is now; not, however, by way of being something new.
Just as it was previously known as a snake.
The rope, even when known as a rope, remains exactly as it was before;
it does not attain another form.
Such is the meaning. (MT 3,15.14)
The world itself is the great space, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) which is without walls;
it does not fill even an atom of space or the measure of a scale.
The world is indeed nothing but the space of consciousness.
Of what nature is the space of consciousness?
It is called "great space" because of its vastness in comparison to external space.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
"Without a foundation":
the phenomenal expansion of living beings and so forth serves as a "foundation" by being the locus for their respective attributes;
it is devoid of that.
He states the conclusion with the word "that":
therefore, this world, consisting of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa),
because it lacks weight and lacks extension, does not fill even an atom-sized space or a scale.
It does not become a fulfiller.
The world [is] in relation to external space;
he further qualifies that very same [space].
It is indeed of the nature of space, transparent and devoid of any grasping as a solid mass;
it is a wondrous expanse within the void, composed of space itself, existing like a city of one’s imagination.
It is of the nature of space alone, being of the nature of nothing at all.
It is transparent, its nature being pure consciousness,
and it is devoid of grasping at a solid mass—
that grasping which is like [perceiving] a solid object.
It is devoid of that;
and it is appropriate that space is free from being grasped as a solid mass,
within the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).

Consisting of space means consisting of the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). "Variegated" means a painting; it is like a city drawn by volition, as if sketched by a mental construction (*saṅkalpa*).
Since it is logical that the city of one's imagination (saṅkalpa-pura) consists of space and does not occupy any physical location such as a scale-pan,
the intended absolute non-existence of the entire world is established.

Furthermore, that which was previously described as "origination" is also established as being merely an absolute non-existence by virtue of its resemblance to non-origination; thus, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

He who consists of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśamaya*) bestows manifold wonders (*citrada*). Now, out of compassion for those desiring to hear his life story, [the author] relates the great narrative that establishes how he did not fulfill the scales or the directions of the world.
He says: "In this regard, listen to this narrative of the pavilion, which is an ornament for the ears,
so that this matter may reach a state of rest within your mind, free from doubt."
You are the one free from doubt;
you are the purpose,
for you are the fulfillment of the world's needs regarding its location and so forth.
The Narrative of Maṇḍapa:
The narrative well-known by the name "Maṇḍapa" is the Maṇḍapākhyāna;
listen.
Of what nature is it?
It means it is an ornament for the ears, that is to say, worthy of being heard. What follows from this?
Regarding this, it says "free from doubt" (*niḥsaṃdeha*).
"Just as by which" means:
*niḥsaṃdehaḥ* is one who has emerged from doubt (*saṃdehāt*).
This refers to what was previously stated;

He will attain rest.
(MT 3.15.17) Overcome by haste, Śrī Rāma requests Śrī Vasiṣṭha regarding the narrative of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
[Overcome by haste: *tvarayā*°.
"O Brahmin, for the sake of increasing true awakening (*sad-bodha*), tell me quickly in brief the entire narrative of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), by which awakening increases.
True awakening is the knowledge that the world does not fill the measure of the scales."
"For its increase. He states the result with the words "by which," meaning "by which [it] has arisen" (uditena).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha relates the very narrative of Maṇḍapa:
"On this surface of the earth, there was a king named Padma, a glorious lord of men who possessed many sons and vast treasuries— a blossoming lotus of a lineage."
Regarding "possessing three sheaths" (*trikośavān*):
on this surface of the earth, there was a king named Padma.
He describes his various specific qualities with the word "in the lineage" (*kule*).
The "family lotus" is one that possesses blossoming;
and the blossoming of a lotus is appropriate.
Here, the word "lotus" (*padma*) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to signify excellence.
Possessing abundant treasuries and endowed with many storehouses;
he was an ocean in the maintenance of boundaries, a sun to the darkness of his enemies,
a moon to the night-lotus of his beloveds, and a fire to the thirst for vice.
The ocean’s observance of its boundaries is indeed well known;
he is the moon to his beloved night-lotus,
for his moon-like nature consists in causing her to blossom.
The state of being a fire for the thirst of the humors is due to its capacity to burn away the thirst of the humors.
He is the moon to the night-lotus of the virtuous, the beloved moon,
the Meru mountain for the hosts of gods, the ocean from which the moon of his fame arises,
the lake for the swans of his excellent qualities, and the sun for the lotuses of his arts.
The wise are the learned;
they themselves are the gods, the *vibudhas*.
Of them.
He is like Mount Meru because he bestows much gold and because he serves as a refuge. Regarding "fame":
it is an ocean, a sea, born from the moon of his fame.
He is a lake for the swans whose forms are the six virtues;
he is the sun because he brings about the blossoming of those very arts which are like lotuses.
He is a wind to the ocean of his enemies, a lion to rutting elephants,
beloved of all branches of knowledge, and a mine of all marvelous qualities.
"Śātravam" refers to the multitude of enemies.
That very cloud;
its wind, because it causes destruction;
and here the "elephants" (mātaṅga) refers to the enemy army intended by the speaker.
The beloved husband of all those heroines who are the embodiments of knowledge; and all those qualities are of a wondrous nature.
He is their mine, their place of origin.
He is Mount Mandara, shimmering as it churns the ocean of Śūrāri;
he is the honey from the clusters of flowers of his own play, with good fortune as his flower-weapon.
And those enemies were heroes;
he who was like that ocean,
in whose agitation Mount Mandara shone forth.
The "graces" are indeed the "bewildering charms";
they are the flowers,
and that which is their flood.
Its spring is Madhu,
because it causes blossoming;
by way of its auspiciousness, that is, its state of being beautiful.
Kusumāyudha is Kāma.
He who is a flood [of compassion] because he causes expansion;
who is the wind for the dance of the *līlā* palm trees, the Keśava of the festival of daring; who is the moon for the white lotuses of goodness, and the fire for the creepers of wicked conduct.
Like a playful creeper;
in her dance,
the wind [blows].
The meaning is "endowed with divine play" (līlā).
"Sāhasa" refers precisely to action that disregards what is beneficial or harmful;
it is a festival, a great celebration.
Keśava is Viṣṇu;
he serves as a point of comparison because of his performance of heroic deeds such as the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa and others. His very goodness is the white water-lily (kairava).
Because he causes it to blossom, he is the moon (śaśin);
because he burns the creepers of wicked amorous play, he is fire (anala).
Karma had a fortunate wife named Līlā,
a playful woman endowed with every charm, like a lotus risen upon the earth.
The wife of that king named Padma was named Līlā; he describes her attributes, saying she was "subhagā" (fortunate/charming).
Fortunate, endowed with praiseworthy beauty;
playful, possessed of grace;
and overflowing with every auspicious fortune upon the earth.
She was like a lotus arisen and born;
she was endowed with all perfections, speaking with playful sweetness,
moving slowly with joy, and smiling like the rising of a second moon.
"Līlā" means she who speaks sweetly with playful grace. "Sānandā" means she whose slow movement is full of joy.
"She" refers to her whose smile is like the rising of a second moon. She is she who possesses such a smile.
She,
whose lotus-face was enchanting with its mass of curls, possessed a cool body and was as fair as a *karṇikāra* flower— she was like a moving lotus-pond.
"Adorned with a lotus-face captivating like Alakāli":
that which is captivating like the face of Alakāli; she who is distinguished by that.
Śītāṅgī means one whose limbs are cool;
Karṇikā means fair-complexioned like a karṇikā flower.
Like what? Like a moving, wandering lotus pond.
The lotus-pond as well, charming with bees and abounding in lotuses, becomes cool-bodied and fair-complexioned through its pericarp.
With a lotus-face that smiles like a cluster of kunda flowers in the grace of a creeper, full of aesthetic flavor,
with sprout-like hands and rich in blossoms, she was like the embodied splendor of spring.
"Śālinī" means she who is beautifully endowed with erotic charm (*śṛṅgāra*). "Prabālā" means she whose hands are like young sprouts (*prabāla*).
"Sā" means "puṣpaiḥ," that is, by means of flowers serving as ornaments.
Rich;
like what?
Like an embodied being.
Like the beauty of spring, she too was smiling with clusters of kunda flowers; "with rasa" means with the essence of spring.
And she becomes graceful;
the rest is the same.
[Śālinī] (She who is distinguished by her face-lotus, which is as captivating as that of Alakā’s consort; she whose limbs are cool.
Śā° (MT_3,15.28) Her pure body is holy, bestowing joy upon the people;

"Avadātā" means one whose body is pure and white;
"puṇyā" means fortunate; "janatā" means people.
She bestows joy upon the people; she is called "Haṃsā" because she possesses the grace of a swan.
Where?
To the earth, the ground;
gone.
Like the celestial river Gaṅgā,
she too becomes exactly like that.
Of that Puṣpa, the showerer of flowers upon the earth, who bestows all delight—
It is said that she arose like another Rati in order to perform service for a long time, because it was appropriate for her to perform service for the Flower-Arrowed One (Kāma).
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he describes her virtuous qualities: "When he was anxious, she was deeply anxious; when he was joyful, she was joyful; when he was agitated, she was agitated;
like a reflection, the beloved was identical to him; only when he was enraged was she afraid."
She was his beloved; "of him" is the ellipsis—meaning of that king.
She was like a reflection.

When he is agitated,
she is agitated.
When that is joyful,

Agitated;

(MT_3,15.31) Thus ends the fifteenth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Oṃ. It is said that the king, whose consort was none other than the Apsaras Bhūtalā, took delight with her, his queen, in play characterized by the essence of unfeigned love; he rejoiced with that beloved. MU 3.16.1.

That king, together with his beloved named Līlā, experienced an unfeigned essence of love; that state of unfeigned love was characterized by specific pastimes to be described in the places that follow.
He sports;
with what kind of woman?
With an apsaras of the earth.
Of what nature was he? He was one whose husband was no other woman; that is to say, his husband was none other than her alone, meaning he took delight in her alone.
Regarding those [places] to be described,
he speaks of the sites for play:
"In garden groves and thickets of *tamāla* trees."
In flower-pavilion beds, in dwellings formed by circles of creepers,
in thickets of *tamāla* trees,
and in garden groves— those shrubs which have been fashioned into houses.
Regarding those:
"with flowers" means those pavilions and couches made of flowers.
Among them,
a *maṇḍapa* is a shelter for people;
*latāvalayasadmasu* means in houses consisting of circular enclosures of creepers.
Upon flower-beds in the inner apartments, on pathways strewn with heaps of flowers,
on swings in the spring gardens, and in the pleasure ponds—
those beds in the inner apartments fashioned from flowers.
Regarding those [streets]:
"Flower" means the streets or paths provided with an abundance of flowers, that is, a collection of flowers.
In those [gardens]:
"in spring" means garden swings constructed in the spring; in them.
In the groves of sandalwood trees, beneath the *santānaka* trees, in the dwellings of *kadamba* and *nimba*, and within the thickets of *pāribhadra* trees; [vīthyaḥ]. (MT_3,16.3–4)
*Ṣaṇḍāḥ* means clusters;
*santānakāḥ* are specific types of trees;
*kadamba* refers to [the *kadamba* tree].
In those dwellings constructed at the bases of *kadamba* and *nimba* trees;
[the word] "pāribhadra" refers to them.
The *pāribhadrās* are specific types of trees.
Those [beings] who dwell in mountain caves and thickets, in cities with lattice-windows,
on the banks of rivers and marshy lands, and in houses atop elephants; MU_3,16.5
In those marshy thickets situated within mountain caves; [the word] "vātāyana" refers to these.
And those cities and the upper stories of the houses were provided with windows;
in them—
[as for] the river— so it is said.
Regarding the phrase "among those": it refers to the multitudes of reeds (*kaṭaprā*) found on the banks of rivers and lakes;
[the word] "elephant" (*vāraṇa*) [is used here].
In dwellings constructed upon elephants;
in summer, in houses of snow and in vine-arbors;
in golden palaces and trees, and in walls of pearls and rubies.
"In the palaces of frost" means in cool houses; "golden" refers to those golden palace-trees planted upon the golden palaces.
In those [houses]:
"muktā" means those houses whose walls are fashioned from pearls and rubies (*muktā-māṇikya*). In them. (MT_3,16.6)
In the forest groves of spring, fragrant with the nectar of blossoming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers,
where rows of cuckoos were warbling; (MU 3.16.7).

Regarding the phrase "in those clusters of forest flowers blooming in spring": the two qualifiers *vikasat* ("blooming") and *kūjat* ("warbling") belong specifically to the term *vasantavanajāleṣu* ("in the forest clusters of spring").
And upon patches of various jewel-like grasses with soft luster,
and at waterfalls where showers of shimmering droplets were falling;
[MU 3.16.8] (sthaleṣu) [sth⟨ū⟩[a]°]
And those various grasses were like jewels; upon what kind of grounds were they?
The meaning is "in lotuses of soft radiance.
Regarding the word *nirjhara*:
in what kind of waterfalls?
"Tarat" means "crossing over"; those who have risen up are the prominent stars.
"Śīkarāḥ" refers to droplets of water.
Their "downpour" refers to showers of rain;
they rain upon such [beings].
On the plateaus of the mountains, upon the golden and ruby stone-slabs,
in the dwellings of divine seers and sages, and in hermitages of remote merit; MU 3.16.9.
Upon the stone slabs of mountains that serve as the source of gold and rubies;
[and] upon the blooming lilies and the smiling lotus ponds.
In forest glades where trees were in full bloom, and where lotus ponds were likewise in full bloom.
When the [lotuses] have blossomed with smiles...
Having described the places for play, he speaks of the modes of play:
"By means of riddles, narratives, and likewise by 'fistfuls of syllables' (*akṣaramuṣṭi*)."

With *aṣṭāpada* (chess), with many *bahūddyota* (games of light), as well as with *gūḍhacaturthaka* (the "hidden fourth" riddle), with narratives (*ākhyāna*)— that is, the telling of accounts— and with *akṣaramuṣṭi*, which are specific types of games.
And by means of dramas and narratives, verses with the confusion of dots (*bindumatī*),
distinctions of regional dialects, and the activities of cities and villages—
those narratives which are spoken within dramas.
By means of those—
namely, the *bindumatī* and *bhrama*, which are specific types of play—
the word "place" (*deśa*) [is used].
"By means of the divisions of regional dialects" means by means of those that differentiate them;
"in the city" is to be construed with "by the activities of the city" and "by the activities of the village."

With wreaths, garlands, and strings of flowers, adorned with various ornaments, moving with playful grace, and partaking in diverse aesthetic sentiments; (MU 3.16.13) [līlāvilolacalanair] [moving with playful grace].
"By turns" means by revolutions.
"In various ways" means by the arrangements of various ornaments, that is, by their mutual combinations.
"Līlā" means playful; those movements and gait that are wavering due to play—
by what kind of [movements] were they characterized?
"Vicitra" means various; that is, of various kinds,
such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other *rasas*.
By means of vessels and bowls.
[They were] with one another,
chewing betel leaves along with moist areca nuts and camphor,
and hiding their bodies within groves of flowering creeper-vines.
*Carvaṇaiḥ* means by those that have been chewed. Regarding *phullā*: they are creepers (*latā*) with blossomed flowers (*phulla-puṣpa*).
In those groves belonging to them,
there is the concealment of the body, which means the act of protecting the physical form.
For that purpose, by those contractions which are shortenings; by them.

With playful acts of anointing themselves with unguents, with the graceful sport of swinging on hammocks, and with the sequence of mutual swaying upon flower-adorned swings within their homes; *kharvaṇāni* [is read as] *svakharva°*. (MU 3.16.15)
*Samālambhana* means the application of body unguents.
*Anyonya* means one another,
mutually.
"Āndolana" means swinging;
[it is performed] by means of its successive movements.
[Amusement: [The amusement of] boats, carriages, yoked oxen, elephants, horses, tamed camels, and so forth, by means of coming and going;
with the playful sport of water-sports and the splashing of one another.
And there are boats and vehicles consisting of draft animals— such as tamed elephants, horses, and camels—
as well as the coming and going [of people].
By them;
the herd of elephants was subdued;
"mutually," etc.
"Mutually" means one another. "Sprinklings" means acts of pouring; by means of those.
[They were adorned] with the modes of dance, song, artistic performance, *lāsya*, *tāṇḍava*, and martial movements.
By means of musical performances, conversations, and the playing of lutes and drums—
those intense and exuberant activities such as dancing and so forth.
Furthermore, he describes the places of sport:
in gardens, on trees by the banks of rivers, in forest groves,
in inner apartments, and in palaces— in those various places, in such various ways.
In this way, through various kinds of pastimes as previously described,
that young woman, who had been raised in comfort and was his devoted and beloved mistress,
once reflected, being possessed of auspicious intentions.
The beloved wife of that king named Padma was she known as Līlā.
Once,
on one day,
the girl reflected; she gave rise to a thought.
Of what nature was she?
She was raised in comfort.
Furthermore, of what nature was she?
"Pure" means endowed with a pure intention—that is, a praiseworthy intention as will be described hereafter. "Śālinī" [means possessed of that].
[Līlā] asks: "What was she thinking? To this he replies:
"This lord of the world, my husband, is dearer to me than even my own life."
"How might he, possessing the splendor of the exuberance of youth, become ageless and immortal?"—the construction is:
"How might this husband of mine be ageless and immortal? that is, free from the defects known as old age and death; by what cause would he be so? This is the syntactical connection.
From living beings, from those endowed with life.
(MT 3.16.20) With this husband, how might I, possessing lofty breasts, sport at will for a hundred years among the flower-pavilions? (MU 3.16.21)

"How might I enjoy myself for hundreds of years with this beloved husband? By what means might I engage in play for a hundred years?"—this is the meaning. "In that manner, I shall strive through the sequence of austerity, recitation, self-restraint, and ritual acts, so that the King, who possesses the luster of the moon, may become free from old age and death. (MU 3.16.22)
The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied [from the context]. Therefore, by means of those [austerities, recitations, and self-restraints] as instruments, I exert effort accordingly.
Just as the moonlight at night dispels the darkness,
may the King be free from old age and death.
[The Moonlight] An explanation without taking into account the nature of the *bahuvrīhi* compound:
(MU 3.16.22) "I ask those twice-born who are advanced in knowledge, advanced in austerity, and advanced in learning: how might death not occur for human beings? (MU 3.16.23)
"I shall ask the twice-born who are advanced in knowledge, advanced in asceticism, and likewise advanced in learning as follows:
'How might death not occur for men? By what cause might it not occur? (MT 3,16.23)
Having stated her resolve, she spoke of the external effort:
then, having quickly summoned and honored the twice-born, she, bowing low, asked them again and again, "O Brahmins, how might immortality be attained? (MU 3.16.24)
Now, immediately after the resolve;
regarding the word "having summoned" (ānāyya),
the word "by the attendants" (parijanaiḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Again and again" (*punaḥ punaḥ*) is intended to indicate the intensity of desire. The Brahmins say in reply:
"O Goddess, all the perfections (*siddhi*) and the powers of the perfected ones (*siddha-siddhi*) are attained through austerity (*tapas*), recitation (*japa*), and self-restraint (*yama*)."
Immortality is indeed attained, yet it is never fully obtained; this refers to the perfections of the perfected ones—
those who are endowed with siddhis.
"But the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) arise through the opposite.
Having heard that the fulfillment of his desires comes from the twice-born, he again expressed his concern regarding them.
Having heard this from the mouth of the twice-born, she, terrified of separation from her beloved, reflected again immediately through her own wisdom.
"By his own wisdom alone, and not by following what was said [by others].
To the question "What did he contemplate?", it is said here:
"If by fate my death should occur before that of my husband, then,
liberated from all suffering, I shall abide happily in my own self.
The meaning is that this is because she would no longer witness the sorrow of her husband's death.
"Now, if my husband should die first after a thousand years,
I shall act in such a way that his life-force (jīva) will not depart from this house.
The phrase "after a thousand years" indicates a blessing.
Now, if the husband or others should die at the end of a thousand years,
then I will employ such a means by which the life-force— the life-force of the husband— shall [be restored].
He will not go out from the house.
Now, if [it is] so, then what? To this he says:
"Because of that delusion, while her husband was still alive, in this very private inner chamber..."
Constantly beheld by my husband, I shall dwell in happiness;
I shall dwell there because of that delusion.
"Thinking through delusion that 'my husband is looking at me,' I shall always,
forever,
return as I please."
Of what nature am I? While this husband of mine, my own, remains alive in this inner apartment (*śuddhānta-maṇḍapa*) by means of the stratagem accomplished by me.
Beheld by her husband means looked at by him.
"I shall return at my ease.
Starting this very day for this purpose, I shall worship the goddess Sarasvatī with prayers, fasts, and observances until she is satisfied.
"Even today, and not tomorrow"—
for this purpose, so that he whose husband is alive would not depart from his own home;
[he addressed] the Goddess Jñapti, the Goddess who is his own intuition.
"Up to satisfaction" means up to the limit of serene confidence (*prasāda*).
[Objection: But how is it heard that [the goal] is through the propitiation of *jñapti*?
[Response: We say it is precisely from the serene confidence (*prasāda*) arising from *jñapti*.
This is because, in all cases, the cause is solely the clarity of cognition (*jñapti-prasāda*).

Furthermore, the instruction on cognition (*jñapty-upadeśa*) to be explained later should be understood as being produced by one's own creative intuition (*sva-pratibhā*); for whatever is performed or heard as a matter of play is [accomplished] by that very same creative intuition.
Even that which is heard through the mouth of a teacher and others is [grasped] by one's own intuition alone,
because one's own intuition is present in all cases.
Having resolved that she would speak of her efforts immediately after her reflection, that beautiful woman, without even informing her lord,
undertook a rigorous penance according to the scriptures, remaining firm in her observances.
Without even stating [this], she remained established in that very restriction; for without it, asceticism would be in vain. (MT 3,16.31)
He describes that austerity by way of its specific qualifications:
"At the conclusion of every three-night period, having performed her breaking of the fast, she was devoted to the worship of gods, twice-born ones, gurus, the wise, and the learned. (MU 3.16.32)
"At the end" (*paryante*) means at the conclusion of three nights; the doubling [of *trirātrasya*] indicates distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
Her body is constantly engaged in bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation.
One whose body is constantly engaged in bathing and other such rites, performing all that is prescribed by the scriptures and right conduct, yet causing affliction.
"She" refers to [the goddess].
"All" means one who possesses faith (āstikya), that is, one who is fit for faith.
Affliction takes the form of ascetic heat.
"Regarding the word 'all' (*sarva*) [in the verse]: ... at the baths and other rites...
"All" (MU 3.16.33) means according to the proper time, according to her exertion, according to the scriptures, and in the correct order;
she thus gratified her husband, whose inner state remained unknown to her. (MU 3.16.34)
Uncomprehended is that play;
his state consists in performing these three as austerity—by means of which he [is such]. (MT 3,16.34)

For three hundred nights, that girl, steadfast in her observances, remained engaged in arduous exertion, dedicated to unceasing austerity. Regarding the word "unceasing" (*anārata*): it refers to that in which there is a constant application (*niṣṭhā*) to austerity.
That is an adverbial modifier; it refers to an arduous exertion consisting of activities such as breaking the fast after three nights, which brings about suffering. (MT_3,16.35)

Then, having been worshipped for a hundred three-night periods, the blessed goddess Gaurī Vāgīśī, who had attained the form [of the image], being pleased, spoke this to her: *atha jñaptiprasādam āha trirātrāṇāṃ śatenātha pūjitā pratimām itā / tuṣṭā bhagavatī gaurī vāgīśīdam uvāca tām //* MU_3,16.36 Then, having been worshipped for a hundred three-night periods, the blessed goddess Gaurī Vāgīśī, who had attained the form [of the image], being pleased, spoke this to her.
[Having been] worshipped, then immediately following the observance (*niyama*),
there is the injunction of Vāgīśī.
Gaurī is of pure nature.
Her status as Vāgīśī (the Mistress of Speech) is to be understood through her being the root cause of all words.
"Having gone to an image" means she has taken recourse to an image made of stone or other materials.
The sense is that, by means of his own creative power (*pratibhā*), he granted her a vision of himself through a reflection (*pratimā*) appearing within it.
He spoke these words being made known through his instruction:
"By means of uninterrupted austerity that surpasses devotion to one's husband..."
"I am well-pleased with you, my child; accept a desired boon. Having heard this formal request, the queen praised her.

Victory to you, O moonlight to the defect of the burning pain of the flames of birth and old age! Victory to you, O sunlight for dispelling the mass of darkness within the heart! (MU 3.16.38) [Note: *hārdāndha* is the corrected reading for *dāhāndha*.]
It is well known that the light of the moon wards off the defect of burning, while the light of the sun dispels darkness.

O Mother, Mother of the three worlds, protect me, this wretched one! Grant these two auspicious boons that I here entreat. [The capacity to ward off the defect of burning. O Mother, protect me, this miserable one; grant these two boons which I here pray for as auspicious.
"Pitiable" means miserable.
"Auspicious" is an adjective qualifying the two boons. Among the two boons, he states one:
"First of all, O Mother, let the life-force of my husband, the Lord of Videha,
not depart from this very pavilion of his own inner apartments;
grant me this one boon from among the two boons."
In response to the inquiry "What [should happen]?", he says: "videhe" etc.
For one who is "videha," that is, dead, let there be no departure;
let him not go.
The second [vow] he declares:
"O Great Goddess, I pray to you for a second time: whenever I desire to see you for the sake of a boon, then grant me your vision."
"Give me this second one. In response to the inquiry "What [second thing]?", he says: "Thee," O Goddess.
"When I pray for a vision of you, then, by virtue of the boon, out of compliance with the boon,
grant me a vision. Having accepted the two boons, he made this known.

Having meditated upon the supreme, indescribable light of direct intuition, and having contemplated in his heart the Lord Śrī Gaṇeśa, the all-pervading remover of the fear of worldly existence, and having placed at his crown the mass of dust from the feet of his guru, Bhāskara now extends this commentary on this excellent treatise titled *Sthiti*.

Having observed that Śrī Rāma had attained conviction, he thereafter begins the appropriate section on the maintenance of the world:

For memory has reached rootlessness because the rememberer has attained liberation.
[The reading] *smṛtiḥ* is found in Ś3; *smṛti°* in N17, Ś1, and Ś6.
It is clear [that it means "memory"].
Therefore, in the absence of a rememberer (*smartṛ*), from what would that memory arise, and how?
For indeed, in the great aeon (mahākalpa), all beings without exception shall partake solely in liberation.
This is clear.
[Clearly] Ś6 omits "spaṣṭam" (MT_4,3.8).

That memory which occurs spontaneously in the experienced and the unexperienced sky of consciousness—that is the glorious majesty of the world; for in the absence of the visible, there is only the radiance of consciousness. MU_4,3.9
Not by itself, but through the assumption of the form of Prajāpati;
not with respect to an object previously unexperienced,
but with respect to an object previously experienced.
The memory that arises within the sky of consciousness regarding an experienced object becomes the matured splendor of the world.
The meaning is that this is not the tradition of Prajāpati.
Why is this so?
To this he says: "Because it is seen."
For because, when there is an absence of the visible— that is, when there is an absence of the visible in the form of memory—
there remains only the radiance of consciousness.
It does not possess the splendor of Prajāpati.
[Thus] N17: "iti" [means] "thus" (MT_4,3.9).
Alternatively, enough with this conceptual construction based on memory;
for, with the intention that the world exists as nothing other than the radiance of consciousness, he says:
It is the radiance of consciousness alone that shines, pure and manifesting without beginning or end;

that which exists as this "world" and as the "Self-existent" (Svayambhū) is nothing other than this. Manifesting without beginning or end means being eternally luminous, devoid of the appearance of a beginning or an end.

That which shines as something transparent is nothing other than the radiance of consciousness itself; it exists as this very world, and it exists as the Self-existent (Svayambhū). Therefore, the sense is that there is no existence whatsoever for either memory or a Self-existent being.
That manifestation of Brahman which has been established since beginningless time, which is its own innate nature—
that is the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) of Virāj, having the form of the universe.
Established from beginningless time, eternally perfected,
belonging to Brahman— the reality of pure consciousness— whatever is its own, intrinsic to it.
It becomes manifest;
that is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) of Virāj, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), who possesses the form of Virāj.
Of what nature is he? He has the form of the world; that is, his essential nature is that of the entire universe.
[The world-form: Within the atom, this world shines forth together with the three worlds, endowed with the succession of place, time, action, substance, day, and night. (MU 4.3.12)
Substance is the category of reality that is the object of action;
[the author] will explain later in the section on Nirvāṇa that it extends down to the atom and manifests throughout the three worlds of Indra.

Then, with respect to each atom, its interior is exactly like that.

Ś6: *bhāsvaritā*; N17: *bhāsuritā* ...
surrounded by such mountain ranges] N17, Ś1, Ś3, Ś6:

Therefore, for that reason,
within each and every atom, there exists that triple world which resides inside the atoms.
Within every single atom,
it is exactly like that and not of any other form;
it has a radiant appearance, surrounded by such mountain ranges and filled with such multitudes of peaks.

it appears as a visible object consisting of light, my dear, yet it is not real. (MU 4.3.14)
Even there, within the three worlds that exist in every atom,
its nature is light— that is, its essential form is knowledge.
He states the result with the words "this [is it]."
Therefore, O dear one, this triple world is real;
it exists as the ultimate truth.
It does not exist,
because its nature is that of light, like a dream.
In the three worlds,
there is no end anywhere to either right view or wrong view;
yet for this [view], O sinless one, awakening has arisen, whether toward that which is awakened or that which is unawakened.
In this manner,

the "end" (anta) refers to the view of existence (*saddṛṣṭi*), which is the view of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), or the view of non-existence (*asaddṛṣṭi*), which is the view of the objectified (*cetya*).
There is no end to this right view and this wrong view.
"Abhyudita" means "arisen" (abhyudaya).
This refers to manifestation. It occurs either with respect to a Buddha or with respect to one who is not a Buddha.
The sequence should be understood as follows: with respect to a Buddha, there is the arising of right view; with respect to one who is not a Buddha, there is the arising of wrong view.

from [wrong] view comes prosperity;

so how can it be said that for the awakened (buddha) there is no end to right view (saddṛṣṭi), while for the unawakened (abuddha) there is no end to wrong view (asaddṛṣṭi)? To this he says:
To one who has awakened, this is indeed only Brahman— solely peaceful and imperishable;
but to one who has not awakened, there is duality, radiant and accompanied by the worlds.
This very world appears as real to one with right view, and as unreal to one without right view.
Just as a single rope appears as a rope to one who has awakened [to its true nature], but appears as a snake to one who has not awakened; such is the sense.
Just as this radiant world shines forth, expanded within a cosmic egg,

That whose essence or intrinsic nature consists of that alone. That.

When that is severed, the tree of karma— the branch of the world— becomes severed.
Of what nature is the tree of karma? It is such that the worlds themselves are its branches; it is like that.
"O Rāma, all this is mind; within that, when it has been investigated, this entire existence consisting of the web of births has been investigated.

apart from the mind, where indeed is the body ever seen?

it is the absolute non-existence of the visible object, and not due to any other cause.

the absolute non-existence of the visible, which is the absolute absence of the visible.]

The mind takes up delusion; it dies and is born again.

[This refers to] someone—the ineffable, pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
Thus the entire world flashes forth when the mind is agitated by mental constructs.

so too this entire expansive world flashes forth and exists within the mind— which is slow-moving in its deliberations yet filled with thought.

it is pervasive and expansive.

Just as a mass of waves exists in water, and just as there is the delusion of two moons regarding the moon; [so is this].
As a mirage appears in the heat, so does cyclic existence appear within the mind;
this is clear.
As a web of rays exists in the sun, and as light exists in fire.
