it is pierced by the falling torrent of rain at the onset of the clouds. (MU 4.9.12)
"Like dry wood" (*śuṣkakāṣṭhavat*): "pierced" (*vinunnā*) means impelled, that is to say, moved. (MT_4,9.12)
On the bank of a mountain river,
flooded by the torrential rush of monsoon cascades, she stood like a forest stone, hissing with loud gasps from the wind.
She stands like a forest-stone; that is, she in whom there is the hissing sound of the wind (*mārutaśītkāraḥ*), and she stands like a stone in the forest (*vanopala*).
Crooked, with strings of dried entrails, foul-smelling, and making a *jhāṅkāra* sound, she is like the lute of the Goddess of the Forest, her belly made of empty skin. (MU 4.9.14) [Note:
*śuṣkāntratantrī* is attested as *śuṣkān⟨d⟩[t]ra°* in N17.]

The lute of the forest's splendor is the *araṇyalakṣmīvīṇā*; he was like it. [Objection: "Surely, how was such a body of his not devoured by the wild predators of the forest? To this, he says: "Because that holy hermitage was free from passion and hatred."
And because of Bhṛgu’s great austerity, [the fruits of his labor] were not consumed by beasts or birds.
Furthermore, the freedom from passion and hatred regarding the holy hermitage is to be understood through the freedom from passion and hatred of the living beings residing there.
Regarding that, [the text] states: "Because of being free from attachment and aversion while abiding therein" (N17: *tatrasthaprāṇirāgadveṣavihīnatvena*).
He expresses this very same point even with the final verse of the chapter (*sargāntaśloka*).
The mind of the descendant of Bhṛgu, Śukra, whose slender body had been emaciated by restraints and observances, was engaged in asceticism;
meanwhile, his body, its blood drained away by the wind, rolled for a long time upon those great rocks.
(MU 4.9.16) [Of the descendant of Bhṛgu, Śukra, whose slender body had been made thin by *yama* and *niyama*.]
The mind practiced asceticism.
Then that body, its blood having been removed by the wind, rolled upon great rocks. May there be auspiciousness.
"luṭhitavatī" [N17: luṭhita]vatī (MT_4,9.16).
Thus ends the ninth canto in the chapter on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Then, after a thousand divine years, Bhṛgu, the Supreme Lord, desisted from his meditative absorption due to supreme awakening. From what kind of meditative absorption? From one characterized by supreme awakening.
Because of his supreme enlightenment, his nature of knowledge was unstained by the impurities of the knowable;
it was not, however, in a state of swoon.
He did not see before him that son, whose face was bowed down in humility.
The boundary of the limit of virtues, standing as if merit were incarnate. (MU 4.10.2) [Note:
*guṇasīmāyāḥ* is clearly read as *guṇasīmāyāḥ* in N17.]
He saw before him a great skeleton, appearing as mere time,
like misfortune embodied or poverty personified—
time that was black.
A skeleton is a skull;
misfortune is the reversal of fortune.
[The text] further specifies the skeleton.
His body was withered by heat; a partridge fluttered within the openings of his skin;
and a frog rested in the shadow of the hollow of his dried-out entrails and belly.
The caves, where peacocks rest in the shade;
the partridges, which are a species of insects;
and the forest-insects sleeping within the hollows of the eyes of the blossoms.
A swarm of cocoon-spinning worms threaded through a cage of flies— meaning,
within the swarms of flies seated in the shape of a cage, a multitude of cocoon-spinning worms is interwoven.
In that [state],

with a body whose extremities were washed by the stream [of tears], laughing with a garland of dry bones, he abandoned his former longing for enjoyments which yield desired and undesired fruits. (MU 4.10.6)
[She who bestows desired and undesired fruits];
[with her extremities washed by the stream]. The meaning is: "as if laughing while laughing. (MT_4,10.6)
With his bright, well-formed head, possessing the luster of the moon,
he emulated the beauty of the top of a *liṅga* smeared with camphor.
With the luster of the moon, possessing the brilliance of the moon;
the *liṅga* is the Śiva-liṅga.
Straight, completely withered and white, with only its own bones remaining.
“With its neck extended, as if lengthening its form” (MU 4.10.8). “Extended by itself” means by its own self.

With his face bearing a nose-bridge as white as a lotus stalk, which was attached and continuous, and from which the flesh had been washed away by the stream [of blood], he maintained a distinct boundary between the upper and lower parts.
Having established the sequence of boundaries, having established the sequence of limits;
surely with her long neck and mouth turned upward,
she was as if watching his life-breaths as they were departing into the belly of the sky.
Surely, in his deliberation:
with his shanks, thighs, knees, and staff-like arms having attained double their length, he was as if measuring the world, fearing the exhaustion of such a long journey. (MU 4.10.11)
The quarters of the sky were unpeaceful.
(MT 4.10.11) With a belly deeply sunken, reduced to mere skin and parched, it seemed to demonstrate to the ignorant the extreme emptiness of the heart. (MU 4.10.12)
This is clear.
(MT_4,10.12) Having gazed upon that dried skeleton, which was like a tethering post for an elephant, Bhṛgu rose up without reflecting on what had preceded or followed. MU_4,10.13
What was Bhrigu doing? Out of affection for his son, he failed to reflect on what had preceded and what followed.
For even among yogis, due to the power of *prakṛti*, there may occasionally occur the falling away of the body as well as a state of lacking reflection on what precedes and follows.
It arises; however, for them, that [arising] is indeed momentary.
"Having arisen" means having moved away from the reflective awareness of one's own essential nature (*svātmatattva*).
[Regarding the reflection on what precedes and follows: Indeed, for Bhṛgu, that which appeared was simultaneous with the light; therefore, [there is] the reflection on what precedes and follows.
"Has this son of mine been dead for a long time?"—thus [he thought] in an instant.
"Thereafter" means immediately after rising; "simultaneous with the light" means simultaneous with the sight of his son's skeleton.
"It occurred to me regarding Bhṛgu; it flashed across my mind.
Why? Because this son of mine has, for a long time—that is, for many years—"
Starting from [this point]: "having departed with the life-force" (utkrāntajīvaḥ) means what? How so? It means "having become fully integrated" (sampanna).
At the very moment he saw the skeleton of his son, by the power of the inevitability of what was to be,
there arose within him an immediate and most terrible anger directed toward Time.
Now, the power of what is to be (bhaviṣyattābala) is the power of destiny (bhavitavyatābala).
Of this Bhṛgu, who was not reflecting— that is, who lacked prior and subsequent deliberation arising at that very moment and thus failed to reflect— [this power operates].
Regarding time— that which consists of the manifold variety of activities residing within pure consciousness—
a most terrible wrath arose. (MT 4.10.15)
"Why has my son been taken away at an improper time?"— thus provoked,

the Blessed One began to cast a curse upon Time (*kāla*). "At an improper time" (*akāle*) means in the absence of Time, characterized by the non-completion of the lifespan of humans destined for that particular age.
This is the intended meaning here:
having attained the state of pure consciousness alone through non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi), this Bhṛgu [realized it].
Having arisen from that meditative concentration,
he then began to be slightly affected by external touch, like a crystal.
There, having first seen his son dead at an untimely hour, he became overwhelmed; immediately thereafter,
by means of his own nature which is pure consciousness, he desired to destroy that time which had manifested as a variety of actions.

And as for this arrival of time, how could it be that one thinks, "I shall destroy this which is self-made and co-existent with its own nature"? This should be understood as the very arrival of discernment (*viveka*).
Let us leave aside the unveiling of such secrets.
Then that Time, whose form was unperceived and who had devoured all creatures,
assuming a physical body composed of material elements, approached the sage.
One whose form is unthought:
he whose form has not entered the state of being an object of cognition because it exists as having reached the nature of the supreme self.
That body, which is of a material nature, should be understood as being essentially of the nature of inquiry from the perspective of ultimate reality;
however, for those who are external [to this], it is of the nature of a deity.
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of means (*upāya*) he possesses, [the text] explains that for those with external views, he has the form of an external deity:
"The glorious one, bearing a sword and a noose, adorned with earrings and clad in armor."
He has six arms and six faces, and is surrounded by a vast army of servants.
This is clear.
(MT 4.10.18) That sky, by means of the leaping mass of flames arising from his body, bore the splendor of a mountain of blooming *kiṃśuka* trees. (MU 4.10.19)
This is clear.
(MT_4,10.19) By the circles of fire spat from the tips of the tridents held in his hands, the quarters of the sky shone as if with rising golden earrings. MU_4,10.20
This is clear.
(MT_4,10.20) When the mountain peaks were exhausted by the wind from his noose, the mountains moved and fell, reeling as if they had mounted a swing. MU_4,10.21
"With their peaks strained" means with their peaks drawn back.
The orb of the sun, darkened by the radiance of the circle of his sword,
shone as if it were obscured by the smoke from the world consumed at the end of an aeon.
It was clearly filled with the smoke from the world consumed by the fire at the end of the eon. (MT_4,10.22)
Approaching that great sage who was enraged and as deep as the ocean agitated at the end of an aeon, the mighty-armed one spoke to him with conciliatory words:
O Sage, those who have understood the nature of the world and have seen both the higher and the lower are not deluded even by a cause, much less without a cause— how much more so the supreme ones!
"Seen" means experienced as one's own essential nature.
The "Supreme and the Subordinate" refers to the reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātratattva*) abiding in the form of both the supreme and the subordinate. By whom? By them.
You are a Brahmin of infinite austerity; we are the guardians of destiny.
Therefore, O holy one worthy of worship, you are honored by me according to my own desire and not otherwise;
for you possess infinite austerity— that is, immeasurable austerity—
and it is by virtue of that infinite austerity that you are so honored.
[Regarding "by virtue of infinite austerity"]:
O you of infinite austerity, do not exhaust yourself with the great fires of the kalpa that are agitated by time.

"What will you burn with your curse against that which is not burnt by me?"—the sense is: "I am who I am; since time, whose nature consists of the manifold variety of the activity of pure consciousness, can never burn anything, [it is impossible for your curse to affect me]."
"You shall burn":
this is the usage of the verb *daha*, meaning "to reduce to ashes," in its future tense (*lṛṭ*) form.
At times,
the cycles of saṃsāra have been swallowed and ten million Rudras have been devoured.
"O Sage, by whom were the hosts of Viṣṇus devoured, and why have we been cursed?
[vayam] Ś1, Ś3: vayam; N17: varam spaṣṭam. (MT_4,10.27)
"For we are the eaters, O Brahmin, while you and others are the food. This is indeed our own destiny; it was not by our own will that this came to pass for us or for you.
(MU 4.10.28) "For us" means for both you and ourselves.
The desired object is what is sought.
(MT 4.10.28) Fire moves upward by itself; waters move downward by themselves;
the eater goes toward the food, and creation also goes toward its end by itself. (MU 4.10.29)
At the time of the end,
O Sage, this form of the Supreme Self appears here in this manner;
within its own self, the Self itself unfolds by its own power.
The Supreme Self unfolds through various activities and sports;
by the vision that has destroyed all stains, there exists here neither an agent nor an enjoyer.

And here, many are the agents [of action] by means of a vision that is free from stain; [many are those] by means of a vision that is stained. "By means of a vision free from stain" refers to right vision (*samyagdṛṣṭi*);
"by means of a vision that is not free from stain" refers to wrong vision (*asamyagdṛṣṭi*).
O Brahmin, agency and non-agency are merely imagined through incorrect vision alone, and not through correct vision for you. This is clear.

Flowers in groves of trees and living beings in the worlds come and go here of their own accord; yet the causality of a Creator is imagined by the deluded. Here, the causality of a Creator is imagined—that is, it is conceptualized through mental construction.
But in the ultimate sense, causality does not belong to anything at all,
because only the solitary, pure consciousness alone exists.
Just as in the movement of the reflected moon there is neither agency nor non-agency— neither real nor unreal— so it is with respect to the creations of time.

Of me, who am Time, whose nature consists in the variety of actions— (MT_4,10.34)— the mind, through false delusion, creates in this world the notion of agency and non-agency, just as one with impaired vision perceives a snake in a rope. MU_4,10.35
This is clear.
He states the conclusion:
"Therefore, O Sage, do not give way to anger; such is the course of calamities."
"Whatever is, let it be exactly so; look at the truth without agitation. For such indeed is the course of calamities.
The sense is that all these [qualities] come to everyone;
whatever exists in whatever way,
let it remain exactly so.
You are agitated and have become overwhelmed;
behold the truth within this net of auspicious and inauspicious karma that has come flowing forth.
The sense is: "Do not fall into agitation.
(MT 4.10.36) We have not been moved by a desire for power, nor are we overcome by pride; rather, we abide solely in destiny through the force of our own inherent disposition. (MU 4.10.37)
We are not established in the determination made by the Blessed One— that is, in the restriction— on account of our power, meaning for the sake of exercising power.
Nor do they remain under the sway of pride; rather,
they abide solely in destiny, arising from their own inherent nature and by the power of their natural disposition.
The sense is that there is nothing whatsoever here that depends upon us.

A wise person, not shrouded by the great darkness of self-conceit, should conform to the established worldly conventions determined by the power of destiny; he should not follow his own arbitrary whims.
"Fixed" means fixed by the scriptures.
Of what nature is the wise one? He is not one who possesses conceit—that is, the sense of "I-making" (ahaṃkāra) itself is not conceit. Conceit...

Such is he whose nature is thus characterized by darkness. (MT 4.10.38) Only that which is to be done is performed by those skilled in action, having resorted to the state of deep sleep and being free from any desire whatsoever. (MU 4.10.39)
The sense is that the wise perform everything entirely without regard for the fruits [of their actions].
(MT_4,10.39) Where is that vision consisting of knowledge, where is your greatness, and where is your fortitude?
For when the path is well-known to all, why do you wander in confusion like a blind man? (MU_4,10.40)
Immediately upon being experienced,
it is established as something entirely worldly;
even while maintaining in his mind the vision of the three times free from defilement.

Without investigating the course of the world, why do you become deluded like a fool? [The state of] possessing stainless vision regarding the three times consists in being the locus of reflection upon what precedes and what follows.

[The state of possessing stainless vision of the three times: Regarding his son, without considering the condition arising from the ripening of the fruit of his own karma, [he spoke thus]. N17: °darśitvam (MT_4,10.41).
"O Omniscient One, why do you wish to curse me in vain like a fool? (This is clear.
"O Sage, for all embodied beings here, the body is of two kinds."
"Do you not know that there is one body, and another called the mind?
The 'body' refers to the gross body;
the 'other' is the second."
In this regard, the body is utterly insentient and solely intent on destruction;
the mind, however, is fixed on exertion, and whether it perishes through hardship or not depends on its engagement in the effort of volitional resolve.
The mind is fixed;
it is exhausted by the affliction of what is worthless. Or else:
By that [mind] also, it is not exhausted.
(MT 4.10.44) Just as, O virtuous one, a chariot is driven by a skillful charioteer who exerts some effort, so too is this body [driven] by the mind. (MU 4.10.45)

It is carried away; it is led toward its desired destination. Having conceptualized what is unreal, the real body is destroyed in an instant by the mind, just as a child destroys a figure made of mud.
"Non-existent" means not being present;
"existent" means being present.
In this context, the mind itself is the person, and what is done by it is said to be "done."
That [mind] is bound because of the cause of conceptualization (*kalanā*); it is liberated when conceptualization has ceased.
"Because of the cause of conceptualization" means due to the cause known as volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*). "When conceptualization has ceased" means that conceptualization has come to an end.
"This body, this eye, this limb, this head—
this [entirety] characterized by expansive modifications is designated as the mind alone.
How is that mind?
This is "of expansive transformation.
"This" refers to that which is expansive (*sphāra*), having the nature of radiating (*sphuraṇaśīla*); it is such a thing as has "transformation" (*vikāra*). Thus it is [described].
That which is designated as "mind" by the wise—
what is that?
It is this body, this eye.
"That this is a limb and that is the head"—this is what occurs.
For it is the mind (*manas*) that is called the "living" (*jīva*), while the intellect (*dhī*) is so called by virtue of its determinative nature;
the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is so called because of its conceit (*abhimāna*), for it is through this that multiplicity arises.
Live, assuming the agency of the act of living; by way of being a determiner— that is, by virtue of being the agent of determination—
because of [the soul's] sense of self-identification [with that role].
[The self] exists as the agent of the conceit "I am the body. Multiplicity consists in the forms of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, which are manifold.
If the mind, through the latent impression of the body, considers other things to be its own...
One perceives as if there were earthly bodies;
"earthly" refers to the mental impression (*vāsanā*) of the body, namely the impression that "I am the body," which arises through the power of the mind.
He sees and experiences other bodies belonging to others as well as his own bodies as if they were made of earth. (MT_4,10.50)
If the mind perceives the truth, then, having abandoned the conception of a body which consists of untruth, it attains supreme bliss. The mind [should perceive] the truth correctly.
If he perceives it,
then that [perception] consists of unreality and has unreality as its very nature.
Having abandoned the cultivation of the body, he attains supreme liberation, which consists of pure consciousness and is of the nature of bliss. Thus he states the result.
While you were established in meditative absorption, your son’s mind traveled far,
even further away, along the path of its own desires;
for it is the mind alone that is the agent in all circumstances, and therefore, for that reason.
Having abandoned this body belonging to Uśanas in a cave of Mount Mandara,
he departed for the abode of the gods, like a bird flying up from its nest. (MU 4.10.53) "Auśanasa" means relating to Śukra.
There, in the groves of *mandāra* trees, in the dwellings of the *pārijāta*,
in the thickets of the Nandana garden, and in the cities of the world-protectors—
this is clear.
O Sage, for eight cycles of four ages, that one of great splendor enjoyed Viśvācī, who was as beautiful as a goddess, just as a bee frequents a lotus.
This is clear.
Then, when the merit produced by one's own volition—conceived through intense spiritual urgency—is exhausted, it vanishes like the nocturnal mist. (MU 4.10.56) [This is clear. (MT 4.10.56)
With his floral crest withered and his limbs perspiring, he became languid from the weight of his armlets; together with her, he fell like a fruit ripened by time.

*yathā*: N17:
(clearly) "Having abandoned that celestial body in the very sky..."
Having reached the elemental ether, he was born upon the earth.
[This is clear.
There was a twice-born man who was a lord of the earth in Daśārṇa and Kosala.
In the great forest of Aṅga he was a fisherman, and on the banks of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) he was a swan.
(This is clear.
In Pauṇḍra he was a king of the Solar dynasty, and among the Sālvas he was a teacher of the Sun-god.
For an eon he was a glorious and wise Vidyādhara, and then, O Sage,
the son of a sage was born as a king of the Solar dynasty in the land of Pauṇḍra.

Among the Śālvas, there was a solar descendant, born into the lineage of the Sun, who became a teacher and a preceptor. Then, among the Madras, there was a protector of the earth, and from him was born Tāpasabālaka.
Known as Vāsudeva, he was staying on the bank of the Samaṅgā river among the Madras. (MU 4.10.61) [The reading "madrīṣu" in N17 is clearly an error for "madreṣu."]
Driven by the power of his own diverse latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
your son wandered through other endless wombs that were indeed full of suffering.
This is clear.
While providing an explanation of the other words, he recounts his previous births prior to those born as an ascetic on the banks of the Samaṅgā:
"In the Vindhya forest there was a cowherd, and among the Kekayas a Kirāta; in Sauvīra there was a feudal lord, and in Traigarta a local guide. (MU 4.10.63)

The *traigarta* is one belonging to the Trigarta country. The *vaṃśagulma* [deer] is found among the Kirātas; the *hariṇa* in the Cīra forest; the *sarīsṛpa* under the palmyra trees; and the *vanakukkuṭa* in the *tamāla* groves. (MU 4.10.64)
This is clear. (MT 4.10.64) Having been that son of yours, the best among those who know the mantras, he formerly recited the lore that bestows the station of a Vidyādhara. (MU 4.10.65)
The excellent one recited— that is, he muttered— the mantra of the vidyā. (MT_4,10.65)
Therefore, O Blessed One, that great Vidyādhara Brahmā [appeared] in the sky,
adorned with necklaces, earrings, and armlets, dancing with a multitude of graceful gestures.
O Blessed One, O Brahmā,
this is your son;
by means of that recitation.
He became a vidyādhara.

The sun to the lotuses that are the heroines, like another god of the flower-bow,
the beloved of the Vidyādharīs, and the ornament of the city of the Gandharvas—
this is clear. (MU 4.10.67) (MT 4.10.67)
Having reached the end of the kalpa, in the abode of the twelve suns,
he was reduced to ashes like a moth in a fire.
[It is] conceptual construction (saṅkalpa); cf.
73a. This is clear.
[Clearly] N17: *spaṣṭam* (MT_4,10.68).
Then, in the vast sky devoid of the creation of the world, that latent impression (*vāsanā*) of his wandered about like a bird without a nest. MU_4,10.69.
This is clear. (MT 4.10.69) Then, when the time had arrived that initiates various undertakings—the commencement of the grand display of saṃsāra—at the end of Brahmā’s night. (MU 4.10.70)
That mental impression (*manovāsanā*) of his, having been stirred by the wind, attained the state of a Brahmin in the *Kṛta* age and was born today upon the surface of the earth.
