MT 4.10.72) This is clear.
"O Great Sage, having become a Vidyādhara for a kalpa,
your son now practices austerities, situated on the bank of the river Samaṅgā.
This is clear.
He describes the entry into the womb of an old woman with a verse at the end of the chapter [on the entry into the womb of an old woman]: regarding the orthography (*jaraḍha*), see MṬ (I) p. 9.
Driven by the persistence of various uneven latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), he has wandered through the world into hollows as formidable as *khadira* and *karañja* trees,
and into the most dense forest regions within the decaying wombs of existence.
Old age [is] more difficult to traverse in the most dense [forests]. N17: more difficult to traverse.
In the side of the decayed womb, amidst the Khadira and Karañja trees that are terrifying and fraught with various kinds of suffering and distress—may there be auspiciousness.
Auspiciousness! N17 omits: "Thus, auspiciousness" (MT_4,10.74).
Thus ends the tenth canto in the Chapter on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Today, on the bank of the most excellent river, whose wind resounds with the gurgling roar of a surging mass of wild waves,
your son is performing austerities. (The "most excellent river" refers to the Samaṅgā.)
He shines and moves about;
wearing matted hair and a rosary, with the wandering of all his senses conquered,
he remained there for eight hundred years, steadfast in his asceticism.
O Sage, if you wish to see that son of yours, who is but a delusion of the mind, [then look at] this one wearing a rosary of beads. (MT_4,11.2)
Therefore, quickly open the eye of discernment and behold:
[this] mental delusion in the form of your own son—that is, the mental delusion regarding your own son;
in other words, "your own son."
When this had been said by Jagadīśa, who regards all with an equal eye,
the sage reflected with the eye of his knowledge upon what was intended for his son.
It was clear. (MT 4.11.4) And in a moment, by the power of his visionary intuition, he beheld the entire account of his son reflected upon the mirror of his intellect. MU 4.11.5
By the power of appearance, he saw— that is, he perceived— through the vision of primordial wisdom.

Furthermore, at the appropriate time, Bhṛgu approached from the bank of the Samaṅgā river and entered his own body, which was situated on the slopes of Mount Mandara and remained there at the peak of time. "At the appropriate time" means at a very brief moment.

Standing at the end of time, positioned before Time itself, the passionless Sage spoke these words to the passionless Kāla, as he gazed upon him with a beautiful glance smiling with wonder: *kālāgrasaṃsthitāṃ kālapurovartinīm* // (MT_4,11.6) *vismayasmerayā dṛṣṭyā kālam ālokya kāntayā / vītarāgam uvācedaṃ vītarāgo munir vacaḥ //* MU_4,11.7*
"Free from passion":
because time is all-encompassing, there is freedom from passion. Bhṛgu says: [N17: v⟨e⟩[ī]ta°]. (MT_4,11.7) Bhṛgu relates:

"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, we are but children, devoid of clarity; O God, only those like you possess the wisdom that perceives the three times without stain. (In this context, "children" means fools.)
This is connected with the second half of the verse beginning with *anāvila*.
"Though it is manifold in form and rich in transformations, appearing as unreal even while being real, this course of the world produces delusion even for the wise man. (MU 4.11.9)
The course of the world is the construction of the world.
O Lord, you alone know that form which resides within you—
the form of this mental activity that creates an illusion like a magician's trick.
"O Blessed One, it exists within you; it dwells in your very midst. (MT 4,11.10) It is said, O Lord, that death does not exist for this son of mine;
therefore, seeing him dead, I have become filled with agitation. (MU 4,11.11)
[He was] filled with agitation because Śukra was long-lived;
[he thought], "Time has carried away my son whose life was not yet exhausted."
"O Lord, it is by the power of destiny that the desire for your curse has arisen in me.
Regarding the word "destiny":
that desire for your curse which has arisen in me is itself nothing but destiny.
Therefore, the sense is that there is no fault whatsoever on my part;
yet we have not recognized the course of saṃsāra as a calamity.
"Or we go to prosperity"—the word "having reached" (*prāpya*) is to be supplied; likewise, "having reached adversity" (*āpadam prāpya*). Indeed, [we go] under the sway of joy or dejection.

"Or having attained prosperity... (MT 4.11.13). "Anger toward one who acts improperly and favor toward one who acts properly should be shown"—this worldly condition, O Blessed One, is firmly established. (MU 4.11.14)
Therefore, the sense is that I became angry because I suspected you of acting improperly.
Having raised this doubt: "This is to be done, this is not"—such is the course of the world as long as one lives;
as long as fire persists, so long are its perceptions of heat, burning, and so forth observed. (MU 4.11.15)
This is clear.

(MU 4.11.15) For one for whom the state of the world consists of "this is to be done" and "this is not," the total renunciation of this very [distinction] is itself what must be abandoned, O Teacher of the World. (MU 4.11.16)
The stability of the world; [N17: *ga*t*sthi°];
O Teacher of the World (jagadguru) / [N17: °guro⟨ḥ⟩] / for whom [there is the knowledge]: "This is to be done; this is not to be done."
Thus, such a state of worldly existence is to be abandoned;
even the complete relinquishing of that [state] is itself to be abandoned.
Because even the abandonment of that [world] consists in the continued existence of the world;
therefore, the sense is that "I have not abandoned the previous state."
When we did not consider such a prior state of affairs— that is, this very thought— [we acted as follows].
"O Blessed One, we have become agitated because of you; therefore, please speak. [She said:
"Tānayī means relating to a son (*tanaya*)."
"Let him be made subject to censure—that is, to the fitness for reproach consisting in being the cause of your anger.
(MT 4.11.17) "O Lord, I have now been reminded by you of what was done by your son;
on the bank of the Samaṅgā, this son was seen by me because of him. (MU 4.11.18)
This is clear. (MT 4.11.18) I think that for living beings in this world there are not two bodies, O All-pervading One;
for the mind alone is the body, by which this world is brought into being. (MU 4.11.19)
O All-pervading One, I think that [it] is not cultivated by anything else.
In this world, there are not two bodies for living beings;
for indeed, the mind itself is the body.
By which mind this world is conceptualized— that is, made manifest through mental cultivation (bhāvanā).
[Kāla said:
"O Brahmin, you have spoken correctly: for us, the mind alone is the body."
Having formed a mental resolve, it creates a body just as a potter fashions a jar.
This is clear.
It produces an unformed appearance and destroys what has been formed in an instant.
Through conceptualization, the fool, out of delusion, [perceives] a Vetālaka, as it were;
"out of delusion" means out of ignorance. And likewise, in a state of agitation, there appear dreams, false cognitions, and the like.
The powers perceived in the mind have the appearance of a city of the Gandharvas.
(This is clear.)
[Clearly] O Great Sage, relying upon this perspective of coarse vision, it is said that for a person there are two bodies: the mind and the physical body. MU_4,11.23
O Great Sage, for one whose vision is coarse,
there are two bodies.

The vision characterized by gross perception is "gross-visioned vision"; that [is what is referred to]. (MT_4,11.23) O Sage, these three worlds are merely a construction of the mind's conceptualization; they have arisen as something vast, appearing neither as real nor as unreal, and nothing else. MU_4,11.24
"Extensive," O Sage,
is this world; that which is the mental activity of the mind is the phenomenon called "thinking."
It becomes that alone;
what is its nature? It means it is neither existent nor non-existent, but indeterminable.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is as if arisen extensively, having manifested with a nature of throbbing vibration.
However, since [the object] is not asserted from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), the word "as it were" (*iva*) is employed.
He states the meaning of the word "only" (*mātra*) in his own words: "and nothing else. (MT_4,11.24)
Through the creeper-like limb of the body called *citta*, fueled by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of duality,
this manifoldness has arisen from ignorance, like the appearance of two moons.
[The phrase] "through the creeper-like limb of the body called *citta*" means in the form of a creeper-like limb.
By the latent impression of differentiation— that is, by the latent impression of duality— which has become powerful,
nourished, and real,
this world-form [arises].
Diversity has arisen and become manifest; how so? Like the appearance of two moons.
The meaning is: "in the same way" as the state of seeing two moons arises from ignorance.
Due to the manifold latent impressions of differentiation, the mind perceives everywhere as distinct the multitude of objects that constitute the world— such as jars, pits, cloths, and so forth.
"Extensive" means vast;
"everywhere" means in all places and at all times.
[I am] emaciated, exceedingly miserable, and deluded; these and other such contemplations [are mine].
Cultivating its own conceptual constructions, the mind enters the state of *saṃsāra*.
"The state of *saṃsāra*" means the condition of cyclic existence.
"Mental fabrication is an artificial form; this is not my [true] nature, therefore I do not fall [into it]."

Thus, through the relinquishing of that, the mind becomes tranquil—the eternal Brahman. "Through the relinquishing of that" means through the relinquishing of mental reflection; "eternal" means beginningless.
The passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*) and ending with "free from affliction" (*nirāmayāḥ*) explains one simile in detail;
[beginning with "Just as"]:
"Just as in the vast ocean, which is spread out and possesses many waves..."
In that which consists of the gentle vibration [of consciousness], graced by a series of many waves;
in the self of water, which is even, clear, pure, sweet, and cool.
In that which is imperishable, vast, of great majesty, manifest, pure,
and of immense power.
The wave, while contemplating its own form as its very nature, creates its own conceptualization through the thought, "I am triangular," by means of that conceptual construction. (MU 4.11.31) [Note:
taraṅgaḥ is corrected from N17: °raṅga[ḥ]]
Falling away through conceptualization and thinking, "I am one whose form has been utterly lost," he goes to the *talātala* [hell],
reaching the surface of the earth by means of such a mental cultivation. (MU 4.11.32)
And when it has been forcibly raised upward, one conceives, "I have risen.
Through various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), one conceptualizes that state as being accompanied by verbal designation (*sābhidha*).
When there is the conceptualization of a reflection of the sun, it is cultivated as "I am luminous"; when there is the falling of a mass of dust, it is cultivated as "I am impure. (MU 4.11.34)
Enveloped by a net of jewel-like rays, he shines with radiant splendor;
yet, pierced by a heavy burden of frost, he experiences the sensation of cold.
With his body blazing with the reflection of the forest fires on the mountains and their slopes, he remains thus.
"Alas, I am burnt! he fears; and having swallowed the fish, he trembles.

Yet, with the reflections of the coastal mountains, slopes, birds, forests, and trees [within him], he shines forth, possessed of a great undertaking and intense exertion, thinking, "I am [the ocean]. (MU 4.11.36–37)
With his flickering body destroyed by the arising of stainless radiance, he cried out as if in a loud lament: "I have been reduced to pieces! (MU 4.11.38)
And those waves are not distinct from the water-mass of the ocean;
nor is there any single form among them that, though existing, is composed of non-existence.
Nor is it that they do not exist; yet those qualities such as brevity and length do not reside in each of those [atoms],
nor do they reside in them collectively, just as waves do not reside in the ocean, yet they are not non-existent there.

In that regard: "O you who abide in your own essential nature, by your mere volition you have rendered them devoid of conceptual construction; they are lost and yet not lost, born again and again, and though born, they are born no more, and are once more destroyed. (MU 4.11.41)
Those born and those yet to be born, through their mutual contact, do not at all attain diversity;
they are indeed free from affliction, consisting of the single nature of water as a commonality.
Possessing many waves, endowed with manifold ripples; consisting of gentle vibrations, having the nature of the movement of gentle water; possessing many circles of billows.
O virtuous one, by those [causes],
in such a self-restraining nature,
just as that well-known wave, triangular in shape and form, its own—
Form is its own form, which is triangular;
manifesting it— that is, making it evident— to the cognizer by its very nature.
By means of its own [conceptualization] arising from itself—

which is non-different from it— in the form of the discrimination "I am triangular," it performs the conceptual construction, that is, the conceptual construction of the triangular form. It does not perform only this one.
But he says that he performs other actions as well, starting with "and falling," etc.:
that triangular wave, thinking "I am falling," falls for that very reason.
Then, by means of that same kind of contemplation, [one perceives] Talātala, known as Talātala, and Bhūtala.
It goes, it moves.
"Arisen" means that the triangular wave has risen upward and is perceived as "I am."
For this very reason, it has arisen through those various conceptual constructions— that is, through the conceptual constructions of arising—
and it is accompanied by designation, meaning it is joined with verbal expression.
The state of that, namely the state of arising,
he conceptualizes and brings about through conceptualization;
"with the sun" is clear.
"With its jewels" (saratna) is clear. "With its waves" (sataṭa):
"having taken the fish" (āttamīnaḥ); "taken by the fish" (mīnaiḥ ātta) means "having taken the fish.
"With reflections" (pratibimbita) is clear.
Regarding "Vimala": Vimala is that which is radiant; by means of that, that which has arisen is destroyed, and its destruction is [the state of] Dhvasta.
He is one whose body is restless;
and [it is] not because of waves.
These are those previously mentioned.
It should be understood that the singular number used previously was with reference to the genus;
therefore, the plural form is employed here.
And not so; those waves do not exist within those qualities.
"Kevalam" means abiding in one's own intrinsic nature,
abiding in one's own essential form.
The conceptual construction which consists in the attainment of the state of being waves—
by that [construction], the waters have been rendered disturbed,
that is, cut off.
"Mutually" (*paraspara*) means one another (*anyonya*). "Grasping" (*parāmarśa*) refers to remaining in close proximity.
Therefore,
they attain diversity;
being of what nature?
That single form which is the commonality of water— [all things] are composed of that alone;
for this very reason, they are free from affliction, being devoid of the diseases known as destruction and arising.
[Śālinī] N17: °li(ri)ni;
bhraśyaṃś; N17: bhraś[y]aṃś; bhraśyan; N17: bhraś[y]an.
"reflected" (pratibimbita); N17:
(sa) pratibimbi°;
"shining forth" (ullasana); N17: °sa*nam*
Lolaṃ;
cor-maya; paraspareti.
Having stated the illustration, he explains the subject illustrated by means of two verses:
"In the same way, within this vast, white, pure, and stainless [space], which has Brahman alone as its singular body and possesses a pervasive form, [therein lies the individual soul]. (MU 4.11.43)
[O You of expansive form! (A Kulaka) Within You,
who possess all powers and are without beginning or end, various powers— unseparated yet appearing as if separate— abide, restless with their manifold and diverse activities.
He explains the meaning of the term *sitapada* (the white-footed) in his own words with the word "pure" (*śuddhe*).
[The phrase] "and free from affliction" (*nirāmaye ca*) means being emerged from the affliction (*āmaya*) so designated.
It is the one, absolute Brahman alone.
To him whose body is such a nature; to him who is thus expansive and characterized by radiance.
"Because it possesses a body"—
in such a one;
in such a Brahman.
The powers are not separate;
nevertheless, like waves, they exist as if distinct. This is a pair [of verses]. (MT 4,11.43–44)
For Brahman, abiding within its own form, attains multiplicity through its various powers; it expands within Brahman like a circle of waves in water.
Brahman is pure, whose essential nature is consciousness alone.
In Brahman, which is one's own body and one's own essential nature called Brahman— being "expanded" (bṛṃhitam) means being endowed with the state of expansion in the form of the universe—
the state of manifoldness (nānātva) is the condition of diversity.
It comes and goes;
of what nature?
Possessing manifold powers; otherwise [it would not].
The sense is that it would not be logical for there to be a transition into diversity.
What, then, is Brahman like when expanded? It is like a circle of waves in water.
as it were.
[Regarding *bṛṃhitatayā*: N17: *bṛṃhita[ta]yā* (MT_4,11.45).
Now, if Brahman alone exists as expanded (*bṛṃhita*) in the form of cloth and so forth, then would it not follow that the objects are each restricted [to their own specific nature]?
"How does form exist? To this he replies:
"Because it takes on various forms, destiny—which produces hundreds of diverse appearances—presides over the object with its fixed form. (MU 4.11.46)
"Adhitiṣṭhati": N17 reads *nānārūpaka* → *adhitiṣṭhati*;
that which is form (*rūpa*) consisting of various forms (*nānārūpaka*).

Because it is conjoined with that [niyati], it produces a hundredfold diversity—that is, it produces a hundredfold irregularity consisting of the restricted forms of individual entities. Niyati is the power called "restriction";
it presides over each entity and brings it under its own control.
The meaning is that by the very power of necessity (niyati-śakti) produced from Brahman, each individual entity possesses its own fixed form.
Having spoken of the category of reality in general, he now describes it slightly more specifically:
"The insentient assumes insentience; it attains consciousness and becomes composed of consciousness."
The power in the form of latent impressions belongs to the Self established in its own essential nature;
it is composed of consciousness and exists in the form of latent impressions.
The power of that Self which abides in its own essential nature is the power of necessity (niyati-śakti).
Having become inert, consisting of the latent impression of dullness (*jāḍya-vāsanā*),
it assumes and takes up dullness,
by which it manifests a stationary form.
Having become the nature of consciousness, consisting of the latent impression of sentience, it attains the state of mind (*citta*),
by which it manifests a moving form.
He states the conclusion regarding that which consists of the latent impression of consciousness:
"O sinless one, it is Brahman alone that unfolds in this expansive form."
O sinless one, because of that reason, this world, with its vast form, appears as if it were a sea filled with various kinds of movements.
Brahman alone unfolds and shines forth;
like what? Like a completely full ocean.
The meaning is: "just as it manifests through various forms of vibration known as waves."
From this cause,
the ocean itself assumes diversity through its dwelling in various forms.

The Self alone, by means of the Self, within the Self—like the water of the ocean within water—for the sake of manifold forms and for the sake of perceiving manifold forms; that which is "vihāra," meaning play; from that [it arises].
Just as various waves are not distinct from the water,
so too all mental constructs are not distinct from the Lord of All,
who exists as the reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) acting as the regulator of everything.

The conceptualizations take the form of the world; these are the conceptualizations. Just as the stalk, flower, creeper, leaf, fruit, and bud exist within a single seed, so do the powers reside within Brahman.

The powers are the forms of the world; they are the powers. Just as there is a multiplicity of powers in the *puruṣa* due to his manifold agency, so too is there always an omnipotence within the omniscient Self.
He states the reason for [the Lord's] omnipotence with the words "omniscient" (*sarvajña*).
For if he were not omnipotent, he would not be omniscient; and here, omniscience is grounded in the capacity to be the creator of all things.
For one who does not know everything does not create everything,
since it is observed that in the case of potters and others, their knowledge of jars and such things is restricted.
Just as a variegated color is seen in the harsh sunlight,
so too does the Lord of Gods possess a manifold power consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
This is clear.
This world of manifold forms arises from the non-manifold Śiva,
just as a streak of Indra’s bow [a rainbow] emerges from a cloud of a single color.
This is clear.
From the non-inert, the state of inertia arises, caused by the contemplation of dullness,
just as a thread emerges from a spider or as deep sleep arises from a person.
(MU 4.11.55) [The term] *jāḍyasya* means "of the state of being inert" (*jaḍatva*).

That which is meditation (*bhāvanā*) or conceptualization (*saṅkalpana*), that very thing is the cause of which [the power]; such is she. By his own will, Śiva [projects] the mental power (*caitasī śakti*) from his own state of non-mind (*acitta*) for the sake of bondage.
Just as a silkworm weaves a cocoon for itself, so too does it weave a web of mental constructs;
being "without mind" means it is devoid of mind due to its absolute purity.
Tāntava means that which is related to threads.
O Brahmin, having by his own will meditated upon his own body as the woven cloth of the Self,
he attains liberation from saṃsāra, like an elephant from its tethering post. (MU 4.11.57)
"Of the self" means by the self;
"by one's own will" means belonging to the self;
"one's own" means innate.
Having contemplated the body— which is one's own true nature called pure consciousness—
as being one's own essential self, having brought it within the scope of contemplation as one's own nature,
[one is liberated] from transmigratory existence, which consists of the contemplation "I am the body."
From cyclic existence, he shall attain liberation, that is, release; what is it like?
Like an elephant;
the meaning is that it is just as when such an animal attains release from its tethering post.
In this context, the word "svecchā" (one's own will) denotes mere will alone.
Liberation:
just as that [is], so it is.
Whatever the self constantly contemplates, that very thing, having been cultivated by itself, [becomes manifest].
By that very power, even a great person is quickly filled;
"whatever" and "whichever" power he has constantly cultivated— that is, always perfumed with.
Even though it is great and all-pervading,
the cultivated power leads the self to its true nature in an instant,
just as a great autumn mist covers the infinite sky.
Cultivated means made the object of cultivation;
"selfhood" refers to that self which exists in the form of a latent capacity (*śakti*).
Tattām:
in the case of mist, this refers to its own nature, that is, the state of being mist.
The unborn one who quickly attains identity with that power which has arisen becomes identical with it;
indeed, whatever state he has reached, he becomes that very thing, just as a tree [becomes one with its root].
(MU 4.11.60) [drumaḥ] N17: °m(ā)aḥ
The Unborn (*aja*) is devoid of birth; the Pure is the reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
"Stability" (*sthiti*) refers to the ground (*bhūmi*) which serves as a support; for [the tree] ascends by conforming to the ground that serves as the support for the tree. (MT 4,11.60)

There is no liberation for the Lord, nor is there bondage for the Self. I do not know from where these notions of bondage and liberation have arisen in the world; they do not exist for the Lord, who is the Self.
[If it is argued:
"In that case, to whom do bondage and liberation belong?"—to this he says: "Bondage... etc.
The intended meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no arising of either bondage or liberation; therefore, what need is there to consider their substratum?
Here it is said:

[N17] "For this [world], there is neither bondage nor liberation; it is perceived as being composed of that very [reality]. Alas! The world is illusory, eternally swallowed by the unreal. (MU 4.11.62)
Because this self is unreal,
from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is no bondage.
Even liberation does not exist;
rather, from the perspective of immediate manifestation, it appears as being composed of that, consisting of both bondage and liberation.
If that is so, how then does the conceptualization of bondage and liberation exist in the world?
To this, he says:
Here, by the word "jagat" (the world), the perceivers residing within the world are indicated. "Aho" expresses wonder. "Jagat" refers to those residing within the world.
The cognizers are swallowed— that is, permeated by their own mental constructs— by something called bondage and liberation, which is unreal and non-existent.
It has been done. Here, he states the reason by means of a qualification: "consisting of illusion" (*māyāmaya*).
The intended meaning is that precisely because it consists of illusion, it is swallowed up by the unreal.
[From the perspective of ultimate truth] N17: °paramārtha°; [even] N17: *api*; [here he says] N17: *katham → āha*
Consisting of illusion; by that which is unreal, [there is] bondage indeed by the unreal. (MT_4,11.62)
Now, one might ask: "How has the Self come to be as if seized by the conceptualization of bondage, liberation, and so forth? To this he replies:
"When the mind is indeed conceptualized by the timeless Self, then this Self is enveloped by it, like a silkworm in its cocoon. (MU 4.11.63)
[By] *akalena*: because it is unfragmented (*akhaṇḍatvāt*), it is devoid of parts (*kalārahita*).
By this very self, at the very moment the mind is conceptualized—that is, made manifest by conceptualization (*kalanayā*)—[it is so].
Then, by means of this very self, the self— its own true nature— is veiled, like a silkworm within its cocoon.
"Enveloped by a sheath consisting of the conceptualization of bondage, liberation, and so forth.
[Objection: "By what material cause has this mind, which is thus conceptualized by the self, emerged? To this, he says:
But these powers of the mind, which are non-different in form yet possess bodies imagined as distinct, issue forth from this [Self] by the millions.
"Non-different in form" means undivided.
These exist as distinct entities.
Residing in that and born from that, they have separate forms like waves from the ocean;
residing in that and born from that, yet existing separately, they are like rays from the moon.
"Marīcyaḥ":
[N17: *ma*⟨v⟩[r]īca°] "Stationed therein" means stationed in that Supreme Self (*paramātman*). "Born from that" means born from that Supreme Self.
These powers of the mind exist in distinct forms;
like what?
"Like waves":
the meaning is that just as waves appear as distinct forms from the ocean, so it is.
He tells the second illustration with the words "tatstha" (situated therein):

In this vast ocean of the Supreme Self, which consists of vibration, in the water of consciousness that is expansive in its extent and characterized by the essence of pure consciousness alone— *MU* 4.11.66.
Some of these surging waves stand as the superior manifestations of the consciousness of Hari, Brahmā, and Rudra; they flash forth, their very nature revealed by their own inherent being.
In that which consists of vibration (*spandamaya*) and consists of the self-reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśamaya*), because here the very self-reflective awareness of "I" is vibration;
in the expansive (*sphāra*) and vast (*vistīrṇa*) consciousness (*cit*).
Consciousness is oriented toward objects; it is in such a state, wherein that very consciousness is the water.
Pure consciousness (cinmātra) is consciousness that is not oriented toward an object of cognition (cetya).
That very [consciousness] is "rasa" (flavor/essence); it is in such [a state] that rasa resides. Rasa should be understood as the essential substance of water, the quality known as taste.
In such a great ocean of the Supreme Self,
these certain waves—
waves of consciousness— quiver forth.
In what manner do the waves abide?
They take the forms of Hari, Brahmā, and Rudra; they are the vibrations of consciousness (*cidvalanā*), the pulsations of awareness (*citspandāḥ*).
Of these, those [waves] are "greater" than which [others].
They remain in such a state.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?
They are manifested—that is, they have come into manifestation—from their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
The meaning is that certain waves, whose very essence is these [deities], manifest in the forms of Hari, Brahmā, and Rudra.
Some are oriented toward objects of thought;
they possess the forms of Hari, Brahmā, and Rudra.
Of whomsoever—certain [goddesses] such as Yama, Mahendra, Arka, Vahni, Vaiśravaṇa, and others—the state [is as follows]: N17: *yāsāṃ* bhāvaḥ; N17: *°v(ā)aḥ*. (MT_4,11.66-67)
The waves of restless desires slay, act, and persist;
"restless desires" refers to those whose longings are fickle. They are such [desires].
From them,
certain fierce waves of Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Suras, and others— leaping up, falling down, and tossing about— arise.
They are leaping and quivering.
Some remain in a slightly fixed form, such as the lotus-born Brahmā and others;
some have arisen and then perished, such as gods, humans, and others.
*kiñcitsthitākārā*: those whose form remains for a short duration; they are called *kiñcitsthitākārāḥ*. (MT_4,11.70)
Worms, insects, moths, and the like, as well as pythons, cobras, and so forth—
some of these flash like mere droplets within that great ocean;
the plural "in these" is used for the sake of completing the meter.
Therefore, it should be connected with the phrase "in this great ocean.
(MT_4,11.71) Some, such as the *calānana*, *mṛgagṛdhra*, and *vañjulaka* birds, flutter about in the mountain thickets like those on the shores of the coastal forests. MU_4,11.72
This is clear.
(MU 4.11.72) Some have very long lives, while others have extremely short lives;
some have hollow bodies due to their own hollow mental cultivation. (MU 4.11.73)
[Because of the cultivation of their own emptiness:
from certain [objects] that are empty and unreal;
because of the cultivation of their own emptiness, that is, from the conceptualization of emptiness regarding their own objects.
They become empty-bodied.
Some [arise] from empty conceptualization; some [arise] from empty conceptualization. (MT_4,11.73)

In the turbulent dream of saṃsāra, some are imagined to possess stability, while others, struck down by their own conceptual constructions, imagine the world to be firmly established. "With stability" means with firmness.

They have cultivated the impression that "this saṃsāra is stable," and have been made possessed of such latent tendencies. Some, having very slight cultivation, are overcome by the fault of dejection;
they are made firm in their suffering by thinking, "I am emaciated, extremely miserable, and deluded. (MU 4.11.74–75)
I myself should understand that here, due to extreme dullness, there is a very slight degree of cultivation.
Some have attained the state of stationary beings; some have reached the state of deities.
Some attained the state of men, while others went to the state of Dānavas.
This is clear.
With the final verse of the chapter, he summarizes the very same point already mentioned.
Some remain in the world for no small number of hundreds of kalpas, while others, being utterly pure, proceed toward the Supreme Person;
for the cognitions of consciousness—known by the other name of "thinking"—arise from the ocean of Brahman, restless like waves.
(MU 4.11.77) [suśuddhāḥ] N17: su(śru)śu°
[The verses] having "mananā" as another name [for their subject].
Thus ends the eleventh canto in the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
"O Sage, these cognitions which take the forms of gods, asuras, and humans are non-different from the ocean of Brahman; this is the truth, and everything else is false.
This refers to those cognitions which take the forms of gods, asuras, and humans.
Non-difference [is that] from the ocean of Brahman;
the other is difference. Gods, asuras, and humans are mentioned because of their predominance.
O Brahmin, cognitions in the forms of gods, asuras, and humans distinguish themselves through false imagination, defiled by one's own conceptual constructions;
for by the internal conviction "we are not Brahman," they have fallen downward.
With the second half of the verse, he states the reason for its being stained: "It is not Brahman.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because.
Even though they are situated within the ocean of Brahman, they are distinct from Brahman.
Cultivating these, they become utterly deluded amidst the terrifying realms of worldly existence—
realms that are "terrifying" because they bestow suffering and are thus extremely fearsome.
O Sage, those cognitions which are of the nature of Brahman are not stained by manifold defects.
Know that this is the seed of actions, or rather,
know it to be action itself;
these [forms] previously mentioned as the shapes of gods, demons, and humans [are produced from it].
The reflections of consciousness;
"brāhmyaḥ" means pertaining to Brahman;
"naikakalaṅkitāḥ" means not stained in any single way.
The meaning is that they are defiled in many ways.
These, then, are those Vedic cognitions;
they are the seed, the cause, of ritual actions.
Know this;
or rather, know it as action itself, because external action, which is intended as such, is prescribed in accordance with this.
For indeed, the arising of external action is neither observed nor logical without the reflective awareness of consciousness.
Know [it] because it has been well-expounded;
N17: *praṇītatvāt* is corrected from *prāṇita*. (MT_4,12.4)
O Sage, he explains that these very [powers] are the cause of the entire world: by means of this internal process of conceptualization (*kalanā*), which consists of volition (*saṅkalpa*),
and which is as formidable as a handful of seeds for the *karañja* trees of the web of karma.
In this vast world, these rows of stone-like bodies stand,
leap about, weep, and laugh;
from Brahma down to a blade of grass, they vibrate like the wind.
O Sage! They flourish, they subside, they wither, and they laugh— by means of that which consists of volition, whose very nature is volition,
which is like a handful of seeds for the *karañja* trees of the web of karma, and which serves as the cause of that web of karma.
To this extent: by this very means— by this terrifying and transformative conceptualization (*kalanā*) which is of the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*)—
in the vast world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, there are rows of bodies, that is, rows of stones in the form of bodies.

They stand, they leap about, they weep and they laugh, they exult and they restrain themselves, they wither and they smile; and this is merely an illustration—the meaning is that they perform all actions. [This refers to] the aforementioned actions in the case of dead bodies.
Because it is not seen. How so? Like the wind.
Just as the wind performs various kinds of actions by means of the vibrations within itself.
The meaning is "so it is."
They remain;
various kinds [of beings]. (MT_4,12.7)
Some of these are extremely clear, such as Hari, Hara, and others;
some are the abodes of slight delusion, such as the serpents, humans, and gods.
This is clear.
Some remain in a state of absolute delusion, such as trees, grass, and the like;
others, utterly bewildered by ignorance, have come to the state of worms and insects.
This is clear.
(MT 4.12.9) Some are carried away like straw, far from the great ocean of Brahman;
these have not attained the [spiritual] stages, just like the serpent-men and others. (MU 4.12.10)
They have not attained the stages; they have not reached the further shore.
Those who have not reached the further shore,
having merely gazed upon the bank, some fall into exhaustion;
whether already born or yet to be born, they are buried by the old rat that is Death.
He merely gazed upon the bank, but did not reach it;
for once he had reached it, it would have been improper for him to be repeatedly buried by the God of Death.
And here, it should be understood that there is a resting in pure consciousness alone.
Having reached the interior of the great ocean of the reality of Brahman, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, and the others have attained its state for the sake of freedom from sorrow. (MU 4.12.12)
That state of being Brahman;
for the sake of freedom from sorrow, that is, for the absence of grief.
Some, possessed of little delusion, [enter] that very ocean of Brahman.
They remain established by relying on that which has not seen the flood of the disease of passion.
"Having relied upon the unseen [reality], the disease of the city," meaning having taken it as one's own self;
the sense is that some are of the nature of those liberated while living.
Some multitudes of births yet to be experienced,
and crores of multitudes of births already experienced; some species of beings remain barren, while others are manifest in the darkness.
*prakāśatāmasyaḥ*: [N17:
*pra⟨kāmatvam asyaḥ⟩[kāśatāmasyaḥ]*] means "one whose darkness has been dispelled," that is, one endowed with the quality of supreme light.
For this very reason, they are barren, being devoid of the fruit known as right knowledge.
*prakāśatāmasyaḥ*: N17:
*pra⟨kāmatām asyāḥ⟩[kāśatāmasyaḥ]*;
*prakṛṣṭatamaso*: N17: *°ta[ma]so* (MT_4,12.14).
Some go from above to below, while others go from below to the Great State;
some go higher and higher from above, and others even lower from below—
lower meaning into the womb of an animal or into hell.
The great state is either human existence or heaven.
[The word] *pada*: N17 reads *°dam* (*mahatpadam*).
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he states the established conclusion:
"This activity, fraught with many joys and sorrows, has come about here due to the failure to remember the supreme state."
Through the realization of the supreme state, one goes to destruction, just as the pain of poison vanishes from the remembrance of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa).
"Of the Lord of Birds" refers to Garuḍa, who is the form of the deity of the mantra of the snake-charmer. May there be auspiciousness! (MU 4.12.16)
"May there be auspiciousness.

Thus ends the twelfth canto in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. [N17: *vihaga* "May there be auspiciousness. May there be auspiciousness.
Twelfth:
Oṃ. The venerable Vasiṣṭha said to the venerable Rāma:
"Those who know reality, while investigating the courses of the world,"
From that bank of the Samaṅgā river, those with flickering rays set forth;
"jāgatīḥ" means belonging to the world,
and "gatīḥ" refers to the movements or arrangements [of the world].
Having gradually ascended into the sky and emerged through the hollows of the clouds, they reached Mount Mandara’s golden cave by way of the path of the perfected ones (*siddhamārga*).
Regarding the word "hollows" (*koṭaraiḥ*): [it refers to the cavities of the clouds].
Regarding the meaning of the word "from the hollows" (*koṭarebhyaḥ*):
on the plateau of that mountain, the descendant of Bhṛgu beheld his own dried-up body from a previous birth, shrouded by moist leaves. (MU 4.15.3)
This is clear.
And he said this: "O father, this slender body is indeed that very one which was formerly cherished by you with pleasant enjoyments."
This is clear.
(MT 4.15.4) This is that body of mine, for which cool beds were prepared with heaps of *mandāraka* flowers upon the grounds of the groves of Mount Meru. (MU 4.15.5)
"It is she; it is not another.
"Behold, this very body of mine, once caressed by the throngs of celestial women, now lies upon the surface of the earth, crushed by the mouths of crawling reptiles."
This is clear.
(MT 4.15.6) This very body of mine, by which I long sported in the groves of the Nandana garden, has now become a withered skeleton. (MU 4.15.7)
The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), meaning "sport.
(MT 4.15.7) "Because of contact with the limbs of celestial nymphs, my body here is wasting away, deprived of that mental activity which was so lofty in its arena of passion. (MU 4.15.8)
In the phrase *uttuṅgānaṅgaraṅgayā*,
the suffix *lakāra* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). (MT_4,15.8)
Having bound yourself with those very same mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) toward those various amorous pastimes and those various states, how can you remain at ease, O embodied one?
Those mental impressions concern the objects of celestial women.
"You are well-established because you are free from fickleness. 'Dehaka' refers to the body; it is an address to that body. (MT 4,15.9)
Alas, where have you been shattered? You have reached the state of being withered by heat; you have become a mere skeleton, yet you, O ill-fated one, still fixate upon me!
(The term *karaṅkatām* means the state of being a skeleton.)
"O unfortunate one, why do you torment me? Do you remember [me] because of being overwhelmed by excessive affection?"
This is the statement:
"By that very body through which I was once delighted in amorous pastimes, I now feel fear as it has turned into a skeleton. (MU 4.15.11)
I am afraid of that very body by which I once rejoiced in pleasures, now that it has become a mere skeleton. (MT 4,15.11)
Behold, where there was once a necklace with the appearance of a web of stars upon my chest, ants are now crawling over it! (MU 4.15.12) [Note:
*nilīyante* is corrected from *°yat*n*te in N17.]
They settle down; they adhere.

Look! By that very body of mine, which once captivated excellent women—drawing them on with its luster like molten gold and leading them to infatuation—it is now dragged along as a garland of skeletons. (MU 4.15.13)
It is carried away and supported.
Behold, with my wide-open mouth, with the dried hide of an ascetic, and with my foul face like a skeleton, the deer in the forest are terrified.
N17: ...they are terrified; being possessed of transformation, they are made to experience fear.
Behold my cave-like belly of a corpse, which is utterly parched.
It shines with a web of rays like the sun, as if through discernment;
the belly of the corpse—the interior of the dead body—is indeed a cave.
This emaciated body of mine, completely withered, lies face up upon the forest floor.

She leads those dwelling in the sky to dispassion by means of her own insignificance; [she leads] the gods dwelling in the sky through her freedom from attachment to sound, form, taste, touch, and smell.
"By means of non-conceptual samādhi alone is my body burned on the mountain.
Regarding my body: by what kind of body?
By one that has entered non-conceptuality—that which is free from conceptualization and is pure consciousness alone.
She whose [nature] is samādhi;
such is she.
When the vampire of the mind has been completely stilled, that subtle digit of bliss which the body [experiences]—[that is she].
Even by means of sovereignty over the world, one does not go to that [state];
"jagatena" means by that which pertains to the world.
Behold [him] whose every worldly effort has come to rest and from whom all curiosity has entirely departed.
The body sleeps happily, with the web of conceptual constructions cast aside.
(This is clear.
The tree of the body is agitated by the frantic activity of the monkey-mind.
It moves with such velocity that it cuts through its very roots.
The "cutting of the roots" should be understood as being of the nature of worldly agitation.
Thus, liberated from the misfortunes of the mind, this [yogin] experiences the shifting movements of elephants, clouds, and lions.
This body of mine does not perceive [anything], as it remains like supreme bliss (*parānanda*).
It is the playful movement, the graceful sport, of elephants, clouds, and lions— that is, of elephants, clouds, and lions.
That is to say, restlessness;
he does not see it, nor does he experience it.

I see no other source of welfare for living beings than non-conceptuality (*acittatva*), which is like the arrival of autumn to the mist of delusion caused by the fever of all desires, and which is like elephants, clouds, and lions. (MU 4.15.22)
The state of being without mind (*acittatva*) is clear.
Those very [beings] have reached the ultimate limit of the enjoyment of bliss.
Those of great intelligence and tranquil minds who have attained freedom from mental distress—
[they] are clearly liberated from the state of all suffering, perfectly peaceful, and free from feverish affliction.
"By good fortune, I behold this mindless body of mine in the forest.
This is clear.
Here, Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, Knower of All Dharmas, it is said that by Bhārgava,
many bodies were consumed again and again.
O Sage, when a body was produced by Bhṛgu, what did he [the soul] have to do with that particular one?"
A great excellence has arisen, or rather, there is only lamentation; "excellence" here means the knowledge of excellence. Thus, Śrī Vasiṣṭha provides the reply.

O Rāma, that very transformation of Śukra which had entered the state of a living being was born as Karmātmikā, the daughter of Bhṛgu in the form of a Bhārgava. (MU 4.15.27) [Bhṛgoḥ: N17 reads °go[r]]

The vibration known as consciousness (*saṃvit*), which brings about the manifestation of the seed-syllable *śukra* and the individual soul (*jīva*), [is the cause]. The word "of Venus" (*bhṛgoḥ*) is in the ablative case. The word "that" (*sā*) is the ellipsis required to complete the sense. (MT 4,15.27)
For she, having first emerged from the supreme state and reached the state of the elemental ether, being set in motion by the wind,
entered the heart of Bhṛgu through the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Having gradually attained vigor, he became endowed with a body like that of Uśanas; "having come together" means having arisen perfectly as the very first, preceded by that [previous state].
The body of Auśanasī was in the form of Śukra’s body; this is a pair [of verses].
Having been provided with the Vedic sacraments (*brāhmasaṃskāra*), she then went before her father.
After a long time, she reached the state of being a withered skeleton. This was the very first time that the body of Brahmā had arrived [in this form].
Therefore, at that time, Śukra uttered this lamentation concerning her for the first time.
*brahmaṇas*: Ś1, Ś3: brahma°; N17: brāhma°; idamprathamam: N17: °ma⟨ṃ⟩m.
This was the first time; that was the previous occasion. That lamentation—such a lamentation as this—was performed.
Even one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), even one who is without desire, though possessing a form like that of a *samaṅgin*, [is as described] previously.
Śukra lamented for his own body, for such is the nature born of the physical frame.
This is clear.
However, by means of that pretext of grief, he demonstrated something to the wise.
That distinction between the body and the embodied being is for the sake of attaining dispassion;
as for "tat" (that),
it is used in the sense of "kiṃ tu" (but rather) to indicate an alternative position.
And thus, the sense is that Śukra uttered his lamentation solely for the sake of benefiting others.
Lamentation:
this sequence applies for as long as life lasts to both the wise and the ignorant body.
"Worldly transaction occurs through power or lack of power, always"—
or else, in another sense,
the connection is "the transaction of the body."
Or, by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it means "of the body" and "of the embodied one.
And thus, it means "of the body of the knower" or "of the body of the ignorant."
The sequence should be understood as follows: by way of non-attachment for the knower, and by way of attachment for the ignorant.
Those who have fully realized the goal and those who are ignorant, following the nature of bound souls (paśu).
In worldly transactions, they remain like a forest thicket;
the forest thicket is to be understood as a metaphor for mere existence.
Just as an ignorant person engages in worldly affairs, so indeed does the wise one.
In this matter, the difference consisting solely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the cause of bondage and liberation.
This difference of latent impressions alone is to be understood in terms of purity and impurity.
For as long as there is a body, so long is there suffering in suffering and pleasure in pleasure.
The wise, whose intellects are unattached, demonstrate [things] as if they were unawakened;
they demonstrate them to others,
but do not see them themselves.
Great-souled beings are always happy amidst pleasures and sorrowful amidst states of suffering; indeed, they are seen to be truly cool within.
"Cool" means free from the agitation caused by pleasure and pain.

(MT_4,15.38) Just as reflections on a pillar are disturbed while the stable body remains unmoved, so too the organs of action of the wise man are disturbed while his steady mind remains unmoved. MU_4,15.39
*Stambhasya*: [N17: *stambha*°] A firm body, a solid nature called a pillar (*stambha*).
[The term] "they agitate" (*kṣubhyanti*) contains the causative sense (*antar-gata-ṇic*).
What are the two applications?
The meaning is that they do not cause agitation.
The organs of action are those which perform the function known as perception; this is the meaning of "organs of knowledge" (jñānendriya).
Agitating [the world] through their state of constant flux, the knower of that remains amidst worldly activities;
like the sun reflected in clear waters, he stays as if situated below.
The knower of that;
situated below; in reflections.
Clear;
due to being moving and unsteady, that is, through extreme instability.
In what state is Bhāskara? He is one whose *sthiti*—that is, his abiding or staying—is *adhas*, in the lower region. (MT_4,15.40)

One whose intellect is unawakened is indeed bound even if he has abandoned worldly activities; one whose intellect is awakened is indeed liberated even if he does not abandon the play of delusion. The point here is that it is precisely the state of having an awakened intellect or an unawakened intellect that constitutes the cause for liberation or bondage.
For one whose faculty of intellect is liberated is liberated even if the faculty of action is bound; likewise,
one whose faculty of intellect is bound is bound even if the faculty of action is liberated.
The word *hi* indicates what is well-known (*prasiddhi*). For one whose intellect is awakened,
there is [the realization of] pleasure and pain in the world, as well as bondage and liberation.
The causes are the very faculties of perception, like fires for the purpose of illumination;
"illumination" means the act of making an object manifest.
One who follows conduct appropriate for the external world, yet is devoid of internal conduct— (MU 4.15.43)
Remain as if you were asleep, with all desires completely stilled;
remaining within the mind,
abide in the Self by means of the Self, liberated from all longings.
Perform your duties; indeed, let your mind remain established in tranquility. O Rāma, you, who are liberated from all worldly desires!
Therefore, by means of the self— that is, by the mind— abiding in the Self and not in objects which are of the nature of the non-Self,
one's duties are to be performed with discipline.
Perform your actions;
indeed, with certainty,
that state which is not in the mind is not a state of being established in the mind.

Do not fall into this pit on the path of saṃsāra, which has great whirlpools of mental and physical afflictions, and which is a deep, bottomless well of intense darkness characterized by the sense of "mine-ness," leading only to downfall.
How is this well of intense darkness characterized?
On the path of saṃsāra, on the way that has the nature of saṃsāra;
in a pit, existing as a pit.
You are not in things, nor are things in you, O lotus-eyed one;
you are of the nature of pure consciousness, established in the Self—be steadfast.
You are the witness, whose form is pure consciousness alone.
Established in the self, one is devoted to one's own nature as pure and awakened;
one is not, however, devoted to the body and so forth.
[One who is devoted to the self whose nature is pure buddhahood] concludes the answer with the final verse of the chapter:
"Having attained the stainless state, free from longing and devoid of the great darkness of the notion of 'mine'— "
O Great-Souled One, if you have mastery over the mind, then homage to you, the great being of transcendent wisdom!
That [mind] from which the great darkness consisting of the form of "mine-ness" has departed.
Such is it;
for this very reason, it is stainless (*amala*), free from seeking (*vigataiṣaṇa*) because of its satisfaction, and devoid of all longing.
Having reached the state called pure consciousness—
that is, having realized it as one's own self— if you prevail over the mind, O mind, you will become capable of conquering it.
O Great-Souled One! At that time, let there be homage to you. To one who is of what nature?
To the one of supreme intellect (*atidhiye*),
to the great one endowed with greatness (*mahate*),
to the existent whose nature is pure being (*sate*)— may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto in the "Stability" chapter of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-Ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Fifteenth [Chapter]:
Then, having set aside those words of his son, Bhṛgu at that time—
The Blessed Lord Kāla, having cast aside [the objection] by making it the object of his censure, spoke these words in a deep voice to Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu.
Having interrupted [the conversation],
Time said:
"O Bhārgava, abandon this body of the ascetic woman Samaṅgā."
O virtuous one, enter this body as a king enters a city.
*Samaṅgātāpasīm* means belonging to the ascetic *Samaṅga*.
"O sinless one, having performed penance again with this body [you possess] from your previous birth, you must at the proper time assume the position of the lords of the Asuras.
This is clear.
"When the end of the great aeon has arrived, you must cast off this body of Bhārgava, like a withered flower, so that it shall not be taken up again.
This is clear.
"O high-minded one, remain in this body with its former form, having attained the state of liberation while living, acting as the preceptor to the great lords of the asuras.
[The phrase] "with its former form" refers to that known by the name Śukra.
"May it be well with you both; we shall go to our desired direction.
There is not even the slightest thing that would not be desired by one [who has attained such a state].
"But how can there be anything desired even for you?"
To this he says: "Nothing at all.
That is not even something slight, for that mind has no desired object.

"Therefore, because I too possess a mind, [the fruit] is desired by me"— this was the thought [of the other]. Having said this, as the two of them were releasing the flower, he vanished from between them, like the sun, the radiant one, disappearing from heaven and earth simultaneously with its rays.
Of the two releasing [light]: *taptāṃśuḥ* means the sun;
*rodasyoḥ* means of heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivyoḥ*).
When the Blessed One had departed after speaking of that destiny,
Bhārgava reflected upon the course of necessity— which is indivisible and fixed by fate—
dried up by the cause of time, yet destined for the auspicious arising of future blossoms.
Mādhava entered that youthful body, which was as impenetrable and impossible to pierce as a well-grown creeper;
it was the cause known as Time.
By that [word], "śuṣkā" (the dry one) refers to Mādhava, which is spring;
by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to the aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*) of spring.
She, whose auspicious rising was like that of a flower about to bloom—
(MT_4,16.8-9)— that body of a Brahmin woman fell to the ground, pale and bodiless, trembling violently like a creeper whose roots have been severed. (MU_4,16.10)
The body of the Brahmin was that of a Samaṅga ascetic.
When the life-force had entered that body of his son, the great sage performed a nourishing rite with mantras and the water from his water-pot.
With the waters from their water-pots,
there was a nourishing filling.
Then all her slender channels shone forth, filled to the brim.
Like rivers in the rainy season whose hollows are filled with floods of water,
all the channels [are filled] from her.
This is clear.
Like a lotus pond in the rainy season or a new creeper in spring, when she was full [of life], her vital breaths appeared as if budding. (MU 4.16.13)
The vital breaths (prāṇas) are this body of Bhārgava;
it is full, being filled with the vital breaths.
Of that body,
the sprouts are those that have swollen in the form of the *apāna* and other vital airs.
Then Śukra arose, carrying forth the vital breaths,
like a rain-cloud from its very roots through the union of sap and wind.
Starting from the very root,
from the foundation itself, he of pure form first saluted his father,
just as a cloud newly risen greets a mountain with its thundering.
This is clear.
Then the father embraced her former body as well,
his conduct moist with affection, like a rain cloud after a long time embracing a mountain slope.
This is clear.
Bhṛgu beheld with affection his former body from which he had been born;
the conviction "this one was born from me" carries away even a man of great intelligence.

"Belonging to her son" means related to her son. [An objection: "But how could such a body, belonging to her son, have been looked upon with affection by him who was possessed of such knowledge? To this, he says: "By me... (MT 4.16.17).

The affection that thought, "This is my son," then overcame even Bhṛgu; for this sense of "otherness" and "self-identity" persists as long as there is a physical form. (MU 4.16.18) "Otherness" (*paratā*) means the state of being another (*parabhāva*).
The state of being one's own is the condition of ownership;
it lasts as long as the form and as long as the body.
It is destined to be and is unavoidable.
Then the father and son became mutually adorned, like the sun and a bed of lotuses rejoicing at the end of the night. "At the end of the night" means at dawn; "rejoicing" means delighted.
[Muditau] N17: °t⟨o⟩[au] (MT_4,16.19). Right here, he tells two other similes:
like a pair of cakravāka birds joined together after a long separation.
Like a peacock and a cloud, they were filled with intense longing and deep affection for one another.
Having stayed there for a moment in that conversation, which was suited to their long-standing and firm yearning, those two of great intelligence then rose.
There they reduced that body of the twice-born Samaṅga to ashes.
For who indeed, born into this world, does not follow established conduct (*ācāra*)? [In this context,] *ācāra* refers to the conduct of the world.
[Regarding worldly conduct] (N17:
[a pair]) (MT_4,16.20-22): Thus those two, Bhṛgu and Bhārgava, remained in that purifying forest, radiant with asceticism like the moon and the sun in the sky. (MU_4,16.23)
Like two clear [lights] in the sky,
those two teachers of the world, who had realized what is to be known and were liberated while living, moved about.
Austerity that is well-calmed and well-steadfast amidst the floods of place, time, and state.
How is that austerity?
It is that in which there is excellent tranquility (*śama*).
That; such was it.
(MT 4.16.24) Then, in the course of time, that Śukra attained the status of preceptor to the Asuras, while Bhṛgu remained in his own appropriate and healthy station. (MU 4.16.25)
In the state appropriate for himself, namely the state known as liberation while in the bodyless form (*videhamukti*).
With a verse at the end of the section on creation, he recounts the account of Śuka in brief, beginning with "This Śuka":
"This Śuka was first born from this supreme state in due order, one of noble fame."
"By his own swift wandering through the paths of memory, he subsequently becomes thus utterly agitated amidst various states.
From this supreme state, known as pure consciousness (cinmātra), which stands before all things as their very self; from that highest station.
In the ten intermediate stages, ending with the states of the Samaṅga and the Tapasattva; thus may there be auspiciousness.
"In these particular states" (etasmād avasthāviśeṣeṣu).
Thus ends the sixteenth canto in the "Chapter on Stability" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

O Blessed One, why is it that the inspired flash of insight belonging to the son of Bhṛgu became fruitful for him through his own experience, yet does not likewise occur for another? MU 4.17.1 O Blessed One!
Of this son of Bhṛgu, who has been described by the account just mentioned—
that "insight" (pratibhā) refers to that manifestation consisting in his passage through various wombs.

In that same way,
for another person— that is, a person distinct from Śukra—
how could that intuition not be fruitful? It would indeed be so.
For the state of being an elephant and so forth, which appears in a dream, is not experienced as being directly perceived by oneself.
Regarding the account:
Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks this reply; at that time, she first arose from the foot of Brahmā.
The intellect of Bhārgava is pure, unstained by any other birth;
this is the first instance, as it was his very first [birth],
belonging to Bhārgava, that is, Śukra.
Because it has arisen immediately from the station of Brahmā,
that intellect has as its object various births and manifestations.

It was pure, untainted by the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous births. Consequently, his visionary intuition (*pratibhā*), which takes the form of traversing various realms of existence (*yoni*), became fruitful.
Others, however, [say it was] from even earlier.

The meaning is that, because they have arisen in the interim, being stained by the network of latent impressions (vāsanā) produced from various other births, they do not experience their own manifestation as a direct perception.
Because they have arisen [from the state of being awakened],
they are stained by the web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that have arisen from various other births. (MT_4,17.2)
"Now, what is the nature of this pure cognition?
To this, he says:
