That state of the mind which is pure when all desires have been completely stilled is called *sattva*; it is described as this stainless consciousness (*cid*).
[Regarding the phrase] "of all desires": [this refers to] all the various longings directed toward the multitude of objects that are to be enjoyed.
When there is pacification— meaning the calming of the mind (manas)— through the power of deep sleep and so forth, or by means of right knowledge and the like.
That which is stability, that which is abiding—
this exists;
it is [perceived] by the wise.
It is called *sattva*;
it is that very stainless consciousness (*citi*), which is described as stainless intelligence (*mati*).
Furthermore, this very pure intellect belongs both to one in whom it has arisen for the first time and to one who is liberated while living;
it belongs to the former as well.
For one who has [merely] arisen [in samādhi], it is directed outward;
however, for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), it is distinguished by being relinquished as it moves outward.
Having spoken by way of specific distinctions regarding all desires, he now speaks in general terms: whatever kind of thing the mind, whose nature is stainless, contemplates, [that it becomes].
That indeed becomes exactly so quickly, just like a whirlpool of water in the ocean;
[it is] the mind whose nature is pure being (*nirmalasattvātman*), having the character of pure being as described in the preceding verse.
Whatever [object], in whatever manner, and as it is endowed [with qualities],
one contemplates— that is, brings within the scope of analytical investigation—
is that very thing.
It occurs quickly, in that manner, and in that way.
What is that object like?
It is like a whirlpool;
just as a whirlpool situated in the ocean suddenly assumes another form.
The meaning is "so it is.
By means of this account, he declares his own intended conclusion:
"Just as this delusion of the son of Bhṛgu arose spontaneously..."

In each case, there is likewise an illustration here: the son of Bhṛgu. Just as this son of Bhṛgu experienced this aforementioned delusion, which consists of the appearance of various wombs, such is the nature of delusion.
Arising by its own nature means having manifested;
"just so" means in that very same way.
It arises for each individual person;
the meaning is that everyone perceives the world as nothing other than the form of a manifestation within their own mind.
Of this point...
To further strengthen [the argument], he again states that Śukra serves as an example, saying: "The example is here" (MT 4,17.5).
He makes this very point easy to understand through various examples:
"Just as the seed produces its own sprouts, leaves, and so forth, with marvelous transformation..."
For all classes of beings, the whirlpool of delusion is likewise;
just as the sprout, leaf, and so forth belong to a particular seed and are not common to other seeds.
It causes wonder; it produces bliss in the form of swelling. Indeed, this is certain.
Of all the multitudes of beings, of all the aggregates of beings;
his own, not shared by others,
is the grove of delusion— the grove of delusion in the form of the world.
In the very same way, it produces wonder and brings about the happiness of various tastes;
the point is that although this saṃsāra appears as something common [to all], it is indeed distinct for each individual.
Whatever is seen as this entire universe, it is exactly like that.
"Each [element] that has arisen is false, and it is indeed falsely that it sets. This entire universe, which is perceived and experienced by us as saṃsāra—
"Hi" signifies certainty;
"evam eva" means in this very manner; "sthitam eva tat" means that it is indeed established as such.
The entire universe arises falsely at every moment; the suffix *kta* here denotes the present tense.
It likewise sets in falsehood, for it remains eternally as such by virtue of its nature being that of the supreme consciousness (*paracit*).
The intended meaning is that it is because [the Self] cannot be the object of arising and setting in reality.
[The suffix] *kta* [is used] in the sense of the present [time] (Pāṇini 2.3.67).

Since it is impossible for that which has been accomplished (*satyabhūta*) to be the object of rising or setting, [the world] does not set nor does it rise for anyone; nothing whatsoever [exists] for anyone.
This is mere delusion; illusion expands in vain.
This world is illusion, having the nature of illusion.
Just as this grove of cyclic existence exists within our own appearance—
For in that same way, thousands of such [worlds] exist, mutually unseen by one another.

Just as this entire forest of saṃsāra— which, though transcending the senses because its nature is pure consciousness beyond all sense organs— resides within our own mental appearance, it nevertheless manifests as "this-ness" (idantā).
Likewise, there are thousands of those groves of saṃsāra. In response to the inquiry as to why they are not seen, he provides the qualification: "not seen by one another" (*mitho 'dṛṣṭāni*).
"By one another" (*mithaḥ*) means mutually.
"Unseen" means not brought within the range of vision.
[The text] provides an example of mutual seeing:
"the example of mutual seeing."
Just as the activities of dreams, mental constructions, and cities [of the gandharvas] are not seen separately from one another, so too are these delusions of cyclic existence.
The summary meaning is this: just as one person does not experience the dream of another, so too one person does not experience the saṃsāra of another.
If it is asked, "But how is there a distinction between creations for each individual?
the answer is: no.
Because, with respect to one and the same object, there is the perception of it as either to be abandoned or to be accepted depending on the difference between persons.
"Another does not experience," [N17: *anyo* (for *antyo*) ... *nānu* (for *nānubha*)].
He provides a summary by showing that [the self] is to be abandoned and to be adopted.
In this way, there exist multitudes of cities whose nature is the mental construction of space; yet they are not seen by one another without the vision of knowledge.

This being the case: "in the sky" refers to the mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) of cities and so forth; those whose form is like that [construction] are such cities, and their "multitudes" are their collections.
The provision of an adjective for the word *nagara* (city), which has become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in a compound, is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).
By those groups of cities, [it means] those various groups of cities.
Without the vision of knowledge— that is, without the vision known as the cognition of pure consciousness—
they are not seen, nor are they experienced, mutually by one another. By means of the vision of knowledge...
But they are indeed seen;
therefore, the meaning is: "For this very reason, I see them, while you do not see them."
[The provision of a qualification: N17: vi(śe)ṣe°;
[the word] "vinā" is [read as] N17: °nā(na) (MT_4,17.11).
This states that even for all well-known beings such as *piśācas* and others, this very nature [of being devoid of self-nature] applies.
For there truly exist Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas of such a nature;
their bodies consist of mere volition and are composed of pleasure and pain.
This is clear.
He extends this very same nature even to himself:
"In this very way, O descendant of Raghu, we and these others have come into being; our forms consist of our own volitions, conditioned by the perception of falsity and truth. (MU 4.17.13)
We have been conditioned by the state of false truth; that is, [we have been conditioned] by the state of falsity within what is taken to be one's own truth.
"Developed" means engaged in cultivation.
Having thus spoken briefly of the distinction, he speaks again in general terms:
"For the cycle of creation and transmigration proceeds for others in this very manner."
But in reality, this [notion of] "establishment" does not truly exist with respect to a non-entity.
Of such a nature, it has the form of a reflection;
when others have crossed over into pure consciousness (cinmātra),
the cycle of creation— so named as "creation" (sarga)— is the flow of worldly existence (saṃsṛti).
It is not real, for it is unreal in nature;
however, from another perspective—
that is, in reality or from the standpoint of ultimate truth— it is so.
This cycle of creation and transmigration persists within that which is non-substantial and empty.
Since it is impossible for pure consciousness, which exists as a reality, to be the substratum of a creation that is itself unreal;
[the author] concludes his own desired position established by the previously stated reasoning: "In this very way, every universe that has arisen is indeed in vain."
Just as the essence of spring [is manifested] in the form of new buds,
so too [is it manifested] in the manner previously described.

The "spring juice" (*vāsantika-rasa*) is the essence associated with spring. This first [state], one's own volition, has attained such great renown that it is thus clearly perceived as being, in the highest sense, firmly established.
This is the first [manifestation] of Brahmā, arisen as preceding him;
it is his very own volition (saṅkalpa).
"In that manner" means by that mode.
He has attained great renown and supreme excellence;
"in this way" means by this manner.
It is firmly established and unshakable;
it is thoroughly discerned and ascertained through its supreme ultimacy and its nature as the ultimate truth.
The word "by people" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Each individual consciousness, abiding within the belly of its own inherent nature,
perishes while perceiving this world as being undertaken in such a manner.
This "own" (*svaḥ*) means one's own;
it is one's inherent nature (*svabhāva*), the essential form known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
In his belly— meaning in that which is like a belly,
but not in a literal belly—
he was situated, meaning he remained there.
"Each" means in each and every one;
"arisen" means produced;
"mind."
Behold— experience— this world as having such an undertaking, characterized by a visible onset;
it perishes, meaning it falls away from the awareness of its own true nature.
Due to the power of appearance, there is existence; due to the observation of the thing-in-itself, there is non-existence.
Long is this dream, the web of the world, the tethering post for the elephant of the mind.
By virtue of appearance;
for it is not logical that there should be an appearance of what is non-existent—this is the meaning.
Because of the observation of the real thing, that is, because of the observation of the ultimate reality (paramārtha).
For the world does not persist by means of right knowledge;
who is there to [perceive] the web of the world?
It is a long dream.
For the existence of the world is indeed the existence of the mind, and the existence of the mind is the world itself;
in the absence of one, both are destroyed, and that occurs through the investigation of reality.
Thus, there is the non-existence of one.
"From the investigation of truth" means from the investigation of reality.
He recalls the answer to the question posed by Śrī Rāma:
"For the manifestation of a pure mind is indeed true."
"For the staining with saffron adheres only to a spotless cloth.
Here he states the illustration: "niṣkalaṅke" means in that which is stainless and free from impurity.
The quality of that which has not been brought by another necessarily increases;
the intuition of the mind arises when it is not assailed by conceptual constructions.
*Anāhṛtasya* means "of that which has not been brought," and *anākrāntasya* means "of that which is not assailed."
Having stated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he explains the illustrated point (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "of that which is unassailed.
*Pratibhā* means manifestation (*pratibhāsa*).
It "arises" (*udeti*), meaning it appears as something possessing fruit.

Just as gold does not remain [pure] when it is in a soiled garment, so a single vision does not remain stable when the mind is withered. (MU 4.17.22) "Suvarṇaḥ" means beautiful, such as the color white and so forth.
When [the mind] is withered and stained by conceptual constructions,
its purification occurs through long-term, firm practice— just as a gem is cleansed by rubbing or copper is purified by the proper application of methods. (MU 4.17.22–23)
Regarding "in the mind" (*maṇesi*):
it refers to a single [object] such as right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Firm practice (*dṛḍhābhyāsa*) is the constant contemplation (*nairantaryeṇa taccintanam*) thereof; from that [practice]. (MT_4,17.23)
Śrī Rāma asks:
How do these sequences of time and action, along with their rising and setting, arise within the mind of Śukra in this world whose nature is mere appearance?
In a world whose nature is mere appearance, it is not logical for the sequences of temporal activity that manifest therein to possess both rising and setting;
and the point is: how could such a thing have arisen for Śukra’s mind?
Regarding the sequence of the processes of death,
Śrī Vasiṣṭha spoke this reply to Śukacetas.
Just as this world was seen by Śukra [to have arisen] from his father and mother, so too did it remain established in his mind, like a peacock within a peacock’s egg. (MU 4.17.25) [Note:
*jagad* is the reading in N17.]
Whatever this world was seen by the semen produced from the father and mother,
that very same thing remained situated in the mind of that semen.
How? Like a peacock;
just as a peacock exists within a peacock's egg.
The meaning is "so it is.
By this, that which has arisen in sequence from the treasury of its own nature is explained,
just as a sprout, leaf, creeper, flower, and fruit arise from a seed.
Then, by means of this semen,
that world residing within the mind [is emitted];
it is the nature which, being of the form of the mind, emerges from the treasury of its own-being.
From that treasury of such a form,
[the nectar] has arisen in succession and been tasted— that is, made an object of savoring.
Regarding this, he states an analogy:
"By the seed":
the living being perceives within itself that very essence which consists of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
A dream is the illustration for this; indeed, this world is a long-lasting dream. (MU 4.17.27)
Now, one might ask: "How can a dream be an illustration here? To this he replies: "It is indeed a long dream. This refers to its length.
And here, it should be understood by virtue of its long-lasting appearance:
"O Rāma, has the thicket of saṃsāra not arisen individually?
At night, it is clearly manifest within one's own self, like the web of dreams of men in an army. (MU 4.17.28)
[Like an army, a man, and a dream-network:
For at night, the forms of an army, a man, and a dream-network arise individually and separately.
Śrī Rāma asks:
This flood of the thicket of transmigratory existence meets together of its own accord;
or perhaps it does not— if so, you ought to tell me that correctly.
This flood of the thicket of cyclic existence, by its very nature,
whether it meets with others or not, [is thus].
They do not even meet;
you ought to speak this correctly and properly—that is to say, you should explain it accurately. (MT_4,17.29)
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Indeed, a defiled mind does not deserve union with vigor, just as iron that is not heated does not adhere to other iron;
but when it is purified and heated, it melts together."
"Hi" signifies certainty. "Malina" means defiled by impurities such as passion (*rāga*).
For this very reason, it is "avīrya" (lacking vigor). "Manah" refers to the mind. "Mithaḥ" means mutually or one another.
It does not deserve adhesion, that is, union.
What is it like?
"Like iron":
the meaning is that just as iron does not deserve adhesion when it is not heated, so it is in this case.
But in the alternative case:
"the mind" means in the pure mind.
*Līyate* means it merges;
and this [mind] merges into the heated iron.
The pure principles of consciousness merge with one another.
For waters of a single form attain unity, but not those that are turbid;
this is clear.
He expresses this very point with the concluding verse of the chapter:
For purity of the mind consists in being free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and having the nature of perceiving what is not real; it is one.
Upon awakening from that state, which is like the condition of deep sleep, through the application of that [purity] alone, it attains union with the Supreme.
(The word *hi* indicates certainty. Having the nature of perceiving what is not real means having the essential character of perceiving objects that are not established.
"State of being devoid of impressions" means the absence of the mental impression (saṃskāra) known as the cultivation (bhāvanā) directed toward objects.
"One" means solitary.
Thus, the purity of the mind comes about.
That mind is the self of deep sleep, having the nature of deep sleep; it is that state,
that place.
Therefore,
for the sake of that purity,
having awakened to the consciousness known as the fourth (turya).
Having attained that through the application of its own subtle elements,
it goes— that is, proceeds— to union with others, which is contact with other things.
By that very reasoning, "union" (melana) should be understood as the knowledge that everything shares a single material cause with oneself. Thus all is auspicious.
And by one's own [effort], in this world and the next, by one's own [power].

Seventeenth [chapter]:
In the *Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by Śrī Bhāskara Kaṇṭha, within the section on "Stability" (*sthiti-prakaraṇa*), the seventeenth [chapter].
Oṃ! But how can the mind, consisting of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), unite with other things? To this he replies:
"In all the clusters of transmigratory existence, there is no difference in the manifestation of that which consists of the nature of the seed-form of the subtle elements. (MU 4.18.1)
That which is the digit (kalā) consisting of the seed, having the nature of the seed—
that [is the power] of that self, of that very nature.

That is to say, of that which has the form of the seeds of the gross elements; [it refers to] the appearance consisting of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which is the appearance of the subtle elements themselves.
In all the clusters of saṃsāra, in every cluster consisting of created forms,
there is no duality within the manifestation or the radiance.
Just as [the nature of] clay manifests in jars and other objects,
the point is that it is indeed logical for the mind to merge with something else through the application of that same principle.

Furthermore, the *tanmātras*— which are the seeds of the gross elements, whose bodies consist solely of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and which are the five [subtle elements] beginning with sound, distinguished from ether and the rest by the intellect— are to be understood as such.
having the nature of seeds;
in the forms of creation; those which have become the seeds of the gross elements.
[Regarding "from ether and so forth"]:
Not only does the merging with the [five] creations occur through the logic of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), but there is also a merging within Brahman.

Intending to say "by that very [state]," he says: "The engagement or the withdrawal of every class of living beings occurs immediately after the attainment of that alone, due to their state of deep sleep. (MU 4.18.2)
Because all classes of living beings, the entire multitude of souls,
are in a state of deep sleep; immediately thereafter, subsequently.
Either it is *pravṛtti*, which is union with other creations;

or it is *nivṛtti*, which is withdrawal from creations or union within Brahman in the form of cessation; this occurs only after attaining the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and only through the conjunction with those subtle elements.
In deep sleep,
because the creations exist as seeds, their cessation is impossible; because the creations do not exist in a manifest state, their activity is impossible.

Thus, because of the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), it is said "immediately after" (*anantaram*). By the mention of "immediately after," the necessary presence of deep sleep here is indicated; for the necessity of deep sleep, which stands as the bridge between Brahman and the creation, is perfectly clear.

In this context, the distinction between the subject matter should be understood as follows: activity belongs to those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), whereas cessation belongs to those liberated after death (videhamukta).
As for the activity of others, however, since it is rooted in ignorance, it is not appropriate to discuss it here.
[The meeting] with others (*itareṣām*):
because the activity (*pravṛtti*) under discussion is preceded by the attainment of those [subtle elements] alone (*tanmātra*), he explains this separately.
Those living beings who possess active engagement have reached the state of the subtle elements;
through their oneness with those subtle elements, they perceive mutually imagined creations.

Those living beings who, by virtue of being one with the subtle elements (*tanmātraikatayā*), possess the nature of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*); yet, because a residue of *sattva* remains, they partake in activity and are joined with worldly engagement.
They exist as being identical with those subtle elements (*tanmātra*) through the logic of the subtle elements;
they are mutually [related] as creations that are imagined as ultimate reality, having an imagined nature.
They see that the minds of those liberated while living meet one another;
herein lies the supreme secret.

Through the single conduit of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the variegated reservoirs of creation mingle with one another and attain density on all sides. (MU 4.18.4) [The term] *tanmātrāṇām* refers to the five subtle elements.
That which is oneness is itself the channel, the path for the flow of water; by means of that,
[it attains] density, the state of being solidified.
Regarding [the state of] density (*ghanatām*): N17 reads *°⟨nānā⟩[natā]m*.
Now, do all the floods of creation (*sargaughāḥ*) converge through the single channel of the subtle elements (*tanmātraikyapraṇāla*), or only some of them? To this, he says:
"the floods of creation" (*sargaughāḥ*). N17 reads *°r(mai)*[mai]*°*.

Some have come to exist separately and have likewise gone to dissolution separately; some world-islands have been established remaining joined together with one another. Some possess impure intellects.
In the latter half [of the verse], some are of pure intellect;
they are produced or constructed,
but not innate.
Now, on what substratum do such floods of creations rest? To this he says:
"Wherein thousands of world-systems, innumerable within every single atom, exist without touching one another—that is the forest named Brahman. (MU 4.18.6)
Not joined to one another, they are unmixed with each other;
in every atom, part by part. Having attained density, it does not undergo mutual merging.
Whatever is established in whatever manner at whatever place, that he perceives as such and nothing else.
"Melana" (conjunction) refers to density, the state of being solidified.
The creation has passed away; it does not meet with one another, nor does it proceed [to do so], because that creation— by implication,
the subject (pramātṛ) residing therein— is [thus characterized].
Whatever is firmly rooted and well-practiced in a particular place,
that alone one perceives there,
and nothing else; such is the case here.
The impurity of the cognizer's intellect has been stated many times as the cause [of error].
Remaining there,
due to the power of current mental constructions,
the successions of living beings are mutually joined together; these are the established conceptions of the creations.
The present mental kingdom is *saṅkalpa*; by its power,
the successions of individual lives are joined together with one another.
They come to be. The sense is that living beings (*jīva*) meet one another because their mental aspirations (*manorājya*) are identical. Of what nature are these successions of living beings?
When the creations have attained their established reality— that is, when they are true— those [mental impressions] which consist of those [realities] are called *bhāvanās*.
This is the meaning:
the creations of those with pure intellects always meet through the channel of oneness with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*);
however, for those of impure intellect, they meet only occasionally through the identity of their volitions (*saṅkalpa*).
[The state of being: N17: *How is the succession of living beings [possible]?

The state of being [is reached] through the channel of oneness with that alone.* (MT_4,18.8) Now, how has this existence of the body attained manifestation, by virtue of which [the world appears] to those whose intellects are covered by the impurity called "volition" (*saṅkalpa*)?
"Because of the channel of oneness with those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), there is no merging with other creations. To this, he says:
"The existence of the body is deeply rooted, while the absence of the body is forgotten;
because it is so thoroughly established as 'bodiness,' the sky of consciousness has forgotten its true Self. (MU 4.18.9)
[Forgotten] N17:

The existence of the body has become established and has reached full growth;
however, in the alternative view,
the non-existence of the body is that which is ultimately real— the absolute negation (abhāva) relative to the body throughout the three periods of time.
By what kind of consciousness-space? By that which has forgotten the Self—that is, by that whose own true nature has been forgotten.
"Forgotten" means brought to a state of forgetfulness.
[In the alternative view:

Just as one whose vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been purified through *prāṇāyāma* and other means is called a "practitioner of breath" (*prāṇayogin*), because his vital breath is pure due to the piercing of the vital breaths of others.
Because of that piercing and pervading [of the vital breaths] within the lives of others.
"From entering another's body" means up to that point; "the kingdom of the mind of the one to be pierced" refers to the person who is to be pervaded by the piercing.
He knows his own kingdom;
likewise, in that same manner, one who has taken refuge in the human body—
having entered another person through the channel of that [subtle] essence alone— is either a person liberated while living (jīvanmukta) or the Puruṣa who first arose from Brahman.
He knows the creations, that is, the creations of the Puruṣa who has taken refuge [in Prakṛti].
The person whose vital breath is pure; [N17:
(Brahma-)person].
Having thus correctly given the answer to the question posed by Śrī Rāma, he relates the various scattered instructional statements that were previously mentioned here and there,
[stating them] correctly.
For all multitudes of living beings,
the Self (ātman) rests in three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; in this regard, the body is not the cause.
Regarding the states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— here, by resorting to these three states,
the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) exists within the Self, which consists of those other three states.
In this [Self], which consists of the three other states, the state of being a body shines forth like the nature of waves in heated water;
"other" means appearing as something distinct from itself.
That which consists of the three states— the three states beginning with waking— is that whose nature (ātman) is such;
[in Him who is] like that.
In this self, which is delimited by the state of being alive.
Having reached the state of the aggregate of consciousness within this [body], and remaining in the state at the end of deep sleep,
the enlightened living being returns [to its source], while the deluded one proceeds toward rebirth.
The state of the digit of consciousness (citkalāpada), called the fourth (turya), returns; the Buddha is one capable of the reflective awareness (vimarśana) of the digit of consciousness.
It turns back and no longer indulges in attachment to sense objects;
it proceeds and indulges in attachment to sense objects.
When there is purity of intrinsic nature, then loving-kindness proceeds.
How is friendship characterized? It is precisely of the nature of oneness between two, serving as the manifestation of perfect affection. How is it?
It is indeed of the nature of oneness between the two.
For the meaning of the word "friendliness" (maitrī) is indeed the oneness of two; furthermore, of what nature is it? It is the manifestation of perfect affection.
It is characterized by excellent friendship and the state of being a praiseworthy friend;
it is that of which this is the illustration or example.
For when there is perfect friendship between two, they become truly one.
The ignorant individual soul (*jīva*) awakens from deep sleep and becomes a partaker of its own creation;
because consciousness (*cit*) is omnipresent, some [souls] are led away by another's creation. (MU 4.18.15)
Because it is all-pervading,
it is led [back]; possessing its own creation, it returns to whatever nature it had prior to the state of deep sleep (suṣupti).
The meaning is that it is precisely of such a nature.
The leading [of the seed] by means of another emission should be understood as a transformation of its inherent nature;
or alternatively, the leading by another emission is illustrated by the example of the emission of semen and so forth.
[This] is to be applied.
[Objection: But in that creation, where is another creation by which he is led? To this he says:
"In every creation there exist other creations as well, each with a distinct form."
Within those as well, there are floods of creations nested within one another like the layers of a plantain leaf;
just as there are other leaves within the leaves of a plantain tree, and within those others yet again, so it is with these creations.
There are other creations;
within those, there are yet others—this is the summary meaning.
In each creation, it possesses a function as vast as the filling of other creations.
The pavilion of Brahma’s plantain leaves is naturally cool. In one creation,
there is that which fills other creations— the multitude of other worlds.
That itself is the leaves; by them, its existence— its subsistence— is plump, meaning of a nourishing nature.
He is such.
Just as there is no difference among the hundreds of leaves of a plantain tree,
so too there is no difference within the reality of Brahman, even across hundreds of creations.
This is clear.
(MT 4.18.18) Just as a fruit arises from a seed and, through its sap, the seed comes into being again, so too Brahman, having become the mind, becomes Brahman again through awakening. (MU 4.18.19)
Just as a fruit arises from a seed that serves as its material cause,
having come into being and manifested from the cause of the sap.
Furthermore, it becomes the seed;
likewise, Brahmā, having become the mind, [arises] from awakening.
Furthermore, one shall become Brahmā.
The seed, having the essence as its cause, unfolds into the state of the fruit;
the individual soul (*jīva*), having Brahman as its cause, unfolds into the form of the world.
This is clear.
[It is] clear.
It is not appropriate to say what the cause of taste might be;
nor is it appropriate to speak of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as something distinct, because it is devoid of differentiation.
How is it that [this] is not tenable?
To this, he says: "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
Intrinsic nature is merely the ultimate.
Because there is no distinction,
it is not appropriate to bring it under the scope of verbal expression or the subject of formal application.

The intention of the phrase "because there is no distinction" is that if an objection were raised against intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then because there would be no distinction, the objection would apply to all intrinsic natures;
and it is not possible to assert non-existence anywhere within that which consists of all things.

The meaning is that there is no causeless first cause, nor is there a first cause other than [the one already established], because it is impossible for that which is non-existent (asat) to consist of everything.
Thus: "not without a cause."
In that which has no cause—
that is, in such a case— in the supreme, primordial cause, the ultimate, pure consciousness alone,
there is no cause or the like.
The meaning is that this is because of the loss of the status of being the primordial cause.
When the seed abandons its own form because it has ceased to be the primary cause, it is seen as having become the fruit;
but Brahman, not abandoning its own form, remains established as both the fruit and the seed.
[It] is observed:
"The fruit and the seed are seen to exist as one; everything possesses the form of the seed, therefore that state is formless."
The reason for the non-abandonment of its own form while Brahman exists in the state of being a seed is precisely this:
everything possesses the form of a seed, whereas that state [of Brahman] is formless;
therefore, it is not possible to equate them, and thus there is no analogy for Śiva.
The entire,
complete nature of the seed becomes possessed of form;
for that reason, from that cause.
In Śiva, whose true nature is pure consciousness alone,
there is no analogy.
It is space itself that arises as the manifestation of space, yet it does not arise as something other than that.
Therefore, O Brahmin, know that the world is neither born nor has it been born;
for from Brahman— which is like the sky due to its absolute purity and luminosity—
only the sky itself is born.
To the question "How is this so?", he says: "And not...
The word "and" (ca) indicates a reason.
For that which is called the world is space; it is "other-sighted," meaning its nature is perception other than Brahman;
it is not born, that is, it does not arise.
It explains the result by saying "from this":
from this, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it is not born;
or, from the perspective of appearance (*ābhāsataḥ*), it is born.
Know that the world is the Brahman-sky, the ether of Brahman.
Seeing the visible world as a mere appearance, the seer does not perceive his own self.

For whom does one's own innate state arise when consciousness is overcome by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)? Seeing the seer, the seen— the multitude of entities that have become the objects of the act of seeing— and the act of seeing itself.
She does not see, that is, she does not experience, her own self, her innate nature as the seer;
for consciousness, overcome by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), has been led away from its own inward orientation.
Of whom? Of such a person;
his own state is his very nature.
It arises and vibrates;
the meaning is that it belongs to no one.
The self;
the form of the seer; the state. (MT_4,18.26)
When the delusion of water in a mirage exists, what is there to be called cleverness?
But when cleverness exists, what indeed is that mirage?
The sense is that, therefore, it is cleverness alone that should be nourished through association with the virtuous and similar means.

The seer, as clear as space and all-pervading, does not see itself, even though it has become the object of sight—like one’s own eye; oh, what a delusion! (MU 4.18.28) "As clear as space" means utterly stainless, by virtue of having the nature of pure consciousness alone.
The seer;
that which has become the faculty of seeing, having attained the state of the visible;
the self known as the seer.
He does not see; how so? Like an eye.
The meaning is: "just as the eye does not see itself.
Oh, what a delusion! This is the sense.
"Clear":
Brahman, as clear as space, is not attained even with effort. (MT 4.18.28) *paśyati*: N17: °śy⟨e⟩[a]ti. "Clear as space" refers to Brahman; it is not found even through exertion.
"But if the visible object is not perceived as something visible, its attainment is very far off.
To the question "Why is it not attained?", he says here: "The visible object."
Therefore, the point is that since the visible is seen as suchness, non-perception itself is the attainment of Brahman.
How could a gross object like you be seen there without focused attention?
In that case, for a subtle observer, the visibility of such an object would be as remote as the distant horizon.
In whatever object,
without attentiveness, one as gross as you is not seen;
in that very object.
For a subtle seer, the state of being an object of sight is utterly cast away.
The expression "one such as you" is said with reference to the body.
The seer remains only a seer; he does not touch the state of being an object of sight.
O Rāma, the visible object is seen by it, but the seer is not seen;
the seer is the agent of the act of seeing,
and he alone remains as the seer.
That seer does not touch the state of being an object of sight;
O Rāma,
by that very seer.
That by which the visible is seen;
the sense is that the visible possesses the quality of being visible. By that seer.
The seer is one's own self, whose nature is that of the seer;
it is not perceived because of its extreme subtlety— this is the intended meaning.
Thus, only the seer exists as a single reality; for here, the visible object does not exist.
If the seer, who is the self of all, remains as the visible object, what indeed would constitute visibility?
"It is possible" means that it alone is capable of withstanding critical analysis; this is the intended sense.
The seer, who is of the nature of all things, abides as the object of vision.
If it exists as something that is visible,
then what exactly is this visibility?
And one must necessarily accept that the seer exists as the object of seeing, according to the analogy of a dream.
Anticipating the objection, "How can the seer exist as the object of seeing?", he provides an illustration.
O observer! Whatever is accomplished by the all-powerful King in whatever manner, that very thing quickly becomes so; he himself arises in that very form. (MU 4.18.33)
Just as by a sovereign emperor, who possesses all power and is endowed with every capacity,
whatever object [is intended], in whatever manner—
"It is accomplished" means it is brought within the scope of the act of accomplishment; that respective object thus comes to be,
or is accomplished, quickly.
When investigation is performed, that very king arises— that is, manifests— in the form of each respective object as suchness.
This is the meaning:

just as an all-powerful king manifests through the medium of his own non-distinct knowledge as the objects being produced that constitute the transformation (*vivarta*) of that knowledge, so too does the seer manifest through the medium of his own non-distinct act of seeing as the perceived objects that constitute the transformation of the act of seeing.
The seer is the manifestation of knowledge through the medium of ignorance that is non-different from itself.
Just as a mango grove becomes radiant while not abandoning its state of being juice, yet remains elevated with fruits, flowers, and leaves; (MU 4.18.34).
Without abandoning that very state of pure consciousness, the radiance of consciousness becomes the individual soul (jīva) and thus becomes the embodied being;
it remains composed of the vision of perception itself.
*Darśanadṛṅmayaḥ*:
This word *darśana* is used here as a *karmasādhana* (instrumental noun). Therefore, the meaning is "consisting of the vision of what is seen. This is a pair (*yugma*).

Just as the essence of the earth arises through thousands of various streams of particles that are non-different from its own self, so does consciousness arise through the delusions of "I. (MU 4.18.36)
"Bhauma" means relating to the earth.

(MT_4,18.36) No end is perceived here for the trees of the effulgence of the essence of consciousness, which shine by themselves within themselves and are laden with hundreds of branches of the visible world. MU_4,18.37
Consciousness alone is the essence (*rasa*). Its manifestation is that of the trees—that is to say, of the worlds. (MT 4,18.37)
Just as a eunuch experiences within himself a distinct aesthetic wonder (*rasacamatkṛti*), so too does this Consciousness perceive the various states of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*) individually.
"Aesthetic wonder produced by rasa" refers to the sense of wonder consisting of a swelling [of emotion] brought about by *rasa*.
In whatever manner and by whichever vital power (jīvaśakti) its own cycle of manifestation arises,
that consciousness within [the self] enters into that very state of existence of the elements and the worlds.
Within one's own mind, consciousness—
whose nature is pure awareness— arises and vibrates.
That is the power of life (jīvaśakti);
within herself, that is, in her own center,
[she perceives] each respective state of the elements and the worlds.
He attains— that is, reaches— the stability and the structural arrangement of the elements (bhūta), which serve as the substratum, and of the worlds (bhuvana).
The transmigrations of certain living beings, whose nature is consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), meet with one another.
Having wandered through cyclic existence by themselves for a long time, some whose minds are joined with purity find peace.
After a long time, following the fall of the body,
you will likewise behold your own self through this subtle and supreme vision,
as well as thousands of world-nets even within the interior of a single atom.
You [should realize] yourself, your own self called pure consciousness (cinmātra),
by means of this supreme (parā), most excellent [knowledge] taught in this present context.
With subtle vision— that is, with right knowledge (samyagjñāna) which is subtle by virtue of having subtle objects as its domain—
you see; you experience.
The word "tathā" (likewise) signifies a conjunction.
Likewise, you see thousands of world-nets even within other atoms.
The word "api" (even/also) indicates the impossibility of seeing thousands of world-nets within other atoms [if one were not a Buddha].
You see [it];
you experience it on the wall, in the sky, in stone, in flame, in wind, and in water.
The marks of *saṃsāra* exist within the whole, like oil in sesame seeds;
the sense is that their essence consists solely of consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is the seed of the world.
When the mind becomes pure, then the individual soul (*jīva*) becomes the Absolute Consciousness (*cit*).
And that [consciousness] is pure and all-pervading; therefore, there is a mutual union between them.
At that time, that consciousness is [pure]; by virtue of that purity.
The long, great dream of the world, which fills the delusion of its own existence for all [beings] such as Padmajā and others, has arisen spontaneously from within itself.
"Filling the delusion of its own existence" means that it causes the delusion of its own existence.
[Regarding the phrase "causing the delusion of its own existence"]:
"Some successions of beings go from one dream to another dream;
therefore, their perception of walls and so forth remains extremely firm. (MU 4.18.45)
Certain successions of beings, rows of beings,
[arise] from one dream— the form of cyclic existence— from another dream.
They go to a dream that has the nature of another [worldly] existence;
for that reason, from that cause.
For these rows of beings who have passed from one dream to another,
there exists a very firm perception [of them] upon walls and other such surfaces.
There exists a cognition in the form "this is a wall," and so forth.
Whatever one meditates upon in whatever state, that very thing quickly becomes fully manifest therein. This is most firm.
Whatever was seen by her even in a dream was indeed real at that time; [this was] because of her consciousness (*cit*).
Within the atom of consciousness (*cidaṇu*) exist all atoms of experience.

Just as within a seed there are atoms of leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits, so too are all the atoms of experience— the minute fragments of experience— present within the atoms of all forms such as jars and cloths.
The supreme atom of consciousness holds the world within itself;
it contains space within space. Cast off the delusion of duality and unity. (MU 4.18.48)
[antar] Irregular meter. Ś1:
jaga*n*ty antar; Ś3: jaganty antar.
The atom of consciousness is the atom whose nature is consciousness;
the world-atom is the atom whose nature is the world—
[all] within the wall of one's own self.
It bears, it sustains. He states the result: "the dissolved.
Therefore, space is that which is called the world; [it is] space within space.
It becomes dissolved in the space called consciousness. He describes its fruit as "the unity of duality. Therefore, you—
Abandon, cast away the delusion of duality and unity;
for there exists only the absolute pure consciousness, which cannot even be described as "one."
The consciousness experiences the atoms within itself through its own very atoms, which are designated as space, time, action, and so forth; for no other atom is possible [within it].
[The phrase] "through its own" means through those that constitute its very nature.
"Minute" means having the form of various elemental substances; "within itself" refers to another minute atom whose nature, such as location and so forth, is distinct from consciousness. (MT_4,18.49)

Itself manifest as everything, the pure mass of atoms of consciousness is experienced through the perception of the body, from Brahmā down to the lowest insect. "Experienced through the perception of the body" means it has been brought within the range of experience.
"Ending with insects" means having insects as its conclusion.
In the word *anubhāvita*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in the sense of the base itself; this is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).
In reality, there is nothing here whatsoever that has been manifested;
rather, the atoms of consciousness themselves experience their own duality as "self" and "property.
Again, what is it that flashes forth?
Regarding this, he says "itself":
the atoms of consciousness (*citparamāṇu*) are fragments of consciousness (*cilleśa*). Duality (*dvaita*) is the nature of duality consisting of forms such as pots, cloths, and so forth.
"Svatva" means one's own nature; they "svādayante," that is, they lead [the object] to become an object of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*). (MT_4,18.51)
The mass of atomic consciousnesses, possessing an expansive body, shines forth by itself,
emitting the fragrance of awareness through the flower-like gates of the eyes and other senses.
"Possessing an expansive body" means having an expansive nature.
The fragrance of consciousness, which is the fragrance consisting of the cognition of jars, cloths, and so forth.
Someone perceives others— consisting of the forms of jars, cloths, and so forth— as being of the nature of dense consciousness (*cidghana*), because consciousness,
being all-pervading and indestructible, is indeed the seed of all that is visible. (MU 4.18.53)
A certain person;
that is to say, one who has entered the waking state.
Of the "seed of the visible," which is called consciousness (cit), [that is,] of the seed of the visible known as consciousness.
Because they are all-pervading and likewise indestructible;
because they are masses of consciousness, being of the nature of consciousness and filled with consciousness;
and as for the others, by their own nature—
One perceives objects appearing as distinct as having an external form, experiencing them with the thought, "These are external.
Another person perceives the entire world in its completeness as being entirely internal.
There, due to the calculation of excessive time, one emerges and sinks;
"sinks" means that someone has entered the state of dream.
"Only within oneself, and not externally.
(MT 4.18.54) Seeing one dream after another there again and again, he rolls about in false pits like a stone fallen from a mountain peak. (MU 4.18.55)
What is someone doing?
He is seeing one dream after another again and again; this is to be connected with the preceding [verse]. Of what nature is that person?
"Vainly" means fruitlessly.
"In the pits" refers to the pits known as existence and non-existence; he has rolled about in them.
Like what? Like a rock fallen from a mountain peak.

Some are closed in on themselves, while others remain in delusion within their own selves; these clusters of embodied beings, throbbing with the essence of their own consciousness, are submerged in it.
(MU 4.18.56) [sphuranto] Ś1, Ś3: sphuranto; N17: sphurato.
Some have entered the state of deep sleep;
they are closed in, seized by slumber,
within their own self enveloped by ignorance.
The "bodies" (*dehi*) are the aggregates of living beings (*jīvasamūha*).
[He] speaks, [he] speaks concerning those who have entered the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*). (MT_4,18.56) [Note: N17 reads *tur°* → *°ti*]
Those few who perceive within themselves the agitation of the world and its living beings—
by them that [world] is seen as such, based upon it as if it were an unreal dream.
These are the living beings who are liberated while alive (*jīvanmukta*).

They perceive within the mind— that is, internally— the agitation of the world's living beings, known as the "world-agitation," which is the delusion of individual souls; but they do not perceive it externally.
By some of them, that object of perception is thus resorted to by way of being internal;
how so?
Like an unreal dream.

For those who have entered the fourth state (turyāvasthā) and are liberated while living (jīvanmukta), they experience even the external world as if it were internal, like a dream, because they perceive its nature to be that of an illusion.
[Outside] N17: [outside], like an unreal dream (MT_4,18.57).
Because the intrinsic nature is the self of all, that which is seen is real within the self.
For wherever that which is all-pervading exists, everything indeed arises there; thus,
that visible world becomes real within the Self, its own essential nature.
Why?
Because of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) called pure consciousness (cinmātra).
Because it is the self of all, it exists in every form.
This is the meaning: the visible object exists in dependence upon the seer.
Although it is unreal insofar as it is perceived by an accomplished one (*siddha*), it is real in its own nature,

because its essence consists in the very nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is synonymous with being established as the form of all things; thus, it is indeed real within its own self-nature.
Now, one might ask: "How is this so?

To this he says: "Omnipresent" (*sarvaga*). For, because it is omnipresent—that is, the state of pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*), which is synonymous with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is all-pervading.
Wherever it exists, there all that is visible arises and manifests.
Therefore, the meaning is that just like consciousness, which constitutes its own nature, the visible world— which is inseparable from its existence— is also truly real.

Within the manifestation of the creation that exists inside the individual soul, which is pure consciousness alone, a multitude of souls arises; and within that [multitude], yet another [creation] likewise arises. (MU 4.18.59)
This is clear.
(MT 4.18.59) From one living being another living being is born, and within that too there is yet another living being;
everywhere, like the fibers of a plantain leaf, the seed of life continues to live. (MU 4.18.60)
It lives; that is, it assumes the agency for the preeminent activity of living.

(MT_4,18.60) This infinite [reality] is equal to the transformation of the intellect regarding the visible world; like the state of being a bracelet or other ornaments in gold, it perishes through mere thorough understanding. (MU_4,18.61)
The infinite appears as being devoid of an end;
this is the visible world.
Through thorough comprehension alone, it is realized that this is nothing but pure consciousness.
Thus, by knowledge alone,
and not by any other cause;
simultaneously, at the same time.
But it does not perish gradually;

rather, it perishes, meaning it goes beyond the range of perception, because its establishment as being experienced consists solely in its nature as pure consciousness (cinmātra). This is the meaning.
Of what nature is this? It is "supreme" (parā), meaning excellent, when viewed with the cognition that "this is the visible" (dṛśya-buddhyā).
That which has growth on all sides—
what is that like?
It is like the state of being a bracelet and so forth;
just as the state of being a bracelet existing in gold perishes through thorough cognition— that is, by the knowledge "this is only gold."
The meaning is "so be it.
For one in whom no inquiry arises as to "Who am I? or "What is this?", for him there persists this long, feverish delusion of being alive, from which neither beginning nor end is ever liberated.
*Ādyantāvimukta-maḥsau*:
liberated from beginning and end; *avicchinnapravāhaḥ*: having an uninterrupted flow.
*Jīvajvarabhramaḥ*: the delusion in the form of a fever consisting of the notion "I am a living being."
The investigation of that wise person whose mind is thus correct should be understood as having borne fruit, for he is liberated from both the beginning and the end.
"Day by day, the greed for enjoyments undergoes attenuation"—
in this context, "it should be understood" is the ellipsis, [meaning] "by the wise."
Greed for enjoyments is the longing for enjoyments.
Just as medicine administered to the body brings about health,
so too does discernment applied to the conquest of the senses become fruitful.
"Applied to the body" means employed within the body.
"Bearing fruit" means endowed with the fruit known as liberation, which is not distant.
This refers specifically to the conquest of the senses.
The sense is that [this] is the direct means toward liberation.
(MT_4,18.64) Discrimination exists only in words, like a brilliant fire in a painting; he by whom it has been abandoned possesses only a discrimination that leads to suffering. (MU_4,18.65)
The word "yasya" (of whom) is connected with the first half-verse;
it is stated with the intention that [the body] has been completely relinquished.
[Regarding the term *parityaktā*: N17 reads *°ty(o)akte*.
Just as the wind attains existence through touch and not through speech, so too is this discernment understood to exist only through the attenuation of desire. (MU 4.18.66)
This is clear.
(MU 4.18.66) Know that the nectar of the painting is not truly nectar; know that the fire of the painting is not truly fire.
A woman in a painting is surely not a woman; by your words, discernment is indeed non-discernment. (MU 4.18.67)
Just as nectar and the like depicted in a painting lack the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyā) such as satisfying thirst, and thus do not possess the nature of actual nectar and so forth;

likewise, that which is described by words alone—specifically, discernment (viveka) that does not accomplish the conquest of the senses—lacks the causal efficiency known as liberation, and therefore its very nature is non-discernment. This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, because of the absence of the performance of purposeful action (arthakriyā) known as liberation,
what kind of discerning person exists?
Regarding this, he says in a verse at the end of the chapter:
[N17: °k*ī*(na)] First, through discernment, passion and enmity reach attenuation along with their very roots;
thereafter, they are completely destroyed. Where that occurs, there is the purifying power of discernment. (MU 4.18.68)
In which person— wherein—
there is passion (*rāga*) as well as enmity (*vaira*), that is, hatred (*dveṣa*);
[this is to be understood] through discernment (*viveka*), that is, through investigation (*vicāra*).
"Previously" means first;
"becomes thin" means it goes toward attenuation.
Thereafter, immediately following that attenuation,
he— that person— perishes indeed; he is destroyed indeed.
It is purifying;
therein, in that person,
is discernment, which consists in being endowed with inquiry.
It exists; however, the meaning is that it is not determined as existent or non-existent by mere words alone. May there be auspiciousness!
"It is exhausted" (N17: *kṣīyate*);
thus ends the eighteenth canto in the chapter on "Stability" (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
In the *Śrīmokṣopāyaṭīkā*, in the section on *sthitiprakaraṇa*, this is the eighteenth canto.
Because it is exceedingly difficult to understand, he explains once again the very meaning previously stated:
"The seed of the living soul (*jīvabīja*) is the Supreme Brahman, situated everywhere like space."
Therefore, even within the world that is the belly of the living being, there exists a living being in manifold ways;
[it is] the seed of living beings, the place of their manifestation.
The supreme Brahman is like the sky, like space,
throughout the entire web of the world that is everywhere regarded as an object of perception.
It remains established by virtue of being the essence of its own nature;
for that reason, from that cause, that which is the belly— the middle region— of the living being [is so].

In that [universe] which exists as the world in the form of a dream and so forth— within that very world, moreover, there exists a living being (*jīva*) of various kinds, in manifold ways consisting of diverse types of stationary and moving entities. To the question "What follows from this?", he says:

Because they consist of the single, solid mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), the various classes of living beings exist within the individual soul like the layers of a plantain tree or like insects in the belly of a man. Therefore, [the Self] is one and alone by virtue of being the solid mass of consciousness.
He whose self is dense—
that state of his is "the state of being a single essence of dense consciousness" (cidghanaikātmatvam).
Therefore, for that reason,
among living beings— within the midst of living beings—
the various classes of living beings exist like the layers of a plantain tree.
For within the leaves of the plantain tree there are indeed other inner leaves;
what are they like? They are like various species of living beings.
"Like insects":
the meaning is that it is just as there are insects within the belly of a man.
Therefore,
the various classes of living beings within [the body] are like the layers of a plantain tree.

"Now, from what is the individual soul (jīva) produced? To this he replied: "O Rāma, just as in the summer a worm may arise from a film of sweat, so too, by virtue of its consciousness, the void itself spontaneously becomes the living soul, assuming various names."
O Rāma! In summer, during the summer season, from the sweat of impurity; "kalka" means filth.
And that is sweat;
that is the sweating with paste.
Therefore.
Whichever worm, in whatever manner and by whatever form, it may exist or be born.
The sky is space;
because it possesses consciousness, it thus becomes a living being by itself in that form.
What kind of "kha" is it?
It is the respective name of each and every worm, whatever its name may be.
This is the point:
first, in the summer, various kinds of worms [arise] from the sweat of the dregs.
They are born; let their body, for its part, consist of impure secretions and sweat.
But as for that moving life-principle (*jīva*), since it cannot otherwise be accounted for as a living being, it must be space itself endowed with consciousness.
Since the mere preparation of the body by means of the paste-sudation (kalkasveda) is complete, and because nothing else is present,
therefore all living beings are indeed of the nature of space (ākāśa).
Because of the steaming of the paste; because of its being present; because of the non-proximity of anything other than that. (MT_4,19.3)
In whatever manner those Jīvakas strive for the realization of their own selves,
in that very manner they quickly become [so], through various methods of worship;
they are composed of space (ākāśamaya).

O Jīvakas, in whatever way living beings strive for the realization of their own selves through various methods of worship— through diverse forms of effort consisting of manifold sequences of worship—
in that very same way they become.
For the sake of establishing one's own self: N17:
[as and as] svātma°;
they become: N17: °va[n]ti (MT_4,19.4).
Having spoken in general, he explains in detail:
"For those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; those who sacrifice to the yakṣas go to the yakṣas;
those who sacrifice to Brahman go to Brahman. One should therefore take refuge in that which is not insignificant. (MU 4.19.5)
He states the conclusion with the word "yat" (that which).
The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied.
Therefore, that by which the person becomes non-trivial— that...
One should rely [upon it].
[One] should rely [on this]. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how did Śukra attain a manifold form without his own sense-base? To this he says:
"For that Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, because of the purity of his own consciousness..."
He was quickly bound by the object seen for the first time due to its inherent nature. He is Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, who was mentioned in the preceding section.
Indeed, this is certain:

because one's own consciousness becomes stainless through the descent of its primordial state, the visible object perceived for the first time naturally causes that [consciousness] to be swiftly bound and turned toward itself, even without deliberate effort.
Therefore, the sense is that there is no contradiction.
O noble one, that consciousness which the fool first attains before him is immediately destroyed;
it becomes of such a nature, and no other whatsoever exists.
She is of noble birth and pure;
for that very reason, she is unfading, having not yet reached any turbidity;
she is young, having just arisen from Brahmā.
Consciousness;
first, at the very beginning,
that which one perceives before oneself.
It becomes of that nature;
it is not some other consciousness that arose prior to Brahmā.
It does not occur without effort;
however, it certainly occurs through effort,
for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of liberation.

At this time, Śrī Rāma asks the question that had previously been indicated.
O Blessed One, you should explain the distinction between the states of waking and dreaming, as they flash forth within the *samaya*.
And how could there be waking within waking? How could dreaming be non-waking? In response to the expectation of what this might mean, he says "how":
how could waking be waking?
A dream that is not waking— how could such a thing exist? "Tell me this very thing," is the sense [of the question].
Thus, in N17: *°thaya⟨t⟩ me iti*, the venerable Vasiṣṭha gives the reply:
"That which is endowed with firm conviction is called the waking state."
That which possesses unstable cognition is declared to be a dream. [Regarding *asthirapratyayam*:
By means of stable knowledge (*sthirajñāna*), that is, by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the form "this is that very same thing," which is capable of such identification.
That which is appropriate for the wise is called "waking";
that which possesses unstable cognitions and is endowed with an unstable knowledge incapable of recognition [is called dreaming].
It may be so;
that is what has been described and declared as a dream by the wise.
In such a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),
it is said that the state of being both dreaming and waking (*svapnajāgrattva*) is sometimes possible for both the waking and dreaming states;
[the text] speaks of the state of being both dreaming and waking (*svapnajāgrattva*).
If that which is seen for a moment in the waking state were to persist through another period of time as a dream,
then that waking state would attain the nature of a dream, and the dream would reach the state of being awake.
"Seen in a moment" (*kṣaṇadṛṣṭa*) means an object that has become the domain of waking cognition by way of the characteristic of being awake (*jāgrallakṣaṇayā*).
"If" (*cet*) means *yadi*.
Seen for a moment, it is seen for only a moment; by implication, it has perished thereafter. Likewise, a dream is an object that has become the domain of dream-consciousness.
If it were the case that [the dream object] persists at another time, meaning it persists even at a time other than the time of the dream; if that were so...
For sometimes even an object seen in a dream is perceived directly at dawn;
that is so at that time.
Waking is cognition that apprehends waking objects; it becomes dream-like because its objects are unstable. Dream is cognition that apprehends dream-objects.
It attains the state of waking because its cognition is stable.
[By way of indication: "N17: [By way of indication] (MT_4,19.10).
But how is this so? To this he says:
"The distinction between the states of waking and dreaming does not exist without stability and instability."
The experience of both is always and everywhere the same.
Since the distinction between the states of waking and dreaming does not exist apart from stability and instability,
[therefore,] of the momentary waking state...
The meaning is that it is indeed logical for a stable dream to possess the status of waking;
herein, he states "equal" (*sama*) to indicate that all experience serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Of these two, waking and dreaming;
"universal experience" (samastānubhava) is the experience abiding in all [states]; "always" (sadā) means at all times.
In all places and in all regions,
he remains exactly the same,
regardless of whether they are stable or unstable.
The word "vineti" (he disciplines) should also be connected here.
Regarding this as well,
he states the result: "That which attains stability is called 'waking'."
Listen to how a dream consists of momentary destruction:
therefore, that which attains stability is called "waking" even while it is a dream by the wise;
whereas that which consists of momentary destruction becomes a "dream" even while it is waking.
Listen to how this comes to be:
the meaning is that you should listen to how there is stability and instability in the waking and dreaming states.
He explains that very point: the life-element exists within the body, by which one lives.
"Lustre, vigor, the life-element," and so forth—this is its designation, O limb.
The "life-element" (jīvadhātu) is the element called "living" (jīva);
it exists within the body.
By which life-element the body is kept alive and the activity of sustaining the vital breaths is performed.
The form "jīvyata" is a usage ending in the causative suffix (ṇic). O dear one! That is the verbal root √jīv.
It is designated as "heat," "vigor," "the life-element," and so forth.
And here, the word *dhātu* is used figuratively because of its similarity to being contained within the body, just like the marrow and other internal constituents.
When the body, through mind, action, and speech, becomes engaged in worldly activity,
then that perfected living element (jīvadhātu) spreads forth.
"When" means at which time.
One is an agent through the body,
through mental action, through activity based upon oneself,
and through speech.
When it is engaged in conventional activity,
then that element of life (jīvadhātu), being accomplished and complete, exists.
"It spreads throughout the entire body" means that it performs a movement [throughout it]. To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
As that [consciousness] spreads through the limbs by means of touch, awareness indeed arises;
because of its fullness, it receives the name "mind" (*citta*), wherein the delusion of the world is internally dissolved.
[This occurs] in that constituent of the living being which consists of consciousness.
While it is spreading forth,
through contact with the limbs— that is, through contact with the element of life (jīvadhātu)—
"hi" indicates certainty; "saṃvit" refers to consciousness, which consists of the vibration of the element of life and takes the form of volitional awareness of cold, heat, and so forth.
It arises, it manifests; that consciousness, while containing within itself the delusion of the world, [arises] because of its fullness— that is,
because of its fullness through the spreading forth of the element of the living soul (*jīvadhātu*).
It attains the name "mind" (*citta*).
If it is asked, "How can consciousness (*saṃvit*) have the delusion of the world latent within it?"—it is true;
consciousness arises first from the element of the living being (*jīvadhātu*).
And at the time of arising, the individual soul (jīvadhātu) arises indeed accompanied by the delusion of the world,
because the delusion of the world is latent within the paternal life-principle (pitṛjīvadhātu).
Therefore, it is established that even consciousness possesses the delusion of the world latent within it. [It is] flowing outward through the apertures such as the eyes, consisting of the external.
That consciousness, moving through the apertures such as the eyes, perceives within itself a form rich with various shapes and transformations.
"Extrinsic" means having an external nature;
[it appears] through various forms and transformations, that is, through forms and transformations such as those of jars, cloths, and so forth.
He perceives and reflects upon his own form as magnificent,
as if it were internally composed of vessels, cloths, and other objects accomplished through mere volition.
Nor should it be asked how this is so,
because it is observed in dreams;
just as in a dream, consciousness itself appears in various forms.
It shines; likewise, it does so externally as well, so there is no contradiction.
Because of its stability within the apertures of the eyes and so forth, one then understands that state as the waking state by means of that very [stability].
This is declared to be the sequence of waking; now hear the sequence beginning with deep sleep.
By that very consciousness alone,
and not by any other insentient thing such as the body;
for that [consciousness] is one's own nature, rich with various forms and transformations.
Its own nature (*svarūpa*) is understood— that is, known— as being "awake" because of its stability, meaning it remains exactly so for some period of time.

Having concluded the procedure concerning the waking state, he makes a formal promise (*pratijānīte*) to explain the procedure concerning deep sleep and the other states, beginning with the sequence of the waking state.
Thus: (MT_4,19.17) He describes the very sequence beginning with deep sleep:
"When the body is not agitated by mind, action, or speech..."
Then that pure element of life (jīvadhātu) remains tranquil;
it does not become agitated because of its exhaustion.
The meaning is that he does not engage in worldly activity;
at that time, the element of life (jīvadhātu).
It is transparent, possessing the impurity known as "slumbering movement";
for this very reason, it is tranquil and free from agitation;
it abides everywhere.
The word "tu" (but) indicates certainty.

Although there is no question posed by Śrī Rāma concerning the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), nevertheless, because it necessarily exists as the intermediate state between waking (*jāgrat*) and dreaming (*svapna*), there is a determination of deep sleep.
For it is not logical for a person, having departed from the waking state, to go to the dream state without first entering deep sleep;
this is because deep sleep exists everywhere as a boundary, like a dam.

Although pure consciousness indeed exists everywhere as a bridge in the midst [of all things], nevertheless, because it is not an object of gross perception— like a flash of lightning or a gem— it is not mentioned as a bridge;
nor is its mention appropriate for those with subtle vision, as it would be of no use to them.
[Like a jewel flashing with lightning] N17: °dyot(i)aratna° (MT_4,19.18).
Then, what will be accomplished? To this, he says:
When the winds have become equanimous, the heart within is no longer disturbed, just as a lamp in a windless chamber produces only light. (MU 4.19.19) [āgatair] N17: °tai⟨ḥ⟩[r]
It is agitated;
the lamp [is steady] because of the absence of agitation produced by the mind, which constitutes its state of equilibrium.
By the incoming winds— that is, the vital breaths—
this element of life within the heart is not agitated; it is not made subject to agitation.

By this it is indicated that through the destruction of the mind (manonāśa) there will be the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇarodha), and through the restraint of the vital breath, the destruction of the mind will be accomplished.
In that regard, for some, the destruction of the mind is held to be achieved by means of the restraint of the vital breath.
For us, however, the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs precisely through the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) accomplished by means of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
If that [restraint of the breath] is an auxiliary factor therein,
there is no fault.
Therefore, the destruction of the mind occurs in every way through the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
However, it is held that this destruction of the mind is not absolute, being like the destruction of the mind induced by liquor and similar substances.
In this matter, only those endowed with intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) are authoritative; enough of this prolixity.
What is the life-element (*jīvadhātu*) like?
It is like a lamp.
The meaning is: just as a lamp that provides light alone in a windless chamber is not shaken by the winds, so it is.
[The element of life: N17: °tu[ḥ] (MT_4,19.19). What follows from that? To this he says:
"Therefore consciousness flows; it does not become agitated within the limbs because of that."
Nor does it enter the apertures such as the eyes, nor does it go outside; therefore,
that element of life does not circulate through the limbs and does not perform movement.
By that taking refuge in the life-element (*jīvadhātu*),
consciousness— which is consciousness in the form of the vibration of the life-element— is neither agitated nor does it arise.
That consciousness does not go outside through the apertures such as the eyes, nor does it come back;
when there arises the inquiry, "In that case, where does it abide? he says:
This consciousness flashes within the *jīva* itself, just as the consciousness of oil is in the sesame seed,
the consciousness of coldness is in the snow, and the consciousness of unctuousness is in clarified butter.
This consciousness is within the *jīva*, that is, in the very midst of the *jīva* which constitutes its own substrate.
It throbs;
like what? Like the consciousness of oil.
Consciousness is like an oil-maker;
"consciousness of oil" means simply "oil"—
just as that [consciousness] manifests within the sesame seed.
The meaning is "so it is.
In this same way, it should also be applied to the other two examples.

[Question: "In that case, what does the living being (*jīva*) do? To this, he says: "To this, he says" [N17: *a(tranya)trā°*].
The individual soul (jīva), remaining for some portion of time within itself in a state of tranquility,
enters the state of deep sleep— a condition that is placid, windless, and devoid of consciousness.

Then the individual soul (jīva), for a certain moment— a minute fraction of time so subtle as to be impossible to describe— remains in a state of tranquility within itself, that is, within its own nature which consists of pure consciousness.
Standing, first standing;
then [he perceives] the unconsciousness consisting of ignorance,
the gentle wind, and the evenly circulating vital breath.
One attains the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptī daśā*).
By this, the entry into the middle abode (*madhyadhāmapraveśa*), which is to be known by those of subtle vision as occurring between the waking and deep sleep states, has been described.
And with this very intention, it was stated that "at the beginning of sleep" is "the end of waking," and so forth; enough, then, of revealing this secret.

In response to the inquiry—"Is it not the case that the individual soul (*jīva*) in deep sleep possesses the fourth state (*turya*), since it is devoid of agitation?"—he says: "vicetanām... saumyavātām" [N17: *sau*⟨s⟩[m]ya°]. (MT_4,19.22)
Having known [this] and when the mind has ceased, one who remains tranquil even while engaged in worldly activity—
awakened throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— is said to possess the fourth state (*turya*).
Having known means having correctly realized one's own self as being of the nature of pure consciousness alone.
When the mind— the mental faculty whose nature consists of conceptual construction—
has ceased and become dissolved,
even while one is engaged in worldly activity, that is, performing actions for the sake of maintaining the bodily life-process;
By means of extreme proficiency, he pacifies the agitation caused by worldly discourse;
likewise, being awakened throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, he is endowed with perfect knowledge as to what the true nature of these states is.
But the insentient [unconscious state] is not so;
it is by the wise that the fourth state is remembered as possessing the "fourth" (turyavat). The meaning is that deep sleep (*suṣupta*) is not like this, and therefore it does not possess the fourth.
He begins to define dream:

when that constituent of the living being is set in motion by the vital breaths— which have attained a state of gentleness from deep sleep— then it arises as consciousness, and from that, as the mind.

therefore,

that element of the living being is moved,
then—
That consciousness, which is consciousness in the form of the vibration of the life-element, has arisen— that is, it has become manifest— by way of being the mind, through its state as the mind.

She perceives the entire web of the world, situated within her own mind, as a vast tree within a seed, through successive revolutions of its constituent parts;
then that consciousness, whose form is the mind, [perceives] that which resides within herself in the form of latent impressions (saṃskāra), established within her own self.

Quickly he beholds it as tending toward the sprout. (MT_4,19.25)
He explains that very point in detail:
when the element of life (jīvadhātu) is somewhat or intensely agitated by the vital winds (vāta), it then moves like the wind in the sky, and one perceives within oneself a movement in the ether.

The meaning of the statement is that it is simply the nature of the predominance of wind (*vāta*) that a person perceives movement through the sky in a dream. When he is flooded by water, he then experiences within himself the agitation of water and so forth, just as a flower experiences its own fragrance.
This element of living beings (jīvadhātu) is flooded— that is, filled— with water in the form of phlegm (kapha).
"Confusion regarding water and so forth" refers to confusion in the form of a flood of water and the like;
when one is overcome by bile and other humors, there is then confusion regarding fire, heat, and so forth.
