And that [state] is false, serving only for delusion, like the work of a mole on the earth;
it is the state of being exclusively intent upon the object of sight, the state of facing toward the visible, belonging to the seer— the agent of the act of seeing.
Know that delusion (mohana) is that which causes delusion; it is the mind (manas), existing for the sake of wandering— that is,
for the production of error.
It is false;
the meaning is that it does not exist as a real entity because it is a mere appearance.
How so?
Upon the great earth; *makkola-karman* is the application of lime-plaster.

In the same way: just as a plastering of lime applied to clay does not exist in reality because the clay remains exactly as it was and exists only as clay, so too the mind appearing within pure consciousness does not exist in reality because pure consciousness remains exactly as it was and exists only as such.
This is the meaning.
In the clay [N17:
°kā*yāṃ* (MT_4,21.37)], one might ask: "How can the mind, which consists of the state of being exclusively focused on the identity of the seer and the seen, exist in a false form? To this, he says:
"[the mind] which consists of the state of being exclusively focused on the identity of the seer and the seen" [N17: d⟨ṛ⟩[ra]ṣṭṛ°].

This experience of the identity with the visible world, which is the very nature [of this state], is called "ignorance" (avidyā), this wine of saṃsāra, by the wise. (MU 4.21.38) [The wise]... the visible world.
Regarding "atimanyatā" (excessive conceit),
it refers to the wise,
that is, to us; [it concerns] the intrinsic nature of the seer-form, which is the intrinsic nature itself.

That state of being absorbed in the visible object—that single-minded concentration on the visible—is perceived by the wise as this very ignorance (*avidyā*), because it produces delusion; it is said to be the form of the intoxicant of *saṃsāra*.
Therefore, the meaning is that the mind is indeed of the nature of ignorance and is thus devoid of substantial reality.
"What harm is caused by this ignorance? To this he replies:
"The world, afflicted by this, does not attain what is auspicious, just as one whose eyes are blinded by a cataract does not perceive the brilliant light of the sun. (MU 4.21.39)
By means of this ignorance, which consists in the identity of the seer with the seen,
[one fails to attain] the auspicious, which is the nature of resting within one's own self.
*Paṭala* is a specific eye disease.
Now, from what does it arise? To this he says: "And that arises spontaneously from conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*), like a tree in the sky."
By the mere absence of conceptualization, it perishes of its own accord.
[It] arises, that is, it manifests.
Now, one might ask: how does it perish?
To this, it is said:
"Merely by non-conceptualization.
That is, merely by the non-formation of conceptualization.
For this very reason, he says "by himself";
for non-intention is not effort,
but rather intention itself.
[Non-conceptualization] (*asaṅkalpanaṃ*): Now, what is accomplished by the destruction of ignorance? To this he says:
"O Mahāmati, by mere non-conceptualization in meditative cultivation... (*asaṅkalpanamātreṇa bhāvanāyāṃ mahāmate*).
When [the mind] has been exhausted through its own serenity and through playful discernment,
and when stability has been attained regarding all objects as being without attachment;
When the vision of truth has become clear and untruth has come to an end,
that Self is attained which is the pure essence of non-conceptual consciousness—
a state wherein there is neither non-existence nor existence, neither pleasure nor suffering.
In meditation upon ignorance;
by means of discernment, that is, by means of inquiry into one's own self;
in what manner?
"By his own grace" means by the grace arising from his own self; the word "arising" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is "playful," meaning endowed with expansion.
In non-attachment and non-clinging;
vision whose object is truth is "truth-vision" (satyadṛṣṭi).
When that [truth] is clear—
that is, when it is accomplished—
in what is unreal, in that which has become untrue.
The meaning is "in the visible.
Of what nature is the Self?
It is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), having the form of that consciousness which has emerged from conceptualization regarding the objects of the visible.
One whose self (ātman) is transparent (accha),
that is, whose essential nature (svarūpa) is such; the meaning is that he does not have the nature of a body or other things which are insentient (acidrūpa).
Therefore, the sense is that the destruction of ignorance is not fruitless.
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of self this is, he says, "not non-existent" (*nāsattā*);
[this refers] to that self (*ātman*).
It does not become non-existent,
because it manifests as the self-nature of all things;
for there is no one [who is not thus].
One does not say, "I am not";
for one who says so would merely be an object of ridicule,
and likewise, existence would not occur.
Because it is not an object of either external or internal organs, like the horn of a hare,
bliss does not exist as "blissfulness" even in a figurative sense.

Because pleasure and so forth have the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as their locus; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of their manifestation even during deep sleep and similar states. Suffering is the state of having suffering as its locus.
It does not exist, for the reason already stated.
Thus,
like the horn of a hare.
[Because of the consequence of [the self] being an object of perception:
"Furthermore, what exists there? To this he replies:
"It is simply the state of being isolated (*kevalībhāva*) which is perceived within."
By means of cultivation that is not [merely] potential, nor by the mind, the senses, or views; rather,
by a person endowed with right knowledge,
[one perceives] that Self.
Within its own wall,
the state of being solitary (kevalībhāva) is the total absence of everything except for pure consciousness alone.
Only [the nature of] being attained is obtained; the expression "it is obtained" is used figuratively, because that which has already attained a single form cannot be subject to further attainment.
The ultimate reality, however, is independent of being attained;

even the state of being an attainer is not tenable therein. Enough, therefore, with words that give rise to conceptual constructions, or with this flawed cultivation that is incapable [of realization]. It is not attained by such [means].
And it is not apprehended by means of mind, faculties, or views.
Of that which has attained a single form; [N17:
of that which has attained (labdhe) a single...]; independent of what is to be obtained; [N17: independent of what is to be obtained].
It is obtainable without regard for that [fault],
by means of its purification.

That which is not obtained even by those who are non-different from the Self, being abandoned by infinite latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as the sky is by rows of forests— [that is the Self]. (MU 4.21.45)
[By the rows of forests: Ś1, Ś3, N17: *ghana*°; MṬ: *vana*°.
That Self, which is devoid of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—though these are non-different from itself, being its very own nature.
It exists because its essential nature is pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that for latent impressions (*vāsanā*) to possess the nature of a self or to have that [consciousness] as their object is necessarily contingent upon their being established as entities. For a latent impression that has not been made an object of pure consciousness cannot truly be a latent impression.
And it is logical that being made an object of cognition belongs only to that which is related to oneself; and when examined, this relation rests upon identity,
for if there were duality, its establishment would be precluded by contradiction.
Because a relationship is impossible precisely due to duality;
for indeed, a relationship between two contradictory things, such as darkness and light, is not logical— enough of this prolixity!
What is it like?
It is like the sky;
just as the sky is devoid of rows of forests.
It exists; that is the meaning.

[Objection: If that alone is the self and is solitary, then from where has this bondage, which consists of the visible world, come? To this he says: "Just as the state of being a snake exists in a rope when it is perceived doubtfully, so indeed is it here."
Bondage is imagined by that which is itself unbound, through the nature of the consciousness-ether;
just as, when a rope is in doubt, the state of being a snake is imagined by a person— certainly, this occurs upon [lack of] ascertainment.
In exactly that same way, by means of the self which is the nature of the space of consciousness—
that is, by means of the self whose very form is the space of consciousness—
while remaining entirely unbound.
Bondage is that which is called "the visible"; it is "imagined," meaning it is produced by imagination. [Objection: But how can this imagined bondage be destroyed? To this, he says:
Every imagined object, through another imagination,
assumes that very otherness, just as the sky appears different by day and by night. Every imagined object is indeed an imagined thing.
By another [conceptualization], that is, by one distinct from itself;
by that very [conceptualization],
it exists.
It assumes another state;
what is it like?
It is like space; just as...
The *kha* [syllable] takes on that very same reality as being something else during day and night;
such is the meaning.
Therefore, it is by means of conceptual construction alone.
The meaning is that there is the destruction of the imagined [nature].
[Regarding the reading] *svasmād*:

"But surely, since that which is distinguished by qualities such as non-triviality (*atucchatva*) is not imagined, how can it be imagined such that the imagination of *saṃsāra*—distinguished by qualities such as triviality—is destroyed? Furthermore, without imagination, the destruction of imagination cannot be effected, just as [the removal of] iron cannot be done without fire. To this, he says:
Whatever is non-vacuous, effortless, free from limiting conditions, and devoid of delusion— that very thing,
when conceived as such, conduces solely to happiness.
That object which is non-vacuous (*atuccha*), meaning devoid of vacuous qualities;
"Effortless" means being devoid of that which must be accomplished through effort.
"Without limiting adjuncts" means being free from adjuncts, because even that which is considered an adjunct does not deviate from its true nature.
It becomes free from delusion because its essential nature is pure, true awareness; it is untouched by delusion.
That is that very reality;
through the conceptualization of it, its non-triviality and so forth arise solely through conceptualization itself.
Such [a nature] is of a non-trivial form and so forth;

it exists because, within its pure essential nature, there is no room for words that depend upon distinctions such as triviality or non-triviality. [Objection: In that case, even that [pure nature] must be abandoned.
To this it is replied: "That is for the sake of bliss alone.
That entity, though conceptualized, possesses qualities such as non-triviality;
it is for the sake of bliss alone—that is, for the sake of resting in the pure essential nature which is devoid of both triviality and non-triviality.
Thus,
the meaning is that by means of the conceptualization of qualities such as non-emptiness, which serves as the antidote, it is possible to destroy the conceptualization of qualities such as emptiness.

[Objection: Since bondage consists of a visible form that is real, how can its destruction be accomplished by mere conceptualization? To this, he says: "Because of its emptiness. [End of MT_4,21.48]
Just as there is fear that "there is a lion inside" an empty granary,
so too is the fear that "I am bound within" this empty body.
A *kusūla* is a small chamber or mechanical enclosure used for the purpose of confining a lion.

Let it be that bondage, appearing as a visible form, is real; nevertheless, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it does not act as a binder for you, whose nature is pure consciousness. The sense is that space is not bound by ropes.
Just as a lion is not found when one looks inside an empty granary,
so too, when examined, that which is fit to be bound by saṃsāra is not found.
This is clear.
[Objection: If that is so, then how does this cognition in the form of the bound and the binder—namely, "this world" and "I am this"—exist?
To this, he says:
"This world" and "this I"—this delusion has arisen among the ignorant, like a fleeting shadow at the time of twilight. (MU 4.21.51) [Note: *śyāmale* is read as *dhṛśyāma* in N17.]
In the dark time of night,
the cognition in the form "this world" or "I am this" arises as nothing but an error.
Such is the summary meaning.
Regarding [the word] *śyāmale*: N17 reads *dhṛśyāma* (MT_4,21.51).
Now, one might ask: "How does such an error arise? To this, he says:
"Through the power of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), for a living being, there are entities and non-entities, as well as the auspicious and the inauspicious."
In an instant they go to non-existence, and again and again they return to existence.
(MU 4.21.52) [The reading *bhāvābhāvāḥ* is supported by Ś1, Ś3; N17 reads *bhābhā°*.]
"By the power of conceptual construction" means by the power of one's own discursive thought.
He explains this very point in detail:
"The Mother herself, having assumed the state of a housewife, hangs from the neck."
Bestowing the bliss of sexual union, she performs the duties of a housewife;
[the phrase] "duties of a housewife" implies [she acts] through delusion.
"Even as a beloved embraced with maternal affection and hanging from the neck,
she utterly causes one to forget the state of intoxication caused by love;
here too, the ellipsis is 'by delusion'."
And this state should be understood to apply to those who are middling sinners and the like;
however, even in this [state], delight indeed arises for great sinners.
They are to be known as belonging to those such as Madhyamapāpīya and others;
thus he states the result.
And having observed the multitude of objects that yield fruits according to one's disposition,
a wise person— one who knows the true nature of things— does not proclaim a single form for these objects here.
Having observed that the flood of objects yields results according to one's disposition, no single form among these objects is proclaimed or described here in this world.
When one who knows the true nature of things thoroughly cultivates the mind through firm meditation in whatever manner they so desire, [the mind becomes that very thing].
The mind perceives that very object as having that specific result and that specific form for that duration of time,
in accordance with how it has cultivated and contemplated it through firm habitual meditation.
That fruit is that which has become the fruit of cultivation;
it has that aspect;
for that duration, at that time.
One clearly perceives [this];
and here, a dream should be understood as an illustrative example.
He states the established conclusion:
there is nothing that is not true, nor is there anything that is not false;
in whatever manner and by whatever means a thing is determined, it is characterized as such by that very means.
This has been determined and cultivated;
otherwise, the point is that a single object would not be a source of joy for one person and a source of suffering for another. (MT_4,21.57)
The mind, having conceived the elephant of space as its own elephant,
pursues the female elephant of the forest of space that dwells in the void.
[The mind] which has conceived the elephant of space as real.
The mind, by way of being an elephant in the sky— that is, through the state of being an elephant in the sky—
having become an elephant in the sky.
...up to: he pursues the female elephant of the forest of the sky.
Of what nature is she?
She stands in the sky, which serves as the foundation for the forest.
Such as that.
...up to the point where it says "having become" (*bhūtvā*);
thus he speaks of the supreme fruition (*paramaphalita*).
Therefore, you [should understand] that volition (*saṅkalpa*) itself consists of the nature of all phenomena.
"O Rāghava, remain well-composed and abide in yourself by means of your own self.
[For] the Self belongs to one who consists of all states of being and whose nature is that of all objects."
That [world] is indeed nothing but mental construction (saṅkalpa) appearing externally in various forms; abandon it, do not bring it forth.
The meaning is that one should maintain equanimity even when [thoughts] have arisen;
for indeed, total abandonment is not possible to perform until the state of liberation while in the body (*videhamukti*).
[Objection: But how can one abandon a thought as it is arising? To this, he says:
For a gem, due to its insentient nature, is incapable of the act of negating reflections; but such is not the case for one like you, O Rāma.
"Due to its insentient nature" means by way of its lack of consciousness.
"One like you" means one whose consciousness is like yours;
for the renunciation of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) is to be accomplished through direct realization (*saṃvedana*),
and that indeed exists in you— this is the meaning.
He describes the means of renunciation:
"O Rāma, whatever appears here as a reflection upon the jewel of your mind,
having determined that it is not a real substance, do not allow yourself to be colored by it."
Attachment is the state of being colored [by passion].
He states another means [to liberation]:
"Or even that which is said to be 'this alone is the truth' is non-different from the Supreme Self."
"Contemplating [the truth], you should realize the Self by means of the Self as being without beginning or end.
For, through the contemplation of the non-difference of all things from the Supreme Self, the realization of the Self as being without beginning or end is indeed accomplished.
O Rāghava, those mental objects which are reflected in your mind—

O Rāghava, how are you? You are one whose self is attached to another—the Supreme Self, whose essential nature is distinct from all other entities. May they not color you, as crystal is colored by other objects.
The sense is that one whose self is the mind—
otherwise, the absence of the coloring by reflected objects would not be logical.
Like whom?
Like a crystal.
Just as a crystal joined with another color is not stained by a coloring produced by that other color.
The meaning is "so it is."

As for the question, "How indeed can the absence of passion toward the body be possible?"—he explains this with a verse at the end of the chapter: N17: *yathā* (MT_4,21.63) [The verse follows: "O King, just as one who has been bitten by a snake does not feel pain in the wound when the poison has been removed, so too, O Lord of the Earth, the wise man experiences no suffering when the poison of desire has been extracted. [He continues: "Even though the body is composed of the three qualities (*guṇas*), it is nevertheless devoid of consciousness; therefore, how could it be an object of passion? It is like a wooden doll or a painted figure. [He further states: "Just as a person who has awakened from sleep does not remember the objects experienced in a dream, so too, upon attaining the state of pure consciousness, one no longer perceives the world of duality. [Finally: "Since the body is merely a collection of elements and is subject to decay, it is like a house made of clay; how, then, can there be attachment to it? Thus, he concludes the point with this final verse.
As various new dyes enter a stainless crystal with full clarity,
so indeed may the desires for worldly existence enter you with full clarity, O Dispassionate One. (MU 4.21.64)
"Vimananam" means being devoid of the mental faculty called *manas* and its associated dharmas.

Just as various colors enter a stainless crystal, so too do [objects] enter You, who are pure due to the absence of *anusandhāna*— the synonym for *manana* (mental cogitation)— even though You are the substratum for the conceptualization (*saṅkalpana*) of objects.
The summary meaning is: "Let the dyes enter.
The sense is that if a dyeing action occurs without leaving a stain, then there is no loss whatsoever. May there be auspiciousness! (MT_4,21.64)
Thus ends the twenty-first canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrī Mokṣopāya-Ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Thus ends the twenty-first canto in the *Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by Śrī Bhāskarakaṇṭha;
he recounts once more the very same matter previously mentioned, because it is established as the subject matter to be expressed in this section on "Stability" (*sthiti-prakaraṇa*).
For a person who has performed inquiry, whose mind’s fluctuations have dissolved,
who abandons mental cogitation through the realization of knowledge, who has partially comprehended the Self,
who renounces the visible world as something to be discarded, and who has attained that which is to be accepted— (Mokṣopāya 4.22.1)
For one who perceives the seer while seeing the visible, yet does not perceive the non-seer;
for one who is awake to the supreme reality while living,
yet is asleep upon the path of saṃsāra consisting of dense delusion.
Because of their ultimate and absolute lack of flavor, even among those pleasures that are flavorful,
he was devoid of taste and free from desire for enjoyments that are delightful when indulged in.
When the dullness of the mind has fully decayed and attachment has dissolved, the self attains oneness with the waters,
just as a mass of snow melts away in the heat;
even amidst those [states] that are wavy and have interiors restless with a multitude of surging waves.
Then, as thirst subsides like rivers at the end of the rainy season,
and the net of worldly tendencies is torn apart— like a bird-net by a mouse— with the swift force of distaste severing the attachment of weak knots; (6–7)
Just as water becomes clear after coming into contact with the *kataka* fruit,
so too does the intrinsic nature of a living being— of a person— become perfectly serene through the power of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*). 4.22.8 *jantoḥ* means "of a living being" or "of a person."
By the power of consciousness— that is, by the power of the knowledge of the pure self—
one's own nature, which is one's true form,
becomes serene and free from defilement.
In what way is it so?
Just as water becomes clear upon coming into contact with the kataka fruit;
in response to the expectation of "under what conditions does it become clear," he says: "The self goes," and so forth.
In that which is free from attachment (*apagatāsaṅge*), where the defect called "clinging" (*asakti*) has perished;
where dullness (*jāḍya*) has decayed and is gone;
and for that very reason, which is dissolving and on the verge of melting away.
When the mind attains oneness with the water called the Supreme Self (paramātman) through the water of the self (ātman), [it becomes pure].
Like what?
Like a mass of snow remaining in the heat of the sun's glare.
Furthermore, while what exists?
Immediately thereafter,
while the cravings are subsiding.
In what state? In those that are wavy, possessed of increase,
and [filled] with masses of billows.
Those whose inner being is restless with the multitude of waves that are the very forms of conceptual constructions.
In such [women].
In what [things] like?
Like rivers.
The meaning is: "just as those [clouds] subside in autumn at the end of the rainy season, so too."
Furthermore, when what exists?
When the net of the latent impressions of saṃsāra has been torn apart by the swift force of revulsion, like a mouse tearing through a web of birds.
In what state?
Unstable;
[unstable] with respect to the knots consisting of desire and so forth.
Of knots:
that which has a "śleṣa," meaning a connection;
in such [a state].
Of what kind of living being?
Of one by whom discernment (*viveka*)—an investigation of the form "Who am I? and "Whose is this saṃsāra?"—has been made;
of such a person, whose mental activity has dissolved.
Of such a person;
for it is only one who possesses knowledge who has the capacity to abandon discursive thought (manana), and thus it is said "because of being a knower."
The meaning is that [it is known] somewhat through indirectness, but not through direct perception; by implication, the object to be accepted is the nature of the pure seer.
The visible object; the seer, whose nature is that of a seer; for one who sees;
the non-seer, distinct from the seer.
"Of one who does not see"—this should be applied even to "one who is asleep among tastes. "Nirāśiṣaḥ" means one devoid of hope. This is a *kulaka* (a group of verses forming a single syntactic unit).
In what [regard]? N17: (e)ka°;
kallolasamūhaiḥ: N17: °⟨m⟩[s]amūhaiḥ;
jantoḥ: N17: ja[n]toḥ.
"By way of direct perception (*aparokṣatayā*).
[Regarding the question] "What else will be accomplished for him?", he says here:
"Free from passion, free from attachment, free from duality, and free from dependence."
The mind emerges from delusion like a bird from a cage—
free from attachment (*nirupāsaṅga*), devoid of clinging,
and independent, without reliance.
Due to delusion— that is, from the lack of inquiry consisting in the conceit of a self in what is not-self—
one whose wickedness of doubt has been stilled and whose curiosity and confusion have vanished, [attains this].
With its interior completely full, the mind shines like the full moon.
In this context, "curiosity" should be understood as pertaining to the nature of reality;
it is "completely full," being replete with innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
That which has such an interval;
such [is it].
Produced with supreme beauty, with its high and low parts raised far apart.
She extends everywhere with equanimity, like a calm wind over the ocean;
she is the one by whom supreme beauty is produced.
For by means of equanimity, a person always possesses a serene countenance;
this is an expression emphasizing the state [of being] where all depression and elation have been cast far away. That [equanimity] is that in which such depression and elation exist.
Consisting of darkness, deluded, and with its interior shattered by dullness,
it reaches a state of attenuation like the night at dawn—
the word "like" (*iva*) being connected with the word "night" (*kṣapā*).
The lotus-pond of wisdom, with its sun of realized consciousness and its sprouts of merit,
blossoms with stainless radiance like the sky at dawn in embodied form.
This is clear.
Wisdoms that captivate the heart and are capable of delighting the world proceed from the splendor of sentient beings like the rays of the full moon.
The glories of being are the perfections of the quality of purity (*sattva*).
He provides a summary:
"What is the use of saying much more here? The one of great intelligence has known that which is to be known."
It neither rises nor sets, being like the sheath of space that has no real existence.
The meaning is that it does not rise, it does not go to its setting, and it does not deviate from its own essential nature called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*),
like the sheath of space within the supreme ether.
Like a vessel of unreal space,
for one whose own nature is known through investigation and whose self has arisen,
these— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara— become objects of compassion.
For one by whom the nature— that is, the own-form— has been fully understood through investigation;
such a person [should feel compassion] even for them.
The meaning is that compassion arises in him upon seeing the agitation involved in the creation and formation of the universe.
(MT_4,22.16) Even though his outward form is manifest, conceptual constructions do not reach him, whose inner mind is free from egoism, just as deer cannot reach the water of a mirage. MU_4,22.17
[The deer-like ones] do not attain self-mastery, nor do they bring it under their own control;
moreover, the absence of egoism in one whose form is manifest is indeed a cause for wonder. (MT_4,22.17)
Like waves, these worlds come and go from all sides; do not embrace birth and death, which arise from the self, as if they were something external to the wise man.
(The term *kroḍīkurutaḥ* means "to bring under one's control" or "to embrace.")
Because there is an absence of identification with the body, there is an absence of identification with birth and death residing therein.
(MU 4.22.18) Manifestation and disappearance constitute saṃsāra, and no other sequence exists.
Thus, one who delights in the vision of those two does not suffer. (MU 4.22.19)
Thus,
by means of those two— namely, such manifestations and disappearances—
he [is affected].
When there is clear vision through the illumination of that very reality,
one rejoices and does not become weary.
For one who has realized the true nature of things indeed delights in objects and is not distressed;
for it is observed that only one who has not realized the truth experiences the distress caused by the fear of a snake and so forth toward a rope and the like.
Through manifestation and disappearance, [it is said]:
"The one whose true nature is unknown alone [is thus described].
Just as the space within a jar is neither born nor dies when the jar is [created or destroyed], so too is the Self.
Whether the body is adorned or defiled, the one who possesses the Self remains likewise;
the sense is that this is due to the absence of identification with the body.
When discernment has dawned, [the suffering] arising from the weight of false delusion subsides like a cold [fever].
Latent impressions (vāsanā) perish like a mirage in a cloudless desert;
they are produced by that mass of delusions which has a false form.
For in a desert with clouds, the mirage surely vanishes, because its very arising consists in heat.
As long as one has not investigated "Who am I? or "How is this?", [the delusion persists].
The grand display of saṃsāra remains for now like darkness;
the inquiry as to what the nature of this darkness is likewise persists for that long.
[Investigation: This body, which arises from the weight of false delusions, is the locus of calamities;
he who perceives it as such through the cultivation of the [true] self, he truly sees.
He who does not perceive this body as a self does see; he sees correctly— this is the summarized meaning.

He who perceives that the pleasures and pains of the body— which arise by the power of place and time— are not his own, being free from delusion, he truly sees. "My" refers to me, who am pure consciousness alone.

He truly sees who perceives both himself and everything else through a vision that is eternally undivided, seeing all as nothing but the light of consciousness. *MU* 4.22.25 (*itarac*: N17: °ra⟨ś⟩[c]*)*

The eternal light is of the nature of the radiance of pure consciousness. He who perceives everywhere that "I alone am" [the one] endowed with action and the infinite limits of space, direction, time, and so forth— he truly sees.
Space, direction, and time—
these are the beginning of the world; that which begins with space, direction, and time is "without limit or end," meaning it is devoid of a boundary or extremity.
And that world, whose nature consists of space, direction, time, and so forth, is indeed myself alone;
for the reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-tattva*), which has the essence of "I-ness" (*ahantā*), exists as the state of being everything.
Otherwise, the notion "I" would not manifest everywhere,
because even though it is not observed in insentient things, there is no difference in their sharing the state of existence as sentient beings.
Even in that case, since it is possible to infer its manifestation, the claim that "it is not so in all cases" is untenable.
Of what nature is that [word]?
It is that which is connected with action (*kriyānvita*).
The separate mention of action, even though it is already implied by the word "and so forth" (ādi), is for the purpose of demonstrating its preeminence.
Thus it is.
Whoever sees [this] in all places and at all times, he truly sees.
The meaning is that there is no other.
Because it is possible [to conceive of] time as a mere flash [of thought],
and because it is possible to conceive of [it] through analogies such as the tip of a hair divided into millions of parts, it has been conceptually constructed in its various divisions.
"He who perceives that 'I am subtle' and all-pervading—he truly sees. (MU 4.22.27) The all-pervasiveness of the subtle is marvelous;
and here, subtlety should be understood as being beyond the external and internal organs.
He who perceives within himself that which is all-powerful, infinite in nature, abiding within all beings, and non-dual consciousness— he truly sees.
Consciousness is the self of consciousness.
He exists.
Of what nature? He possesses all powers; otherwise, the world in its manifold forms would not manifest.
He is infinite in nature because even the end is swallowed within him alone; thus he is devoid of an end.
For that which has been swallowed cannot conceal the form of the swallower.
He is within all things.
Abiding within the interior of all existents,
it would not manifest as "I" otherwise;
it is non-dual, yet [appears] as duality.
Because even for the dead, that nature does not depart, he is "devoid of a second.
Thus [it is said].
"Within" means in the mind.
But it is not by means of the eye;
he who sees, he truly sees.
One who is free from that [identification],
who is agitated by the fear of mental and physical ailments, and subject to birth, old age, and death—
only the wise person who perceives, "I am not the body," truly sees. MU 4.22.29
The wise one is one who possesses the certainty that the self is the reality of pure consciousness alone.
My majesty pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards;
he who perceives that "there is no second to me" truly sees.
Of me, who am of the nature of pure consciousness alone— not of the nature of the body and so forth—
everything here is strung together as if a multitude of gems upon a thread.
"He who sees that 'I am indeed the mind-stuff'—he truly sees.
To the question, "How is everything woven upon you?", he says here: "The mind-stuff."
For pearls are strung upon a thread;
and the nature of the thread should be understood as being pervasive and subtle in relation to the intellect (*citi*).
"Neither I nor anything else exists here; Brahman alone exists, yet even that does not exist. (MT_4,22.31)
Thus, he who perceives the middle between existence and non-existence—he truly sees.
In this world, [one might think], "I am," regarding oneself as having the form of a limited body and so forth; yet, "I am not" [in that sense].
The world, which exists as something other than me and distinct from me, does not exist,
because it is not perceived in deep sleep.
Brahman is all-pervasive, consisting of pure consciousness alone;
it exists as such in the ultimate sense, for it is impossible to assert that it is non-existent in every respect. Indeed, not...
The delusion we have pointed out cannot possibly exist;
that Brahman neither exists nor does not exist.
Because it transcends both external and internal faculties, it is thus:
that reality called pure consciousness alone, which is the middle between existence and non-existence and serves as their junction—
whosoever sees this, he truly sees.
The reality of pure consciousness alone (cinmātratattva) has been pointed out;
it is called pure consciousness alone (śuddhacinmātrākhya).
Whatever name exists in the three worlds, known as "measure" (*mātrā*), that is a single limb of mine;
he who sees it within like a wave in the ocean—he truly sees. (MU 4.22.33)
For me, whose nature is pure consciousness alone—
indeed, in a dream, everyone experiences the world as being composed of parts of that very consciousness—
this [world] is to be pitied and protected by me alone; she is my own younger sister.
He who looks upon the three worlds as fragile truly sees;
"fragile" means fearful of destruction.
A younger sister is just like this.
When the states of "selfhood" and "otherness," as well as "thou-ness" and "I-ness," have ceased through the realization of the Great Self,
then that one of clear vision surely sees.
The sense is: because of the existence of the mind;
that is, because one perceives the state of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) everywhere.
The body consists of the Bhairava of Consciousness, free from the pursuit of objects of thought (*cetya*).
He who perceives the entire web of the world as filled [with consciousness] truly sees.
Free from the pursuit of objects of thought (*cetya*), he is the Bhairava of Consciousness; because he devours all things, he is the Bhairava known as Consciousness (*cid*).
His body is his very nature, which consists of that [Consciousness].
Whether one views pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, and the various notions of discrimination as "I am," or indeed as "I am not," such a person certainly does not fall away from the truth.
(MU 4.22.37) That is to say, one who views pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, and the mental constructions of discrimination as "I am"— [does not fall away].
Whether viewing it as "I am this" or "I am not this," one does not fall away; one does not incur loss.
For in either case, there is the attainment of the nature of pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*).
Indeed, apart from pure consciousness, nothing can be all-pervasive or transcendent.
[This occurs] when the world is filled with the existence of one's own self and devoid of anything else.
Seeing what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, the man who perceives correctly [regards] his own self,
which is of the nature of pure consciousness alone.
That existence which is the nature of manifestation—
by that [existence], because it abides as the essence, it is filled and rendered full.
Otherwise, the manifestation of "I" would be impossible;
likewise, in a world devoid of anything else distinct from pure consciousness.
What is to be abandoned?
Since it is impossible for one's own self to be abandoned, the meaning is that nothing at all is to be abandoned.
What is to be accepted?
The meaning is that because one's own self is always already attained, there is nothing whatsoever [to be gained]; thus, seeing— that is, experiencing— in this manner,
a person [is liberated].
He is endowed with sight like [that of others]; the meaning is that others are blind.
I bow to Him for whom the notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have ceased, who is beyond reasoning, devoid of appearance, and is simply pure Being— sufficient unto Himself—
thinking, "This is [He]. This world is "beyond reasoning," meaning it is impossible to conceptualize through logic.
Because it abides in its own nature, which is tranquil and without appearance, it is devoid of manifestation;
it exists as pure being alone.
By this certainty,
for that person whose discrimination between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted has perished.
I bow to that person;
the sense is that he alone is superior to all.
He who,
like space, is of a single nature even while pervading all existents, and who does not undergo the coloring of existence— he is the Great-Souled One, Maheśvara.
The person who has gone to all states of existence.
Like space, the Self is one, the all-pervading Self;

although it exists within all things, and although it is engaged in worldly activity regarding all objects that serve as the means for bodily sustenance, [it remains free from] the coloring of objective phenomena.
In the mind toward existence,
he does not undergo attachment— that is, attachment in the form of joy or resentment.
He is a Great Soul, a Great Person;
he becomes Maheśvara because he is endowed with great power.
Pervading all states of being,
he is free from the conceptualization of darkness and light, and has attained the nature of time.
I bow to him who has attained that state— he who is gentle, perfectly equanimous, and established in his own nature;
he who is the conceptualization of darkness and light, and of insentience and consciousness.

He was released by her; [released] from Time— that is, from Time whose nature consists in the diversity of activity— from its very essence (ātmatām), that is, from its own form as the bestower of existence.
He has gone;
he is gentle, cool,
and established in his own true nature.
I bow to him who has attained that state;
here, moreover, the sun is described as being unprecedented.
He expresses this very same point with the concluding verse of the chapter:

"Homage to that Śiva, possessed of supreme awakening, whose infinite activity is entirely uniform throughout all the manifold and beautiful manifestations of the world’s arising and passing away, for he alone is the one who moves everywhere. (MU 4.22.42)
Of him who has attained all things as one, whose sole refuge is the totality;
in those [powers] of beautiful majesty, endowed with praiseworthy capability,
diverse and of many kinds.
In those arts existing within the world, which consist of the combinations and collisions of rising and setting,
she is infinite and devoid of destruction.
The mental modification (vṛtti) becomes indeed equanimous;
and here, "endlessness" is in reference to its firmness.

It has been said: "Let there be salutation to Him, the one possessed of supreme awakening, who is endowed with the realization of the reality of the Supreme Self, the auspicious one who has become Śiva, the Puruṣa."
And Śiva is of equal disposition toward all, the sole refuge for everyone, and of the nature of supreme awakening;
may there be auspiciousness.
Thus it has been said for the sake of Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-second canto in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Thus ends the twenty-second canto in the section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! Furthermore, he describes once more the majesty of the discerning one (*vivekin*).
Taking hold of the supreme state, he remains like the whirling of a wheel;
even while exercising sovereignty over the city of the body, he is not defiled.
The "supreme state" refers to the highest station known as pure consciousness alone.
"Grasping" means one who relies upon the supreme state;
"standing" like the whirling of a wheel means being situated all around.
"Remaining without further attachment in his activity"—
that is to say, he is one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). Even while exercising sovereignty over the city of the body, he is not defiled.

The meaning is that one is not seized by the pleasures and pains arising from those [objects]. Even a king, who relies upon the highest station, remains engaged in ruling while wandering everywhere throughout the city.
For such a knower of reality, this [city] is like a pleasure grove for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.

For one who knows that, his own body is like a great city for happiness alone, not for suffering; it is comparable to a pleasure grove because it is the means for attaining the ultimate bliss of liberation.
"It does not lead to suffering because there is no staining by suffering. (MT_4,23.2) Regarding this, Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Great Sage, how indeed can the body possess the nature of a city?"
And how could a yogin, dwelling in this [state], be a sole enjoyer of the pleasures of sovereignty?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Rāma, this city of the body is delightful and endowed with all virtues;
for the knower, it is rich in infinite diversions and illuminated by the sun of self-perception."
One's own light is the self-luminosity;
that itself is the sun.
By means of it, through the medium of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), there is manifestation toward oneself.
She was led away. He describes her possession of all virtues:
"With the light from the radiance of the windows of her eyes illuminating the interior of the world."
Her lower legs are as broad as the gateway of her hands,
and the interior of her world is illuminated by the light shining from the windows of her eyes.
The calves of her legs reached as far as the width of the gateway;
her eyes were like windows.
The radiance and light of those two—
by that light, the various worlds were illuminated and made manifest.
In that city,
within which the centers of the worlds were contained, even the interior spaces of the worlds were visible through the windows constructed at the city gates.
The visible parts become [the gates];
the two hands themselves are the two gate-towers at the entrance,
and by means of those two, the feet themselves are reached as the two inner gate-piers.
That [city] which has regions near the forest; such cities and the upajaṅgala region have, for their part, a main street (pratolī). (MT_4,23.5)
Her line of body hair was like a thicket of creepers, her skin was garlanded with watchtowers,
and the circles of her calves, thighs,
and pillars were supported by the resinous burs of her ankles.
"Garlanded with bastion-towers of bark":
the bark itself is the bastion-tower, that is, the rampart;
she is adorned by it.
Guggulu is the stone that serves as the foundation for the pillar.
[Śilā] N17: *°bhūtālitā*. The letter *bhū* is in the *āradā* script. The text follows MṬ (I) 17,25.
(MT_4,23.6) The first creation, a stone slab with feet clearly demarcated by lines, beautiful with its boundaries of skin, vital points, veins, essence, and joints. MU_4,23.7
Those two feet, divided by two lines,
are Ugra and Śilā;
of these two, the first was created.
For in the initial creation, stones are established having been divided [into parts];
the essence of skin, vital points, and veins is indeed the very collection of skin, vital points, and veins.
That [earth] which has junctions and boundaries as its limits and frontiers.
The stone slabs formed the panels for the two thighs, while the opening for the private parts was fashioned from the tips;
it was covered by a roof of shimmering rows of hair, like a covering of shining leaves.
With the opening of the vulva fashioned from the tips of the two thighs as its door-panels:
"the two thighs themselves are the door-panels; those which are their tips..."
By those two, it was fashioned and constructed with the arrangement of door-panels;
its very lap is the location of the anus,
which serves as its exit— the position of the doorway.
That which is a shimmering mass of hair is itself a covering fashioned from pieces of glass;
she is veiled by that.
[The Garland of Hair] (N17: *cakāva*kacāvalī):
Adorned by the garden of her face, which possesses the beauty of her eyebrows, forehead, and mouth;
its broad expanse of cheeks is strewn with the blue lotuses of her falling glances. (MU_4,23.9)
That face, which possesses a beautiful luster through its eyebrows, forehead, and mouth,
is itself the garden;
by it she is adorned.
The lake of her chest had the buds of her breasts fixed within it,
and the mountain of her playful shoulders was covered by the dense line of hair.
[Her] shoulders are like playful mountain peaks covered by thick rows of hair; that is,
she is both one whose shoulders are covered by thick rows of hair and one who sports upon mountain peaks.
Covered by a dense line of hair,
with mountain-like mounds for playing upon the shoulders.
With the bowl of her desired food cast into the pit of her belly,
she makes a sound through the agitation of wind expelled from the cavity of her long throat.
In the cavity of the belly, that is, in the pit of the stomach;
those excellent foods, meaning beautiful foods, which have been cast therein— by means of them.
"Under that pretext" means to that extent.
She is one who possesses a broken vessel for her desired food— that is, a broken bowl for the food she desires.
In the royal city as well,
there are vessels of desired food;
that which is the long cavity of the throat.
In that [state],
there is an upward-moving,
circulating wind; whatever agitation belongs to that [wind], [that is what is meant].
By that [wind], sound is produced, being endowed with sound;
even within the city or in the caves,
the sound of the wind occurs.
Adorned with whatever objects are obtained as determined by the marketplace of the heart,
the city of the vital breath flows incessantly through its nine gates;
the heart itself is the marketplace, the place of assembly.

In that [work], it is adorned by those meanings which have been determined as worthy of adoption— that is, meanings established as such— and which are obtained according to their respective contexts, having arrived through their own natural flow.
In the marketplaces of the city as well, matters of business were settled.
The sitting posture: as for those who have attained their goal,
their mouths are wide open, and they are filled with fragments of teeth and bones that have been seen.
In that city, there are pits where food is chewed by *cilla* birds with tongues flickering from their mouths;
furthermore, in the pits of that city, there are fragments of bones abandoned by flesh-eaters.
The *cilla* is a specific kind of bird.
The hollows of her ear-cavities were concealed by a mass of hairy grass;
the edges of her buttocks were bound by chains, and her broad back was like a vast wilderness.
Here, "chains" refers specifically to the buttocks.
She whose back has its edges curved by those two [breasts], and whose vicinity is beautiful;
she whose very back is a broad wilderness.
Furthermore, iron chains are placed at the junctions of the city and the wilderness for the purpose of obstructing thieves and others.
With its edges gracefully curved; [N17: °topāntam] [N17:
sā⟨ḥ⟩] (MT_4,23.14) The endless mire was drawn out from within the water-wheel whose axle-pole was severed at the base.
The excellent woman of self-reflection, who gallops upon the ground of the garden of the mind,
has her water-wheel severed right at the anus; thus, with the mechanism of the water-wheel broken,
she is drawn up from within— that is, from the internal region.
She from whom endless mire— meaning mire in the form of excrement— has been cast out.
She even clears away the mud from the city.
Regarding "the garden of the mind":
for in the wise mind, the contemplation of the self alone vibrates day and night.
In the garden of the mind:
the restless monkeys of the sense-faculties are firmly bound by the leather thongs of wisdom;
it is delightful with the blossoming flowers of laughter from the garden of the face.
For the wise man binds his restless senses with the rope of discernment (*jñāna*).
He says, "It is like a garden";
for it is fitting that flowers should bloom in a garden.
Thus,
for the knower, his own body-city is the most beautiful of all auspicious things;
it leads only to happiness, not to suffering, and to the highest benefit.
The city of one's own body possesses all the qualities of the cities previously mentioned; it is one's own bodily city for the sake of the supreme benefit, meaning for the sake of liberation.
Is this [pleasure] a giver of happiness for the ignorant, or not? To this, he says:
"Furthermore, for the ignorant, this is a treasury of endless sufferings."
But for the wise man, this is a garland of treasuries of infinite joys. (MU 4.23.18) "A garland of treasuries" means a series of storehouses.
The meaning is that it produces endless suffering;
the intention is that because one who does not know the pure reality experiences torment day and night for this reason.
[Objection: "In that case, would not such [a state] belong to the knower as well?
To this, he says: "But for the knower... The word "but" (tu) indicates a distinction.
For one who has realized the pure reality of the self, there is no possibility of experiencing distress for that purpose;
the sense is that one person does not become a partaker of distress on account of another.
"But surely, at the time of its destruction, this [ignorance] will cause suffering to the knower? To this he says:
"O subduer of enemies, when this has been destroyed, nothing of the knower is destroyed;
when it remains, everything remains established. Therefore, this [knowledge] brings happiness to the knower. (MU 4.23.19)
The intended meaning is that its essential nature consists solely of pure consciousness (cinmātra), distinct from these [states].
Now, one might object: "In that case, even during the state of persistence (sthiti), there would be no purpose for this [consciousness] by means of that [state]."

Here he says, "While it remains," meaning that everything is well-established because it accomplishes all tasks useful for liberation while living (jīvanmukti). He provides the conclusion with the words, "Therefore, this..."
Established; [the conclusion]. N17: *saṃ*sthi[ta]m upasaṃhāraṃ ] N17:
Regarding the summary [of the metaphor]: "Is it not true that some have even stated that this [body] is a chariot? To this he replies:
"Since the wise man, having mounted it, dwells at ease within saṃsāra..."
For the sake of attaining all enjoyments and liberation without exception, this city of the body is known as the chariot of the Knower;
for from it [proceed] the splendors of sound, form, taste, touch, smell, kinsmen, and wealth.
For it is by this very [means] that they are obtained; therefore, this [knowledge] bestows gain upon the wise one.

[Regarding the verse: "Sound, form, taste, touch, smell, kinsmen, and prosperity"—if it is asked, "What gain is there for the wise one through the acquisition of sound and the rest? [the answer follows].
No,
because the attainment, which consists in the knowledge of the collection of powers of the reality of the Supreme Self through the medium of sound and so forth, is already established.
O Rāma, when this [intellect] itself bears the web of the activities of pleasure and pain, then it is everywhere capable of supporting the weight of all things;
this is the city of the body.
For the knower perceives pleasure and so forth as belonging only to the body, not to itself.
Indeed, exercising sovereignty in that city of the body,
the knower remains free from delusion and agitation, like Indra in his own city.
Free from delusion regarding this matter, I am devoid of self-conceit; with my agitation gone, I am undisturbed. I do not let the intoxicated horse of my mind gallop toward the pride of arrogance.
One does not bestow the daughter of wisdom upon that which has the form of the duality called greed—
a duality consisting of the arrogance of the pit, the form of sense-objects, and the ostentation of the abyss.
To him he does not give his daughter Prajñā; he does not give the wisdom that has been seized by greed.
That which acts is "bhāva" (existence/activity).
In the [passage containing] "śvabhrāḍambare," N17 reads °bhrā(ta) *ḍa*ṃ⟨bha⟩[ba]re;
in "lobhākhyo," N17 reads °ākhy⟨ā⟩[o]. (MT_4,23.24)
And he does not perceive any vulnerability in that foreign kingdom of ignorance;
rather, he cuts away the internal roots of the fear of the enemy that is saṃsāra.
Here, "the foreign kingdom" is ignorance itself, which, by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), functions as the hostile king.
He does not see;
what talk can there be of his going? This is the vulnerability of this king of ignorance.
The word "tu" has the sense of "eva" (only/indeed). He does not see [it], because it has been conquered.
Because it has been conquered by way of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇayā*):
in the revolution of the essence of craving (*tṛṣṇāsāraparāvarta*), which is difficult to grasp due to the agitation of sensual desires (*kāmasaṅkṣobhadurgraha*).
They do not sink into the game of the senses, wherein pleasure and pain are cast about;
[it is] such as that which consists of the reversal and recurrence of the essence of craving.
That which is the agitation of desire; by that, they are seized,
overturned, and impelled.
The two dice are pleasure and pain; pleasure and pain themselves are the dice. Their casting, their play—that is to say, gambling—is what is meant.
In that regard, they do not sink;
for the king’s immersion in gambling is indeed a fault,
and even playing with dice is surely enveloped by craving and desire.
He plays with dice;
for the king,
bathing occurs incessantly, both externally and internally, moment by moment.
The movement of one's desires proceeds in sequence through the confluences of rivers and sacred fords;
externally, in the outer world;
internally, in the mind.
The mind alone is the chariot because it is under one's own control; he whose movement is by means of that [mind] is [the rider].
Internal bathing, however, should be understood as immersion in the cavity of consciousness.
Unseen by all the senses, with his face turned away from observing the city [of the body],
he dwells eternally in bliss within the inner apartment known as meditation.
(The word *pura* refers to the body.)
And the king of the city, invisible to all people, remains wandering through the city with his face turned away from observing the town;
and here, "meditation" (dhyāna) should be understood as the very awareness of the reality that is one's own self, which is pure consciousness alone. (MT_4,23.28)
This divine city, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is always a source of happiness for one whose soul is eternally delighted— just like Amarāvatī belongs to Śakra;
[the word] "of the knower" (*jñasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Everything remains established by that which is stable; nothing is destroyed by that which is destroyed.
How could that city of the king not bring happiness?
This is clear.
When the city of the body has perished, nothing at all is lost for the knower, just as when a jar is destroyed, the space within it that had occupied the jar remains unchanged. This is clear.
Just as the wind touches an existing jar but not one that is no longer present—that is, one that has perished—so too does the embodied soul [touch] this city of its own body. MU 4.23.32:
*asthitam* means "no longer present" or "perished."
One who knows the Self as distinct from the body is a knower of that [Self].

The knower of that [reality], though this Blessed Lord, the Self, is omnipresent, remains situated here; having experienced the state of manhood created by his own conceptual construction, he has attained the vision of the Self. (MU 4.23.33)
Even while acting, he does not act; though fully intent upon all activities, he sometimes presides over all the matters at hand. Being established here means being situated within the body.
The word "api" (even/also) indicates the contradiction involved in the enjoyment of a universal self by a male [body].
One who has realized the vision of the Self is a knower of that [Self],
not a fool.
Because such a state [of agency] is impossible for him; "acting" means acting through the medium of the body and so forth; "not acting" means because of the certainty that "I am not the doer."
He presides over— that is, he determines as tasks to be performed— the purposes and objectives that are relevant and have come into the current flow.
But not those imagined by one's own reflective awareness.
[He] illuminates: "N17: °tayati (MT_4,23.33-34).
Now, if he performs this at some time, what does he do at other times? To this he replies:
"At times he ascends a swaying celestial chariot (*vimāna*) out of sport."
The stainless mind, desiring to sport in the lovely state of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*),
sometimes that knower of reality ascends by means of his own self-play upon a celestial chariot— the mind itself, which is a chariot in form.
To do what?
To sport— that is,
to engage in internal diversion.
Of what nature is the mental vehicle? It is "unwavering," meaning free from flickering.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
He whose movement is unstruck and nowhere obstructed.
The masculine gender [of the pronoun] "tam" is used in reference to the word "vimāna. It is "amala," meaning free from the impurities of passion and so forth.
For this very reason, it is beautiful.
The knower of that [asks]: "But what does he do there? To this he replies:
"Established there, with Lokasundarī, whose limbs are perpetually cool..."

He who indeed always delights in loving-kindness (maitrī) abiding within his heart— he, the knower of that, remaining there, seated in the celestial chariot of the mind, [unites] with Lokasundarī, the beloved of the world.

He delights constantly with Maitrī—the woman named Maitrī—who dwells eternally in his heart and whose limbs are ever-cool; the sense is that at times, being inward-turned, he becomes composed entirely of loving-kindness.
[Regarding *lokasundaryā*:
Not only does he have loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as his beloved, but he has two others as well; thus it is said:
"Two beloveds stand at his sides, Truth and Solitude."
Like the two stars Viśākhā belonging to the moon, their minds were equally gladdened.
(This is clear.
The wise one [beholds] all these worlds as if torn apart by the saw of suffering.
Seated upon his throne, he beholds the worlds as Vālmīki did, or like the sun from behind its back; in what manner does he behold them?
Suffering itself is a saw;
by it they are split and tormented,
like anthills by ants.
The meaning is: "having ascended from peak to peak.
(MT_4,23.38) Having long fulfilled all his aspirations and being beautiful with every perfection, he shines like the full-bodied moon, never again to be eclipsed. MU_4,23.39
With every prosperity and every excellence, he is beautiful.
Even when indulged in, the flood of enjoyments does not produce weariness for him;
rather, the *kālakūṭa* poison shines upon the neck of his afflictions.
*Rājate*: The sense is that the flood of enjoyments (*bhogaugha*) leads to weariness by way of destruction.
[Objection: But how is it that this does not lead to his weariness? To this, he says:
For when enjoyment is consumed with full understanding, it leads to contentment; likewise,
a thief who is recognized and reassured becomes a friend rather than an enemy.
Ś3: *°śvāsito*; N17: *°svāmito*.
The meaning is: having fully understood and correctly determined [it] as being of the nature of the self (*ātmarūpatva*).
For enjoyment (*bhoga*), when known as being of the nature of the self, [is liberated].
Even when destroyed, it does not give rise to weariness, because it remains as one's own essential nature;
nor is the destruction of the self logical,
because even in the event of destruction, it remains as the witness of that destruction.
Because of its stability: [N17:
*tathā* (always remaining firm)] by means of that stability, [it is] far-reaching during the quarrels of the multitudes of men, women, and dancers.
To the wise man, the splendor of enjoyments appears like a beautiful festival procession;
even another skilled person keeps far away from a quarrel among a multitude of actors,
as well as from the performance of the drama they have begun.
He perceives it:
just as a village procession unexpectedly encountered by travelers on the road is watched by them, even so is the activity consisting of worldly transactions perceived by the ignorant. (MU 4.23.43)
The sense is that he gazes without any mental attachment (*niranusandhāna*).

Just as the eye falls effortlessly upon objects such as the directions or substances situated before it, without any passion (*nīrāga*), so too does the intellect of the steadfast one fall upon its objects. (MU 4.23.44)
Just as the eye, when objects in the various directions are presented without effort,
falls [upon them] free from passion— that is, devoid of attachment—
so does one of steady intellect.
The intellect of one who knows that [reality] descends upon its tasks in the same manner. The sense is that such a person performs actions while remaining entirely free from passion.
He never seizes an object already attained by the senses, nor does he fail to give what has been attained; thus complete, the Knower remains steadfast. (MU 4.23.45)
For this indeed is perfection: the non-grasping of what has been attained and the non-desiring of what has not yet been attained.

Those of fickle minds, who worry about what they have not attained and remain indifferent toward what they have already attained, do not conceive of the noble mind; they are like peacock feathers that cannot steady a mountain.
Free from thoughts of attainment, they neither conceptualize nor cause agitation. With all doubts completely stilled and all curiosity dissolved, [they remain].
With the web of conceptual constructions completely destroyed, the knower shines like a sovereign emperor.
This is clear.
He does not fit within himself; he expands by his own self within the Self.

Self-possessed like the ocean of milk, reaching to its full and limitless bounds, it does not admit [anything else]; because it is filled with bliss, it expands within itself by means of its own self. The sense is that it perceives no other whatsoever within.
And it is both complete and without limit or end; thus, it is "complete and without limit or end."

Neither from within nor from without [does he find delight]; toward beings wretched in their craving for enjoyments and those with dejected senses, he—calm and with an undisturbed mind—laughs at them as if they were madmen. (MU 4.23.49)
The intended meaning is: "What need is there to speak of attachment to that?"
At that time, when there is attachment, [the letter] *u* is attached to *kā*.
Just as one who desires another’s wife is ridiculed by others,
so too is the one who desires sense-objects ridiculed by the wise.
(MU 4.23.50) "Another’s own" means belonging to another.
For a man who desires such a future wife—
that is, who desires a wife for another purpose—
he is laughed at, meaning mockery is performed by others.
In the same way, the ignorant person who desires the enjoyment of the senses is laughed at by the wise.
One should bring under control with discernment the mind that abandons its own equanimity and happiness, fleeing toward sense objects,
just as one would bring a lordly elephant under control with a goad.
Equanimity is one's own happiness, the bliss of the Self known as equanimity;
[this is attained] through reflection in the form: "What essence is there in these enjoyments?
To whatever mental tendency the flow toward enjoyments is granted—
That mental fluctuation, too, must be destroyed at the very outset, just like the sprouting of a poison.
[it refers to] that mental fluctuation (*manovṛtti*).
"At first" means prior to the bestowal of the spreading [of the ritual substance].
The intention of the word "api" (even/also) is to suggest: "What need is there even to speak of her to whom it is not given?
[Objection: But what is the result of bestowing the spreading upon one who has already been struck first? To this, he says:
For even the honor shown after one has been struck is infinite;
even a meager watering acts like nectar for a rice plant scorched by the summer heat.
(MU 4.23.53) [tāḍitasya] N17: °ḍi⟨-⟩[ta]°
"Honor" (*sammāna*) means respect; it signifies, that is to say, the act of bestowing [gifts] with full extension. (MT_4,23.53)
Now, how is this so? To this he says:
For honor consisting of great respect is not perceived by one who is not in need;
the flood of the rainy season shines but slightly upon rivers that are already full. (MU 4.23.54)

For [the word] *pūrṇānām* means "because they are full. By one who is *anārta*, meaning not subject to affliction, *sammānaḥ*—that is, great honor—is not perceived, meaning it is not known. This is the point.
He supports this with an illustration: "Of full rivers... Even a small amount of water from full rivers shines brilliantly during the flood of the rainy season.
The meaning is that they lack the quality of bringing joy to the minds of people; for the minds of people indeed become joyful upon seeing the floods of rivers swollen by the monsoon rains.
Even when full, the ocean, though already beneficial, desires yet more; even for the sake of filling the world, the single ocean takes up all the water. (MU 4.23.55)
[He] is joined with the filling of the world—"with joy," is the remainder [of the sentence].
(MU 4.23.55) That which is the subsequent embellishment of the restrained mind, he prizes highly precisely because it has attained what was previously unattained in its expansion. (MU 4.23.56)
*Leśena pūraṇā* means filling by way of a small portion; *tām eva bhāgamaṇḍanām eva* means that very same filling by way of a small portion.
And this [person] has not yet attained expansion, yet it has been attained.
And it is that which has obtained expansion where none was previously obtained;
its state is "reality" (tattva);
therefore [it is so called].
One who has not attained expansion considers even what is very little as much;
for a king who is bound [by desires] is satisfied with a mere village once he is liberated.
Unbound by others and not overcome, he is not satisfied even by sovereignty.
One who was bound at first and later liberated is "bound-and-liberated" (baddhamukta);
likewise, a mind that has been restrained is satisfied by even a mere fragment of enjoyment.
The state [of being].
(MT 4,23.57) Since the restraint of the mind is to be accomplished by means of the restraint of the senses, he speaks specifically of the restraint of the senses:
"Having crushed hand with hand and having ground teeth against teeth."
"Having assailed them as one limb might another, conquer your own enemies, the senses.
The meaning is that the senses which have turned toward their objects must be withdrawn by means of the power of right knowledge.
By men who are eager for victory and desirous of rising upward, the sense-faculties must first be thoroughly understood as enemies of the heart.
(MU 4.23.59) [udbubhūṣubhiḥ] N17: °bhūṣ(i)u°

"Another," meaning one in the form of a king or similar authority; "by those wishing to rise," that is, by those desiring to attain power; "should be known as enemies"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
And the enmity of the sense faculties toward the heart should be understood as their tendency to draw one toward objects of enjoyment.
[Regarding *udbubhūṣubhiḥ*: N17 reads *°bubhūṣ⟨i⟩ubhiḥ*.
He offers praise to those who are endowed with mastery over the mind.

On this vast expanse of the earth, those men are truly fortunate and possess virtuous intentions who are counted among the subjects of human discourse yet have not been conquered by their own minds. (MU 4.23.60) [subhagās] Ś1, Ś3:
subhagās; N17: su--
gaṇyā] Ś1, Ś3: gaṇyā; N17:
— spaṣṭam //
[Clearly] N17: *spaṣṭam* (MT_4,23.60).
He expresses this very point even with the verse at the end of the chapter:
"The serpent of the mind, having made its coils in the cavity of the heart, possesses the virulent poison of conceptual constructions."
I pay homage to that subduer of enemies (*arindama*) who has attained tranquility. The meaning is that he alone is the most excellent of all. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-third canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Thus ends the twenty-third canto in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīmokṣopāyaṭīkā*, composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Now, one might ask: "In that case, what is the difficulty in conquering the senses? To this, he says:
The sovereigns of the great hells, whose elephants are intoxicated misdeeds;
they are difficult to conquer, for their enemies are the senses, which are bristling with the shafts of desire.
(MU 4.24.1) Those whose elephants are indeed intoxicated misdeeds.
Those emperors were such that their very hopes were like arrows and shafts.
Moreover, they are equipped with both elephants and arrows.
Those ungrateful ones who first destroy their own bodies, which are their own support—
those enemies of their own senses are difficult to conquer, being great treasuries of evil deeds.
They cause one to strive for enjoyments that are impossible to attain.

Having reached the abode of the body, out of greed for the bait of sense-objects, the vultures of the senses—those fierce birds whose wings are what ought and ought not to be done—flit about restlessly. (MU 4.24.3)
[The abode of the corpse: N17: *ka(re)le*°.
"Vultures of the senses" (*akṣagṛdhrā*): those whose two wings are precisely the fierce [distinctions] between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; such are they.
Those rogues who are caught in the web of discernment regarding what should and should not be done—
no one can sever their limbs, just as one cannot swallow a mouthful of stone.
They are vultures greedy for sense-objects;
for vultures do not seize a mouthful of stone.
Those who delight in sense objects that are charming only at first sight fall into hells that are utterly devoid of flavor at their end. They are like vultures. (MU 4.24.5)
This is an adjective qualifying "in the objects" (viṣayeṣu), meaning "those whose inner essence is utterly devoid of flavor."
One who possesses the wealth of discernment (*viveka*) in this city of the wretched body is not overcome, against his will, by the enemies that are the senses dwelling within. (MU 4.24.6)
While this contemptible body is being experienced,
for one who is strong is not overcome by enemies against his will.

Those who dwell in formidable cities made of clay are not as happy as those whose minds are self-dependent and who are lords of their own bodies as cities. "Those who dwell in formidable cities made of clay" refers to kings of external cities.
"Having a mind under one's own control" is the reason expressed by way of this qualification.

(MT_4,24.7) For one who has brought the servants of the senses under his own command and has well captured the enemy that is the mind, the insights of a Buddha flourish like blossoms in the springtime. MU_4,24.8
The wisdoms of the Buddhas, the knowers; the wisdoms of the Buddhas,
the awakened ones.
For one whose mental pride has been destroyed and who has subdued the enemies that are the senses,
the latent tendencies for enjoyment wither away like lotus ponds in winter.
In the winter [of existence],
the latencies of enjoyment (*bhogavāsanā*) and the formative forces of enjoyment (*bhogasaṃskāra*)—
to that extent do the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) dance about in the heart like Vetālīs in the dead of night.
As long as the mind has not been conquered through firm practice on a single principle (ekatattva), [the senses] do not cease their wandering; this is the sense.
The single principle is the all-pervading reality of pure consciousness alone.

(MT_4,24.10) I consider the mind to be the servant of the discerning person because it performs desired actions; a minister because it accomplishes tasks through counsel; and a vassal because its own senses are under its command. (MU_4,24.11)
The vassal is appointed for the conquest of enemies.
Because of his fondling, the mother is affectionate; because of his protection, the father is purifying;
because of supreme trust, I consider the friend to be the mind of wise men.
Because of trust in the mind (*mano*),
and because of fondling— that is, acting out of fondling—
the term refers to one who is both affectionate and possessed of tenderness.
The *lalanā* is the woman.
Having looked upon it with the vision of the scriptures, well-pondered, and earnestly entreated,
the father of the mind, having surrendered his own self, bestows supreme accomplishment.
It was entreated and begged most earnestly;
having abandoned and destroyed oneself—
for it is the mind that destroys its own self.
It accomplishes what is beneficial.
Since even a father brings about the welfare of his son by sacrificing his own life, he serves as a point of comparison for it.
Well-polished, well-scrubbed, well-held, and well-attuned.

The heart-pleasing jewel of the mind shines in the heart when joined with excellent qualities; in the case of the gem, it is well-polished and properly examined, and [the mind-jewel] is set upon excellent,
praiseworthy qualities as its threads.
Completely applied [to all things],
this master of the mind-mantra bestows upon the doer of auspicious deeds those actions which are axes for the tree of birth and which result in future prosperity.
*Udarkaḥ* means that which has become the subsequent fruit; *udayaḥ* refers to those [actions] for which there is such a result.
Regarding the person of auspicious karma, who performs auspicious deeds,
he states the result:

Thus, O Rāma, having washed this mind-jewel— which is stained by much mud— with the water of discernment for the sake of perfection, become one who possesses light. (MU 4.24.16) "For the sake of perfection" means for the sake of perfection known as the attainment of the reality of the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure consciousness alone.
It possesses light; it possesses illumination.
Even one who cleans jewels becomes possessed of light in the darkness, due to the radiance of the gems.
Because of its existence.
For the sake of attaining the reality of the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure consciousness alone:
"Even though you are expanded by discernment, do not fall helplessly like an ordinary man into these terrifying realms of worldly existence, which are full of calamities. (MU 4.24.17)
In these fearsome and terror-inducing [places],
do not fall, do not go;
even if I am possessed of discernment, should I go?
The word "api" (even) is used to indicate that one should not go even when certain that it will benefit oneself;
the meaning is that while an ordinary person is devoid of discrimination,
you yourself were not possessed of discrimination at the time of your fall.
What [is there for me]?
Do not fall into those things that cause fear;
do not [allow them] to manifest.
Do not disregard this illusion of saṃsāra, which has arisen crowded with hundreds of misfortunes and is like a mist of great delusion.
Do not disregard it; do not treat it with contempt by asking, "What can this possibly do to me?"
Resorting to supreme solitude and perceiving the truth with your intellect,
thoroughly conquer the enemies that are the senses, and cross over the ocean of existence.
