(MT 4.25.12) Indra was defeated by the infinite Daityas who possessed the machinery of jewels;
he created garden pavilions with the flames of fire cooled by snow. (MU 4.25.13)
[He] has constructed garden pavilions with the flames of fire that are cold as snow; [these] consist of jewel-machines, manifested through illusion, having the very nature of jewel-machines.
By him, Vāsava was utterly defeated by those infinite Daityas. He is that one.
[Endless] (N17: [ḥ]na⟨na⟩ntā):
He surpassed the sandalwood trees of the Nandana grove with gardens blooming with flowers in all seasons;
he surpassed the sandalwood of the Malaya mountains, from which the serpents were carried away by illusory snakes. MU_4,25.14.
He whose sandalwood trees surpassed the Nandana grove with their blossoms in every season;
he for whom the sandalwoods of Mount Malaya had their natural serpents driven far away by illusory snakes that had stolen [the real ones].
With his inner apartments rendered dull by the beauty of the world’s golden women, he [was like one] who has driven away the innate serpents with illusory snakes.
For the sake of playful competition, the Lord, the wielder of the discus and mace, was surpassed—
overcome by the beauty of the world of golden women produced through his illusory power (*māyā*). By that splendor of the golden-limbed ladies, he was eclipsed.
He whose [there were] women of the inner apartments; he. For the sake of sport, a rivalry manifested through illusion is "sportive rivalry";
by that, [he was] overcome.
He by whom Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus and mace, was slain by Mahārudra;
he whose own sky-like city is enriched with stars that are a multitude of jewels flying up incessantly.
Its courtyards were filled with heaps of various flowers reaching up to the knees;
clearly,
during the nights, its sky was filled with hundreds of moons from all the netherworlds.
He whose excellence of qualities was celebrated in songs sung by the world and by his own statue;
(this is clear).
He caused the celestial elephants to flee before the lordly elephant Airāvaṇa created by Māyā.
The interior of his harem was filled with the excellence of the splendors of the three worlds;
he was clearly fortunate with every prosperity and endowed with all sovereign powers.
His supreme instruction was honored by all the vassal lords of the Daityas;
clearly,
the circle of Asuras rested in the shade of the forest of his great arms.
Adorned with earrings made of the essence-jewels from the caves of all the oceans:
all the oceans themselves are the caves;
the "essences" are the jewels within them.
Their earrings;
by them he was adorned.
Of that god who had been destroyed, whose form was harsh and terrifying—

There was a vast army of asuras, the destroyers of the gods, by whom the gods had been uprooted and brought to exhaustion; such was its power. When that army, relying on its illusory strength, was asleep or had departed to another region.
Having found a vulnerability, the gods indeed advanced against that other army of Śambara.
That which is the army;
its *antara* is the middle,
the opening, or the opportunity.
"Having obtained [it]";
the sense is that otherwise they would not have possessed that capacity.

Then, by the Daitya Śambara, Dudrika, Havadruma, and others were appointed over his own armies as intoxicated vassals for the sake of protection. (MU_4,25.23)
"Appointed" means urged or dispatched.
Having found an opening even against those [demons], the leaders of the gods struck them down,
like hawks moving through the sky striking agitated sparrows.
They struck them— namely Dudrika, Havardruma, and the others—
having found an opening and gained an opportunity.
They struck; they were striking.
They slew the generals, and then the best of the asuras created yet others—
restless and with fierce roars, like the ocean creating its waves.
And others who have a fierce roar;
[others who have a fierce roar].

fully equipped and accompanied by a great army.

those gods there, terrified by his illusion,

With the faces of the goddesses drenched in tears,
that Śambara,

that which is a very great gurgling sound is the *gharghara* sound.

"ghasmarāḥ" [N17: °r*ā*ḥ] (MT_4,26.59).

When the army of the Dānavas had swelled like the sun at midday,
the divine hosts fled like waters without banks, their limbs and weapons cast down and their blood flowing forth.
"Cast down" means they were thrown to the ground by the asuras;
"those whose limbs and weapons were halved" means, in short, those whose limbs were severed and whose weapons were shattered.
For this very reason, those divine armies—with blood flowing from them—fled in fear; they were driven away like what? Like [the following].
Like waters through dams; when what exists? "In that," and so forth;
in the great asura named Dāma, who is called Dāman.

A battle (*saṅgara*) is a conflict involving intense fury (*kaṭhina-saṃrambha*). When such a battle exists, in which the immortals (*amaras*) were overwhelmed—this constitutes a *kulaka* [of verses]. (MT 4,27.1–5)
Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa followed those [demons], even though they had long since vanished,
with a resonant roar, just as fires follow their fuel.
These were the armies of the gods.
"Anujagmuḥ" means they followed behind, running after; the word "api" indicates that following those who have vanished is not appropriate.
Even though they searched with great effort, the asuras could not find the gods who had vanished,
just as lions cannot find deer that have flown up into a dense forest canopy.
The asuras did not obtain [them];
[the birds] that had flown up from the forest of dense nets [were clearly visible]. (MT_4,27.7)
When the hosts of immortals had not been captured, Dāma, Vyāla,
and Kaṭa then went with joyful hearts to their lord, Śambara, who resided in the treasury of Pātāla.
Then the gods, being dejected, having recovered for a moment,
went to the immeasurably radiant Brahmā in order to find a means of victory;
"dejected" means fainting.
Having regained their breath and recovered their consciousness,
Brahmā appeared before them— whose faces possessed a beauty as crimson as blood—
as the moon appears over the oceans whose waters have been turned red at twilight.

"With blood" means with gore;
those whose faces are red [are so described].
"Of such [beings]" means at evening,
that is, during the evening twilight; or rather, the moon should be understood as the agent in the act of making [the sky] red.
Because it is red at the time of sunrise;
thus, "then" means "in the evening," that is, at the time of sunset.
Having bowed to him, those gods [reported] that matter which had been uttered by Śambara.
They correctly explained the sequence of Dāma,
Vyāla, and Kaṭa— that sequence known as Dāma and the others— which had been set forth by Śambara and manifested by Śambara.
Having paid homage to him, they related the matter exactly as it was.

Having heard all this from him and having reflected upon it, Brahmā, the discerning one, spoke these words of consolation to the host of gods: MU_4,27.12: "To him [N17: *tasmai* (MT_4,27.11)], having heard that and having deliberated, Brahmā, the knower of inquiry, spoke these words which provided reassurance to the army of the gods."
Brahmā spoke of that army of gods, the host of deities, which had Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa as its vanguard.
"Alas! At the end of a thousand years, Śambara must die at the hands of Hari, the Lord of the Immortals; therefore, wait for that time.
Alas, what a tragedy!
By Śambara as the agent;
at the end of a thousand years, [following] the sequence known as battle from the Lord of the Immortals, Hari Viṣṇu.
"Martavyam" means "to be died.
The sense is that he will not die for that long;
you should wait for that duration of time.

"Now, what shall we do with Dāma and the others who continue to cause us harm for so long? To this he replied: "O best of immortals, today you must fight these Dānavas—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—by means of illusory warfare and then flee."
O best of the immortals,
you, while fighting these Dānavas— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa— by means of illusory combat, shall cause the battle to take place.
"Run away! [They ask: "But what will be achieved for them by our fleeing? To this he replies:
"By virtue of their practice in battle, in the minds of these [enemies], it is like [the reflection] in a mirror."
The wondrous manifestation of egoism will attain the status of a reflection for these [qualities], such as generosity and the rest;
that is, the savoring of the sense of "I," taking the form: "We are victors in battle."
It will appear as a reflection within the mind—that is, in the mental disposition. [Objection: But what will be accomplished by that? To this, he says:
But these gods—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—having taken up latent impressions (vāsanā), will be easily conquered by you, like birds caught in a net. (MU 4.27.16) [Ś₁ gloss: "he"]
Because, according to the method that will be explained, it is the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) themselves that act with necessity.
[Objection: "But why can these not be conquered today? To this he says:
"But today these are without latent impressions and are devoid of pleasure and pain."
Slaying their enemies with fortitude, they have become invincible even to the gods. (Regarding "dhairyeṇārīn": in an alternative reading, [the text reads] "dhairyeṇārīn tu").
Today they are without latent impressions (*avāsanāḥ*), being devoid of the impression of "I" (*ahaṃvāsanā*);
for this very reason, they are free from pleasure and pain;
and for this very reason, by means of fortitude, [they conquer] their enemies.
"Striking down" means that they have gone [to a state] where even the gods are difficult to conquer, which is to say, they have become difficult for you to conquer.
For one who is devoid of pleasure and the like becomes difficult to conquer because of being free from fear.
"Now, how will these [beings] become submissive through latent predisposition (*vāsanā*)? To this he replies:
"through latent predisposition."

Those who are bound by the threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and brought under control by the snares of desire fall into subjection in this world, like birds tied with ropes. Those who are bound by the threads of latent impressions are those bound by the thread of the latent impression of "I" (*ahaṃ-vāsanā*).
They become such that, being brought under the control of the snares of hope,
they become subject to the world.
What are they like? Like birds bound by a rope.
This is the meaning: the person (puruṣa).
One becomes possessed by an internal latent impression of "I," a disposition consisting of thoughts such as "let this be mine" or "let this not be mine.
Through that, one falls into wretchedness;
because of that, one comes under the power of another.
"But how can those who are free from latent impressions (vāsanā) be difficult to conquer? To this he says:

"For those wise ones who are free from latent impressions, whose intellects are unattached to anything, who neither rejoice nor feel anger—they are of great intelligence and are difficult to conquer. (MU 4.27.19)
They rejoice in all things, whether they are to be abandoned or accepted;
they are unattached, being devoid of attachment in the form of passion and hatred.
Those whose intellects are such [as described]: a person is to be won over only by attachment to what is to be adopted and aversion to what is to be rejected;
otherwise, they are those who have understood the method.
Kings do not strive to conquer their enemies merely by the giving of wealth;
rather, the point is that a person who is free from attachment even toward his own body cannot be conquered by anyone in its absence.

The non-attachment of hatred should be understood as being due to its producing attachment; for a person who has turned away from things to be abandoned through hatred becomes possessed of a stronger attachment—synonymous with passion—toward things to be accepted. (MT_4,27.19)
The embodied being whose knot of bondage is formed by the rope of internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—
even if he is great and possessed of vast knowledge— is conquered even by a child.
A knot [of pride]; Ś1, Ś3: *granthi*.
The meaning is that otherwise, even among the ignorant, those advanced in learning and age would not offer salutations even to those wealthy in riches.
"This is he," "I am this one," "this is mine"—thus is one who has constructed such conceptualizations.
He becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is for waters.
"Ākalitā" means held or grasped on all sides; [he is one] by whom conceptualization—that is, volitional construction—is [held].
He [is the one who acts] regarding calamities of such a nature as "may this happen to me" or "may this not happen to me."
Even one who has become a worthy person through cultivation, whose self is limited by only this much,
though he be omniscient, has everywhere fallen into a state of supreme wretchedness.
O worthy one, O Indra!
By which [means] the self, its own true nature,
is delimited by only this much.
And it is of such a measure, consisting merely of the body and so forth; for that very reason, it is limited— such is its nature.
Cultivated means made the object of meditative cultivation;
that person,
though omniscient, [attains] the supreme, unsurpassed [knowledge] regarding everything.
"Miserliness" means wretchedness; "gone" has the sense of "going.
For one who is attached to the body and desires the welfare of the body necessarily falls into a state of miserliness.
By him who has conceived a limit for the infinite and immeasurable reality of the self, the self has been brought under control by his own self. (MU 4.27.23) [N17: °t⟨ā⟩[a]ḥ]
Because it abides as the witness of the end of the infinite, it is devoid of that [end];
because it abides solely in the form of the knower, it does not touch the state of being an object of knowledge, for it is immeasurable.
Of the reality of the self; by which [intellect], through conceptualization, its limitedness— known as being delimited by the body— is imagined as being merely this much.
It was cultivated by that ignorant one;
thus, by his own self, he has made himself subject to another.
For the helplessness resulting from attachment to enjoyments is inevitable for one who is delimited by a body.
[Regarding the term] *aspṛśamānasya*: [it is] as it stands.
[Regarding the term] *ātmāvaśīkṛtaḥ*: N17 reads *°t(ā)aḥ* (MT_4,27.23). Now, how is this so? To this, he says:
Whatever exists in the three worlds that is distinct from the self, there one becomes bound by the notion of it being an object to be acquired (*upādeya*).
This occurs because the self has been cultivated as something limited (*paricchinna*).
Whatever is distinct—this is the remainder; it has been cultivated;
it exists as something cultivated.
In that regard, through the sense of "mine-ness" (upādeyatā) produced by the conceit of non-attainment,
cultivation (bhāvanā) becomes bound; and the very state of being bound by cultivation is what is termed "subjection" (vaivaśyam)— this is the intended meaning.
N17: (The word "because" is to be supplied as the remainder; since [it is] conceived as distinct from the self. N17: [distinct] from the self;
N17: conceived (MT_4,27.24).
By the phrase "the helplessness of the bond of mental cultivation," he explains that the state of being subject to the influence of others is a cause of suffering:
"The wise know that mere attachment is the cause of endless sufferings;
they know that mere non-attachment is the cause of all happiness. (MU 4.27.25)
[The wise] know:
"It is merely a basis, merely a bond of cultivation.
Having provided a general justification, he recalls the specific detail.

"As long as you remain without attachment to the persistence of existence, just as the wind is not to be conquered by gnats, so indeed shall you not be conquered. (MU 4.27.26) "Without attachment" means devoid of reliance.
While established in existence— that is, established in the reality of the body and other such objects—
a living being succumbs to wretchedness through internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Otherwise, even a mere gnat would be like the immovable mountain Meru.
Otherwise, in the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [liberation occurs].
Wherever latent impressions exist, there one falls into wretchedness;
for it is observed that being permeated by qualities and defects belongs to that which exists, not to that which does not exist.
And where a latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) exists, there wretchedness (*dīnatā*) arises.

The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of completing the meter. For (*hi*), because of this, the state of being permeated by virtues and non-virtues is that which brings about wretchedness, as it is the state of being connected with the beneficial and the harmful.

Of that which exists—possessing the reality of a body established by latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—it is seen. Of that which does not exist—which, due to the absence of latent impressions, is like a non-entity because its nature is pure consciousness alone—it is not seen.
He states the conclusion:

"O Śakra, act in such a way that [beings] cultivate within themselves the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of 'this is I' and 'this is mine,' just as Dāma and others do. The word "from this" (*ataḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
O Śakra, just as Dāma and others [perceive], this is that very "I" and "this is mine"— such is their own latent tendency (*vāsanā*),
namely the latent tendency of ego-grasping (*ahaṅkāra-vāsanā*).
Within the mind;
they cultivate and conceptualize;
act accordingly; therefore, it should be known.
The meaning is that they will come to be.
[Objection: But how is it that they will not be conquerable by me? To this he says:
"Whatever misfortunes there are for people, and whatever states of existence and non-existence," and so forth.
These are the pungent and tender blossoms of the thorny creeper of craving.
Craving itself is a thorny creeper because it causes suffering; [the phrase "of that" refers to it].
Bound by the threads of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), this world revolves like a thorny creeper.
That world, having reached its extreme old age, comes to destruction for the sake of great suffering and [fleeting] pleasure;
it revolves, undergoing a state of perversion.
That is the latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Annihilation means destruction.
(MT_4,27.31) Even one who is steadfast, even one who is extremely learned, even one born of noble lineage, even one who is great—
A living being is bound by craving, just as a lion is bound by a chain. It is bound and rendered helpless; for one who is seized by craving clearly becomes powerless.
For this bird of the mind that is perched upon the tree of the body and dwells in the abode of the heart, a snare has been fashioned. (This is clear.)
The world, wretched due to its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is dragged away by Kṛtānta, like a bird, helpless and gasping incessantly, by a child with a rope.
[Kṛtānta] is Yama in the form of possessiveness (*mamatā*).
For Śrī Vyāsa himself has designated Mamatā as Death (kṛtānta); see Mahābhārata XIV 13.3–7. Also see Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa I 130 (Hanneder 1998: 80f; 183).
[Regarding Mamatā:
"Enough with this burden of weapons and with wandering through battles; by means of reasoning alone, you must eliminate the enemy's latent tendencies along with their distortions. (MU 4.27.35)
It is accompanied by error, joined with perversion;
it is of no avail against you, the enemy who takes the form of the triad beginning with the "dā" [the giver], by means of weapons and the like.
The intention is that he will indeed succeed.
(MT_4,27.35) While the enemy’s inner fortitude remains undisturbed, neither your weapons, nor your treatises, nor your missiles shall prevail over you. (MU_4,27.36)
When you are unshaken, being free from agitation due to the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
then Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, by virtue of their practice in combat,
will seize within you a latent impression consisting of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*).
"We shall fight"— of such a nature is this [army] consisting of egoism. If those mechanical beings created by Śambara do not rely upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they will attain invincibility.
"Invincibility" (*ajayyatām*) means that the mechanical beings (*yantrapuruṣāḥ*) are devoid of conscious deliberation. Therefore,
O gods, first awaken them by means of rational warfare (*yuktiyuddha*).

Until, through the power of practice, they become possessed of latent impressions (*savāsanā*); awaken them, endow them with latent impressions, and make them so. Then those whose mental cultivation is firmly established will become [easy] prey for you.
In this world, there are no one at all whose hearts are not pierced by craving,
nor any who are not tender-hearted.
Regarding the use of *na*-compounds, see also MṬ (I) 30,7.
[Objection: "But if, at some point, they will not be killed even by that, then what should be done?
To this he says: "Thirst (*tṛṣṇā*)."
With hearts pierced by craving and minds permeated by craving,
they are fragile and wretched;
indeed, all who are seized by craving become fragile.
Therefore, the sense is that they too will certainly come to exist.
[Delicate: N17: pe⟨valāḥ⟩[lavāḥ] (MT_4,27.40). He concludes Brahmā’s speech with the final verse of the chapter:
"This entire world, both even and uneven, has attained stability through its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*)."
And just as the mass of waves moves upon the ocean, therefore it is that very [mind] which has gone forth here that must be treated;
this world, consisting of pleasure and pain, is experienced as both even and uneven.
The entire world [arises] from its own latent tendencies— that is,
from the latent tendency of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
That latent impression (vāsanā) has attained stability in this world.
It moves and it sparkles; like what? Like a mass of waves, as a mass of waves [moves] in the ocean, the sea.
"It moves" means "so it is. Therefore, that is indeed the latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Let it be treated; let it be made fit for treatment.
"May you depart safely.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh canto in the Chapter on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having said, "I shall tell of the disappearance of Brahmā," the Blessed Lord vanished right there,
like a wave of water that has made its sound upon the shore of the ocean.
In that very place, at that very spot; not by going elsewhere.
"Antardhi" means concealment or obstruction.
But the gods, having heard those words, departed toward their own respective quarters,
taking with them the fragrance of the lotuses, like winds carrying a forest garland.
This is clear.
For some days, they rested in their own beloved palaces, which possessed steady splendor,
just as bees rest within lotuses.
This is clear.

(MT 4.28.3) Having found an auspicious moment for a short while that would bring about their own exaltation, they made a sound like the roar of kettledrums, resembling the thunder of clouds at the time of universal dissolution. (MU 4.28.4)
This is clear.
(MT 4.28.4) Then, in the sky, a terrible battle ensued once more with the Daityas who had risen from the depths of Pātāla, one that caused a great delay of time. (MU 4.28.5)
[War] causes a waste of time and does not bring about the destruction of Śambara,
because Brahmā has declared that his death will occur only at the end of a thousand years.
This is the meaning. The word "of the gods" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
*Samavartata* means he came into being.
The meaning is:
"Thus [it is said].
Swords, arrows, spears, and multitudes of mallets, pestles, clubs, axes, and fierce discuses fell in great numbers.

In response to the inquiry as to what kind of battle took place, he says "vavuḥ" (they blew), [describing] weapons such as thunderbolts, mountain rocks, fire, trees, and the mouths of serpents, Garuḍas, and so forth.
They blew; they were blowing, [the remainder of the sentence being] "released by the gods and the daityas. (MT 4.28.6)
A river created by magic, with a dense torrent of great waters and weapons fashioned by illusion, quickly surged forth in every direction;
that river, possessing a roar as deep as a turbulent flood of water, instantly overwhelmed hundreds of thousands of rocks, mountains, riverbanks, and trees.
"Created by magic" means produced through the illusory power (*māyā*) of the *rākṣasas*.
Of the great water joined with weapons—
that which has a dense flow [of such water]. She is she.
Likewise, repeatedly, very rapidly, and swiftly toward the mountain of stone;
agitated and wandering among hundreds of thousands of trees on the earth's edge;
that flood of water, a flood of water equipped with weapons.
That river possesses a dense roar;
such is the river consisting of weapons.

In all directions, that army of gods, asuras, and siddhas— composed of the harsh bodies of earth and other elements in its striking and seizing, yet having a body of light-rays in the sky— which subsides, arises once more with its very same essence, created by illusion.

N17: (meaning "even though she was capable of both delivering and receiving blows") "consisting of earth and so forth" means that her body, which is as harsh as earth and other elements in the delivery and reception of blows, is composed of those very things.

That is to say, by Indra and Śambara.

Then the faces of the quarters became like great oceans filled with floods of blood from mountains shattered by weapons resembling crags, and they were adorned with forests of *kunta* and *tālī* trees planted by the gods, the lords of the asuras, and the divine mountains. (MU 4.28.10)
The mountains shattered by weapons that resemble mountains are the divine mountains,

Then there fell a rain of iron lions, from whose mouths were disgorged spears, arrows, javelins, clubs, swords, and discuses; which had effortlessly swallowed the mountains hurled by gods and demons; and which possessed fierce rows of saw-like teeth and claws that produced a harsh, grating sound.
Then there was a rain of iron lions; a shower of iron lions fell. Of what nature were they? They were vomited forth.
She is the one from whom spears,
arrows, pikes, clubs, swords,

She by whom the mountains were [shaken];
she,
upon the grindstone, on the stone for grinding.
Resounding means making a sound by virtue of friction;
those teeth and nails are like that saw.

[She who possesses] spears, arrows, javelins, clubs, swords, and discuses;
whose army of suns at the end of the eon is manifested by the burning of the quarters arising from the heat of the poison-flames of her blazing eyes.
The row of venomous serpents leaped up like a sea in rut, as the long earth and its mountains seemed to fly upward.
[MU 4.28.12] "Venomous serpents" refers to snakes;
"row" means a line.

By that [light],

By which;
she;

(MU 4.28.13) [That is,] those thunderbolts which were loud-sounding...
Those very things are the *makaras*; the heap (*utkara*) of them is the *karkara*, so called because of its gravelly nature.
That intermediate space which possesses such a particular sound; that which is of such a kind.
That very thing is the ocean, the sea; by its circles of waves, in the form of wave-mandalas, it is thus whirled,
that is, enveloped.
By those which are like immovable mountains;
likewise, by those that are "āvartins," meaning possessed of whirling motion.
The various weapons are like the currents of a river;
by them,
his limbs are rendered extremely constricted.
The entire world was of an absolutely perfect nature.
The atmosphere was adorned with mountains, missiles, weapons, Garuḍas, and high peaks, and filled with hosts of Nāga women and celestial maidens.
For a moment it was filled with oceans, for a moment with masses of fire, for a moment with suns, and for a moment with darkness;
[it was filled] with the women of the *nāgas* and the women of the hosts of gods.
By the repetition "for a moment, for a moment," it is stated that the oceans and the other elements were created by illusion (*māyā*).

What is the nature of the intermediate space? It consists of mountain-forms, missiles, and weapons—these are the "mountain-missile-weapons. In their midst are the Garuḍa-mountains, which are rubies (māṇikya) peaks.
"By them" means by those [beings] who were adorned and supported.

"High" refers to that place where the women of the Nāgas and the women of the Asura hosts reside. As for the women of the Suras, however, they dwell directly in the sky; therefore, they are not mentioned here. "Garuḍa... [and so forth].
The absence of a long vowel for the letter *ga* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
However, the mountains manifested by the mantra were sent forth directly in the form of missiles (*astra*), appearing as actual weapons (*śastra*).
The state of being created by illusion:
with masses of mountains of fire and weapons spread through the sky, agitated by the *guḍaguḍa* sound of *garuḍas*, along with hosts of Asuras and the women of the Asura clans.

The world became such that the space between the celestial abodes and the earth blazed with the fires of an unbearable kalpa; the atmosphere was agitated by the *guḍaguḍa*— the rumbling roar— of the Garuḍas.
There, having employed those masses of mountains that had spread forth as floods of weapons and fire;
The world;
that unbearable period of the eon, the time of dissolution,
wherein the realms of the gods, the earth, and the intermediate spaces are set ablaze.
It became like that.
Right there, the gods leaped from the surface of the earth into the sky like birds from a mountain slope; yet,

The phrase "by the exceedingly powerful" is connected with the first half [of the verse]. Then, the gods and demons, scorched by the great conflagration clinging to the forest-like rows of trees formed by the lofty weapons fixed upon their bodies, assumed the appearance of mountains shaken by the winds at the end of an aeon within the expanse of the sky. Then the gods and asuras [beheld] the splendor of those mountains which were shaken by the wind at the end of the eon within the sky, in the midst of the firmament.

Those for whom there is burning; such are they.
With streams of blood released from the bodies of the lords of gods and asuras and swirling all around,

from their bodies,

He bore a body that was perfectly full, like the rising Gaṅgā with its hundred branches reddened by the twilight.
Those experts in the ways of policy brought to an end their mutual downpours of mountains, showers of water, various fierce weapons, and the raining down of terrible thunderbolts,

Afflicted by that, they were agitated;

Causing a tumultuous uproar,
with severed heads, hands, arms, and thighs wandering through the sky like inauspicious locusts in the firmament at that time—

trunks, arms,

[He saw] the intoxicated fire, with its agitated waters, winds, and sun; the forest bursting asunder, and the multitudes of gods and asuras shattered.

That [place] was such:

intensely bewildered, with its horizons whirled into confusion by mountain peaks that resounded as they were struck by massive weapons equal in size to themselves; [the place was filled] with the winds from the multitude of caves at their summits that seemed to warble in distress, and with the abundant roars of lions that had descended, crying out as if in lamentation.
It was known by the agents who were mountain peaks; it was intensely whirled about, being possessed of delusion. How was it whirled about?
Where the horizons have been made whirled, that is, possessed of a spinning motion.
That [was filled] with mountain peaks; of what kind were they? Equal in size to oneself.
They were struck by those dense weapons, which were as large as mountain peaks.
By them;
for this very reason, by those resounding;
furthermore, by what kind of beings?
The winds of the foremost caves and torrents are "foremost-cave-torrent-winds";
by means of them—
that is, under that pretext.
As if warbling with agonies—
for one joined by agony indeed warbles—
furthermore, of what kind were they? They had fallen upon [him].
Those which are lions; their roars; by means of those—that is to say, under the pretext of them.
With what kind of sounds? With loud (*adabhra*) and intense (*utkaṭa*) cries.
[The world was filled] with illusory rivers, oceans, armies, dense fires, and conflagrations; with trees, the corpses of gods and asuras, mountains, and masses of rocks.
Within the expanse of the sky, there was a swirling rain of helmets, arrows, spears, and maces, like forest leaves scattered by the wind;
"within the expanse of the sky" means in the midst of space,
and "scattered by the wind" means tossed about.
Just as a forest leaf [is moved by the wind],
so too was it deluded, possessed of wandering.
By whom was it perceived as moving? In response to the inquiry—“Indeed, movement in the midst of the sky is not logical”—he says “the river of illusion,” and so forth.
[The phrase] ends with “the end of the sky.”
The delusion regarding rivers of illusion and the like, which move within the sky, is superimposed as being the very rotation of the sky itself.
Scattered by the wind,
through the fierce blows of his palm— which was as irresistible as the flight of the wings of the Lord of Mountains—

[Instantly] N17: And those hands, which were as large as the wings of the king of mountains and difficult to restrain in their coming and going—those such as these, their... [which]...
By means of those palms; by means of those blows; having performed them; "drāk" means quickly.
Those who fall are the very bodies of the warriors, which are like great mountains;
those who strike them are the blows.
By those [beings], the celestial cities were cast down;
and by them, that flood of the ocean— the seven seas— was filled with full water.
"He was" means he was born.
The atmosphere was filled with a deep, humming roar, and the interior of the mountains was washed by blood.
Or rather, the cave that is the expanse of the world became filled with that [blood], as it lay within the pool of blood;

At that time, at that moment,
she became agitated.

She whose atmosphere was filled with that dense, humming clamor of battle; such was she,

The mode of existence that consists of a lake of blood is the "abode";

The formulation is like [the expression] "possessing stability in stability. Furthermore,
the cave is one whose interior space is filled with the humming of mosquitoes, whose inner reaches of the mountains have been washed by rain, and which exists within a lake.

With a verse at the end of the chapter, he describes the similarity between this battle and *saṃsāra*:
"It causes transformations that spread through infinite directions; it bestows pleasure and pain that are oriented toward decline and arising."
Then, indeed, that battle-campaign involving the conflict of the hosts of gods and asuras became truly like this cycle of existence (*saṃsṛti*).
The word "khalu" expresses certainty;
that battle-campaign here became similar to *saṃsṛti*.
Of what nature?
That which is the expansion into infinite directions;
by that, the modification known as violence—that is, the state of being modified—is [prevented].
It is such that it "acts";
it is such that it "bestows" those pleasures and pains which are oriented toward decline and arising.
The cycle of existence, crowded and congested by the hosts of asuras and suras,
also brings about through its expansion a transformation known as bondage.
It bestows both pleasure and pain and is crowded with various objects; thus may there be auspiciousness.
resembling the cycle of existence,
bestowing pleasure and pain,
and crowded with various objects.

By means of illusion, as well as by dispute, by alliance and by war, by flight, by fortitude, by deception, by stratagem,
by wretchedness, by combat with missiles, and by frequent disappearances;
That battle was waged by the gods for thirty-five years with a wretched contest of missiles.
He fought with the gods for thirty-five years— that is, thirty-five years—

[and] "by means of an expedient" (upāyanena), that is, by approaching [him].

By the asuras— of what kind?— who were characterized by miserliness (*kārpaṇya*), by dejection (*dīnatā*), by their own disappearances (*svāntardhānaiḥ*) manifested through illusion (*māyā*), and by their self-concealments (*nijagopanaiḥ*).
By those for whom such an undertaking is generally of this nature.
By those who carry away merit and take away life;
by those who are impetuous and possessed of fury in great acts of violence;
by them.
Furthermore, by what kind [of beings]?
By those who, through their battles, have undertaken death.
They,
with such [marks], have a tilaka.
"By means of illusion," and so forth;
"by approaching" is a marginal gloss on Ś1.
(MT_4,29.1-3) Years, days, months—ten, eight, five, and seven.
Showers of trees, fire, weapons, water, thunderbolts, and mountains fell. "Showers" means rains;
they fell.
For how long? For ten years and eight months.
"Five, seven, and twelve"—
that is to say, days; by implication, at other times such as during the twilight periods (*saṃdhyā*).
Thus it should be understood.

However, after such a length of time, due to the firm habituation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*), Dāma and the others—whose minds were swallowed up by it—adopted the conviction that "I am [the body]. (MU 4.29.5)
"From firm practice of egoism" means from the form of egoism such as "We shall fight."
Those whose minds are seized— that is, possessed by egoism— are such [persons].
Just as a mirror becomes like the reflected object due to the excellence of its proximity, so too [is it with the mind].
Due to the excellence of their practice, they too have attained a state of egoism, just like that [of the primary self],
because of the intensity of proximity— that is, due to the abundance of its presence—
just as a reflection is possessed of the original object.
Just as an object that is very distant does not reflect in a mirror,
so too the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of an object does not arise due to a lack of practice. "Very distant" means from a great distance.
Regarding objects— that is, states such as fighting and so forth—
*vāsanā* is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the thought, "This was done by me."
When Dāma and the others were born, having developed the latent impressions of egoism,
they fell into a state of wretchedness, thinking, "This is my life; this is my purpose."
When Dāma and the others— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—
were born, that is, produced.
Those for whom there is the latent impression of egoism;
such are they.
When they were born and had reached maturity,
they fell into such a state of wretchedness and dejection, thinking, "This life of mine is my only purpose."
[They] have arrived at this conclusion: for in the absence of egoism (ahaṅkāra), there could simply be no wretchedness in the form of possessiveness (mamatā) which lacks a foundation;
however, when that [egoism] exists, because it has found its support, it is indeed difficult to ward off—this is the intended meaning.
Seized by the latent impression of fear and struck down by the latent impression of delusion,
those who are bound by the snares of hope have consequently fallen into a state of wretchedness.
Then, immediately after approaching in a state of wretchedness,
those [servants] beginning with Dāma were seized by fear— that is, by the terror arising from the apprehension of the destruction of their bodies and so forth.
That which is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the formative force (*saṃskāra*);
they are seized and brought under control by it.
Likewise, [they are seized] by delusion (*moha*) regarding what is not the self, such as the body and so forth.
By that latent impression (*vāsanā*) of ignorance, which consists of the cultivation of the notion of a self, [beings] are struck down, that is, afflicted.
Bound by the snares of desire— that is, by the snares of desire for objects such as wealth for the sake of the body and so forth, which have been made the objects of the conceit of "self-identity"—
they are brought under their own control.
They have reached the utmost limit of wretchedness and dejection.
[The limit: "N17: kāṣṭhām" (MT_4,29.9). [Objection: "But what has been achieved by them because of that? To this he says:
"For in vain indeed has the sense of 'mine' (mamatva) been imagined by those who are free from egoism (anahaṅkāra)."

and the others.
Indeed, O serpent,
this is certain: by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, who are free from egoism— that is, devoid of the sense of "I."

there arises "mine-ness" (mamatva), which is the state of possessiveness (mamatā).
"Vainly" means in vain;

the meaning is that it is absolutely unreal.

(MT_4,29.11) "May my body become firm; may my wealth lead to happiness"—for those whose minds were fixed on such thoughts, their fortitude vanished. MU_4,29.12

Because it is devoid of attachment to the body;
*mārjitā*: polished.
"Thinking, 'How may we become stable in this world?
they fell into dejection, like lotuses deprived of water.
(MU 4.29.14) [Note: Ś1 reads *bhavemeti ca*; Ś3 reads *bhavemeti*]
"May we exist"—
thus pierced and pervaded;

[one should place it] upon their heads; "thus" means in the manner previously described.

Furthermore, he explains this very point regarding the subject of the awakened one: "O Rāma, it is in the domain of the awakened that this speech truly shines. [N17: for one who knows the nature of Brahman called pure consciousness.]

"O Rāma, there is indeed nothing whatsoever [to be grasped] by means of the form 'I am the Buddha'; this speech, namely 'all is Brahman,' is the object known as the awakened one, the fit location. In that place—*mukta* (liberated). *Mukta* is derived from the root *muc*, meaning "one who has been released. It refers to one who has abandoned all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is liberated from the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). *Buddha* is derived from the root *budh*, meaning "one who has awakened. It refers to one who has awakened to the true nature of reality (*tattva*). *Rūpa* is derived from the root *rūp*, meaning "form" or "appearance. It refers to the physical body (*deha*), which is the support for the senses. *Asmi* is derived from the root *as*, meaning "I am. It refers to the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), which is the cause of bondage. *Kila* is a particle used to indicate hearsay or tradition. It serves to show that what follows is based on the teachings of the sages. *Nāsti* is derived from the negative particle *na* and the verb *asti*, meaning "there is not. It negates the existence of anything real. *Evā* is a particle used for emphasis. It serves to exclude any other possibility. *Kiñcana* is derived from the pronoun *kim* and the suffix *-cana*, meaning "anything whatsoever. It refers to the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*), which are the causes of suffering. *He rāma* is a vocative address. It serves to attract the listener's attention. *Eṣā* is a demonstrative pronoun. It refers to the preceding statement. *Vāk* is derived from the root *vac*, meaning "speech" or "word. It refers to the teaching of the scriptures (*śāstra*). *Sarvam* is derived from the adjective *sarva*, meaning "all" or "everything. It refers to the totality of phenomena (*dharma*). *Brahma* is derived from the root *brh*, meaning "the Great One" or "the Absolute. It refers to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). *Iti* is a particle used to mark the end of a quotation. It serves to indicate that the preceding words are the exact teaching. *Prabuddha* is derived from the prefix *pra* and the root *budh*, meaning "awakened" or "enlightened. It refers to the state of liberation (*mokṣa*). *Ākhya* is derived from the root *khyā*, meaning "called" or "named. It serves to identify the state. *Yaḥ* is a relative pronoun. It refers to the subject. *Viṣaya* is derived from the root *viṣ*, meaning "object" or "domain. It refers to the sphere of experience. *Yogya* is derived from the root *yuj*, meaning "fit" or "suitable. It refers to the capacity for realization. *Deśa* is derived from the root *diś*, meaning "place" or "location. It refers to the ground of being. *Tatra* is a locative adverb. It refers to that aforementioned location. It serves to connect the preceding description with the following explanation. *Tatra* means "in that [place]. It indicates the context of the following discourse. *Muktasya* is a genitive singular noun. It refers to the liberated one. It serves to specify the subject of the following attributes. *Muktasya* means "of the liberated one. It distinguishes him from those still bound by worldly existence. *Buddhasya* is a genitive singular noun. It refers to the awakened one. It serves to specify the subject of the following attributes. *Buddhasya* means "of the awakened one. It distinguishes him from those who have not yet realized the truth. *Asmīti* is a compound of the first-person pronoun *aham* and the particle *iti*. It refers to the ego-identification. It serves to illustrate the nature of delusion. *Asmīti* means "the notion 'I am'. It represents the fundamental error of self-clinging. *Rūpeṇa* is an instrumental singular noun. It refers to the means or instrument. It serves to show how the notion arises. *Rūpeṇa* means "by means of the form. It indicates that the notion is produced through the perception of the body. *Kila* is a particle used for emphasis or tradition. It serves to confirm the common understanding. *Kila* means "indeed" or "it is said. It acknowledges the conventional view. *Nāsty eva* is a negative existential construction. It asserts non-existence. It serves to negate the reality of the notion. *Nāsty eva* means "there is simply not. It emphasizes the absolute absence of such a thing. *Kiñcana* is a pronoun with an indefinite suffix. It refers to any possible entity. It serves to exhaustively deny existence. *Kiñcana* means "anything at all. It leaves no room for doubt. *He rāma* is a vocative address. It serves to maintain the dialogue. *He rāma* means "O Rāma. It addresses the interlocutor by name. *Eṣā* is a demonstrative pronoun. It refers back to the preceding statement. *Vāk* is a feminine noun. It refers to the verbal expression. It serves to identify the content. *Vāk* means "this speech. It points to the specific utterance. *Sarvam brahma iti vāk* is a descriptive phrase. It states the nature of the speech. It serves to define the teaching. *Sarvam brahma iti vāk* means "the speech 'all is Brahman'. It identifies the core doctrine. *Prabuddha-ākhyaḥ* is a bahuvrīhi compound. It describes the subject. It serves to qualify the following term. *Prabuddha-ākhyaḥ* means "known as the awakened one. It provides the designation. *Yaḥ viṣayaḥ* is a relative clause. It specifies the object. It serves to locate the subject. *Yaḥ viṣayaḥ* means "that which is the object. It identifies the domain. *Yogyaḥ deśaḥ* is a descriptive phrase. It defines the location. It serves to complete the description. *Yogyaḥ deśaḥ* means "the fit location. It indicates the appropriate ground. *Tatra* is a locative adverb. It connects the description to the context. *Tatra* means "in that [regard]. It establishes the setting. *Muktasya buddhasya asmīti rūpeṇa kila nāsty eva kiñcana* is the main proposition. It asserts the non-existence of the ego-notion. It serves as the central thesis. *Muktasya buddhasya asmīti rūpeṇa kila nāsty eva kiñcana* means "for the liberated and awakened one, there is indeed nothing whatsoever by way of the form 'I am'. It summarizes the entire argument.*
It shines forth;
by implication, it should be understood that it does not shine in the domain of non-Buddhas.

Being certain, he also knows that the things conducive to that [goal] are real;

"Not for one who is ignorant."
Regarding the phrase "not for the ignorant":
one might ask, "Is there ever a denial of this experience by one who knows it, or not? To this he replies:

thus indeed, thus indeed, he becomes one who experiences [it]. Therefore, for that knower—

He becomes absorbed in that;

The denial— that is, the repudiation— of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), which consists of both that called false egoity (mithyāhaṅkāra) and that called ultimate reality (paramārtha).

It does not exist;
for a non-existent entity cannot become existent merely by being perceived,

therein,

This sky-like form of the Great Consciousness is dense with the appearance of a crystal interior and is profoundly tranquil;

Chapter [N17]: Oṃ. Śrī Rāma asks:

[They are like] children, yakṣas, and piśācas.
Regarding suffering, which consists of wandering through various wombs,
the venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke this reply for the sake of Dāma,

"O scion of the Raghus, listen to this which was spoken by Yama when he was entreated.
This clearly states the words of Yama.
"When Dāma and the others shall undergo separation and hear their own story,

The word "iti" marks the conclusion of Yama’s speech.

"O Blessed One,

In which country, at what time, by whom being described, and in what manner will they hear this account of their own history?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
"In the marshlands on the shore of the great lotus lake in Kaśmīra,
these two have repeatedly experienced a succession of births in the womb of fish."
In a small pond on the shore of the Great Lotus Lake; cf. (IV) 31.10.
The succession of births in the womb of fish: "Those whose intentions were bound by desire, being fickle, have met their end through time."
Right there in that lotus lake they will become cranes,
their intentions tethered and their minds bound.
There, amidst garlands of white water-lilies and clusters of lotuses...
Upon the excellent creepers of *śevāla* moss and amidst the undulations of the waves;
upon the swaying cradles of blooming white lotuses and the vines of blue water-lilies;
amidst streaks of clouds formed by masses of spray and within the movements of cool whirlpools.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of the lake with the cranes, those ornaments of the world,

The story related to Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and others;

such being the case.

From the horn of Pradyumna: [the reading] °gā⟨ś⟩[c] is clear.

This entire sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa has been told to you;

its true nature remains unknown when it is not investigated. (MT_4,32.26-27)
Even from a great position, fools who are deluded fall downward through the power of ignorance regarding the Rāma[-mantra], just like Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa. Thus,

[The space between the trees in Rājagṛha] is clearly visible.

Not abandoning [it] at all;
"as if disfigured" is a statement in which the abstract state is the primary focus.
Like deformity,
like insentience which is contrary to its own nature,
it perceives— that is, it experiences.

just as a person desiring to go to a certain place [perceives it] through the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that place...
Just as [a traveler] goes to intermediate places by way of delusion,

Those who [rely] upon the treatise as a means— that is, the treatise on the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra).

there is no other entity whatsoever called "the world."
The sense is that the world is nothing other than the self-reflective awareness (*svātmaparāmarśa*) which has consciousness as its substratum and object.
[Objection: Even so, how is it that difference appears as if it were real? To this, he says:

Experience, which takes the form of the three worlds, is the orb of rays from the sun of consciousness; O you who are free from boastfulness, tell me, where is the difference between these two—the moon and the sun? (MU 4.33.22)
Having the form of the three worlds, having the appearance of the three worlds; it is experience,
which is to say, the three worlds.
Consciousness alone is the sun;
its orb of rays comes into being.
"O you who are free from boasting, O you who do not speak untruths!
Let it be told by you. To the question "What [is it]? he says:
"Where?
[refers to] the moon and the sun, whose forms are the solar discs reflected in the orb of water.
Where does division occur? At what time or in what place does it occur?
For example, as in the case of the form of the solar disc reflected in water.

The meaning is that although a distinction appears between the moon and the sun, in the ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ) there is no difference; likewise, although a distinction appears between the world— which consists of the orb of rays from the sun of consciousness reflected in the external and internal organs— and the sun of consciousness itself, there is indeed no difference at all.
*bhedaḥ*: N17: *paramārthataḥ* → *bhedaḥ*. *arthaḥ*: N17: *ar⟨-⟩[thaḥ]*.
(MT_4,33.22) This states that there is an absolute absence of difference.
The opening and closing of this consciousness-vision,
which by its very nature consists in the experience of the world-form, are these two: its setting and its rising.
[Regarding] "setting and rising": cf. *Spandakārikā* 1.1.
"By nature" means effortlessly.
"Of this [power]" refers to that which stands before one as one's very self (*ātman*).

Of the vision called consciousness (*cid-dṛṣṭi*), which is the vision known as consciousness (*cit*); its opening and closing (*unmeṣaṇa-nimeṣaṇe*) consist of opening, which takes the form of a reflective awareness of what is distinct from itself, and closing, which takes the form of a reflective awareness of itself alone. It is precisely these two that constitute the opening and the closing.
The experience which is the form of the world—
that is to say, "the world"—
its setting and its rising.
For you, closing the eyes is setting;
opening the eyes is rising. Alternatively, opening the eyes is the expansion of one's own nature.
Considering that *nimeṣaṇa* (closing) is the contraction of one's own nature,
*unmeṣaṇa* (opening) is setting,
and *nimeṣaṇa* is rising.
This is to be applied [to the present case as well]; and thus, there is not even a scent of difference.
For the point is that the opening and closing of the eyes do not themselves differ from the one who possesses the power of opening and closing them.
And this is witnessed by all experience in both dreams and deep sleep.
Thus it is; no effort is required here.
of that which stands before; [N17: °ra[ḥ]sthā°]; opening and closing [N17: °ṣa*ṇanime*ṣaṇe].
[Regarding the phrase] "possessing opening and closing":
he introduces the description of the *ahaṃkāra* (I-maker), which is the primary cause of the entire world, as follows:
"The referent 'I', when not fully understood, is a stain in the sky of ultimate reality."
But when the referent of "I" is fully understood, it becomes the sky of the ultimate reality.
The referent of "I" is the entity denoted by the word "I.
When not fully understood from the perspective of ultimate reality, what is its nature?
Thus, being unknown,
impurity exists in the sky of the ultimate reality, the space of pure consciousness alone.
Because it exists in the form of the body, it conceals that [reality];
for concealment is indeed the very nature of impurity (mala), and not otherwise.
When it has been fully understood— that is, known as being of such a nature from the perspective of ultimate reality—
it becomes the sky of ultimate reality, which is the very space of pure consciousness.
Because it comes to rest in that very state of being.
By abiding in the form of the body;
because it covers that [body], [it is called] "covering" (*ācchādaka*);
the space of pure consciousness (*cinmātrākāśa*).
For the sake of practice, he says this again and again:
"The sense of 'I' has been fully understood; it no longer exists within the state of non-I.
It attains oneness with the Self of the consciousness-ether, like water merging into water. (MU 4.33.25)
In the state of "I-am-ness" (*ahambhāva*), it is fully understood from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*) that this [state] has no final basis; thus it is known:
"I-am-ness" is ego-construction (*ahaṅkāra*). In the state of "I-am-ness"...
This is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*):
it does not have the coarse conception of "I" as its cause.
Why is this so?

Regarding this, it is said: "oneness. For that sense of "I" (ahambhāva) attains oneness with the Self by way of the sky of consciousness (cinnabhas), which is the nature of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
What is it like? It is like water;
just as water attains oneness with water.
The meaning is "so it is.
As for the question "In what does this [I-consciousness] ultimately rest?", once the ultimate nature of the I-consciousness is known, the I-consciousness comes to rest in the Supreme Self;
therefore, the sense is that it does not fall into limitation, which consists in resting in the body.
[By the self] N17: *ātmanā* (MT_4,33.25).
Now, how is it that the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*), once fully understood, attains oneness with the conscious self (*cidātman*)? To this he replies:
"The world of perception, beginning with the 'I', does not exist at all in reality."
Why indeed must that [notion] necessarily remain for one who investigates the "I"?
[The word] *kila* indicates certainty. [The portion beginning with] *aham-ādi* is missing from the manuscript pages.
